- A-IC3 (2026)
    - title: A-IC3: Learning-Guided Adaptive Inductive Generalization for Hardware Model Checking
    - what: A-IC3 adds an online proof-aware contextual multi-armed bandit to IC3 generalization. A PA-LinUCB agent chooses among static and activity-aware CTG/EXCTG strategies from local CTI and global proof-state features, then updates from clause quality and propagation feedback. The method defines an eight-feature context, push-aware reward, seven arms, and globally fixed hyperparameters, then integrates with rIC3 without offline training. Experiments separate safe/unsafe solving, PAR-2, arm-selection phases, and termination-frame counts; case plots show adaptive choices rather than a fixed arm.

    - number: rIC3-CtgDown solves 629
    - limits: The study targets Boolean hardware transition systems and rIC3's existing strategies. Results use a 914-instance HWMCC suite, one-thread runs, a 3600-second timeout, and fixed reward hyperparameters. Bandit gains are empirical and do not establish better proofs for unseen designs; future work includes other verification phases and reinforcement learning.

    - what: Reports a Lean4 library for empirical-process learning theory: Gaussian functional inequalities/concentration, covering and chaining culminating in Dudley’s entropy integral, localized least-squares error bounds, linear regression and ℓ1-image covering. Authors report about30,000lines, over1000theorems/lemmas, about500supervised hours with Claude Code/Opus4.5, and compilation without sorry/custom axioms. Provides a detailed human–AI proof-engineering case study; it does not experimentally establish autonomous research or a causal speedup. Builds coordinate-resampling invariance for heterogeneous independent distributions; Efron–Stein, Rademacher/CLT Gaussian Poincaré, entropy duality/subadditivity, Bernoulli-to-Gaussian log-Sobolev and Herbst concentration. Explicit C1/Sobolev density and mollification handle analytic extension. Dudley uses recursive projections with step distance εk rather than3εk/2, finite-net bounds, a nonnegative shift for Fatou, and separability/path continuity. Covering numbers use WithTop Nat; entropy/integrals have ENNReal canonical versions and real wrappers. Least-squares master theorem exposes sphere nonemptiness, supremum integrability/boundedness and critical-radius hypotheses; ℓ1 covering uses Maurey’s probabilistic finite-net construction. Four preserved task specifications show the entropy-convergence proof evolving from a vague Fatou instruction to a shifted ENNReal proof with explicit API dependencies.

Reported Gaussian concentration is for finite positive dimension, positive Lipschitz constant and threshold under standard product Gaussian measure. Dudley requires σ,D>0, a nonempty totally bounded index set, a pathwise-zero anchor, measurable coordinates, integrable exponential increments, finite entropy integral and continuous sample paths; not arbitrary stochastic processes. Displayed Sobolev density/LSI theorems require differentiability and continuous derivatives plus square-integrability; the LSI listing additionally assumes integrability of g²log(g²). The master error theorem assumes f*∈F, star-shaped shifted class, any positive radius satisfying the critical inequality, an ERM for every noise vector, a nonempty sphere at sqrt(tδ), integrable localized absolute suprema at two radii and boundedness. The displayed theorem does not require δ to be the smallest solution. It bounds fixed-design empirical prediction error, not arbitrary population excess risk. Local Gaussian-complexity capacity control additionally assumes total boundedness of the empirical image, finite entropy integral, path continuity and positive/negative supremum integrability. These are proof premises, not a demonstration that every new function class satisfies them. - AKR probabilistic knowing-how checker (2026)
    - title: AKR: A Model Checker for an Adaptative Probabilistic Knowing-How Logic
    - what: Presents AKR, an open-source Python checker for adaptive probabilistic knowing-how logic. It parses PRISM probabilistic LTS models, regular-expression perceptions, and Khq properties; builds live DFAs, synchronizes products, and delegates minimum reachability probabilities to PRISM. The paper states the polynomial recursive checking algorithm: Boolean cases recurse over states, while Khq builds a product for each perception DFA with a fresh source state and checks minimum probability of reaching DFA-final goal states. The hotel-cleaning example makes adaptation concrete: action outcomes change room-cleaning counts and plans may switch based on outcomes. Experiments vary room counts 4–100 and three regular-expression perceptions, isolating star-operator and expression-length effects.

- An End-To-End Verification of Keller’s Conjecture (2026)
    - what: Lean4 formalization resolving Keller cube-tiling conjecture in positive dimensions: true through7 and false from8 onward. Closes earlier gaps between a verified geometric-to-clique reduction and external SAT solving by verifying an improved coloring/CNF encoding, semantic symmetry transformations, certificate-checked propositional symmetry breaking and cube coverage, plus reflected checking of an8-dimensional counterexample and upward extension. Replaces arithmetic-heavy graph vertices by Keller colorings with Gap/No-Faceshare predicates; this enables the general s=2^(n−1) reduction to be solved directly at n7,s64, avoiding difficult unformalized discretization reductions to s3/4/6. Splits symmetry obligations at the conditional index-bit-flip boundary: this transformation is proved semantically in Lean, remaining clauses are manually designed and mechanically checked with substitution redundancy. Uses trestle’s scoped auxiliary variables and verified encoding combinators; optimized case splitting and checked cube-cover refutation complete the automated proof chain.
    - limits: Tiling means axis-aligned translates of half-open unit cubes with exactly one covering cube for every point of R^n. Faceshare means corners differ by1 on one axis and agree on all others. This does not cover rotated cubes, overlaps, gaps or other tile shapes. The positive-dimension restriction matters: the displayed reduction theorem uses dimension n+1. The geometric reduction uses periodic tilings, finite clique/coloring existence with s=2^(n−1), and proof of encoding soundness in the direction needed to infer absence of colorings from UNSAT. Verifying only the SAT certificate would not suffice without those upstream connections. The authors avoid relying on Kisielewicz/Łysakowska discretization results, which Clune had not formalized, by solving s64 directly. Rows with s2 or s6 are additional experiments, not substitutes for the full n7 proof. Initial fixed-color symmetries for n≥3 assume the conjecture in dimension n−1. The authors prove n2 directly and proceed successively, rather than assuming the desired lower-dimensional cases. A unit-clause symmetry restriction is valid by existence of a transformed solution, not because every original solution satisfies it. Coordinate/color permutations and bit flips preserve the coloring conditions. Conditional index bit flips may change index adjacency yet preserve No-Faceshare. They are not expressible in the employed SR proof system; that portion requires separate Lean reasoning. The remaining SR clauses were found manually, not discovered automatically by a verified symmetry search. SR addition preserves satisfiability through a repair substitution and checked unit propagation, rather than necessarily preserving every satisfying assignment. Unverified C dsr-trim adds hints; verified trestle LSR checking validates its output. Failed or wrong hint generation should not be accepted merely because the converter terminates. The stated single-threaded CaDiCaL solving and proofix split suggestions are heuristic/unverified producers; solver results have certificates checked by verified LRAT/SR tools, and the cube-cover condition is separately refuted with negated cubes. The paper reports proof by reflection into Lean; it does not give a complete axiom/native-evaluation/trusted-executable inventory in this proceedings description. CNF auxiliaries yi,j,d and zi,j,d impose the implications needed for encoding, not an unconditional biconditional identification in every model. Exactly-one color constraints are essential for deriving color inequality from the no-shared-color clauses. Reported solve/check totals are hours over all cubes; they are not specified as elapsed wall time or normalized by a stated hardware/thread configuration. No CPU, RAM, repetitions or variance is supplied. Qualitative comparisons to BHMN are not a controlled ablation isolating encoding, splits and tooling. Authors explicitly report no LLM/AI use for the formalization; paper-writing use was limited to occasional Tikz-style questions. Thus this is evidence for human-designed hybrid formal proof workflows, not a measured LLM proof-agent success.

- Apply2Isar: Automatically Converting Isabelle/HOL Apply-Style Proofs to Structured Isar (2026)
    - what: Isabelle/ML tool replays procedural proofs, records intermediate proof states and prints a declarative Isar proof with explicit dependencies. It handles common command interactions, optional compact printing and partial conversion around schematic goals. Evaluates conversion success on4461 apply-style proofs selected from five AFP entries. Explains why simply reversing procedural steps fails with introduced facts, subproofs, all-goal methods, unfolding, shadowed names, schematic goals and printing/type inference. Provides concrete translation choices and fallbacks, including use of sorry during replay and retention of broken/partial inputs, making final independent proof acceptance essential. Kernel checking alone does not remove source axioms or sorry admissions; input placeholders and replay failures are deliberately representable, so assurance requires a complete final proof without admissions. The intended output faithfully exposes intermediate goals/dependencies, rather than selecting a natural human style. Readability, maintainability and robustness improvements are motivations and reasoned examples; no user study, maintenance experiment, perturbation benchmark or readability rating is reported. Supports14listed commands and15AST cases, with the additional case for preexisting introduced facts. Custom commands are unsupported. Original method bodies are parsed through existing functions rather than analyzed deeply, limiting safe renaming and deautomation. Schematic intermediate goals are collected into unchanged apply-style blocks under one declarative have, yielding partial translations. Output may change very little when schematics dominate; partial success is not equivalent to fully declarative proof. Printing and reparsing terms is not guaranteed to round-trip. print_types=necessary checks reparsed equality modulo alpha-equivalence and can trigger slow parsing; it does not solve arbitrary custom syntax ambiguity. Label shadowing can also break output unless users change prefixes. subgoal_fix_fresh defaultsfalse and handles cases where the shadowed variable is absent from relevant goals. Turning it on can fix conflicting printed names but break explicit method references to renamed variables. No universal option solves all cases. Copied structured Isar is not parsed/replayed internally: replay uses sorry to simulate its terminal effect. A broken copied block can survive in the generated text until final checking. Comments are lost in tokenization. The procedure is a refactoring aid, not an unconditional proof certifier. Benchmark selects five AFP entries with most textual apply occurrences, and only ten primary-session files for AutoCorres2. This is deliberately apply-heavy coverage, not a random sample of the AFP or all Isabelle proofs. Exact Isabelle2025-2 is stated; no precise timing distribution, repeated-run uncertainty, cross-version stress test or generalization theorem is reported.

- APR safety/liveness framework (2026)
    - title: Abstract Framework for All-Path Reachability Analysis toward Safety and Liveness Verification (Full Version)
    - what: Reformulates all-path reachability (APR) proof rules for abstract reduction systems so they correspond one-to-one with LCTRS rules, adapts cyclic APR proofs, reduces safety properties to partial APR validity, and introduces total validity that quantifies over finite and infinite execution paths for liveness. Defines DVP+ and a complete disproof rule DVP-bottom, proves equivalence with the original DVP, and formalizes finite APR pre-proofs, bud/companion links and proof graphs. Safety APR predicates characterize non-reachability of error states, illustrated with Peterson mutual exclusion. For liveness, Theorem 6.3 proves that an APR proof graph is acyclic iff the APR predicate is totally valid; the Peterson starvation-freedom example obtains an acyclic proof. Appendices establish decidability under finite reachable closure and detail limitations of reduction and cyclic generalization.

    - number: partial validity considers finite maximal paths; total validity considers finite and infinite paths
    - number: Theorem 6.3: acyclic proof graph iff total validity for a partially valid APR proof
    - number: APR proof/disproof decidability when reachable closure finite and side conditions decidable
    - limits: ARS reductions may be nondeterministic; partial validity alone ignores infinite paths and is insufficient for liveness. Total-validity criterion assumes a partially valid APR proof and its finite proof graph; decidability additionally needs finite reachable closure and decidable emptiness/intersection/runnability. Current cyclic buds must match companions exactly, the full cut rule is omitted, and process fairness/generalized companions are future work. Safety reduction uses error sets and normal-form conditions.

    - what: Defines a coinductive CSP deadlock-freedom specification and reports its equivalence to a failures-divergences refinement specification in Isabelle/HOL. Builds proof tactics for RoboChart transition processes enriched with active-node parameters and invariant assumption/guarantee checks. Full state-machine/controller composition and environment compatibility remain future work. Reduces recursive-process deadlock goals by coinduction,node case splits,universally quantified inputs,invariant hypotheses,guard coverage and proofs of every enabled continuation. Trigger events are treated as available; synchronization/event availability and compatibility of component contracts need separate system-level proofs. Exactly one simple leaf node is active; composite states with multiple active nodes are excluded. Invariant I is supplied manually as a design/environment assumption. Initial satisfaction and preservation by other components are environmental obligations. Checking a component under I does not establish that the deployed sensor/memory/environment enforces I or that interacting components are mutually consistent. The CSP notion permits successful termination through Skip. It is the deadlock_freeSKIPS variant,not the usual never-terminating deadlock-free CSP process. Coinductive DFI requires a nonempty observable event sequence before recursion,while DFI* permits empty sequences after progress is already accounted for. Correctly distinguishing those variants prevents unguarded circular proof. Isabelle/HOL and the HOL-CSP semantic libraries support kernel-checked proofs of generated logical terms. Model translation runs through Eclipse EOL RoboChart→Circus and EGL Circus→HOL-CSP; the paper claims semantic faithfulness but does not give a machine-checked end-to-end translator correctness theorem. Enrichment adds an explicit active-node parameter,final-state branch and assume/guar wrappers. Equivalence to the original process is conditional on successful contracts and surrounding operational structure. Assuming an invariant is a meaningful restriction on admissible inputs,not an unconditional theorem about the original unrestricted model. False assume emits aviol and recurses to a fallback; false guar emits gviol then STOP. These behaviors differ. Component proofs distinguish environmental violations from internal errors; a deadlock-free enriched process can still rely on an unrealized environment contract. Automation is specialized to the prototypical Trans structure and available normalization/reduction rules. Simple logical/arithmetic goals use simp,auto or Sledgehammer. A failed tactic does not establish a deadlock; Nitpick/Quickcheck witnesses of uncovered guards must be assessed for reachability,environment assumptions and the actual original model. Counterexample search concentrates on enabled-guard coverage. It does not claim completeness for arbitrary transition action failure,interacting process deadlock or infinite-state reachability. Real-valued symbolic proofs avoid enumeration but still require dischargeable mathematical obligations. Authors declare GenAI only for language polishing: technical content,proofs and formalization are human work. The study evaluates theorem-prover automation,not LLM-generated specifications/proofs or agents. No Verus,Rust or TLA+case is included.

    - what: Experience report on qrhl-tool, a Scala quantum cryptographic proof frontend using Isabelle/HOL for ordinary mathematical reasoning. Explains coupling-based relational logic, quantum predicate subspaces, a failure of emulating locals with persistent globals, dependency-sensitive memoization, and gradual migration from trusted tactics to kernel-checked reasoning. The complete worked example relates inversion of f composed with f to inversion of bijective f, proving equal game success probabilities while leaving runtime reduction outside the tool. The body exposes the actual assurance boundary: fully formalized Hilbert-space predicates coexist with axiomatized program/probability constants and hardcoded qRHL tactics. It walks through all commands of a reduction, its frame restriction on the adversary, the coupling x mapped to (x,f(x)), and the simplifier closing the residual subspace inclusion. It also explains why persistent entangled pseudolocals break quantum equality and how dependency tracking avoids rechecking after presentation-only or proof-only changes. These are qualitative implementation and worked-proof observations, not quantified performance or soundness evaluation.

A useful adversary bound also needs τ≥τf. Quantum reinterpretation strengthens both assumption and conclusion to quantum adversaries. - Dreier Torunczyk merge-width (2026)
    - title: Merge-width and First-Order Model Checking
    - what: Introduces radius-r merge-width via construction sequences that merge vertex parts and resolve default edges/nonedges. It unifies structural graph parameters and proves first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable on classes of bounded merge-width when a witnessing construction sequence is supplied. The paper defines construction/merge sequences, radius-r width, and translations from twin-width, degeneracy, bounded expansion, clique-width, generalized coloring numbers, and flip-width. It proves bounded twin-width and bounded expansion imply bounded merge-width, bounded merge-width implies bounded flip-width, and gives almost-bounded results for nowhere-dense classes. The model-checking algorithm maintains local first-order types through merge and resolve operations; distance-FO locality and scatter types yield Theorem 5.4, with O_{σ,q,w}(|V|²m) for a sequence of length m and O_{q,w}(|V|³) for graphs. Closure under first-order interpretations/transductions is proved. Examples and case arguments include bounded-degree/degenerate graphs, planar/minor-excluding classes, ordered structures, graph squares, and the relationship to twin-width and clique-width.
    - number: radius-r width for every fixed r
    - number: Theorem 1.11 O_{q,w}(|V|³) graph model checking
    - number: binary-structure bound O_{σ,q,w}(|V|²m)
    - number: radius needed r=2^{O(q²)}
    - limits: The FPT theorem assumes the input includes an effective construction sequence and a bounded radius-r width for r exponential in the quantifier rank; finding or approximating such sequences in general is open. The proved graph algorithm is cubic in |V|, weaker than linear bounds known in special bounded-expansion/twin-width settings. Structural equivalences with flip-width and monadic dependence are conjectured in general. The method is for finite binary relational structures and first-order model checking, not temporal/distributed traces; width constants and sequence length dominate practical cost.

- Driving by Disproof (2026)
    - title: Driving by Disproof: A Practical Model Checking Approach to Fleet Coordination
    - what: Recasts fleet coordination as model-checking disproof: submit the negation of the desired joint requirements to nuXmv, then use the resulting counterexample trace as a driving plan for all vehicles. A central observer updates an environment model with vehicle states and requirements, obtains a shortest bounded trace, and sends actuation instructions. Formalizes the specification as G¬(r1∧…∧rn) over an SMV environment model, explains conditions for expected counterexamples (pairwise-compatible requirements, non-dead-end initial scene, requirements covering the full traversal), and distinguishes entering/leaving events and fallback behavior. The POC aligns nuXmv BMC with HighwayEnv via discretized lateral and rounded velocity controls. Five tasks test longitudinal, lateral, and dynamic ordering maneuvers, with 1,000 runs each; runtime and trace-drift analyses identify lateral mismatch, no-CEX events, safety-distance constraints, and state-space scaling as the main practical risks.

- Enhancing Interactive Theorem Prover Error Messages with Hints (2026)
    - what: Heuristic enhancements to three Agda v2.8.0 error messages, evaluated with novice-Agda programmers in a university course. Measures successful repairs, time among retained successful submissions and perceived helpfulness. Confusable hints improve measured success and speed; correct whitespace hints improve retained-success timing; correct hints consistently improve perception. Incorrect hints show no statistically significant performance effect in this study, which is not an equivalence or harmlessness theorem. Documents exactly when each hint is shown, false-positive/false-negative limits, counterbalanced error-message variants on distinct snippets, timing-data exclusions and uneven participation. Results separate objective repair outcomes from subjective ratings. Conditional timing, repeated observations per participant and unsupported no-practical-danger language materially limit generalization to proof-development or agent workflows.
    - limits: Participants are final-year bachelor CS students in one elective functional-programming course: experienced programmers, new to Agda/ITPs after four Agda lectures, not general programming novices. Recruitment during lecture limits population to that course and language/demographic setting. Two survey variants swap original/enhanced error messages (OEM/EEM) across distinct A/B or C/D tasks. Every participant may see both conditions across different snippets, without seeing the same snippet twice. Per-snippet comparisons are between participants; pooled observations reuse participants. This is not a simple all-hints versus no-hints participant split. Ten one-error snippets represent three correct hint types and two incorrect ones, with two snippets per type/intention. No incorrect Confusable task was included because authors found no sufficiently realistic scenario. Incorrect hints are therefore a selected set, not all possible harmful hints. Whitespace heuristic splits an unknown name into in-scope names, without proving resulting application typechecks. Confusable compares unknown names only against in-scope names using generic Unicode spoof data. TooFewArgs triggers at function application sites with inferred function result type, not bare references with zero supplied arguments. Heuristics do not rerun a repair and certify its correctness. Compiler stops at the first error, making interpretation of a subsequent failure ambiguous. No semantic-correctness proof of suggested edits or trust theorem for modified Agda is presented. After removing 17 single-open/no-rating participants, analysis has 56 participants (32/24 variants), 412 submissions (228/184), average about 7 tasks and median 10; task response count 37–55. Random task ordering activated only after first TooFewArgs#A, so all users saw that task first. Timing analysis removes 136 failures, nine successful submissions interleaved with other tasks and 25 with >2-minute compilation gaps. Thus 242 retained successful observations inform timing, not all attempts. Successful-case conditioning and missingness can change group composition; results do not measure time-to-success including failures. Single-tailed Mann–Whitney U tests use directional hypotheses chosen by correct/incorrect intention, p<0.05. Table 3 has 21 p-values across five type/intention groups plus two pooled summaries and three outcomes. No multiplicity correction or participant-cluster model is described; pooled independence and multiple testing are reader concerns, not rerun statistical results. Online environment uses Haskell highlighting, no Agda Unicode-entry support or cursor-column display, and snippets use visible small libraries rather than standard Agda library. This differs from normal local Agda editing. Eleven-day access and 1–2-minute advice do not impose a strict per-task time limit. Subjective ratings range very misleading through very helpful, plus did-not-read option; Table 3 labels epsilon no rating. Exclusion of disengaged participants and differing availability of ratings affect denominators. No long-term learning/retention, error fatigue or realistic multi-error proof-development study is performed. Non-significant incorrect-hint performance tests do not establish zero harm or an acceptable bounded harm. No equivalence margin, confidence interval or statistical-power calculation is reported. The authors recommendation is broader than the exact study sample evidence. Only stated GenAI use is activated GitHub Copilot in PyCharm during data analysis. Hints themselves are designed heuristics, not evaluated LLM-generated hints or proof attempts. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or distributed protocol result is supplied. Authors report that cleaning gaps above two versus five minutes made no statistically significant difference (§3.4), without presenting a detailed comparison. Uneven task topics and recency across hint types constrain comparisons between types; Confusable material was more recent than TooFewArgs material (§5).

- Faster Verified Real Root Isolation with Descartes’ Rule of Signs (2026)
    - what: Reports Isabelle/HOL verification of termination, soundness and completeness for Descartes-based real root isolation: classical interval bisection Dsc and a Newton-accelerated NewDsc. Uses existing sign-variation and Three Circles theorems, proves a Bernstein splitting lemma to justify discarding gaps, and refines to fraction-free integer-coefficient SML code. Eight small benchmark cases compare with a customized verified Sturm baseline. The authors report mixed results using ChatGPT 5.1 Thinking for newdsc proofs; they also used ChatGPT to help write the SML benchmark driver, without specifying its model. Partial recursive definitions expose a domain predicate, separating termination assumptions from conditional correctness. Square-free complex-root separation plus Three Circles proves bisection terminates. NewDsc accepts a much smaller window only if it preserves the interval’s variation count; a strengthened splitting lemma excludes roots in discarded gaps and on window boundaries. A list-of-lists de Casteljau triangle supports sign-combinatorics induction. Integer coefficient pre-scaling eliminates rational GCD overhead before SML generation. Results distinguish easy polynomials, where Newton overhead hurts, from clustered Mignotte roots, where acceleration helps.
    - limits: The mathematical input is a nonzero real polynomial P, an open interval a<b, and natural degree bound p with degree(P)≤p. The displayed termination theorem further assumes p≠0 and square_free(P). Interval endpoints are excluded from the target root set; exact midpoint roots are returned as degenerate pairs. General integer input needs a square-free factorization and a global Cauchy root bound, which are future wrapper work rather than a completed all-roots interface here. Descartes counts positive roots with multiplicity and bounds them by coefficient sign variations after removing zeros; the difference is even. Only counts zero and one determine the exact root count directly. Transform x to (a x+b)/(x+1) and multiply by (x+1)^degree to map the positive line into (a,b). Bernstein coefficient variations provide the interval test. The paper bridges two prior formalisations when p=degree(P), while correctness statements use a degree upper bound. Dsc returns no interval for variation zero, returns (a,b) for variation one, and otherwise emits the midpoint if it is an exact root then recurses on both open halves. The function package’s domintros mode generates dsc_dom and conditional recursion/induction rules. A separately proved domain theorem establishes termination under its preconditions; total syntax alone is not a proof that every input evaluation terminates. Termination uses the existing formal Three Circles theorem and positive separation among distinct complex roots of a square-free polynomial. Once interval width is small enough, the relevant complex-disc region contains at most one root and variation is at most one. Repeated halving eventually reaches that scale. Square-freeness is a sufficient hypothesis, not a claim that no nonsquare-free input can ever terminate. Soundness dsc_pair_ok permits either a degenerate exact root (m,m) or an interval with exactly one root in its open interior. The displayed dsc_sound assumes domain membership, degree bound, P≠0 and a<b. The displayed dsc_complete assumes domain membership, degree bound and P≠0 and says every root strictly between a,b lies between the endpoints of some output pair. It uses closed endpoint inequalities in the coverage conclusion. Neither displayed theorem by itself states a globally disjoint, ordered or duplicate-free output list; those properties should not be attributed without an additional statement. NewDsc uses N≥2 in the prose. For variation nu≥2, first try one boundary block of width (b−a)/N; if its variation remains nu, recurse only on it with N². Otherwise try windows of the same scale around endpoint corrections lambda=a−nu P(a)/Pprime(a), then from b. A candidate is accepted by a variation-preservation test, rather than by trusting Newton convergence. Helpers’ full definitions, derivative-zero handling and complete newdsc theorem preconditions are not printed. If both jumps fail, bisect, test the exact midpoint and recurse on both halves with Nprime=max(4,floor(sqrt(N))). Successful jumps square N for more aggressive future shrinking; fallback reduces that aggressiveness. The paper says NewDsc termination and soundness are similar to Dsc and reports all three properties verified, but only gives a detailed new completeness argument in the article. The full source proof scripts were not independently inspected. Ordinary splitting proves Var(a,u)+Var(u,v)+Var(v,b)≤Var(a,b). If the retained window has the original variation count, both discarded open gaps have variation zero and therefore no root. This does not by itself exclude roots at u or v; the paper explicitly invokes a strengthened lemma for these boundary cases but does not display that stronger formula. Treat boundary exclusion as a reported formal lemma, not a consequence of the weaker printed inequality alone. The de Casteljau triangle takes convex combinations with positive weights summing to one. Its two boundaries encode the subinterval Bernstein coefficients. Inserting a convex combination between adjacent real numbers cannot add sign changes. The authors represent successive rows as a list of lists and prove monotonicity by strong induction on the coefficient list, then induct on the triangle for splitting. This differs from the cited Rocq pointwise-recursive algebraic representation because the current proof needs coefficient-list combinatorics. For code generation, decompose interval transformation into a Taylor shift by a, scaling by width b−a, polynomial reversal and a Taylor shift by one. A list-based Ruffini algorithm implements shifts; an iterative mapping loop implements scaling. Equivalent polynomial transformations can have very different arithmetic costs, so this is a separate refinement step from abstract termination/correctness. Fraction-free shifts use a=n_a/d_a and pre-scale coefficient c_i by d_a^{k−i}; denominator signs/normalization must preserve the intended nonzero scaling and sign-variation result. The adjusted width (b−a)d_a is represented by numerator/denominator and further coefficient scaling clears fractions before they appear. The text reports verified integer root tests and partial tail-recursive dsc_int/newdsc_int suitable for SML. It does not give all refinement equations or the complete integer implementation in the paper. Benchmark baseline is Joosten/Thiemann/Yamada’s verified Sturm isolate, customized to remove square-free factorization and algebraic-number packaging. Thus timings compare core isolation on already suitable inputs, not complete algebraic-number pipelines. Four random polynomials P1–P4 come from [22]; four Mignotte-type polynomials have form x^n−2(2^tau x−1)^2 and tight root clusters. This is a targeted eight-case experiment, not a broad random-distribution benchmark. Runs use Poly/ML 5.9.2 on an Apple M4 CPU with 16 GB memory. Table 1 gives milliseconds, median of five runs or average of 100 runs when runtime is below 10 ms. No spread/confidence intervals, memory/GC measurements, exact M4 model, optimization flags or Isabelle build version are specified here. No comparison with an unverified state-of-the-art root isolator is reported; approaching that performance is future work. Table 1 has two side-by-side groups: P1–P4 compare isolate,dsc_int,newdsc_int,dsc_exec; Mignotte cases compare isolate,dsc_int,newdsc_int,newdsc_exec. The unoptimized column is different in the two groups. The author claim of 10–200 times optimization speedup is rounded: P2 has dsc_exec/dsc_int=6.7/0.5=13.4 and M32,32 has newdsc_exec/newdsc_int=88617/449≈197.4. Do not treat cross-group unoptimized timings as the same algorithm. Direct GenAI report: ChatGPT 5.1 Thinking received corresponding dsc proofs as reference for newdsc proofs. Authors call its generated soundness proof largely correct with a few Sledgehammer-repaired errors, and say the other generated proofs were less valuable and not worth using overall. The SML experimental runner was also written with ChatGPT help. There is no trial count, prompt transcript, proof acceptance rate, cost, human-time measurement or controlled comparison. This is a specific qualitative human-assisted proof-reuse report, not autonomous end-to-end theorem proving. Formal artifact is linked at https://github.com/Aeacu2/Dsc with a Software Heritage snapshot and artifact DOI 10.4230/artifacts.26768. Reported machine checking is author evidence; no local build or artifact audit was performed. Future work includes square-free/all-root wrappers, dyadic rationals, approximate arithmetic and refinement to LLVM using Isabelle/LLVM. These are not current measured deliverables. There is no distributed-system protocol, verified Rust, Verus or TLA+ result; relevance to proof agents comes from the explicit LLM report and the distinction between abstract correctness, completeness boundaries and executable refinement.

- Formalization of a Realistic Verification-Condition Generator for an Intermediate Verification Language (2026)
    - what: Reports Dafny definitions and soundness proofs for a B3 intermediate verification language, an executable verification-condition generator (VCG), and a coinductive reference semantics supporting nondeterminism, unbounded loops, scopes, abrupt exits and recursive calls. Proves valid generated conditions imply procedure correctness for a closed set of procedures. A structural invariant/specification semantics makes most proofs amenable to SMT automation; a separate coinductive refinement connects it to reference execution. The authors report Cursor auto-completion only, without an LLM evaluation. Postcondition stacks model escape depth while continuation stacks guide VCG control flow and variable removal. Fresh variable incarnations distinguish assignment histories from current program states. The general statement theorem connects an arbitrary symbolic context, incarnation map and continuation stack to a reconstructed scoped statement; procedure soundness is derived from an assume-pre/body/check-post wrapper. Mutual coinduction handles both recursive procedure calls and loop unrolling. The paper explicitly separates the verified formal generator from incremental SMT interaction and evolved public B3, and excludes user axiom definitions.
    - limits: Only source-IVL-to-VC generation is proved sound. Source-to-B3 translation, B3-expression-to-SMT translation and actual solver validity remain outside the theorem. The conclusion is conditional on mathematical validity of every generated VC, not on any unchecked SMT response. Dafny, its own verification pipeline, logic and underlying SMT automation are trusted for the author-reported proofs; no independently checked small-kernel certificate or self-verifier proof is supplied here. The paper simplifies the grammar: Boolean/integer/uninterpreted types; mathematical operations, quantified expressions and function calls; check/assume, assignment, nondeterministic choice, conditionals, unbounded loop, vars scopes and escape depths. It assumes unique variable declarations with no shadowing. Only distinct-variable inout parameters are shown; the accompanying formal implementation handles all parameter kinds, as does B3. Interpreted-function semantics and expression refinements are described but omitted from printed formal definitions. Correctness is partial: nontermination is permitted, and the work does not prove termination of B3 loops or recursive source procedures. VCG itself is reported terminating by measures on statements and continuations. Assertions must hold on relevant execution prefixes; reference omnisemantics is not merely an arbitrary overapproximation that can hide a failing check, since Check demands both the expression and post-state membership. Omnisemantics relates a statement and initial state to a sequence of overapproximating post-state sets. Its head handles normal completion; index i handles escape i. A scope duplicates the current head, adds arbitrarily initialized fresh locals, and lifts every post-set by allowing those locals and projecting them away. An escape does not execute the rest of its current statement sequence: it targets the indexed enclosing-scope postcondition. Escape zero is a no-op. A loop introduces no control-flow scope. To break out, wrap it in vars and use escape 1. Structural loop semantics existentially chooses any suitable invariant state set containing the initial state and preserved by normal body completion; body escapes still answer to the unchanged tail of enclosing postconditions. The syntactic invariant annotation is ignored by the semantics and is separately validated by VCG. Reference loop semantics instead unrolls body;loop using a greatest fixed point. Structural call semantics checks the instantiated precondition and universally considers post-states satisfying the instantiated postcondition, with the same domain and all nonargument variables unchanged. It omits checking the callee body. Reference call semantics adds RefMeetsSpec for the callee. A procedure without a body is treated as meeting its specification; its specification remains an assumption, not a proved implementation. Aliased inout actuals are excluded by the displayed distinct-variable requirement. Theorem 1 requires a closed set of procedures: every called procedure belongs to that set. Valid VCs for every procedure imply all reference MeetsSpec predicates. Recursive specifications may be assumed modularly only because all available bodies are checked and the mutually recursive reference predicates are coinductive. The article does not present a global liveness theorem or a termination argument for arbitrary recursion. Proof decomposition: Lemma 2 derives structural MeetsSpec from one procedure’s valid VCs; Lemma 3 derives reference MeetsSpec for a closed, structurally correct procedure set. Theorem 4 is the generalized statement-level VCG invariant used for Lemma 2. Several prose cross-references call Lemmas 2/3 Theorems 2/3; the numbered statement labels remain Lemma 2 and Lemma 3. VCG state contains incarnation map I, symbolic path context C and stack B of (introduced variables, continuation statements). Check generates C implies substituted E and leaves C unchanged; assume conjoins substituted E. Assignment creates a globally fresh incarnation xprime, constrains it to E evaluated under the old map, then updates I. This freshness and substitution bookkeeping is part of soundness, not a source-level assignment simplification. Conditional generation follows each branch with its continuation under opposite guard assumptions and unions the VC sets. Scope entry allocates local incarnations and pushes its following statement with its local-variable set. Normal and abrupt scope exit remove local entries from I, while accumulated formulas may still mention their incarnation values. The paper describes this symbolic-execution choice as more stable for automation but potentially producing more VCs; it gives no comparative measurement. Theorem 4 assumes all free variables in S and B are mapped by I; each jump depth fits its corresponding continuation suffix; the stated VCG judgment holds; every VC is valid; and incarnation state ist satisfies C. It concludes structural correctness of mkScope(S,B) from AdjustState(ist,I) against the universal post-set. AdjustState projects current program values from I-selected incarnations; conflating it with the full symbolic-history state would misstate the theorem. Printed equation (2) gives mkScope(S,B)=mkScope(Bprime,(vars nu in S);Sprime) in the nonempty case, reversing the declared statement/continuation argument order. Reader diagnosis: the type-consistent intended recurrence is mkScope((vars nu in S);Sprime,Bprime). This is a presentation issue; no claim is made that the Dafny implementation contains the same error. The detailed inductive proof of Theorem 4 is delegated to the artifact. Coinductive SemRefine and MeetsSpecRefine are mutually recursive greatest lemmas. Structural loop-unrolling first proves Sem(body;loop,...); the coinductive hypothesis gives RefSem of that unrolling. Calls invoke the procedure refinement, which in turn invokes statement refinement for all precondition states. Recursive interpreted expressions require a similar omitted refinement. About 100 manually supplied proof lines connect the semantics; this is not the size of the full soundness proof. The formal AST/state, semantics, generator and proofs total about 4.7 kLoC: about 2.0 kLoC AST/state, 660 LoC omnisemantics, and about 2.0 kLoC VCG/proofs. Roughly 1.5 kLoC are actual code and 3 kLoC annotations/proofs. Authors report four months by one person previously inexperienced with Dafny proofs. These are rounded development-effort reports without timing trials, benchmark corpus, proof acceptance rates or independent reproduction. Manual proof work concentrated in incarnation/substitution chains, sequence folds for continuation unwinding, and quantified/uninterpreted expression semantics. The paper calls these higher-order semantics difficult for SMT. It does not measure how much automation replaced manual work or compare alternative provers. The GenAI declaration says only Cursor auto-completion was used; it gives no model, prompts, accepted-completion counts or agent autonomy evidence. The formalized VCG stays close to the public B3 generator but is not a verified release of every public-tool path. Public B3 sends branch contexts incrementally to SMT and has evolved; integrating proofs into a release remains future work. User-defined axiom definitions are excluded; public lazy delivery of axioms and interpreted-function definitions is also future work. Thus the abstract phrase realistic features does not mean all current B3 features are covered. Artifact is linked at https://github.com/dafny-lang/b3, Software Heritage swh:1:dir:1795668a148637332f93759bb96a4cd4283d6e32, DOI 10.4230/artifacts.27039. No artifact files, source-build logs, generated binary or model of the compiler/runtime were inspected. Related claims about HOL4/Dafny, core Why3, Viper, Boogie certification and Featherweight VeriFast are author comparisons, not independent re-evaluations in this reading.

- Formally Verified Linear-Time Invertible Lexing (2026)
    - what: ZipLex is a Scala/Stainless lexer that verifies maximal munch with rule-order tie breaking and lossless lexing/printing under explicit token transformation and separability conditions. It refines simple list/regex specifications to zipper derivatives, tail recursion, balanced sequences and mutable memoization. Experiments compare adversarial and JSON grammars and hash-table variants. Explains why arbitrary token concatenation is not invertible, how an all-rule prefix test yields a sufficient adjacent-token invariant, why a natural zipper induction fails, how an explicit stack preserves tail recursion while filling a cache, and which proof/resource and runtime claims remain conditional. Retains the untokenized suffix, client injectivity obligations, collision qualification, sparse-cache parameters, proof-count discrepancies and combined runtime/memoization ablation.
    - limits: §2: lex returns tokens and a possibly untokenized suffix. The informal print(lex(s))=s notation must retain all consumed text and any suffix appropriately; printing just successfully recognized tokens cannot reconstruct an arbitrary unrecognized suffix. Maximal munch picks the longest prefix and earliest rule on ties. Non-nullable rule expressions ensure each emitted token consumes input. §§2–3.1: alphabet elements have arbitrary type. Each rule must supply transform/charsOf and a client proof of charsOf(transform(s))=s on its required domain. Surjectivity is unnecessary for values created through transform. A noninjective semantic conversion can retain the original string alongside the value. This is a precondition on clients, not automatic correctness of arbitrary user token constructors. §§3.2–3.4: lex(print(ts))=ts does not hold for arbitrary token lists. PrintableTokens carries a sufficient R-Path separability invariant over suitable valid tokens; it is not a maximally permissive condition. Relation sep(t1,t2) rejects a boundary when any rule has a word with prefix text(t1) followed by the first character of text(t2). All rules matter, not only the producing rules. Nonempty tokens justify first-character access. §3.3: R-Path means the relation holds at each adjacent pair. Slicing preserves it. Concatenating nonempty paths needs one boundary relation check; empty sequences need their ordinary boundary-free cases. The displayed indexing equivalence omits that qualification. A constant number of relation checks is not constant character work: prefixMatch traverses the first token plus one character and considers rule languages, with rule/token/cache costs. §3.5: disjoint-character separator tokens provide a sufficient special case. Programming-language whitespace also occurs within strings/comments, so that approach is restrictive. The all-rule R-Path method is more general; it does not prove every possible token rearrangement printable. §4: regular expressions use explicitly enumerated character sets, concatenation, union and star. No richer regex feature such as arbitrary complement or lookaround is established. A zipper is a set of contexts, each a list interpreted as concatenation. Correctness relates matchZ to matchR(unfocus(z),s), and matchR to ghost matchRSpec. Reachable derivative finiteness is discussed through cited prior work, not independently audited here. §§5–7: verified equivalence steps connect list recursion to tail recursion and BalanceConc (balanced trees, immutable array leaves, default N=512, zero-copy leaf slices). No universal constant-time concatenation or machine-level JVM resource guarantee follows from functional equivalence. The proof relies on Stainless, SMT reasoning, compilation/runtime and prior verified LongMap. §6.1: generic HashMap[K,V] decorates LongMap[List[(K,V)]], indexed by hashes; collision buckets are linked lists. Functional correctness tolerates collisions, while performance explicitly requires reasonable collisions. Memoization invariant is that each stored (k,v) satisfies v=f(k). Mutation avoids threading an immutable cache through all functions/proofs. §6.2: longest-prefix memoization works on full input and indices. An explicit stack records parameters; after the tail-recursive result returns, cached values for recorded calls are filled. The paper cites Reps for O(n) longest-match time. For fixed rules/finite derivative state space and appropriate cache/hash assumptions this supports linear input-length reasoning; no separate machine-checked resource theorem or adversarial-hash worst-case constant lookup proof is shown. §6.2: sparse caching stores one of every k calls for inputs longer than M, default k=10,M=10^6. Pure opaque parameter functions may depend on input/rules, and functional correctness is agnostic to their settings. Arbitrary such functions do not automatically preserve a uniform linear-time bound. Turning memoization off in the JSON experiment relinquishes the general anti-backtracking guarantee. §7: authors report 21961 VCs, including 8802 cache hits, approximately 130 minutes, 44 VCs above 10 seconds and slowest 58 seconds. Final 100-line SMT-LIB query for the slowest VC rechecks in under a second with cvc5; that does not mean its original unfolding/approximation run took under a second. Aside from simple VSCode completions, authors explicitly report no LLM reliance. §7/Table1: 1915 executable lines and 13200 specification/proof lines sum to 15115; computed ratio is about 6.89, whereas prose says roughly ten times. §6.1 says approximately 1600 additional lines for hash-table work, while Table1 mutable HashMap excluding LongMap totals 2790. Scopes are not reconciled by the paper; retain both without inventing an explanation. §8: sequential benchmark algorithms on Linux, two 24-core AMD EPYC9254 sockets,96 virtual processors,128GB,2.9GHz base/up to4.15GHz. JMH/OpenJDK21.0.2; 99.9% confidence intervals. Figures are selected grammar/JSON workloads, not arbitrary parser or communication-protocol verification. The paper supplies no independent reproduction here. §8: full memoized ZipLex is about 3.5 times slower than Coqlex on JSON in detailed prose, rounded to 3 times in conclusion, and approximately two orders faster than Verbatim++. Verbatim++ incurs roughly two seconds DFA preprocessing. No-memo GraalVM21.0.11 variant is 1.37 times slower than Coqlex; this changes both runtime and memoization, so the improvement cannot be attributed solely to GraalVM. ASCII specialization/boxing is a hypothesis, not established causal attribution. §8: map benchmark inserts N random pairs, removes half and reinserts/updates all N. Generic verified mutable HashMap is slower than standard mutable HashMap, faster than standard immutable HashMap; LongMap is also plotted. This workload does not establish superiority for arbitrary key distributions or adversarial collisions. Data Availability: authors report artifact evaluation for Zenodo version4 DOI10.5281/zenodo.20084365, 1.35GB SMT-LIB, Bolts lexers/regex and nightly CI. These are author reports; no current CI status, artifact proof replay or extended arXiv2510.18479 verification was performed. Formal verification of distributed protocols, Verus/Rust, TLA+ and LLM proof generation are not evaluated.

- Fractional Separation Logic in Isabelle LLVM (2026)
    - what: A shallow Isabelle/HOL fractional separation logic with unbounded positive rational scaling and nominal resource labels. Labels preserve a concrete resource witness so arbitrary labeled assertions can be split and recombined. A kernel-checked VCG automates fractions/labels/frame inference,integrates with fork-join Isabelle LLVM,and verifies shared-input/disjoint-output parallel matrix-vector multiplication. Defines fractional separation algebra type classes,scaling of assertions by inverse resource scaling,and a uniform same-label recombination equality. Extends concrete-state abstraction and access-report frame compatibility to distinguish shared reads from exclusive writes/frees. Gives bottom-up refinement rules and normalization/matching automation,then an explicit recursive proof with shrinking input fractions,fixed labels,decreasing index,and ownership extraction/reinsertion for output elements.
    - limits: Fractions in the algebra are arbitrary positive rationals and compatible equal-valued resources can sum above1. Physical ownership is bounded by embedding assertions and frame into sα of a concrete state,which assigns fraction1 at each allocated-block address. Introductory sum≤1 intuition concerns realizable states,not a global restriction on the algebra. Uniform recombination requires the same label/resource witness;arbitrary unlabeled assertions remain noncombinable in general. Labels may be introduced existentially and forgotten,but two independently chosen witnesses cannot simply be assumed equal. Extended labels include undef,and annotations explicitly require l≠undef. Hoare triples quantify over frames and require successful termination in Isabelle LLVM semantics,with frame-compatible access reports. Reads cannot intersect frame-full addresses,writes/frees cannot intersect even partially framed addresses. Race freedom follows because modeled data races are semantic errors;this is relative to the trusted semantics. Trusted boundary includes Isabelle inference kernel plus Isabelle LLVM semantics and code generator. Frame inference,VCG,and derived separation rules produce kernel-checked proofs. Paper does not provide an end-to-end proved target-compiler/OS/hardware theorem or re-establish the LLVM backend soundness here. Concurrency supported here is fork-join parallel function calls with shared immutable resources and disjoint writes. Additional concurrency patterns,full Sepref stepwise parallel refinement,and higher-level map-reduce rules are future work. No verified Rust borrowing semantics or distributed/network protocol is supplied. User supplies inductive pre/postconditions,termination relation,and separate pure lemmas registered with simplifier. Explicit sep_split/sep_join annotations guide sharing;the paper’s fully automatic final proof is conditional on that setup,not automatic invariant/specification discovery. Matrix dimensions and storage use natural-number abstractions of signed fixed-width indexes,with m*n<2^63 and width representation in mtxA. Result array must own every index initially. Executable version uses64bit entries,but the paper does not spell out an unbounded-integer no-overflow theorem for entry multiplication/addition;do not conflate index bounds with arithmetic bounds. Constructors for the data structures are proved correct to address vacuous preconditions. This supports their realizability under constructor preconditions;it does not establish satisfiability of every arbitrary user assertion or external intended specification. Case-study generality remains limited to a few examples.

    - title: Three Roads to de Finetti’s Theorem in Lean 4
    - what: Freer reports a Lean 4 formalization of the de Finetti–Ryll-Nardzewski equivalence for infinite random sequences: contractability iff exchangeability and conditional identical independent distribution. Three routes converge on one finite conditional-factorization interface; only reverse martingales cover general standard Borel targets, while the L2 and Koopman routes assume real square-integrable variables. Human-selected definitions, architecture and accepted edits guided Claude proof generation and GPT review/repair. The reported 42,745-line research artifact builds on a pinned Lean/mathlib toolchain, but needs substantial library refactoring. A reusable skill records proof patterns, concrete instance-management failures, LSP feedback and library search.     - limits: Figure 1 assumes StandardBorelSpace Ω, measurable/standard-Borel nonempty target α, probability measure µ and each X i measurable, with X indexed by natural numbers. It concludes Contractable µ X ↔ Exchangeable µ X ∧ ConditionallyIID µ X. The theorem concerns infinite sequences. The Ω standard-Borel assumption is explicitly attributed to Lean conditional-expectation infrastructure; this reading does not claim it is a minimal mathematical necessity (§2, Figure 1). Exchangeability is invariance under arbitrary index permutations; equivalence with finite-support finite-marginal invariance is also reported formalized. Contractability compares equally long increasing subsequences. Conditional i.i.d. is relative to a directing random probability kernel, not unconditional independence. The paper also reports the converse conditional-i.i.d.-to-contractable direction. Exact formal definitions of all predicates and complete proof bodies are not printed here (§2). The common ending takes a sub-sigma algebra G and conditional factorization for each finite initial block, constructs a G-measurable probability kernel and packages ConditionallyIID. It centralizes measurability/product-measure uniqueness. Three routes sharing this interface reportedly exposed definition/support-lemma drift; reader inference: this checks agreement between routes, but is not an independent oracle for intended semantics, and common definitions/ending can share an error (§3.1, §5). Route A alone handles general standard Borel target spaces. Contractability supplies reverse-filtration symmetries; reverse martingale convergence supplies factorization. Real-valued conditional expectations must be converted to event indicators and transported through measurable embeddings back to arbitrary target-valued finite blocks. Supporting work includes Levy downward convergence, time reversal of filtrations and demonstrating the reversed process is a forward martingale (§1, §3.2). - Generalised bit-vector quantum circuit verification (2026)
    - title: Generalised Bit-Vector Abstractions for Formal Verification of Quantum Error-Detection and Entanglement Circuits over {H, X, C-NOT}: CSS Constructions, Soundness, and Mutation-Based Validation
    - what: Extends a two-bit-vector abstraction for H, X, and C-NOT quantum circuits to parametrized repetition/concatenated codes, arbitrary CSS syndrome extraction, a formally characterized sound fragment, mutation validation, and large GHZ circuits. The abstraction separates superposition tags from basis-state XOR behavior and reduces verification to bit-vector SMT constraints. The paper defines fragment F conditions under which the abstraction is sound, proves an explicit invariant theorem, gives necessity counterexamples, and differentially tests against exact state-vector simulation. Properties cover arbitrary error patterns, detection limits, and classical-decoder recovery; tested codes include Steane, [[15,7,3]], [[15,1,3]], and rotated surface codes. Direct Z3 encoding uses bit-vectors, XOR code-word constraints, and cardinality-bounded error variables. Evaluation finds all 12,000 in-fragment random circuits agree with state-vector simulation, while unrestricted circuits agree only about 55%; all 622 non-equivalent single mutants are detected. GHZ verification reaches 262,144 qubits, but random dense parity networks become very hard as depth/support grows.
    - number: All 12,000 in-fragment differential tests agreed with exact simulation; unrestricted tests about 55%
    - number: 682 mutants generated, 60 equivalent, 622 non-equivalent; all 622 detected
    - number: Largest GHZ star 262,144 qubits: 9.01 s solve, 46.1 s build, 1,397 MiB peak RSS
    - number: At 32 qubits, depth 4 solve 0.033 s versus depth 7 27.5 s; depth 8 had timeouts
    - limits: Soundness is only for fragment F: no non-phase gate between Hadamards and no Hadamard after a qubit has interacted; S/Z gates, genuine Y stabilizers, entangled-qubit Hadamards, and general stabilizer circuits are outside scope. Logical circuit faults are modeled, not hardware noise, decoherence, measurement errors, or fault propagation/hook errors. Code-word preconditions and error-location assumptions are explicit. Mutation coverage is single-modification classes only; the 100% rate is not complete fault coverage. GHZ scale is family/solver-specific; Python term construction and memory dominate at large sizes, and comparison with prior work is observational.

- Gholami-Sarjoughian Constraint-DEVS (2026)
    - title: Constraint-Driven Modeling Enabling Dual Model Checking and Simulation for Discrete Event Systems
    - what: Introduces Constraint-DEVS, a bounded variant of Parallel DEVS, and extends DEVS-Suite so the same component models support simulation and exhaustive reachability/model checking. A state-exploration protocol wraps one-cycle simulation, with bounded state variables, bounded ports, discrete-time events, selective state exploration, and transducer-based trace/property analysis. NoC and circular-buffer models demonstrate the framework. The paper gives concrete finiteness conditions and an algorithm: state and port values are specified by regular expressions, input events include an explicit null value, and a Q/V/U exploration loop injects every possible input into each reachable state, using simulation for one cycle. It defines explorable versus unexplorable variables to reduce state space without changing simulation behavior, and reuses an experimental-frame generator/transducer for state, path, and QoS-like checks. The circular buffer verification catches a simultaneous-event bug; NoC experiments compare round-robin and adaptive task distribution and quantify the severe state-explosion tradeoff. An appendix details VerifiableAtomic, StateVar/PortState, VerificationEngine, and integration with existing simulator classes.
    - number: circular buffers: 3,200, 12,600, 201,600 states
    - number: circular-buffer times: 4.55, 14.90, 273.78 s
    - number: adaptive distributor: 15x state-space increase; 15.78 to 245.20 s
    - number: NoC 4x3: 25,255,495 states and 39,211.6 s
    - limits: Exhaustive checking requires finite bounded state variables, bounded port values, discrete external-event times, finite time-advance values, and no converging time-advance sequences. Selective state exploration can omit information needed by a property, and complex Java data/trace processing raises cost. Results are reachability checks, not automatic proof of an unbounded DEVS model. NoC models simplify packet/data behavior and rely on abstraction; the framework does not remove state explosion: a 4x4 network was not completed, and authors propose partial verification and multiresolution modeling. Property expressiveness through an experimental frame may itself require validation.

- Guidelines for Producing Concise LNT Models, Illustrated with Formal Models of the Algorand Consensus Protocol (2026)
    - what: # Whole-paper read: Guidelines for Producing Concise LNT Models, Illustrated with Formal Models of the Algorand Consensus Protocol (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Hubert Garavel. MARS2026, EPTCS443,pp43–83,doi10.4204/EPTCS.443.5;arXiv2604.05006,41pages. The paper refactors a finite LNT model of Algorand's BBA* phase and reports equivalence/model checks. Its strongest directly measured result is model compaction with strong bisimilarity checked for two four-node configurations. It supplies a detailed transformation sequence, printed model code and property scripts. It does not establish correctness of the deployed Algorand implementation or arbitrary-size Byzantine consensus. [Q0,Q1,Q2,Q10,Q11]  ## What changes, and what is preserved  The original Urbino model has967LNT lines. Application-specific changes produce U0 with769lines. These changes include new observations, merged/split events, a different attacker and a fair-coin correction; the paper explicitly says many “do not preserve bisimilarity properties.” Thus equivalence of U0–U4 does not imply equivalence with the original967-line model. [Q2,Q11,Q14]  Four generic transformations then produce U1–U4: extract shared modules, replace duplicated control branches with data parameters, merge common sequences, and replace mutually recursive tail calls with assignments and explicit loops. Strong bisimilarity means corresponding states can match every labelled transition in both directions. Authors report BCG_CMP checks for A4,0(four honest nodes) and A2,2(two honest/two malicious), with incremental checks after individual changes. They give structural/algebraic explanations, not a mechanized theorem covering every use of every transformation. The common-suffix choice law is explicitly qualified as failing for common prefixes. [Q3,Q4,Q5,Q6,Q7]  The §2.2 table gives total/nonblank-noncomment lines: U0=769/705,U1=607/552,U2=320/282,U3=288/250,U4=250/212. U0→U4 therefore removes67.49%of total lines and69.93%of substantive lines, ratios3.076and3.325 respectively; these are reader arithmetic. The original967→250comparison also includes semantic changes. Readability and reduced maintenance effort are the author's qualitative judgments; there is no reader study or maintenance-cost experiment. [Q3,Q11]  State counts illustrate that fewer source lines need not produce fewer unminimized states. For the honest-node/malicious-node/A4,0/A2,2 LTSs, U0 has1740/3190/24230/42509states; U1 is identical; U2 has1761/3190/24599/42509;U3 has1681/3046/20665/34679;U4 has1723/3130/20905/35059. After strong-bisimulation minimization every version has558/840/12059/19486states. Identical minimized counts alone would not prove bisimilarity; the reported equivalence checks supply that evidence. No runtime or memory benchmark is given. [Q3]  ## Concrete transformation cases  U1 extracts duplicated node/counter code and splits data definitions into types/constants/channels. U2 merges honest, malicious and disguised behaviors using a MORALITY parameter; node IDs≤H identify honest nodes. U3 factors common suffixes/prefixes and reduces NODE's process calls22→9. Its final branch-factorization example is acknowledged as harder to understand despite being shorter. U4 exposes an inner three-step coin loop inside an outer block-processing loop, replacing12recursive calls across node/counter code with3loops. [Q4,Q5,Q6,Q7]  The loop discovery uses pairs of control location and step residue, rather than control locations alone. The initial random-bit process had combined graded-consensus abstraction with a later fair coin; separating these roles restores the nested-loop structure. The earlier probability P_H used for the later coin is corrected to0.5 among the specific changes before the equivalence-preserving sequence. The counter independently accepts propagated/self-propagated bits, increments K0/K1 and resets them after TALLY. AnnexB prints U2/U3/U4 node code and recursive/imperative counter variants, enabling direct comparison. [Q7,Q14,Q15,Q16]  ## What is verified  Visual checking first hides irrelevant events and minimizes by branching bisimulation, which allows matching behavior across internal steps. Four-node models have roughly12000–20000strongly minimized states,43000–69000transitions and131labels. SYNC-only slicing exposes alternating BEGIN/END barriers. The block interface exposes proposal bits0/1 and commit-proposed/commit-empty events: for H≥T the observed model allows acceptance or rejection; for H<T the illustrated attacker systematically rejects bit1 proposals. Earlier pre-v5models have visible deadlock traces. These are observations of the stated abstract models and attacker, not an arbitrary-fault resilience theorem. [Q8]  Equivalence checks compare sliced systems with small hand-written expected processes: TALLY events form a cyclic four-dimensional hypercube; SELF_PROPAGATE has a more involved loop with optional per-node propagation. Hidden bit/counter values are renamed toX, so those checks establish event-pattern behavior after abstraction, not correctness of discarded values. SET_BIT slices remain difficult to inspect, motivating value-passing MCL formulas. [Q9,Q10]  AnnexC reports16named property scripts checked on both U4configurations: P1deadlock absence;P2SYNC alternation;P3aTALLY counter sum≤4 andP3bhypercube;P4a/bPROPAGATE patterns;P5a/bSELF_PROPAGATE patterns;P6a/bselection P_IN/P_OUTpatterns;P7a/bP_ZERO/P_ONEpatterns;P8ablock-interface classification;P9a/b/cper-node SET_BITinitialization and step progression. The latter formulas require an eventual next bit-setting event or, in P9b, a new proposal, without intervening conflicting events. They are local sequencing checks. The conclusion leaves formulas connecting all nodes' votes to the expected consensus decision as future work. The printed P9cdescription is grammatically incomplete, while its formula explicitly targets SET_BIT(ID,0,any). [Q17,Q18,Q19,Q20]  The models have infinite loops. Absence of deadlocks does not itself prove eventual block commitment. The paper does not report probabilistic model checking or almost-sure termination; probability values occur in observable choice labels, and probabilistic verification is proposed as future work. The evaluated equivalences and MCL results should not be turned into a quantitative probability-of-failure guarantee. Larger configurations of6,8,10nodes are mentioned as explored compositionally, without this paper providing comparable property outcomes or resource measurements for them. [Q10,Q11,Q15,Q16]  ## Model assumptions and limits  AnnexA fixes node population, honesty and equal stake; omits money/rewards, cryptography and leader election; abstracts graded consensus by a probability; reduces step numbers modulo3; and synchronizes every voting phase with global BEGIN/ENDbarriers. Committees are independently selected possibilities ranging from0toNmembers rather than fixed sizeC. The attacker does not fork: it manipulates votes to reject selected proposed blocks. U0 replaces shared BOYCOTT synchronization with independent malicious behavior triggered by proposal bit1. Therefore the model covers one censorship-style strategy, not all Byzantine behavior or dynamic corruption. [Q12,Q13,Q14]  Two documented interpretation choices are fresh committees per step rather than per round, and a persistent per-node bit across steps. Printed constants use N=4,C=3,T=2,H=2(or4),P_V=C/N,and P_H=p²(1+p−p²),p=H/N. The main process synchronizes nodes on proposals, propagation, barriers and both commit events. Reader observation: agreement at those shared commit events is constrained by the model composition; the paper's checks do not independently establish all implementation behaviors fit that composition. Relaxing synchrony and moving from historical BBA* to deployed ABFT remain future work. [Q12,Q13,Q15,Q16,Q11]  For this collection, the paper contributes a concrete workflow for simplifying distributed-system specifications while checking equivalence and targeted temporal properties. Its relevance to LLM-generated specifications is my inference: proposed cleanup should retain an explicit preservation target, and success on self-chosen event slices should not substitute for the intended protocol guarantee. The paper has no Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment.  ## Read and evidence scope  Read all41pages, §§1–8,29reference entries and AnnexesA–C, including all32specific changes,9model-code subsections,16property scripts and auxiliary processes. Inspected all5figures, the full §2.2table and dense formula/code renderings; complete extracted text supplied the remaining material. No external author artifact was linked or acquired beyond the full code printed in the paper. Official arXiv and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. Publisher PDF differs in66bytes but yields identical raw extracted text; hashes and comparison saved. No author code, compiler, model checker, solver or generated LTS was executed or loaded. All reported tool results remain attributed to the author.

- HSTL automotive model checking (2026)
    - title: Hybrid Spatiotemporal Logic for Automotive Applications: Modeling and Model-Checking
    - what: Defines Hybrid Spatiotemporal Logic (HSTL), combining temporal next/until, grid-neighbor spatial modalities, and hybrid nominals/binders that name vehicle positions over time. It gives semantics, modeling idioms for vehicle assumptions, a memoized formula evaluator, and baseline, globally optimized, and motion-aware trace generators. HSTL nominals name grid positions rather than worlds and can be static, relatively moving, or fixed-motion vehicles. The evaluator is proved correct with O(|t|²|φ|) runtime. The motion checker is correct under partitioned consistent assumptions and has trace bound O(s·Σ_{k=0}^{n−1}∏_v b_v^k), where static/dependent branching is 1 and fixed motion branches by |M|. Specifications cover safe following, hazard evasion, intersection crossing, overtaking and platooning; motion assumptions dramatically reduce traces.

Motion algorithm requires consistent assumption partitions, no nominal both dependee/dependent, and each dependent nominal in one relative assumption. It is intended mainly for offline planning/test generation; discretization omits continuous vehicle dynamics and uncertainty, and experiments use a 10-minute timeout and wall-clock measurements.

- Hybrid synchronous refinement types (2026)
    - title: Towards Formal Verification of Hybrid Synchronous Programs with Refinement Types
    - what: Defines operational semantics and a refinement-type verification system for synchronous programs combining discrete reactions, ODE evolution, and zero-crossing-triggered resets, and proves type safety. The paper gives a modular zero-crossing definition, hybrid stream operational rules for finite and non-terminating continuous segments, and typing rules that combine differential invariants with an Active predicate for guards known to interrupt flow. Type-preservation lemmas show safety throughout continuous traces and after resets; appendices provide detailed proofs and worked water-tank and automatic-braking derivations.
    - number: zero-crossing case analysis identifies 85 subcases in the appendix taxonomy
    - number: two worked examples are verified in §8 with detailed proofs in Appendix E
    - number: no runtime or benchmark aggregate is reported
    - limits: Safety is an invariant over reachable continuous traces and reset states, under the stated Zélus-style semantics and differentiable guard/flow assumptions. The Active predicate only captures guards whose initial value and derivative establish activity; zero-crossing choice is semantic and syntactic-order dependent. The authors explicitly make no liveness claim for Zeno executions, and the paper is a formal development with examples rather than a scalability benchmark.

    - title: HyperQB 2.0: A Bounded Model Checker for Hyperproperties
    - what: Introduces a Rust push-button bounded model checker for synchronous HyperLTL and asynchronous A-HLTL over NuSMV and Verilog, using SMT or QBF encodings and returning counterexamples or existential witnesses. HyperQB2.0 unifies NuSMV and Verilog into a program-graph IR, supports unbounded integer/array domains through Z3 ASTs, and adds loop-condition encodings for completeness on finite-state fragments. It offers pessimistic/optimistic and halting bounded semantics, three interfaces, asynchronous trajectory-position quantification, synthesis of existential traces, and explicit/implicit simulation encodings for ∀∃ and ∃∀ loops. Case studies cover information flow, linearizability, robotics, fairness, co-termination, deniability, cache attacks and hardware constant-time properties.
