- Improving LLM Code Reasoning via Semantic Equivalence Self-Play with Formal Verification (2026)
    - what: # Improving LLM Code Reasoning via Semantic Equivalence Self-Play with Formal Verification (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Poon Tsz Nok and Antonio Valerio Miceli Barone use generated Haskell program pairs to train a language model to reason about code. Alice generates a transformed program and either an equivalence proof (SEQ) or a distinguishing input (SINQ). Bob judges equivalence. The paper evaluates rejection-based supervised fine-tuning and downstream benchmarks. It supplies no new soundness theorem for Liquid Haskell or the complete training pipeline. Its reported verifier labels require an additional qualification: the inspected current wrapper does not independently enforce that the model submitted the intended equality obligation.  This record covers arXiv:2604.17010v2, dated 3 May 2026, all 20 pages, 34 references, 19 figures, eight tables, two numbered listings and Appendices A–H. The official and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. ACL Anthology lists “Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026,” July 2026, pages32273–32292, DOI10.18653/v1/2026.findings-acl.1615 (saved publication metadata). That publication metadata is separate from the arXiv version actually read. The paper does not identify an experimental repository revision. Static findings below concern commit `490fe084d705cb501e0fe34e592f17db2eb44a7b`, not an authenticated historical run.  ## What the method establishes  The reference corpus starts with OpenCodeInstruct programs translated into Haskell by DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B. Compilation and execution on a generated input filter the candidates, yielding about 28,000 functions (§3.2, Figure2). Passing that filter establishes that a particular candidate compiled and executed on one input under the filter. It does not prove that the translation preserves the original task, that the reference function meets its intended specification, or that it behaves correctly on every input. AppendixA's recursive versus fold-based reverse example illustrates alternative Haskell implementations; its typing discussion does not establish that every Haskell program is pure, total or safe.  SEQ asks Alice to generate Q and a Liquid Haskell proof of equality with P for all inputs of the declared type. The intended mechanism uses reflected definitions and proof by logical evaluation (PLE). SINQ asks for an input on which their observations differ. AppendixB's SEQ example compares `double x = x + x` with `double' x = 2 * x`; its SINQ example distinguishes `"zero"` from `"non-positive"` at zero. These are concrete proof and witness examples, not distributed-system specifications. Conditional equality in the checker semantics remains distinct from a specification of the original natural-language task.  Bob samples answers, normally ten, and difficulty is `10 * (1 - N_success/N)` (§3.4). Alice generates with target difficulty10 and separately learns to predict observed difficulty. The paper retains hard generator cases and a smaller easy sample, difficulty-prediction examples, and successful proof-generation traces. Bob is fixed throughout seven Alice rounds and fine-tuned once afterward. Each Alice training round restarts from the original base model on accumulated examples; generation uses the previous adapter. This is supervised fine-tuning with rejection sampling. AppendixC discusses reinforcement learning as a possible extension; it is not the evaluated implementation.  The base model is DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, with LoRA adapters. AppendixE gives temperature0.6, top-p0.95, top-k20, presence penalty1.5 and a32,768-token context. The actual reported hard threshold is3, rather than the example/default5. A main run takes “about 3 days on 4 NVIDIA L40S GPUs” (AppendixE.4). That is an author-reported duration, not a reproduced measurement.  ## Static checks of the verification and selection boundaries  Seven selected repository files were read completely: root and SEQ_v2 READMEs, `run_liquidhaskell.py`, `SEQ.py`, the seven-round launcher, the dataset compiler filter and the EquiBench evaluator. The full nontruncated repository tree was used only as metadata. Stored datasets, predictions, checkpoints and scientific result JSON were not loaded. No author code was imported or executed; no GHC, Liquid Haskell, solver or training run was performed.  The main equivalence wrapper accepts a generated code block, post-thinking response or entire response as the proof body (`generate_proof_body`). Its fixed refinement lemma template is commented out. It inserts the model's text into a module containing reflected P and Q, rejects an empty body, invokes GHC with the LiquidHaskell plugin and returns `"proved"` on exit0 (`verify_equivalence`). No inspected check independently requires a refinement annotation asserting the intended equality, fixes the proposition outside model control, or rejects model-supplied additional assumptions/options. A successful process exit alone therefore does not show that this wrapper submitted and checked the target equality. This is a static obligation-integrity issue, not a demonstrated successful bypass or evidence that any reported training example was mislabeled. The small `run_liquidhaskell.py` example overwrites its initial annotated double example with an addNumbers proof lacking an explicit equality refinement annotation; it is source text, not a saved successful run. The paper's second few-shot proof example has the same omission.  The inequivalence wrapper rejects a Q compilation error and accepts different successful stdout. It also accepts one successful and one failed execution, or differing failure statuses (`check_divergence`). Runtime and timeout statuses can thus contribute to labels. An observed timeout is not proof of semantic nontermination. Reference compilation is checked separately, but that does not remove every execution failure. The record does not infer the frequency or historical impact of these cases.  Selection differs from the paper in the pinned driver. Both generator branches append candidates only when difficulty is at least the threshold; the later easy-generator sample therefore has no candidates. The difficulty-prediction sample takes at most `0.5 * n_hard` easy items, at most one third of the resulting subset, rather than half the subset. SEQ generation training retains the original target10 prompt; SINQ generation training rebuilds its prompt with observed Bob difficulty. Both difficulty-prediction branches use observed difficulty as their output label. The source uses `>=`, while the paper's hard-case definition uses `>`. The launcher sets threshold1, versus the paper's reported3 and README example5. Its base-model restart and single final Bob training do support the described schedule. These differences do not identify the configuration actually used for the paper's experiments.  `parse_bob_output` normally returns a Boolean, but a missing match falls through as None and an exception returns `(None,None)`. `run_bob` uses truthiness: ordinary missing output is treated as an inequivalence answer; the exception tuple is treated as an equivalence answer. That can affect difficulty and training selection. No stored-output audit establishes how often either case happened.  The selected dataset validator checks function-binding heuristics and compilation; its input-argument filter is commented out. It does not itself implement the paper's one-input execution stage, which may occur elsewhere. The EquiBench evaluator uses a Haskell-specific system prompt on the loaded benchmark pairs, extracts the first regex match rather than necessarily the final answer, and skips parse failures/exceptions before computing accuracy, precision, recall and F1. It saves parsed/unparsed counts, but the paper tables do not give those counts. These are current evaluation-path limitations, not a reanalysis of stored experimental outputs.  ## Evaluation and numerical evidence  The main E0 regime attempts SEQ/SINQ50/50 over500 reference programs per round. E1 is SINQ-only with500, E2 is96/4 with500, and E3 is SINQ-only with40 (Table1). Tables6/8 and Figures6/12/15/18/19 report total accepted pairs:  - E0:34SEQ and903SINQ, total937 - E1:1,839SINQ - E2:62SEQ and78SINQ, total140 - E3:156SINQ  AppendixF estimates E0 yields as34/1750≈1.94% and903/1750=51.6%, using expected branch-attempt counts. It defines expected accepted volume `K=P*(p*r_SEQ+(1-p)*r_SINQ)`, predicts E2≈19.632 pairs per round and chooses E3≈38.04 references, rounded to40. This controls an estimated pair count. It does not equalize actual accepted counts, proof tokens, difficulty, class balance or compute. E2 and E3 actually have140 and156 pairs. The text's “isolates the causal effect” and “fixed compute resources” claims exceed that control. The paper itself acknowledges residual difficulty/class differences and small samples, and asks for stronger statistical evidence (§7). No independent training-seed replication or uncertainty for those causal differences is established by averaging16 evaluation samples/trials.  Intrinsic Bob accuracy increases87.57→91.34% on training-split generated challenges and88.24→88.79% on unseen-split challenges (Table2). The latter is0.55 percentage points. The seven overall difficulty means are0.50,0.50,0.65,0.87,0.66,0.93,1.18 (Figure3); they increase overall but not monotonically. Figure7's SEQ means end1.89, after2.17,3.00 and1.00, so AppendixH's “2.0−3.0 in later ones” is only a loose description of some rounds. Difficulty is performance relative to this Bob and these accepted cases, not an independent measure of semantic complexity.  Table3 reports Haskell HumanEval Bob Pass@1 rising17.7→26.4%, with compilation errors130→110; final Alice is26.3%/104errors. On MBPP Bob rises26.7→36.9%, errors250→203; Alice is34.3%/218errors. Figure9 labels final Alice MBPP errors212 instead of Table3's218. This discrepancy remains unresolved. Plot averages over16 trials do not establish independent repetitions of the complete training process.  EquiBench's largest E0 accuracy increase is OJ_V56.5→69.8%, or13.3points (Figures4–5). OJ_A rises50.2→57.4, OJ_VA55.8→55.9, STOKE48.0→51.8; DCE falls55.1→51.9 and TVM51.7→50.1. F1 improves on OJ_A/OJ_VA/OJ_V/STOKE and declines on DCE/TVM. PySecDB accuracy rises67.6→68.8 and F151.3→54.0 (Table4). CodeXGlue accuracy rises48.8→50.5, while recall falls51.1→41.7 and F147.9→43.2 (Table5). The authors describe near-random defect detection; no statistical chance-baseline analysis is supplied.  Table7 does not support universal dominance by the mixed or volume-controlled SEQ arms. E0 loses to E1 on MBPP Bob36.9 versus38.8 and Alice34.3 versus39.3, and HumanEval Alice26.3 versus28.1. E2 loses to E3 on OJ_V accuracy63.2 versus65.8/F161.5 versus64.7, TVM accuracy48.8 versus50.8/F133.5 versus33.9, and CodeXGlue F144.1 versus48.5; PySecDB accuracy ties68.7. E2 wins several other comparisons, including the four Haskell generation scores. These small, mixed results support investigating complementary supervision, not a general proof that SEQ uniquely improves reasoning.  The validated-count plots contain percentage-denominator errors. Figures12,15,18 divide labels by250, even though E1 uses500SINQ attempts, E2 expects480SEQ/20SINQ attempts, and E3 uses40SINQ attempts. E1 consequently prints yields above100%. For example248/500=49.6%, not99.2%; E3's26/40=65%, not10.4%. Figure15's actual branch counts are random, so480/20 are expected denominators rather than authenticated attempt totals. The reported raw accepted counts and Table8 totals need not be wrong merely because the percentage labels are wrong. Figure19 reuses the raw counts. All figures, tables, count trajectories and these qualifications are retained separately.  ## Contribution and limits  The useful contribution is a concrete way to generate semantic reasoning tasks and combine proof-oriented examples with distinguishing-input examples. The study exposes low positive-equivalence yield, verification-wrapper obligations, label handling and the need to compare training volumes and costs carefully. Its strongest direct relevance is to evaluating LLM agents that write proofs: successful verifier invocation must be tied to a fixed intended theorem, and benchmark gains require checks beyond accepted proof labels.  The paper explicitly notes proof-generation failures, Liquid Haskell/reflection limitations, partiality/nontermination and the gap to low-level, stateful and memory-manipulating programs (§8). There is no Verus, Rust, TLA+ or distributed-protocol experiment. Applying these ideas to distributed verification is a reader inference. The record claims a whole paper and selected static-source read, not a fresh proof, experimental reproduction, exhaustive repository audit, historical configuration recovery or verification of every generated item.

    - what: Characterizes graph classes where FO model checking parameterized by the number of variable names is FPT in monotone settings, gives a kernel for shallow colored trees, and proves AW[*]-hardness already on paths and on monotone classes of unbounded tree-depth.     - what: Introduces Linear Chain Logic (LCL) for spatial, size-indexed properties of periodic matrix product states and approximate model-checking algorithms based on completely positive transfer maps, irreducible decomposition and semilinear evidence sets.     - title: Multi-Objective Statistical Model Checking using Lightweight Strategy Sampling
    - what: Introduces the first statistical model-checking approach for multi-objective Pareto queries. It samples deterministic strategies with lightweight strategy sampling (LSS), estimates all objective values by Monte Carlo confidence intervals, and constructs convex-hull underapproximations and incremental overapproximations of the achievable/Pareto set. The paper formalizes simultaneous confidence boxes across strategies and objectives using Bonferroni/union-bound error allocation. Its incremental algorithm assigns geometrically shrinking error budgets to batches and almost surely converges, under ideal LSS on finite contracting MDPs, to a confidence band of precision sqrt(2d) epsilon. Three fixed-budget algorithms (weight-vector refinement, fixed-iteration budget, fixed-strategy budget) combine strategy-discarding heuristics with an independent evaluation phase to retain sound lower bounds. The modes implementation evaluates 40 instances from quantitative-verification and reinforcement-learning benchmarks, and reports when SMC remains usable while Storm PMC times out.

    - what: Introduces two-dimensional bounded model checking (2D-BMC) for unbounded Petri nets, bounding both execution length and token count, and implements SMT encodings in DCModelChecker 2.0 for LTL with linear integer arithmetic (LTLLIA) under interleaved and concurrent firing semantics. Sections 2–3 define interleaving versus concurrent firing, LTLLIA counting syntax/semantics, and loop/no-loop bounded semantics. Section 4 gives Algorithm 2, which enumerates macro-bound k and all (lambda,kappa) time/token pairs, plus SMT encodings for markings, loops, arithmetic terms and temporal operators. Section 5 describes PNML/ANTLR preprocessing, Z3 workflow and counterexample traces. Experiments compare 352 MCC fireability instances with ITS-Tools, test 320 fireability-cardinality properties across 20 models, and evaluate five synthetic unbounded nets against DCModelChecker 1.0, ITS-Tools and TAPAAL.

    - number: 352 comparison instances; 7 false positives; confidence 0.90
    - number: 320 properties, 20 benchmarks, 1,280 runs
    - number: bound 100 explored without counterexample in workflow example
    - limits: 2D-BMC is bounded and incomplete: UNSAT means only that all traces within the explored bound satisfy the property. Current DCModelChecker 2.0 does not use truly concurrent execution on every run, and its encoding/tool is slower than ITS-Tools/TAPAAL in some categories. Formula translation caused seven false positives among 352 comparison instances (confidence 0.90). Concurrent firing removes intermediate interleaving markings, so semantics must match the intended system.

- Pischke-Yoshida top-down bottom-up (2026)
    - title: Top-down = Bottom-up: Sound and Complete Characterisations of Liveness by Multiparty Global Protocols
    - what: Develops a principal global-type synthesis algorithm from safe-and-live local typing contexts and proves that top-down global-type projection and bottom-up local verification characterize exactly the same live multiparty sessions (Ptop = Pbot) under precise synchronous subtyping, balanced global types, and coinductive full-merging projection. Beyond the headline equivalence, the paper gives operational semantics for processes, local contexts, and global types; a deterministic fair round-robin scheduler that linearizes independent interactions; termination and balancedness proofs for synthesis; a combined projection/subtyping relation establishing trace inclusion and principality; and a complexity bound O(n^2 b |Delta|^n) for graph synthesis. The Monte Carlo MapReduce example shows why subsumption removes an unused crash branch. The implementation includes four projection algorithms, process/local inference, safety/liveness checking, and global synthesis, and benchmarks literature protocols including MapReduce, independent workers, rings, wallets, e-voting, and binary counters.
    - number: Ptop = Pbot
    - number: PSPACE-complete synchronously
    - number: undecidable in the asynchronous semantics
    - number: O(n^2 b |Δ|^n) graph synthesis bound
    - limits: Assumes synchronous session semantics, finite guarded recursive local types, finite labels, safe-and-live input contexts, fair scheduling, precise synchronous subtyping, and balanced global types. Process-level liveness is undecidable, so bottom-up checks context properties that soundly imply it; synchronous context checking is PSPACE-complete and asynchronous liveness is undecidable. Synthesis can incur exponential syntactic expansion because recursive syntax cannot share branch subterms; benchmarks show stack overflow/timeouts on largest coinductive-full cases. Tool results cover representative examples rather than production deployments.

- Proof-based coverage (2026)
    - title: From Execution to Necessity: Proof-Based Metrics for Code Coverage (Short Paper)
    - what: Introduces proof-based coverage: translate a C program with an assertion to SSA and an SMT formula, extract an unsatisfiable core proving the assertion, and map core constraints back to source statements. Proof line coverage measures statements necessary for validity rather than merely executed. Defines Trace(P) and Proof(P), line coverage LC(P)=|Trace(P)|/|N(P)| and proof line coverage PrLC(P,T)=|Proof(P)|/|N(P)|. The prototype translates a restricted loop-free C subset to SSA/SMT and marks a minimal unsat core. The paper adds non-trace conditions using undefined-variable metadata, states Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 that proof statements share one execution trace, and derives PrLC≤LC. A Siemens TCAS experiment found lines repeatedly execution-covered but never proof-covered; replacing the relevant if with result=0 left all tests outputs unchanged.

    - number: fan example LC=11/15≈0.69

Current encoding does not model short-circuit evaluation (sound but coverage may change), and scaling to larger datasets may be problematic. Theorem 1/PrLC≤LC rely on added non-trace conditions.

    - what: Defines a UPPAAL methodology for quantum protocol models: stabilizer-state locations for noiseless Clifford verification, and external C++ density-matrix functions plus statistical model checking for arbitrary noise and timing.     - title: HyPOLE: Hyperproperty-Guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observation
    - what: HyPOLE turns finite HyperLTL relational/temporal objectives into quantitative robustness rewards for value-based centralized training and decentralized execution. Universally quantified trace policies use local histories; existential traces use learned Skolem-witness/history representations, aided by a predictor of other agents’ state prefixes. Authors claim satisfaction-optimal policies under exact path reconstruction, optimal value learning and Individual–Global–Max factorization; simulations compare against shaped rewards across SMAC, MessySMAC and WildFire. The printed proof does not establish several required equivalences, recorded below. Complete witness/predictor construction, finite semantics, robustness equations, conditional theorem/proof chain, practical neural approximations, seven supplied tactic specifications, repeated-run performance and runtime overhead. Separates stronger semantic claims from the evidence and records concrete mismatches among path-consistency, logical satisfaction, maximum robustness, expected return and empirical pair frequency.

Policies map observation-action histories to fixed actions. The logic uses finite episodes, strong-next length checks and until before the shortest assigned trace ends. Each quantified trace variable ranges over behaviors of its corresponding policy, not automatically all possible executions of a deployed system (§§3–4). A hyperproperty relates several executions; HyperLTL quantifies trace variables then applies a temporal formula to their joint behavior. ∀∃ allows a later existential witness to depend on preceding universal traces, while ∀∀ requires all combinations to satisfy the inner body. This changes the requirement itself, not merely an algorithmic tuning parameter. Claims that ordinary shaped rewards are inherently universally quantified are authors’ framing, not an established general limitation of arbitrary reward design (§§1–3.2). The semantic objective in Figure 3 maximizes the probability that sampled trace sets satisfy a HyperLTL formula, with histories drawn from each policy and mapped to most-likely paths using Φ. The sample-set cardinality and probability measure are not fully specified. This is not a model-checking guarantee over all reachable traces or a statistical lower confidence bound on satisfaction (§4). Skolemization gives one trace function f_i for each existential quantifier, depending only on preceding universally quantified trace variables; with no preceding universal it is constant. An ordered union preserves variable indices; zip combines traces pointwise, truncated to the shortest prefix. The proof relies on witness traces being realizable under the corresponding policy and history map, not arbitrary unrelated traces (§5.1, Equations 1–3, Appendix C). Section 5.3 defines H(t) as histories whose selected most-likely path induces t, assumes H(t) nonempty and chooses Ω(t)=Sel(H(t)). The ideal existential policy consumes Ω(f_i(...)), requiring preceding universal paths. At decentralized execution these paths are unavailable, so the implementation predicts them from its local history and learns the composite Ω∘f_i using an RNN. No general finite-state synthesis or causal realizability algorithm for arbitrary trace Skolem functions is proved (§5.3, Appendix D.2). Training uses global state/other-agent information through CTDE, with local execution using VDN, QMIX or QTRAN utility decomposition. Independent Q-learning is evaluated only for universal formulas. IGM (Individual–Global–Max) means joint greedy maximizing actions equal the tuple of local greedy maximizing actions. Theorem 5.3 assumes an actually optimal joint Q satisfying IGM; it does not prove neural training reaches that optimum. General Q need not fit additive/monotone factorization (§5.3, Definition 5.2, Theorem 5.3). Theorem 5.1 author claim: path-consistent Φ and policy tuples optimizing the Skolemized formula also optimize original-formula satisfaction probability. Theorem 5.3 author claim: optimal IGM-compatible joint Q induces decentralized policies optimizing Skolemized satisfaction. Appendix A.2 adds a material premise absent from the theorem box: during execution f_enc-dec accurately reconstructs the universal trace prefixes needed by witnesses. No finite predictor-error, sample-complexity, failure-probability or convergence-rate guarantee is provided (§§5.2–5.3, Appendix A). Path reconstruction gap, reader inference: §4 defines path-consistency only as the true generating path belonging to argmax Φ(h,·). Appendix A.1 strengthens this to the selected argmax coinciding with that actual path. Membership does not ensure a unique maximizer or trace-equivalent ties. Two hidden states labeled p and ¬p with the same observation and constant Φ have both paths in argmax; any fixed selected path is wrong for one latent case. Exact reconstruction needs uniqueness or an appropriate equivalence/tie assumption; arbitrary partial observation does not supply it (PDF3,13). Robustness equivalence gap, reader inference: Figure 9 defines atomic robustness c−f(L(s)), with min/max for conjunction/disjunction/temporal aggregation, but §§5.2/C.2 and Appendix A.1 assert satisfaction iff robustness converges to ρmax. A satisfying predicate can have any positive margin below the global maximum: with c=1 and f=.9, a constant satisfying trace has robustness .1, not 1 if another reachable state has f=0. Maximizing margin is stronger than Boolean satisfaction; the paper supplies no normalization making every satisfying finite trace attain a common maximum. Thus the asserted equivalence is not established by Figure 9. Return-to-probability gap, reader inference: Appendix A.2 moves from expected discounted cumulative robustness to maximizing the probability of satisfying the formula (or reaching maximum robustness). IGM only preserves greedy decisions for the learned Q and cannot justify that objective change. One-step fully observed example: a safe action always yields predicate margin .1; a risky action yields margin 1 with probability .9 and −.1 with probability .1. Expected robustness favors risky (.89>.1), while Boolean satisfaction favors safe (1>.9). This uses the atomic Figure 9 semantics and demonstrates the missing equivalence; no artifact run. Horizon/discount and repeated prefix rewards can introduce additional preferences (§5.3, Appendix A.2). Sample-set versus pair-frequency mismatch, reader inference: Appendix B says three of four pairs satisfy its ∀∀ inner body and reports .75. Under §3.2’s universal trace-set semantics, a fixed set containing a violating pair fails the ∀∀ formula as a Boolean statement. A .75 uniformly sampled-pair frequency is a different probability, requiring an explicit distribution/sampling event. The example’s ∀∃ witness and all-pairs proportion illustrate useful dependencies but do not resolve the Figure 3 set-satisfaction probability definition (PDF3–4,14). Finite-semantics boundary qualification: Figure 9 evaluates always/eventually/until over [ℓ,k), although the path segment and pointwise zip are described with endpoints through k; strong-next is stated only for k>ℓ. Its empty-trace convention and final-position cases need an explicit consistent convention before building a verified monitor. The supplied text contains no machine-checked equivalence between its Boolean monitor and quantitative monitor (PDF3,5,16). Specifications are supplied manually in Appendix G. Focus-fire combines all allies being in range of a common enemy, enemy health decrease, increasing kill count and eventual victory. Medivac adds staying near the lowest-health ally and comparing allied/enemy health loss, with universal versus existential healer. Corridor holds a choke point until damage/kills/win. Defense always keeps enemies outside observation range and allies above a health threshold. The formula is a spatial/readiness condition and does not itself contain an explicit action predicate enforcing that attack description. The WildFire display also has duplicated dist( syntax. - REAL Ramsey elimination (2026)
    - title: Fast Ramsey Quantifier Elimination in LIRA (with applications to liveness checking)
    - what: Presents REAL (Ramsey Elimination for Arithmetic Logic), a solver-agnostic implementation eliminating Ramsey quantifiers from existential LIA, LRA, and LIRA formulas, with SMT-LIB extension and Alchemist translation from FASTer/Armoise reachability relations. The resulting existential formulas can be solved by standard SMT solvers to check liveness/termination. The paper defines the infinite-clique semantics and gives a worked arithmetic elimination argument using arithmetic progression witnesses. REAL adds SMT-LIB parsing/export, formula sharing and normalization, and compact Boolean/theory encodings. The FASTer pipeline verifies McCarthy91 termination and checks liveness of sliding-window, Lamport bakery, and cache-coherence protocols (SYNAPSE, Berkeley, Dragon, futurbus, MOESI). On eight pipeline benchmarks, REAL elimination/solving times and formula sizes are reported; parameterized integer/real families scale near-linearly in elimination, with solving dominating, and comparison to the prototype shows orders-of-magnitude speedups.

    - title: Realizability Is Not Enough: Encoding, Liveness, and Auditing of Synthesized Robot Supervisors
    - what: Builds an open-source ROS2/FlexBE pipeline that generates capability-based GR(1) specifications, performs well-separation analysis, synthesizes with slugs, audits explicit Mealy strategies, merges equivalent states with a proof, and emits executable HFSM supervisors. Four domains compare one-hot versus enumerated capability encodings and Fair-Outcome versus System-Goal liveness. Formalizes activation/outcome protocols and pending memory, explains how Fair-Outcome assumptions can be falsified by system-controlled retry bookkeeping, and introduces a post-synthesis explicit-state auditor. The auditor is sound and complete for protocol violations, deadlocks, bounded-failure violations and goal-unreachable SCC traps under completed exploration. A reducer is proven to preserve core capability output traces while explicitly documenting that pending propositions and full GR(1) winning status need not be preserved. Experiments expose ordering sensitivity and the gap between realizability, structural progress and executable deployment.

    - what: Reports Rocq mechanization of safety, deadlock freedom and liveness for a synchronous multiparty session calculus. Uses coinductive local/global type trees, process-oriented subtyping, plain-merge projection and association of local environments to balanced, well-formed, projectable global types. Operational correspondence plus induction on finite grafting contexts proves associated environments live on fair paths; session typing transfers guarantees to processes. Authors report about14K added Rocq lines, with public/archived source and classical choice/excluded-middle assumptions explicitly used in path construction. Records exact balancedness, well-formedness and projectability standing assumptions; asymmetric label matching under subtyping; environment versus session liveness quantifiers; mixed fixed-point path encoding; graft-height proof and its constructive_indefinite_description use; fair-session-path construction with excluded_middle_informative; stuck-recursion definition repair; precise output safety and synchronous reactive-semantics limits. Earlier record omitted axioms and conflated environment path guarantees with the existential session definition.
    - number: About 14K lines of Rocq
    - limits: Simple synchronous, rendezvous communication calculus, not asynchronous network queues. Guarded recursion, finite nonempty labeled branch sets, conditionals, sends/receives and inactive processes; values/expressions include bool/int/nat and nondeterministic choice. No crashes, Byzantine behavior, loss, timeout or network implementation are modeled. Subsorting is reflexive with nat≤int. Communication payloads are typed but do not encode arbitrary dependent data properties. Processes/sessions are inductive syntax, recursive variables encoded with natural indices; local/global types are possibly infinite coinductive trees corresponding to guarded recursive syntax. Continuations are lists of optional branches: label index k exists only for Some, not None/out-of-bounds. Raw Rocq constructors allow lists without valid branches; environment well-formedness tctx_wf imposes nonempty well-formed local trees. Participant maps use natural-number keys, disjoint domains for composition, and MMaps extensional equality M.Equal. Standing assumptions after Remark3.8: global types satisfy wfgC, encompassing inherited well-formedness/balancedness, and projectableA. Balancedness: for every subtree there is a finite depth k by which each participant in that subtree appears on every path long enough or ending. This is a structural protocol requirement, not scheduler fairness. Theorem5.8/6.9 concise statements suppress these standing conditions; arbitrary global trees or any collection of locally typed processes do not receive the theorem. Projection is coinductive plain merge. A participant at a root send/receive gets corresponding local branch; an uninvolved participant must project all continuations to the same local type. Absent participants project end. Stronger full merge is future work; projectability is assumed rather than proved for every global syntax. Process-oriented subtype may receive more labels and wider input sorts, or send fewer labels and narrower output sorts; continuations subtype coinductively. Association Γ⊑G requires every participant of G in Γ with Γ(p) subtype of its projection; any extra environment participant is absent or end. Local environments have individual send/receive readiness and synchronized reductions requiring compatible sorts. Global reduction permits root branch selection and disjoint communication in all branch continuations; printed GR-Ctx also requires both root participants in every continuation. Association is more than matching syntax, and must be preserved under reduction. Theorem4.8 soundness: if G can communicate between p/q under labelℓ, Γ can communicate between the same participants with possibly different labelℓprime, and both resulting objects remain associated. It does not simulate every exact global choice. Theorem4.9 completeness: each Γ synchronized step has the same-label G step preserving association. Counterexample in Remark4.10 has a sender restricted toℓ0 while the global type allowsℓ0/ℓ1. Calling this bidirectional same-label bisimulation would be inaccurate. Environment safety coinductively requires every mutually ready sender/receiver to synchronize using the sender label and compatible payload sorts, preserved under all synchronized reductions. It does not require a counterpart ready for every unilateral request; safety is distinct from progress. Example5.2 int sender/nat receiver is unsafe because int is not a subtype of nat. Associated environments satisfy Theorem5.3. Paths may be finite or infinite. Fairness Definition5.4: whenever synchronized pair(p,q) is enabled at positionn, some later communication of that same ordered pair occurs, possibly with a different label. It is pair fairness, not fairness of every branch label. Live paths require every unilateral send or receive request eventually gets its corresponding pair communication. An environment is live if every fair path from every reachable reduct is live. The universal condition is over fair paths only; unfair starvation schedules are excluded. Paco encodes coinductive predicates as greatest fixed points of parameterized inductive relations. Paths are cosequences with conil/cocons; eventual is inductive least fixed point, alwaysCG coinductive greatest fixed point. This avoids explicit index bookkeeping and Rocq native cofix guardedness limitations. These are proof representations, not a runtime scheduler or finite model checker. Balancedness supplies a finite p-grafting context containing no p, with holes beginning at p-related communication or end. Theorem5.8 first proves liveness for direct projections (actual Rocq uses equivalent global enabledness predicate), using height of p-grafting versus q-grafting as a decreasing induction measure until the pair becomes enabled, then fairness forces communication. Proof transfers to subtyped Γ by associating paths pointwise and preserving transition labels. Detailed grafting/projection definitions and inherited results are referred to [16]/[20]. Theorem5.8 path lifting extracts witnesses of Theorem4.9 from Prop to construct a CoFixpoint cosequence, explicitly using constructive_indefinite_description. Theorem6.9 additionally constructs a fair session path using constructive_indefinite_description and excluded_middle_informative. Thus reported machine checking has these logical assumptions; do not describe the whole development as axiom-free or constructive merely because it uses coinduction. Full artifact assumption audit/build was not performed. Reactive semantics folds finite internal conditional evaluation/recursion unfolding into communication transitions using an unfolding relation; no explicit τ-only LTS transitions. Structural congruence rearranges parallel composition/unit. This lets subject reduction match each session communication with exactly one same-label environment step, rather than a weak simulation with silent stuttering. Does not establish equivalence to arbitrary calculi with internal divergence or a concrete distributed runtime. Table2 session rule requires each component process be typed by an environment already associated with a suitable global type. Lemma6.1 preserves typing through unfolding. Theorem6.2 sends every session step to a same-label type step; Theorem6.3 permits a type step to be matched by a same-participant session/type step with potentially different label. Theorem6.5 explicitly guarantees the sender label belongs to the waiting receiver branch set in every reachable unfolded typed session. Theorem6.6 says a typed session either can communicate or every unfolding can further reach all-inactive processes, not global termination. Session liveness Definition6.7 is an existential continuation property at every reachable unfolded send/receive: from that unfolded state there exists a finite reduction sequence reaching the corresponding continuation. It is not syntactically the environment definition quantifying every fair path. Authors identify it as Padovani lock-freedom/lock-freedom under full fairness; Theorem6.9 proves it by choosing a fair session path, lifting it to a fair live environment path, then extracting a finite communication prefix. No bounded latency or unconditional all-schedules termination theorem is claimed. Remark6.8 repairs a prior liveness formulation that started its required continuation at the pre-unfolded state. In stuck sender µX.q!ℓ(0).X with q inactive, the original state coincides with the apparent post-send recursion, allowing zero steps to fake progress. Their definition starts at the unfolded pending-send state, excluding that example. This is a semantic definition correction, not a discovered bug in their checked theorem. Printed Table1 R-comm has p receiving from q but labels the communication(p,q), whereas Definition4.2 and environment/global send rules use(p,q) for p sending to q. Read literally this reverses the sender/receiver order and conflicts with same-label subject reduction for a one-way session. Likely presentation convention/typo; this reading has not checked artifact definitions and does not establish a Rocq inconsistency. Endpoint order should be checked before transcribing the rule into another verifier. Examples4.4/4.7/5.6 use G=p→q:{ℓ0(int).G,ℓ1(int).q→r:ℓ2(int).end}. The infiniteℓ0 path is fair under pair fairness, since p/q always communicate, but r waits forever. G is projectable and associated yet unbalanced. This is an explicit negative example outside standing balancedness, demonstrating why association alone is insufficient for liveness. The finiteℓ0,ℓ1,ℓ2 path terminates and is fair/live. Reported contribution around14K lines is added code on top of prior subject-reduction development [16], not necessarily whole artifact size. Proofs of subject reduction/deadlock freedom were rewritten for environment-based typing; operational correspondence, environment safety/liveness new. No checking-time, memory, theorem counts, admitted-proof count, dependency audit, industrial protocol benchmark or verified endpoint extraction measured here. Paper links GitHub omerskeskin/mpstlive and an SWH archive; reader has not built or audited artifact. First mechanization claims are author-qualified to their knowledge and not independently surveyed here. No completeness theorem saying every live session typable is provided. Fair termination is explicitly stronger; stronger liveness under instruction fairness or justness may require different global types/projection. Full merge, other calculi and weak simulation support are future work, not delivered extensions. Crash-stop/asynchronous association results mentioned are other work. Explicit declaration says no AI-generated text or code is present. This is authors stated provenance, not an independent audit. No Verus, Rust or TLA+ implementation delivered. - RustyDL: A Program Logic for Rust (2026)
    - what: Presents RustyDL, a source-level dynamic logic and sequent calculus for a safe Rust subset, plus a Rusty KeY prototype. The logic models ownership moves, shared and mutable references, arrays, integer overflow, loops and non-standard control flow directly over Rust compiler HIR, aiming to support inspectable human-in-the-loop proofs instead of translating to an intermediate language. RustyDL maps Rust primitive, array and reference types to logical sorts, uses mutating updates for mutable borrows, and treats moved values with fresh constants. Dynamic-logic box/diamond modalities express partial/total correctness; updates decompose deterministic state changes. Symbolic-execution rules split conditionals, model moves and borrow/deref/mutation operations, branch on debug-mode overflow versus panic, and check array bounds. Loop-scope rules record break/continue/return exits and permit invariants for Rust loops that compile to unconditional loops. The prototype implements taclets in KeY and demonstrates borrowing, loops, arrays, tuples and enums; a binary-search proof is reported.
    - number: 4,260 rule applications for binary-search proof in 2.1 s
    - number: safe-Rust subset; lifetimes, traits, iterators, pattern matching and generic functions deferred
    - limits: The logic focuses on safe Rust and assumes unsafe code is encapsulated and separately verified. It covers primitive values, shared/mutable references and arrays; structs/enums are analogous, while unions, smart pointers, traits, lifetimes and a fuller specification language remain future work. Rust programs are assumed deterministic; the Rust transition function is left abstract and rule soundness is described as relative to ongoing formal semantics. Integer rules target debug semantics and must prove absence of overflow. The KeY proof system is not foundational and relies on integer/sequence theories. Verification is a proof of concept with limited automation, not a mature benchmarked verifier.

- SA interval abstraction (2026)
    - title: Effective Stochastic Automata Model Checking by Interval Abstraction (extended version)
    - what: Presents a dedicated stochastic-automata model-checking method that abstracts continuous timer distributions into probability intervals and applies big-time-step semantics to construct an MDP. Value iteration returns lower and upper bounds on minimum and maximum reachability probabilities. The paper defines the abstraction and refinement process, extends Modest and Jani input support, and supplies a Rust prototype. Evaluation covers small stochastic automata, bounded M/M/1/100 and Weibull/Erlang queues, and file-server models compared with mcsta’s STA digital-clocks approach. The study reports how interval granularity affects accuracy, state-space size and runtime.
    - number: M1 at pI=0.01: result [0.245, 0.755], 82,657 MDP states, 1.6 s
    - number: M5: result [0.117, 0.883], 260,395 states, 20.6 s
    - number: queue 150/200 jobs: M/M/1 total runtime 95.0/143.8 s; Weibull total runtime 96.8/137.4 s
    - number: queue abstractions have 2,229,270–3,334,270 MDP states
    - limits: The abstraction produces bounds whose tightness depends on per-interval probability and interval generation; smaller intervals can cause large MDPs. The queue experiments use finite buffers and bounded arrival counts, and the file-server model replaces continuous nondeterminism and an initially uniform queue with specific distributions/empty-queue initialization. The implementation is a prototype; exponential interval choices can be much slower and run out of memory, and future work includes deterministic delays and time-bounded properties.

- Schirrmacher et al. FO+dp (2026)
    - title: Model Checking Disjoint-Paths Logic on Topological-Minor-Free Graph Classes
    - what: Proves an algorithmic meta-theorem: model checking first-order logic extended with vertex-disjoint-path predicates is fixed-parameter tractable on graph classes excluding a fixed graph as a topological minor, with runtime f(H,phi)*n^3 and a witness tuple when the formula is true. Proof strategy decomposes graphs into strongly unbreakable tree decompositions, collapses FO+dp predicates to FO on unbreakable regions containing large clique minors, computes bounded-size folio/type-preserving representatives for boundaried subgraphs, proves compositionality under gluing, and runs a bottom-up dynamic program. The collapse uses generic folio and partition-linkedness lemmas; replacement preserves topological-minor exclusion, unbreakability, and annotated types. The result improves the earlier minor-free theorem and yields O(f(k)n^3) applications such as F-Topological Minor Deletion when a large clique certifies a no-instance.
    - number: f(H,phi)*n^3
    - number: O(f(k)*n^3) F-Topological Minor Deletion
    - number: q(k) in 2^{O(k)} decomposition bound
    - number: extended folio representative size computable
    - limits: Assumes a finite colored graph and an excluded fixed topological minor H; the parameter dependence f(H,phi) is computable but can be very large. The algorithm is uniform and does not need H as input, although runtime depends on it. It handles subgraph-closed topological-minor-free classes; dense non-subgraph-closed classes and constant-time postprocessing queries remain open. The dynamic program relies on deep decomposition, irrelevant-vertex, folio, and bounded-treewidth machinery; no implementation benchmark is reported.

- Schwarzweller GALOIS_4 finite correspondence 2026 (2026)
    - title: The Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory
    - what: Schwarzweller completes a Mizar series formalizing the finite Galois correspondence. Intermediate fields K correspond bijectively and with reversed containment to subgroups Aut(E,K); the inverse sends a subgroup to its fixed field. The article proves degree/order/index formulas, isomorphism–conjugacy equivalence, normality criteria and a restriction quotient theorem. It also shows that the two maps exchange joins and meets for binary and nonempty families. Records the finite-Galois guard, the extension-of-isomorphisms dependency, distinct assumptions for defining restriction versus proving it onto, and nonempty-family scope. Distinguishes normality of K/F from E/K being Galois, and generated lattice joins from set unions. Separates this culmination of imported results from an independently rerun artifact or comparison with Lean.
    - limits: MML GALOIS_4 version 8.1.15 5.100.1509 identifies the article. The Introduction calls it the last of five articles and cites earlier Mizar field extensions, simple extensions and splitting-field work. It points to a similar Lean development but offers no measured comparison of proofs, automation or checker performance (pp.9,16). Results 1–3 characterize a normal subgroup by conjugation invariance and, for strict subgroup H, by being a homomorphism kernel. Definition 1 packages subgroup index as a cardinal; Definition 2 packages conjugacy for groups that are subgroups of the ambient group. These representation/strictness guards are retained rather than identifying arbitrary isomorphic subgroup records literally (p.10). Definitions 3/4 form h(K) as the induced subfield on the range of h restricted to carrier K. For finite E/F and normal intermediate K/F, results 4–6 make each F-fixing E-automorphism restrict to an F-fixing K-automorphism, preserve composition under restriction, and stabilize K as a field. Result 7 gives a fixed-field inclusion. Normality and finite-extension premises are explicit, not assumed for all intermediate fields (p.11). Result 8 uses a normal extension represented as a simple algebraic adjunction to identify it as a splitting field of the generator’s minimal polynomial. Result 9, for finite Galois E/F, extends any F-fixing isomorphism K1→K2 between intermediate fields to an F-fixing E-automorphism. Its sketch chooses a primitive generator and invokes splitting-field extension results. The imported extension-equivalence symbol and proofs of those dependencies were not independently audited (pp.11–12). Results 10/11 transport fixing groups and fixed fields under an automorphism using the corresponding conjugate subgroup; their inverse/conjugation order depends on the imported convention. The record uses these as stated, without silently treating conjugated subgroups as equal or an F-isomorphism of fields as literal field equality (p.12). Results 12/13 identify the existing maps Ψ_E(K)=Aut(E,K) and Φ_E(G)=Fix(E,G). Under finite Galois E/F, 14–16 make them inverse bijections; 17/18 recover every intermediate field/subgroup by applying both maps; 19/20 give reversed containment in both directions. The correspondence is over intermediate fields inside this E and subgroups of Aut(E,F), not over all abstract fields/groups (pp.12–13). Result 21 gives [E:K]=|Aut(E,K)| and [K:F]=[Aut(E,F):Aut(E,K)]. Result 22 equates F-isomorphism of K1,K2 with conjugacy of their fixing subgroups in Aut(E,F), using 9,17,11. Isomorphism does not force the intermediate fields to coincide in general; nor does subgroup equality mean merely equal order (p.13). For every intermediate K of a finite Galois E/F, 23 says E/K is Galois. Result 24 says K/F is Galois iff K/F is normal; separability comes from the enclosing finite Galois setting. Results 25/26 equate this normality with invariance under every F-fixing E-automorphism and with Aut(E,K) normal in Aut(E,F). It would be wrong to infer every K/F is Galois merely because E/K always is (p.13). Definition 5 defines the restriction homomorphism ρ(K):Aut(E,F)→Aut(K,F) for finite E/F and normal K/F, without requiring E/F Galois. Results 27/28 give the associated fixed-field inclusion and kernel Aut(E,K). Surjectivity in 29 adds finite Galois E/F. Result 30 therefore obtains Aut(K,F) isomorphic to Aut(E,F)/H when H=Aut(E,K) is normal, using 26,28,29 (p.13). Results 31/32 give binary field/subgroup lattice inclusions for arbitrary extensions. Under finite Galois E/F, 33/34 upgrade them to equalities: field meet becomes subgroup join, field join becomes subgroup intersection, and fixed fields exchange the analogous operations. Join means the smallest containing field/subgroup, generally not the set union; a union of two subgroups may not even be a subgroup (p.14). Definitions 6/7 collect the pointwise Ψ/Φ images of nonempty families; 35/36 identify those image families explicitly. Results 37/38 recover a family by both maps under finite Galois E/F. Results 39/40 give general-extension lattice inclusions; 41/42 give equality and reversal for nonempty families in the finite Galois case. The article’s printed square union/intersection notation and raw extraction S/T must be read as lattice join/meet, consistent with its Introduction, not arbitrary set operations (pp.10,14–15). The family theorems explicitly require nonempty M. Empty-family top/bottom conventions are not handled by their printed statements. In 42, M is a family of subgroups of Aut(E,F), not a mere subset of individual automorphisms; the Introduction’s shorthand wording is less precise than the typed theorem (pp.10,14–15). Reading example, not printed: E=Q(sqrt2,sqrt3), F=Q has group C2×C2. For K=Q(sqrt2), its fixing subgroup consists of identity and the sign change of sqrt3; [E:K]=2 and [K:F]=2 match order and index. K1=Q(sqrt2), K2=Q(sqrt3) have meet Q and join E, while their order-2 fixing subgroups generate the full group and intersect in identity. Every subgroup is normal, so these quadratic intermediate extensions satisfy the quotient conclusion. Reading scope check, not printed: E=Q(cuberoot2) is finite but not normal over Q and has only the identity Q-automorphism. Its full fixed field is E, not Q, so the recovery identity 17 cannot be generalized to every finite extension. The article does not state the infinite-Galois correspondence or its topology/closed-subgroup qualifications. All eight pages, seven definitions, 42 results with every clause and supplied sketches, registrations, 15 references and dates read; both sheets and enlarged p.15 inspected. Quotations are exact plaintext excerpts, with separately labelled visual transcriptions for lattice formulas damaged by extraction. This reading did not execute formal artifacts. The paper reports no proof time/size, empirical or automation benchmark, and no distributed/Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM-agent experiment.

- Second-Order Hyperproperty Complexity (2026)
    - title: Complexity of Model Checking Second-Order Hyperproperties on Finite Structures
    - what: Analyzes Hyper2LTL model checking on finite tree-shaped and acyclic structures and its Fixpoint Hyper2LTLfp fragment, proving decidability and tight complexity bounds. The paper proves PSPACE-completeness on trees and EXPSPACE-completeness on acyclic models for unrestricted Hyper2LTL, while the fixpoint fragment is P-complete on trees and EXP-complete on acyclic models. It also gives alternation hierarchy results and combined-complexity bounds, motivating the fragment for monitoring growing trace sets.

- Securing the Foundations of an Intermediate Language for Probabilistic Program Verification (2026)
    - what: Formalizes in Lean/mathlib a chain from probability spaces for discrete-time Markov chains through optimal expected costs of MDPs and sound expectation calculi to correctness of HeyVL encodings for probabilistic programs. Covers unbounded loops,nondeterminism,resource ticks and failed observations. Adds a fault-tolerant calculus to establish liberal-preexpectation soundness with conditioning,and idle k-(co)induction that preserves values of variables unmodified by the loop. Provides a deep embedded verification-condition generator and a small interactive proof case. This is foundational encoding/logic verification,not end-to-end verification of the production Caesar implementation or a new distributed-protocol case study. Theorem3 constructs a probability measure over infinite valid paths with cylinder probabilities equal to finite transition products; reconciles textbook path cylinders with mathlib measure cylinders via successor-of-finite-path spaces,Ionescu-Tulcea and pushforward. History-dependent deterministic schedulers induce Markov chains whose states are paths. Expected nonnegative extended-real cost is a supremum of finite-horizon path sums. Theorem12 gives angelic/maximizing Bellman least-fixed-point equality generally; Theorem19 gives demonic/minimizing equality for finitely branching MDPs by constructing an optimal memoryless scheduler,avoiding an unjustified interchange of infimum and supremum. pGCL has dependent typed states and shallow function-valued expressions inside a deep program syntax; small-step rules lead to a sink-extended operational MDP. The soundness recipe sandwiches an expectation transformer against a higher-order Bellman least fixed point. wp includes tick costs and a least loop fixed point; wlp uses one-bounded expectations,a greatest loop fixed point and ignores ticks. wfp uses least loop fixed points and counts failed observations; complementing expectations and swapping the nondeterminism optimization relates it to wlp. Conditional expectation is defined as wp/wlp(1),rather than a compositional transformer. Idle induction checks states agreeing with the initial values of all unmodified variables. HeyLo is deeply embedded with Nat,ENNReal,Bool variable types; HeyVL is loop-free and its computable vp produces formulas. Syntax-level spGCL loops carry invariants. Encoded wp overapproximates wp; encoded wlp underapproximates wlp. Assuming a candidate bound,encoding the program and asserting the postexpectation yields a sound bound when the VC is valid. Loop encodings use modified-variable havoc and validate,with dual operations for upper bounds.

- Simplicial Actions for Distributed Protocols (2026)
    - what: # Simplicial Actions for Distributed Protocols (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Philip Sink represents distributed communication steps as actions on simplicial models of knowledge and belief. The main contribution is a mathematical representation, with worked examples and six claimed structural results. It is not an implemented verifier or an experimental comparison. Some universal protocol claims need qualifications: the printed proofs do not establish that every input perspective has an output, and the revision proof confuses one preimage with all preimages. Concrete reader counterexamples are given below, separately from the author's claims.  This read covers arXiv:2608.16881v1, 17 August 2026: all 31 pages, 24 references, 37 figures, definitions and all proofs in §8. All page renders were inspected through eight contact sheets; pages 2,16,20,29,30,31 were additionally viewed at full size. The official and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. The only PDF hyperlink is its arXiv page. No implementation or supplementary artifact is claimed here; simulation is explicitly future work.  ## Definitions and intended results  A node is an agent's local perspective; its color identifies the agent. A face is a compatible set of perspectives, and a facet is a maximal such face. The paper assumes uniquely colored facets (UCF): every facet has exactly one node per agent. Node assignments give each propositional atom one of three values: true, false or unspecified. A global facet is propositionally consistent. Knowledge quantifies over facets sharing the agent's node. Belief instead quantifies over an agent-specific subcomplex, permitting a false view of the world (§2). If no considered facet shares a node, the universal belief condition can hold vacuously; seriality is not separately imposed.  The protocol definition uses an input complex, an output complex and an execution map from input faces to collections of output faces (§3, Definition 3.1). It requires monotonicity, preservation of intersections, equality of the input and output color sets, and coverage of the output by the execution map. Those are structural representation conditions, not agreement, termination, validity or resilience specifications for a consensus implementation.  Section 4 first explains ordinary Kripke action models. Output worlds are compatible input/action pairs; accessibility intersects the input and action relations. It then translates message sending, uncertain receipt and an uninformed third party into that setting. Its first alternating-message construction deliberately fails on the second step because it lacks the persistent sender/receiver state needed to stop after a lost message. This motivates postconditions in the simplicial construction.  A simplicial action carries colored action nodes, literal preconditions and postconditions (§5, Definition 5.1). Mode3, the chosen compatibility rule, rejects explicit contradictions but allows an unspecified input value to be filled by a precondition. A postcondition overrides an input value; otherwise the precondition fills an unspecified value, and an existing specified input value survives. The paper restricts preconditions and postconditions to atomic information/literal assignments. General non-atomic and modal conditions are not implemented by this definition.  For knowledge, an output facet consists of compatible same-color input/action pairs whose two projections are input and action facets and whose updated assignments are consistent. Theorem 5.1, proved as 8.1, shows that every admitted output facet retains UCF. Its argument uses full projected facets and injective coloring; it does not establish nonempty output or survival of every input node. Theorem 5.2/8.2 claims the resulting execution map `Ξ(F)={X in I[A] | π0(X) subset F}` always forms a protocol. Monotonicity, intersection preservation and output coverage follow directly for this map, but the printed equality-of-colors claim has the missing-survival condition described below.  Belief updates use one facet family and execution map per agent (§5.2, Definitions 5.2–5.3). Theorems 5.3/8.3 and 5.4/8.4 repeat UCF preservation and the protocol claim. The belief protocol preserves only the relevant agent's projected intersections. Color preservation still requires equality of all colors for each input face; the same survival issue applies.  Revision changes which facets are retained (Definition 5.4). For each full input/action product facet X, `R_a(X)` chooses consistent candidates Y that preserve the a-colored node and maximize the number of nodes retained from X. Ties are all retained. Candidates need an action-facet projection but need not have a facet projection in the agent's original belief complex. That permits belief change. Theorem 5.5/8.5 establishes UCF by restricting candidates to UCF facets. Theorem 5.6/8.6 claims a belief protocol for an execution map requiring **every** preimage of an output face to project inside the input face. This universal condition is material to the proof problem below.  ## Concrete protocol cases  The two-agent alternating-message protocol starts with private bits and uncertainty about the other bit (§§3–5.1). One designated sender sends its true bit; after successful receipt the roles switch. A lost message stops further sending. The final action has ten perspectives. S and R flags distinguish sending, receiving and an inactive state, and postconditions change those flags. A central edge preserves inactivity. The paper gives one- and two-step outputs and an induction describing a square with four extending alternating-color strings. The sender differs between the preliminary examples; the construction is symmetric, so that is not a contradiction.  The layered-message protocol is synchronous: both agents send each interval, at most one fails in an interval, and agents stop after observing failure. A six-perspective restricted action assumes a=0,b=1; stitching four bit combinations yields a sixteen-perspective action (§5.1, Figures 22–29). Additional bit preconditions/postconditions prevent receiving a bit and later its opposite. The author acknowledges that these constraints seem overly restrictive and leaves a better encoding open. The text's side-length formulas disagree: it prints `2n-1`, then assumes `2(n+1)` in the induction. Visually, the initial square has one edge per side, the one-step output three, and the two-step output five. With n counting completed steps, those drawings have `2n+1` edges or `2(n+1)` vertices per side. No formula was silently repaired.  Both examples also conflict with the printed consistency rule. Section 2,p2 requires jointly consistent assignments across every facet; §5,p11 repeats that no atom may be true at one node and false at another. Yet §5.1,p13 assigns b the shared flags “S and ¬R” and a “¬S and R”. Every displayed alternating input edge therefore contains S/¬S and R/¬R; its action edges likewise mix contradictory flags. They are not facets of the stipulated maximal complex. For the layered output, Figure 24,p16 joins `(a,5)(¬Pa,¬S)` to `(b,4)(¬Pa,Pb,S)`; that outer edge, and the other end's outer edge, are excluded by Definition 5.1's consistency requirement. Thus the drawings and their induction are intended constructions, not established instances under the printed literal assignments. Agent-specific flags S_a/R_a and S_b/R_b might repair this, but the paper does not supply that encoding. Footnote1,p3's remark about lifting examples to local variables does not define it. This reader observation survives the injective-color correction below.  A three-agent belief example models a sending its bit to b with possible loss while c falsely believes nothing was sent (Figures 30–31). Adding two facets to c's action complex changes that to uncertainty among successful sending, failed sending and no sending. This illustrates belief-state modeling, not an empirical advantage of revision.  The final example compares a→b→c→a communication with a broadcasting to b and c (§6, Figures 32–37). In the cited structure-aware, known-message setting, the cyclic protocol complex remains connected while broadcast separates the two possible decision values. It illustrates a topological obstacle and a successful broadcast case under those assumptions. It is not a general consensus solution under asynchronous loss, Byzantine faults or hidden schedules. The paper explicitly leaves complete representation of the distributed local model and the scope of action-model expressiveness unresolved.  ## Reader checks of the universal claims  These are hand-derived observations about the printed definitions and proofs. No solver, prover, model checker or author implementation was run. The flag-consistency problem above concerns the printed encodings of the examples; the following witnesses concern universal structural claims.  First, the maximal-complex formula on page2 prints `forall u,v in x: V(u) != V(v)` without restricting u and v to distinct nodes. Taken literally, u=v makes every nonempty witness x impossible. The preceding UCF definition correctly states injectivity: equal colors imply equal nodes. The following counterexamples use that intended injective-color reading; otherwise the printed foundational formula already fails to describe its examples.  Second, compatible actions need not cover every input perspective. Take one agent a and atom p. Let the input have two singleton facets `{x0}` and `{x1}`, with p false at x0 and true at x1. Let the action have one a-colored node y requiring p, with no postcondition. Both structures satisfy intended UCF. The update is nonempty but contains only `(x1,y)`. The execution map at `{x0}` has no nonempty output face. Its input color set is `{a}` and its output color set is empty, contradicting Definition 3.1's equality. Theorem 8.2's singleton proof starts “if X ∈ Ξ({n})” and shows the color of an existing output; it does not prove an output exists. Taking all agent-specific belief complexes equal gives the same issue for Theorem 8.4. An applicability/coverage assumption or a weaker definition is needed before accepting these universal statements.  Third, the revision map's output-coverage proof uses one preimage where its definition quantifies over all. On page31 it selects `X'` from the inverse relation, observes that `π0(X')` is an input face, and concludes `X ∈ Ξ_a,BR(π0(X'))`. A different preimage may project outside that face. The following finite example demonstrates this problem under the intended inherited-color interpretation of product preimages.  Let agents be a,b, with nodes u colored a and v1,v2,v3 colored b. Atom p is unspecified at u, false at v1 and v2, and true at v3. Let the global complex S have all three facets `{u,vi}`. Let a's belief complex have just `{u,v1}` and `{u,v2}`; b's can be S. Let the action have the single facet `{α,β}`, with colors a,b, p unspecified at α, p true at β, and no postconditions. Both action belief complexes contain that facet. All stated consistency and UCF conditions hold under the intended coloring convention.  The compatible output node set is `{(u,α),(v3,β)}`. For a, the raw product facets are `X1={(u,α),(v1,β)}` and `X2={(u,α),(v2,β)}`. Each has the unique consistent replacement `Y={(u,α),(v3,β)}`: it retains the a-node and the maximum possible overlap, one node. Consequently a's revised complex has facet Y and both X1 and X2 are preimages of Y. For Y to belong to `Ξ_a,BR(F)`, F must contain both `{u,v1}` and `{u,v2}`. No face of a's input complex does. Thus Y belongs to the revised output but to no execution-map image, contradicting the output-coverage requirement. At input face `{u,v1}`, the a-singleton survives, but the b-singleton has preimages through both v1 and v2 and is excluded. The output therefore loses color b. This is a reader counterexample to the universal claim as interpreted, not a machine-checked theorem.  There is a typing ambiguity here too: the inverse-face definition applies `V[A]BR` to raw product preimages that may lie outside `N[A]BR`. The natural extension assigns a product pair its input color, as the proofs implicitly do. Without that extension the inverse definition is not fully typed; with it the example above applies. The record does not assume an unprinted alternative inverse or execution map that could repair the theorem.  Other presentational problems include using facet projections on general faces/sets without fully spelling out their extension, leaving `L(x)` instead of `L(x)(P)` in a scalar assignment branch, and inconsistent figure references in the cycle-versus-broadcast discussion. These should not be confused with the substantive existence and universal-preimage issues. UCF preservation of admitted facets remains distinct from these stronger protocol claims.  ## Evaluation, limitations and contribution  The evidence is mathematical definitions, paper proofs and small worked diagrams. There are no runtime, memory, scalability, proof-effort or protocol-success measurements, no mechanized proof artifact inspected, and no implemented simulation reported. Section 6 proposes testing larger models; §7 says implementation and controlled comparisons with/without revision are future work. The author asks: “Firstly, does belief revision actually help with fault tolerance? If so, how? In what contexts?” (§7, p27). Forthcoming NASA gossip-protocol work is mentioned but not supplied or evaluated in this paper.  The direct contribution to distributed-system verification is a reusable representation of communication and uncertainty, including incorrect beliefs, and the separation of a repeated action from its input state. It does not verify a production protocol or establish revision-based resilience. The record preserves the claimed structural theorems with the reader's explicit qualifications. There is no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM proof-generation evaluation. Using these constructions as specifications for such tools would require an explicit semantics translation, fixed task properties and repaired structural assumptions; that is a reader inference, not a reported result.

- Spatiotemporal robustness for STL (2026)
    - title: Spatiotemporal Robustness of Temporal Logic Tasks Using Multi-Objective Reasoning
    - what: Defines spatiotemporal robustness (STR) for discrete-time temporal-logic tasks as the Pareto-maximal set of jointly admissible spatial and temporal perturbation magnitudes. It gives sound under-approximating robust semantics with min/max operations over Pareto sets, predicate-level algorithms and case studies for fighter-jet and robotaxi trajectories. STR treats spatial noise and asynchronous per-signal time shifts as separate objectives; a scalar pair of independent robustness values can be unsound. For STL in positive-normal form, robust semantics recursively combine predicate STR using downward-closure min/max. Theorem 1 proves every robust-semantic point is dominated by a true STR point, yielding sound task satisfaction but conservative margins. Predicate STR is reformulated as a monotone worst-case-margin constraint; Algorithm 1 scans temporal shells and solves robust spatial optimization, with a signed-distance shortcut from 1-Lipschitzness. Algorithm 2 propagates Pareto envelopes through parse trees.
    - number: F-16 path length 1848; temporal perturbation up to 50 and spatial Gaussian variance [100,100,10] in illustration
    - number: F-16 predicate runtimes: avoidance 53.23 s, threat 2.91 s, climb 13.62 s; conjunction 0.0001 s
    - number: robotaxi runtimes 0.67 s (vehicle+pedestrian) and 0.03 s (fixed pedestrian)
    - number: F-16 limiting subformula changes at temporal budget ΔT=30
    - limits: Signals are discrete-time and nominal; temporal perturbations are integer vectors and spatial budget uses the infinity signal norm. The robust semantics require STL positive-normal syntax and can under-approximate true STR. General predicate functions induce nonconvex/bilevel optimization; complexity grows with signal dimension and temporal horizon. Signed-distance results assume closed sets (tight for convex sets). Case studies are illustrative and use finite traces, not closed-loop dynamical guarantees.

- Structural Liveness of Conservative Petri Nets (2026)
    - what: Proves EXPSPACE-completeness of structural liveness for conservative and structurally bounded Petri nets, with doubly-exponential bounds on minimal live markings. The paper models Petri nets as action vectors and develops a proof chain: reversible virtual reachability is represented by bounded linear systems; conservative, structurally bounded and live-bottom-SCC properties are related; dead markings are represented by disjunctions of bounded restricted markings; quasi-dead markings and extractor cases reduce non-liveness to linear-system constraints. Small-solution theorems then yield a 2-exp bound on a live marking, enabling an exponential-space nondeterministic algorithm. A strengthened EXPSPACE lower bound completes hardness for conservative nets and transfers it to structurally bounded nets. The proof extends integer-solution bounds with divisibility constraints.
    - number: The complexity result is theorem-based; no runtime data or benchmark suite.
    - number: Linear-system dimension in the construction is d·2^d; solution norms are bounded by (2+||A||)^{2^{poly(d)}}.
    - number: The upper-bound algorithm guesses a binary-encoded live marking and checks liveness in polynomial space in that encoding.
    - limits: Results concern standard finite-dimensional Petri nets with nonnegative markings and conservative/structurally bounded subclasses; general structural liveness complexity remains open. Bounds are doubly exponential and not practical algorithms. Several technical ingredients are cited from prior work (Rackoff/Leroux), and the proof uses virtual reachability, reversibility and large-component extractors. No implementation or experimental evaluation is reported.

    - what: Defines a quantified SMT/BMC encoding that synthesizes fixed absolute-time update schedules for safety-critical timed systems modeled as two-player timed games.     - what: Reports a Rocq implementation and soundness/completeness proof for checking rational piecewise-affine feed-forward neural networks against finite-arity universal relational specifications. Reduces a network plus hyperproperty to a joint piecewise-affine function, enumerates affine segments and searches each segment for a negative satisfaction value by a verified mixed-strictness Fourier–Motzkin solver.
