Printed solver theorem and robustness example contain concrete inconsistencies, which this record separates from uninspected artifact correctness. A computational real-subset interface and reduced-rational dependent type support evaluation while retaining embeddings into reals. Total piecewise-affine functions prevent partial-domain gaps from vacuously proving network properties. The formal specification restricts input preconditions to a convex polyhedron and both generator/satisfaction maps to total piecewise-affine functions. A specification-equivalence proof guards manual encoding, then verified decomposition, segment splitting and strict-negative feasibility compose into the final boolean iff theorem. Prototype limits and differing GitHub/evaluated-artifact content are explicit.
    - limits: Targets feed-forward, finite piecewise-affine networks with rational arithmetic, exemplified by affine Linear and elementwise ReLU layers. It does not support arbitrary sigmoid/nonlinear activations, recurrent cycles, training correctness or deployed floating-point/parallel semantics. The formal interface generalizes to ordered real subsets with suitable operations; its computable exact solver requires division. Exact mathematical soundness does not remove a mismatch with finite-precision inference. RealSubsetOAM packages an embedding into real numbers preserving order, addition and multiplication; Coquelicot algebra/matrix support is extended around it. QDEP is the dependent subtype of rationals fixed by rational reduction, removing multiple representatives. The authors explicitly assume proof irrelevance to identify equal reduced-rational values under standard Rocq equality. Rationals with division support FME; merely being an integer subset is not enough for the solver’s division interface. AffineSegment pairs a convex polyhedron with an affine map. Segments can be partial and domain membership is tested. Total piecewise-affine functions (TPWAFs) have composition/concatenation preserving totality. Neural-network affine decomposition returns a total function. Segments can overlap at activation boundaries; a function representation must agree there, not count each segment as a distinct execution. The supported hyperproperties quantify universally over finitely many executions of the same deterministic network. Arity r is fixed in the specification. This is a finite-input/output relational class, not arbitrary temporal hyperlogic, probabilistic fairness or infinite-trace properties. The paper uses monotonicity, robustness and individual fairness as examples of this class; only monotonicity and one-dimensional robustness receive worked formal encodings. Informal NNDH uses input tuples X generated from W by netIn and output acceptance netSat>=0. Formal NNHyperproperty narrows W to a convex polyhedron, netIn to a total piecewise-affine generator and netSat to a scalar total piecewise-affine map over the restricted real subset. Thus not every mathematical relation or arbitrary precondition is accepted. Rational instances quantify through the chosen representation/embedding; no theorem about floating-point inputs is supplied. Specifications are manually translated into the framework. The recommended method first writes a natural predicate and proves equivalence to the encoded hyperproperty. Monotonicity1d uses r=w=2, precondition x1<=x2, identity generator and affine netSat=y2−y1; the paper displays monotonicity_1d_correct. This protects the property encoding when the equivalence is proved, but the prover does not infer the human’s intended specification. joint_pwaf composes netSat with concatenated netIn and r copies of the network composed with netIn. Because concatenation takes separate inputs, evaluation duplicates x as colvec_concat x x, explaining the 2w segment input dimensions. The network-to-piecewise semantics theorem asd_preserves_satisfiability connects this construction to natural network satisfaction. Partial pwaf_eval None is treated as True; using total network/generator/satisfaction components is essential to avoid certifying an undefined input. Segment splitting universally requires satisfaction on each segment under W. Linear constraints combine W, segment domain and strict violation of the required nonnegative scalar output. Feasibility gives a counterexample; infeasibility for every segment proves the universal property. A zero satisfaction value is allowed, so the negated output condition is strictly<0 rather than<=0. Mixed strict/non-strict inequality support is therefore a correctness requirement. Fourier–Motzkin solver returns Some assignment when feasible and None when infeasible according to the intended algorithm and subsequent equivalence theorem. Reader visually confirmed that displayed fme_correct on p.494 instead says None => exists sol,is_linear_system_solution sys sol, missing negation. Both printed branches assert feasibility. This cannot be the claimed correct theorem for an inconsistent system such as0<0; record it as a printed theorem defect. Artifact proof may differ and was not inspected. The final verify_hyperporperty_correct states boolean true iff nn_satisfies_nndh, composing decomposition, split and linear-system correctness. The counterexample interface returns a solver assignment on first failing segment; None across the finite list yields boolean true. Correctness is author-reported machine formalization, not established here by executing the shown code. Some displayed type parameters/dimensions and theorem names are abbreviated or inconsistent; this record does not treat the printed snippets as a compilable standalone artifact. Robustness predicate on p.496 has parameter order (epsilon,delta), and requires |x1−x2|<=delta implies |N(x1)−N(x2)|<=epsilon. For fixed epsilon, robustness is downward closed in delta. The prose on p.497 claims robust for delta=.096,epsilon=.1 but not for smaller delta=.0959,epsilon=.1, which contradicts that order property. The theorem calls actually supply first arguments .096/.0959 and second .1, so they instead vary epsilon with delta=.1; the prose swaps meanings. The displayed example_not_robust2 statement on p.498 also omits negation before is_robust_1d, while its proof starts by introducing the positive property and deriving contradiction. That script shape proves a negated proposition. These are source presentation defects, not reader evidence that the kernel accepted contradictory proofs. Reader Figure3 check after independent visual review: the middle output weight is −.3. The network is ReLU(.66 ReLU(−x+.1)−.3 ReLU(x+.25)+.99 ReLU(.7x)+.1). Its four slopes on regions divided at−.25,0,.1 are−.66,−.96,−.267,.393, and its outer ReLU stays positive. Hence it is globally .96-Lipschitz, consistent with the positive call epsilon=.096,delta=.1. Inputs−.2 and−.1 produce .283 and .187, differing exactly .096; this refutes epsilon=.0959,delta=.1. These are exact reader calculations, not artifact execution. The earlier record misread the negative weight and has been corrected. Robustness encoding uses two halfspaces for |x1−x2|<=delta and a two-segment output absolute-value function; the paper reports equivalence to is_robust_1d. Robustness example was added during two-stage review after artifact evaluation. GitHub includes it, but peer-evaluated Zenodo artifact explicitly does not. It must not be described as checked in the evaluated artifact or as evidence that all published snippets compiled. Authors give O(2^n) network segments for n ReLU activations, O(n) constraints per segment, and O(2^(nr)) systems of O(rn) constraints when r network copies are combined. These estimates suppress complexity contributed by netIn/netSat and W, so should be read for fixed/simple specifications. FME has exponential elimination blow-up; no polynomial-time performance claim is made for the full prover. Replacement by a polynomial linear-feasibility solver is future work. Runtime evaluation uses nine positive-weight networks with1–9 activations, at most3layers, weights sampled in[1,2], biases in[0,1], rounded to3decimals to ensure monotonicity. Each monotonicity check repeats5times. This is a synthetic guaranteed-positive benchmark, not a diverse trained-network suite, hyperproperty variety study or adversarial/counterexample evaluation. No comparison with state-of-the-art solver timings is provided; authors acknowledge slower performance. Hardware is32GB RAM and Intel Core Ultra7 155H at3.80GHz. The figure plots mean seconds on a log scale, rising from roughly10^-3 at one ReLU to roughly10^3 at nine. Values are graphical orders of magnitude, not exact spreadsheet measurements. Ten or more activations take over an hour and often exhaust Rocq memory. Raw data.xlsx, software version/OS, precise seeds, error bars and per-run values were not inspected or specified in the paper. FME formalization exceeds3000 Rocq lines; no total-development size, labor time, proof-acceptance rate or formal trust audit is reported. Proof scripts demonstrate rewriting semantic equivalences then vm_compute/reflexivity for a small monotonicity example. This is executable decision-procedure automation inside Rocq, not an LLM proof agent or empirical theorem-proving model evaluation. Artifact locations are https://github.com/verinncoq/rocq-nn-roll-prototype and DOI10.5281/zenodo.19798155. A prior verified ONNX converter is cited as an import path; its theorem, parser coverage and correspondence to inference engines were not independently inspected. Rocq kernel, real-number assumptions, proof irrelevance, imported libraries and any extraction/compiler boundaries remain part of the stated or uninspected trust chain. Future work includes clipping by precondition, incremental polyhedral generation, symmetry, faster verified linear solver, abstract interpretation, floating-point library Flocq and parallel verification library SyDPaCC. Extraction of verified networks/prover is proposed, not delivered as a verified efficient execution pipeline. No Rust, Verus, TLA+ or distributed protocol is verified in this paper.

- three-layer agent-skill capability verification (2026)
    - title: Methods for Formal Verification of Agent Skills: Three Layers Toward a Mechanically Checkable Capability-Containment Proof
    - what: Defines two-sided semantics for agent skills—deterministic script-side and nondeterministic LLM-side—and composes three verification layers: static capability analysis, refinement-typed tool-call envelopes, and SMT-bounded checking of runtime traces. A proof-carrying skill bundle is rechecked at bootstrap. Separates script and LLM projections of traces, states containment against declared capabilities, proves soundness and incompleteness for each method, and gives a composition theorem whose sole residual is the LLM’s refusal-to-act surface handled by the runtime biconditional. The implementation includes JavaScript modules, signed evidence files, a bootstrap checker, and a worked SKILL.md example.

    - number: All 53 tests pass (§8.4)
    - number: Layer 3 takes a few seconds per skill at Kmax=100; bootstrap re-check runs in milliseconds (§9.6)
    - number: Implementation ships as zero-runtime-dependency JavaScript modules (§Abstract)
    - limits: The paper explicitly does not verify model weights, training data, or decoding stochasticity; the LLM is treated as an adversarial nondeterministic oracle constrained by typed dispatch. Method C is bounded by transaction-buffer horizon Kmax, while methods A/B cover only their respective script and dispatch surfaces. Soundness depends on the underlying analyzers, type system, SMT encoding, and runtime biconditional.

- Transition Invariants Revisited: Termination Witnesses and Their Validation (2026)
    - what: Extends the standard machine-readable proof format that program verifiers hand to each other so it can carry termination proofs. The proof is a transition invariant: a relation between any earlier and later state of a run that must decrease in a well-founded way. Three checkers re-validate such proofs independently of the tool that made them.
    - number: Evaluated on all SV-Benchmarks programs expected to terminate, 900 s CPU and 15 GB per run
    - number: Witnesses validated by at least one validator: CPAchecker 366 of 422 (87%), CPAchecker-TransVer 192 of 200 (96%), UAutomizer-TransVer 375 of 389 (96%), Goblint-TransVer 176 of 286 (62%)
    - number: Validators solved about 40 programs that CPAchecker's own verification mode could not, using other tools' witnesses
    - number: Validation often faster than verification (Wilcoxon p = 2.1e-10 and 1.1e-13 for the two CPAchecker validators on ranking-function witnesses)
    - limits: Termination of sequential C programs only; the authors say "We do not consider other reasons for non-termination, such as deadlocks." One reduction route needs finite state spaces and TransVer has limited support for arrays and structs. Witnesses with many invariants (Goblint) often could not be validated within limits. Not about fairness or liveness of concurrent or distributed systems.

- Transitive Relation Learning (TRL) (2026)
    - title: Infinite State Model Checking by Learning Transitive Relations
    - what: Transitive Relation Learning (TRL) extends bounded model checking with learned transitive relations and blocking clauses so that finite-depth search exhaustion can prove safety of an infinite-state transition system. Uses model-driven conjunctive variable projection to select transition cases, recurrence-based transitive projections, loop detection, redundancy checks and backtracking. Learned relations need not over- or under-approximate a loop’s full transitive closure. Soundness instead depends on blocking only paths covered by the learned relations. Section 5 recursively substitutes accelerated under-approximations to validate possible counterexamples. Appendix A proves Theorems 22 and 28.
    - number: 626 unique LIA-Lin CHC competition 2023/2024 problems, 300 s and 10560 MiB each. TRL solves 386 (267 safe/119 unsafe), GSpacer 373 (287/86), ABMC 272 (142/130). Unique-proof counts depend on which overlapping solver configurations are excluded.
    - limits: May diverge; finite-image projection does not ensure complete loop closure. Implementation is limited to linear integer arithmetic; reals, arrays, bitvectors and temporal verification are future work. Main algorithm can return unknown when an error is reachable only through learned transitions. Author empirical and proof claims were read but neither code execution nor machine-checked proof was performed.

- Unit proofs study (2026)
    - title: Do Unit Proofs Work? An Empirical Study of Compositional Bounded Model Checking for Memory Safety Verification
    - what: Studies a systematic bottom-up method for compositional CBMC unit proofs. Analysts iteratively build harnesses, ensure termination, increase coverage, and refine models of unknown variables/functions from error traces; objective completeness requires graceful termination, full reachable-line coverage, and resolution of every memory-safety violation. The study selects 73 functional units from 89 known defects across FreeRTOS, Zephyr, Contiki-ng and RIOT. Initial harnesses set loop bounds to one; coverage gaps trigger larger bounds or allocation limits, while error traces drive minimal preconditions and function models. The blind construction protocol separates defect identification from proof writing. Analyses quantify model types, loop bounds, development/execution cost, comparison with engineer-authored FreeRTOS proofs, and generalizability to larger functions.

    - title: Scalable Deductive Verification of Data-Level Parallel Programs
    - what: Improves VerCors scalability for array/matrix data-parallel programs with three linked techniques: rewrite nested quantified array expressions into equivalent single-variable forms with usable SMT triggers, use unique type qualifiers to rule out array aliasing, and use immutable qualifiers to model unchanged arrays as mathematical sequences. Kernel-body extraction further reduces solver context. Section 2 explains permission-based separation logic, Viper translation and nested GPU parallel blocks through OpenCL XswapFast and PVL examples. Section 3 defines a bijective inverse for linear index expressions, states conditions for correctness, and reports a 2,500-line Lean 4 proof of the rewrite theorem; nonlinearity and unsupported modulo patterns remain limits. Section 4 explains Viper quantified heap chunks and snapshot comparisons, then defines immutable and unique typing, including struct/pointer examples. Section 5 evaluates CLBlast BLAS kernels, earlier Halide/HaliVer benchmarks and a Radio Telescope Pipeline containing the Padre algorithm. On an i7-11800H/32GB Ubuntu 23.04 machine, ten runs per experiment and one-hour timeout show all techniques up to 150× speedup, 8.5× total Level-1 and 10.8× Level-2 CLBlast speedups, more than 1.9× on earlier experiments, and previously unverifiable xger/xher2 and Padre cases becoming verifiable. The rewriter was essential for every reported experiment; gemm_3 failed because modulo is unsupported.

    - what: Develops a statistical theory for finite-budget agentic theorem proving. It models verifier-backed proof search as a deterministic finite-horizon reachability MDP and defines statistical provability as the probability that a specified prover reaches a verified proof within a verifier-call budget on a problem distribution. Under a faithful state abstraction, optimal MDP success equals budgeted syntactic provability. For offline depth-wise action-value regression followed by greedy proving, Theorem3.1 bounds the gap to the optimal prover by an occupancy-weighted sum of value-estimation errors; the multiplier is the learned prover’s average truncated proof length. Error terms separate approximation, training-region coverage geometry and Monte Carlo rollout noise, with a faster rate under an action-gap margin condition. Defines full proof states as multisets of open goals so branching remains Markov, deterministic verifier transition F, solved set G, hitting time TG, budgeted value V and average truncated length Len. Assumption3.1 requires compact concentration sets, Lipschitz optimal values and hypothesis classes, local-mass coverage of i.i.d. query pairs, conditionally independent binary rollout labels with mean Q*, and minimax regression. Theorem3.1 gives εt=approximation+covering term+Hoeffding rollout noise and regret 2Σ unsolved-mass×ε. A margin condition changes ε to ε^(β+1). Budget allocation balances Nt and mt under total labels nt=Ntmt. Appendices prove deterministic MDP, faithful abstraction, Bellman recursion, greedy regret, covering and uniform regression; truncation adds overflow penalty δW. Appendix C proposes representation selection by Bellman-certificate tightness and a complexity penalty; Appendix D interprets scaling through horizon, effective dimension and margins.

The paper explicitly says a new prover leaving the occupied region is no longer certified without added coverage assumptions. Binary rollout labels are idealized verifier-backed success labels with conditional mean Q*. - A Layered Formal Methods Approach to Answering Queue-related Queries (2025)
    - what: QuASI decides whether any packet trace consistent with per-port received/sent/dropped counts can satisfy a queue query. The enqueue-rate abstraction removes packet origins. A cheap first layer uses a disjunction of necessary constraints, constructs a purported most-uniform trace per component and checks input consistency via Gale-Ryser binary-matrix existence; negative answers are intended conclusive. Positive answers proceed to an exact Z3 switch model. Simulation evaluates tighter queue/buffer upper bounds, burst exclusion and runtime. Records concrete switch/count/query semantics, conservation-derived cover constraints, exact representative/input-labeling reductions and supplied proofs, all benchmark configurations/results and ambiguity about matched FPerf measurements and selected-negative query populations. Separates possible history from actual measured history, first-layer upper bounds from second-layer model-relative exact maxima, and common-path early exits from general scalability. Reader checks expose printed pseudocode boundary conditions, a tie-dependent MUC counterexample and unsupported exact multi-switch composition claim without claiming reproduced artifact defects.
    - limits: Finite single output-queued switch model, N input ports/Nq output queues/T discrete steps, at most one packet per input/output port per step, negligible forwarding time, known finite queue capacity and drops at full queue. Initial queues may be nonempty; sent+dropped totals can exceed received totals. Counts are treated as accurate and interval-aligned; counter wrap/loss, heterogeneous packet sizes/link rates, internal pipeline delay, uncertain measurement error and real scheduling refinements are not modeled in detail. Existential feasibility question: Mi∩Mo∩Q nonempty, where Mi fixes all input counts and Mo fixes output/drop counts. A positive answer means a behavior is possible, not that it occurred in the observed execution. A negative answer rules it out only under the modeled switch assumptions. Query grammar permits bounded existential/universal time and queue quantifiers, conjunctions, comparisons of enq/cenq/qlen, queue sums or differences, against K or K*t. Gives concrete reader checks of displayed size inequality, heap environment links and return-value correspondence without attributing these printed defects to unchecked HOL4 scripts.

- Ahvonen-Jaakkola-Kuusisto MSC formula-size game (2025)
    - title: Formula size game and model checking for modal substitution calculus
    - what: Defines game-theoretic and formula-size semantics for MSC, GMSC, GGMSC and SC, then characterizes expressive power and model-checking complexity, including asynchronous variants and a universal reduction. The paper gives two co-inductive semantic games (bounded-round and global interpretation tracing) and proves their correctness, then builds formula-size games whose winning strategies characterize separation of classes of pointed Kripke models, including non-uniform finite-model strategies. It identifies asynchronous MSC/GMSC/GGMSC with corresponding modal mu-calculus and computation-logic fragments, and encodes deterministic linear-tape-bounded Turing machines over words. Detailed reductions establish PSPACE-completeness for standard MSC/GMSC/GGMSC and SC, PTIME-completeness for asynchronous variants, constant SC data complexity, SC satisfiability bounds, and a computable reduction from every recursively enumerable problem to MSC model checking when input padding is allowed.
    - number: PSPACE-complete standard MSC/GMSC/GGMSC model checking (combined and data)
    - number: PTIME-complete asynchronous MSC/GMSC/GGMSC
    - number: PSPACE-complete SC model checking and satisfiability
    - number: PTIME-complete asynchronous SC model checking; NP-complete asynchronous SC satisfiability
    - limits: Results are semantic and complexity-theoretic over finite or word-like Kripke models; asynchronous semantics omit iteration clocks. The universal reduction relies on padding/extended word models. Formula-size games characterize fixed program size but do not provide a practical verifier. Undecidability of MSC/GMSC/GGMSC satisfiability remains, and succinctness questions are open.

- AMC effectivity-frame model checking (2025)
    - title: Efficient Model Checking for the Alternating-Time µ-Calculus via Effectivity Frames
    - what: Implements full alternating-time µ-calculus (AMC) model checking over concurrent game frames (CGFs) and equivalent effectivity frames (EFs). Conversion precomputes coalition capabilities so modal checks become set lookups; the paper measures whether this amortizes conversion cost and compares against direct CGF checking and MCMAS. It defines CGF and playable EF semantics, proves the induced-frame translation preserves every AMC formula, and instantiates local/game-based coalgebraic µ-calculus algorithms in COOL. Random formulas, castle games and modulo games separate regimes: EF conversion has an upfront exponential-in-agents/moves cost, while EF evaluation benefits when many joint moves have equivalent outcomes or fixpoints repeatedly revisit modalities. The full AMC implementation supports Büchi-style formulas unavailable in MCMAS; MCMAS instead benefits from symbolic OBDD representations on succinct cases.

- Automatically Generalizing Proofs and Statements (2025)
    - what: Lean proof-term generalization tactic that takes an existing proof and a selected constant, then returns a more abstract statement with a proof when transformation typechecks. It generalizes repeated occurrences independently, discovers related constants through type mismatches/antiunification, and abstracts composite proof fragments into hypotheses. Demonstrations include arithmetic, set cardinality, algebraic cancellation and Bézout. Six-stage description explains separate metavariables per occurrence, hypothesis abstraction from inferred types, iterative detection of dependent constants, unification to recover required equalities, metavariable-to-binder extraction, and type inference for the resulting statement. Contrasts accepted proof with useful/general/nonvacuous generalization, and shows how definitional computation or opaque proof steps obstruct extraction. Distinguishes implemented tactic from ideal future proof-discovery uses.
    - limits: Requires an existing formal Lean proof and user-selected expression/constant, optionally occurrence controls. Soundness relies on successful final proof typechecking in its Lean environment and the assumptions of referenced declarations. It is not a stand-alone axiomatic proof of the algorithm, an audit of input axioms, or a guarantee that a formal statement matches human intent. Accepted result is a provable conditional statement. This alone does not establish weakest hypotheses, nonvacuity, strict generality, novelty, usefulness or a canonical mathematical abstraction. Paper explicitly describes a true output hypothesis that forces n=2 and thus adds no genuine generality. Outputs depend on the exact proof, including how facts are encoded, not just the original theorem statement. The transformation operates on proof terms and loses tactic-script structure. Default abstracts all occurrences; coincidental equality may change output, and user can restrict occurrences. Dependent-constant search uses syntactic antiunification and a heuristic favoring fewer metavariables. No completeness, optimality, termination or runtime complexity theorem is reported. Related mismatches may remain unresolved, especially when generalized types lose definitional equality. Definitional-equality example fails when generalizing integers because divisibility no longer unfolds as the required existential. An explicit rewrite via Int.dvd_def records the connection as a proof step and permits an added divisibility-definition hypothesis. Merely unfold does not change the proof term and therefore does not provide that evidence. Computation can erase the dependency trace needed for abstraction:paper’s reduceMul example leaves 6 rather than how 2*3 produced it. Generalizing proofs cannot independently solve newly exposed mathematical subproblems. Original specialized computations may need to become hypotheses instead. Bézout output is a long collection of sufficient algebraic/size/quotient/remainder conditions from a particular proof, not a recovered canonical Euclidean-domain definition. Typeclass simplification and simultaneous generalization from two proofs are future work. Several application sections discuss an ideal algorithm or mathematical motivation rather than demonstrated execution:inductive proof discovery, intermediate-value abstraction, conjecture generation, learning from counterexamples, and interesting-question generation. No integrated LLM/automated proof-discovery evaluation is reported.

    - title: Sound Statistical Model Checking for Probabilities and Expected Rewards
    - what: Surveys statistical methods used by SMC tools, identifies unsound confidence procedures, recommends Clopper–Pearson for probabilities and DKW for bounded rewards, and introduces theoretical bounding-set and limit-PAC methods for unbounded reachability rewards implemented in modes. The paper distinguishes fixed-k and sequential PAC settings and requires worst-case coverage over all true probabilities, exposing why CLT/Wald, Wilson/CC and Chow–Robbins procedures can be unsound. It proves the DKW confidence band yields a tighter expected-reward interval than Hoeffding, derives bounds for instantaneous, cumulative and reachability rewards, and shows a finite-state DTMC geometric path-length construction is theoretically sufficient but often unusably large. DKW-E-Lower is a new lower-bound procedure for any nonnegative finite-expectation random variable, with a limit-PAC theorem. A survey of tools shows no sound and efficient default for sequential probabilities or fixed reward estimation before their modes implementation.

- Canonical for Automated Theorem Proving in Lean (2025)
    - what: Presents Canonical, a Rust implementation of backward type-inhabitation search linked to Lean, using beta-normal eta-long terms, explicit substitutions, equational constraints, arbitrary argument refinement order and entropy-guided parallel iterative deepening. On an adapted Natural Number Game with manually selected premises, solves 62/74 statements versus Aesop 27 and Duper 45; reports 51 seconds for the 62 successes. Also solves 46 of the first 50 Lean Prelude statements under a specified inhabitant-equality criterion. Search supports higher-order premises, indexed types and induction, but the translation omits universes and quotients, and default iota pruning is incomplete. Separates source-dependent type theory, Rust search, translation obligations and returned Lean terms; records universe-erasure unsoundness admitted by the authors, iota/structure-eta incompleteness, manually chosen premises and benchmark adaptations, per-world results, exact proof-size metric, successful-proof timing denominator, Prelude success definition, and examples requiring supplied lemmas or generalized recursors. Distinguishes proposed LLM integration from measured proof search.
    - limits: §§3.1–3.2, pp.5–6: terms are beta-normal eta-long and have parameter bindings, simultaneous let declarations, a local head and arguments. Types annotate bindings. Parameters/lets may refer to each other circularly; the encoder must supply a signature valid in the target theory. A missing variable type prevents its use in proof construction; a missing let body makes it an opaque constant. Recursor and projection annotations add reduction behavior. Static arity is an input-format property, not a general property of Lean expressions. §3.2, p.6: start with a goal metavariable, choose a local head and create all its argument metavariables together. Refinement creates typing and definitional-equality constraints. Violations undo a head assignment; metavariable choice need not be backtracked because any completed term admits arbitrary refinement order. This is a structural algorithm argument, not a mechanized implementation-correctness theorem. §3.3, pp.6–7: de Bruijn indices with explicit substitutions permit partial beta reduction without knowing a metavariable’s eventual free variables. Reduction either exposes a rigid head/arguments or becomes stuck. Different rigid heads violate equality; equal heads yield subterm equations. Refinement revisits equations stuck on that metavariable and undo restores them. There is no separate dedicated unification algorithm; constraints guide the same search. §3.3.1, p.8: equality of a blocked recursor/projection and a rigid term may become true after the major argument is instantiated. Default mode treats it as violated, deliberately sacrificing completeness. Program-synthesis mode (+synth) treats it as stuck, admitting more search. A constructor cannot be chosen as the major-argument head of a recursor/projection because that would create a reducible term outside canonical form. This paper does not establish completeness for all Lean definitional equality. §§3.4–3.4.1, pp.8–9: iterative deepening DFS bounds a custom entropy product, mutates assignments in place and runs large branches with fork-join parallelism. Successive thresholds aim to double node counts. Refined metavariables contribute branching factors; unrefined ones use empirical completion estimates from bins keyed by source type ignoring explicit substitution and rigid-equation status. Estimated chance of later rigid equality mixes entropy 1 with average completion refinements; each metavariable estimate is capped at 1000, and unsuccessful refinements incur an extra penalty. Independence is an estimating assumption, not a proved property of dependent subgoals. §3.4.2, pp.9–10: prefer rigid equations for propagation and early failure, then statistically likely impossible metavariables, then high estimated entropy and later arguments whose types constrain earlier values. Meta-level choice and head-level choice serve different purposes. No general theorem of optimality, fair coverage under changing statistics, or global resource bound accompanies this heuristic. §4, pp.10–11: Rust solver communicates through Lean FFI and translated Term/Typ structures. Translation follows Lean Expr constructors, uses lets to retain beta-redexes, and replaces universe-indexed sorts by a single declaration Sort : Sort. The authors explicitly admit possible unsoundness by Girard’s paradox. This affects the search abstraction; a returned term accepted by Lean’s kernel would still have to satisfy Lean’s original universe rules. The paper supplies no mechanized translator-correctness proof or separate measured return-path/kernel-rejection experiment. Rust implementation alone is not evidence of verified Rust or Verus use. §§4–4.1, p.11: Pi structure packages function-valued terms to enforce static arity, with Pi.f/Pi.mk wrappers and eta expansion. Unfolds Set, Not, reducible definitions and typeclass instances where possible to avoid excess wrappers. Literal constants are generally opaque; only natural literals at most 5 receive constructor definitions. Quotient types and universe levels are outside the translation’s supported scope. §4.2, p.12: recursively include constant definitions down to primitives; provide recursor definitions as usable abstractions while hiding types of certain definition-only constants to reduce redundant expressions. Inductive declarations bring constructors/recursors, structures bring projections; local assumptions are included and users supply extra constants in brackets. Recursive expansion can violate abstraction and explode for real numbers. Relevance filtering and automatic premise selection over all Mathlib are outside scope. §5, pp.12–13: Natural Number Game has 79 levels across 9 worlds but 74 unique statements. Authors replace its pedagogical custom naturals/axiomatic operations with standard Nat. Premises are manually selected, mostly from reference solutions and earlier levels. Added Nat.le.intro/dest convert inequality definitions; one level needs Classical.byContradiction; an If structure lets Canonical encode implication induction predicates. Report results for this adapted benchmark, not the untouched game or an unseen randomly sampled theorem library. §5, p.13: Aesop uses default options, Duper portfolio mode, Canonical timeout 15 seconds. Natural-number simp attributes are removed until the corresponding game level, while Duper gets needed definitional equations. Hardware Mac Mini M4 Pro, 24GB RAM; Lean/Mathlib 4.16.0, Duper 0.0.23. No complete matching CPU/thread/time budget table for all solvers. Artifact reference 45 names CanonicalLean v4.22.0, distinct from the benchmark Lean version. §5, pp.13–14: 62/74 Canonical, 27/74 Aesop, 45/74 Duper. Authors attribute much advantage to induction support absent from the compared tactics. 51 seconds is explicitly the time to generate 62 successful proofs; it does not include all failed attempts as a benchmark-total wall-time measurement. On nine successes taking over one second, averages are 23 million attempted refinements/s, 2.1 million/s without equation violation and 1.2 million/s below threshold, branching factor 1.6, final iteration 17% of solve time. §5, p.14: proof length counts constants, free/bound variables, sorts, literals and projections, excluding lambda/let binder types. On common successes Canonical proofs average 251 times shorter than Duper and 18 times shorter than Aesop. Available constants and use of domain-specific lemmas differ. This metric does not measure human readability, checking time, bytes, or whole-benchmark proof-size performance. §5, p.14: Prelude test uses first 50 statements, not a random held-out set. Nonpropositions allow multiple generated inhabitants; success requires one definitionally equal to the library implementation. Constructor-disequality proofs supplied instead of noConfusion. 46 successes; three failures due to missing structure eta encoding, one due to iota incompleteness. Per-problem timeouts and count limits are not comprehensively tabulated. §§6–8, pp.15–16: compares its approach with sauto, Agda inhabitant tools, TWELF, hammers and tactic prediction. Cut-free backward search does not invent local lemmas, call domain solvers on partially instantiated goals, share conflict clauses or table results; branches mostly share statistics. Learned forward reasoning, tactic integration, other DTT languages, AI data generation and LLM use are future directions, not evaluated contributions.     - title: A Behavioral Theory for Distributed Systems with Weak Recovery
    - what: Introduces DπFR, a distributed pi-calculus with dynamic nodes and links, crash failures, weak recovery, imperfect local knowledge, and incarnation numbers; defines reduction and labelled-transition semantics and proves weak bisimilarity fully abstracts weak barbed congruence. It handles undefined instruction results/flags, instruction bundling, deterministic metering and load-address independence, and integrates with Groundhog. Evaluation measures selected SPEC integer benchmarks, payment-contract scalability, startup and Rust zero-knowledge proof-verification code. No machine-checked correctness proof of DeCl is reported. Preserves precise runtime/hardware trust assumptions, ISA differences and undefined-input/flag guards, the full conservative two-pass dataflow algorithm, CPU-fuzzer coverage limit, gas accounting/overcharging and timer observability condition, position-oblivious register/pointer/flag handling, verifier passes and padding treatment. Guarantee covers valid microarchitectures within one chosen ISA, not agreement between separately compiled x86 and Arm programs. Hardware must implement accepted ISA correctly; required extensions such as BMI2 restrict deployment. Deterministic runtime call API, no shared-memory multiprocessing and deterministic sandbox initialization are assumed. Runtime API implementation, input state and memory protection remain trusted. §§2.1/2.2: Memory isolation is necessary to prevent reading external nondeterministic data; hardware or software isolation can provide it. Sandbox code cannot be writable and executable by untrusted code. Arm64 fixed-width alignment prevents executing alternate instruction decodings; x86 uses 32-byte instruction bundles, no spanning instructions, aligned direct targets and masked aligned indirect targets. Code/data must be separated. Unknown instruction encodings are rejected. Runtime can use a separate writable alias for loading code; this trusted action must not expose mutable code while the sandbox executes. §2.1: On Arm64, torn store straddling mapped/unmapped boundary may or may not partially alter mapped memory. DeCl terminates after a memory fault rather than simulating precise stores. This termination rule alone does not define a deterministic post-fault sandbox memory snapshot; runtime must respect the stated externally visible-effect boundary. Side-channel paragraph claims removal of in-sandbox timers/parallelism/atomic timing vectors; it does not provide an empirical side-channel evaluation or establish that an external observer cannot measure execution time. §3: Integer and integer SIMD subset only; floating-point instructions excluded because some permit implementation-dependent approximations. Armv8.0 supports approximately180 base plus430SIMD instructions by chosen decoder classification; rejects malformed SBZ/SBO, unpredictable/unallocated/undefined encodings except intentional udf#0 trap. Despite October2024 manual prose changing BSR/BSF zero-input behavior to unchanged, conflicting pseudocode/other sections lead authors to retain conservative undefined-result handling. §3.2.2/Algorithm 1: Undefined-flags analysis tracks set U through each basic block: reject read of U, clear defined flags, add undefined flags. Initialize every block IN to all-undefined, analyze without reporting, union predecessor OUT sets, analyze again with reporting. Indirect jumps are preceded by AND alignment which defines observable flags, so static-branch CFG suffices; AF remains undefined but accepted instructions cannot observe it. A full fixpoint could accept more programs; two-pass algorithm may falsely reject but is claimed sound, and author-compiled LLVM/GCC cases pass within two. No mechanized soundness proof or machine-code refinement accompanies this claim. §3.3: Fuzzer generates random candidate instructions, filters through verifier, concatenates verified basic blocks into MB–GB programs and compares final register/memory state across5+microarchitectures for each architecture. This tests handwritten verifier/ISA understanding; it is not necessary trusted enforcement, exhaustive ISA validation or proof of all accepted programs. No precise campaign duration, samples, machine list or verified-code bug count reported. §§4/4.1: Gas is instruction accounting, not real elapsed CPU duration; instruction timing varies. Meter register x23/%r12 decremented at block epilogue. Bundling prevents jumps past required accounting: x86 already32B, Arm branch16B/timer8B with x24 aligned-target register. Initial gas/counter arithmetic, runtime calls and periodic interrupt handling must satisfy implementation constraints. No arbitrary wall-clock bound follows from a gas count alone. §4.2/Figure 3: Branch scheme checks high sign bit after decrement and traps on negative. Arm SUB/TBZ/BRK preserves flags; x86 flag-preserving LEA/PUSH RCX/MOV0x3f/SHRX/JRCXZ/INT3/POP sequence is costlier than SUB/JNS/INT3 when flags may be clobbered. Indirect jumps into middle of a statically recognized block may be charged for its full length, deterministically overcharging. Forward-branch gas checks can be elided if whole program size N bounded (example10M instructions); at most N further instructions until checked backwards branch or termination. This is not exact preemption at precisely the requested instruction count. §4.3/Figure 4: Timer scheme keeps gas decrement but removes per-block sign checks; runtime checks sign before every externally visible call effect, and timer interrupt terminates negative-gas programs. Execution may continue nondeterministically after gas exhaustion for at most timer slice t, while external call trace stays deterministic. Requires calls be the only observable effects and program memory be externally invisible. Short slices add overhead; tiny gas budgets may favor branch metering. Ordinary LFI leaks absolute load/stack/code addresses and therefore lacks determinism. Position-oblivious code allows only low32-bit observations of absolute-address registers, zeros high bits after PC-relative address formation, and requires runtime-returned pointers be offsets too. This is stronger than ordinary position-independent executable code. §5.2: x86 CALL stores absolute return address, so POC replaces it with LEAL/PUSH/JMP; returns are aligned masked indirect branches re-adding base. String instructions must zero high32bits of RSI/RDI afterward. OR-based branch target guard flags must not reveal base: PF depends only low byte, SF requires same address-space half, ZF requires never allocating zero sandbox; LEA guard can avoid flags changes if both halves needed. POC supports same-process sandbox relocation/fork only under runtime’s address-hiding obligations. §§5.3/6: Runtime call table moved outside sandbox, first metadata page unmapped; new dedicated call register x25/%r13 prevents reading nondeterministic metadata. Simplified redundant-guard elimination saves reserved registers. Compiler/rewrite/assembler/linker are untrusted for determinism because final code is checked, but rejection or changed source-program semantics remains possible. Section8 explicitly permits replacing unwanted FP instructions with NOPs; acceptance then establishes the altered binary’s restricted behavior, not faithful implementation of original FP source. §6.2: Trusted standalone linear-time verifier decodes enumerated subset, checks instruction/configuration safety, bundle control flow, LFI addressing/reserved registers and x86 flags. Meter validation uses leader construction (entry/post-branch/direct target), checks debit immediate against block size, same-bundle epilogue/branch, exclusive meter-register operations and aligned targets. Unmetered fallthrough padding may merge with next block and be charged, introducing deterministic overcharging. No verifier LOC/TCB-size count, formal proof, verification throughput benchmark, or comprehensive adversarial bypass results reported. §7.1: Eight supported SPECrate CPU2017 integer C/C++ programs compiled Musl/LLVM19.1.4+LTO; excludes unsupported languages/toolchain cases and floating point, uses rate instead of speed because LFI4GiB versus16GiB requirement. Platforms AMD7950XUbuntu and bare-metal M2DebianAsahiLinux, fixed base clock/shielded core. SPEC runtime intentionally supplies nondeterministic APIs including time, so this experiment measures transformation overhead, not end-to-end deterministic program execution. No trial count/confidence intervals supplied. §7.1/Table 4: Figure6 means include eight programs; Figure7 means only four WebAssembly-supported ones. DeCl-HWx86 overhead4.40%/5.47% in table differs from rounded prose∼3%; retain actual table values. Wasmtime24.0.0 uses deterministic fuel/128-bitSIMD. Reduced overhead by>2× does not mean total runtime or throughput improves>2×: compare 1+overhead, and distinguish SPEC subset from separate cryptography runtime measurements. §7.2.1: Groundhog replaces wasm3 with metered DeCl-LFI using picolibc/freestanding contracts and specific runtime storage/block APIs. - Extended threshold automata (2025)
    - title: Parameterized Verification of Round-Based Distributed Algorithms via Extended Threshold Automata.
    - what: Extends threshold automata with decrements and resets of shared variables, develops sound and complete semi-decision procedures for general coverability and reachability, and evaluates an implementation on fault-tolerant distributed algorithm models. The counter-system model retains arbitrary process counts satisfying a linear-arithmetic resilience condition. Parametric intervals abstract shared counters; an abstract counter system leaves location counts unbounded. Lemmas 1–2 relate concrete paths to non-spurious abstract paths using quantifier-free linear-integer constraints, including acceleration multiplicities. Lemmas 3–4 establish a well-structured system with effective predecessor bases. Algorithm 1 must preserve transitions from subsumed states to enumerate all abstract error paths, because one spurious path cannot settle verification. Corollary 2 and Lemma 5 give soundness/completeness; Theorem 1 proves termination for nonnegative updates without resets. A second abstraction keeps only occupied/empty location bits, allowing zero tests in reachability specifications; PRA implements this symbolically. General coverability can express two leaders at the same location, whereas ordinary positive-location coverability cannot. Experiments reveal the narrower scope of the phase-king and full Red Belly results than the abstract suggests.

All possible finite orders of parametric thresholds must be considered. Abstract transitions can be spurious and require SMT concretization. The extended model is undecidable; error-path unfolding can diverge on cycles containing decrements/resets. Termination holds for monotone increments/no resets, acyclic error graphs, or cycles without decrements/resets. Evaluated properties are selected safety/reachability properties, not full liveness or implementation refinement. - Formal Verification of Parameterized Systems based on Induction (2025)
    - what: # Formal Verification of Parameterized Systems based on Induction (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Jiaqi Xiu and Yongjian Li, arXiv 2503.18030v1, 23 March 2025. This is a whole-paper record: all nine PDF pages, 23 references, two figures, four algorithms, nine numbered equations and both tables were read. All pages were visually inspected, including six dense pages at 1900px. No appendix or checklist appears. The acquired official PDF and pool copy are byte-identical. [quotes.json](quotes.json) supplies exact passages with section/page pointers; [tables.json](tables.json) preserves the complete table pages, and the two row sidecars transcribe all cells. Cited papers were not independently read for this assignment.  The paper presents wiseParaverifier, a system for discovering and generalizing auxiliary invariants of parameterized safety protocols. Its main contribution is a search procedure: use small protocol instances and counterexamples to suggest invariants, select quantifiers, merge related formulas, and ask Ivy to prove the parameterized result. It reports success on seven cache-coherence and ten distributed protocol models. The evidence is an algorithm description and benchmark measurements. The paper contains no numbered theorem, lemma or complete end-to-end soundness, completeness or termination proof. I did not run a solver, checker or author program, and acquired no generated proof files or verification logs.  Section I p1 states the central limitation of starting small: an invariant’s inductiveness on a small instance “does not imply that these invariants will retain their inductive characteristics when applied to larger scale system concretizations” (Q1). The workflow addresses that gap with two stages. `invFinder` constructs concrete auxiliary invariants; `Verifier` generalizes them and checks induction (§III p2, Q2). Figure 1 p3 adds an essential detail: a successful Ivy proof yields “Passed”; a failed proof increases N and returns to invariant discovery. Thus the intended acceptance condition is parameterized induction, not agreement at two finite instance sizes. The paper says, “wiseParaverifier employs Ivy for automatic inductive verification” (§III.C p5, Q15). No acquired artifact lets this reading independently check that step.  The initial concretization is based on overlap between parameters in an invariant F and transition rule R (§III.A.1 pp2–3). With two invariant parameters and one rule parameter, the rule may use either existing index or a fresh third index, so N=3 represents the listed overlap cases. With two rule parameters, representatives can require N=4, including the all-fresh pair. These are concrete examples of reducing redundant parameter instantiations. The stated selection principle requires the concrete protocol to simulate the same or symmetric transition behavior under arbitrary parameters (Q4). The article does not prove a general cutoff theorem or define a complete supported protocol language that makes that principle automatic.  For each rule/invariant pair, the system constructs `indOblg`, a formula involving the rule guard, assignments, unchanged-variable equations and a violated postcondition (§III.A.2 p3, Eq1). Z3 satisfiability produces an assignment used to propose an auxiliary invariant by negating the conjunction of its state equations; unsatisfiability eliminates that obligation (Q7–Q10). Rules that do not change relevant invariant variables can be filtered. Candidate invariants are checked through a client/server service wrapping Murphi, NuSMV and NuSMV-BMC (§III.A p2, Q3). The server retains information about previously executed protocols, a detail relevant to interpreting timings (§IV p7, Q24).  The heuristic Generalize search uses earlier invariants to narrow which equations matter (§III.A.3 pp4–5, Figure 2 and Algorithms 1–2). Shared terms form `join`; terms unique to the current counterexample form `diff`. It tests `join` plus increasingly large subsets of `diff`, then removes unnecessary terms or uses an increasing search to obtain a smaller checked candidate. It falls back to nonheuristic search if that fails (Q11–Q14). This is a useful concrete distinction: previous formulas guide candidate generation, while an external checker checks candidates against the concrete model. Although the paper repeatedly calls the result “most concise,” it gives no global minimality proof or formula-length/readability evaluation.  Quantifier promotion uses type saturation γ(t)=#(Ω,t)/C(t), the number of concrete values of type t in a clause divided by that type’s concrete domain size (§III.C p5, Eq3). An unsaturated type is proposed as universally quantified. A saturated type triggers a check at N+1; a surviving clause can receive universal quantification, while failure prompts existential or finer mixed grouping. Equations 4–7 describe extending groupings and expressing existential alternatives. The following page says existentially treated groups may be joined by disjunction (Q16–Q20). These tests generate candidate quantifiers. They do not by themselves establish correctness at every size; the final Ivy induction check in Figure 1 remains necessary.  The merger has three distinct cases (§III.C p6, Q21). Equivalent parameterizations share a representative. If one existing invariant implies the whole conjunction, Eq8 permits retaining it. Eq9 permits a strictly stronger replacement that implies the old conjunction while the converse fails. A stronger formula still needs an invariant proof: implication alone does not establish that initial states satisfy it or that transitions preserve it. Algorithms 3–4 add another optimization, generating symmetric formulas and asserting already accepted auxiliary invariants and their images to prevent redundant counterexamples. The paper distinguishes unrestricted universal-type permutations from restricted existential and mixed cases (Q22–Q23); a transfer must preserve those quantifier distinctions and the modeled protocol’s symmetry.  Several printed details limit treating this presentation as a fully specified formal argument. Eq2 p3 writes `f_k = eq_i ∨ ¬eq_i`. Read literally as logical disjunction, each factor is a tautology and its negated conjunction is false. That conflicts with the surrounding candidate-invariant explanation; a notation or presentation error is plausible, but its intended repair was not established. Eq1 does not explicitly include a prestate F conjunct, so this record does not silently substitute the conventional `F ∧ R ∧ ¬F′` formula. Algorithm 1 p4 line12 shows a function index without recursive arguments, and line24 converts `solution` while iterating over `subS`. These details were visually checked. They are unresolved presentation issues, not an independently demonstrated failure of an implemented verifier. [reader-diagnostics.json](reader-diagnostics.json) separates these observations from the authors’ claims.  The evaluation has a 17-model comparison and a four-strategy ablation (§IV pp7–9). The cache models are MutualExNodata, MutualEx, MutualEx_M2, GermanNodata, German, FlashNodata and Flash. The distributed models are Decentralized_lock, Lock_server, Multi_lock_server, Ricart-Agrawala, Shard, Two_phase_commit, two client/server variants and two consensus variants. Four distributed rows require mixed universal/existential quantifiers. The paper does not print the benchmark safety formulas, instance sizes, full transition models or failure/network assumptions. Verifying a model named Flash or Consensus_epr therefore supports that model-level claim; it does not establish correctness of a deployed cache implementation or every consensus variant.  Experiments used an 18-core Intel Gold 6254 CPU at 3.10GHz. Table I reports completion seconds and final parameterized-invariant counts for wiseParaverifier, Paraverifier, DuoAI and IC3PO. Counting numeric successful entries gives 17, 7, 14 and 12, respectively; these are reader counts. “error” means compilation failed after modeling, while “fail” means verification could not complete (Q25). Neither means a discovered safety violation. The prose says Paraverifier failed on all distributed models (§IV.A p7, Q26), but its Two_phase_commit row succeeds in 6.18 seconds with ten invariants. The table supports one distributed success and nine compilation errors. That conflict is preserved rather than resolved in favor of the prose.  The comparative gains vary. Flash takes wiseParaverifier 585.68 seconds and 135 invariants versus Paraverifier’s 589.23 seconds and 162 invariants; DuoAI and IC3PO fail. GermanNodata takes 19.14 seconds/39 invariants versus DuoAI’s 535.80 seconds/892, about 28× less time by reader arithmetic. On Consensus_epr, however, DuoAI takes 28.88 seconds/seven invariants, wiseParaverifier 43.10/16, and IC3PO 1248.26/eight. Coverage and low invariant count therefore do not imply universal speed or concision superiority.  Table II compares simple increasing, simple decreasing, heuristic increasing and heuristic decreasing search using seconds and NuSMV calls. They complete 15, 15, 16 and 17 models; “/” denotes more than 86,400 seconds with continuing counterexample discovery. Heuristic decreasing is fastest or tied on 15 rows. For FlashNodata it reduces heuristic increasing’s 1669.69 seconds/1818 calls to 329.91/674. On Consensus_epr, simple increasing takes 183.23 seconds/2909 calls versus 43.10/753. The tradeoff reverses on small Ricart-Agrawala: simple decreasing takes 0.43 seconds/eight calls versus heuristic decreasing’s 0.54/ten. These are author-reported measurements, with no stated repetitions, seeds, variability or error bars. Software versions, memory use and a clear cold/warm-server timing boundary are absent. GermanNodata, Lock_server and Ricart-Agrawala have differing timings across Tables I–II; the row sidecars retain each printed value.  Bibliographic provenance also needs care: §II’s “I4 [20]” points to a listed 2003 cache-coherence paper, “Ivy [21]” to Ironfleet, and reference13 retains a literal placeholder venue. This record does not treat those mappings as validated provenance. No author repository, model, log or certificate URL was identified in the paper or acquired arXiv metadata; this was not an exhaustive artifact search. The arXiv TeX and experimental HTML links were not acquired.  For distributed-system verification, the paper contributes a practical combination of counterexample formulas, earlier-invariant-guided search, mixed-quantifier proposals and symmetry blocking, evaluated across two protocol categories. It presents no Verus or verified-Rust implementation, TLA+ experiment or LLM-agent study. A reader proposal for agents writing specifications and proofs is to reuse earlier invariant terms as search hints, make quantifier changes explicit, and require an independent parameterized induction check before accepting them. Its measurements suggest evaluating completion coverage, checker calls, runtime and formula size separately, while separating compilation failures, verification failures and timeouts. Those are transfers from the method and evaluation, not capabilities demonstrated for LLM agents by this paper.  Whole9pages/23references/2tables/2figures/4algorithms/9equations. Reconstructs overlapcase concretizations, Z3CTIformulas, join/diffheuristic andfallback, type-saturationN+1quantifier proposals, three merging cases, quantifier-aware symmetry blocking and finalIvyfeedbackloop. Alltablecells transcribed, coveragecounted, representative speed/call/invariant tradeoffs and printedformula/pseudocode/citation/table/prose inconsistencies retained.
    - limits: Parameterized protocol safety models and representative overlap/symmetry cases; trustworthy translation and final symbolic Ivy induction. SmallN/N+1checks alone do not prove all sizes. No complete end-to-end soundness/completeness/termination theorem or acquired authorcode/models/logs/certificates.17successesauthorreported; no execution/reproduction. NoVerus/Rust/TLA+/LLMagentstudy.

- Formally Verifying a Vertical Cell Decomposition Algorithm (2025)
    - what: Rocq/Mathematical Components verification of a functional sweep algorithm returning triangular/trapezoidal cells whose interiors and specified lateral doors avoid nonvertical segment obstacles. The proof handles vertically aligned events without producing zero-width cells and proves each returned cell has an interior center. Complete free-space coverage and shared-door completeness remain unproved. Preserves precise obstacle/numeric model, executable/proof representation split, two-stage safety contracts, orphaned events, four scan branches, hazard inheritance and six levels of invariants. Explains ownership plus obstacle-boundary coverage as the safety argument. Distinguishes nonempty individual cells from nonvacuous output coverage, empirical trajectory usability from a planner correctness/completeness proof, and event alignment from excluded vertical obstacles.
    - limits: §§1–2/4.5, pp.1–4/9–10: input obstacles are finite straight segments, not filled polygons. Endpoints can be shared, but other intersections are excluded; duplicates are excluded. Each edge has strictly increasing x from left to right, so vertical and zero-length segments cannot satisfy the proof edge type. A well-formed bounding box has distinct lateral sides and low/high edges; every obstacle point must lie inside it. This is point motion in a 2D scene, without finite robot shape, dynamics, sensors or uncertain coordinates. §2.1/5.1, pp.3–4/11: proofs assume a Mathematical Components real field, with exact arithmetic and boolean equality/order. Rational numbers suffice; no completeness of the real numbers is required. The generic executable accepts a number type, four arithmetic operations and two comparisons. Its user must instantiate them consistently with field laws. Ordinary floating point does not satisfy that exact model; no rounding-error theorem is given. §2.1, pp.4–5: a determinant computes signed area for above/below/collinear tests using ring operations. Vertical-cylinder tests ensure projections lie within segment x range. Vertical projection is the only operation using division, returning an option outside its range. The edge_below relation is transitive for outgoing edges sharing a left endpoint, but is not a global partial order. §2.2/5.4.1, pp.5/13: cells store low/high edges and ordered unique left/right boundary point lists. Closed cells have both sides; open cells have no right side yet. Safe part consists of strict interior plus lateral points strictly between low/high edges excluding recorded unsafe points. Owned part excludes bottom and left boundaries, allowing unique ownership even when cells meet. Safety is not a claim that every boundary point is free. §§3–4, pp.5–8: scan state stores vertically arranged open cells as prefix/last/suffix, closed cells with the last one separate, and cached last x/high edge. Initial processing needs a first event strictly beyond the left boundary to construct a first closed cell. Event preparation uses insertion sort merging equal positions, then separately sorts outgoing edges when processing each event. Recursion consumes the finite event list; no asymptotic complexity theorem is reported. §4, pp.6–8: event order is lexicographic in x then y. Four branches distinguish x advance, same x above the last high edge, same x below it, and same x on it. Same-x handling updates/discards would-be zero-width cells and preserves old unsafe-side points. Vertical alignment of separate events is supported, while vertical obstacle segments remain excluded. §4.5/second_phase_safety, pp.9–10: eight prerequisites are well-formed box, permitted endpoint-only intersections among boundaries/edges, inside-box events, strict lexicographic event ordering, outgoing edges starting at their event, later events covering right endpoints, no event in an edge interior, and duplicate-free outgoing lists. Each resulting cell has center strictly inside, well-formed side lists and safe part disjoint from unsafe events/edges. Isolated events are supported by this more general contract. §4.5/two_phase_safety, p.10: composing preparation with processing reduces prerequisites to well-formed box, unique edges, endpoint-only intersections including box edges, and all edge points inside the box. The conclusion gives interior center, side well-formedness and obstacle avoidance for every returned cell. Input preparation must preserve the original edges, since safety relative only to the generated event set could otherwise omit an obstacle. §5.1, p.11: generic_trajectories avoids Mathematical Components structures and drops the dependent edge proof field for extraction. Proof files instantiate this same generic algorithm with field operations via notations and generalize theorems across sections. Rational implementation uses integer numerator/positive denominator. No verified foreign-function wrapper, machine-integer overflow proof or independent extraction replay is provided in this reading. §5.2, pp.11–12: six nested invariant groups describe open cells/remaining events; cache consistency and event/edge relationships; special last open cell; disjointness/nonempty cells; coverage of processed obstacles by high boundaries; and safe lateral-side exclusions. A preliminary proof under no vertically aligned events verified fewer branches; the main result described here is the stronger proof including degeneracies. §5.3, pp.12–13: pairwise order of all earlier/later open-cell high edges replaces relying on adjacent sortedness under a nontransitive relation. Projection comparisons require the point x coordinate to be in both edge cylinders. These assumptions make local geometric order reasoning sound. §5.4, pp.13–15: unique owned parts and coverage of each processed obstacle by cell high boundaries imply interior safety by contradiction. An interior point on an obstacle would belong to its own cell and a distinct boundary-covering cell. Separate invariants show events appear in side lists, and inherited side hazards survive degenerate replacements. Disjoint ownership does not imply closed cells have no shared boundary. §§1/6.1, pp.3/16–17: proof does not establish union of owned parts covers the box or that adjacent cells with a safe passage share a represented door. Tests reportedly support both properties, with no described count/distribution/ground truth. Missing either could cause the application to miss an existing path. Per-cell nonemptiness does not prove the output list is nonempty or complete. §6, pp.16–17: integration in a larger path tool assesses usability, but path search, smoothing with Bezier curves and full trajectory proof are outside this paper. Proof effort is almost 15000 lines in 12 files. No runtime, memory, compilation time, hardware, systematic benchmark or independently reproduced build is reported. Adjacency lookup currently scans all cells; cached neighbours, vertical/crossing obstacles and trajectory verification are future work.

- FRAIG-BMC (2025)
    - title: FRAIG-BMC: Functional Reduction to Speed Up Bounded Model Checking
    - what: Introduces FRAIG-BMC, an on-the-fly functional-reduction procedure integrated into each BMC unrolling. It simplifies trivial logic, reuses structurally hashed nodes, and SAT-checks simulation-equivalent nodes before CNF encoding, reducing variables and clauses while preserving the BMC property check. The algorithm maintains an unrolled-AIG-node to SAT-variable map and performs three ordered reductions: constant/idempotent AND simplification, structural hashing, then simulation equivalence classes checked by SAT. Equivalences are checked across time frames, which a standalone pre-BMC FRAIG cannot exploit. For constrained properties Ck, the paper adds filtered random simulation over the constraint cone of influence and a SAT-sampling alternative with blocking clauses and optional random unit clauses. Large equivalence classes are capped and treated as unique to avoid excessive checking. The implementation extends AIGER aigbmc with CaDiCaL and compares it to CaDiCaL-backed baseline and ABC-BMC3 on SEC, partial-retention (PartRet), and information-flow (IFC) benchmarks.
    - number: SEC Table I includes 17 named cases; FRAIG-BMC reaches bound 243 on i2c and 907 on ss pcm
    - number: SEC cases show hundreds of thousands to over one million trivial/structural merges (e.g., des3 area 597,798 trivial and 1,069,415 structural)
    - number: time limit 3,600 seconds; server Intel Xeon 8375C, 256 GB memory
    - number: PartRet 61 cases and IFC 56 cases according to figure captions
    - limits: The method targets bit-level AIG transition systems and safety properties checked to finite bounds; it does not establish unbounded safety. Functional equivalence is relative to the current simulation candidates and then validated by SAT, while constrained simulation assumes constraints can be represented and sampled from their cone. An excessively large equivalence class is deliberately not fully checked, trading possible reductions for runtime. Benchmarks contain repeated circuit copies and all runs use a 3,600-second timeout on one 256-GB Xeon server, so gains may depend on structural redundancy and hardware.

- Ganesha-Chakrabarti CRV SEU hardening (2025)
    - title: A Formal Verification Approach to Safeguard Controller Variables from Single Event Upset
    - what: Defines conditionally relevant variables (CRVs): variables whose single-event-upset bit flip can change a controller safety-property result. It combines static slicing with CBMC bounded model checking, instrumenting a shadow program and one nondeterministic bit flip per candidate variable; a counterexample establishes relevance while no violation establishes irrelevance within the bound. The paper gives a two-case formal CRV definition covering both upset-induced violation and upset-masked violation, a concrete instrumentation algorithm that duplicates the program and asserts XOR disagreement of safety outcomes, and a compiler-facing selective-hardening workflow. In three C benchmarks, slicing retained 4 relevant variables in each case; CBMC removed 1, 2, and 1 false positives for motivating, temperature-control, and fan-speed programs respectively, with reported efficiencies of 25%, 50%, and 25%.

Safety is a domain-provided output property, often weaker than functional correctness; the method models one bit flip at one use and uses bounded model checking. Experiments are three small single-procedure C programs (30 or 45 LoC), Frama-C 30.0 and CBMC 5.12; no industrial-scale or complete-state-space validation. Future work is interprocedural analysis, other model checkers, and automated safety-property derivation.

- GOL in GOL in HOL: Verified Circuits in Conway’s Game of Life (2025)
    - what: HOL4 proof that an infinite tiling of Game of Life mega-cells simulates ordinary Game of Life. A compiler maps arbitrary initial GOL states to detailed circuits; after n×60×586 low-level steps, sampling one designated pixel per 3150×3150 mega-cell recovers exactly n original steps. Modular I/O semantics, symbolic gate proofs, delayed-signal abstraction and proof-producing circuit assembly account for geometry and signal propagation. Records the exact sampling theorem, three coordinate/time scales, partial I/O runs and cancellation, phase-dependent port ownership, exact versus approximate signal semantics, delayed half-adder issue, deferred crossover/connection proof obligations, infinite tiling, external symbolic discovery versus kernel confirmation, and 512-case high-level truth check. The result includes transport delays and clock windows but not physical hardware or asynchronous execution.
    - limits: §§1.1/3.1, pp.2/7: states are sets of live cells over the unbounded integer plane. All cells update synchronously under standard eight-neighbour B3/S23 rules. The theorem quantifies over arbitrary input sets, not only finite patterns. No bounded-grid boundary, stochastic update, asynchronous schedule, physical implementation or finite machine overflow model is included. §2/4.1, pp.5/9: tiles are 150×150 low-level cells; coordinates for ports/gates use 75-cell half-tile units, and gate centers are double-even. A mega-cell is 21×21 tiles, or 3150×3150 cells. One circuit tick is 60 GOL generations. One simulated update takes 586 ticks, hence 35160 low-level generations. Spatial scale is not a count of live cells or a measured memory footprint. §3.2, p.7: the area of influence includes all cells within Chebyshev distance one of a live cell. Disjoint influence regions suffice for one-step evolution of a union to equal the union of evolutions. This condition is deliberately stronger than necessary. Runs need composition arguments; disjointness at time zero alone is not a perpetual noninteraction theorem. §§3.3–3.4, p.8: io_step first requires influence within the owned region, executes ordinary step, checks specified output-region contents, then deletes outputs/inserts inputs. It is functional but partial: an assertion or boundary failure prevents a run. run requires every finite prefix to exist under the prescribed modifier sequence. Assertions express observed behaviour; indefinite run is part of the proved component specification. §4.2, pp.9–10: each tick has two 30-generation phases. North/south port transfer occurs halfway through; east/west transfer occurs after 60. Ownership flips between producer and consumer around transfers. This phase separation and 60 rather than 30 generation stream spacing permit noncolliding crossovers; identical geometric crossings without timing assumptions are not valid. §4.3, pp.10–11: binary composition requires disjoint owned tile areas and matching port direction/position/entire signal at internal boundaries. The result unions areas, ports and initial patterns. Internalization removes matched ports from both input/output sets without changing initial pattern; at modifier level matching assertions, insertions and deletions recover ordinary GOL. Infinitary composition handles arbitrary sets of circuits. §4.4, pp.11–12: delays do not generally commute with logical identities involving repeated signals at different ages. The raw half-adder formula depends on a at delays 12/15 and b at delays 15/18; one cannot simply erase delay annotations and claim exact XOR at all ticks. Approximate values allow arbitrary transients and track settling deadlines within each simulated-clock stability budget. §4.4, p.12: approximate values are boolean expressions over nearby simulated cells, indexed by mega-cell position. Refinement means inclusion of the sets of permitted streams; a smaller settling deadline refines a larger one. Exact values are limited combinations of clock and current-state signals, with integer time shifts extending into the past. This supports negative shifts mathematically without negative low-level simulation steps. §4.4/5.2, pp.12/16: the exact clock is high for 22 ticks per period of 586. The current-state signal holds each macro-state for 586 ticks. Delayed gates consume the stability window, and an exact clock/latch masks transient data and retains the next state. Special rules require timing inequalities and equality with the particular nextCell formula. Values outside supported operations become top, which admits every stream and therefore cannot certify a meaningful sampled result by itself. §§4.5–4.6, pp.13–15: floodfill tracks occupied even half-tile positions within [0,42)², multisets of unmatched inputs/outputs, pending crossover ports and gate placements. Adding regular gates matches all input values against known outputs; crossovers can be staged one input at a time. Teleport reindexes streams across copies separated by 42 half-tiles; it is neighbour communication in an already infinite tiling, not physical instantaneous transport. §4.6, pp.14–15: floodfill has existential input/output streams and universal admissible crossover streams, plus position/direction uniqueness and conditional matching obligations. Intermediate placement can leave unresolved outputs, but the circuit_run consequence is guarded by connection completeness. Unmatched outputs are proof obligations; the final cancellation discharges them. Individual gate validity is also required. §5.1, pp.15–16: SML first searches for a symbolic steady state outside kernel inference. The proof assistant then checks one complete tick of that symbolic state and confirms equality with every variable aged by one, yielding arbitrary repeated-tick behaviour. Boolean cell updates enumerate all assignments to relevant local variables, simplify to expressions, and use fast kernel computation. Discovery code need not be trusted for correctness of accepted theorems. §5.2, p.16: an SML program parses an ASCII gate diagram, inserts initial clock/latch gates, traverses outputs depth first, stages crossings and reindexes boundary outputs. It repeatedly applies proved floodfill lemmas and simplifies concrete side conditions. nextCell correctness is checked over all 512 configurations of center plus eight neighbours. The final two outputs match and cancel the two initial inputs. Final theorem, p.17: for every n and input S, step^n(S)=read_mega_cells(step^(n×60×586)(build_mega_cells S)). Sampling selects p when 3150p+(1726,599) is live. Two mega-cell variants differ in latch state. The theorem guarantees sampled-state equality at designated times, not that intermediate circuitry resembles the macro-state at all times or that off-the-shelf simulator code itself is verified. §6, p.17: roughly 9500 LOC is author-reported proof effort. No benchmark timings, build duration, hardware, gate count, live-cell counts, formalization-person effort or independent simulator replay is provided. The source snapshot is available; no source inspection or kernel replay was done in this reading. Formal links to traditional universality models and generalization to other automata/hardware remain future work.
