    - title: A Certified Proof Checker for Deep Neural Network Verification in Imandra
    - what: Implements and formally proves a checker for Marabou UNSAT certificate trees in the Imandra functional language and interactive theorem prover. DNN queries are represented as affine tableau equations, bounds and ReLU constraints. The checker parses inductive proof trees with ReLU or single-variable splits, updates child bounds, and checks Farkas contradiction vectors at leaves. A polynomial Farkas lemma and its DNN specialization connect negative linear combinations to UNSAT; covering lemmas show every satisfying assignment falls into one split child, enabling functional induction over the tree. The formalization includes 2,113 lines and 267 auxiliary lemmas. SAT assignments remain directly checkable; this work certifies UNSAT trees.

Imandra’s arbitrary-precision arithmetic avoids floating-point error but costs time and uses list-based structures.     - title: LeanLTL: A Unifying Framework for Linear Temporal Logics in Lean
    - what: Presents a Lean 4 temporal-logic library with a shared semantic representation for finite and infinite nonempty traces, arbitrary Lean propositions/data expressions, LTL-like macro notation, and preliminary simplification-based automation. Gives machine-checked embeddings of LTL and LTLf and a traffic-light safety/liveness example. Trace uses an Option-valued sequence N→Option σ, extended natural length, nonemptiness proof, and a proof that values are defined exactly before length. TraceSet is a predicate on traces; TraceFun maps a trace to Option α, with strong/weak get interpreting undefined values as False/True. The LLTL macro recursively rewrites host connectives, pushes next into trace-function arrows, binds strong gets before weak gets, and coerces remaining propositions/predicates into trace sets. The push_ltl simp set translates satisfaction into first-order semantics so existing Lean tactics can finish arithmetic obligations; Figure 1 proves an invariant of the recurrence n=5 initially and n_next=n² by globally_induction and nlinarith. LTL/LTLf embeddings use inductive syntax, evaluation, translation, and a satisfaction-equivalence theorem. The traffic-light example includes queue arithmetic and environment assumptions, proving exactly one light green globally and both lights green infinitely often for traces satisfying those assumptions.
    - number: 9-page short paper; Lean 4; tagged artifact vITP25
    - number: two traffic lights with queue/arrival/departure fields
    - number: no empirical performance or agent-evaluation numbers
    - limits: Discrete linear time; all traces are nonempty. Finite-trace strong/weak next and exceptional TraceFun accesses need deliberate truth-value handling. Arbitrary Lean theories improve expressivity but do not provide general decidability or a fully automated procedure. Automation is an initial simp-based prototype; integration of LTL/LTLMT solvers, formal embeddings for LTLMT/LTLfMT, and past/bounded-time operators are future work. The traffic-light system behavior is assumed from external specifications; complete example/embedding proofs are in the cited software repository rather than fully printed in the short paper. No repository execution, solver speed comparison, distributed implementation, or agent evaluation was performed in this reading.

    - what: # Whole reading: PyCaliper (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  This CAV 2025 paper supplies hardware specification/synthesis infrastructure and two case studies. Its directly relevant LLM result is GPT-4o ordering existing invariant candidates under formal-oracle checks. The record below separates source reports from reader interpretations and preserves scope limits.  Source report: PyCaliper is a Python-embedded domain-specific language (DSL) and infrastructure for register-transfer-level (RTL) hardware specification, verification-backend integration and invariant synthesis. The paper contributes an extensible common specification/oracle interface and two case studies. Its algorithms build on existing incremental invariant synthesis and counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS). Reader assessment: no new soundness/completeness theorem, mechanized correctness proof of the framework, or general distributed-system verification result is presented. The framework delegates checks to existing proof engines. [Q1, Q2, Q13]  Source excerpt — §1 Related Work and Figure 1; physical PDF p.3, printed p.410, [paper.raw.txt:96](paper.raw.txt#L96):  ```text PyCaliper on the other hand, is not a veriﬁcation tool in itself: our main contribution is Python-embedded infrastructure that enables programmatic RTL speciﬁcation and interfaces with (SVA and BTOR2)-based veriﬁcation engines. We use these veriﬁers as oracles to implement invariant synthesis techniques such as syntax-guided synthesis via CEGIS [3] and incremental invariant synthesis [11,36] (the latter itself uses an approach based on PDR). ```  Source report: SpecModule/Struct/Group/Logic/LogicArray mirror RTL modules and signals. input, state and output mean global assumptions, state invariants and output assertions. A miter is two copies of the design; eq and conditional eq relate their signals, while inv is a single-copy assertion. The displayed inductive obligation is input(S) ∧ state(S) ∧ T(S,S′) ⇒ state(S′) ∧ output(S′). Reader qualification: this is preservation under the assumed invariant; the formula does not itself show that every reachable initial state satisfies state. The SVA harness includes clock/reset assumptions, but the paper does not provide a separate base-case proof or a complete initialization-semantics argument. Correct results depend on correct assumptions, RTL mapping, translation, solver and oracle handling. [Q3, Q4, Q7, Q8]  Source excerpt — §2.1 Specifications and Figure 2; physical PDF p.4, printed p.411, [paper.raw.txt:141](paper.raw.txt#L141):  ```text Inductive Specification. Inductive speciﬁcations in PyCaliper consist of three components: input, state, and output blocks. These correspond to global assumptions, the state invariants, and output assertions, respectively. In general, the input, state, and output functions can be thought of as predicates over the state of the RTL design. ```  Source examples: Figure 2 gives a parameterized FIFO specification for no stale-data leakage: equal control signals and pushed input data, equal pointers and selected live storage entries, and equal output data when nonempty. These are printed schematic examples with omitted code, not separately measured case studies. Figure 3 uses @unroll(2): assume two chosen input constants at step 0 and assert the adder output at step 1 while reset is deasserted. Reader qualification: the printed Python randomly chooses constants before the bounded check, so that illustration alone does not cover every input pair. It computes sum(vals) % MAX with 32-bit constants, but MAX is undefined in the displayed excerpt; the exact wrap modulus is unspecified. [Q3, Q5]  Source excerpt — §2.1 bounded specifications, Figure 3; §2.2; physical PDF p.6, printed p.413, [paper.raw.txt:197](paper.raw.txt#L197):  ```text Example 1. Figure 3 provides an exam- ple for an Adder module in which the simstep function speciﬁes that the output with two (randomly chosen) inputs a and b equals a + b modulo wrap-around. ```  Source report: elaboration introspects Python objects and resolves hierarchical paths, e.g. a UART tx_fifo.wr_ptr. Parameterized FIFO depth/width can be packaged as a Python library. Section 2.3 presents input-side and output-side implication obligations under a relation R and illustrates FIFO refinement to a Counter. Only synchronous lock-step module transitions are currently supported; stuttering is discussed as a more general form. Reader qualification: the displayed implications alone are not a full transition-simulation proof; initialization and preservation of R are not separately established in this paper. The printed FIFO/Counter relation is preserved in rendered transcriptions without correcting its direct pointer/incdec equalities. [Q5, Q6, Q7]  Source excerpt — §2.3 lock-step restriction; §3.1; Figure 4; physical PDF p.8, printed p.415, [paper.raw.txt:264](paper.raw.txt#L264):  ```text PyCaliper currently supports reﬁnement proofs where both M1 and M2 mod- ules transition synchronously in lock-step. In general, reﬁnement relations may allow one module to stutter, i.e., not transition while the other module tran- sitions. Such stuttering reﬁnement [16,32] can be used to relate two modules that have similar functional behaviors but diﬀerent timing behaviors. For exam- ple, Burch-Dill reﬁnement [33] allows veriﬁcation of a pipelined processor design against its non-pipelined counterpart. ```  Source report: the SVA backend emits a clock/reset harness and a k-step counter, compiles assumptions and assertions, and invokes the licensed Jasper FPV App through TCP/Tcl. Its oracle enables/disables assumptions, covers/checks properties and retrieves traces. The BTOR2 backend uses Yosys lowering with memory flattening, hierarchy removal and technology mapping, retains signal-name correspondence, symbolically unrolls the design and checks bit-vector formulas with Boolector. Other engines/solvers are proposed through interface/operator extensions; the paper does not report an implemented SymbiYosys backend. Reader assessment: the comparison measures two concrete integrations; it does not verify translation correctness or establish equivalence of all engine results independently. [Q7, Q8]  Source excerpt — §3.1 oracle; §3.2 BTOR2; §4.1; Table 3; physical PDF p.9, printed p.416, [paper.raw.txt:306](paper.raw.txt#L306):  ```text PyCaliper currently supports the (licensed) Jasper Formal Property Ver- iﬁcation (Jasper FPV) App [13] as the proof engine. However, we can enable support for other engines (e.g., open-source tools such as SymbiYosys [15]) by implementing the oracle interface. PyCaliper interacts with Jasper FPV via a TCP interface which is used to send Tcl commands (e.g., prove P_asrt for a check queries) and receive responses. ```  Source report: ceqhole searches for a conjunction of conditional equalities selected from a supplied signal list. Its fuel-limited incremental search maintains speculative assumptions and relatively inductive assertions, adds candidates via a strategy, saturates provable assertions, backtracks, and succeeds only when a self-inductive set proves output. Running out of candidates or fuel can fail. ctrlhole searches a bounded-size control-to-dependent-signal lookup table using traces, then checks inductiveness; counterexamples refine the trace set, and unsatisfiable trace constraints increase table size up to a bound. Reader qualification: these are template-restricted searches; unsuccessful bounded search does not show no invariant exists. The two reported experiments do not benchmark ctrlhole/CEGIS. This is a discrepancy in the paper presentation; author code was not inspected, so the implemented guard and its behavior are unknown. No repaired rule is asserted. [Q9, Q10]  Source excerpt — §4.1 synthesis target; §4.2 incremental synthesis; Figure 5; physical PDF p.10, printed p.417, [paper.raw.txt:364](paper.raw.txt#L364):  ```text The algorithm admits a fuel parameter f∗ that imposes an upper bound on |assms| − |assrts| during the search. Intuitively, a higher f∗ allows for more speculative guessing (with higher coverage), while a lower f∗ forces the algorithm to be more conservative. ```  Source report: domain tags are added to an open-source TAGE indirect-branch predictor so an entry is used only in its creating privilege domain. The stated checked property assumes privileged true targets targ_i < BDRY and an invariant that every PRIV-tagged table target is below BDRY; it asserts prev_mode = PRIV ⇒ targ_o < BDRY. Both backends reportedly verify this using 2-induction. Reader qualification: the formal claim is a privileged-target range property under those assumptions. It does not itself assert full target correctness, independence from all attacker-controlled state, whole-processor security, or complete prevention of every branch-target-injection behavior. No attack experiment, independent proof-certificate check or reproduction was performed here. [Q11, Q12]  Source excerpt — §5.1 IsoTAGE security property and two backends; physical PDF p.12, printed p.419, [paper.raw.txt:428](paper.raw.txt#L428):  ```text We formalize this as a property that says that provided the true branch target in privileged mode (PRIV) is in the valid kernel-code segment (less than a boundary BDRY), the generated prediction is also in the valid kernel-code segment. Formally, we iden- tify the inductive speciﬁcation: ```  Source measurements: Table 4 varies BHT_WIDTH from 4 through 9. SVA total/solve/parse seconds are 4.0/2.6/1.4 at width 4 and 12.7/11.4/1.3 at width 9. BTOR2 is 3.6/2.6/1 at width 4 and 753.9/11.9/742 at width 9; all six rows are saved in evaluation.json. BTOR2 program statements grow 5,465→116,186 and elements 598→14,486. Solving times are comparable in these cases; total BTOR2 time becomes dominated by parsing, and is slightly lower than SVA only at width 4. The authors call the Python-based parser a likely cause; no parser ablation establishes causation. Hardware, software versions, repetitions, run uncertainty and precise timing boundaries are not supplied. These figures support a bottleneck diagnosis for this benchmark family, not a broad solver ranking. [Q11, Q12]  Source excerpt — §5.1 IsoTAGE security property and two backends; physical PDF p.12, printed p.419, [paper.raw.txt:438](paper.raw.txt#L438):  ```text Interestingly, we observe that the solving times (ST) of the BTOR2 backend (using the Boolector solver [12]) is comparable to SVA backend using the Jasper FPV App. However, the parse time (PT) is where BTOR2 backend falls behind. This is likely due to the fact that we currently use a Python-based btor2 parsing library - we plan to report this result and improve the parsing performance. This insightful comparison was possible due to PyCaliper’s compatibility with both veriﬁcation backends. ```  Source report: DAWG dynamically partitions cache ways to prevent cross-domain information leakage, formulated as noninterference. Prior work manually supplied invariants. This experiment synthesizes k out of 8 cache-way invariants for k=2,3,4 as invariant width increases. It compares built-in random ordering against GPT-4o ordering of existing candidates, given current invariants and the partitioning property. The authors report about 80 Python lines and 30 minutes of human effort to add that strategy. Reader qualification: this LLM supplies a search heuristic; it is not reported to invent the desired property, write arbitrary invariants, prove a theorem or produce a verified Rust/TLA+ specification. Backend oracle checks determine acceptance. [Q12]  Source excerpt — §5.1 Table 4; §5.2 DAWG and GPT-4o strategy; Table 5; physical PDF p.13, printed p.420, [paper.raw.txt:467](paper.raw.txt#L467):  ```text We attempt two strategies for selecting the invariant candidate order: random (in-built) and a custom (rudimentary) neural strategy. In the latter, we prompt an LLM (gpt-4o) to provide an order of candidates, providing the current set of invariants and the cache partitioning property as context. Implementing this strategy with PyCaliper required ∼80 lines of Python code and around 30 min of human eﬀort. ```  Source measurements: Table 5 reports means ±σ over 20 runs using the SVA backend and Jasper FPV. For k=2, random/neural verification calls are 16.7±2.3 / 14.3±2.6 and nodes 5.5±0.6 / 4.9±0.9. For k=3, calls are 101.6±47.1 / 54.0±21.8 and nodes 13.3±5.5 / 8.5±3.9. For k=4, calls are 785.7±91.2 / 163±74.2 and nodes 54.3±4.8 / 11.6±8.6. Reader assessment: this shows lower mean search/oracle effort in three configurations on this design. The paper does not report end-to-end wall time, LLM/API cost, exact prompt/model snapshot/temperature, random seeds, fuel setting, success/failure counts or held-out designs. It supplies no statistical significance test or measured generalization claim. These counts cannot establish overall speedup or cost savings after LLM overhead. [Q12]  Source excerpt — §5.1 Table 4; §5.2 DAWG and GPT-4o strategy; Table 5; physical PDF p.13, printed p.420, [paper.raw.txt:484](paper.raw.txt#L484):  ```text We use the SVA-backend with the Jasper FPV App as the veriﬁcation engine. We see that even our very rudimentary neural strategy outperforms the random strat- egy, likely by being able to detect a pattern in the invariants using the provided context. The takeaways from this experiment are twofold. Firstly, PyCaliper allows leveraging industry-scale backends as veriﬁcation oracles in an invariant synthesis task. Secondly, PyCaliper uses the Python ecosystem to enable easy prototyping of new ideas. ```  Reader synthesis: directly useful for LLM-assisted formal-verification evaluation: separate a heuristic candidate proposal/order from a trusted verification oracle, constrain the search language, expose assumptions and search budgets, and distinguish oracle-call count from end-to-end runtime/cost. - Model Checking and Synthesis for Optimal Use of Knowledge in Consensus Protocols (2025)
    - what: # Model Checking and Synthesis for Optimal Use of Knowledge in Consensus Protocols (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Alpturer, Huang and van der Meyden use MCK to check whether small synchronous consensus protocols decide as soon as their available information permits, and synthesize concrete decision predicates from knowledge-based programs. The contribution is empirical and methodological. They “do not attempt to give a full characterization or a proof” of general optimality (§1, p.3, Q3). The 22-page arXiv 2505.02353v1 is the full version of the PODC 2025 paper, ACM pp.131–140, DOI 10.1145/3732772.3733552 (Q37; saved arXiv metadata). No new parameterized proof or new synthesis engine is presented.  ## Assumptions and specification (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The system has synchronous message rounds and two layers: an information exchange defines observed state, messages and updates; a decision protocol chooses noop or a decision. Failures are crashes or sending omissions. A crashing agent can send an arbitrary subset of its messages in the crash round and then sends nothing; an omission-faulty agent can omit sends but receives messages sent to it (§3, pp.5–6, Q6–Q7). “Byzantine Agreement” names the coordination problem here; the experiments do not evaluate arbitrary malicious message values, asynchronous scheduling or a cryptographic implementation.  The base simultaneous agreement specification requires at most one decision per agent, agreement at the same time among nonfaulty agents, and a decision value initially held by some agent, possibly faulty. The paper explicitly says “termination is not a requirement of this specification,” while reporting additional termination checks in its scripts (§4, p.6, Q8). Eventual agreement permits different decision times (§8, Q20). These distinctions matter when calling a synthesized result correct.  Optimality is relative to the same information exchange and failure model, comparing runs with identical initial preferences and failure patterns (§4, p.7, Q9). The paper distinguishes an optimum protocol, which decides no later than every competitor, from an optimal protocol, which no competitor systematically improves. This is not optimality across arbitrary messaging designs or execution costs. The semantic order as printed compares every agent; this record does not silently narrow its quantifier to nonfaulty agents.  MCK uses finite variables and ordered binary decision diagrams. The chosen clock semantics gives an agent its current observable variables plus the time, rather than perfect recall. Synthesis replaces boolean template variables with local predicates equivalent to knowledge tests (§6, pp.8–9, Q11–Q12). Uniqueness under clock semantics and the optimality characterizations are attributed to prior theory, not proved anew. EBA’s simpler knowledge-based program P0 also requires technical side conditions on information exchange: learning 0 through decision-message chains and suitable possibilities involving nonfaulty agents (§8, pp.11–12, Q20).  ## Concrete cases and results (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Four SBA information exchanges are modeled: FloodSet, FloodSet plus current received-message count, the Count variant plus previous count (“Diff”), and the concrete Dwork–Moses protocol. Two EBA exchanges, Emin and Ebasic, respectively send decision values and additionally send initial 1 messages with a count. The models have parameters n agents, t maximum failures and the decision-value set. The main FloodSet/Count timing table fixes two values (§§7–11, Q13–Q28).  FloodSet retains values seen and broadcasts their union. The naive earliest-knowledge hypothesis t+1 fails at n=3,t=2. Revised Eq 2 uses time=n−1 when t≥n−1, otherwise t+1; model checking and synthesis agree in the instances checked (§7.1, pp.9–10, Q14–Q15). The authors report an all-n proof in companion work [7]; this read does not include that proof (Q17). Adding the current message count exposes the early condition count≤1, meaning only the agent’s own message was received (§7.2, Q16). Diff gave no stronger SBA stopping condition than Count in checked cases, although previous-count memory can help a different EBA specification (§7.3, Q18).  The printed Count formula needs reconciliation at a boundary. Eq 3 uses “time = t” in its t≥n−1 branch (§7.2, p.10, Q16), whereas FloodSet Eq 2 uses time=n−1 (Q14). At n=3,t=3,time=2,count=3, Eq 2 is true and Eq 3 false. Count adds an observation while retaining FloodSet’s values and clock; its stated earliest condition should not require later knowledge on that account. No-crash histories allow count 3 even when t=3 is the failure upper bound. This is a reader-derived discrepancy in the printed conditions, not a replayed MCK counterexample or a refutation of the companion theorem. The benchmark inputs needed to resolve it were not obtained. The source’s formulas are retained unchanged in Q14/Q16 and static-witnesses.json.  There is a second printed EBA ambiguity. Ebasic’s jd update stores 0 on receiving 0 and otherwise ⊥, but its decision 1 rule includes “jd𝑖 = 1” (§9.2, pp.12–13, Q22). Under that update description the jd=1 branch cannot be reached. I have not silently repaired the update or inferred which rule the actual model used.  Appendix A gives a complete FloodSet synthesis example for n=3,t=1,two values. It uses finite time 0..3, communicates while time<2 and has four decision templates for knowledge times 1 and 2 (pp.18–21, Q32–Q35). The reported output makes both time 1 predicates false; at time 2 the predicate for v is values_received[v], with 0 taking priority in the decision code. The authors report that the accompanying formulas all hold (p.22, Q36). State at time m means information after round m; the decision follows in the next modeled round (§7, Q13). This accounts for the appendix’s AX3 completion check.  The appendix checks ordinary and uniform agreement, validity and termination at AX3, and knowledge predicates. Its printed agreement formulas compare values when both agents have decided; they do not explicitly require simultaneous decided flags (Q34). Thus the displayed formulas alone are not a direct check of every SBA clause. The knowledge-based theory may establish simultaneity; no counterexample to the synthesized protocol is claimed. Likewise the finite AX3 termination check is not a general unbounded liveness proof. The appendix uses currently ALIVE agents in knowledge tests, which should not be casually substituted for permanently nonfaulty agents without the cited crash-theory correspondence.  ## Evaluation and limits (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The experiments used one core of a 3.7 GHz six-core Intel Core i5 with 256 KB L2, 9 MB L3 and 32 GB memory. The final run’s timeout was 10 minutes (§10, p.13, Q23). Early exploratory trials sometimes ran 5 hours or 2 days; those are not the table timeout. No MCK build/version, BDD variable ordering, repetition count, variance, raw trial set or memory measurements are supplied. The measured costs are model-checking and synthesis runtime, not consensus latency or deployment throughput.  All three timing tables are transcribed with printed values and converted seconds in numeric-evidence.json: 16 parameter rows in Table 1, 15 in Table 2 and 6 in Table 3, totaling 118 timing cells. TO remains a timeout rather than a measured 600-second completion. Representative results show the steep scaling:  - FloodSet at n=5,t=2: checking 34.635 seconds, synthesis 162.015 seconds; synthesis times out at n=5,t≥3. Checking still finishes at n=6,t=1 in 72.863 seconds, while n=6,t=2 times out (Table 1, Q24) - Count at n=4,t=2: checking 23.328 seconds, synthesis 120.892 seconds; synthesis times out for t=3/4 and both tasks time out at n=5 in the listed rows (Table 1) - Diff at n=3 takes roughly 258–304 seconds depending on failure bound/rounds; Dwork–Moses times out for every listed n=3 case. Both time out at n=4,t=1,one round (Table 2, Q26) - Emin EBA synthesis succeeds through the listed n=3 cases, with crash costs 31.219–178.142 seconds and omission costs 11.371–66.735 seconds. Every n=4,t=1 cell times out. Ebasic succeeds only at n=2 in Table 3 (Q28)  Table 3’s prose says Emin scales to 4 agents before blowup, then names Emin again for the worse count-containing model. The table has no successful 4-agent row, and §9.2 attributes the extra count to Ebasic. This record preserves the cells and flags the prose ambiguity instead of recording 4-agent success or swapping labels without evidence. Receiving/general omissions are reported to have similar successful cases, but no separate timing rows are provided (§11, Q28).  For comparison, the authors report 125 seconds for purely temporal SAT-based SBA checking of Dwork–Moses at n=5,t=4 (§13, p.16, Q30). This checks a different obligation with a different algorithm from the BDD epistemic runs, so it is not a like-for-like solver speedup. They suggest quadratic messages and BDD size explain the difficulty; the paper does not measure a causal ablation. Their conclusion is appropriately limited: “a manual proof of correctness and optimality will” still be needed for all numbers of agents and failures (Q30).  ## Contribution to the requested topic and evidence scope (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  This adds concrete epistemic verification and protocol-synthesis benchmarks for distributed consensus, including examples where stronger local observations permit earlier decisions but make automated analysis harder. It supports a workflow of synthesizing small instances, checking hypotheses on larger finite instances, then proving the general claim manually. That workflow is the authors’ proposal; this paper does not demonstrate LLM agents. There is no Verus or verified Rust experiment. Appendix A calls its nondeterministic transition construct “refinement calculus/TLA action style” (Q33); it does not report TLA+/TLC verification.  For LLM-generated specifications and proofs, I infer evaluation lessons from the record: state the failure and information-exchange scope, declare observation/recall semantics, distinguish agreement from simultaneous agreement, inspect every printed guard and boundary case, separate finite checking from general proofs, and retain timeouts and source/script mismatches. These are reader-derived lessons, not measured LLM results.  Read every one of 1099 layout-text lines, all 22 pages, all 39 references and the complete appendix input/output. Inspected 11 contact sheets and fullsize pages 10,13–15,19–22; the paper has three tables and no figures. The bundle retains 44 literal excerpts with line/character/page anchors, 19 diagnostics, all 37 timing rows and raw hashes. Local/official PDFs are byte-identical. The paper identifies no benchmark archive/repository link. The primary MCK site links a related consensus demonstration. I read its page/loader and all 551 logical lines (550 newline characters) of four static source scripts: FloodSet, optimized FloodSet, Count and Dwork–Moses. They are pinned by content hashes and fetch times; no direct association with the paper’s benchmark version was established.     - title: Model Checking as Program Verification by Abstract Interpretation
    - what: Introduces MOKA, a Kleene-algebra/fixpoint language encoding ACTL and universal modal µ-calculus formulas as programs that enumerate counterexamples, then combines sound abstract interpretation with local-completeness logic and abstraction repair to eliminate false alarms. It lifts arbitrary state abstractions to stack abstractions, defines sound abstract interpreters, and extends Local Completeness Logic with least-fixpoint rules (µLCL). A failed local-completeness obligation guides Abstract Interpretation Repair by adding relational abstract elements; traffic-light and control-flow examples show a false alarm removed by refinement. - Nanopass Back-Translation of Call-Return Trees for Mechanized Secure Compilation Proofs (2025)
    - what: Rocq-verified back-translation from a finite well-formed collection of finite call/return trace prefixes into generated source whole programs sharing a context. Organizes the construction as initialization plus four small compiler passes over call-return trees, using identifiers, ghost call stacks and flattened rules before code generation. Proves each requested prefix can be produced by the back-translated source program. Handles stateful, arbitrarily reentrant callbacks and returns separated from their calls by nested interactions. Private loc, is_call and res distinguish external callbacks from internal recursion and recover the correct branch after a return. Separates determinacy and stack invariants across intermediate semantics, then relates ghost locations/stacks to concrete memory/frames. Gives an informal path to stronger finite-relational security, while explicitly leaving integration into a complete compilation-chain security theorem unmechanized.

The exposition assumes one procedure per compartment; the actual development supports multiple procedures and records procedure identifiers in call events. Fine-grained sharing of secure data/code pointers is future work. Theorem3 establishes inclusion of each requested finite prefix in generated-program behavior. It neither states equality of all trace sets nor forbids extra generated behavior, and it does not establish infinite-trace/liveness properties. It relies on the chosen trace/context/source-target models and the remaining compilation-chain proof. It does not directly translate the syntax of an arbitrary low-level adversary or prove that every original source program already behaves like the generated replacement. Reuse across languages and proof-effort improvements are author expectations/experience reports. Taint includes both explicit data dependence and writes in secret-controlled regions. Chain invariants prove uniform vertices cannot be dummy. Security transfer to lower IRs/assembly remains unproved, while a proposed memory relaxation has an explicit axiom and inconsistent location wording. The recovered prose is the same-paper deferred proof supplement, not a different paper or an implementation audit. Appendix A restates main-paper Claim 23 as supplement Claim 1. It defines c1≼c2 by ipd(c1)∈ir+(c2) and c1≺c2 by ipd(c1)∈ir(c2). Lemma 2 compares intersecting regions; Lemma 3 gives either a strict first comparison, a nonincreasing chain, or a shorter intersection chain. Strong induction proves that an intersection chain with ipd(c1)<idx ipd(ck) has some i with ipd(c1)∈ir(ci): the nonincreasing case contradicts the topological order, and the shorter case recurses. Figure 1 shows the three postdominator configurations. The text identifies development theorem chain_containment; no mechanized proof was opened or checked. Appendix B states recursive unicdep(v) through control-dependence edges c→w where v postdominates w but does not postdominate c, alongside uni(v) excluding secret conditions whose strict influence regions contain v. Lemma 5 maps control dependence into an influence region. Lemma 6 finds an appropriate controlling edge for influence-region membership. Theorem 7 proves ∀v, uni(v) iff unicdep(v), in both directions by topological-index induction; text names uni_cdep_equivalent in the development and says it is not required for the main proof. This establishes the stated equivalence with the notion in Hack and Moll’s Theorem 4.1 for the original graph under the inherited acyclic-graph setting. PCFL assumes a secret_cond labeling and guarantees a topological transformed graph, one successor at each secret condition, and detour_spec: each original edge v→w maps to v→detour(v,w), with w postdominating the new target. Postdominance alone needs progress/definedness and acyclicity to justify reaching the original target. - POPACheck: A Model Checker for Probabilistic Pushdown Automata (2025)
    - what: POPACheck translates finite-data recursive probabilistic MiniProb programs to probabilistic operator precedence automata and checks LTL plus a stack-aware POTL fragment. A support-chain semi-algorithm distinguishes positive nontermination from positively almost-sure termination using numerical upper bounds and expected-runtime certificates. Separated formula automata avoid determinization; experiments cover nested conditioning, games, branching populations and finite-array randomized search. Explains why numerical approximations alone cannot decide exact probability one, how finite expected time is stronger than almost-sure termination, why conditioned support-chain edges need probability ratios, and how stack-aware properties differ from ordinary trace order. Preserves finite data versus unbounded stack, incomplete decisions, all measured rows, two quantitative timeouts, approximate probabilities, formula/code mismatches and absent cross-tool comparison.
    - limits: §§1–2,4: pOPA is a subclass of probabilistic pushdown automata with finite control states and label-driven stack actions, while its induced Markov chain has unbounded stack configurations. MiniProb integers have a chosen finite bit width and arrays fixed size. Arbitrary chosen width does not mean unbounded integer values in a single model. Recursion/nested query depth can be unbounded; this is not arbitrary unbounded array or concurrent distributed-state verification. §2.1/Definition1: precedence matrix is total over labels; bottom symbol # yields to all program labels, so first move pushes. Push records current state/label, shift changes the top label, pop depends on current and saved state. The extra pop-label condition preserves precedence compatibility. Precedence relations are not assumed reflexive/transitive orders. These restrictions enable synchronized stack-aware formula products; do not replace the model by unrestricted pPDA and assume identical algorithms. §§1–2: observe failure rejects and restarts the current query. obs unwinds only to nearest qry boundary, preserving outer queries, so nested posterior sampling is modeled. A conditioning event of zero probability gives an ill-defined query, not an ordinary normalized posterior. Markov probabilities model specified sampling distributions; no adversarial scheduler or Markov decision-process strategy synthesis is evaluated. §2.2: supported logic is LTL and POTL_fχ, not all POTL. Atomic propositions include program events/function names and finite-variable arithmetic tests. Directional next and chain-future/until operators move through procedure frames. Call-return/postcondition matching can be context-free and beyond LTL. Full formal semantics/proofs are referred to [10,40], not fully redeveloped or mechanized here. §3.1: termination triple probabilities are least nonnegative fixed-point solutions of a monotone nonlinear polynomial system. Nontermination at node c is 1 minus the sum of termination outcomes. Support-chain states include only c with strictly positive nontermination; division by that positive quantity conditions push/shift/support probabilities. Support edges summarize finite nested runs. This chain captures limit behavior with the intended probabilistic construction, not a claim that all time-indexed observations can be erased without the formula-aware machinery. §3.1: upper bounds on termination give lower bounds on nontermination. A positive lower bound includes the node. Otherwise the algorithm tries a stronger certificate: stack symbol popped with probability one in finite expected time (PAST). A valid linear expected-time solution implies almost-sure termination (AST), excluding the node. Failure to prove PAST is inconclusive, not nontermination. AST with infinite expected time can fail this stronger test; no total decision procedure is claimed. §3.1: zero variables are removed through value iteration; decomposed Newton computes lower bounds. Upper bounds either satisfy lower<=v<=lower+epsilon and v>=f(v) in Z3, or come from optimistic value iteration initialized at the lower bound. SCC decomposition solves bottom-up. Exact epsilon, stopping tolerance, rational/floating implementation details and independent certificate validation protocol are not supplied in this tool paper, so printed approximate probabilities are not exact certified decimal values. §3.2: separated Büchi/omega-operator-precedence automata have disjoint languages from distinct starting states, allowing synchronized products without determinization. Qualitative checks analyze product SCCs; quantitative checks solve additional support-probability equations with OVI. Theoretical claims: singly exponential time in formula size, polynomial space in pOPA size for qualitative theory, and EXPSPACE for quantitative model checking, citing [40]. These are not guarantees that the implemented semi-algorithm terminates on every valid input. §4: function parameters pass by value or value-result; actual value-result arguments must be variable identifiers. Boolean operators treat zero as false. Bernoulli(e1,e2) has success probability e1/e2; Uniform(e1,e2) is stated half-open [e1,e2). Distributions need valid parameters; general C/Rust overflow, pointer aliasing and undefined behavior are not analyzed. Fig6 supports while, recursion, query and observe, not arbitrary source-language execution. §5: benchmark has three nested-query programs and 16 distinct Q formulas, yielding 20 program/formula rows, plus Sherwood with four S formulas and varied finite sizes. This is a demonstration suite, not a random production corpus. AMD 8-core 4.5GHz,64GB,Ubuntu24.04; one-hour timeout. No timing variance, independent replay or directly measured PRISM/Storm/PReMo/Pray comparison. PReMo/Pray are excluded because they only compute termination probabilities, which OVI handles below one second here. §5/Table3: all three OVI upper-bound runs are below one second, but Z3 times out on Schelling/Virus. Thus the blanket below-one-second prose concerns the chosen successful method, not every attempted solver. - Position: Formal Mathematical Reasoning—A New Frontier in AI (2025)
    - what: A position paper arguing that formal mathematics should complement language-model reasoning to supply checked reasoning steps, automatic training feedback and a path toward verified software/hardware generation. It organizes research challenges around data scarcity, faithful autoformalization, proof search, abstraction, retrieval, specification trust and proof maintenance. Its main original contribution is an agenda with separate levels for autoformalization, theorem proving, verified natural-language reasoning and verified system generation; it supplies no new proving algorithm, experiment or formal theorem. The paper separates producing a proof of a fixed formal statement from ensuring that the statement captures human intent. It proposes collecting human repairs and synchronizing informal/formal pairs, using semantic rather than string-match autoformalization metrics, comparing provers under explicit hardware/time budgets, growing libraries through useful subgoals and abstractions, and evaluating agents on projects and change histories. Software verification receives a distinct treatment: bespoke datatypes, repetitive case splits, large evolving codebases and specification management differ from isolated mathematical theorem proving. It discusses an alternative neural-only view and identifies self-verification and easy-to-hard generalization as unresolved prerequisites rather than demonstrated impossibilities.
    - limits: This is an explicitly selective position paper, not a systematic survey or controlled comparison. The claim that formal reasoning is indispensable and forecasts of lower verification cost are author positions, not results established by experiments in this paper. Formal proof checking establishes the exact encoded claim relative to the proof system, its assumptions and trusted implementation. The paper itself makes fidelity of generated specifications a key open problem; checker acceptance alone does not establish developer intent or correctness of the translation. The milestone levels are proposed organizing categories, with no validated thresholds, measured reliability requirements, human-cost study or proof that capability rises in the stated order. Theorem-proving level 2 explicitly includes human-built tactics without machine learning. Numbers about NuminaMath, Proof Pile, AlphaProof and seL4 are cited contextual examples, not new measurements. IMO 2025 claims are explicitly attributed to blogs/X without further details, and no such external evidence was fetched in this reading. The discussion of current systems is tied to the supplied 2025 proceedings version. Its model capability and benchmark-availability claims are historical author assessments, not a current exhaustive inventory. Arguments that informal scaling alone cannot resolve advanced mathematics and that neural-only self-verification remains weak draw on prior work; no impossibility theorem or decisive experiment rules out future neural-only systems. Software, hardware and mathematical verification are discussed broadly. Verus and AutoVerus appear as examples, but Rust memory/concurrency semantics, TLA+ specifications, distributed protocols and their fault assumptions are not evaluated. Formalizing or solving selected substeps while interleaving natural language does not by itself certify every unformalized claim or the full natural-language conclusion. This boundary follows from which parts are actually checked, not a new end-to-end guarantee shown here.

- PoWER (2025)
    - title: PoWER Never Corrupts: Tool-Agnostic Verification of Crash Consistency and Corruption Detection
    - what: PoWER encodes crash consistency as a precondition on each storage write: every durable state introduced by a partial write must be permitted by a ghost permission. Prophecy-based storage views and recovery-equivalent writes simplify proofs. A bounded-bit corruption model and an eight-byte corruption-detecting Boolean support atomic data/checksum updates. CapybaraKV in Verus and CapybaraNS in Dafny demonstrate the method, with coarse concurrent KV variants and performance comparisons. Records exact permission quantification, prophecy flush semantics, state versus transition and blanket versus single-use permissions, all four write strategies and concurrency restrictions. Includes correspondence-proof trust boundaries, CRC corruption bounds, Tick-Tock counterexample and CDB protocol, full type/LOC/startup/resource tables, all workload setups and adverse performance cases. Separates conditional detection from arbitrary-media-error recovery and reported proofs from independent proof replay.
    - number: CapybaraKV 5,531 executable / 14,255 spec+proof / 5,244 trusted lines; CapybaraNS 278 / 673 / 414
    - number: verification 54 s single-thread, 23 s eight-thread for KV, 12 s for NS
    - number: Table 2 KV total: 5244 trusted, 14255 spec/proof, 5531 implementation lines; notary 414/673/278
    - limits: Core technique requires Hoare pre/postconditions, ghost variables and quantification over crash states. Each asynchronous write requires all chunk-wise old/new durable outcomes to satisfy its permission; executable annotations erase. Soundness depends on every actual storage mutation using the controlled API, correctness of the storage model and a meaningful allowed-recovery predicate. A permission that allows all states proves no useful crash property. Natural storage semantics distinguish readable last-written bytes from outstanding writes. Atomic persistence chunks can survive independently until flush. The prophecy model instead stores read_state and one prophesized durable_state; write updates all readable bytes and chooses a subset of chunk subwrites for durable state. Flush constrains these two states to agree without changing either in the ghost model. This is a logical modeling device, not a runtime ability to predict crash outcomes. The authors report a Verus proof implementing the prophecy model over a natural model using prophecy variables. The PoWER-to-Crash-Hoare-logic proof in Rocq/Perennial is metalogical and trusts a translation of PoWER semantics, since PoWER was not implemented in Rocq. The Verus correspondence to crash invariants is entirely machine-checked within Verus. Formal theorem bodies are in artifacts; this reading examined paper explanations only. Crash states can be specified through rec(bytes), commonly allowing pre-operation or post-operation abstract state. Transition permissions instead authorize pairs of durable states. Blanket permissions cover arbitrary recovery-equivalent transitions; single-use permissions authorize a mutating transition once and are consumed or invalidated. A blanket permission can manufacture single-use permissions only for its allowed transitions. Initial recoverability and all permission constructions remain proof obligations. Tentative writes change only addresses irrelevant to rec and need no value-specific proof. Committing writes are a single aligned atomic chunk, typically after flushing tentative data, so only old/new durable states matter. Recovery writes rely on idempotent recovery that overwrites all possibly torn bytes on retry. In-place writes can use weaker specifications with many allowed outcomes, but the authors have no verified examples or helper-library support for that category. Atomic PoWER adds durable ghost resources owned by atomic invariants, proof callbacks and completion objects for consumed transition permissions. Completions witness an issued/applied operation even if another thread later changes its key. This extension needs concurrency facilities beyond the minimal core features; a tool-agnostic core does not imply arbitrary concurrent proofs in plain sequential Dafny. Concurrency allows multiple readers, or disjoint statically allocated storage regions with exclusive access during writes. It excludes read/write or write/write overlap within one region because callers must know its current logical state. Sharded wrappers establish linearizable individual create/read/update/delete/list operations, not cross-shard transactions. The reusable inner implementation still supplies a transactional API to wrappers. Corruption is modeled by a fixed device bitmask with at most c potentially faulty physical bits. A zero mask bit reads correctly; a marked bit can return either value independently on each read. The trusted CRC axiom distinguishes byte strings at Hamming distance 1 through c. Current ECMA CRC-64 implementation uses c=1 for arbitrary lengths; the cited c=3 for data shorter than about1 GiB is not exploited. Detection is conditional on that device-wide bound, not a guarantee against arbitrary bursts, malicious rewrites, rollback or unbounded media failure. Reader qualification: integrity proofs must cover corrupted data and checksum bytes, repeated/noncontiguous address mappings, and the chosen CDB codeword distance under the same physical-bit bound. The paper reports verified checking and a trusted CRC library; it does not derive an unrestricted cryptographic collision-resistance guarantee. Detecting a mismatch permits reporting corruption, not necessarily repairing damage or preserving availability. Tick-Tock’s old-checksum/new-data mismatch after a crash is not a small-bit corruption event relative to the old data. CRC(D0) can collide with CRC(D1-prime) even if D1-prime differs by only bounded media corruption from D1, because D0 versus D1-prime may differ arbitrarily. The paper gives a logical counterexample to the algorithm in its model, not an independently reproduced NOVA-Fortis artifact exploit. CDB stores one of two known eight-byte values CRC(0) and CRC(1), with aligned crash atomicity and sufficient corruption separation assumed/proved for the primitive. Two data/CRC slots accompany it. Write the inactive slot and checksum, flush, atomically switch CDB, flush. The selector identifies the committed slot independently of potentially matching stale checksums. This costs extra storage and flushes; it does not remove hardware atomicity assumptions. CapybaraKV values contain a fixed-size item and a list of fixed-size elements, with fixed-size keys. The abstract state has on-abort and on-commit maps. Ordinary operations affect the latter; abort restores it from the former; commit publishes it to the former. A crash during commit may commit or abort, while other uncommitted operations abort. Reads within a transaction see tentative operations, so visible results need not already be durable. Implementation uses main/item/list tables, per-field CRCs, validity CDBs, copy-on-write updates and a physical redo journal. Journal commit writes a CRC of pending entries then flips a CDB; replay installs operations and clears the journal. Volatile key index and free lists rebuild on startup. Correctness depends on recovery traversal, bounds, allocation and CRC checks, not merely the commit selector. Capacity is statically allocated at initialization with maximum key/item/list counts and sizes. No dynamic resizing, partial-value updates or range queries. All keys reside in a volatile Rust HashMap and must be indexed again at startup. Designed target is small records on tens of GiB of dedicated PM in a cloud-storage service. Prototype integration into an Azure Rust system is reported, not evidence of production deployment of all verified variants. Trusted pmcopy bridges Verus and compiler-generated representations. It requires repr(C) and derive(PmCopy), implements PmSafe/PmSized/Clone/PartialEq, generates specifications and static layout assertions checked by Rust. PmSafe includes numeric types, bool and char; composites require safe fields. Casts still require correct layout, valid discriminants/values and prior corruption checks. Compiler assertions caught a u128/i128 layout change; this is a concrete consistency check, not a proof of the macro or compiler. CapybaraNS stores a 64-bit logical timestamp and last hash. Advance increments and atomically persists them using CDB; Sign signs their binding. A trusted C# wrapper supplies CRCs, cryptography and serialization. This paper does not supply a complete distributed-notary protocol, a cryptographic implementation proof, remote attestation argument or availability theorem. Counter overflow handling and full security assumptions require the external specification. PM model permits independent eight-byte chunk reorderings until flush; backend write uses PMDK non-temporal stores or mov followed by clflushopt/clwb, and flush uses sfence. It deliberately overapproximates strongly ordered clflush and same-cache-line hardware ordering, including potential compiler reorderings. Eight-byte alignment/atomicity, backend calls and hardware behavior remain trusted. PoWER can use other models; current model is not a universal storage-device specification. Table 2 counts unverified pmcopy source but not its generated code. KV trusted count includes mock byte-vector PM plus Windows/Linux backends, concurrency and sharding wrappers. Trusted versus proved LOC therefore should not be interpreted as executable core size alone. Reported proof/code ratios are2.6 KV and2.4 NS; LOC is not a measure of specification adequacy. KV design, implementation and verification took about1.5 years by a team of experts and newcomers; headcount and person-time are unspecified. After that experience, porting the PM spec to Dafny took under an hour, porting helper lemmas about an hour, and implementing/verifying NS about nine hours after its spec and C# wrapper were already written. This is author experience, not a controlled productivity comparison. On Linux6.9.3 with i7-11850H eight physical cores and32 GB RAM, KV verifies in54s with one thread or23s with eight; NS takes12s with one. Appendix expects KV1–2min serial or15–40s parallel on other hardware. Paper gives no independent proof replay in this reading and no controlled comparison against alternative verification approaches. Performance setup is a two-socket32-core machine with128 GB RAM and one128 GB Optane DC PMM, Debian Trixie/Linux6.12.10. All KV runs use the sharded variant with one shard per thread. Redis client/server run together but retain communication overhead; RocksDB uses memory-mapped files and non-temporal log appends; Viper preallocates enough capacity except in utilization measurement. Different supported features and durability architectures affect comparison. Microbenchmarks use25M records,64-byte keys,1 KiB values and8-byte list elements. Append adds16 elements per record in random order; read-list returns the entire list; trim removes it. Other operations run once per record. Figure2 uses logarithmic latency axes and95% confidence intervals. KV matches or beats RocksDB but Viper is faster on several operations, including most writes; Redis is slowest. Windows/Azure20 GiB battery-backed DRAM tests run only KV, with up to2× improvement; other systems lack Windows support. YCSB uses15M keys,24-byte keys,1140-byte values and five executions per system. RunE range queries are omitted and RunA/RunB partial updates become full-value updates. X is uniform75% updates,5% read-modify-write and20% reads; Y/Z use50/50 or5/95 read/update with90% accesses to10% records. LoadE is omitted only from Figure4 as similar to LoadA. These modified workloads must not be called an unmodified full YCSB suite. At one thread KV is broadly comparable to Viper and often slightly slower. - Reusable Formal Verification of DAG-based Consensus Protocols (2025)
    - what: # Reusable Formal Verification of DAG-based Consensus Protocols (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Nathalie Bertrand, Pranav Ghorpade, Sasha Rubin, Bernhard Scholz and Pavle Subotić, arXiv2407.02167v2,18March2025. The inventory year2024 identifies the original submission; this read uses the retained2025revision. The authors report TLA+/TLAPS safety proofs for five protocol models by combining three DAG-construction components with two ordering components. The five are DAG-Rider, Cordial Miners, Hashgraph, Eventually Synchronous Bullshark and a minor variant of Aleph. The result concerns Integrity and Total Order; eventual delivery, probabilistic progress and implementation correctness remain outside it (Q0,Q1,Q2,Q12).  ## Reading scope and source identity  Read all21PDFpages, sections1–6 and51reference entries, all three figures including both panels of Figure2, seven listings and numerical Table1. Individually viewed pages6–16, covering the figures, listings, refinement mapping and numerical table. The paper refers to “Appendix ??” but includes no appendix. References were read as bibliography entries, not recursively read papers.  Acquired the paper-linked repository's complete nontruncated tree and22static blobs at9e4c9629eb283c7c34b6ffcf7956bc72a3e26e5d,22December2024, the latest retained commit before this paper revision. This selects a historical version without establishing that it produced the reported timings. Whole reads cover README and the five component Specification.tla files. Proof files and complete-protocol sources are inspected only in explicitly recorded ranges. Acquisition of a file does not imply its whole read. No author code, specification, checker or solver was executed/imported; no serialized experimental data or model was loaded.  ## What is proved and how composition works  A vertex embeds its entire rooted causal history, rather than only an opaque identifier. Thus two processes possessing the same vertex have identical histories for it. A separate anchor-agreement property requires processes that have selected anchors for a frame to select the same anchors. Delivering each frame's previously undelivered causal-history vertices in a fixed deterministic order then prevents duplicate delivery and gives consistent delivery order. A lagging process may deliver a shorter prefix; the proof is not simultaneous equality of local delivery states (Q2,Q3).  The decomposition is three construction models, reliable structured, unreliable structured and unreliable unstructured, plus Global Perfect Coin (GPC) and Virtual Voting (VV) ordering. Reliable construction ensures one agreed vertex per position. Unreliable structured construction allows equivocation and uses ratification to agree on a vertex at a position. GPC ordering separately agrees on leader positions; combining these properties establishes anchor agreement. Hashgraph first converts its unstructured events to a structured witness DAG. Reference consistency constrains witnesses' predecessor references; VV establishes agreement on famous witnesses (Q4,Q6,Q7,Q8).  The full protocol maps constants and new state variables into an INSTANCE of the ordering specification. Each construction action performs an appropriate ordering action or leaves its mapped variables unchanged. Protocol-specific refinement obligations remain necessary: five reusable components do not eliminate the proofs connecting five concrete models to them. DAG-Rider and ES Bullshark share reusable components but differ in wave lengths and commit/leader rules. Aleph is explicitly a variant; neither the paper nor its one-line repository README gives a precise delta against every published Aleph rule (Q4,Q9,C6).  ## Assumptions and abstractions  The system explanation assumes signed identities and fewer than one-third Byzantine processes. Reliable broadcast is weakened to integrity because validity and eventual agreement support liveness. Its model retains the first broadcast for each creator/round; the authors argue a faulty process's chosen delivered message could equivalently have been sent first. This is an abstraction argument to retain in correspondence work, not a separately measured implementation equivalence (Q1,Q5).  Unreliable communication copies a vertex from another local DAG; Byzantine participants can insert arbitrary modeled vertices. Procedures retain input/output behavior while omitting internal loop states. GPC becomes an arbitrary fixed function shared by all processes: randomness, unpredictability and fairness are absent. Agreement of the function's answers suffices for the stated safety argument; it supplies no probability-one termination theorem or implementation of a cryptographic coin (Q5,Q7,Q8).  The retained component models use finite symbolic bounds on waves/rounds or event IDs, with no fixed numerical test instance. Proof claims quantify over their parameters; a single TLC run at one bound would not establish that claim. The record does not independently establish an infinite-execution refinement beyond these bounded model families. The VV component incorporates its reference-consistency premise directly into both the prestate and poststate of Next. Its source proof of that premise therefore depends on the action restriction; a concrete protocol still must justify the mapping (C1–C5).  ## Consequential findings in the retained artifact  The printed self-referential VertexSet listing is explanatory shorthand. ReliableStructuredDAGconstructionSpecification.tla instead constructs vertices recursively by decreasing round with UntilRoundVertex. That resolves the apparent circular-definition concern for this component. However, its received/added-vertex guards access v.edges, while the actual constructed records contain strongedges and weakedges. This is a static field mismatch in the saved model; no checker error or reachable protocol failure was observed (C1).  In the unreliable structured component, Approves(v,u) requires Observes(v,u) and forbids observing every vertex with u's source and round. Taking that quantified vertex to be u yields both Observes(v,u) and its negation. Thus the literal definition admits no approval. With n-f positive under3f<n, ratification requires a nonempty set of approving sources and cannot occur under this reading. Since ratified vertices initialize to Nil, the displayed agreement property can hold without any ratification progress. This is a reader derivation from the retained definitions, not a claim that the real Cordial Miners protocol fails (C2).  The unstructured component's DonotSeeFork(v,u) has the same self-including universal condition. Taking x=u contradicts its Path(v,u) conjunct. Its Sees predicate consequently cannot witness a seen ancestor under the intended reflexive Path interpretation. This is another source-definition concern to resolve before trusting correspondence to actual Hashgraph behavior; the paper excludes liveness and no safety counterexample is established (C3).  VVOrderingProofs.tla contains several named lemma statements without proof text. Most concretely, intInv14 asserts, for integers a,m, that a>=m and m+a>2f imply m>f. The permitted assignment f=1,a=2,m=1 makes both premises true and its conclusion false. The file cites this lemma in its Inv1 preservation proof. The nearby intadd statement has the plausible intended conclusion a>f with strict a>b. This suggests a proof-support defect or mistaken statement in the retained artifact; it does not show a checker accepted a false theorem. The actual preservation goal is a majority-count fact that can be mathematically true even though this cited general lemma is false (C7,C8).  The same proof preamble asserts, without accompanying proof text, that every witness has more than2f predecessor sources in the preceding frame. Combined literally with its positive finite frame range and predecessor-frame condition, that leaves no nonempty witness set: a witness of minimum frame would require an earlier witness. This preamble should not silently become an established domain theorem. A simpler nonvacuity concern appears in the VV specification itself: all witness-DAG cells initially are empty, while adding a witness requires more than2f predecessor sources already present. With f nonnegative and no genesis exception, no first witness can be added under the intended typed interpretation. Whole proof closure and tool handling of unproved declarations have not been replayed. These artifact findings limit independent confirmation of the paper's mechanized-proof claim; they do not refute the high-level decomposition or establish a reachable fork (C5,C7).  ## Evaluation and significance  Table1 reports, in order reliable structured/unreliable structured/unreliable unstructured/GPC/VV: specification lines403/160/230/272/136; invariants6/6/7/10/18; proof lines460/594/554/822/2120; maximum proof depths10/9/8/9/13; maximum degrees7/8/7/7/11; leaf obligations633/895/665/1302/3316; and checking seconds49/68/74/125/651. Environment:2.10GHzCPU,8GBRAM,Windows11,TLAPS1.4.5. These are author-reported component checks, not reader replications or total timings for every full-protocol refinement. No repeated-run variability or controlled comparison appears (Q10).  The authors report approximately14person-months across five people. Their “almost half” proof-effort claim corresponds to reducing an illustrative ten separate construction/ordering components to five reusable ones. There is no controlled person-time baseline or ablation demonstrating a50% labor saving; refinement work and component complexity also differ. A reusable component count is concrete, while a measured causal labor reduction remains unestablished (Q0,Q4,Q10,Q12).  This is directly relevant to reusable TLA+ specifications and distributed-protocol proofs. It has no Verus/Rust artifact or LLM-agent experiment. A reader proposal for evaluating proof agents is to score specification correspondence, nonvacuous progress examples, closure of helper lemmas and refinement obligations separately from reported leaf-obligation throughput. The retained field/predicate/lemma issues make those distinctions concrete without treating static concerns as observed solver results.
    - number: approximately 14 person-months across 5 people

- rIC3 (2025)
    - title: The rIC3 Hardware Model Checker
    - what: Introduces rIC3, a Rust bit-level IC3/PDR checker with a portfolio of IC3, BMC, and k-induction. It combines COI-reduced SAT queries, optimized VSIDS data structures, GipSAT, dynamic generalization (DynAMic), CTG/EXCTG, and optional internal-signal/localization abstractions.     - what: Extends standpoint linear temporal logic (SLTL) with four history-information semantics in addition to step semantics: pure observation, public-history, decremental, and incremental. The formal semantics use separate finite transition systems Ta whose labels expose subsets Pa of propositions and define future-history satisfaction.     - what: Rocq perm_solver Ltac tactic reifies list concatenations into binary trees of natural-number labels, searches for a multiset rewrite using permutation hypotheses, and applies a proved reflection theorem to obtain the standard-library Permutation result. Goal and hypotheses are standard-library Permutation statements over list concatenations/cons. Cons is normalized into singleton append. Mapping associates distinct atomic list subterms with labels. A multiset of labels retains repeated occurrences; interpreting the paper’s word sets as ordinary sets would discard multiplicity and invalidate permutation reasoning. Reflection theorem requires a correct semantic permutation proof for every tree pair in the substitution environment and check_unify=true for the flattened goal. It proves soundness of success, not completeness or automatic truth of arbitrary context hypotheses. Ltac constructs terms/environments and discharges their obligations; the proof assistant checks the resulting theorem application. CUD depth0 returnsfalse before testing equality; positive depth first cancels common occurrences to detect equality, otherwise searches applicable left-side substitutions in either direction. It is a bounded backtracking rewrite search, not general complete logical unification or a decision procedure for all consequences of permutation assumptions. Default check_unify uses depth values at quartiles of the substitution-environment length and rpt=false, dropping a used hypothesis from that search branch. The fixed-depth variant takes user depth and rpt=true. Author’s observation that typical proofs rarely need reuse is empirical experience, not a theorem that a hypothesis may safely be discarded without losing solutions. Submultiset guards are required before replacement, and substitutions preserve multiplicity through occurrence removal/addition. Hypothesis reuse changes search power while preserving soundness. - van der Leer Wullaert Ahrens Scott Karoubi UniMath 2025 (2025)
    - title: Scott’s Representation Theorem and the Univalent Karoubi Envelope
    - what: Authors report two Rocq-UniMath proofs of Scott’s Representation Theorem: every beta lambda-theory is recovered as the endomorphism theory of a reflexive object, by Scott’s syntactic retract category or Hyland’s presheaf category. Univalence converts theory isomorphisms to identities. Setcategory and univalent Karoubi envelopes are compared by Rezk completion, yielding a fully faithful embedding of Scott’s model into Hyland’s. An extensible Ltac2 tactic reduces substitution terms and emits explicit rewrites, with two reported timing examples. Records exact section-retraction versus equivalence scope, beta/eta boundary, synthetic initial syntax assumption, four displayed-category layers and tuple costs, explicit Scott/Hyland constructions, idempotent splitting/truncation, monoid counterexample, precise envelope completion versus full-presheaf embedding, source notation errors, generated proof timing versus tactic execution, component size caveats and open categorical lifting.
    - limits: Core foundation is Martin-Lof type theory with univalence; hom types are sets (unique identity proofs), objects need not form a set. A setcategory requires a set of objects; a univalent category requires identities of objects to correspond to categorical isomorphisms. These are distinct conditions. Proposition 6/13 use univalence of Set and displayed layers; semantic isomorphism is constructed first, then transported to identity. This is mathematical equality through an assumed foundation, not definitional equality by evaluation (§1.3, Remark 3). Algebraic theory T consists of sets T_n, projections and simultaneous substitution satisfying variable/unit/associativity laws. Lambda-theory adds abstraction lambda:L_(n+1)→L_n and application rho:L_n→L_(n+1), compatible with substitution, with beta rho∘lambda=id on L_(n+1). Main formal results cover beta theories, not beta-free or beta-eta variants, despite definitions and informal generalizations being discussed (§2.1, §2.3). Pure syntax Lambda is presented informally as a higher inductive syntax with variables/application/abstraction/substitution and equations. Formalization instead assumes a sequence of sets with these operations, equations and an induction principle, because UniMath core disallows inductive types. Initial Lambda→L morphism uses that interface. This does not assert a separately constructed concrete inductive syntax artifact; main SRT is parameterized over arbitrary theories and does not depend on constructing initial Lambda (Remark 10, Example 12). E maps a reflexive object X with X^X retract of X to E(X)_n=C(X^n,X), substitution by product composition, abstraction/application via exponential adjunction and retraction. Beta needs app∘abs=id_(X^X); eta additionally needs abs∘app=id_X. Definitions only need finite powers/binary products with nullary product and the relevant exponential, although introductory RO uses a Cartesian closed ambient category. Singleton in Set is trivial model; nontrivial models require other categories (§1.2, Definitions 16–17). Two functions S,H:LamTh→RO satisfy E∘S=id=E∘H. There is no claimed two-sided inverse RO→LamTh→RO. Scott and Hyland give distinct models with same endomorphism theory. Scott hom sets are inhabited; Hyland presheaves include empty objects with absent morphisms from nonempty objects. Remark 19’s phrase no morphisms into the empty object cannot literally include its identity; interpreted as the distinguishing lack of hom-set inhabitation. No equivalence between all theories and all reflexive objects is proved (§1.2, §2). Displayed categories build LamTh over AlgTh over Set^N, with four layers hiding structural details but making modular univalence proofs and avoiding duplicate object-type definitions. Two n-tuple encodings, nested pairs versus finite-index functions, require switching; paper reports this as implementation cost, not a measured algorithmic overhead (Remark 21, §1.4). Scott R has closed idempotent lambda terms A with A∘A=A and morphisms f with B∘f=f=f∘A; identity at A is A. Encoded pairing/projections supply products, lambda terms supply exponentials, terminal I=lambda x1 x2.x2. U=lambda x.x has each object A as a retract, hence U^U as a retract, and is reflexive. Explicit bijections E(U)_n↔L_n preserve projections/substitution/lambda/rho and yield E(S(L))=L by univalence. Closed constants must be weakened under binders to typecheck (§2.2). Hyland uses algebraic T-presheaves: sets P_n with substitution action satisfying unit/associativity. Pshf_T is univalent. Shift A(Q)_n=Q_(n+1), with weakened action and fresh variable, is Q^T; lambda/rho exhibit theory presheaf L as reflexive. Lawvere category has natural-number objects and hom(m,n)=T_m^n. Its presheaves equal the algebraic interface; Yoneda yields Hom(T^n,Q)≅Q_n. These bijections preserve operations to prove E(H(L))=L. Informal observation about dropping beta does not enlarge the stated completed main formal scope (§2.3). Karoubi envelope D splits idempotents, fully faithfully contains C and every D object merely is a retract of an image object. Merely means propositional truncation, not chosen witnesses. Add setcategory or univalence condition for the corresponding foundation. Set construction R^S(C) uses pairs (X,f) with f idempotent, morphisms g satisfying f2∘g∘f1=g, identity f; it is a setcategory envelope if C is a setcategory. It defines a completion monad on setcategories, multiplication ((X,a),b)↦(X,b) (§3.1). R^S(C) univalent implies C univalent, converse false: Example 42 uses commutative matrix monoid {I,diag(1,0),diag(-1,0)}. Only I is a unit so its one-object category is univalent; at retract diag(1,0), both diagonal rank-one matrices are automorphisms while identity type has one member, violating univalence. This concrete counterexample is source mathematics; reader checked displayed matrices and c^2=b, not a replayed Rocq test (Proposition 41, Example 42). Univalent R^U(C) is full subcategory of Set-valued presheaves consisting of mere retracts of representables. Equalizer of an idempotent f and identity splits f; composition of retracts keeps object within subcategory; Yoneda gives full faithfulness. Full subcategory of univalent presheaves is univalent. R^S(C)→R^U(C), sending (X,a) to equalizer of Yoneda(a) and Yoneda(id), is fully faithful and essentially surjective: R^U(C) is Rezk completion of R^S(C) for arbitrary C. This theorem concerns envelope subcategory, not all presheaves (§3.2). Comparison identifies Scott R with set-envelope of monoid of eta-fixed closed terms, not all closed terms without restriction. Lambda/rho identify this monoid with substitution monoid L_1. Proposition 49 assumes target D has all colimits; applying D=Set^op relates presheaves on Lawvere category and L_1 one-object category. Diagram (8) passes through set-envelope, its Rezk completion and inclusion into full presheaves. Composite R→Pshf_L is fully faithful and preserves U as L, powers and relevant exponential/morphisms, hence endomorphism theory. Full Pshf_L need not itself be Rezk completion of R; introductory phrasing is coarser than Theorems 47/50 (§3.3). propagate_subst is deterministic syntactic rewriting in Ltac2: traverse left goal term, match registered traversal/rewrite patterns, execute applicable equalities and print explicit refine/maponpaths composition steps. It replaces slower repeated Ltac rewrite search. Ten trivial rewrites occur in shown substitution term (one abstraction, four applications, five variable substitutions); other proofs need 40+. Extensible lists cover constructors then composition/pair/projection/curry/n-tuples. Modular traverse also underlies generate_refine for targeted subterm rewriting; generalized tactic handles arbitrary identity sets and hyperdoctrine formulas (§4). Reported illustrative timings: U_term substitution, repeat reduce_lambda≈100ms, propagate_subst≈35ms, generated explicit script≈5ms. First nine lines of subst_compose≈40ms, propagate_subst≈330ms, reduce_lambda≈1s. These are two source-reported examples without hardware, repetition counts, uncertainty or benchmark corpus. Generated proof replay is distinct from tactic search/execution, and examples do not establish whole-project speedup. Longer explicit proofs trade size for checking performance and avoid extensive retained automation per UniMath maintainability preference (§4). Project reports >11,000 lines, roughly equal definitions/proofs. Approximate component counts: categories 3,000; Scott 3,000; envelopes 2,000; algebraic-theory constructions 1,000; comparison 1,000. These rounded listed components total 10,000, not an exhaustive exact project total; no independently counted repository size or development person-hours. Integrated into UniMath, HTML commit 5941f44e3c13d2ac385f5a8b9b486c0088dd3f46, archive 93afb3f22a54064c0baa8493bd326f385fc96ebe. Compilation instructions linked but no reader build/axiom audit or timing reproduction (§1.4). Printed notation has apparent typing/copy errors, checked visually: Definition 8 writes rho_n∘lambda_n=id_(L_n) though maps compose on L_(n+1); Corollary 32 shows correctly indexed shifted object. Theorem 36 final proof line writes E(S(L)) rather than E(H(L)); theorem/§2 state H correctly. §3 preliminary idempotent-splitting paragraph reverses X/Y retract relation for f:X→X. Theorem 45 equalizer proof labels Y→E witness s while diagram and following page use r. These are exposition discrepancies; no corresponding artifact error established. Open: lifting the type-level section/retraction to categories or bicategories, with right-hand RO structure unsettled. Domain-equation/Scott D_infinity/PCF formalizations are complementary related work, not supplied proofs here. No distributed protocol, TLA+, Verus/Rust or LLM agent evaluation. Indirect contribution is foundational assumption auditing, abstraction cost, multiple-proof comparison and explicit generated proof replay evidence (§5–6).
