- VEP: A Two-stage Verification Toolchain for Full eBPF Programmability (2025)
    - what: VEP separates eBPF verification into C-level symbolic execution and SMT proof generation in user space, compilation that translates code, assertions and proofs, and independent bytecode symbolic execution/proof checking intended for kernel space. Separation logic describes owned memory and helper-acquired resources. Annotations expose loop invariants and contracts unavailable to fully automatic verifiers. The paper reports acceptance/rejection, time, memory and annotation/proof sizes on 41 small programs, and claims Coq proofs of the separation-logic transformation properties. It does not present a mechanized soundness/refinement theorem for the entire executable toolchain. Records proof-generation/checking boundary, trusted helper specifications and bytecode semantics, assertion restrictions and conversion rules, compilation passes and source-property loss, safety versus intended functionality and termination proof limits, concrete string/list/socket examples, all Table 2–5 results and deployment/version uncertainty. Separates sample success from universal no-error/full-programmability claims; checks discrepancies in memory/speed/acceptance prose and proof-line terminology; preserves printed illustrative inconsistencies without claiming implementation defects.
    - limits: §§2/5: Claimed small trusted computing base excludes the C verifier, compiler and SMT solver because bytecode is checked again. Guarantee still depends on correct executable bytecode checker, faithful eBPF instruction/memory/arithmetic semantics, actual helper contracts, and correspondence with kernel execution/JIT. The paper supplies no whole executable-checker soundness or code-to-kernel refinement theorem. §5 specifically reports Coq proofs for separation-logic transformation properties, not all these components. §§2.1/3/5: VEP-C computes strongest postconditions, eliminates spatial entailments, and uses its own SMT solver producing cvc5-style proof terms. VEP-eBPF independently symbolically executes bytecode and checks spatial/pure proof steps without solving. Checked proof terms remove the need to trust SMT answers only to the extent proof rules and their checker/semantics are correct. Kernel-space deployment is the intended architecture; evaluation does not clearly distinguish an in-kernel deployment benchmark from standalone checker measurements. §§2.2–2.3/7: Introduction and capability section claim functional correctness, but §2.3 explicitly makes user intent the user’s responsibility and §7 lists functional correctness as future work. The reported Key_connection annotations are expressly memory-safety-only. Accepting bytecode safety does not establish intended lookup/copy semantics or preservation of arbitrary source assertions. §2.2: Termination within finitely many steps is claimed. The shown loop reasoning uses invariants and exit conditions; no explicit general ranking-function, decreasing variant or fuel/step-bound rule is explained. Invariant preservation alone establishes partial correctness, not termination. This is a limit of the presented justification, not a reproduced checker counterexample. §§2.1/6.2/Appendix B: Full programmability and no false positives/negatives are author claims. Finite examples and annotations do not establish completeness for all safe programs; general entailment is acknowledged undecidable. Spatial-expression scope restrictions reject some natural quantified array assertions, requiring custom predicates. Appendix B DNF normalization can multiply branches, so approximate linear symbolic-execution cost in statement/assertion length excludes assertion-size growth and SMT solving. §3: Memory ownership uses disjoint spatial conjunction; duplicated ownership is inconsistent. Built-in helper contracts are derived from documentation, not proved against kernel helper implementations. Resource acquire/release soundness depends on their completeness and accuracy, including permitted null returns, flags and sizes. Contract variants are selected for supported contexts. §§2.3/4: Source C undefined behavior can compile into memory-safe bytecode. Early source rejection protects source semantics beyond kernel bytecode safety. Maliciously altered bytecode with a valid safety proof may pass without matching original program intent. Neither final safety checking nor an unverified compiler automatically proves C-to-bytecode functional refinement. §4: Compiler uses nanopasses, member-to-offset conversion, calling convention transformation, iterated register coalescing, and explicit stack frame preconditions. Few optimizations supported. Dead source variables become existential logical variables. Figure 14 deliberately turns a false source assertion x==1 after x=0 into satisfiable exists _x,_x==1; source assertion truth is lost even though bytecode safety can survive. §4 Figures 13/15, Appendix A: Printed illustrations contain apparent inconsistencies. Figure 13 sets R1=0 then asserts R1==*(R10-4)+1 while stack value is0. Figure 15 declares fields x,next but accesses l.head. Appendix A transforms forall n,v!=n*n into forall n,n!=n*n, which fails for n=0/1 and is not generally equivalent. These are source illustration issues; artifact behavior was not tested. Appendix A prose also describes x as a nonsquare although displayed condition constrains v with x=2*v. §3 Figures 4/6/9/12: An arbitrary owned output list proves initialized memory/ownership, not that memset filled every byte or strncpy copied/padded correctly. Figure 9 uses stronger repeat(v,n) content predicate; Figure 6’s displayed successful strncpy postcondition is weaker than complete C-library functionality. Keep actual predicate content when evaluating generated proofs. Appendix B: Internal assertions separate program-variable addresses, pure facts and owned memory; logic variables in spatial facts require permitted existential binding. Printed array-address conversion shows V(e1+e2) without explicit element-size scaling; semantics/type conventions would need inspection before inferring a compiler defect. §6: Evidence is 41 selected small C programs, not large production services or adversarial bytecode fuzzing. Linux Kernel5.15 and PREVAIL August2024 used. Hardware, trial repetitions, confidence intervals, human annotation time/user study and whole-tool LOC are not specified. No independent reproduction performed. §6 Tables 2–5: Passing rate means acceptance for safe cases and rejection for unsafe cases. All ten unsafe cases stop at VEP-C; compiler/eBPF columns are dashes. Thus data demonstrate C-front-end rejection, not independent final-checker rejection of ten crafted attacks. Safe VEP outcomes are 30 category samples plus one Key_connection, all accepted. §6.2: Linux 6/10 acceptance is for the PREVAIL sample category, not all safe programs; Linux category is9/10 and Stringlib3/10, with Key0/1. PREVAIL10/10,8/10,1/10 and Key0/1. Source attributes PREVAIL variability to SMT dependency/nondeterminism although introduction describes abstract interpretation; no experiment establishes that causal claim. Claimed version regressions30%/20% lack paired version tables, and no cross-version VEP study is shown. §6.1: Claimed predictable2–3MB VEP-eBPF memory is contradicted by Linux sample maximum8034KB (lathist); VEP-C maximum32569KB. Linux average.94ms applies to its accepted Linux sample subset, not all benchmarks, and Stringlib maximum2.69ms. Claimed3–5x faster than PREVAIL is not uniform: Linux category12.48/8.42≈1.48x, while39.46/8.42≈4.69x relative to VEP-C. Different acceptance sets complicate average comparisons. §6.3: Table3 labels proof counts as proof lines, while prose calls64840 proof obligations. Do not infer64840 independent obligations. Annotation lines are a size proxy, not measured effort or expertise. Key proof5819lines in table versus about5800 in text; preserve rounding. §7: LLM generation of annotations, broader functional correctness and advanced optimization support are proposed future work. No LLM agent experiment, Verus/verified Rust/TLA+ proof, distributed-protocol theorem or code execution reported in this reading.

- Veri-QEC (2025)
    - title: Efficient Formal Verification of Quantum Error Correcting Programs
    - what: Defines assertion and program logics for quantum error-correcting programs, proves a sound proof system, reduces Pauli-error verification conditions to classical SMT assertions, and implements the automated Veri-QEC verifier.     - number: Benchmark includes 14 stabilizer codes
    - limits: Verification scales exponentially with code size and uses a 24-hour timeout; parallel experiments use 250 of 256 cores. User constraints can improve scale but require logical encodings and may change the verified scope. Relative completeness is established for finite programs without infinite loops; completeness for while-loops remains open.

Tracks numerator residues instead of potentially undefined rational residues, all three modular cases, Kummer range reduction, nondeterministic refinement emptiness versus concrete LLVM, relaxed-accumulator bounds, 64-bit chunk table/reciprocal correction, certified prime-budget checks and sign-aware CRT. Preserves exact wrapper guarantees and external GMP/compiler/I/O boundaries, all benchmark table numbers, source inconsistencies and optimization-versus-mathematical proof effort.
    - limits: §2, pp.2–3: Bernoulli convention B1=−1/2; B0=1 and odd indices above 1 vanish. Even indices congruent 2 mod 4 are positive, multiples of 4 negative. Rational modular reduction requires denominator coprime to modulus. The denominator is the squarefree product of primes with p−1 dividing even k. The pre-existing AFP supplies Bernoulli foundations; Voronoi/Kummer congruences and concrete prime bounds were added for this development. §3, p.4: compute numerator N_k mod p for all odd primes, including denominator primes where B_k mod p is undefined. For p−1 dividing k, use −D_k/p mod p. Otherwise compute B_k mod p and multiply denominator factors modulo p. Fast sum requires 2^k≠1 mod p; slower fallback handles equality. Restricting to only fast primes lacks the required a priori coverage bound. Theorems 5–7, pp.3–4: Kummer gives range reduction using k prime=k mod (p−1), with k prime nonzero under the denominator exclusion, and factor k/k prime. Fast-sum theorem requires prime p≥5, 2≤k≤p−3 and primitive root g. It reindexes into m outer terms and n inner terms using the order of 2. These arithmetic assumptions differ from the later wrapper handling p=3 and larger original k. §3.1.1, p.5: nondeterminism-error monad refinement means implementation results belong to specification results and failure is controlled, but an abstract implementation with no results is still allowed. Refinement to LLVM later rules out an empty result set. The remainder-sum loop tracks power x^j, doubled residue 2^j s mod p and modular accumulator; explicit assertions expose bounds to later refinements. §3.1.2–3, pp.6–7: Montgomery state uses W=32, 64-bit accumulator and explicit nonoverflow arithmetic/casts. A relaxed accumulator is below (n+1)p and only needs final reduction. Refinement assumptions include a valid Montgomery context, n<2^W and correctly represented input. Export uses 32-bit modulus/inverse/value/residue parameters and 64-bit length/result; an interface width alone does not eliminate the stronger length proof condition. §3.2, pp.7–8: w=w prime=8 gives 64 binary digits per chunk and eight byte-indexed tables of 256 double-width words, 16 KiB total. Entries use relaxed Montgomery form so the hot loop mostly performs shifts, masks, indexed updates and additions. A precomputed floor(2^128/p) replaces division; a possible quotient error of one is corrected, requiring p<2^31. Remainder terms not divisible by 64 use the simpler loop. §3.3, p.9: final modular wrapper requires even nonzero k, odd prime 3≤p<2^31, denominator factor list, correct primitive root below p and correct order of 2. It creates the Montgomery inverse by Hensel lifting, applies range reduction or denominator-prime shortcut, multiplies denominator factors and converts out of Montgomery representation. The final result is exactly N_k mod p. §4.1–4.4, pp.10–12: an initial analytic bit-size bound and explicit prime-product inequality bound required sieve size. Reject if Y≥2^31; success is proved through k=105946388. Sieve produces odd primes and a smallest-prime-factor cache, denominator factors sharpen the bit budget, and fixed-point log bounds prune primes without floating point or huge integers. Tasks contain prime, primitive root, order and a placeholder residue. §4.4–4.5, p.12: primitive roots are found by testing candidates against prime factors of p−1; the factor cache also computes order. Parallel map preserves every task’s first three fields and fills the correct residue. t>1 is the map precondition, while the caller uses max(2,t). Parameters t,d affect parallel execution, not the mathematical result. This is shared-memory LLVM parallelism, not an asynchronous distributed protocol. §4.6, pp.12–13: special cases return 1,−1/2,0 for k=0,1,odd>1. General processing returns a success flag, numerator and denominator. Add N_k≡1 mod 2; all moduli are distinct primes and their product exceeds |N_k|. CRT returns residue num in [0,m); known sign gives N_k=num for positive indices and num−m for multiples of 4. This is not unsigned residue reconstruction without a sign theorem. §4.6.1–2, pp.13–14: fast CRT uses product/remainder trees, independent recursive branches and array refinement instead of explicit pointer trees. CRT and denominator product need arbitrary precision; GMP operations are imported through specified Hoare triples with an existence model. The model prevents contradictory specifications but does not prove GMP’s implementation correct. Replacing GMP with a verified library is discussed as independent work. §5, p.14: final wrapper Hoare triple assumes separate valid output memory locations, nonnegative signed 64-bit t,d and unsigned 32-bit k. It ensures valid GMP numerator/denominator outputs, k≤105946388 implies success, and every successful result equals the canonical numerator/denominator. A larger k is not guaranteed to fail; a successful larger case is still correct. Trust includes Isabelle, LLVM generator/compiler, separation-logic/model assumptions and specified GMP operations. §5/6, pp.14–15: generated C/C++ header and LLVM are used by a handwritten command-line driver. Timing callbacks instrument exported LLVM. Decimal conversion/file writing use an unverified GMP routine. The correctness triple is not a verified filesystem-output, command-line parser or OS/hardware theorem. §6, pp.15–16: benchmarks use Clang 18.1.8 and a LEO5 node with two 32-core 2.60 GHz Xeon Platinum 8358 CPUs and hyperthreading, nominal maximum CPU factor 128. Comparison also uses Ryzen 9 9900X single/12-core and Ryzen 7950X3D 16-core. Reported relative performance improves with k; cluster code is slightly faster over roughly 3e5–5e6, but authors explicitly deny a statistically rigorous comparison. No confidence intervals, run counts or repeatability protocol are given. §§7–8, pp.16–17: the cited O(k² log^(2+o(1)) k) complexity and practical-record history concern Harvey’s algorithm, not a newly mechanized cost theorem in this paper. A later subquadratic prime-power algorithm lacks an implementation according to the authors at publication. The development totals 32578 LOC; about 6 kLOC/20% is mathematical core. No artifact build or independent benchmark replay was performed.

- Verifying Datalog Reasoning with Lean (2025)
    - what: Lean 4 certificate checker for positive, function-free Datalog conclusions. Formalizes least-model and proof-tree semantics and their equivalence; verifies computable ground-rule matching and tree/DAG validation. Offers unordered hash-map graphs with verified DFS acyclicity/local checks and ordered arrays with backward-index references. Adds preliminary safe-rule model checking; evaluates certificates converted from Nemo traces. Separates checking individual derivations from checking closure/model completeness. Gives partial-substitution matching equivalence under inhabited constants, ordered-body indexing, a reusable DFS correctness invariant based on reachability from cycles rather than cycle membership, and compact topologically ordered proof graphs. Benchmarks show sharing can greatly reduce tree certificates, while explicit input facts are absent from the prototype JSON and must be treated as leaf assumptions.
    - limits: Datalog fragment has finite programs/databases, constants/variables/relations with fixed finite arities and no function terms. Signature constant domain may be infinite. Herbrand interpretations use unique names. Negation, aggregates, existential heads, datatypes and complex values are future work, not supported logic covered by this checker. Grounding maps every variable to a constant; computable matching uses partial substitutions. grounding_substitution_equiv explicitly requires Inhabited constants so unmatched variables can receive a default. Atom/relation comparisons and hash-based executable representations require suitable equality/hash instances. Tree validity uses ordered children exactly matching the grounded rule-body list, or a database leaf; empty-body rules can also justify leaves. It proves a supplied derivation of a fact, not completeness of a reasoner or all facts being listed. Program indexing by head/body relation sequence must contain the correct source rules. Unordered graph is complete as a data structure: every predecessor is a vertex key. Acyclicity plus locally valid nodes yields a proof tree for every vertex. This completeness means no dangling graph references, not completeness of logical consequences. All vertices checked, not merely one selected root. HashMap/HashSet DFS distinguishes current walk for cycles from fully verified nodes for sharing. Theorem9 is scoped to calls from the driver and valid verified-node invariant; no unrestricted correctness claim for arbitrary bogus cached sets/walks. Ordered arrays require each predecessor index strictly less than current index and validate local rule steps. §5 model check requires safe rules (head variables also appear in body). It checks all matching body substitutions against a finite candidate interpretation, with partial ground rule activeness invariant. This is unoptimized preliminary functionality, not the procedure whose scalability Table 1 establishes. Prototype JSON does not explicitly encode original database facts; every no-predecessor node is treated as an assumed fact. Thus validation is relative to those supplied leaf assumptions. It cannot catch an invented leaf unless original database membership is separately supplied/checked. Authors explicitly call for explicit facts for production. Input fact/rule ingestion from original sources such as CSV is outside certification scope. Python Nemo-trace conversion and JSON parsing are described but no verified parser/translation theorem is established here. Lean kernel theorem checking and compiled standalone execution are distinct trust paths; paper does not verify Lean compiler/runtime. Certificate soundness for selected facts is not complete materialization correctness. A sound certificate plus checked modelhood and inclusion of original database would establish least-model equality, but those conditions must all be enforced; benchmark selection 1000 GALEN conclusions is not verification of all 1.8 million facts. Ordered-check LogSpace statement is a theoretical encoding observation, not measured peak RAM or a proved bound on the actual loaded-array/JSON/Lean implementation. Table 1 sizes are compact JSON bytes, not resident memory. No formal runtime complexity proof of the complete prototype is supplied. Nemo reasoning baseline excludes tracing and cannot directly express total certificate-generation/translation/checking overhead. Checker times are whole prototype wallclock means 5 runs on one laptop; no dispersion, raw generation cost or extensive invalid-input dataset is reported. Reader ran no artifacts.

- Verifying maximum link loads in a changing world (2025)
    - what: Velo computes a separate worst-case offered traffic load for each network link over specified failures and independent BGP egress changes. Strictly isotone routing reduces each destination’s worst case from arbitrary egress subsets to one egress; exception tunnels require combinations of their endpoints. A top-k heap limits changed destinations. Weighted normalized traffic clustering reduces matrix size with an absolute error bound. Rust prototype evaluation compares analysis time and approximation accuracy; a real ISP topology/configuration with synthetic demand illustrates configuration and capacity planning. Records full optimal-subpath/ECMP and exception-path proofs, topology-by-topology failure enumeration, independent-destination and iBGP visibility assumptions, route-change budget semantics, complete clustering bound proof and its unaddressed count-preservation issue, qualified Algorithm2 listing concerns, all Table1/2 numeric cells, real-data reconstruction limitations, exact QARC comparison scope, synthetic case-study demand, and contradictions between summary claims and printed maxima.

Predicted loads conditional on that demand matrix and allowed events, not probabilities of congestion or guarantee about future offered traffic. Different matrices require separate runs; optional total additional traffic y covers arbitrary additive uncertainty, not arbitrary correlation/protocol dynamics. §§3/9: All routers must learn preferred iBGP routes and preference-affecting attributes must not change on iBGP sessions. Egress abstraction inspects external ingress filters and LocalPref; other attributes can take arbitrary values/ties. Route visibility problems, aggregation and conditional advertisements coupling destinations are excluded. Requires correct mapping from configurations to all feasible egress subsets; no full BGP convergence/transient-safety proof. §3: Traffic splits equally across optimal next hops at each router, a fluid ECMP model. Strict isotonicity means path ordering remains strict when same prefix/suffix weights added; positive acyclic shortest-path behavior is needed for DAG/topological propagation. No loops/negative-cycle generalization. §4 Theorem1: For each fixed topology, destination, link and nonemptyegresssetB, someb∈B alone produces at least as much linkload. Proof chooses egress preferred by downstreamv, uses optimal subpaths/next-hop set inclusion and equal-split reachability to show crossing fraction cannot decrease. Different links can need different egresses; outputs are individual maxima, not a single scenario simultaneously maximizing all links. §4.1.1 Algorithm1: Per-border-root forwarding DAG, initialize node load from Md, topologically add l[u]/outdegree to successors and take each edge maximum. Appendix A Algorithm2 printed listing: Builds Gdag[b] and merged Gfw, then calls TopoSort(Gdag), out(Gdag,u) as if Gdag were one graph. Likely intended Gfw but not specified. Global max y update is nested only inside ordinary forwarding-edge loop after adding exception contributions to y′; a tunnel-only edge with no active ordinary-forwarding edge may never update y. - Wang et al Chevalley presentation rewrites 2025 (2025)
    - title: Algebra Is Half the Battle: Verifying Presentations of Graded Unipotent Chevalley Groups
    - what: Authors report Lean 4 verification that full Steinberg relations for the A3, B3-small and B3-large graded unipotent Chevalley presentations follow from codimension-1, lifted and chosen definition relations. Proofs exhaust missing relation families using explicit group rewrites, interchange lemmas, degree casework and reflection. Automation controls simplification, generates boilerplate theorems and handles reassociation. The application to higher-dimensional expanders and a field-size-independent derivation bound are not formalized. Examines exact relation-vanishing theorem, bounded-degree dependent generator type, hand-enumerated roots and constants, relation-accessor/equation interfaces, chosen missing-root definitions, 15/21/26 absent commutator families, eight lift patterns, reflection reduction, representative degree cases, controlled simp/macros/grw behavior, missing Dehn-function bound and several visibly inconsistent informal notations.
    - limits: Formalized cases are fixed A3, B3-small and B3-large presentations, not all ranks or all Chevalley groups. B3-small has seven roots from base beta/psi/omega; B3-large has nine from alpha/beta/psi. Generators are triples (root, natural degree i, coefficient) with proof i≤height(root). Base roots have height 1. Generic interfaces use Ring R, while concrete weak definitions use Field F and divide by 2; odd characteristic is explicitly required in the matrix discussion. Printed top-level excerpt omits surrounding typeclass/characteristic context, so this record does not infer arbitrary-ring validity of the final theorem (§3–4). Full relations include linearity for each root/degree, mixed-degree commutation for each root, and commutator relations for distinct roots with constants and degree sums. Commutator convention is ghg^-1h^-1. Unipotent positive-root restriction avoids diagonal/opposite-root relations. Monomial generators represent polynomial generators under linearity and mixed-degree rules. Extension parameter m used to motivate matrix families is absent from the formalization; no formal infinite HDX family construction follows (§3). Weak presentation has codimension-1 relations, images of ungraded present-root relations under lifting, and explicit missing-root definition words. Codimension-1 commutator relations require the pair to lie together in an appropriate two-base-root span: alpha+beta and beta+psi are individually present but their mutual commutator is excluded. The prose phrase every pair of distinct present roots is therefore too broad without the common-span condition shown by its own example. A fixed definition expression e is chosen; general invariance under arbitrary admissible e remains future work (§3.3). PresentedGroup is FreeGroup T modulo Subgroup.normalClosure rels. The exact displayed B3-large theorem states every full relation projects to identity in weakB3LargeGraded. Paper states this yields isomorphic weak/full presentations. This is an equality/consequence result for encoded presentations; the printed theorem is not itself a formal spectral/topological expansion theorem or a displayed matrix-representation isomorphism. Reader did not audit all definitions or execute source (§4). PositiveRootSystem excerpt only packages a height map; concrete roots and additive relationships are manually enumerated rather than obtained from general root-system geometry. This avoids partial addition/Option obligations and makes degree constraints easy for ht/omega, but authors acknowledge scaling limits. PartialChevalleySystem stores present roots and zero-/single-/double-span root pairs, with handwritten roots/constants later checked. Classification is tailored to A/B systems; more complex systems need more fields. Typechecker feedback alone should not be generalized to certification that every intended geometric root/constant was encoded correctly (§4). GradedPartialChevalleyGroup adds liftedRels and define to the partial system; define is identity on present roots and must commute with lifting. In full case liftedRels empty/define identity. Weak B3-large uses an explicit five-factor word with -1/2,1,-t for alpha+beta+psi, and commutator words for alpha+beta+2psi and alpha+2beta+2psi. split3/4/5 partition total degree into legal component degrees, preserving i=j+k. Definitions, not an automatically discovered arbitrary presentation, determine proof targets (§4). Three presentation-interface obstacles are handled explicitly: unpack one union of relation subsets into accessors; move from free-group relators to equations inside the quotient; turn r=1 relators into rewrite-friendly r1=r2 equalities by an equivalence lemma. Double-span relation has degree i+j and i+2j terms with coefficients C1*t*u and C2*t*u*u. These interfaces let rw/simp and standard group facts act on the right objects (§4). Authors derive each missing relation family individually: missing commutator counts 15 A3, 21 B3-small, 26 B3-large. These counts are root-pair relation families parameterized by coefficients/degrees, not just 62 individual scalar equations. A3 and small B3 each have one missing root, large B3 has three. Interchange lemmas shuffle degree/coefficient choices; eight are obtained by the 2^3 base-degree 0/1 lifts. Others require explicit rewriting. Several relations need separate concrete degree pairs (§5). Representative B3-small linearity proof expands the missing-root definition, commutes the target across smaller-root factors, combines linear terms and contracts to the desired generator. Printed Lean lin_of_beta_psi_omega follows these specified steps via grw, not autonomous search. For alpha commuting with the highest B3-large root, paper lists 00/01/02 and nine further degree cases (12 before reflection). Involution i↦height(root)-i preserves relations and derives the other half; this is a symmetry reduction, not a universal decision procedure (§3.1, §5). Automation has three parts. chev_simps controls linearity/identity/inverse normal forms without unrestricted simplification; height_simps plus omega discharges height arithmetic. Theorem macros generate names/statements/proofs for repeated linearity/identity/inverse, commuting and reflected consequences, removing 3–10-line boilerplate. greassoc_of% adapts category-theory reassociation by left multiplication. grw first tries a supplied rule directly, then its reassociated form, then project-specific simplification. General group multiplication is not assumed commutative; mul_comm in the exposition is an illustration of a supplied equality, not permission to commute arbitrary group elements (§6). Authors report faster development/compilation and readability/maintenance from automation, but no timings, controlled baseline, effort totals or automation success rate. Few thousand proof lines and 80 source-calculation pages are approximate descriptive counts. Macros generate checked proof scripts, not a reported LLM workflow; bounded exhaustive rewriting search is proposed future work. grw is expressly project-specific (§1, §6–7). Critical omitted result: quantitative HDX application needs a Dehn-function bound for deriving full relations from weak ones independent of field size q. Formalization establishes derivability, not this bound. Authors describe source papers as observing derivations lack field dependence, but do not formalize accumulated rewrite length or the HDX corollary. Proposed proof-length tracking tactics would address this gap. Spectral expansion and topological expansion differ in higher dimensions (§2, §7). Reader source caveats, visually confirmed: Definition 5 says q=p^m while quotienting by an irreducible polynomial of degree m+1; standard quotient cardinality would instead be p^(m+1). §3.3 calls G prime the ungraded group but prints lift G→G prime while text says ungraded→graded. Worked example p. 7 has a missing negative sign in the prose commutator expansion and swapped degree-split bounds relative to its stated beta/psi+omega heights; subsequent displayed derivation uses negative 1. These are informal exposition inconsistencies, not demonstrated failures of linked Lean code. Quotes retain original text rather than silently repairing it. Additional reader scope caution: p. 6 footnote broadly says all quadratic forms are equivalent in odd characteristic; this is not generally true over finite fields. Its purpose is explaining the displayed split orthogonal form, not the presented relation-vanishing theorem. Paper excerpts have omitted proof/context and inconsistent shortened class/type names, so they should not be treated as a standalone compilable file. No artifact replay, source axiom audit or independent matrix/geometry verification was performed. Future work includes general An, B4/C3, diagonal/non-unipotent presentations, general root-addition API and bounded proof search. Those are plans, not delivered cases. No Rust/Verus/TLA+ result, distributed-system safety/liveness experiment, LLM model or proof-agent benchmark appears. Relevance is checked rewriting infrastructure and the distinction between proving equations and certifying quantitative application requirements.

They explicitly distinguish instantiation completeness, meaning the necessary proof instances can be made, from instantiation termination, meaning no endless sequence of instances; “In this paper, we focus on instantiation termination.” The contribution is an operational model, a termination argument for an adapted set axiomatisation, and a method for building such arguments. There is no reported runtime benchmark, solver performance comparison, mechanized proof certificate or implementation refinement proof. Avoiding all instantiations would terminate trivially but fail the intended usefulness requirement, as the authors' footnote explains. Termination is not a proof of completeness, set-library correctness or a distributed protocol's correctness. [Evidence: Q1, §1 introduction/contributions/scope/technical-report pointer, PDF pp.1–3; Q17, §6 conclusion/future work/acknowledgments, PDF pp.18–18; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]  Examples 1 and 2 show why equality, history and case splitting matter. The trigger [diff(s1,s2),member(x,s2)] requires both terms, with consistent variable assignments modulo known equality. Knowing a=c lets diff(b,c) and member(t,a) support the match (b,a,t); recording it prevents the equivalent later match (b,c,t). Changing the trigger to [member(x,s1),member(x,s2)] initially gives four combinations from two member applications. Instantiating produces a clause but does not alone populate the E-graph with all its literals. Splitting that clause can assume ¬member(t,diff(b,a)), making the term member(t,diff(b,a)) known and enabling five new combinations and an indefinitely repeatable pattern. These are worked logical cases, not measured solver runs. [Evidence: Q2, §2.1 E-matching/Examples1–3 including §2 introduction, PDF pp.3–5; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]  Example 3's subset-elimination axiom adds a second difficulty: instantiating the outer variables can introduce an inner quantifier. Its inner [member(x,s1)][member(x,s2)] denotes alternative triggers, so either shape suffices; it is not the conjunction used inside one comma-separated trigger. A termination bound must anticipate newly introduced quantifiers and their possible instances, as well as terms. The model abstracts solver choices rather than claiming to reproduce one configured solver. An extended literal is an ordinary literal or a tagged universal quantifier; extended clauses are disjunctions and formulas are conjunctions of them. Every trigger set is nonempty, covers every bound variable, and each term contains a bound variable and an uninterpreted function application; interpreted function symbols are excluded from triggers. The initial input is therefore not arbitrary unprocessed SMT syntax. Definition 2 states are current tagged quantifiers W, current clauses A and E-state E, or the terminal saturated/inconsistent markers. [Evidence: Q4, §3 introduction/§3.1 syntax/Definition1, PDF pp.6–7; Q5, §3.2 states/Definition2, PDF pp.7–7; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]  Definitions 3–4 replace a concrete congruence-closure implementation with an E-interface. Its judgments track known terms and equalities/disequalities, including known subterms and equality substitution; extending it adds literals with the required closure. Positive/negative predicates are represented using equality to Boolean true/false. A basis chooses one representative per known equivalence class. A finite number of classes does not imply only finitely many syntactic terms, and a finite basis at each step does not alone prevent unbounded growth across steps. This last limitation is explicit in the related-work discussion. [Evidence: Q6, §3.3 E-interface/Definitions3–4, PDF pp.7–8; Q16, §5 complete related work, PDF pp.17–18; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]  Definitions 5–7 pair the E-interface with an instantiation history containing a quantifier tag and a tuple of ground terms. A candidate is enabled only when an appropriate trigger matches known terms and no prior instance with that tag has a pointwise equal tuple under current equalities. History thus blocks semantic duplicates, not merely identical printed expressions. Example 4 applies this to (b,a,t)/(b,c,t). The model's counting argument depends on preserving this history discipline. [Evidence: Q7, §3.4 E-history/E-matching/Definitions5–7/Example4, PDF pp.8–9; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]  Definition 8 has four transition rules. Split chooses a nonempty collection of disjuncts from currently unsatisfied clauses and must make progress; it adds ordinary literals to the E-interface and quantifiers to W. Instantiation selects an enabled match, puts unit literals/quantifiers directly into their components, keeps non-unit clauses in A and records the instance in history. Bot ends an inconsistent state. Sat ends a consistent state with assumed satisfaction of every current clause and no enabled instances. Instantiation and splitting may interleave without a fixed order or fairness requirement for this case. Reader scope limit: the saturated marker records this trigger-relative exhaustion; the chapter does not establish first-order satisfiability or completeness from it. [Evidence: Q8, §3.5 all four transitions/Definition8, PDF pp.9–11; exact source and character/LF/page anchors in quotes.json.]  Section 3.6 parameterizes an inner quantifier's tag by all outer bound variables. Instantiating an outer quantifier substitutes those tag parameters as well as its body. Both insertion of new quantifiers and history-enabled matching compare tags modulo equality of their parameters. This prevents equivalent outer instances from creating fresh identities that evade deduplication. These details are part of the abstraction; the full definitions are delegated to the technical report. Reader scope limit: the four displayed rules also have no explicit CDCL backtracking/restart, clause deletion, MBQI or concrete solver implementation state. It uses 12 uninterpreted functions, removes cardinality because that depends on external linear arithmetic, and splits bidirectional definitions into separate introduction/elimination implications with independent triggers. Example 5's union elimination offers one single-term trigger and two alternative multi-term triggers. Most are non-generative. Union elimination yields Boolean literals whose non-Boolean subterms were already known through the trigger; under this model Boolean literals do not add new classes. Four generative non-nested introduction axioms can create Skss(s1,s2), Skeq(s1,s2), Skdj(s1,s2) or Skie(s), respectively for subset, extensional equality, disjointness and emptiness. O1(B) is the set-sorted basis. O2(B) contains the element-sorted basis plus every possible application of the three binary and one unary Skolem functions over O1(B). Potential match sets then cover original quantifiers and parameterized inner quantifiers, including those not yet introduced, while excluding history-equivalent instances. - A Generalised Union of Rely–Guarantee and Separation Logic Using Permission Algebras (2024)
    - what: GenRGSep is an Isabelle/HOL library generalizing rely-guarantee separation logic to resource models without guaranteed units or cancellativity. It supplies permission/multi-unit/single-unit algebra classes,compositional resource constructions,a generic relational-action concurrent language,explicit stabilization operators,and a reported mechanized operational soundness theorem. Identifies why Vafeiadis-style operational safety nearly extends to noncancellative resources but needs stronger preservation of local state on silent framed steps when external choice retains its surrounding command. Conjunction still needs all local resources cancellative. Distinguishes a weaker atomic framing condition from requiring the atomic relation to admit the corresponding unframed transition. Paper’s result concerns the generic logic/library,not a production implementation.
    - limits: Permission algebra requires partial commutativity/associativity,compatibility laws and positivity;it need not have units or cancellation. Multi-unit and single-unit classes add those respective structures. Total HOL addition is only constrained by algebra laws on compatible resources;behavior on incompatible sums cannot silently be used as valid resource composition. Proof system works over local/shared state pairs and relational atomic actions. Environment rely relation constrains shared changes;guarantee constrains observable updates. Local state splits under parallel composition while shared state remains common. Instantiating a real language requires sound resource and atomic-action models beyond this generic framework. Theorem2 says a derivable triple and its precondition imply safe n for every finite n. safe enforces postcondition only when command is skip,checks rely/program/framed steps,and records observable guarantee updates. It does not prove termination,fairness,progress,deadlock freedom or network-fault tolerance. Conjunction rule retains a global side condition:every possible local state must be cancellative. Removing cancellation from the base algebra does not make all standard conjunction reasoning available over arbitrary noncancellative instances. Silent τ transitions must preserve the same unframed local resource in the strengthened frame-safety clause. This is essential to the external-choice proof;allowing merely some decomposed residual resource is insufficient. Observable updates generate guarantee obligations without forcing guarantee reflexivity for silent actions. Predicates are shallow HOL functions;rely/guarantee,stabilization and atomic proof obligations are supplied mathematical relations/predicates. Paper reports an Isabelle mechanization and supplies GitHub/SWH artifact,but does not demonstrate an automated verifier,code extraction or verified compiler connection. The supplied PDF has substantial apparent notation/rule inconsistencies detailed in reader caveats. The record distinguishes the authors’ mechanized-soundness claim from the displayed formulas;no artifact execution checks which formulation is implemented. Displayed rules alone should not be treated as a coherent independently validated formalization.

- A Verified Earley Parser (2024)
    - what: Isabelle/HOL formalization of an inductive Earley recognizer, refinement through a bin-wise fixed-point algorithm to executable functional lists, and a pointer-guided parser producing one parse tree. Recognizer correctness and successful parse-tree existence equivalence require terminal-only input and an epsilon-free grammar. Returned-tree soundness and a termination argument are proved for generated pointer structures. Explains why one-pass list-bin processing misses completion opportunities for epsilon rules and retains an explicit epsilon-free premise. Separates item equality, refinement, pointer invariants, single-tree soundness and tree-existence equivalence from enumeration of all parses. Uses first reduction-pointer monotonicity to terminate even for cyclic grammars; gives informal O(n^4) time and O(n^3) pointer-space estimates, rather than attributing optimal Earley bounds to this implementation.
    - limits: Grammar is a finite rule list plus start symbol over a common symbol type. Nonterminals are all rule LHS symbols plus the start symbol; terminals are the remaining symbols. is_word G omega excludes nonterminals from the input. Abstract item completeness and correctness explicitly assume is_word. The inductive Earley specification supports epsilon rules, but executable Earley_eq_Earley_L, correctness_recognizer and correctness_build_tree_Earley_L require epsilon_free G: every RHS is nonempty. Lifting this restriction is future work. No verified epsilon-elimination preprocessing is delivered here. Each bin contains distinct items with end index equal to bin index. List insertion appends new items and merges reduction pointers into existing entries. Termination of bin processing relies on well-formed bounded items and finite candidate counts, not arbitrary malformed bin arguments. build_tree_prime termination requires wf_tree_input: sound_ptrs, mono_red_ptr, valid bin/input indices and valid entry index. Pointer soundness includes earlier origin bins for reductions, bounds and operation semantics. Only the FIRST reduction triple is required to have a strictly earlier reduction entry within the current bin. wf_item_yield_build_tree_prime additionally assumes wf_bins. Returned-tree corollary assumes epsilon_free and successful build_tree over Earley_L-generated bins, and proves rule-tree well-formedness, start root and full input yield. Existential successful tree iff derivation additionally assumes is_word. The algorithm extracts one parse tree, not a forest enumerating every ambiguous or cyclic derivation. Nevertheless the final theorem DOES establish existence of a returned tree iff a valid derivation exists under its premises. The phrase no completeness for trees concerns all possible trees, not failure to recognize some valid word. Partial functions in HOL use domain-theoretic definitions; termination is proved on stated valid inputs. Option None representing undefinedness is not a runtime detector that can return after discovering an infinite computation. Arbitrary externally supplied pointer cycles are outside the proved termination domain. Complexity is explicitly informal with fixed grammar: rule count and maximum RHS size are constants. More than 6,000 formalization lines are reported, but no formal complexity theorem or proof-effort breakdown is supplied. Scala extraction and execution do not constitute a verified compiler/runtime chain. Evaluation measures the exported recognizer, not a full byte-level lexer or full parse-tree production pipeline. Five toy grammars, unary inputs a^n and ten-run means do not establish representative production workload performance. Hardware, Scala/JVM versions, exact source dataset, variance and raw timings are not supplied in §7. Imperative cached refinement, grammar indexing, next-symbol grouping and epsilon support remain future work. No Verus, Rust, TLA+, distributed-system implementation or LLM agent is evaluated.

- Affeldt Stone Coq Lebesgue differentiation 2024 (2024)
    - title: A Comprehensive Overview of the Lebesgue Differentiation Theorem in Coq
    - what: Affeldt and Stone report Coq/MathComp-Analysis formalization of the real-line Lebesgue Differentiation theorem, implying the first Fundamental Theorem of Calculus for integrable real functions almost everywhere and the density theorem for measurable real sets. Supporting work connects subspace/uniform-convergence topology, extended-real filter limits, regularity/Egorov/Lusin/Tietze, continuous L1 approximation and a finite Vitali covering argument for the Hardy-Littlewood inequality. A new Urysohn proof uses coarser uniform separators and reusable gauge-pseudometric infrastructure. Main theorem scripts and statements total approximately 1,497 lines, excluding uncounted supporting theories. Reads exact local-integrability/Lebesgue-point/FTC/density premises; explicit bounded-support localization and two error estimates; full-carrier subspace design preserving arithmetic; weak-topology uniform function alias; right-filter tactic issue; finite-measure versus prose boundedness; separator equivalence and gauge construction; finite ball selection with factor 3; unused infinite covering results; all table counts and future second-FTC scope.
    - limits: Main theorem is real-valued f on realType with Lebesgue measure on the real line, assuming locally_integrable [set: R] f. Definition requires measurability, open domain and finite integral of absolute value on every compact subset. It concludes a.e. Lebesgue points, not differentiability of every integrable f itself. Lebesgue point means average |f(y)-f(x)| over centered open balls tends to zero as positive radius tends to zero. iavg is average absolute value; davg centers f first. Extended-real fine maps infinities to 0, so meaningful normalization relies on the finite positive ball measures used under radius premises (§2–3). First FTC result assumes global integrability of f. FTC1_lebesgue_pt differentiates its variable-upper-bound integral at a Lebesgue point x with lower interval bound a<BRight x; bound type handles open/closed finite lower endpoints and negative infinity. Corollary FTC1Ny integrates over ]-infinity,x] and asserts derivative=f(x) a.e. Direction 1 is the derivative direction, not an extra smoothness hypothesis. Proof uses a nicely-shrinking-set generalization. No continuity of f is needed, and the result is not differentiability everywhere (§10.1). Density theorem assumes only measurability of A, not finite total measure. It concludes local ball-volume ratio converges a.e. to indicator_A(x), hence 1 inside A and 0 outside up to a null set. This local consequence uses the indicator as locally integrable, not global integrability of an infinite-measure set (§10.2). Proof localizes f to f_k=f*indicator_(ball 0 [2(k+1)]), obtains a.e. Lebesgue points in each ball, and uses countable localization for the full line. Positive-threshold limsup exceptional sets are controlled through continuous approximation: Markov bounds approximation error and Hardy-Littlewood bounds maximal error. Continuous L1 density depends on Lusin/Tietze, while maximal inequality uses regularity/finite Vitali. The overview explicitly identifies bounded-to-general steps often omitted in informal notes (§4, Figure 1). Subspace A is a type alias for the entire carrier T, not the subtype of points satisfying A. Neighborhoods restrict ordinary neighborhoods within A for points of A; outside A the topology is discrete. Thus continuity depends only on values within A while x+eps remains well-typed for arbitrary numeric carrier values. Hierarchy-Builder factories assemble proper-neighborhood/topological laws. This avoids needing A closed under addition; it does not assert x+eps remains in A (§5.1). Uniform_fun A V aliases all U→V functions, then pulls back uniform convergence on restricted functions via sigL_arrow and weak_topology, copying the uniform structure using Uniform.copy. Values outside A are ignored by the induced convergence condition. Extended-real limsup extends sequence-only infrastructure to arbitrary filters as inf_V_in_F sup(f[V]), specializing to deleted real neighborhoods and right-radius limits. Development exposed/fixed near-tactic right-filter handling quirks; no performance numbers are reported (§5.2–5.3). Egorov, outer/inner epsilon-regularity, Lusin and continuous L1 approximation formally use finite-measure hypotheses mu A<+infinity or mu D<+infinity, with measurability and positive epsilon; they do not formally require geometric boundedness. Prose repeatedly says bounded, which is stronger for real Lebesgue sets. Egorov additionally assumes measurability of each function and limit and a.e. pointwise convergence. It obtains uniform convergence outside a measurable epsilon-small set. Inner-regularity supremum version removes finite-measure restriction by sigma-finiteness (§6, §8). Uniform_separator A B means some uniform structure coarser than original topology has an entourage avoiding A×B. uniform_separatorP equates this with a continuous function into [0,1] taking 0 on A and 1 on B. No normal-space assumption appears in that equivalence; normality plus closed/disjoint sets supplies a separator, yielding Urysohn. A point outside a closed set in a uniform space supplies another separator, yielding complete regularity. Range/image inclusions support empty sets without needing equal nonempty singleton images (§7.1). New Urysohn proof replaces explicit rational-index induction with a countable entourage basis/gauge pseudometric, extended distance to A and truncated distance function min(d(A,x),epsilon)/epsilon. Coarser uniform topology ensures continuity in original topology. For normal spaces basis relations are U2×U2 union complement(closure U1)×itself, indexed by nested opens A subset U1, closure U1 subset U2. Most work proves a coarser uniformity and a separating entourage. Additional countable-product metrizability and uniform-space complete regularity are reusable consequences, not all needed by the differentiation proof (§7.2, Figure 2). Tietze theorem formally assumes normal X, closed A, f continuous within A, positive M and |f|≤M on A; extends to global continuous g equal to f on A with same bound everywhere. Uniform limits preserve continuity. Lusin gives compact K subset A, small measure A minus K, f continuous within K, via Egorov/inner regularity. Combined Lusin/Tietze yield globally continuous g_n integrable on A with L1 error over A tending to 0; proof then restricts approximants to localization ball. No stronger all-space globally integrable approximant conclusion is inferred (§8). Finite Vitali lemma takes a list of indices for nonempty sets satisfying is_ball. It returns duplicate-free sublist D of disjoint selected balls; each original ball intersects a selected ball of at least its radius and is contained in its triple-radius dilation. Set-based predicate avoids committing to center/radius-pair representation; cpoint/radius recover witnesses. Infinite Vitali lemma and covering theorem were also formalized but are expressly unnecessary for this differentiation proof (§9.1). Hardy-Littlewood operator is supremum over positive-radius averages of |f|. Formal weak-type bound: measure{x:HL(f)(x)>c}≤(3/c)*norm1(f) for locally integrable f and c>0. Global norm may be infinite, making bound uninformative in that case; useful quantitative estimates apply to localized/integrable functions. Factor 3 comes with one-dimensional ball cover. Lower-semicontinuity theory establishes measurability of maximal operator (§9.2). Table 1 counts approximate lines including theorem statements for selected main/intermediate lemmas: 87,61,118,108,108,118,75,180,165,143,265,69, summing to 1,497. Subspace and uniform-convergence support are explicitly N.A., not zero effort. Counts depend on boundary between lemmas and supporting theories, so total is not complete project size, human effort, automation throughput or runtime. No controlled benchmark, proof-generation rate or LLM intervention is described (Table 1). Reader exposition caveat: Lusin prose p. 12 prints measure(K minus A)<epsilon while K subset A, which is vacuous; exact formal lemma correctly prints measure(A minus K)<epsilon. This record follows the formal statement. Similarly formal finite-measure premises are preserved over prose shorthand bounded. These are distinctions in supplied paper, not evidence of source-code proof failure (§6–8). MathComp-Analysis extends MathComp with classical axioms. Paper supplies exact declarations, proof outlines, repository/archive and source-file pointers, not complete printed proof scripts or an independent axiom/build audit. Reference snapshots list MathComp-Analysis 1.2.0 and MathComp 2.2.0 (2024), and Coq manual 8.19.2; these references alone do not pin a tested build configuration. Artifact archive 603335be2da03f1a37b210f027047f94aa0ed2c6 identifies supplied source; reader did not execute it. Authors explicitly acknowledge mathlib differentiation statements are more general in domain/measure/codomain/Vitali-family formulations and sometimes stronger differentiability conclusions. Comparative claims describe cited 2024 snapshots and were not rechecked against current libraries. Their belief that Banach-space generalization should be engineering work is a proposal, not completed generality. Second FTC for absolutely continuous functions is future work using Radon-Nikodym plus bounded/total variation (§11–12). No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+ result, software safety/liveness evaluation or LLM proof agent appears. Relevant evidence is human proof-engineering decomposition, exact semantic hypotheses, reusable topology interfaces, proof-gap repair and library integration. Authors claim first Coq Lebesgue first-FTC formalization; reader has not independently established priority.

Define window equivalence E(x,y): (y≤a⇒x≤a) and (a<y<b⇒x=y) and (y≥b⇒x≥b). Symmetry is stated only when a<b. Reported val(t) E hard(a,b,t) implies hard(bottom,top,t)=val(t). Values outside the window need only indicate the correct side; narrow-window outputs need not equal the exact tree value. §2: Define a second relation R(y,x): (y≤a⇒x≤y) and (a<y<b⇒x=y) and (y≥b⇒x≥y). This is a relation parameterized by(a,b), not ordinary ≤ or numerical-distance comparison. Paper reports R(soft,val), R(hard,val) and R(hard,soft), with hard/soft equal search spaces. It would be incorrect to infer soft superiority merely because it satisfies a stronger property than the classic hard theorem; hard satisfies that property too. The direct hard-to-soft relation expresses the actual refinement. §2.1: Single-player-perspective evaluation/search requires unary negation satisfying −min(x,y)=max(−x,−y) and −(−x)=x. These are abstract algebraic assumptions, not reliance on numeric subtraction or negative integers. They allow swapping the player perspective while preserving the order structure. §3: Generalization requires a bounded distributive lattice: meet/join replace min/max. The weak relation B(x,y) is a∨(x∧b)=a∨(y∧b). It recovers exact valuation for full bottom/top window. Equivalence with the classic E relation is stated for linear orders and a<b; it cannot be transferred blindly to partially ordered values. §3: Strong lattice relation S(y,x) means x∧b≤y≤x∨a. On a linear order with a<b it coincides with R(y,x). Distributivity gives S(y,x)⇒B(x,y), but B alone does not imply S. Paper reports S(f(a,b,t),val(t)) for hard,soft and Bird–Hughes bh, after modifying variants for lattices. It does not reproduce their algorithms or provide direct proof scripts. §3.1: For lattice negamax, −(x∧y)=(−x)∨(−y) and involution are assumed, forming a de Morgan algebra. Arbitrary bounded lattices or arbitrary unary sign functions are not enough. No theorem for nondistributive lattices is stated. §4: Caching/reusing earlier calls is cited as work by Li et al., outside the variants covered here. No verification of transposition tables, concurrent cache updates, distributed search or graph-cycle handling is reported. §4: A Hughes-derived program was suspected to prune less; Hughes reportedly used Haskell Quickcheck privately to compare its search space with the canonical implementation and confirmed the suspicion. - Basold, Bruin and Lawson directed Van Kampen 2024 (2024)
    - title: The Directed Van Kampen Theorem in Lean
    - what: Reports a Lean4/mathlib formalization of directed spaces and their fundamental categories, culminating in a Van Kampen theorem: covering a directed space by two open subspaces makes the induced fundamental-category square a pushout in Cat. This gives a compositional description of directed path-equivalence classes. Introduces 5.6k lines across30files and detailed correspondence between the handwritten universal-property argument and Lean obligations. Concurrency is motivated by irreversible executions and a two-program obstacle picture; no concrete distributed implementation or verified protocol is evaluated. Reads directedness/covering definitions, asymmetric homotopies and symmetric zigzag quotient, category/functor laws, complete eight-step proof and matching Lean construction. Records exact two-open-cover and overlap-compatibility assumptions, index offset, partition-refinement/representative independence, Classical.choose and quotient descent, artifact version/limits, and small printed type/order slips without inferring formal artifact failures.
    - limits: Directed space means a topological space with selected continuous paths closed under constants, concatenation and monotone subparametrization. Directed maps are continuous maps preserving those selected paths. This is more general than giving every space a global partial order; no finite-state, finite-dimensional or path-connectedness assumption appears in Theorem21. One must supply an appropriate directed-space model before applying the theorem (§2,§5.1). Figure1 contrasts two sequential schedules, concurrent schedules differing only in progress speed, and concurrent schedules around a shared-memory-access obstacle. The obstacle excludes simultaneous access and separates access orders. These are geometric motivation examples, not verified source programs, a memory-model soundness theorem, or measured race-detection results. Literal exactly-two-paths language should be read at the schedule/deformation level, since parametrized paths allow many timings (§1,Figure1). Implementation extends TopologicalSpace with IsDipath and three closure fields. Dipath extends endpoint-indexed Path with a proof of directedness. General path reversal is unavailable because it may violate direction. Products and directed structures induced along continuous maps are provided. For strict subparametrizations with changing endpoints, the authors reuse Path.map by treating the parameter map as a monotone path in the unit interval, overcoming a mathlib interface that only handled endpoint-preserving reparametrization (§2.1). Directed homotopy is a directed map I×X→Y with fixed map values at deformation times0/1; directed path homotopy also fixes both path endpoints. Direction applies to both product coordinates and a homotopy cannot generally be reversed. PreDihomotopic is existence of one such homotopy; Dihomotopic is its smallest generated equivalence relation, implemented by EqvGen. Symmetric equivalence of paths does not assert physical reversibility of executions (§3). Example12 uses linear interpolation H(t,s)=(1−t)γ1(s)+tγ2(s) for monotone interval paths ordered pointwise. Directedness uses coordinatewise monotonicity. Lemmas14–16 extend zigzags through directed maps, prove endpoint-preserving reparametrization invariance, and establish concatenation congruence, identities and associativity modulo equivalence. These are the exact conditions needed to descend path concatenation to a category (§3). Fundamental-category objects are all points; morphisms x→y are directed paths modulo Dihomotopic; identity is constant path and composition concatenation. It is a category rather than a groupoid because reverse paths may not exist. The dπ functor maps points by directed maps and path classes by composition; it is not an algorithm that enumerates every execution or yields a numeric count of schedules (§4). Path pieces γ_i,n are equal-parameter subpaths. Being n-covered means every piece lies in one cover member. Lean covered_partwise γ n represents n+1 mathematical pieces, with zero as one covered path; the recursive split therefore uses n+2. This index convention matters in refinement/induction and is explicitly explained rather than a theorem off-by-one bug. Homotopy covering is a rectangular n×m grid (§2.1,Definition20). Theorem21 assumes X1 and X2 open in X, unionX, and X0 their intersection, all with induced directedness. Inclusion maps induce the Cat square. Conclusion is the universal property of a pushout: for any target category and two functors from the local fundamental categories agreeing exactly on the intersection, there is a unique global functor restricting to both. No connected-intersection/basepoint hypothesis is required in this full-category formulation. General arbitrary covers are not formalized (§5.1,§6). Proof Steps1–2 force the global object map by local membership and the path map by a composite of local images of finitely many covered subpaths. Compactness/Lebesgue Number Lemma yields finite subdivisions for a path/homotopy under the open cover. This is an existence theorem for arbitrary topological paths, not a stated effective subdivision procedure or complexity bound (§5.1). Step3 uses overlap agreement to eliminate the cover-branch choice. Step4 refines n- and m-piece partitions to a common mn-piece partition, using functor composition and reparametrization to eliminate subdivision choice. Step5 proves constants and concatenation. These independence obligations prevent a local-piece construction from depending on arbitrary choices, rather than merely checking one chosen partition (§5.1 PDF12–13). Step6 reduces representative independence to a single directed homotopy and then to one row of covered rectangles by induction. Step7 strengthens the induction to homotopies with moving endpoints: the images of lower path followed by right boundary and left boundary followed by upper path agree. For a single rectangle, min/max endpoint homotopies make a fixed-endpoint path homotopy; induction glues columns. Constant boundary paths recover the original path-equivalence result. Step8 descends to the quotient, obtains a functor, verifies restrictions and uniqueness (§5.1 PDF13–14). Formal construction follows the proof but reorders it: covered-path maps and refinement independence are defined/proved before choosing a subdivision. FunctorOnHomAux explicitly uses Classical.choose_spec on has_subpaths. Then representative independence permits Quotient.liftOn; separate map-id/map-comp and unique-extension lemmas build Functor and IsPushout. Calling the proof constructive refers to its explicit mathematical functor construction; the printed use of classical choice does not establish an extracted executable algorithm (§5.2). Theorem/proof snippets have small printed slips. PDF13 Step5 begins F′(delta⊙gamma) although gamma:x→y and delta:y→z, so the composable order is gamma⊙delta; the preceding equation and Lean functorOnHomAux_trans PDF16 use the correct order. PDF14 final homotopy chain writes id_x as the left identity after the y-constant path; the typed identity should be at the target image. PDF14 prose calls F1/F2 maps out ofC and names the wrong inclusions for h_comm, whereas displayed Lean types are local categories→C with agreement along intersection inclusions. These are paper-text/type-description slips, not evidence of failed checking in the linked artifact. Implementation version is Lean4.6.0-rc1, built on mathlib; reported size5.6k lines in30files. Publication says not yet integrated into mathlib. These are2024source statements; this reading does not assert current2026integration status or a current first-formalization claim. The related2023arXiv version uses Lean3, so its version should not be conflated with the conference artifact (§1.1–1.2,front matter). Archived code is version1.1 at https://github.com/Dominique-Lawson/Directed-Topology-Lean-4/tree/v1.1 with Software Heritage directory479a73373a2bf508149f7d1b889b42304fe78a9e. File pointers include directed_space.lean, constructions.lean, dipath.lean, path_cover.lean, directed_homotopy.lean, directed_path_homotopy.lean, fundamental_category.lean and directed_van_kampen.lean. Paper excerpts deliberately replace proof bodies with comments; those omissions are not evidence of sorry in the repository. No build, axiom audit or independent kernel acceptance was performed in this reading. Authors do not formalize the undirected groupoid Van Kampen corollary, though they explain that making every path directed should yield it. Arbitrary open-cover generalization is proposed but not investigated in depth. Formal links to higher-dimensional automata and their languages are future work. Thus a concurrent program→d-space semantics bridge and any system safety/liveness theorem remain outside the reported formalization (§6). Evaluation is a mathematical formalization case with definitions, lemmas, theorem statement and archived artifact, not empirical protocol verification. No benchmark suite, checker runtime/memory, person-effort, defect count, LLM success rate, Verus/TLA+/Rust implementation or distributed-system model is evaluated.     - title: Verifying Global Two-Safety Properties in Neural Networks with Confidence
    - what: Defines confidence-based global 2-safety properties unifying robustness and fairness, and verifies them by self-composing a DNN and replacing softmax with a sound piecewise-linear over-approximation checked by Marabou. The property compares every sufficiently close input pair when at least one output has confidence above a threshold, allowing class changes near low-confidence decision boundaries while requiring high-confidence predictions to agree. The paper proves soundness and bounds softmax approximation error, gives a complete Marabou-based counterexample procedure for the approximated network, and uses binary search to synthesize minimum robust/fair confidence. Experiments cover German Credit, Adult, Law School and COMPAS models with global robustness and sensitive-attribute fairness queries.

Marabou completeness removes solver false positives, but abstraction can produce spurious counterexamples. High confidence as a precondition can make poorly calibrated networks vacuously safe; current method handles roughly two to five outputs and does not establish training-data generalization.

    - what: Proposes a concrete pointer-as-integer C memory interface with explicit allocation/access failstops and an implementation-specific allocation oracle hidden behind axioms. Demonstrates it in Coq with a toy RTL-to-tagged-Mach compiler/runtime, proving two-way behavior refinement under a matching memory-model instantiation. Public/private protection isolates compiler control data while allowing defined out-of-object effects among public data. Connects finite allocation/failstop behavior to compilation rather than treating OOM as undefined. Context labels let the oracle predict target stack offsets and heap placements without exposing private layout in interface axioms. A perturb operation models private-layout changes between public allocations. Gives executable tagged stack/allocator design, relational state/memory matching and explicit optimization losses from concrete addresses. Scope remains toy data-pointer compilation, with full C,function pointers and phase composition future work.
    - limits: Public/private(PvP) protection allows arbitrary accesses among public regions, but prevents ordinary source data-pointer accesses to compiler-private state such as saved return addresses,locals,parameters and heap headers. It is not object-granularity spatial/temporal safety or protection against data-only attacks. The axiomatic byte-addressed interface has finite word-representable nonoverlapping regions,positive nonnull bases,alignment and minimum-size constraints,heap-base uniqueness,stack/heap observation functions,load/store stability and free/perturb laws. New allocations need not be initialized to zero; contents are defined but unpredictable. Any integer may be used as an address. Loads/stores within allocated regions succeed. Outside them they may succeed,warp to public storage or failstop depending on instantiation; source axioms do not expose private addresses. LdStEq applies to any successful store; LdStNeq only restricts stores whose destination lies in an allocated region, permitting OOB warping side effects. Allocation may report OOM at any time under the generic axioms. Nonvacuity/behavior equivalence is established for the particular program-indexed instantiation matching compiler/runtime allocation, not every arbitrary oracle and not a source-only universal resource guarantee. Proof-of-concept memory is64-bit-word-addressed with no alignments, unlike the proposed byte-indexed interface. Source RTL has unlimited local pseudoregisters,straight-line function bodies,+/−,loads/stores,calls and fixed local arrays. Mach has fixed registers,abstract code pointers/separate code,tagged word memory,privileged/unprivileged accesses and direct named calls. Code-pointer corruption is excluded by this representation. General function-pointer protection is explicitly future work; abstract blanket control-flow-attack language does not prove secure arbitrary-C compilation. Theorem1 assumes source behavior under I(S) is not Stuck; a source typing judgment can rule that out. It compares termination with same result,divergence and failstop. Its stated ≈ equates failstops for any reason,so it does not by itself equate exact OOM versus OOB labels or failure timing/step counts.     - what: Extends probabilistic model checking from expected rewards to full reward distributions for DTMCs and MDPs, supporting variance, quantiles, value-at-risk and CVaR for rewards accumulated until co-safe LTL goals. DTMC forward computation is often faster than DVI on large PRISM benchmarks, but DVI can be faster when Vmax is high.

    - title: Formal Verification of the Empty Hexagon Number
    - what: Formalizes in Lean the geometric-to-SAT reduction behind h(6)=30: every set of 30 planar points in general position contains an empty convex hexagon. A distributed CaDiCaL/cake_lpr computation supplies the n=30 unsatisfiability certificate. Sections 3–4 connect Lean convex-hull predicates to triangle emptiness and determinant-based orientations; σPtInTriangle_iff under four-point general position closes an implicit gap in prior work, and OrientationProperty proves that holes depend only on triple orientations. Section 5 constructs a six-step canonical-position transformation (rotation, translation, projective map, sorting, reflection and return from infinity) and proves existence of a σ-equivalent canonical set. Section 6 defines orientation, triangle, cap/cup and hole variables plus 16 clause families; variable-defining and orientation clauses are proved, while forbidden configurations imply six-holes. The n=30 CNF is partitioned into 312,418 subproblems, solved by CaDiCaL 1.9.5 with LRAT proofs checked on the fly by cake_lpr in 25,876.5 CPU hours (~3 CPU years). The Lean encoder emits CNF below 1 s on a laptop; a comparison g(6) corollary takes 28 s to solve versus Marić's 787 s and uses O(n⁴) rather than O(n⁶) clauses. The formalization required ~300 hours/3 months and ~4.7k Lean lines, and corrected an orientation-map error and a lex-order/code mismatch in prior work.

- ForEx hyperliveness verification (2024)
    - title: Automated Software Verification of Hyperliveness.
    - what: Introduces Forall-Exist Hoare Logic (FEHL) and ForEx, a constraint-based verifier for finite-program ∀k∃l relational properties (Forall-Exist Hoare Tuples). The method symbolically postpones existential nondeterministic choices as parameters, computes parametric strongest postconditions, and discharges resulting first-order constraints with SMT. FEHL provides self-composition, sequencing, conditionals, loops and consequence rules; the paper proves soundness and completeness relative to sound/complete unary Hoare and under-approximate systems. ForEx implements eager restriction satisfiability checks, a minimal C-like language with arrays/bitvectors, Z3 support for linear integer arithmetic, arrays and finite bitvectors, and guess-and-check invariant generation. Experiments compare ForEx against HyPA, PCSat and HyPro on k-safety, GNI, refinement and related benchmarks. ForEx is faster on solved instances but its counting-based loop alignment misses context-dependent alignments and it cannot prove termination of existential loops, leaving some GNI instances unsolved.

It tracks interrupted accepting-state searches with a restart set, proving that the algorithm finds an accepting lasso iff one exists and terminates otherwise. Hitchhiking adapts the Map accepting-predecessor algorithm to exploration-time GPU execution. It maintains open, active, and interrupted sets plus a monotone maximal-predecessor function; detailed lemmas establish finite rounds, propagation invariants, cycle detection, and no-cycle termination, and a thread-safety argument explains atomic maxima and barriers. GPUexplore 3.0 integrates the algorithm with a compressed tree hash table, work claiming, generated CUDA successor functions, and Spot NBA construction. The evaluation compares Hitchhiking with Map, Spin NDFS, and 1/32-core LTSmin over 96 BEEM instances spanning 150,000–1.2 billion states.
    - number: Titan RTX 4,608 cores, 24 GB
    - number: 512 threads/block and about 3,000 blocks
    - number: 96 instances
    - number: 150,000–1.2 billion states
    - limits: The model is a finite Kripke structure with total transitions and an NBA product; correctness assumes a strict total order on accepting states, atomic thread-safe updates, and global barriers between parallel loops. GPU memory and state-hash capacity limit scale; work claiming is not BFS, making runtime exploration-order dependent. Benchmarks omit communication-channel models, partial-order reduction, and precise Spin hashing; one telephony family exposed incorrect LTSmin results attributed to overflow.

    - what: Introduces Isabelle/Scala technology for distributed AFP builds without shared memory or shared file systems. A master analyzes session dependencies, synchronizes workers with SSH/rsync, stores coordination state and compressed ML heaps in PostgreSQL, and workers execute sessions independently. A runtime predictor scales historical timings across hosts/threads; a heuristic solves the multi-mode resource-constrained scheduling problem quickly and reschedules as measurements change. The implementation sets concrete infrastructure assumptions (same platform, local SSDs, SSH/bash, PostgreSQL, repository clones) and explains why Slurm was rejected for cross-platform, low-privilege academic clusters. Build phases include dependency extraction, worker initialization, optional benchmark sessions, queue execution and HTML/LaTeX finalization. The scheduler uses Amdahl-law interpolation, conservative overestimation, host/thread modes and a parallel serial-generation scheme; experiments compare classic, heuristic and CPLEX schedules on preliminary, heterogeneous and Isabelle2024 release data. Three datasets contain 19,263, 30,510 and 30,203 session data points. On release hardware the heuristic finishes AFP in 35:40 (40:50 with slow sessions, 1:59:13 full), while distribution classic mode takes 8:10; full AFP CPU/elapsed speedup exceeds 100.
