- Lean Formalization of Completeness Proof for Coalition Logic with Common Knowledge (2024)
    - what: Reports a Lean 4 formalization of soundness, completeness and the finite model property for coalition logic with individual/common knowledge. Uses reusable syntax and proof-system typeclasses across CL, CLK and CLC, canonical coalition models and finite filtration. Main contribution is mechanized logical metatheory and proof engineering, not an implemented distributed-system case study. Records exact semantic/frame assumptions, positive-length common-knowledge paths, canonical effectivity cases, closure changes needed for deep embedding, finite-state construction, staged Set/Finset/List proofs and the concrete N-maximality derivation. Identifies a printed semantic discrepancy for empty-group common knowledge between the usual reflexive-transitive interpretation of starred notation and the shown Lean path constructors. Separates reported sorry-free artifact from abridged paper snippets; no independent replay.

Syntax is an inductive deep embedding with bottom, variables, conjunction, implication, coalition effectivity, individual knowledge and common knowledge. Syntax itself accepts arbitrary agent types; Fintype and Nonempty hypotheses are introduced where needed. Semantics uses classical reasoning and noncomputable finite-set conversions within Lean/Mathlib. §4, p.4: effectivity E(s,G) is a family of outcome sets a coalition can force, abstracting away explicit actions and strategies. True playability requires six conditions: empty outcome never forceable, universal outcome forceable, grand-coalition maximality relative to empty-coalition complements, outcome monotonicity, superadditivity for disjoint coalitions and a least empty-coalition outcome set. These are model assumptions, not distributed runtime liveness or memory-safety claims. §4/5, pp.4–7: each individual knowledge relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (S5-style equivalence). Coalition effectivity means the satisfying-state set belongs to E(s,G). Individual knowledge quantifies over indistinguishable states. Printed mathematical common knowledge uses a starred union relation, whereas Lean snippets use paths with at least one edge. For a nonempty coalition reflexivity bridges these conventions; empty coalition requires a different convention and exposes a discrepancy. §6/Table 1, pp.5/7: reported soundness Theorem 4 is theoremhood implies validity in the defined class of models, proved by induction on derivations. Axioms for coalition operators correspond to playability conditions; knowledge axioms use equivalence relations. Common-knowledge axiom C and induction rule RC use path-constructor arguments. This is not correctness of any specific program or natural-language requirement. §7, pp.8–9: Pformula gives constructors, Pformula_ax adds propositional derivability, CLformula adds effectivity and laws, Kformula individual knowledge, Cformula common knowledge with finite agent type. Typeclasses state minimum operations/laws; they are not generic inductive syntax. Generic semantics is omitted, so some proofs by induction remain tied to particular formula datatypes. §8.1, p.9: canonical coalition states are maximal consistent sets. For proper coalitions, X is effective iff some formula has its truth set inside X and its effectivity formula in the state. The grand-coalition case uses complements and absence of empty-coalition effectivity. Generic construction assumes nonempty agents and propositional bottom is not derivable. Initial canonical model has only five playability conditions and no epistemic relations. §8.2, pp.9–11: finite closure contains every subformula of every closure member, single negations, Ki CG ψ for members of common-knowledge groups and CG[G]ψ for effectivity formulas. Finiteness of agent groups enables finite expansion. Filtered states are canonical-state intersections with closure, represented by a filtered powerset and attached membership proof. There are at most 2^|cl(φ)| possible filtered states; this is a reader counting bound, not a paper runtime measurement. §8.2/8.3, pp.10–14: filtered effectivity treats grand coalition existentially and proper coalitions universally over canonical representatives. Finite models make empty-coalition principality follow from playability. Proofs use pairwise incompatibility of distinct filtered states and provability of the universal state disjunction. Set-to-Finset-to-List conversions require preserving disjointness, membership and absence of duplicates. §8.4/8.5, pp.14–15: Truth Lemma 5 equates filtered-state membership and satisfaction for formulas inside the finite closure. Common-knowledge proof inducts on positive-length paths from the front. Completeness Theorem 6 is validity implies theoremhood, using a maximal consistent extension of {¬φ} and a finite filtered countermodel. This establishes formula completeness/finite countermodels under the chosen semantics, not strong completeness for arbitrary infinite theories or a measured decision algorithm. §§1/3/9, pp.2–3/15–17: authors report all artifact proofs sorry-free, Lean 4.4.0-rc1 and Mathlib 98fe17fd, after completing an original Lean 3 proof and porting it. Paper snippets omit proof steps and even show an explicitly explained sorry. Code size about 6,000 lines: 300 CL, 700 CLK, 1,100 CLC and almost 4,000 shared. No exact build timings, proof-search benchmark, independent axiom audit or implementation replay provided in this reading. §9, pp.16–17: main engineering burden is finiteness/datatype conversion and long routine inductions. Native quantified representations and more generic semantics/inductive structures are proposed improvements, not implemented evaluations. IoT and metro systems motivate the introduction but are not verified cases. No Rust, Verus, TLA+, LLM agent or deployed distributed protocol experiment.

- Modular Verification of Intrusive List and Tree Data Structures in Separation Logic (2024)
    - what: A modular separation-logic method for intrusive data structures, where clients embed link nodes inside data objects. The representation separates node topology from attached data. Coq/Iris proofs in HeapLang reuse node-level specifications to verify cyclic/doubly linked lists, deques, and unbalanced binary-search-tree maps, including internal pointers and insertion. Shows that singly linked intrusive sequences compose into cycles, two oppositely directed cycles compose into a dcycle, and data fields framed alongside dcycles give a deque. For search trees, separates shape, key ordering and attached values; uses functional one-hole contexts and separating implication to retain the traversed tree while returning a pointer to an interior link. Locate is proved once and its contract makes insertion a modular, non-inductive client proof.
    - limits: Object programs are in unmodified Iris HeapLang, a simplified language with dynamic allocation, arrays and location arithmetic. The paper deliberately omits C fixed-width integers, byte representation and alignment. It does not verify actual Linux/Boost C/C++ code, C container_of provenance rules, a compiler, or machine execution. Hoare triples guarantee no crash under their ownership preconditions, and the stated result if execution finishes. This is partial correctness, not a proved termination/cost bound. The illustrated operations are sequential; the use of the concurrent Iris framework does not establish concurrent linearizability or thread-safe list mutation. Node APIs require ownership of supplied link cells and return detached ownership after removal. Clients allocate/deallocate enclosing objects. Data-layout predicates require separate ownership of topology and payload fields; arbitrary aliasing between those fields is not admitted. Concrete BST API uses natural-number keys and ordinary comparisons. Generic functional discussion uses a Boolean comparison p, but the printed assumptions/as-stated lemmas have apparent gaps detailed below. No balanced-tree invariant, rotations, deletion API or logarithmic complexity theorem is provided. Partial-tree reconstruction requires a valid one-hole context and a subtree whose insertion preserves the whole-tree BST invariant. A magic wand does not allow plugging an arbitrary key arrangement into the hole. Functional correctness lemmas and context generalization are part of the proof effort. Formal checking depends on Coq, Iris reasoning about HeapLang, and the declared definitions/specifications. Diaframe assists proof search and small pointer-arithmetic support is added in Setup.v. The paper supplies a Zenodo mechanization, but this reader has not replayed it or compared printed inconsistencies to source. The deque proof-size claim is less than30Coq proof lines for the deque API after underlying dcycle specifications, Iris lemmas and Diaframe support exist. It is not the size or cost of the full library or tree development. Scaling to more graph-like shared structures remains open.

- SCYTHE distributed protocol synthesis (2024)
    - title: Efficient Synthesis of Symbolic Distributed Protocols by Sketching
    - what: Introduces SCYTHE, a syntax-guided and counterexample-guided synthesizer for completing TLA+ sketches of parameterized distributed protocols. It enumerates typed expressions with cache/equivalence reduction and short-circuiting, uses TLC to check finite instances, and generalizes counterexamples into pruning constraints for safety, deadlock, liveness, and stuttering. The tool synthesizes protocols including consensus, 2PC, locks, sharded stores, and Raft reconfiguration. The paper formalizes protocol instances, fairness, sketches with pre/post holes and regular-tree grammars, and distinguishes finite-instance synthesis (Problem 1) from all-parameter-instance synthesis (Problem 2). Candidate generation uses cache-based size enumeration and semantic normal forms for Boolean/set/equality expressions; pruning constraints are disjunctions of hole interpretations. Safety constraints are optimal, while deadlock/liveness/stuttering encodings are sub-optimal but non-over-pruning; fairness and explicit implementability/environment constraints prevent vacuous solutions. TLC exhaustive checks each finite instance. In 22 benchmark rows, equivalence reduction cuts generated expressions by orders of magnitude; final TLAPS proofs establish safety for arbitrary instances in all but the two-process-only Peterson cases. Extra-checks expose finite-size overfitting: two Raft variants initially correct up to 3 nodes failed at 4+ and required larger-instance checks.

The model is xdot=f(x)+g(x)u with safe set C={h>=0} and inner set D={bθ>=0}. Proposition 1 requires feasible controls on every boundary activation set and D⊆C. Training combines correctness, derivative/feasibility, and a boundary activation regularizer; outer CEGIS adds verifier counterexamples. The verifier finds an initial boundary activation set by a line segment and LP, enumerates all boundary hyperplanes with neural breadth-first search, enumerates boundary hinges by LP, then applies cheap sufficient checks before nonlinear exact checks (dReal where needed). Theorem 2 gives a valid NCBF when all checks pass. Experiments on Darboux, obstacle avoidance, hi-ord8 and spacecraft rendezvous show major speedups; SR 6D L4/M8 falls from 298.7s baseline to 60.1s, while dReal/Z3 are unavailable or time out in many cases. Regularization cuts SR boundary hyperplanes from 6218 to 627 at equal coverage in one configuration.

    - limits: ReLU piecewise linearity, continuous f and g, connected unsafe and initial sets for the boundary enumeration argument, and exact dReal checks are assumed. - Taming Differentiable Logics with Coq Formalisation (2024)
    - what: Coq/MathComp formalization of six differentiable logics through one intrinsically typed syntax and separate real/extended-real interpretations. Mechanizes algebraic properties, soundness and equal-input conjunction derivative properties, repairs incorrect informal soundness claims and completes previously omitted STL shadow-lifting analysis. Adds reusable partial-derivative, Cauchy mean-value and L’Hôpital results. Shows that truth extraction from a loss value needs a specified threshold and syntax fragment: finite STL equality evaluates to zero for a true equality and its negation, so sign-based soundness must omit negation. Handles constants by either extended reals or finite signed representatives. Encodes dimensions and availability of negation in dependent types. Proves inversion lemmas for n-ary connectives and formalizes missing limit cases rather than inferring soundness or useful optimization from a well-typed real expression.
    - limits: The core LDL syntax deliberately omits quantifiers, lambda and let from the earlier language. It embeds real constants, finite vectors/indices, arbitrary vector functions and applications, comparisons, n-ary conjunction/disjunction and optionally negation. Intrinsic typing prevents ill-typed terms, not false properties or ill-chosen loss semantics. Gödel, Łukasiewicz, Yager and product interpretations use [0,1]; DL2 uses nonpositive values and STL signed values. Interpretations over ordinary reals coexist with extended-real alternatives. Domain invariants are proof obligations. STL parameter nu is positive; Yager associativity statement requires p>0. Closed-interval soundness means only that an interpretation at a designated extreme truth/falsity value implies the corresponding Boolean truth. It is not a claim that every intermediate fuzzy value is classically true or false, or that arbitrary training loss minima meet the specification. DL2 and STL soundness is for the negation-free syntax. DL2 has no compositional structural negation. STL negates by arithmetic minus, which makes a zero-valued true equality and its negation share zero; the real-valued soundness theorem therefore uses >=0 for true, <0 for false and excludes negation. For finite-real constants the paper selects DL2 True=0/False=−1 and STL True=1/False=−1. Alternative extended-real semantics use domain endpoints. These choices repair a generic-syntax mismatch; they are not interchangeable numerical training implementations without further interpretation/geometry checks. Shadow-lifting is a local partial-derivative property at equal input coordinates, not a statement of strictly improving every unequal conjunction, differentiability everywhere, convergence of gradient descent, global optimum attainment, data generalization or universal network correctness. Disjunction shadow-lifting, weak smoothness, scale invariance and unequal-input generalization remain future work. The displayed Coq shadow_lifting definition quantifies p>0, whereas informal Definition6 allows any nonzero interpreted value. The printed stl_and_lt0 derivative lemma also assumes p>0 despite prose labeling its target branch amin<0. Record preserves that presentation mismatch; negative-domain coverage of the full formal implementation was not independently inspected. The paper formalizes differentiable logics, not neural networks themselves. Vehicle/CAISAR compiler certification is motivation/future integration, not an end-to-end certified specification-to-training/compiler result delivered here. No distributed-system proof, Rust/Verus, TLA+ or LLM proof-generation evaluation is presented. Proof reports rely on Coq, MathComp/MathComp-Analysis and their real/extended-real definitions. Partial is defined using a filter limit; substantive derivative lemmas additionally establish convergence. Artifact repository and Software Heritage archive are linked, but scripts and their axiom inventory were not run or audited by this reader.

- The Rewster: Type Preserving Rewrite Rules for the Coq Proof Assistant (2024)
    - what: Extends Coq definitional reduction with user rewrite rules and presents a bidirectional type-preservation criterion for PCUIC with universe cumulativity and SProp proof irrelevance. Pattern types and metavariable types are inferred generally; right sides are checked against those types, optionally using equality constraints safely forced by a well-typed match. Coq implementation is reported, while confluence checking and justified conservative rules remain future work. Explains why checking a propositional equality at some common type is unsound under cumulativity and why ordinary unification can infer unjustified symbol injectivity. Gives higher-order metavariable substitution, restricted symbol-headed patterns, triangle/confluence restrictions, a matching antisubstitution proof and a constraint-extraction relation robust under later environment extensions. Separates type preservation from consistency, confluence and termination; implementation status is explicitly dated to publication.
    - limits: Underlying setting is annotated PCUIC with metavariables plus universe/sort-quality variables. Typing depends on a well-formed environment, local/metavariable contexts, structural guard conditions for fixpoint consistency and usual positivity for inductives. Virtual sort annotations matter to principal pattern types but do not carry observable matching content. Pattern matching is restricted: head of main elimination branch must be a declared symbol, not an arbitrary metavariable; variables may occur in argument holes. Patterns are left-linear, contain no β/ι-redexes, and cannot inspect syntactically irrelevant/SProp terms. Holes at irrelevant positions are allowed. These restrictions support the confluence/postponement argument. Subject reduction is conditional on appropriate confluence/triangle and pattern restrictions as well as the type-preservation criterion. Implementation of arbitrary rewrite declarations alone does not establish these global conditions. §8 says porting the Agda confluence checker is an immediate future goal. Definition4 requires a pattern-inference derivation at Tp with exactly its pattern metavariables Θ, and ordinary typing of the right side at Tp. Definition5 permits typing the right side under equalities E extracted soundly from pattern typing; it does not permit arbitrary assumptions selected to make the right side typecheck. Constraint extraction relies on rigidity/injectivity stable under environment extension. Symbols may receive future rules, so eliminations headed by symbols do not justify injective decomposition. Bare metavariable equality can be retained; equalities under higher elimination contexts are discarded, and if several equalities are extracted for one pattern variable, all but one are discarded. The full relation returning no equalities is sound but less useful. Type preservation is not consistency: symbols and rewrite principles may already be inconsistent propositionally. Consistency transfer is attributed to prior extensional-type-theory interpretation when proposed rules are admissible as propositional equalities. Justified-rules support proving this connection is future work, not required/checked automatically for every declaration. Termination is not assumed for subject reduction. The paper states a checker can be correct when it answers while potentially diverging. Its repeated decidable-criterion wording must therefore not be read as a proved total decision procedure for unrestricted user-supplied nonterminating rewrite systems. Article formally presents metatheory in the PCUIC framework and reports implementation. It does not provide a demonstrated machine-checked end-to-end proof that the modified Coq kernel implements this metatheory. No proof-checking session, kernel audit or artifact run was performed by the reader. At publication, rewrite PR18038 was integrated in development, expected for Coq8.20; type-preservation PR19290 was implemented but not yet integrated. These are historical paper statements, not checked current Coq/Rocq release status. Implementation extends presented syntax to primitive projections, universe/sort polymorphism and unfold_fix symbols. Exceptions example has acknowledged potential universe-inconsistency warnings on the if/match rules. No claim that all examples/rules are automatically safe, terminating or conservative. No runtime benchmark, corpus acceptance/rejection rate, proof-size comparison or user-study evaluation. Evidence consists of formal rules/proof arguments, counterexamples and implementation examples. Abstract formally-expressed wording is not interchangeable with fully mechanized verification.

    - title: Timed Multiset Rewriting and the Verification of Time-Sensitive Distributed Systems
    - what: Defines a multiset-rewriting language with explicit time for systems such as drone surveillance, where goals must hold perpetually under environment interference. For progressive timed systems (PTS), both are PSPACE-complete; bounded realizability is NP-complete and survivability lies in Δ2P. PTS limits actions in bounded time, enabling finite abstractions and complexity proofs. The Maude executable semantics checks bounded traces, with timed drone actions, energy and wind interference. The paper distinguishes finite bounded search from infinite recurring obligations and proves upper/lower bounds via configuration equivalence.

    - what: Introduces Trace Inlining, a lazy BMC algorithm that alternates under- and over-approximation, extracts Craig-interpolant procedure summaries from verified traces, and reuses/refines summaries across call contexts; implemented as Saransh. The inlining tree tracks overapproximated, inlined, blocked and summarized call sites. A verification oracle encodes passified procedures as SMT VCs; a verified partial trace yields an interpolant summary that replaces a subtree. - Using Dynamically Layered Definite Releases for Verifying the RefFS File System (2024)
    - what: The RefFS project page links a separate 124-page draft, Progress of Concurrent Objects with Dynamic Dependencies, authored by Mo Zou. Its PDF metadata dates it May24,2024; the project says “A separate paper” illustrates MoLi's metatheory (P1). This is a complete fresh reading of that PODD paper, not an appendix of the OSDI paper and not a new reading of the RefFS implementation. The original RefFS main-paper account remains inherited from formal509. Whether this precise draft proves every rule of the released MoLi framework is not established by the link alone.  PODD makes a thread's progress depend on definite actions, obligations that their owning threads must fulfill once enabled. Actions have state-dependent layers, and dependencies must preserve strict relative order even when numeric layers change. Layers have a total order, not necessarily a well-founded one. Finite dependency sets and decreasing local/stack metrics supply the termination argument. The LIVE-FRM rule extends action/layer context while preserving old ordering, so an acquisition proof can be reused without expanding every nested wait chain. Tokens account for unblocked loop progress and finitely many levels of delaying interference. Theorem4.2 states linearizability and deadlock-freedom; starvation-freedom additionally requires rely and guarantee actions at level0 (S12,S14,S15).  AppendixA supplies the fuller resource/ownership logic, fences, rules and ideal shared-memory semantics. AppendixB first gives judgment simulations with finite-height while stacks: arbitrary-length lexicographic lists would not be well-founded (S31). B.3 expands new while/live-frame cases. B.4 maps these to a common simulation, directly for starvation-freedom and through a lock plus nondeterministically decreasing finite-wait wrapper for deadlock-freedom (S45,S48). B.5 combines thread simulations using finite active-thread dependency sets, scheduler rounds and a lexicographic metric. LemmasB.22–B.30 connect coinductive fair traces to refinement (S54,S57,S58,S66,S69). B.6 defines progress over complete fair traces, permitting abort alternatives, and uses three most-general clients to relate finite refinement to linearizability and fair refinement to linearizability plus starvation/deadlock freedom. The deadlock equivalence wraps the atomic specification; it must not be replaced by the stronger starvation refinement (S72,S74).  AppendixC provides all printed proof outlines for nested TAS/ticket locks, ticket-lock coupling lists, optimistic/lazy TAS lists, and two-list transfers. Ticket queues support starvation-freedom; unfair TAS permits only the weaker deadlock-freedom claim. Lists use local lock obligations, node order and finite traversal metrics. Optimistic/lazy cases retain removed nodes in ghost garbage, not a proved memory-reclamation scheme. Lazy contain is explicitly omitted. Transfers use one mutex to serialize moves, list levels0/1/2 and lexicographic (listlevel,distance-to-tail) layers; their add/remove proofs are referred to earlier lists. The two-list move is a useful dynamic-dependency example, rather than a distributed network/crash model (S87,S90,S94,S102,S109,S116,S122,S124).  Evaluation consists of paper proofs and worked examples; no numerical benchmark, proof-time table or replayed mechanization is supplied here. Section6 explicitly makes mechanization and automation future work (S20). Section5.1 admits that common rely conditions and frame stability can prevent reuse across objects (S17). - Validating the eBPF Verifier via State Embedding (2024)
    - what: SEV tests the Linux eBPF verifier with deterministic closed programs. It profiles accepted programs, folds their observed register states into R9, then inserts a conditional illegal operation that must be reachable under the observed execution. Accepting that transformed program exposes an unsound approximation. A one-month upstream campaign found15root-cause-distinct verifier logic bugs, including12soundness/3completeness bugs and two reported privilege-escalation cases;10were fixed at submission. This is empirical validation of a verifier, not a whole-verifier correctness proof. Records the self-checking containment oracle and paper-only argument, deterministic-input and trace-preservation assumptions, concrete folding/operator/tracer design, false-negative paths and lack of detection-equivalence proof, all bug class/location counts and overhead values, manual triage, precise sample failures/diagnostic errors and privilege conditions. Separates verified-component claims from incomplete specification/implementation correspondence and records no bugs found in tnum.c rather than treating that as proof.
    - limits: §§1,3.1: Necessary soundness invariant is that every concrete execution state belongs to the corresponding abstract state. The testing oracle embeds an observed value with a branch to an invalid operation; a correct analyzer must consider that branch feasible. A rejected transformed program due to the sink passes this particular test, not every state/path or full verifier soundness. §§3.1–3.2: Inputs are accepted, closed, deterministic eBPF programs without external input/interactions so a single profile is repeatable. Correct interpretation/tracing, folding evaluation and transformed control-flow/register behavior are assumed. The method does not directly validate arbitrary nondeterministic production BPF workloads, concurrent shared map changes or every environment-dependent helper. §3.1 Proposition3.1/Corollary3.1: Paper argues embedding adds no invalid operation except the sink, using branch-state partition Ai=Aj union Ak and safety under subset Ak. This is a prose argument, not a mechanized proof of the generator/transformer/verifier semantics. It presupposes correct construction and original accepted program behavior; it cannot establish that all verifier rejections are bugs without diagnosing their cause. §3.1 folded variant/§4.5: Paper calls folded detection capability equivalent to direct embedding based on likely propagation over continuous campaigns. No injectivity or detection-equivalence theorem/probability bound is proved. §4.5 explicitly allows arithmetic to hide some non-contained states. Folding collisions/precision loss and missing generated programs can produce false negatives; longer testing is not a completeness guarantee. §3.2: R9 is reserved for folded state. One random ALU function is generated per basic block, then reused each time that block occurs in a loop trace; folded expected value is evaluated in execution order. Folding excludes division and unary operations and uses nonzero registers to reduce collapse to zero. These restrictions concern folding instructions, not necessarily every original generated instruction. §3.2/§4.2: Structured generator tracks lightweight register/stack types, encodings and control flow to make accepted tests likely. Tracer records instruction indices/register states at basic blocks using an internal buffer, virtual device and mmap. It does not snapshot all accessible memory; load/store issues are detected only if they propagate to observed registers or yield another diagnosed failure. §§3.2,4.1: Interpreter bpf/core.c is patched for tracing, so runtime ground truth is relative to this interpreter/instrumentation. No claim of testing every JIT compiler, processor or architecture follows. A verifier behavior not exercised by generated accepted programs may remain unchecked. §4.1: Campaign boots compiled upstream kernels in QEMU/KVM guests, restarts dead VMs, and retains original program/profile/transformed program. Root-cause analysis/deduplication is manual; automatic discovery does not mean automatic explanation, exploit construction, patching or independent validation. §4.2: Counts are15unique roots within one month and10fixes as of submission. These historical results do not imply all bugs are fixed today or each has a CVE. Two reported exploitable cases require CAP_BPF or CAP_PERFMON; they are not both demonstrated unprivileged-without-capabilities attacks. All15roots are reported in verifier.c, not arbitrary kernel-memory bugs. §4.2: Soundness bugs wrongly accept unsafe programs; completeness bugs wrongly reject safe ones. Rejection for a reason other than the sink prompts a completeness-bug diagnosis under valid transformation assumptions. A wrong diagnostic for an already-invalid program, as in Figure5d, is a logic-error case but by itself does not demonstrate acceptance of unsafe code or rejection of safe code. §4.4: Overhead comparison runs24hours and repeats measurements for each program, but does not report number of repetitions/programs, distributions, absolute throughput, confidence intervals, per-VM vCPU allocation or accepted-program rate. Total1.6%throughput impact is small partly because only infrequently accepted programs are profiled/transformed. No direct controlled bug-yield comparison with Syzkaller/BVF/Buzzer is shown. §4.5: No false positives observed is an empirical author report, not a proof of the whole oracle implementation. Accepted-program search diversity is the main acknowledged source of false negatives. Raw coverage refers to execution paths in generated programs and induced coverage to verifier code; optimizing induced coverage is left outside scope and no measured coverage percentage is supplied. §4.5: Directly inserting many sinks can halt checking early or fork repeatedly; verifier state pruning cannot remove these paths because precise registers have different ranges. One final folded sink avoids that multiplication. It also tests newly inserted arithmetic, which can expose a bug absent from the untransformed program. §5: Authors report range-analysis bugs in the same Linuxv5.19 version Agni claimed to verify and cite incomplete conditions/divergence issues. This challenges scope/specification correspondence, not validity of every formal proof. No bugs found in previously verified tnum.c (~200LOC) is a testing observation, not a newly proved soundness result. Agni range analysis is~2100LOC against~20000LOC overall verifier. §5: Compared with offline abstract-log comparison, the target verifier itself interprets embedded predicates, avoiding a second full abstract-state parser/reference verifier. This is a metamorphic testing oracle with a semantic containment requirement; without predefined per-component specs does not mean without any specification or modeling assumptions. §§5–6: Kernel-local case applicable to evaluating proof/checker trust and generated specifications. No distributed protocol, Verus/verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent evaluation. A real adaptation to proof assistants/distributed verifiers requires a corresponding executable semantics, valid transformation and oracle; none is implemented here. No SEV repository/artifact appendix pointer in saved PDF; external references and bugs not replayed.

    - title: End-To-End Formal Verification of a Fast and Accurate Floating-Point Approximation
    - what: Develops a fully verified, fast binary64 enclosure implementation of exp for CoqInterval, including bit-level argument reduction, polynomial approximation, tables, exceptional values and reconstruction, and reports a 20× speedup over the prior implementation. The new algorithm reduces x via k=round(x·1/ln2), computes t=(x−k·log2_64h)−k·log2_64l, evaluates a degree-5 polynomial, adds ±d bounds, scales by 2^k and applies next_down/next_up. The paper stresses that seemingly algebraic rewrites break accuracy because floating-point lacks associativity/distributivity. Arithmetic expressions are typed ASTs with IEEE-754 (flt) and real-plus-rounding (rnd) interpretations; exact operations reduce proof burden. A recursive well-behaved predicate WB ensures finite IEEE results equal rnd values (Theorem 1), and simplify_wb automates most exceptional-behavior goals while Gappa handles exact-rounding side conditions. The extracted text reaches §2.2; later strategy details and benchmark tables are unavailable.
    - number: Abstract reports 20× speedup in CoqInterval relative to previous exponential implementation. Prior Rump-integral proof took minutes with bit-at-a-time arithmetic and a few seconds after hardware floating-point support; exact new end-to-end timing is not in the extracted sections. Algorithm uses binary64 (53-bit precision), degree-5 polynomial terms p1…p5, and 64-entry constant table indexed by ki land 63.
    - limits: Correctness targets finite binary64 inputs and Coq’s executable function; theorem relies on WB side conditions (nonzero divisors, no overflow, exact representability for OpExact). Floating-point operations must retain implementation-specific parenthesization; algebraic simplification can invalidate results. The prior interval algorithm supports arbitrary precision, whereas fixed 53-bit hardware precision motivates the replacement. Available extraction omits Sections 3–7, so proof effort, benchmark counts and complete speedup table cannot be independently reported.

- Verifying Peephole Rewriting in SSA Compiler IRs (2024)
    - what: LeanMLIR(X) gives intrinsically typed SSA with nested regions and user-defined operation semantics. A mechanized generic rewriter lifts local semantic equalities to whole-program equality along SSA def-use chains, with verified DCE/CSE and tactics exposing domain-level obligations. Cases cover a fragment of LLVM arithmetic, bounded structured control flow and an FHE polynomial-quotient IR. Explains typed context/variable machinery, zipper splitting/insertion and matching substitutions, structural treatment of region matches, pure-expression invariant for monadic contexts, and how operation/region signatures assemble semantics. LLVM case explicitly collapses poison and immediate undefined behavior, leaving a manual condition for division/remainder rewrites. scf generic loop laws are not all supported peephole patterns; Poly representative-dependent operations require additional choices.
    - limits: Theorems concern the user-provided embedded syntax and denotation in Lean. Kernel acceptance establishes properties of that model under its assumptions, not automatically faithful semantics of actual evolving MLIR/LLVM or a complete native compiler pipeline. Parser/elaboration errors can affect intended statement fidelity even when resulting terms are well typed. Core value semantics are pure, total Lean functions with structured regions. General unstructured CFGs, irreducible control flow, divergence, arbitrary memory effects and inter-IR linking are not fully modeled. Bounded loops are deliberately selected to avoid nontermination semantics; noncomputable algebraic denotations are allowed but not executable interpreters. Matching follows SSA expression trees and structural region equality; it does not recursively match inside regions as metavariable patterns. Rewriting can recursively visit region bodies, but free region arguments in rewrite patterns are unsupported. These are distinct capabilities. Side-effect extension only rewrites operations markedpure, denoting them in Id while other operations use an IR-specific monad. User semantics/effect classification must be appropriate. Current mechanization conservatively treats all regions as potentially effectful. LLVM instance models selected scalar arithmetic/bitwise/shift/select/icmp instructions and all comparison flags, but excludes nsw/nuw flags and most LLVM. It collapses immediateUB and poison into Option.none despite their different contextual behavior. The manual corresponding-division/remainder check is outside the mechanized collapsed-value proof. Treating UB and poison identically is safe only under an additional condition preventing a new immediateUB on the right when absent on the left. Authors report manually checking both directions for translated division/remainder rules via matching operations/arguments; this is not a proved general full-LLVM refinement theorem. Exhaustive instruction tests enumerate inputs only through bitwidth8 and use LLVM opt constant folding as ground truth. They provide empirical consistency with those cases, not proof over all widths or an independent formal LLVM semantics. Arbitrary-width rewrite proofs concern the Lean model, with some rules inherently restricted to specific widths. Alive corpus selection retains only93 of435 tests matching supported instructions and no preconditions. Automatic success54/93 and six additional selected manual proofs must not be presented as full-suite coverage or full automation. No proof times, runtime optimization speedups, hardware, repeat-count uncertainty or comparative prover-cost benchmark is provided. Poly models a pinned evolving IR’s algebra, not encryption security, ciphertext noise bounds, a complete FHE implementation or correctness of lowering quotient operations to arrays/machine code. Operations using representatives depend on a chosen section of quotient projection and need more than abstract ring laws.

- Verifying Randomized Consensus Protocols with Common Coins (2024)
    - what: # Whole-paper record: Verifying Randomized Consensus Protocols with Common Coins (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Song Gao, Bohua Zhan, Zhilin Wu and Lijun Zhang. DSN 2024, IEEE, pp.403–415; DOI 10.1109/DSN58291.2024.00047. Read arXiv 2409.17627v1, submitted 26 September 2024, all 13 PDF pages, §§I–VIII, all 27 references, six figures and four tables. Inspected every page image. Publication pagination comes from Crossref; this PDF has no printed page numerals (Q52). Exact extracted passages with PDF pages and source lines are in quotes.json and combined.quote-source.txt. No author code, compiler, checker, prover, solver or serialized experiment/model data was executed or loaded.  ## Contribution and claimed guarantees (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The paper extends parameterized threshold-automaton verification from independent local coins to a shared common coin. It adds a separate coin automaton and communication variables, giving an infinite-state Markov decision process with process-location counters, per-round shared variables and resilience parameters (§III,Q9–17). Byzantine processes are represented through their effect on threshold guards rather than explicit Byzantine automata (§III-A,Q8). This is a verification method for protocol models, not an implementation refinement or verified executable.  Safety and termination follow different reductions. For safety, two one-round invariants imply agreement and binary validity (Proposition 1,Q20–21). Theorem 1 states that any finite schedule can be reordered by rounds while preserving its final configuration and per-round stutter equivalence (Q22). Theorem 2 relates one-round LTL without next-time properties to a single-round system, assuming nonblocking behavior and termination of every fair single-round execution for all initial configurations (Q24). These assumptions matter; it is not an unrestricted equivalence between arbitrary multi-round properties and one bounded run.  For termination the paper distinguishes three categories (§V-B,Q26–28). Category A has no decide event and targets eventual convergence to a common final value. Category B has binary messages and explicit decisions. Category C uses a Binary Crusader Agreement stage that may output ⊥, meaning undecided. C1 requires a uniform positive probability of converging during a round. C2 preserves unanimity; C2′ instead gives a positive probability of deciding when the round starts unanimously. Proposition 3 supplies a two-round geometric argument: the probability of not deciding after 2r rounds is at most `(1−p·p′)^r` (Q29).  Binding fixes a bit at the first relevant execution prefix and excludes its opposite in every continuation. It is a property of sets of executions, beyond ordinary single-execution agreement (Definition 4,Q30). The model refinement introduces N0, N1, N⊥ locations so that five sufficient safety conditions, CB0–CB4, imply binding (Proposition 4,Q31–32). Proposition 5 combines binding and C2′ for termination (Q33). Lemma 2 states that, in the single-round setting, a uniform positive probability under every admissible adversary is equivalent to each adversary having some satisfying path (Q35). That quantifier order is stronger than merely finding one favorable schedule.  The proof record is mixed. Lemma 1 has a one-line justification. Proposition 2 calls its proof trivial after a geometric-tail argument. Propositions 3–5 provide paper proofs; Corollary 1 cites them. Proposition 1, Theorems 1–2 and Lemma 2 explicitly omit proofs for length (Q21,Q24–25,Q35). proof-inventory.json records all ten named results and their assumptions. No proof-assistant artifact was inspected, and this reading does not independently establish their soundness.  ## Assumptions and limits (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The network is asynchronous and reliable: a sent message is “eventually received” without “loss, duplication or modification,” and receivers identify senders (§I(a),Q3). Byzantine faults are bounded by the selected resilience condition. The common coin is a trusted, fault-free abstraction, and only strong coins are considered: both bits are common outputs with probability 1/2. Cryptographic implementation correctness is future work (Q2–3,Q41).  The model separates shared-message guards from coin guards. Correct processes cannot update coin variables; coin rules cannot modify shared variables. Automata are canonical: rules on cycles have zero updates (§III-B,Q10–13). The method is parameterized by the environment's admissible n,t,f values, rather than verifying only the example cluster sizes.  The termination specification is explicitly “under Round-rigid Adversaries” (§IV,Q19). Such an adversary is fair and schedules all actions of round k before those of round k+1 (§III-E,Q17). Removing this restriction is future work (§VIII,Q41). Finite safety-trace reordering does not establish probabilistic termination for arbitrary asynchronous adaptive schedulers.  No benchmark archive, model file or proof-artifact URL is identified in the read paper. The paper says it builds two one-round automaton versions per protocol, but those inputs and their transformations were not available in the inspected sources (Q36–37). This does not assert that no artifact exists elsewhere. No ByMC run was reproduced.  ## Cases and reported evaluation (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The benchmark comprises Rabin83, CC85(a), CC85(b), FMR05, KS16, MMR14, Miller18 and ABY22 (§VI,Q36; Table II,Q45). Their protocol descriptions give different Byzantine bounds: for example Rabin83 uses t<n/10, CC85(b) t<n/6, and CC85(a), KS16 and ABY22 use n>3t. These protocol descriptions should not be substituted for the undisclosed exact checked input environments.  Table II reports model locations/rules, execution-schema counts and verification time for agreement, validity and almost-sure termination. The authors “ran each experiments 10 times” and report averages, without raw trials or dispersion (§VI,Q37). The first six rows use an Intel Core i7-12650H laptop; the final two use a 216-core AMD EPYC7702 server in parallel mode. Times measure verification work, not consensus latency or throughput.  Small examples complete quickly: Rabin83 has 7 locations/17 rules and reported times 0.25s for agreement, 0.20s for validity and 0.43s for its convergence target. CC85(a) uses 342 schemas/4.93s for agreement and an average 171.5 schemas/2.70s for termination. Fractional schema counts are averages. All eight rows and all table values are retained in numeric-evidence.json.  MMR14 has 17 locations/29 rules. Its agreement and validity checks take 298.90s and 8.74s. The termination column says CE, with no time. Separately, §VI reports a CB2 violation “within 10 seconds at best,” with an example witness n=193,t=64 (Q38). A failed sufficient condition alone does not prove nontermination. The authors additionally analyze the returned execution, compare it with a known adaptive attack and describe repeating its final actions to recreate the opposite estimate distribution.  The motivating four-node example has three correct processes and one Byzantine process. Two correct processes obtain the coin result s, while the adversary delays messages to the third until it can force estimate 1−s; the round can repeat (§II,Q7). This is a prior attack, not a new vulnerability discovered by the paper. Miller's 2018 issue credits Ethan MacBrough and explains that the actual coin instantiation lacks the independence assumed by the earlier ABA proof (Q48–49). The issue proposes an extra CONF phase before revealing coin shares (Q50). Its later implementation comments were read as allegations, without auditing the linked code (Q51).  The two repaired category C variants reportedly pass their obligations. Miller18 takes 11h46m47s and ABY22 takes 10h13m14s for all termination conditions, each exceeding 10^8 schemas; agreement takes 605s and 583s, respectively (Table II,Q45). The paper also describes 24-hour timeouts for the earlier technique on category C models, without a controlled cross-hardware speedup comparison (Q37).  Table IV changes milestone counts from 10 to 6 in five same-size ABY22-based automata. Calculated maximum schemas fall from 98,182,294 to 28,918 for CB0 and 7,479,057 to 3,592 for Inv2 (Q39,Q47). These are calculated search bounds, not measured runtime reductions or proof that the variants preserve protocol semantics. Table I supplies MMR14 transition guards and updates; Table III lists selected value 0 formulas and an ellipsis, rather than complete checker inputs. Figures 1–6 provide pseudocode, voting and MMR14 automata, and the binding refinement.  ## Source discrepancies that qualify interpretation (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Three points remain unresolved from the printed sources. They are recorded as static comparisons, not reproduced checker failures or counterexamples to a full theorem.  - Example 2 gives the MMR14 environment `n>5t` (Q9), while §II describes n>3t and §VI reports n=193,t=64. That witness satisfies 193 > 192 but not 193 > 320. The exact checked resilience condition cannot be recovered from the paper alone. - Proposition 5 reasons that no correct process has executed a coin-based rule, “in other words” the coin “is not yet tossed,” and therefore its result is independent of the binding bit (Q33). Figure 4 and Table I instead show rb with guard true, from initial coin location I2 to N0/N1, followed by unconditional rc/rd publishing its outcome (Q13,Q43–44). Under the initial-state and action definitions, a finite round 0 prefix can execute rb then rc before any correct-process transition. The adversary observes configuration histories (Q15,Q17). Thus the stated timing inference needs a further visibility or scheduling condition that is not enforced by these displayed rules. This prefix does not refute the full theorem or a benchmark protocol; it identifies an unsupported step in the supplied model-to-proof account. - Table III labels C1 with a universal implication excluding mixed final values along every path after a 0-valued final event (Q46). Body C1 is a positive-probability convergence condition, reduced through a per-adversary existential-path condition (Q27,Q35). The displayed statements differ. Separate model versions might explain a stronger checked obligation, but their concrete transformation is not supplied here, so the table cannot establish that correspondence.  The coin prefix, resilience arithmetic and quantifier comparison are in static-witnesses.json. All relevant formulas and table entries were checked against rendered PDF pages, rather than relying only on text extraction.  ## Relevance to the requested topic (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  This work directly addresses parameterized verification of randomized Byzantine consensus, especially the relation between common randomness, adaptive scheduling, binding and almost-sure termination. It supplies concrete verification-cost evidence and an example of using failed proof obligations to investigate a known attack. It also shows why a safety-preserving reordering theorem, a probabilistic termination argument and a checker result must retain their separate assumptions.  For evaluating LLM-written specifications or proofs, the reader-derived lesson is to check scheduler quantifiers, coin secrecy and independence, the exact resilience environment, source-to-formula correspondence, proof availability and what a counterexample actually disproves. The paper contains no LLM, Verus or verified Rust experiment. Its TLA proof-system reference concerns related HotStuff work, not this paper's verification method (Q40,Q42). HoneyBadger/Dumbo composition and cryptographic primitive verification remain future work (Q41).

Nonblocking and all fair single-round termination are prerequisites for reduction. - WSR and DR register specifications (2024)
    - title: Hyperproperty-Preserving Register Specifications
    - what: Constructs two non-atomic shared-memory register specifications preserving finite-trace hyperproperties under strong adversaries. WSR is complete under forward simulation for write strong-linearizable registers, including single-writer ABD. Introduces decisive linearizability, which preserves relative order of already included operations while allowing insertion, and constructs complete register specification DR. A forward simulation from multi-writer ABD to DR establishes decisive linearizability and lets client proofs use DR. Conference paper gives algorithms, formal finite-execution definitions, examples and proof sketches; full proofs are deferred. Captures exact scheduler quantifiers and finite-trace scope, class completeness versus generic history tracking, three randomized client distinctions and fourth overwritten-value example, WSR set-collection stopping rule, DR guarded rollback/version/lock behavior, lazy-linearization hardness construction and ABD majority-publication simulation. Separates safety/refinement from progress and pseudocode from its stated LTS formulation. Replaces an incomplete introductory record.
    - limits: Model uses labeled transition systems with possibly infinite states/labels, finite transition executions including intermediate states, calls/returns with thread and action identifiers, per-thread sequential well-formed histories, and response-before-invocation real-time order. Registers hold natural numbers and initially contain 0. Prefix-closed sequential specifications and interface composition synchronize calls/returns while interleaving client/implementation internal actions. A hyperproperty is a set of sets of client traces. Satisfaction universally quantifies deterministic schedulers. A scheduler maps a complete past execution to a set of transitions; either at most one transition is allowed or all choices are client-internal. Thus it resolves scheduling and implementation nondeterminism while allowing unresolved choices only among client-internal transitions. It sees previous coin outcomes, not future ones. Authors avoid the prior step-determinism restriction by using executions rather than label traces. Strong observational refinement I≤sI# preserves every client hyperproperty of I# in I. Lemma3.4 says every concrete deterministic scheduler has an abstract deterministic scheduler with the same projected client trace set. Theorem3.5 equates this with call/return forward simulation: initial states related, each concrete step matched by a finite abstract sequence with the same interface projection, allowing stuttering. This is a finite-trace theorem. No fairness, infinite-trace, termination, or quantitative time guarantee follows automatically. A class is downward closed under forward simulation. A hard implementation is simulated by every class member; complete additionally means it belongs to that class, yielding membership iff forward simulation to it. Proposition4.3 constructs a generic complete linearizable object by tracking history and enabling only linearizable responses. Lemma4.7 generalizes to any preorder R relating linearizations of prefix executions, with state storing history and a suitable linearization. These existence constructions are not the compact useful reference programs sought here. Ordinary linearizability completes selected pending calls, drops others, and preserves thread behavior/real time. Strong linearization maps every execution to a legal history and preserves prefixes. Write strong-linearization preserves prefixes only after projecting to writes, permitting read repositioning. Decisive linearization preserves the whole prior linearization as a subsequence: new operations may be inserted before old ones but cannot reverse any already included pair. Decisiveness is defined for any object; the compact completeness results here concern registers. For registers the hierarchy is strict: strongly linearizable, write strongly linearizable, decisively linearizable, linearizable. ATR belongs to first; DLR separates first/second; TNSR and multi-writer ABD separate second/third; generic history-tracking linearizable register separates third/fourth. Write strong implies decisive through WSR⊑FDR and completeness, not by simply assuming every given write-strong mapping already preserves all read pairs. Single-writer linearizable registers being write strong is attributed to [15], not newly independently proved here. Motivating programs use fair coin values1/2 and target Pr[a=b]=1/2 under every strong adversary. P1 has sequential write1/write2/coin versus concurrent read. P2 has write1/coin/barrier versus write2/barrier/read. P3 moves coin after both writes complete at barrier. Figure3: ATR satisfies all; DLR fails P1 only; TNSR fails P2 only; ABD with at least three processes fails P1/P2; all satisfy P3. These are concrete semantic counterexamples, not a statistical experiment. DLR atomically loads X twice then adversarially chooses one value. TNSR atomically reads, and writes load X twice, optionally skip their store only when observed values differ. ABD uses lexicographic(counter,writerID) timestamps, majority query maxima, read writeback to majority, write timestamp increment, monotone background updates/acks. Fewer than three processes do not support the stated adversarial schedules; ABD2 requires all processes in each quorum. The finite-trace study does not establish the usual asynchronous ABD liveness/failure theorem anew. P1 ABD schedule buffers a homogeneous old-value1 quorum plus a newer-value2 reply; after coin, deliver an appropriate majority. P2 buffers old write2 query replies, lets write1 finish, and obtains a fresh reply. After coin, choose old replies so equal counters favor writer1 ID, or fresh reply so writer2 chooses a larger counter. For P3, after both writes finish every quorum intersects the maximum-timestamp publication quorum, so subsequent read value is already fixed. Probability manipulation follows scheduling information and operation overlap, not Byzantine messages. WSR Algorithm1 writes X atomically. A read initializes V={X}, repeatedly atomically sets (Vprev,V)=(V,V∪{X}), stops when V no longer grows, then chooses any member. It stops at the first observed value already in the set, which need not equal the immediately previous observation. Arbitrarily many distinct intervening writes can extend collection and memory; no bounded-read or wait-free property under endlessly new values is established. Adversary may delay final selection until after a client coin. Theorem5.4 makes WSR complete for write strong registers, hence single-writer ABD⊑FWSR. Remark5.3 gives k-load registers Ik with Ik+1 not strongly observationally refining Ik, while every Ik refines WSR. Calling WSR the limit is explanatory language, not a stated analytic convergence theorem or finite bound on loads. DR Algorithm2 adds natural version Ver and lock L. A new read waits for L0 then atomically saves start version and value. Later collection adds X only when Ver≥start. A writer saves start version under L0, then normally stores v/increments Ver, or, if a concurrent store made Ver>start, locks, saves current X, temporarily stores v and decrements Ver, then separately restores X/version and unlocks. Existing reads may see the temporary value; new read initialization/writers are blocked while L1. Version rather than value comparison detects concurrent writes even with equal values. The rollback and restoration are separate atomic steps. Treating them as one atomic block removes overwritten values visible to existing readers and loses the Figure4 behavior needed for ABD. Conversely, new reads cannot initialize from the temporary version. The read collection itself does not universally await L0; its version guard determines which temporary values an already active read may collect. Authors explicitly state the simplified DR pseudocode may choose overwrite before its guard can be satisfied and get stuck, whereas their LTS formulation avoids this. Thus a literal implementation of Algorithm2 is not automatically the full LTS with the same progress behavior. Conference finite-trace linearizability claims tolerate this stuck execution; the full LTS definition/progress equivalence is not supplied here. Figure4 P4 adds a third concurrent read c=2 before barrier to P2. TNSR cannot return2 there in a branch where write2 later skips its only store and b reads1. DR permits the temporary store; ABD permits the third reader to obtain2 through its query/timestamp schedule. This demonstrates why TNSR is too restrictive as the general decisive/ABD reference even though it is itself decisive. AppendixA Lemma4.7: simulation gives a prefix-preserving execution mapping π with identical history; compose a suitable linearization L with π for downward closure. Generic complete object stores a linearization and permits each interface action only if there is an R-related next one. Full proof details are in separate extended version. AppendixA WSR membership linearizes writes at stores and completed-choice reads retroactively at their first load of chosen value. Hardness cannot eagerly store whenever an arbitrary write-strong linearization first includes a write: that may remove older values still needed by overlapping readers. Construct lazy L* changing only on responses, including pending operations only if they are non-last writes, and additionally decisive. Simulate each newly added write by a store, and let pending readers collect new values they lack. Key lemma places returned value either at rightmost write when read invoked or at a later-added write. Lemmas establishing L* and full simulation relation are deferred. AppendixA DR membership assigns each included write its stored version and each chosen read its version at first load of chosen value, orders by version then associated transition order. Version/rollback guards are said to establish real time; immutable assignments preserve pair order. Hardness uses the lazy construction but temporarily rolls back when a newly included write must precede an already included one, maintaining X as rightmost linearized write. Conference sketch does not supply the full invariants or every insertion case; no independent mechanized proof performed. AppendixA ABD simulation tracks first majority publication of a value/timestamp pair, whether caused by a write update or read writeback. New maximum timestamp becomes a fresh DR version/store collected by active readers. Older timestamp uses temporary rollback, collection by eligible concurrent readers, restoration of latest value. Timestamp publication and version correspondence are proof state, not an executable conversion of network messages into a shared-memory algorithm. Example5.2(iii) ends with linearizes h1 although the branch is extension h2; the surrounding argument requires h2. This is a printed naming typo, not a counterexample to completeness. Other compressed diagram/proof wording is interpreted in its stated context, without inferring a main theorem failure from absent extended details. Related work: tail strong linearizability depends on chosen effect-free preamble and is not comparable to decisive; its repetition/random-choice transformation is ineffective on WSR/DR.     - title: Automating Unrealizability Logic: Hoare-Style Proof Synthesis for Infinite Sets of Programs
    - what: The paper introduces Wuldo, the first proof-synthesis algorithm for Unrealizability Logic (UL), a Hoare-style logic over potentially infinite program sets described by regular tree grammars. Wuldo computes syntax-directed proof skeletons, generates parametric verification conditions, and checks or synthesizes nonterminal summaries and loop invariants using SMT/SyGuS solvers. Summaries are reusable inductive facts about grammar nonterminals, enabling compositional proofs of unrealizability and infinite-state/input properties. The implementation supports whole-cloth proof generation for some cases and emits interpretable proof certificates, unlike black-box satisfiability encodings.
    - limits: Wuldo's main relative-completeness result is for loop-free program sets; loops require summaries/invariants and can be difficult. Effectiveness depends on solver support for quantified linear arithmetic, infinite arrays, and SyGuS grammars; Wuldo may prove unrealizability but does not generally establish realizability. Experiments use regular-tree grammars, finite benchmark suites, 5-minute timeouts, and a 4-core i7-7700HQ/16GB Windows machine. The authors note unsupported nondeterminism and hard quantified summaries as open limitations.

- Akshay et al. affine MDP invariants (2023)
    - title: MDPs as Distribution Transformers: Affine Invariant Synthesis for Safety Objectives.
    - what: Treats MDPs as transformers of probability distributions and synthesizes affine inductive distributional invariants together with strategies proving distribution-based safety. AlgMemLess targets memoryless strategies with relative completeness; AlgDist handles distribution-dependent general strategies with sound but incomplete Handelman-based constraints. The paper proves that distribution strategies depending only on the current distribution suffice, and that an inductive distributional invariant contained in the safe set is a sound and complete certificate. AlgMemLess templates action probabilities and a conjunction of affine inequalities, uses Farkas' lemma to eliminate universal quantifiers, and has soundness, relative completeness, and PSPACE bounds. AlgDist uses quotients of affine expressions for action probabilities; positivity constraints remove denominators, and Handelman's theorem produces a sound bounded-product translation, losing completeness. The framework handles initialized and uninitialized cases, restricted initial constraints, and can extend to polynomial invariants via Putinar's Positivstellensatz. A prototype in Python/SymPy/PySMT with Z3 and MathSAT solved Running, Chain, Split, PageRank, and Insulin-131 I examples.
    - number: AlgMemLess PSPACE, sound and relatively complete
    - number: AlgDist PSPACE for fixed K, sound but incomplete
    - number: Running 3s, 92 vars, 123 constraints
    - number: Chain 10s, 69 vars, 82 constraints
    - limits: Safety sets are finite conjunctions of affine inequalities over finite-state MDP distributions; initialized safety is Positivity-hard even for Markov chains. AlgMemLess is complete only relative to affine invariants and memoryless strategies; AlgDist's Handelman translation is incomplete, parameterized by product bound K, and assumes compact antecedent sets for the theorem motivation. Existential nonlinear real arithmetic is decidable but solver performance varies by orders of magnitude and can take hours. Experiments are unoptimized and small; no claim of scalability or complete decision procedure for general distribution safety is made.

    - what: Presents AutoHyper, a complete explicit-state model checker for arbitrary HyperLTL quantifier prefixes, using automata quantifier elimination and practical language-inclusion backends. HyperLTL trace quantifiers are eliminated inductively into T-equivalent Büchi automata; existential elimination composes with the transition system, while universal elimination is negation plus complementation. Random formulas with up to four alternations show practical growth milder than worst-case theory. A complete AutoHyper baseline quantifies strategy-based verification's incompleteness and runtime trade-offs.

Contributions include cyclotomic-extension definitions, prime-power rings of integers and discriminants, unit/coercion lemmas, a splitting-field typeclass repair and early upstream integration. Case II permits p dividing xyz and is still ongoing (§1,§3). Regular number n is positive and coprime to the cardinality of the class group of the ring of integers of cyclotomic_field n Q. For prime p this means p does not divide that class number. Existing mathlib finite-class-group results are prerequisites. Its examples 37/59/67 irregular below 100 and roughly 60% expected regular primes are mathematical context, not formalized classification or experimental success rate (§1,§3). Cyclotomic extensions are a property of A-algebras B relative to a set S of positive integers: specified primitive roots exist and B is generated over A by roots with those orders. Positive orders rule out n=0. cyclotomic_field is concretely a splitting field of the cyclotomic polynomial; field/algebra/inhabited structures derive from it, but cyclotomic-extension instance needs proof. Property encoding supports subextensions and transporting lemmas rather than forcing every construction to use one definitional field representation (§2). - BMC for Asynchronous Hyperproperties (2023)
    - title: Bounded Model Checking for Asynchronous Hyperproperties
    - what: Generalizes asynchronous HyperLTL (A-HLTL) with nested trajectory quantifiers and gives a QBF-based bounded model checker for a fragment, with complexity results for acyclic Kripke structures and case-study experiments. The extended logic quantifies traces and trajectories independently, where trajectories choose which traces advance or stutter and must be fair. The bounded encoding unrolls Kripke structures to depth k and trajectory schedules to m, with pessimistic and optimistic halting semantics; Theorem 1 establishes equivalence at the structure diameter and a finite trajectory bound. For acyclic frames, one trajectory quantifier gives NL/coNP-polynomial-hierarchy bounds depending on trace alternation, while nested trajectory quantifiers raise complexity one level; arbitrary trace alternation with one trajectory remains PSPACE. The HyperQB implementation translates the encoding to QuABs QBF and finds security counterexamples and classifications in concurrent, speculative, compiler, and cache examples.

    - what: Lean3 formalization of unrestricted (type-0) grammars and closure under union, reversal, concatenation, and Kleene star. This structurally guarantees a nonterminal on every left-hand side; terminal-only strings are irreducible. A grammar stores its nonterminal type, initial symbol, and a finite rule list. Ambient terminal/nonterminal types need not be finite; each concrete grammar has finite symbol support. §2.2: A language is a set of terminal lists. Generated words are terminal-only images reachable from the initial nonterminal by reflexive-transitive rewriting. is_T0 means existence of a grammar with exactly that language. Grammar/Turing-machine equivalence is background knowledge, not formalized here; the conclusion lists it as future work. §1: Development uses Lean3/mathlib, small metaprogramming tools, nondependent data types with proof-bounded list indexing, and no attempt at constructivity. This is not a verified algorithmic extraction or complexity analysis of recognition. §3: Union adds a fresh initial symbol and marked disjoint copies of both nonterminal sets, with two branch rules. The lifted_grammar interface requires injective lift, a partial inverse sink injective on defined inputs, matching forward rules, and preimages of applicable larger rules; the correspondence is not automatic for arbitrary embeddings. §4: Reversal swaps/reverses rule contexts and reverses outputs, preserving the central nonterminal and initial symbol. List reverse distributes over concatenation in reversed order and is involutive. No new terminal-alphabet restrictions are introduced. §5: Simply adjoining S→S1S2 is unsound for unrestricted grammars because terminal context can cross the factor boundary. The repair uses disjoint source tags and separate proxy nonterminals for terminals on each side. Simulated rules match proxies, never actual terminals. Proxy conversion may happen early, disabling matches, so the hard proof relates every arbitrary intermediate string to two source-derivable strings rather than assuming a prescribed execution order. Induction on every rule preserves one case; only the fourth permits a generated terminal word. The empty-word case follows Z→R#→ε, even if L is empty. §6.2: Ellipsis-based compartment expressions become nested list.map/list.join. - CompMDP string-diagram checking (2023)
    - title: Compositional Probabilistic Model Checking with String Diagrams of MDPs
    - what: Defines CompMDP, a compositional probabilistic model-checking algorithm for open Markov decision processes composed as string diagrams, computing optimal expected cumulative rewards while retaining reachability probabilities and scheduler alternatives. The paper formalizes open MDPs with entrances/exits, rewards, transition probabilities and almost-sure termination, then derives decomposition equalities for reachability and expected rewards under sequential composition and loops. A categorical construction builds solution functors from rightward Markov chains to MDPs and bidirectional diagrams; semantic arrows retain pairs of reachability probability and expected reward for each memoryless scheduler, with a meager subsumption optimization. CompMDP implements this in Python, supports freezing subdiagrams and delegates frozen components to PRISM, and records an optimal scheduler result. Experiments on Patrol, Wholesale and Packets test reuse, freezing and scale, including models with 10^8 positions.
    - number: Patrol/Wholesale up to 10^8 positions
    - number: Packets 2.5×10^5 positions and 5×10^5 transitions
    - number: 6–130 s high-identification runs
    - number: Packets intermediate freezing 1–3 s vs PRISM 56–65 s
    - limits: The core framework assumes finite nonempty action sets, finite positions, unique exit access, and almost-sure termination of the top-level composed MDP; memoryless schedulers suffice under this termination assumption. Expected rewards are unconditional probability-weighted sums, differing from PRISM’s infinity convention for unreachable exits. The meager semantics and implementation optimization are described as correct but deferred for full categorical formalization. Sequential/task composition is better supported than parallel system composition; performance degrades with many locally optimal schedulers, low component reuse, loops, or poorly chosen freezing. Experiments run on one Apple dual-core laptop and synthetic benchmarks inspired by real tasks.

- Conschecker (2023)
    - title: Optimal Stateless Model Checking for Causal Consistency
    - what: Develops a stateless model-checking framework for causal consistency variants CC, CCv and CM. The DPOR algorithm explores executions represented by program-order (po) and reads-from (rf) relations, maintaining model-specific consistency edges; it is sound, complete and optimal because each consistent po-rf trace is explored once. Conschecker implements the algorithm at LLVM IR level and reports assertion violations. The paper formally defines CC overwrite cycles, CCv conflict/arbitration cycles and CM happened-before cycles, then gives a uniform trace semantics and DPOR schedule construction. Conschecker extends Nidhugg and validates outcomes against Herd simulations. Evaluation spans 9,815 litmus tests, SV-COMP stress tests, five database applications, classical anomaly benchmarks and parameterized programs; model strength differs (e.g., Delivery Order unsafe under CC/CCv but safe under CM).

- continuous-time decision-tree policy safety (2023)
    - title: Safety Verification of Decision-Tree Policies in Continuous Time
    - what: Introduces the first direct continuous-time reachability algorithm for systems controlled by decision trees. It propagates set enclosures through policy branches and nonlinear ODEs, using Taylor models for dynamics and axis-aligned predicate splitting for the tree, thereby detecting between-sample safety violations. A DTCS samples a tree every control period while applying the selected action continuously. Algorithm 1 queues state sets, postT partitions them among actions, and postf computes interval and endpoint enclosures; Theorem 1 proves termination/soundness and relative completeness under exact post procedures. The implementation uses TaylorModels.jl/JuliaReach and handles fixpoints for unbounded-time results. Even state-independent dynamics f(x,u)=u yield PSPACE-complete bounded-time reach-avoid and undecidable unbounded-time reachability via reductions from LBAs and two-counter machines. Experiments distill trees from neural policies: a depth-10 six-dimensional quadrotor is verified in 6.5 minutes; cart-pole is proved safe forever by a fixpoint; acrobot policies reach goal in about 100–112s; mountain-car reaches its goal within 132 steps in 16s. A generic hybrid-automata tool stalls at bisections, showing the value of exploiting tree structure.
    - number: PSPACE-complete bounded-time and undecidable unbounded-time even for state-independent dynamics
    - number: quadrotor depth 10/177 nodes, 84s table average and 6.5min full verification
    - number: cart-pole 40s finite analysis and infinite-time fixpoint
    - number: mountain-car at most 132 steps, 16s
    - limits: Solutions to ODE initial-value problems are assumed unique; predicates are axis-aligned xi≤c; Taylor-model overapproximations and bisections can accumulate wrapping error. Fixpoint checking is for time-invariant systems and may be hard with general Taylor sets. The proof-of-concept focuses on relatively small trees and simple tasks; nonlinear reachability remains undecidable in general and exactness depends on post procedures.

    - what: DiaToM is a proof-of-concept LCF-style SML prover for classical first-order logic with term-dependent sorts, formula-schema variables and a configurable equality/specification policy. Authors encode ETCS and SEAR and demonstrate proof-producing bounded comprehension translation, quotients and group homomorphisms, natural numbers/integers/lists/co-lists, a simulation-preservation characterization of modal formulas, and a set receiving injections from every finite powerset iterate of any given set. The body explains explicit context tracking for possibly empty dependent sorts, the danger of evaluating arbitrary relations as functions, specification unique up to a chosen equivalence, and proof-producing conversion from external bounded formulas to categorical internal logic. Concrete modal quantification and powerset-collection statements show what the chosen foundation adds, while a 2,443-line kernel and elementary SML infrastructure give qualitative implementation evidence.

Formula variables encode axiom schemas by instantiation, not ordinary higher-order quantified predicates. Theorem Γ,A⊢φ retains all needed variables in Γ, including dependency information, so possibly empty sorts are not silently inhabited. Universal specialization adds free variables of its witness; generalization checks assumptions, sort dependencies and schema-sort lists. Substitution/matching must preserve well-formed dependent sorts; equality transport is deliberately restricted rather than a full dependent type theory.     - what: Extends differential Floyd–Hoare logic (dFHL) with assume-guarantee Hoare quintuples and interruption/fallback constructs to prove safety envelopes and graceful degradation in automated-driving controllers. The layered simplex combines a goal-aware RSS controller with a collision-avoiding RSS fallback around a black-box advanced controller. The paper gives trace semantics for nondeterministic hybrid programs with continuous physical dynamics and environment variables, defines α↓A interruption, fallback α on β, and a two-way simplex that switches back to α. Margined switching conditions, counters, or timers prevent infinite controller oscillation. Simulations with a sampling-based planner answer safety, strong goal, and best-effort goal questions, including POV2 braking that interrupts and later returns control to GA-RSS.
