    - title: Contextuality in distributed systems
    - what: Defines a lattice of distributed-program specifications as subpresheaves of relative execution traces paired with maximal covers of a finite topological variable space. The lattice order captures refinement and parallelism; associated information algebras define local and global consistency, with global consistency related to sequential consistency. The paper constructs relative traces from nondegenerate simplicial cells of products of variable prosets, proves the trace presheaf is flasque and a tuple system, and derives an ordered adjoint information algebra of relations. It characterizes local consistency by flasqueness and global consistency by an inference/join test. A dining-philosophers specification is locally consistent but globally inconsistent: three singleton traces induce a causal loop in chopstick acquisitions. Isabelle/HOL formalizes several constructions and proofs, while an explicit local-computation reformulation reduces join cost by projecting pairwise overlaps.

    - title: Tailoring Stateless Model Checking for Event-Driven Multi-Threaded Programs
    - what: Introduces Event-DPOR, a dynamic partial-order-reduction algorithm for stateless model checking event-driven multithreaded programs whose handlers process mailbox messages in arbitrary order. The paper defines a finite-thread/shared-variable model with handler mailboxes, happens-before traces and trace equivalence. Event-DPOR extends Optimal-DPOR using happens-before prefixes, weak initials, wakeup trees, parked wakeup sequences and race reversal that can reorder serialized messages. Weak-initial redundancy checking is proved NP-hard; the implementation uses a sequence of inexpensive incomplete tests and a final decision procedure. Correctness proves at least one maximal execution per equivalence class; optimality proves exactly one for non-branching programs. The Nidhugg implementation stores vector clocks and handles first-conflict reversals. Benchmarks compare Event-DPOR with Optimal-DPOR, GenMC DPOR and LAPOR on posters, buyers, ping-pong, consensus, prolific, sparse-mat and plb programs.

    - what: Establishes fixed-parameter first-order model checking on every monadically stable graph class and proves monadic stability is the tractability boundary for hereditary edge-stable classes. The tractability proof first establishes almost-linear neighborhood complexity: for every ε, the number of distinct closed-neighborhood traces on a parameter set A is O(|A|^{1+ε}). A reduction using branching index, sampling and nowhere-dense machinery yields this bound. Welzl's low-crossing-number order then gives distance-r neighborhood covers of constant diameter and subpolynomial overlap via a greedy compact-interval partition; the cover can be computed in O(n^{4+ε}). Substituting it into the Flipper-game model-checking framework improves the overall bound to O_{C,ε,φ}(n^{5+ε}). For hardness, Ramsey refinement and k-flips characterize non-stability by induced subdivided cliques or webs. Careful existential “deobfuscation” yields effective interpretations of all graphs, giving AW[*]-hard FO model checking, W[1]-hard existential FO model checking, and W[1]-hard induced-subgraph isomorphism under Turing reductions.

    - what: Reports Isabelle/HOL proofs of Iwamura’s directed-set decomposition, equivalence of directed completeness and nonempty well-related completeness, and equivalence of Scott continuity and preservation of nonempty well-related suprema. Uses cardinal-indexed well-orders on the original carrier instead of a universal ordinal type. Generalizes from partial orders to quasi-orders and removes all codomain order/completeness assumptions in the continuity theorem. The uncountable construction closes each strict prefix under chosen finite upper bounds by countable iteration, bounding its size by the larger of the prefix size and countable infinity. Countably infinite carriers require a different finite-stage sequence; an inverse order isomorphism reconciles its natural-number index with the carrier index. Cardinal induction chooses possibly nonunique suprema of smaller directed sets, turns their monotone image into a well-related set, and transfers its supremum back to the original directed set. A strengthened simultaneous induction proves continuity for every possible supremum without assuming transitivity in the codomain.

The familiar nonempty plus pairwise-upper-bound definition needs transitivity for equivalence. Iwamura’s theorem assumes reflexivity and an infinite directed carrier but does not assume transitivity; completeness and continuity equivalences assume a quasi-order, meaning reflexivity and transitivity, without antisymmetry. A well-related set is one whose every nonempty subset has a least element. This implies reflexivity but is defined without assuming transitivity or antisymmetry. A pre-well-order additionally assumes a quasi-order. In the main theorem’s quasi-ordered ambient carrier, well-related subsets inherit transitivity. Nonempty qualifiers exclude a requirement for a least element/bottom arising from an empty supremum. Choice is used to select a least-cardinality well-order of the carrier and a bound f(X) for each finite X using SOME. Later it selects a supremum for each smaller directed set. This last selection cannot use unique choice because removing antisymmetry makes suprema potentially nonunique. More constructive proof organization does not mean a choice-free or computational construction. Isabelle/HOL cannot collect arbitrarily large ordinals of every type into one ordinal type. The workaround represents an ordinal by a well-order relation and uses cardinal-library comparisons across types. The index order on A is the particular least well-order representing |A|; it is different from the original relation whose directedness is being studied. Locales permit both relations, unlike fixing one order per type through a type class. For the least well-order, every strict prefix A_prec(a) has strictly smaller cardinality. Leastness is essential: an arbitrary well-order may have a strict prefix as large as the whole carrier. An infinite least-cardinality well-order has no greatest element, since deleting one point preserves infinite cardinality. Therefore the union of all strict prefixes equals A. That equality fails for nonempty finite carriers, which are handled separately. Uncountable case: F(X)=X union {f(Y):Y is a finite subset of X}; F^omega(X) is the union of its finite iterates. Any finite set in this union is contained in one common stage, so its chosen upper bound is in the next stage. This argument needs no transitivity. F and its closure are monotone; closure stays within A and includes X. Cardinality control splits finite and infinite prefixes. A finite starting set has finite stages and at most countable closure, which is still smaller than uncountable A. For infinite X, finite subsets have the same cardinality as X, each iterate preserves that cardinality, and a countable union has size at most |X|. The proof uses existing cardinal-library lemmas; it does not assume that the original uncountable cardinal is regular. Countably infinite case: choose order isomorphism seq from natural numbers to the least well-order on A. Seq(0)={f(empty)} and Seq(n+1)=Seq(n) union {seq(n),f(Seq(n) union {seq(n)})}. Every stage is finite and directed because the added bound also bounds itself by reflexivity. This avoids countable closure becoming as large as the entire countable carrier. This proves directedness even without transitivity. Forward direction uses cardinal induction on directed D. A finite D has a greatest element by directedness; an infinite D is decomposed by Iwamura and each smaller I(d) receives an inductively obtained supremum s(d). Monotonicity of I and of taking suprema makes s monotone from the chosen well-order on D to the original relation. A monotone image of a well-related set is well-related even without injectivity. Completeness supplies a supremum x of s(D). Covering D by I(d) and ambient transitivity shows x bounds D; any bound of D bounds each I(d), hence s(D), so x is least among bounds of D. C-continuity includes f(A) subset B and preservation of every existing supremum for each nonempty C-subset. It does not require preserving empty suprema. Under a reflexive domain and class C containing every related pair {i,j}, this property implies monotonicity. Well-related sets meet that condition, without requiring codomain reflexivity or transitivity. The continuity equivalence assumes only a quasi-ordered, nonempty-well-related-complete domain. The codomain is an arbitrary carrier and binary relation, with no reflexivity, transitivity, antisymmetry or completeness assumptions. The proof establishes completeness and preservation simultaneously by cardinal induction. It does not compose codomain inequalities through an unstated transitivity assumption. For continuity, a supplied supremum x of D may differ from the one constructed through the well-related set C. Domain transitivity proves the supplied x also is a supremum of C, so preservation applies to f(x) itself. A bound b of f(D) bounds each f(I(d)); the induction hypothesis gives f(s(d)) related to b. Thus b bounds f(C), and the least-bound property of f(x) completes the proof without codomain transitivity. Authors report 726 Isabelle lines in AFP entry Directed_Sets, plus refactoring of Complete_Non_Orders with new Continuity.thy and Directedness.thy totaling 427 lines. These counts describe different development scopes; they are not runtime or proof-success measurements. The article reports machine formalization but no build log, tactic-time statistics, independent replication, empirical benchmark or proof-agent evaluation. AFP and cited prior developments were not opened or rebuilt in this reading. The paper motivates directed sets through nets in topology, fixed-point semantics for loops and ideals in reachability/coverability of well-structured transition systems such as Petri nets. These are motivating applications, not a verified protocol, Rust implementation, Verus/TLA+ specification or applied model checker delivered here. It contains no LLM-assisted proof experiment.

    - title: Liveness Properties in Geometric Logic for Domain-Theoretic Streams
    - what: Defines LTL over the algebraic cpo of partially defined streams JStrAK and studies formula denotations through Scott topology, sobriety, frames and geometric logic. Negation-free LTL formulas translate inductively to geometric theories whose models are exactly the denotations; the paper applies the translation to prove a liveness specification for the non-productive stream filter function. The stream domain is DCPO[N,JAK] with a pointwise flat order, so finite-support streams are compact approximants and total streams are their directed suprema. The authors prove negation-free denotations are upward-closed and induce sober subspaces, while negation can destroy sobriety (e.g., J¬□aK excludes aω). They stratify negation-free LTL into G, Gδ and full fragments, define geometric-formula operators for next/until/weak-until, and prove model equivalence (Theorem 3). A frame/deduction treatment establishes spatiality for countable theories and gives complete deduction for Gδ formulas. For filter, ordinary fixpoint induction fails because the bottom function does not satisfy total-output liveness; finite-occurrence formulas ψn,k and output approximants φk yield Lemma 13 and prove that infinitely many predicate-satisfying input elements imply a total filtered stream.

    - title: Quantitative Safety and Liveness
    - what: Generalizes safety, liveness, the safety-progress hierarchy, and safety-liveness decomposition from Boolean properties to quantitative trace properties over complete lattices. The paper introduces quantitative properties Φ:Σ^ω→D over complete lattices, quantitative safety via finite witnesses for wrong lower-bound hypotheses, and the safety closure Φ*(f)=inf_{s≺f} sup_g Φ(sg). It proves safety iff upper semicontinuity iff equality with safety closure, safety iff inf-property, co-safety iff sup-property, and characterizes lim-inf/lim-sup levels. New liveness and co-liveness definitions are shown to generalize Boolean liveness; every property decomposes as min(Φ*,Ψ) with Ψ live, and as the minimum of two live properties. Approximate α-safety/β-co-safety are characterized by closure gaps; for real-valued limit properties these imply suffix influence eventually falls below any δ>α+β, yielding a finite-state (δ,δ)-monitor. Examples include minimal/maximal/average response times and discounted safety.

Explains which propositional equivalences and limited quantifier rules the efficient kernel handles, why automatic quantifier instantiation is excluded from F(OL)^2 comparison while explicit instantiation proof steps remain kernel-checkable, how standalone proof imports differ from justified theory theorems, and why schematic axiom schemas make existence-only definition unsound as a conservative extension. Polynomial/quadratic complexity claims concern checking explicit proof data and formula comparisons, not general proof search. No machine-checked verification of the whole Scala kernel/compiler/runtime or empirical complexity benchmark is reported. Ortholattice equivalence is a restricted propositional theory excluding Boolean distributivity. F(OL)^2 extends it with equality symmetry/reflexivity, universal monotonicity and congruence for schematic connectors. It is not a complete validity or equivalence decision procedure for first-order logic. Standalone proof checking establishes derivability from explicitly listed imports; it does not prove imported axioms/theorems themselves. Theory validates imports against its own stored axioms/theorems/definitions, and a theorem remains relative to that theory’s assumptions. Calling the result unconditionally true in the paper does not establish consistency of arbitrary user axioms. Theorem type depends on a specific Theory instance; host language path-dependent types prevent ordinary mixing of facts from distinct theories. Scala type checking is a usability/encapsulation mechanism, while kernel proof checking remains the proof-validity boundary. Function definitions require fresh symbol and proof of unique existence. Existence alone could yield a global pick function and Choice when new symbols are usable in replacement schemas. Underspecification weakens the exposed fact after checking a unique construction; it does not discard the existence/uniqueness obligation. Tautology is a non-clausal DPLL-like propositional proof search with worst-case exponential atom branching, most-frequent-atom heuristic and ortholattice simplification. Its stated completeness is for propositional reasoning, not quantified mathematical proof or all first-order validity. Quantifier automation/external ATP integrations are future work. If all A_p/B_p null then W equals C_p a.e. for every prime, hence is almost invariant under translation [1/p]. Unbounded prime orders and the translation lemma give final dichotomy. Shrinking errors enter through Cassels, explaining why the unfinished branch cannot simply be dropped (§6.2). Reported 27 PRs and just over 3,500 net new lines include mostly generic library code contributed directly to mathlib master. Final ~30-line informal proof corresponds to 101 formal lines excluding comments, after supporting libraries exist. This is not total proof effort, proof-check time, autonomous automation output or a model benchmark. Author recommends upstream-first development as a belief supported by this case, without controlled workflow comparison (§1, §6.2, §7.4). Missing general branch first normalizes δ to max(δ,0). For this nonnegative sequence, failure to tend to zero yields literal WA=S by a separate arithmetic argument. Normalization matters: failure of a signed δ to tend to zero by negative values alone does not imply full approximation. Needed divisor-count/totient growth bounds partly existed in external Unit Fractions Project and would need migration. Duffin–Schaeffer convergence/divergence criterion for nonnegative approximation errors is motivating context, not proved here. Easy convergence direction uses Borel–Cantelli; hard converse and Pollington–Vaughan lemma are future targets. Later quantitative work can bypass Gallagher according to author correspondence; source does not formalize those quantitative results. - Neural Activation Patterns as Specifications (2023)
    - title: Towards Reliable Neural Specifications
    - what: Proposes neural representation as specification: mine partial neural activation patterns (NAPs) shared by most examples of a class, then verify classification and robustness for the whole input region following that pattern. A relaxation factor δ controls precision/recall. NAPs can be encoded directly in Marabou, support non-ambiguity checks between labels, and augment input norm-balls to verify larger regions. The method’s mining algorithm counts neuron activation frequencies on class training data, selecting activated/deactivated neurons above δ and below 1−δ. The paper distinguishes NAP robustness (all inputs following a pattern are classified as the label) from NAP-augmented robustness (norm-ball intersected with the pattern region). Controlled 2-D visualization explains why activation regions are flexible and larger than boxes. VNNCOMP-21 MNIST and CIFAR10 experiments quantify precision/recall, timeouts, coverage and robustness bounds; δ=0.99 yields an MNIST digit-1 NAP covering 84% of test images and verifies ε=0.3 for six of seven previously non-robust inputs. CIFAR10 verifies some examples at ε=0.12 (10× the prior bound) when δ=0.9.
    - number: MNIST δ=0.99 digit-1 NAP recalls 959/1135=84% test images; δ=1.0 recalls 1124/1135=99% but admits 8 wrong-label images
    - number: Table 3: ε=0.2 without NAP fails/timeout, while δ=0.99 NAP robustness verifies all tested labels; ε=1 augmented NAP also verifies all tested labels
    - number: Table 4: with δ=0.99, all six mnistfc_256x4 and one mnistfc_256x6 non-robust inputs verified at ε=0.3; largest VNNCOMP ε was 0.05
    - number: CIFAR10 Table 5: at ε=0.12 and δ=0.9, 3/7 tested inputs verify; ε=0.12 is 10× the prior bound and an input volume ratio of 10^3072
    - limits: Targets feed-forward ReLU classifiers and uses Marabou; extension to other activations/architectures is conjectural. Mining is approximate, requires δ>0.5 and trades recall for precision; lower δ can cover fewer inputs. NAP guarantees concern the network’s classifier, not semantic correctness of labels or distribution shift. Noisy/mislabeled data can violate ideal same-label patterns. Marabou has timeouts and complete verification remains expensive; abstract verifiers can be inconclusive. Experiments use MNIST/CIFAR10 VNNCOMP models, not deployed systems.

- Okazaki RUSUB6 Gram Schmidt 2023 (2023)
    - title: On the Formalization of Gram-Schmidt Process for Orthonormalizing a Set of Vectors.
    - what: Okazaki formalizes exact Gram–Schmidt orthonormalization in a real inner-product space. For a nonempty injective sequence whose range is linearly independent, the output has equal length, is injective and orthonormal, spans exactly the input span, and preserves span equality at every prefix. The paper constructs finite projection-term sequences and recursive prefix states, then defines PROCESSGramSchmidt by this contract. It does not verify floating-point stability or give a compiled implementation. Records finite linear-combination helpers, inner-product summation, the exact projection/subtraction/normalization formula, division safety from prefix independence, dual recursion state and per-prefix span/orthonormality invariants.
    - limits: MML RUSUB_6 version 8.1.12 5.74.1441 identifies the Mizar formalization. H is a real unitary space, meaning a real inner-product space in this library, not an arbitrary normed space or complex unitary matrix. No completeness of H or finite dimension of its entire carrier is required; the input sequence is finite (pp.53–55). Theorem 9 assumes x is one-to-one, rng x is linearly independent and len x≥1. Set-level linear independence alone would not exclude repeated entries of a sequence; the injectivity guard matters. Zero vectors and dependent later vectors are excluded, rather than detected and skipped by a specified branch (p.55). Definition 1 makes r◦x the sequence of scalar-vector products r_i x_i with length len x. Proposition 1 assumes equal coefficient/vector lengths and input range in A to put its sum in Lin(A), by induction. Propositions 2/3 turn mutual generator containment in spans into equality of subspaces (pp.53–54). Definition 2 forms the real coefficient sequence ((u|x_i)) of inner products. Proposition 4 gives its pointwise vector product, Proposition 5 moves inner product through a finite sum, and Proposition 6 reduces such a sum to the sole potentially nonzero term. These support orthogonality of residuals, not numerical approximations to it (p.54). Proposition 7 constructs a total function on H×H* returning the finite sequence ((x|e_i)e_i); Definition 3 names it SeqProj(H). The function returns projection summands, not their sum. For a general e it is just this formula; interpreting the sum as an orthogonal projection requires the orthonormal prefix invariant (p.55). Proposition 8 proves every orthonormal family linearly independent by showing a zero-sum linear combination has empty support. Theorem 10 later applies it to the constructed output range; the main same-span theorem is already part of Theorem 9 and the defining contract (pp.55,57). Theorem 9 sets e_1=x_1/||x_1|| and e_(k+1)=r_(k+1)/||r_(k+1)||, with residual r_(k+1)=x_(k+1)-sum_(i≤k)(x_(k+1)|e_i)e_i. It requires equal input/output lengths, orthonormal output range, injectivity, same final span and the recurrence, plus orthonormality/injectivity/same span at every prefix k≤len x, including the empty prefix (p.55). The residual is orthogonal to each earlier e_j because the prefix is orthonormal and inner product distributes over the sum. It is nonzero because otherwise x_(k+1) lies in the earlier output span, equal by induction to the earlier input span, contradicting independence plus injectivity of x. Thus every normalization divides by a strictly positive norm. These are the mathematical obligations of the printed recurrence; the PDF abbreviates the final induction rather than displaying its full checker proof (pp.55–56). For span preservation, each new e is a scalar multiple of x_(k+1) minus a combination of earlier e, so it lies in the enlarged input span. Conversely x_(k+1)=||r||e_(k+1)+the projection sum lies in the enlarged output span. Nonzero normalization plus orthogonality also makes the new output distinct from earlier unit vectors. This reading explains the invariant step; it is not a separate executed proof trace (Theorem 9). Theorem 9 proof first constructs E(k), a finite sequence of partial output sequences in the union of H^i for i≤len x. Its transition appends the normalized residual. It then extracts a vector sequence e with E(n)=e restricted to n and proves the prefix predicate by induction. Maintaining E and e agreement connects a state of prefixes to the advertised output recurrence (p.56). Definition 4 names PROCESSGramSchmidt(x) under the same nonempty/injective/independent assumptions and repeats all seven substantive contract clauses, including prefix-span equality. The recurrence mathematically determines the output for a fixed ordered input, but this PDF does not present a separate uniqueness proof script or code extraction. Its output is an orthonormal basis of Lin(rng x), not necessarily all of H (pp.56–57). The arithmetic is exact real arithmetic. No rounding, conditioning, classical versus modified Gram–Schmidt stability bound, reorthogonalization, rank-deficiency handling, operation-count benchmark or executable numeric example appears. Error-correcting-code/cryptology applications and Isabelle/HOL work are introductory related-work context, not evaluated case studies here (pp.53,57). Exact quotations preserve raw extraction artifacts such as inequality glyphs, U+0016 for prefix restriction and broken denominator/index ordering; renderings were checked. Five pages, four definitions, ten propositions/theorems, all supplied sketches, acknowledgement, eight references and acceptance date read. Mizar source/checker and cited developments not independently inspected/run. No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM proof/specification-agent evaluation.

- Petrification (2023)
    - title: Petrification: Software Model Checking for Programs with Dynamic Thread Management
    - what: Reduces verification of dynamically forked/joined concurrent programs to fixed-thread Petri programs. Petrification instantiates at most β thread copies, separates control flow from data, and adds safety and bound specifications; iterative β increases detect semantic thread width. The Conc semantics permits non-unique thread IDs and sequentially consistent arbitrary interleavings. Petrification renames local variables per template/instance, adds inUse/notInUse/insuff places, and labels Petri transitions with assignments and guards. Lemmas connect bounded-width executions and Petri firing sequences; Theorem 3.10 equates bound-specification satisfaction with thread width ≤β, yielding soundness and completeness for bounded-width correct programs and incorrect programs. Three iterative algorithms differ in whether they check safety or bound first.

Completeness is relative to the modeled language and Petri verification backend.

    - title: Bel-Games: A Formal Theory of Games of Incomplete Information Based on Belief Functions in the Coq Proof Assistant
    - what: Formalizes normalized belief functions, conditioning, expected utilities and complete/incomplete-information games in Coq/SSReflect/MathComp. Reports utility preservation and Nash-equilibrium correspondence for three transforms from Bel games to hypergraphical complete-information games. Extends the TBM transform beyond Dempster conditioning by enlarging local-game participation. Records the finite algebra and exact conditioning contracts, three score semantics, type-specific deviations and profile flattening, transform restrictions and locality caveat, weak-conditioning TBM repair, theoretical versus verified complexity, illustrative payoff errors and limits of the reported proof evaluation.
    - limits: The development uses finite state/player/type domains, finite sets/functions and realFieldType scalars; field operations suffice, without a general infinite measure/integration construction. A normalized basic probability assignment has zero mass on the empty set, nonnegative masses summing to one. Bel sums masses of contained focal sets; Pl sums intersecting ones. A probability measure is the singleton-focal special case (§3.1). Dempster-Shafer evidence and upper/lower probability interpretations are distinguished; the formal development chooses the former. The Mr. Jones example assigns mass 1/2 to {P,Q} and 1/2 to {R}. The paper’s objection to a Bayesian posterior concerns the specific equiprobable-within-men prior and its intended evidence interpretation, not a mathematical proof that Bayesian models cannot represent any such decision situation (§§2–3.1). Conditioning packages a revisability predicate, a mass-transforming function requiring its proof, and Bel(C-complement | C)=0. This is weaker than Bel(C|C)=1 or Pl(C-complement|C)=0. For example, mass 1 on Ω and a proper nonempty C satisfies Bel(C-complement)=0 while Bel(C)=0 and Pl(C-complement)=1. The introductory certainty/impossibility wording must therefore be qualified by the actual axiom; the paper explicitly acknowledges weak conditioning can yield Bel(C|C)<1 (§3.2; reader example). Dempster requires Pl(C)≠0, intersects each focal set with C, discards empty intersections and renormalizes. Strong conditioning requires Bel(C)≠0 and retains only focal sets contained in C. Weak conditioning requires Pl(C)≠0 and retains whole focal sets intersecting C, renormalized without intersection. These encode distinct updates, not interchangeable implementations of one posterior (§3.2). Printed notation errors, checked on rendered pages: Definition 13 types revisable as a predicate on Ω although it is applied to events; the Coq pred {set W} has the intended event domain. Definition 19 uses an unbound B in the denominator/overlap test; its Coq rule consistently uses C. Definition 27’s final mathematical inequality omits the prime on the deviating action, becoming vacuous; the adjacent Coq change_strategy expression correctly changes to a'_i. These presentation defects do not establish formal-artifact unsoundness. XEU is a focal-mass weighted sum of φ(u)(B). CEU takes minimum utility within B; JEU mixes its minimum and maximum using local pessimism coefficients (mathematically in [0,1]); TBEU averages within B, equivalently using a pignistic probability after conditioning. Each agrees with ordinary expected utility on singleton masses. The displayed Coq fJEU accepts an arbitrary scalar coefficient function; its type alone does not enforce the stated coefficient interval (§3.3). Pure complete-information Nash equilibrium excludes a strictly improving unilateral deviation; ties are allowed. Mixed strategies use a product of each player’s probability distribution and expected utility, hence independent randomization, not an arbitrary correlated distribution. Mixed equilibrium is represented as pure equilibrium in the mixed extension; this is a representation theorem, not a general existence proof or a computed equilibrium solver (§4.1). Hypergraphical games sum local utilities for each player, who must use the same action in every local game. Bel games add a common mass assignment over joint private-type configurations and utilities depending on joint actions and types. A pure strategy maps own type to action. Properness requires every own-type event to satisfy the chosen revisability predicate, excluding otherwise undefined posteriors, even for types assigned zero plausibility under Dempster conditioning (§§4.2–5). Bel equilibrium checks each player and each of their types for a profitable change at that type. Flattening turns a type-contingent strategy into a vector over abstract players (i,θi). The reported transform theorems establish equality of utilities for each such pair and one-to-one pure-equilibrium correspondence, not equality of information available to the original decision makers or a distributed implementation (§§5–6). Direct transform computes Dempster conditioning on the fly, indexing local games by prior focal sets and including types possible within that set; weights divide by the corresponding type-event plausibility. Conditioned transform precomputes posteriors for any permitted conditioning, uses the union of posterior focal sets and posterior masses; local contribution can be zero for a posterior in which the set is not focal (§§6.1–6.2). Reader qualification of the printed any-XEU claims in Theorems 34/36: the displayed score types allow φ(u)(B) to inspect u outside B, but the transformed local game only knows actions for types appearing in B. Utility preservation needs locality: agreement of u,v on B implies φ(u)(B)=φ(v)(B). CEU/JEU/TBEU satisfy this, but no such premise appears in the displayed statements. Counterexample to unrestricted printed generality: one player, types 0/1, actions 0/1, prior singleton masses 1/2, Dempster conditioning, utility u(a,θ)=a and φ(v)(B)=v(1). Original type-0 utility equals strategy σ(1), while only the positive-mass local game for {0} contributes to abstract player (i,0), whose local payoff cannot observe σ(1). Two profiles agreeing at type 0 and differing at type 1 thus refute universal utility equality. The full repository may contain omitted assumptions; it was not inspected. This is a statement-scope concern, not a finding that Coq accepted a false theorem. TBM uses TBEU/pignistic probabilities and one local game per joint type configuration. For arbitrary conditioning it expands participation beyond matching own types: include (i,θi) if a posterior focal set contains the local state and a state matching θi. This is necessary because weak conditioning can retain states not matching the conditioned type. Dempster/strong posteriors stay within the own-type event and the original smaller participation condition suffices (§§6.3). Table 4 reports Direct and Conditioned time/space O(k*Size(G)^k), TBM under Dempster conditioning space O(k*Size(G)) and time O(Size(G)), with k the largest focal-set cardinality. These bounds are imported from prior work; §7 identifies complexity proofs as future work. They are not demonstrated machine-checked complexity guarantees, measured runtimes, or a uniform polynomial bound when k varies. The enlarged arbitrary-conditioning TBM graph is not assigned the same unconditional complexity bound. Concrete examples use two players choosing P/Q/R; avoiding the culprit gives 3 each for different innocent partners and 2 each when sharing one. Table 2 has equilibria (Q1,R2)/(R1,Q2) when P is guilty. Example 32’s type-dependent strategy yields CEU 3 for every player/type, hence is an equilibrium. Table 3 center (Q guilty) nevertheless prints (2,2) at (Q1,R2), conflicting with the stated culprit-zero rule, which gives (0,3). Example 32 also mislabels σ2(R-bar) as σ1(R-bar); its following prose disambiguates. These local illustration errors do not refute the general transformation proofs. Reported size is about 2.5 k lines of Coq/SSReflect, including roughly 1 k lines for belief functions. Proofs mostly rewrite finite sums, often using under beneath binders; authors report no special additional recurring automation need. They report formal verification clarified conditioning pre/postconditions and proof presentation. Paper gives no checker runtime, extracted implementation test, empirical solver benchmark, independent human-behavior study or LLM-agent success evaluation (§§3.1,7). Artifact is linked to GitHub/Software Heritage and reported MIT/OPAM availability, but no repository audit or proof execution was performed here. Separate 2022 paper was not read. No Verus/verified Rust/TLA+ or distributed-protocol safety/liveness result appears. Relevance to proof/specification-agent evaluation is inferred: compare intended semantics, formal premises and checked statement; conditional transformations do not prove the empirical adequacy of a decision model.

    - what: Constructs a Coq interpreter for possibly nonterminating µ-recursive algorithms whose extraction resembles direct functional evaluation rather than fuel-based repeated approximation. Domain existence proofs guard Coq computations, then erase. A tailored unbounded-search termination predicate and forward proof invariant handle minimization; ordinary structural recursion handles syntax, vectors and primitive-recursion helpers. Discusses erasure choices that eliminate generic Obj.t placeholders or replace them with unit. Records exact search pre/postconditions for partially decidable predicates, functionality/disjointness role, existential proof versus computational witness distinction, impossible-branch dependent inversion, forward invariant for tail recursion, all six arity-indexed constructors and semantics, nested-recursion guard conditions, vector-projection design and two higher-order extraction encodings. Ackermann and universality are background, not new executable benchmarks. §§1/4.3, pp.4/12–13: compute(P)=(exists x,Px)->{x|Px}; Coq computation requires a noninformative existence proof and returns value plus specification proof. It does not turn arbitrary existential propositions into extractable witnesses without a program specific to P. Footnote explicitly says compute is not a definition of traditional computability. Within Coq no value is required when guard lacks proof. §3.1, pp.6–7: test n takes a proof Dtest(n) and returns proof of P(n) or Q(n); on domain P and Q cannot both hold. Q need not equal global negation P and test need not be defined everywhere. Prels(s,x) requires x>=s, domain at all points s<=i<=x and P(x), but does not assume x is the first hit or prior Q. Postls returns m>=s, domain/P at m and domain/Q at each s<=i<m, establishing first hit under disjointness. §3.2, p.7: Dls has stop(domain/P at n) or next(domain at n,Dls(n+1)). Loop is structurally recursive on Dls proof, which erases. Dls projection at n supplies test-domain proof; when test chooses Q, stop constructor is impossible by P/Q disjointness and false elimination yields the needed structural subterm. This carefully chosen inversion matters to guard acceptance. §§3.3–3.4, p.8: existential Prels builds Dls entirely in Prop using interval induction. Search never reads the witness as runtime data. Forward btwn(Dtest and Q,s,n) proof accumulator records already rejected prefix, so recursive call is syntactically tail-position before extraction rather than reconstructing result proof after it. Correctness is proof-carrying, not runtime certificate checking. §3.5, pp.9–10: F(n,y) must be functional and comes with a program computing y under exists-y guard. Minimized output m satisfies F(m,0) and every smaller n has a defined positive F(n,*). Instantiating Dtest=domainF,P=zeroF,Q=positiveF meets disjointness via functionality. A zero after an undefined earlier point is not a valid minimum under these semantics. §3.5, p.9: generic test creates a dependent Boolean then immediately branches; extraction would retain that unnecessary intermediate structure. Specialized six-line loop directly pattern-matches computed natural output, with zero return/positive recurse. Shared termination/search reasoning is retained, but code deliberately specializes instead of maximizing generic abstraction. §4.1, p.10: syntax A_a indexed by arity. zero:A0,succ:A1,projection idx(a)->A_a,composition A_b with vector b of A_a yields A_a,primitive recursion A_a with A_(a+2) yields A_(a+1),minimization A_(a+1) yields A_a. Input tuple order is reversed so recursion-driving natural is first vector element. Coq types rule out malformed arities before extraction. §4.2, pp.10–12: semantics is a functional input/output relation over fixed-length vectors. Composition existentially supplies all inner outputs, primitive recursion relates successive intermediate outputs, minimization enforces prior positive definedness. ra_sem_fun proved by structural induction establishes at most one output. No assertion of existence for every algorithm/input. §4.3, p.13: interpreter follows same syntax recursion as semantics; composition passes recursively interpreted subalgorithms through vector traversal. Coq guard checker sees structural subterms because helper recurses on vector itself. Minimization uses Braga-style domain machinery only inside search; recursive interpreter call is on proper child syntax. Display leaves three proof obligations as underscores and points to source, which was not inspected here. §4.4, pp.14–15: finite indices and length-indexed inductive vectors are tailored for extraction. Projection recurses on vector, not index, so a projected child remains recognizable structural subterm. Empty vector+inhabited index contradiction is eliminated with idx_inv; dependent inversions enable one match instead of separate head/tail matches. Vector extensional equality is provable componentwise without assuming functional extensionality for arbitrary functions. §5, pp.15–16: extraction erases arities, maps indices to naturals/vectors to OCaml lists and inlines selected helpers. - Propositional proof skeletons (2023)
    - what: Introduces semantic proof skeletons: selected learned clauses that summarize an unsatisfiability proof and allow later reconstruction of a complete DRUP/DRAT proof by incremental SAT solving. Online glue/reason-clause filters and offline LRAT-activity filters are implemented in CaDiCaL and DRAT-trim, with independent chunks enabling parallel reconstruction. The paper formalizes the reconstruction invariant: each skeleton clause is proved as a RUP under preceding clauses, then chunk proofs are stitched into a complete proof; variables in skeleton clauses are frozen to prevent unsound incremental inprocessing. It gives online Glue, Glue+Trail and Dynamic filters, offline activity-based Offline/Offline+Units/Offline-Opt filters, UNSAT-core restriction, and post-reconstruction shrinking. It also adapts DRAT-trim to concatenate chunk LRAT proofs and explains when deletions must be removed.

Runtime and compression depend on heuristic clause selection and chunk balance; the study uses CaDiCaL/DRAT-trim and does not establish comparable gains for satisfiable cases or other proof systems.

Tests exported dependency graphs from portions of Isabelle/HOL. Repairs an earlier proof’s incorrect strict type-size argument by tracking both size and number of free type variables. Analyzes most-general solution paths modulo renaming, eliminates infinitely many strict instantiation extensions, and reduces nontermination to a self-instance cycle under composability. Monotonicity requires every type variable on a dependency’s right occur on its left; the kernel checks the corresponding definition-name condition. Main equivalence requires finite, well-formed, monotone and composable dependencies. Composability says a reachable endpoint and any next edge source are comparable by type instantiation or have no common instance. Without it, nonterminating instantiated chains need not contain a cycle of the restricted uninstantiated-start path form. A cycle means a restricted path ends at an instance of its starting symbol, modulo variable renaming, not necessarily identical concrete syntax. A typed dependency graph must account for substitutions/unification rather than ordinary finite graph cycle detection. The executable breadth-first checker is clocked and always returns at the supplied depth limit; Maybe_cyclic means inconclusive, not a cyclicity witness. Acyclic means the explored frontier actually became empty after checked steps, allowing a proof about all lengths; absence of a discovered cycle at finite depth alone is insufficient. Cyclic_step gives a self-instance path witness; Non_comp_step gives a failed composability witness. Neither a noncomposable input nor a cyclic dependency automatically proves a logical contradiction in the user’s equations. They prevent acceptance by this sufficient termination-based foundation. No unconditional decision procedure for all overloaded theories is claimed. General termination is undecidable; a finite clock does not guarantee a decisive answer on every input. - Automating cutoff proofs (2022)
    - title: Automating and Mechanizing Cutoff-based Verification of Distributed Protocols
    - what: Formalizes cutoff-based verification for parametric distributed protocols in the Relational Modeling Language (RML). A finite cutoff instance is sufficient when every safety violation in any larger instance can be simulated by a trace of the cutoff; the paper encodes this simulation in first-order logic and uses SMT to check it. The paper gives initial, step, and safety simulation conditions and a first-violation refinement that removes the need to simulate behavior after a violation. A backward static analysis starts from instantiated negated safety clauses, follows action updates into guards to a fixed point, and emits the relevant action set, simulation relation, and lockstep. In the sharded key-value example, the analysis reduces eight actions to four and proves a two-node cutoff. The implementation checks the formulas with Z3 and handles seven protocols: four cutoffs are synthesized automatically; three require small manual changes. Two-phase commit exposes a limit: universally quantified guards force actions of all larger-instance nodes into the simulation, requiring an extra failure-simulating node and constraints.
    - number: 7 protocols
    - number: 4/7 automatic synthesis; 3/7 small manual changes
    - number: 20–40 ms per protocol
    - number: 2-node sharded-key-value cutoff
    - limits: RML domains are finite per instance but may have infinitely many valid interpretations; safety properties are assumed universally quantified. The result is for safety, not liveness. Cutoff correctness depends on a simulation relation for every valid larger interpretation and on a safe finite cutoff. Automatic synthesis can fail when universal guards or side effects conflict, as in two-phase commit, and the basic key-value store needs an added precondition.
    - how much was read: most of it read

- Bapanapally and Gamboa Banach–Tarski 2022 (2022)
    - title: A Complete, Mechanically-Verified Proof of the Banach-Tarski Theorem in ACL2(R)
    - what: Reports a complete ACL2(R) formalization of Banach–Tarski: a finite partition of the unit ball can be moved by rotations into two copies of the ball. Encodes reduced words as lists, proves a faithful free rotation group, chooses canonical orbit representatives, removes countable poles, then handles radial extension and the origin. Paper lists five subsets for the sphere minus poles decomposition,14 for the sphere, and 52 for the ball. Provides concrete Lisp definitions/theorem statements and archived source pointer, but no runtime/proof-size benchmark or fresh certification log. Follows every construction and printed code listing, including strengthened defchoose representative consistency, enumeration of poles/bad angles, origin absorption via arbitrary-axis rotations, matrix closure/inverse/distance lemmas and exact final theorem forms. Distinguishes a mathematical existence proof with noncomputable choice from an executable geometric algorithm; records abbreviated hints/unions and two prose slips without extrapolating them into failures of the linked formal artifact.
    - limits: The theorem is about abstract non-measurable subsets of the real unit ball, not physically cuttable pieces or a volume-doubling program. It relies on an Axiom-of-Choice mechanism and prior non-denumerability of real intervals. ACL2(R) extends ACL2 real reasoning via non-standard analysis. The paper cites existing formalized matrix algebra, modular arithmetic, trigonometry and uncountability; this reading does not audit their foundational implementation or consistency (§1,§7). Infinite sets are represented extensionally by membership predicates, not allocated data structures. Existential predicates use defun-sk with witness functions; defchoose with :strengthen t selects a common representative for all inputs in the same orbit equivalence class. Canonical consistency is essential to disjointness; an arbitrary unrelated witness per input would not suffice. These choices establish logical existence and need not compute a constructive enumeration of all chosen points (§2,§5.1). Words use four character encodings for a,a^-1,b,b^-1; weak words allow adjacent inverses, reduced words do not. word-inverse reverses the word and swaps each letter with its inverse. word-fix recursively cancels inverse neighbors and compose fixes concatenation. Closure, associativity and inverse are shown as defthmd statements; the empty list is identity. The reduction/isomorphism invariants make an abstract group argument tractable as list induction (§2,Listings1–5). Corollaries 1–3 partition all reduced words into identity plus four leading-letter classes and reconstruct the whole group as a^-1W(a) disjoint-union W(a^-1), and similarly for b. This is the algebraic source of two reconstructions. It does not by itself prove a partition of physical ball pieces; later arguments transfer it to a free group action (§2). §2 PDF 5 prose says the witness word-a for x=compose(a^-1,word-a) is a^-1x. In the stated no-leading-a^-1 case the witness should be ax. Reader example x=b: compose(a^-1,ab)=b, whereas compose(a^-1,a^-1b)=a^-1a^-1b. This is a printed explanatory slip, not evidence that the formal corollary is false or its certified proof fails; no linked source was run (§2 PDF 5). Rotation generators A± rotate about x and B± about z with cos 1/3 and sine ±2sqrt2/3. array2p stores real 3×3 matrices. rotation maps a reduced word to the product of corresponding matrices. Faithfulness is shown using image of(0,1,0), rescaling coordinate x/z by 1/sqrt2 and all coordinates by 3^|w| to obtain integers. Nonempty reduced words yield a nonzero mod 3 triple; base cases 4 and inductive letter-pair cases 16 underpin nonidentity and injectivity (§3). Definition 4 characterizes rotations by 3×3 real matrix, inverse=transpose,determinant1. New helpers compute determinant and inverse; Lemmas 5–12 establish multiplication closure/determinants/identity/inverse laws, rotation product/inverse closure and distance preservation. Lemma12 uses x^T x and R^T R=I, without a geometric determinant argument. These are exact real algebra statements, not floating-point error guarantees (§4). D consists of unit-sphere points fixed by a nonidentity group rotation. Its complement is invariant under group action, proved by conjugation: if r(p) is fixed byrw, then p is fixed by r^-1 rw r. Choosing one representative M per orbit outside D transfers the word partition to disjoint representative-rotation classes. Intersection of two distinct classes would imply a nonidentity rotation fixes a point outsideD, a contradiction (§5,§5.1). Listing 6 reports five disjoint sets covering S²−D and two reconstructions from transformed class pairs. The printed iff/or statements express coverage/equivalence; disjointness is argued in prose and depends on separate properties. Listing 6’s conjunction-free union formula alone does not constitute the whole partition proof. Paper explicitly describes witness and orbit-consistency reasoning rather than reducing the result to a finite test (§5.1). For each nonempty reduced-word rotation, symmetry would force rotation=its inverse, contradicting faithfulness and the free group’s absence of nontrivial self-inverse words. Thus skew-entry vector(m32−m23,m13−m31,m21−m12) has nonzero normK. Its normalized positive/negative vectors are exactly the two unit-sphere poles. Enumerating all finite words and both poles yields coverage of D, even though generation includes weak words/duplicates; countability only needs a covering sequence (§5.2). Uncountability yields an axis point outsideD. General rotation-3d supports angle addition and iteration. Bad angles that send some pole to another after a positive number of rotations are countable via pole pairs and integer indices. A good angle yields pairwise-disjoint translated copiesD,RD,R²D,…; with E their union, RE=E−D. This countable shift absorbs the poles and transfers the paradoxical decomposition from S²−D to S² (§5.3). §5.3 PDF 11 says alpha is uniquely determined by p1,p2,n, but its own alpha=(2πk+beta)/n expression also depends onk. For fixed n there may be several roots in[0,2π). The argument enumeratesk as well as n/pole pairs, so uniqueness over onlyp1,p2,n is unnecessary and overstated; countability survives finite/countable multiplicity. This reading does not infer a formal-artifact defect from that prose statement (§5.3). Listing 7 shows14predicate classes covering the sphere and two displayed six-term reconstructions; proof hints are elided. Count14is the displayed construction’s author-reported size, not a claimed minimum number of Banach–Tarski pieces. Union equivalences and rotations in the paper must be read with the stated disjointness/construction arguments, not as a standalone complete certification transcript (§5.3,Listing 7). For nonzero points of the ball, p maps to p/||p|| on the sphere; linear rotations preserve radial scaling. Thus sphere pieces lift along radii to B³−{0}. The origin needs a separate transformation since every origin-axis linear rotation fixes it. rotation-about-arbitrary-line combines translation and rotation about an off-origin axis close enough that the entire origin orbit stays inside the ball (§6). Off-origin rotation is shown to return an R³ point, have zero-angle identity, compose by angle addition, and keep the chosen origin orbit insideB³. Return-to-origin angles requirecos(nθ)=1, hence rational multiples2πk/n. Uncountability supplies a nonreturn angle. Z = {R_(l,nalpha)0:n∈N} givesRZ=Z−{0}, allowing the same shift/absorption strategy to restore the origin. Listing 8labels 52 sets and three ball equivalence theorems, but abbreviates several terms and all hints (§6). Evaluation is formal construction and authors’ reported machine acceptance in ACL2(R), with source link and Software Heritage archive. There are no empirical benchmark datasets, theorem-generation agents, success-rate comparisons, proof-checking times, memory figures, source line counts or person-effort measurements. Printed listings give concrete definitions and obligations but include ellipses, so this paper reading is not a fresh reproduction of all event admissions (§§1–7,Listings5–8). Source pointer https://github.com/acl2/acl2/tree/master/books/nonstd/nsa/Banach-Tarski and archive swh:1:dir:964ff589fe9739a46201bbeac71a6733aa4f274b establish where the authors locate the formalization. Reusable rotations.lisp and countable-sets.lisp are identified in§7. This reading does not certify current master contents, exact checker version/options, absence of unsound admissions or a full dependency closure; the paper supplies no reproduced audit log. No distributed protocol, concurrency/liveness model, Verus, verified Rust, TLA+or LLM agent is evaluated. Transfer to the human’s topic is methodological: specification representation, explicit witness/choice assumptions, intermediate algebraic invariants and replayable named theorem artifacts. - Bayesian HyperPCTL* SMC (2022)
    - title: Bayesian Statistical Model Checking for Multi-agent Systems using HyperPCTL*
    - what: Presents Bayesian statistical model checking for probabilistic HyperPCTL* over DTMCs. A multidimensional Bayes test handles joint probabilities; an approximate Bayes test bounds parameter error when recursively sampled nested subformulas are uncertain. BayesSMC propagates Type-I/II errors, uses top-down on-demand sampling, and is implemented in HyProVer alongside an SPRT comparator.
    - number: HyProVer Python toolbox, macOS Big Sur quad-core i7, 16 GB RAM, 50-run averages, 30-minute timeout. For collision avoidance, Bayesian method decided all tested n=4–10 cases in 0.019–0.382 s with 8–8,786 samples where SPRT often exceeded 1,800 s or remained undecided. For nested goal reaching, Bayesian completed in 0.216–6.316 s with 16–62.72 samples; SPRT never completed within 30 minutes.
    - limits: Finite DTMCs, finite-bounded until operators, independent path samples and Beta priors (uniform for comparisons). Approximate testing has an indifference region near expanded/reduced hypothesis boundaries and requires nonempty reduced sets; guarantees are probabilistic, not exact. Experiments use two-robot grid worlds and no public HyperPCTL* checker comparison.

- BlueCov/JBMC coverage integration (2022)
    - title: BlueCov: Integrating Test Coverage and Model Checking with JBMC
    - what: Introduces BlueCov, a Java bytecode coverage tool that consumes JBMC’s own coverage goals, instruments exactly those bytecode locations, records runtime hit counts and feeds uncovered goals back to JBMC for incremental test generation. This avoids criterion mismatches and redundant tests when formal test generation augments an existing suite. JBMC translates Java bytecode through CProver GOTO, inserts assert(false) goals for location/branch/path/MC-DC criteria, and synthesizes inputs; a greedy subset-cover heuristic minimizes generated tests. BlueCov takes JBMC’s JSON goals, instruments bytecode with ASM 6 using bytecode indices, records hits in an in-memory map, persists them with MapDB and uses a JVM shutdown hook. A FloatTools.sign example maps nine goals to three existing tests, then uses a NaN input to reach otherwise apparently dead code and complete coverage. The implementation discusses Java interfaces, erased generics, modeled JCL functions, exceptional termination, Maven integration and the difference between source lines and bytecode goals.
    - number: JBMC location coverage generates 9 goals for FloatTools.sign
    - number: 3 existing tests before augmentation
    - number: NaN test reaches previously uncovered goal 9
    - number: ASM 6 instrumentation
    - limits: Coverage is defined by JBMC’s bytecode model, so model/library approximations can differ from deployed JVM behavior; unsupported or nondeterministically modeled JCL functions may reduce precision. Test generation is NP-hard subset cover approximated greedily and object construction is proprietary/outside the paper. BlueCov records coverage rather than percentages, and persistence depends on shutdown-hook execution. The work demonstrates tool integration and one small example, not proof that generated tests establish functional correctness or broad industrial scalability.

- Candle: A Verified Implementation of HOL Light (2022)
    - what: A HOL Light-like interactive theorem prover whose soundness theorem reaches from higher-order-logic inference rules through source/kernel/REPL/compiler to modeled machine-code execution. Exported statements on a dedicated kernel-controlled channel must encode derivable HOL sequents and contexts. Implements runtime compilation of user declarations using CakeML Eval,with safety and datatype-protection proofs in HOL4. Combines a prior verified HOL kernel with whole-program simulation preserving soundness-critical values,syntactic restrictions that protect constructors/references/export channels,an interactively verified Eval-based REPL,and in-logic compilation. Distinguishes unverified user-customized display/input behavior from a verified invertible theorem-export format. Shows actual HOL Light-style sessions and documents incompatible language/library features and required wrappers.
    - limits: Top theorem is conditional on repl_ready_to_run:the generated code is installed in the prescribed machine state with correct entry point and FFI setup,plus other compiler/runtime premises hidden in that predicate. It is a theorem about machine_sem with basis_ffi,not a proof of physical processor/OS behavior or arbitrary binary loading. Guarantee concerns special kernel_ffi events. Ordinary stdout can contain any theorem-looking string;pretty printing is customizable and mostly unverified. Only the protected export,which includes a recoverable context and sequent,has the stated semantic guarantee. Logical result is THM ctxt th:derivability in the encoded HOL calculus relative to a context,connected through prior kernel/semantic soundness work. It does not establish that a human’s intended theorem was faithfully parsed/formalized or that arbitrary printed prose is true. Safe declarations cannot directly call protected constructors or kernel FFI,and cannot obtain writable kernel references;pattern matching and kernel-function calls are allowed. Runtime checks,environment/type-stamp freshness and valid-state invariants protect this boundary. Unrestricted native code/unsafe operations are not granted to arbitrary users. REPL theorem rules out Fail,meaning a stuck/type-error behavior in the formal semantics. It does not guarantee termination,successful compilation of every declaration,absence of exceptions,resource sufficiency or eventual theorem production. Compiler refinement permits early resource-limit exits. REPL functional input-output correctness is deliberately not proved. A parser,quote filter or pretty-printer could choose the wrong intended statement while the exported formal sequent remains sound. Verifying safety suffices for this soundness theorem,but not for full user-interface equivalence. Eval is integrated into CakeML compiler/proofs but not typeable in the source type system used to validate user code;users therefore cannot mention Eval. Its detailed verification is deferred to another publication. Current top-level proof uses interactive reasoning rather than ordinary whole-REPL type inference. 2022 HOL Light library port is incomplete. Some record-using files omitted;open/include unsupported,polymorphic comparison/hash rewritten or removed,value restriction affects code,and parser needs explicit arguments in let rec. No drop-in compatibility/completeness theorem or performance study is reported. Proofs developed in HOL4 depend on the correctness of the host prover and formal logic/machine/compiler/FFI models. The paper uses prior kernel,CakeML compiler/type-inference/bootstrap results;it does not independently re-prove their entire development here.

- decentralized shielding (2022)
    - title: Shield Decentralization for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
    - what: Defines decentralized multi-agent shielding and decomposes a centralized DFA shield into per-agent shields that require no communication while preserving safety. The paper identifies two requirements for communication-free shields: Cartesian safe action sets so any combination of local choices is safe, and unambiguous local state transitions inferable from each agent’s label and action. Algorithm 1 starts from one safe joint action, greedily adds individual actions only when the induced Cartesian set is safe and next-state mapping remains unambiguous; Algorithms 2–3 compile these sets into transient and interface-compatible individual shields. Theorem 1 proves safety preservation for environments with all actions enabled. If the input shield is Cartesian and unambiguous, the result is maximally permissive; otherwise it is at least the trivial one-action solution. Gridworld experiments retain 22.07 of 23.30 average safe joint actions, and Q-learning obtains zero violations; a momentum particle task shows zero violations even under partial observability.
    - number: Theorem 1 safety preservation under E(s)=A
    - number: gridworld 23.30 centralized vs 22.07 decentralized safe joint actions
    - number: 2.5 million training steps, 240 agents, 10 seeds/configuration
    - number: particle shield 21.67 vs 20.81 average actions
    - limits: Safety depends on a correct environment abstraction, a centralized shield, and shared labels independently computable by every agent; theorem assumes E(s)=A. Decentralized synthesis is generally hard or undecidable, so the method decomposes an existing shield and makes order/arbitrary choices that affect permissiveness. State explosion is severe (71,130 gridworld and 170,348 particle shield states before reduction); asymmetric observations may lack a shared label set. Evaluation is simulated tabular Q-learning/DQN, not physical systems.

- Event monads in Isabelle (2022)
    - title: Compositional Verification of Interacting Systems Using Event Monads
    - what: Defines event monads, event systems and Hoare rules in Isabelle/HOL, then composes independently verified handlers into correctness results for distributed summation, a German cache-coherence model and real-time partition scheduling. An event monad returns a set of value/state/output-trace triples and a failure flag, supporting nondeterminism, state updates, signal, bind and while loops. Preconditions and postconditions can depend on traces; an append-only trace frame rule preserves prior output, unlike simply treating traces as arbitrary state. Event systems map events to handlers; unhandled events become environment output, while emitted handled events execute recursively in sequence. Separate inductive reachability and guaranteed-termination predicates support partial/total Hoare rules. Pair and indexed-array lifting rules preserve untouched subsystem properties. The MapReduce model proves that alldone implies the accumulated sum is correct. Cache-coherence proves an invariant ensuring exclusive access for arbitrary N clients. The scheduler case proves watchdog representation refinement, scheduler refinement, their product composition and a final tick-level specification. Both no-switch and next-tick/next-window/next-frame switching cases reuse the watchdog proof.
    - number: 8948 total implementation/example lines
    - number: 1131 foundations; 726 MapReduce; 1261 cache coherence
    - number: 2572 watchdog lines reused by both scheduler versions
    - number: 723 no-switch scheduler; 2265 switching scheduler/system
    - limits: Interactions send events without waiting for immediate replies; all output events may be placed at function end. Handlers and the recursive event-dispatch semantics execute sequentially, so this is not a general concurrent interleaving or network-failure model. Unhandled events are delegated to the environment. Termination must be proved for recursive event chains and loops; MapReduce permits a server to skip progress forever and proves correctness conditional on alldone, not eventual completion. RTOS verification is at design level: parts resemble C, but AutoCorres C translation is not used; the concrete doubly-linked watchdog is abstracted to a list/array of relative deadlines. Case studies demonstrate functional correctness/refinement, not measured end-to-end implementation performance, schedulability for arbitrary workloads, or spatial separation of an entire OS.

- Felli-Montali-Winkler CTL-star DDSA (2022)
    - title: CTL* model checking for data-aware dynamic systems with arithmetic
    - what: Introduces a finite-history-constraint abstraction and CTL*f model-checking procedure for data-aware dynamic systems with arithmetic (DDSAs), synthesizing initial-variable conditions for branching-time properties. The procedure recursively reduces CTL* subformulas to LTL checks over configuration maps, computes history constraints with quantifier elimination, and terminates when finitely many constraint formulas exist up to equivalence at the property quantifier depth. This criterion yields decidability for rational/real monotonicity constraints and integer periodicity constraints, while a two-counter-machine reduction proves feedback-free and bounded-lookback systems remain undecidable for branching time. The ada prototype accepts DDSA or bounded Data Petri Net models, calls CVC5/Z3, returns configuration maps and product graphs, and reports detailed SMT counts and runtimes on mined and normative business processes.

- FLAQR availability and integrity types (2022)
    - title: Applying consensus and replication securely with FLAQR
    - what: FLAQR is a typed core calculus for composing confidentiality, integrity, and availability policies around remote evaluation, equality comparison, and replicated choice. The paper gives paper proofs of blame soundness, a conditional majority-quorum failure bound, and noninterference; it does not verify a concurrently executing Paxos or PBFT implementation. The substantive addition is a principal algebra with availability authority and partial conjunction/disjunction, plus a fails judgment that follows failures through nested protected types. Quorums arise by composing compare and select rather than being a special type-system parameter. Blame constraints connect an observed failed comparison to possible faulty principal sets. These are language metatheory results in a sequential global stack model, with two worked banking programs rather than an implementation benchmark.

    - what: Formalizes a generalized divergence theorem for rectangular boxes in Lean/mathlib using a distortion-controlled gauge integral (GP). This avoids assuming integrability of each individual partial derivative. The GP theorem transfers to the Bochner integral when divergence is integrable, then yields Cauchy–Goursat and Cauchy integral formulas for Banach-valued complex functions, including countable exceptional differentiability sets. Describes reusable integration infrastructure and proof-design tradeoffs. Records actual derivative/continuity/integrability distinctions, exceptional sets, domain and Banach-space restrictions, partition/filter nontriviality, four integral parameter settings, box-additive abstraction and choice, totalized integrals, proof chain through annulus and disk to analyticity, displayed corollaries, code presentation caveats, and unfinished extensions.

The GP partial-derivative theorem assumes Fréchet differentiability within the closed box outside a countable set and continuity within at exceptional points. Summing diagonal components gives divergence. No separate derivative integrability hypothesis is needed for GP, but full differentiability is stronger than existence of partial derivatives alone. §§3.3,4.10–4.11: The Bochner conclusion additionally requires Bochner-integrable divergence, continuity on the closed box, and differentiability in its interior outside a countable set. Exhausting the interior by smaller boxes removes differentiability requirements on the boundary; a≤b permits degenerate boxes, with both sides zero. The informal Theorem8 says continuity on an open-closed I, but displayed integral_divergence explicitly assumes continuity_on f (Icc a b); retain the formal closed-box condition. §§1–2: Domain shape is rectangular; no theorem for arbitrary elementary regions is formalized here. The comparison with Abdulaziz–Paulson Isabelle Green is the author’s: that result allows broader plane domains and only partial derivatives, while this result allows higher finite dimensions/Banach codomains and weaker derivative regularity. Neither formalization subsumes the other. No independent source-to-source comparison was performed. §3: Gauge δ is point-dependent; Henstock tags belong to their own closed subbox. Riemann uses a constant gauge; McShane allows tags outside their own box but inside the ambient closed box. GP further bounds partition distortion, with its gauge permitted to depend on that bound. Ordinary multidimensional Henstock–Kurzweil/Fubini-compatible generalizations cannot integrate every divergence, motivating the different integral. §3.1: The one-dimensional Henstock–Kurzweil definition and derivative FTC are explanatory background. The author explicitly did not formalize a separate one-dimensional interface; a wrapper over the R¹ box integral is future/easy work, not an existing wrapper demonstrated here. §4.1: Boxes are nonempty products (lower_i,upper_i] with strict coordinate bounds, making partitions disjoint and endpoints uniquely recoverable. Empty boxes use with_bot; intersections and bounding-box joins form a lattice. Face coordinates use fin.succ_above, with distinct front/back embeddings. Degenerate domains enter later through the generalized theorem, not the box structure. §§4.2–4.3: One prepartition structure plus is_partition predicate permits shared operations and filter lemmas. The author is unsure about this design because proofs must carry the predicate. Tags are total functions on all boxes to avoid membership proof arguments. Extending structures does not automatically inherit namespace lemmas, so one-line wrapper definitions/lemmas are repeated. §4.4: Cousin’s lemma guarantees subordinate tagged partitions, preventing vacuous integral limits. Nested center splits produce homothetic boxes with the original distortion; a common point and positive gauge give a contradiction. Refining each box and merging preserves union/distortion. These existence results ensure GP filters are nontrivial, rather than merely defining an unrestricted limit. §4.5: Three booleans encode constant-gauge, Henstock-tag and distortion requirements. Riemann=(true,true,false), Henstock=(false,true,false), McShane=(false,false,false), GP=(false,true,true). Filter bases additionally require a complementary prepartition of bounded distortion when applicable. This condition is trivial for full partitions; the author includes it to avoid an extra c>1 side lemma for partial partitions. The design proves common lemmas uniformly but is difficult to extend to other integrals. §4.6: Box additivity means partition sums equal the whole-box value, either globally or on subboxes. Additivity for binary coordinate splits suffices via common hyperplane refinements. Measures, integrals, and upper-minus-lower face integrals instantiate this interface. Complement partitions are obtained by classical choice, not an extraction of an executable partition algorithm. §4.7: The integral is a selected filter limit if integrable and zero otherwise. Therefore an equation involving its value alone is not an existence proof; has_integral/integrable premises matter. Integration supports continuous-linear-map-valued box-additive volumes, but the project uses only measure-scaled vectors; the author calls the unused generality possible overengineering. §4.8: Henstock–Sacks estimates control sums on partial partitions covering the same union, with error ε1+ε2, or compare a partial sum with a sum of subbox integrals within ε. The convergence gauge packages hypotheses. This yields restriction to subboxes and box additivity uniformly across the four integral settings. §4.9 proof: Differentiability gives a local linearization error controlled by ε times box volume at fixed distortion. At countably many exceptional points, continuity permits summably allocated local errors κ(x), whose sum is <ε/2. This is a countable-point exception, not arbitrary almost-everywhere differentiability or a null-set exception without further hypotheses. §4.10 proof: Bochner→McShane starts with measurable indicators, extends to simple functions, proves invariance under changes on measure-zero sets, and approximates an integrable function by simple functions. The displayed transfer theorem uses a locally finite measure and bRiemann=false; it does not imply every Bochner function is Riemann integrable or conversely characterize Bochner integrability. §5: Complex results use a complex Banach codomain with second-countable topology, required by this mathlib Bochner setup. Continuity on closed domains and complex differentiability off a countable interior set suffice. No continuous derivative assumption is introduced. Annulus results require 0<r≤R; center disk formula uses R>0; disk Cauchy theorem permits R≥0. §5 proof chain: A real vector field (−if,f) has zero divergence by Cauchy–Riemann, giving rectangular Cauchy–Goursat. Applying it to e^z f(c+e^z) on a logarithmic rectangle gives equality of annular circle integrals. Apply this to f(z)/(z−c) and shrink the inner radius for the center formula. Applying the center formula to (z−c)f(z) gives the disk theorem. A removable difference quotient gives the formula at arbitrary w, extended to exceptional w by continuity. Preserve these limits without claiming a kernel defect. §6: Other integral definitions permitting countable coordinate-hyperplane exceptions, multivariable complex analysis, arbitrary-domain Cauchy–Goursat, and Ilyashenko’s finite-limit-cycle theorem are plans rather than completed results here. - Hage et al. SMC4PEP (2022)
    - title: SMC4PEP: Stochastic Model Checking of Product Engineering Processes
    - what: Introduces SMC4PEP, which converts pool-based or event-based BPMN product-engineering processes into PRISM Markov Decision Processes, removing redundant processes and replacing cross-abstraction message flows with events to reduce model size while preserving stochastic, timing and reward analyses. The architecture has differentiator, converter and generator stages. The converter eliminates exactly identical processes, removes pools/message flows and inserts events; the generator builds one PRISM module list per diagram and adds timeline rewards. Two automotive OEM cases compare pBPMN and eBPMN models: event-based models reduce states/transitions substantially, including orders-of-magnitude reduction in the four-level case, though one build time increases. PRISM checks A-SPICE properties for deadlock freedom, objective fulfillment and conformance, plus minimum duration and expected cost. The authors explicitly acknowledge state-space explosion and rely on model minimization as future mitigation.
