- Holistic Verification of Blockchain Consensus (2022)
    - what: Parameterized model checking verifies binary Byzantine consensus associated with Red Belly Blockchain under n>3t and0≤f≤t. First verifies binary-value broadcast, then substitutes a smaller specification-based automaton into the outer consensus and checks safety and progress properties with ByMC. Agreement and validity do not require the added good-round fairness; termination does. The verified algorithm is the coordinator/timeout-free pseudocode variant under that fairness, rather than a proof of the deployed implementation or its partial-synchrony mechanism. Makes the decomposition concrete: global sent-message counters replace local receive counts; Byzantine effects lower enabling thresholds by f; four temporal broadcast properties support a replacement gadget; round communication closure reduces selected all-round LTL obligations to one-round checking. Manual meta-arguments connect per-superround invariants to global agreement/validity and good-round existence to eventual decision. Gives a fair-round definition, a nonterminating4-process trace, detailed automaton rules, explicit liveness preconditions and measured schema counts.
    - limits: Fixed n sequential processes communicate through reliable fully connected asynchronous point-to-point links; delays are finite but unbounded, steps interleave, each receive is atomic and sender identities distinguish quorum members. Up to t<n/3 are Byzantine; f≤t is the actual fault count. The threshold abstraction assumes faulty senders cannot impersonate arbitrarily many distinct processes. Communication closure is essential: each process uses only messages for its current round, discards earlier tags and buffers later tags. Monotone send counters and threshold guards admit the prior ByMC reduction. Guarantees do not automatically extend to arbitrary protocols with cross-round data dependencies, timing constraints or changing membership. Reliable communication is encoded by progress assumptions on enabled rules and source-location emptiness. This excludes scheduler executions that indefinitely withhold enabled productive actions. Added consensus fairness is different: some round r has every correct process first deliver r mod2 in that round’s binary-value broadcast. Neither fairness follows from asynchronous reliability alone. Algorithm1 is the DBFT variant without coordinator/timeouts. The second DBFT variant uses partial synchrony, but this paper replaces that mechanism with a good-round assumption. It does not prove a synchronizer, coordinator rotation, timeout correctness or that the deployed environment enforces the assumption. Threshold models describe correct processes and abstract Byzantine influence with f-offset guards; global send counters abstract possible local receipt histories. Parameterized checking ranges over symbolic parameters satisfying n>3t≥3f, rather than testing a list of network sizes. Soundness still depends on faithful manual abstraction and ByMC’s reductions/SMT checks. Inner broadcast verification establishes justification,obligation,uniformity and termination. Replacement must preserve all behaviors relevant to the outer consumer because contestants is shared and the outer algorithm can proceed before the broadcast finishes. The paper argues this and supplies encoded preconditions; it is not a machine-checked source-to-source refinement of production code. ByMC handles a restricted LTL fragment and one-round systems. Cross-superround agreement,initial validity and existential good-round termination require manually chosen intermediate formulas and mathematical composition arguments. The model checker does not directly discharge each final quantified formula as written. The proof covers binary agreement,validity and eventual decision for the displayed algorithm. It does not prove blockchain transaction semantics,multi-value reduction,ledger consistency across all block heights,network/cryptographic code,resource bounds or end-to-end behavior of the deployed Red Belly software. Processes continue participating after deciding so others can finish; only the first decision matters.     - title: Inferring Invariants with Quantifier Alternations: Taming the Search Space Explosion
    - what: Presents a PDR/IC3 invariant-inference algorithm that learns first-order invariants with quantifier alternations. It lifts quantifier-prefix choice to the inductive-generalization level for parallel breadth-first search, introduces k-term pseudo-DNF (k-pDNF) matrices, and combines EPR restrictions, incremental SMT, multi-block generalization and heuristic may-proof-obligations. The IG procedure partitions prefix space into categories/workers, orders prefixes by quantifier depth/alternations/universals/existentials, shares constraints only from immediate sub-prefixes, and interleaves separation with SMT checks of Init and relative inductiveness. k-pDNF represents a negated cube followed by up to k−1 cubes, expressing implication-shaped Paxos lemmas more compactly than CNF/DNF. The complete P-Fol-Ic3 algorithm has learning and heuristic tasks, optional EPR edge restrictions, and solver robustness via restarts, parallel Z3/CVC5, and incremental assertions. Evaluation covers 30 safe distributed-protocol problems, including Paxos variants, with ablations for pDNF, EPR, incremental SMT and multi-block generalization.
    - number: 30 benchmark problems
    - number: 5 trials per algorithm; 16 threads, 20 GiB RAM, 6-hour timeout
    - number: paxos-epr 920 s (5/5), flexible-paxos-epr 418 s (5/5), multi-paxos-epr 4272 s (4/5)
    - number: k=1 universal and k=3 non-universal pDNF settings
    - limits: Benchmarks are safe transition systems with known human invariants; inference success is not a refutation method for unsafe systems. EPR requires a user-provided acyclic set of allowed sort/function edges, and prenex separation may need a special push-down mode. Full FOL search can be intractable; the method failed vertical-paxos-epr and several hardest cases, and stochastic parallelism yields variable success. Experiments use fixed 6-hour timeouts and 16 threads/20 GiB; performance and learned lemmas depend on solver behavior, random seeds and prefix restrictions.

- IPA compositional TLA+ checking (2022)
    - title: Compositional Model Checking of Consensus Protocols Specified in TLA+ via Interaction-Preserving Abstraction
    - what: Introduces Interaction-Preserving Abstraction (IPA) for compositional checking of TLA+ consensus specifications. Actions are partitioned into modules, dependency/interaction variables are identified, internal actions are abstracted, and each module is checked in a context formed from abstractions of the others. Strong refinement proves that passing all compositional checks implies refinement of the original specification to the abstract one. IPA defines recursive dependency and interaction-variable sets and four abstraction constraints: abstract dependencies cannot use other modules’ locals; interaction updates depend only on interaction/dependency variables; abstract locals avoid other-module locals; and every externally visible action has a mapped abstract action preserving effects. A strong action mapping is used because ordinary refinement does not record correspondence of omitted actions. Case studies identify polling, centralized control-flow and brute-force replacement of performance optimizations as practical patterns. Raft is split into PreVote, Vote and Replication; ParallelRaft merges Replication into LeaderRecovery when it offers little abstraction. The theorem composes per-module refinements into S⇒A.

    - number: ParallelRaft ratio 1.9–3.1
    - number: 3 servers
    - limits: The framework checks finite-state safety invariants and explicitly excludes liveness. Correctness assumes the abstract specification already passed model checking, and module/interaction-variable classification and strong refinement mappings are manually supplied or checked; TLC checks only ordinary refinement. The PRaft specification is confidential. Experiments use three servers and bounded term/command parameters, so measured ratios do not establish unbounded protocol scalability.

- Jaakkola polyadic Boolean modal logic (2022)
    - title: Complexity of Polyadic Boolean Modal Logics: Model Checking and Satisfiability
    - what: Studies complexity of satisfiability and combined model checking for polyadic modal logic with relation permutations and Boolean operators (negation, intersection). It proves ExpTime-completeness for PML(¬), ExpTime-completeness for PML^c(p,s,¬,∩) when the accessibility vocabulary is bounded by a constant c, and PTime-completeness for combined model checking of PML(p,s,¬,∩). The paper defines k-ary relation terms, cyclic/swap permutations, Boolean operations, k-tables, and their Kripke semantics. For PML(¬), it gives a polynomial reduction replacing R and ¬R by fresh relations R1,R2 plus a coverage formula η, then reconstructs a model with a two-copy domain. For bounded-vocabulary full Boolean polyadic logic, Lemma 11 first converts modalities to table terms; formulas ξ1–ξ3 force table coverage and closure under permutations, after which a layered domain W×{2,…,m}×N reconstructs a model. The PTime model-checking proof normalizes negations to leading form, evaluates relation terms as polynomial-size sets, and uses a subformula-labeling algorithm with pointer enumeration for complemented relations.

PML+global-diamond ExpTime-completeness is imported through a guarded-forward-fragment translation. The model-checking result concerns explicit finite relational structures and formulas, not distributed protocols or infinite-state verification.

    - what: The official five-page Appendix A supplies case-study training, rectangular verification domains, partition widths, model/policy architectures and two illustrative 100-step simulations. These additions make the learned-model experiments more concrete; they do not resolve the main account's printed controller-optimality proof concerns, establish exact numerical certificate checking, or transfer the model certificate to physical dynamics. Source spans S1–S5 preserve every appendix page, including Tables2–4, Figures2–4 and Equations11–12.  A.1 trains Pendulum/Cartpole models for up to300epochs with early stopping and5,000–50,000points as depth increases. Pendulum has1–5hiddenlayers of64neurons, training angle±π and angularvelocity±1, safeangle±π/15, initialangle±π/36, actuator±1. Thus the supplement strengthens the need to distinguish an abstract NN state-box guarantee from physical Acrobot safety.     - title: Towards the Combination of Model Checking and Runtime Verification on Multi-Agent Systems
    - what: Combines static model checking of decidable MAS submodels with runtime monitors for residual strategic/temporal properties, returning conclusive or inconclusive partial results even when full ATL* checking is undecidable. - Modular Formal Verification of Rust Programs with Unsafe Blocks (2022)
    - what: # Modular Formal Verification of Rust Programs with Unsafe Blocks (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Nima Rahimi Foroushaani and Bart Jacobs, December 2022 technical report, arXiv:2212.12976v1. This is a proposal and early VeriFast implementation for checking unsafe Rust using modular symbolic execution and RustBelt semantic types. The demonstrated prototype verifies one small allocation example. A soundness proof relating successful execution to RustBelt, general generics, and panic safety remain future work. Its worked Cell proof explains an intended resource discipline; the literal Rust listing also omits UnsafeCell, an important source-language qualification (Q1,Q2,Q10,Q11,Q12,R1).  ## Reading and evidence scope  Read the whole 23-page PDF: cover, abstract/contents, printed pages1–22, sections1–7, Appendix A, all13 bibliography entries, all13 listings, three figures and the six-row Table1. No numbered theorem, completed soundness proof, benchmark-results table or checklist appears. Figures1/2 show concrete/symbolic execution trees; Figure3 is a screenshot whose code and “0 errors found (28 statements verified)” message were read in its page18 render. Individual page renders inspected:9,11,16,17,18,22,23. Appendix listings12/13 are clipped at the right edge in the PDF itself; their visible text was read, without claiming recovery of missing characters. References were read as entries, not recursively followed.  Acquired the paper-linked Zenodo7472607 v0.1.0 record and its7,879,059-byte Git bundle; checked published MD5 and pinned ref rust-tr-drop at58197015846357c14553fd514a3d357abaee378a. Inventoried1,861 Git-tree entries through static object inspection. Retained eight plaintext assets. Seven were read whole: repository README, soundness.md, frontend Readme, exporter toolchain/Cargo configuration,217-line rust_fe.ml and alloc.rs. Read translator lines400–505 and735–965, plus selected search hits; this is not a whole1,316-line translator or repository audit. Manifest hashes/Git blobs identify the exact files. The current official Rust UnsafeCell documentation was consulted for its introductory and aliasing paragraphs; it is2026 documentation, not a pinned2022 language definition. Other documentation sections, repository files, experiments and cited papers were not read. No author code was executed/imported, checker/solver invoked, or model/checkpoint/serialized experiment data loaded.  ## What the proposed verification means  The input is assumed already type- and borrow-checked. User separation-logic contracts, ghost commands and lemmas complement obligations extracted from Rust types. The aim is to check unsafe implementations against their safe interfaces, so safe callers can rely on ownership, validity and borrowing guarantees. The report's “Our target claim” explicitly quantifies over all safe abstractions and the unsafe hierarchy behind them; §6.1 then proposes proving the checker sound or generating function-specific Iris proofs. These are intended guarantees, not completed meta-theorems of this prototype (Q1,Q9,Q12).  The distinction between a valid address and a valid Rust value is concrete. Listing3 dereferences null; its other function overwrites an inner mutable reference with null without directly accessing unallocated memory. That operation corrupts the reference's type invariant and can make later safe code fail. Thus tracking allocation alone cannot establish Rust safety (Q3). The paper's UB examples and safety ambitions do not exhaust every Rust validity, aliasing or concurrency rule.  ## Modular symbolic execution and the deque example  An execution state consists of a variable store, owned heap chunks and persistent path facts. An allocation may abort through handle_alloc_error or yield aligned allocated memory. Fresh fields carry an uninitialized marker; reading that marker causes verification to get stuck. Figures1/2 contrast arbitrarily many concrete allocation addresses with two symbolic cases, null and nonnull. This is an explanatory abstraction argument, not a measured path-reduction result (Q4,Q5).  The create_deque example allocates a sentinel Node, writes its prev/next pointers to itself and leaves value uninitialized. Heap predicates separately own allocation and fields. A write needs a matching owned chunk; a successful write updates its value. The postcondition transfers all allocation/field chunks and nonnullness to the caller. At calls, the checker consumes the precondition and produces the postcondition rather than repeatedly executing the callee body. Consuming ownership prevents duplicating permission when transferring resources. Empty residual heap in this example accounts for all chunks; this does not establish that every Rust program must be leak-free (Q4–Q6).  The raw-pointer-only deque has little type-induced interface information. Safe abstractions need stronger semantic types: check the implementation from the resources its parameter types provide and reestablish the interface resources at return. Although §3.3 describes weakest-precondition/strongest-postcondition ideals, the method uses user contracts; it does not automatically infer maximally precise contracts or eliminate the need to justify lemmas (Q6,Q7).  ## RustBelt resources and the worked Cell outline  RustBelt interprets a type by its size, ownership predicate and sharing predicate. Shared-reference ownership refers to the pointee's sharing predicate, so sharing a Cell can have a different logical meaning from sharing an ordinary immutable integer. The Cell example uses a thread-dependent non-atomic persistent borrow. Its lifetime token, with a positive fraction at most1, witnesses the borrow is live; the thread's non-atomic token controls access in that thread. Opening a borrow supplies writable resources together with an obligation to restore them before reclaiming the tokens (Q8).  Table1's six rows show the intended sequence: initial reference/lifetime/thread resources; unfold shared-reference ownership; unfold Cell sharing; invoke the lifetime access rule; write the new integer; close the borrow and recover tokens. The token discipline prevents ending a lifetime while borrowed resources remain outstanding. The authors omit details, including representation of local variables as owned pointers, and present the table as an outline. It is neither a complete mechanized Cell proof nor a verified Rust-library result of the demonstrated prototype (Q8,Q9).  There is a separate source-language problem. Listing2 stores a plain i32, obtains a mutable raw pointer from &self.value and writes through it. It declares !Sync and does not expose deep references. The authors conclude “The usage of unsafe code in Cell library is sound” (Q2), reasoning about race avoidance. Current official Rust documentation says “Mutating that data, for example through an alias or by transmuting a &T into a &mut T, is considered undefined behavior” and “All other types that allow internal mutability, such as Cell<T> and RefCell<T>, internally use UnsafeCell to wrap their data” (R1). A single-thread restriction alone does not grant permission to mutate shared plain-i32 storage under these documented rules. Accordingly, preserve the authors' intended RustBelt-style Cell resource model but do not present the literal Listing2/6 as valid production Rust. This is static source/documentation comparison, not a compiler/Miri experiment or a proof about the historical prototype's acceptance. The current documentation itself says precise aliasing rules remain in flux; the core immutability/UnsafeCell distinction is explicit (R1).  Appendix A labels its examples “intended” encoding and translation. Listing12 writes self.value under &self with a comment invoking an unsafe superpower; this is illustrative code rather than ordinary compilable Rust. Listing13 introduces abstract lifetime/thread/borrow predicates and bodyless access/closing lemma declarations. Those declarations express obligations and trusted rules to implement/justify; their presence is not a proof of those rules or evidence that the prototype generated and checked this translation (Q14).  ## Prototype, artifact and trust boundary  The architecture invokes the official compiler frontend for type/borrow checking, extracts MIR and annotations through Cap'n Proto, then translates into VeriFast's C AST and separation logic. MIR supplies explicit control flow while retaining type information. Reusing the frontend helps source correspondence; it does not prove the MIR-to-C translation preserves Rust semantics. Contracts for allocation/library operations, translation, type encoding, VeriFast and its solver remain relevant trust assumptions (Q10).  At publication, the authors report support for a “very limited subset of Rust.” They demonstrate alloc.rs allocating one u8, checking allocation failure, writing42, testing the impossible branch *p!=42, and deallocating. The unreachable branch contains two deallocations. Its acceptance would show path-sensitive exclusion of that branch under the example's assumptions, not acceptance of a reachable double-free or general exception safety. The paper screenshot reports28 statements verified, not a benchmark score, runtime or reader reproduction. No additional verified Cell/deque/library suite is reported here (Q11,C1).  The pinned translator agrees with the admitted limits: Layout::new becomes sizeof; pointer is_null becomes comparison with zero; other generic functions hit an unsupported case. Type translation handles Layout specially, rejects nonempty tuple types in the inspected branch and rejects generic lifetime/constant arguments. The call translator follows the ordinary destination, and Resume is explicitly unsupported. These inspected regions support limited functionality, not a claim that every source path was audited. The frontend is tied to nightly2022-01-31 and explicitly takes only the first decoded Cap'n Proto message. No serialized message was loaded during this read (C2–C5).  The pinned backend soundness document states “VeriFast does not check that the program obeys strict aliasing rules” for its C verification claim, and lists known issues. Its C-compiler caveats do not automatically establish a bug in this Rust example. They do explain why translating Rust into an accepted C AST cannot, without further justification, discharge Rust's distinct shared-reference rules. No claim is made that every listed C/Java unsoundness affects this Rust path (C6).  ## Panic safety and evaluation limits  Listing9's swap_nonoverlapping contract is explicitly hypothetical. Listing10 demonstrates unsafe temporary state in BinaryHeap::sift_up and a comparison that may panic. Listing11 exposes a MIR unwind successor, motivating analysis of exceptional paths. However, MaybeUninit::<T>::zeroed().assume_init() already creates an invalid value when all-zero bytes are invalid for T; this example's risks cannot all be attributed to later unwinding. §6.2 leaves the exact necessary post-panic checks and RustBelt extension as future work. There is no timing comparison, benchmark population, proof-size study, RustBelt derivation count or controlled usability experiment.     - title: Lifted Model Checking for Relational MDPs
    - what: Introduces pCTL-REBEL, a lifted probabilistic model checker for relational Markov decision processes that reasons over first-order abstract states instead of grounding all objects, and proves decidability for state-bounded infinite domains via finite abstract RMDPs and probabilistic bisimulation. The paper defines OI-subsumption relational states, grounding semantics, relational pCTL including next and bounded/unbounded until, and a relational Bellman operator whose V and Q rules store probabilities rather than rewards. Logical regression, Q-rule combination, V-rule maximization and three mutually recursive Check/CheckUntil/CheckNext algorithms implement lifted checking, including absorbing goals and state-bound filtering. Theorem 1 proves that an abstract RMDP for a state-bounded infinite model is probabilistically bisimilar for a formula, so checking the finite abstraction is equivalent to checking the infinite MDP. Worked blocks-world regressions and nested formulas expose rule construction. The unoptimized SWI-Prolog prototype checks infinite blocks/box worlds and compares against PRISM/STORM; pCTL-REBEL handles 15 blocks (6.6e13 ground states) under 1800 seconds while PRISM explicit handles 8 and STORM sparse 9, but indefinite-horizon checking grows exponentially and road-map constraints cause runtime explosions.

    - what: Adds parallel execution to the Isabelle Refinement Framework and generates verified LLVM. A parallel introsort/pdqsort-style algorithm is proved total-correct and benchmarked against C++. The memory model uses never-reused blocks, so use-after-free and allocation conflicts are detectable. The M-monad invariant requires consistency and an execution avoiding every finite forbidden block set. The disjoint concurrency rule composes Hoare triples; with_split and npar refine independent list subcomputations to same-array disjoint slices. Parallel psort partitions, falls back when depth/size is small or partition is unbalanced, and uses median-of-64 sampling. The final theorem states in-place return of the original pointer and sorted-permutation contents. Generated LLVM is instantiated for uint64 and strings. Figure 2 compares verified, std::sort(par-unseq), and Boost sample_sort over many distributions on laptop/server; Figure 3 shows speedup versus core count. Results are comparable on laptop integers, slower for server strings and highly parallel speedup. The semantics and generated LLVM text remain within an explicit trust boundary: Isabelle’s kernel, the shallow LLVM embedding and the code generator are trusted, and parallel execution uses an external C++ TBB primitive.

- SPsCGF model testing (2022)
    - title: Improve Model Testing by Integrating Bounded Model Checking and Coverage Guided Fuzzing
    - what: Presents SPsCGF, a two-stage test-generation workflow for Simulink/Ptolemy control models: CBMC bounded symbolic execution supplies initial seeds, then coverage-guided fuzzing mutates signal inputs using signal-pattern operators. The implementation translates models through an intermediate representation to C/C++ drivers and measures coverage. The paper explains why indirect time-series effects defeat symbolic execution (an ONDLC shutdown model can yield 2^n combinations while only one signal pattern reaches the target), and why ordinary fuzzing creates irregular signals. SPsCGF combines CBMC branch/MC/DC seeds, an efficient dynamic-programming n-wise generator for constant ports, seed selection based on half-flipped conditions, and time/signal mutation operators. It supports nonlinear elements by executing generated raw code and directly embeds complex Simulink code in the IR. Experiments compare SPsCGF, raw coverage-guided fuzzing, SimCoTest, and Simulink Design Verifier across benchmark and industrial vehicle-control models.

    - title: Specification and Verification With the TLA+ Trifecta: TLC, Apalache, and TLAPS
    - what: Uses a TLA+ specification of asynchronous termination detection and Safra's ring algorithm to demonstrate complementary verification with TLC explicit-state checking, Apalache bounded/SMT and inductive-invariant checking, and TLAPS theorem proving, including refinement from the algorithm to a high-level state machine. The high-level module specifies active nodes, pending messages, termination detection, safety, liveness under weak fairness, and quiescence. TLC finds 4,097 states for N=4,K=3 in the abstract model and 1.3 million (N=3,K=C=3,Q=9) or 219 million (N=4 with same bounds) in the algorithm model, exposing state explosion and a token-color bug. Apalache checks bounded prefixes, proves an inductive invariant for N=100 in 20 seconds, and checks quiescence for N=100 in 11 seconds. Refinement is checked for small N; TLAPS proves type, safety, liveness, and refinement for arbitrary instances, with an invariant proof taking about 230 lines and liveness/refinement about 245 lines. The conclusion recommends TLC first, Apalache for inductive invariants, TLC/random exploration for liveness, then TLAPS for higher confidence.

Functional proof assumes modeled persistence behavior; experiment does not validate actual power-failure retention of physical FRAM. §7.1.3: Host supplies timestamps; nondecreasing checks reject rewind but do not establish real elapsed time or trustworthy clock. Audit deliberately reveals last timestamp and helps detect future-code requests. Equal timestamps are allowed by the less-than test. TOTP cryptographic security relies on chosen functional algorithms, not a new proof of SHA1/HMAC security. §8.1: Computational security requires efficient emulator so it cannot justify a key leak by factoring/brute force. Knox does not formalize/check efficiency: manual audit supplies this obligation. Case emulators reportedly use at most one spec query per circuit cycle and roughly equivalent computation. Do not describe whole cryptographic result as fully mechanically checked. §8.2: Specs deterministic; true hardware randomness unsupported. Stateful CSPRNG plus explicit host seed/add-entropy operation is proposed compatible design, not a fourth demonstrated/verified case. §8.3: Permitted leakage can be made explicit as spec leak operation; functional equivalence need not be checked for that adversary-only operation. Enlarging allowed leakage changes guarantee and needs policy review. §8.4: Monolithic proof avoids intermediate ISA specs and proves only particular HSM program/circuit behavior. Scaling to sophisticated CPUs/crypto is unresolved; no public-key signatures in three simple cases. Delayed fixed worst-case response with separate correctness/WCET reasoning is a future proposal. §9: Noninterference/declassification/secure-compilation comparisons concern formulations described by authors. Their limitations do not establish impossibility for all generalized information-flow or simulation frameworks. No direct distributed-protocol, Rust/Verus/TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment. §7.2: Single-threaded verification timings on one older CPU; no distribution of proof time or independent reproduction. Implementation latency at12MHz/2Mbaud, no confidence intervals/run count given. Claimed interactive suitability is author interpretation. Originality/relative-simplicity comparisons not independently surveyed.

- VPN polynomial-network verification (2022)
    - title: Sound and Complete Verification of Polynomial Networks
    - what: Presents VPN, a branch-and-bound verifier for polynomial networks using alpha-convexification to obtain global lower bounds and convergence guarantees. VPN exploits low-rank polynomial-network structure, interval bound propagation, Hessian lower bounds, a power method for spectral-radius estimates, and uniform or non-uniform diagonal shifts. It recursively splits the widest input interval; projected gradient descent gives an adversarial upper bound, while the convexified objective gives a sound lower bound. Branch-and-bound terminates with global verification under the stated assumptions. Experiments compare VPN with Gurobi, IBP, and DeepT-Fast on MNIST, CIFAR10, and STL10, including degree 2–7 networks and 96×96 images.
    - number: MNIST 2×16 VPN 1.43–1.78 s per listed epsilon
    - number: CIFAR10 VPN about 0.92–1.03 s for 2×16
    - number: STL10 VPN 1.39–5.06 s versus Gurobi out of memory
    - number: degree 2–7 MNIST bounds
    - limits: The method targets twice-differentiable polynomial networks and uses finite input boxes, bounded Hessian estimates, and a time-limited practical search. PGD alone is not a certificate; soundness comes from convex lower bounds and branch-and-bound, while timeout leaves instances unresolved. Black-box QP solvers scale poorly in input dimension and degree. Higher-degree/deeper architectures and other functions remain future work.

- ZonoDual (2022)
    - title: Zonotope Domains for Lagrangian Neural Network Verification
    - what: Introduces ZonoDual, combining zonotopic intermediate bounds with Lagrangian decomposition to produce tighter lower bounds for ReLU-network verification. The paper formulates verification with duplicated layer variables and dual equality multipliers, replacing independent hyperboxes by zonotopes that preserve neuron dependencies. A zonotopic ReLU program is equivalent to two-layer verification and NP-hard; coordinate partitioning gives tractable relaxations, with exact 2-D candidates computable in near-linear generator time. ZonoDual initializes DeepZ/IBP bounds, performs GPU-friendly 2-D dual ascent, optionally merges later partitions into MIP subproblems, and retains valid lower-bound guarantees. Stagewise use of tighter boxes further improves zonotopes.
    - number: 2-D zonotope evaluation O(dm) after O(dm log m) preprocessing
    - number: 2-D zonotope has 2m vertices
    - number: CIFAR network 6,244 ReLUs/4 layers
    - number: MNIST-Deep 5,196 neurons/6 layers
    - limits: The core setting is scalar feedforward affine/ReLU networks and axis-aligned input boxes; the method is an incomplete bound procedure, not complete verification. Weak duality and sound pushforward bounds are required. Higher-dimensional ReLU programs need MIP or another incomplete solver, and stagewise optimization has substantial memory/parallel cost. Reported experiments are MNIST/CIFAR-10 networks and compare bounds, not end-to-end branch-and-bound completion.

- A Formal Proof of Modal Completeness for Provability Logic (2021)
    - what: HOL Light deep embedding of Gödel–Löb provability logic (GL) proves soundness and modal completeness for nonempty finite irreflexive transitive Kripke frames. Finite duplicate-free maximal consistent formula lists replace an inappropriate infinite canonical construction, yielding finite countermodels without compactness. Polymorphic bisimulation transfers completeness from formula-list worlds to any infinite carrier type. A semantic MESON tactic proves some modal lemmas but fails even on the Löb axiom. Records object/meta-level distinction, frame endpoint constraints, transitive converse-well-founded semantics, theoremhood-only derivability,120lemma engineering effort, finite subformula extension and strict-box-growth accessibility, truth/valuation clauses, carrier-size condition and bisimulation variance. Separates formal theorem from incomplete tactic; concrete terminal/loop/infinite-chain/small-carrier/valuation examples expose exact assumptions.
    - limits: §§1.2/2, pp.4–6: classical polymorphic HOL Light with infinity and choice. Modal syntax is a separate inductive form datatype with string atoms and classical/Box constructors. Recursive holds interprets this object language under valuation V. Object provability is distinct from HOL theoremhood. The paper manually restores some type annotations omitted by the printer. §2.1, pp.5–6: frame (W,R) has a set W of carrier values and binary accessibility relation R. Box p at w checks every u in W with R w u. Frame validity quantifies all valuations and all worlds in W; class validity quantifies every frame in that class. Raw holds_in allows empty W and vacuous validity; nonempty worlds and relation endpoint constraints belong to the relevant frame classes. §2.2, pp.6–7: TRANSNT requires nonempty W, every R endpoint in W, transitivity and well-founded converse R (no infinite forward R chain). ITF requires nonempty finite W and irreflexive transitive R with those endpoint constraints; ITF_NT proves inclusion. TRANSNT_EQ_LOB characterizes transitive/converse-well-founded frames by validity of the Löb schema under the endpoint constraint. Finite world sets differ from infinite carrier types: the latter must accommodate arbitrary finite countermodel sizes. §3, pp.7–10: classical Hilbert axioms plus K: Box(A=>B)=>(Box A=>Box B), and Löb: Box(Box A=>A)=>Box A. GLproves closes axioms under modus ponens and necessitation of theorems. Derivability with assumption contexts is not formalized; the authors leave its necessitation restrictions and deduction theorem aside. Soundness for TRANSNT/ITF yields GL does not prove False. This is theoremhood completeness, not arbitrary-premise strong completeness or arithmetic incompleteness. §3.1, pp.8–9: about 120 internal theorems and derived-rule lemmas, including reusable classical/K/K4 facts. Propositional axiom naming follows Arithmetic/derived.ml; lemmas are proved for this GL calculus. Internal _th forms and external derived rules aid list reasoning. The authors report that MESON/METIS sometimes fail to infer middle implications or schema instantiations, requiring manual search. No success distribution, annotation burden or timing benchmark is reported. §4.1, p.11: CONJLIST []=True, singleton [p]=p, larger lists use nested conjunction. CONSISTENT X means GL cannot prove Not(CONJLIST X). Either extending a consistent X with A or with Not A remains consistent. MAXIMAL_CONSISTENT p X adds no repetitions and a decision q or Not q for each subformula q of p. This is relative maximality over relevant formulas, not every formula in the language. The world definition separately restricts all members to subformulas or their negations. §§4.1–4.2, pp.12–13: extension takes a consistent list X of subsentences of p and returns a relative maximal M with X SUBLIST M and the same closure restriction. It iterates over missing subformulas, appending a formula if consistency survives, otherwise its negation. This is an existence proof, not an efficient executable consistency test. Nonprovable p gives a world containing Not p. Duplicate-free lists over the finite closure yield finitely many worlds, including order variants; no 2^n world bound is stated. §4.2, p.13: GL_STANDARD_REL p w x requires appropriate maximal worlds; every Box B in w persists in x together with B; additionally some Box E is in x while Not(Box E) is in w. The new-box witness gives strict progress needed for irreflexivity. Merely preserving boxed facts permits self-loops. ACCESSIBILITY_LEMMA derives boxed membership from universal successor membership for relevant Box subformulas under its nonprovability/world hypotheses. §§4.1/4.3, pp.12/14: for w in W, standard V a w iff Atom a is a member of w AND a subformula of p. Under nonprovable p, a standard model, and q a subformula of p, the truth lemma equates membership of q with its truth at w. Extending consistent [Not p] gives a countermodel. Completeness initially uses carrier form list; the Noetherian-frame version follows by class inclusion and soundness. No claim that an infinite canonical maximal-set construction works. §4.4, pp.15–16: bisimulation across two carrier types requires related points to belong to their world sets, agree on atoms, and satisfy forth/back successor conditions. BISIMILAR_HOLDS preserves all modal formulas. Class-validity transfer requires coverage of every source model point by a bisimilar target point. Embedding finite countermodels in carrier A proves generalized completeness only under INFINITE(:A), not for every fixed finite carrier. §4.3, pp.14–15: the finite-model property gives mathematical decidability; a complete efficient procedure is outside scope. GL_TAC applies completeness, unfolds semantics/ITF and calls MESON_TAC []; GL_RULE invokes prove after universal generalization. The tactic is incomplete because first-order automation does not handle essential finite/Noetherian reasoning. It fails on the Löb axiom despite that axiom being available in GL. Its successful Box-biconditional example has a printed MESON trace. No total termination or completeness guarantee for the tactic. §4, p.11: the authors suggest reusing finite subformula extension for other normal modal calculi with different accessibility relations. This does not prove that all normal modal logics have the finite-model property; logic-specific semantic obligations remain. §5, pp.16–17 compares S5, IS4 and HOL4 via cited work, not independently replayed artifacts. Supplement/§1/§1.2, pp.1–4: HOL Light GL source comprises modal.ml, gl.ml, misc.ml and completeness.ml, loaded by GL/make.ml. January 2021 archive identifier is provided; the authors report using original HOL tools. No independent load/build here. The paper intentionally omits proof bodies. No total LOC, elapsed checking/runtime, hardware, large benchmark or LLM-agent evaluation. Solovay arithmetic completeness is background, not this formalized result.

- A Mechanised Proof of the Time Invariance Thesis for the Weak Call-By-Value λ-Calculus (2021)
    - what: Reports Coq proofs that weak call-by-value lambda calculus L and multitape Turing machines simulate each other with polynomial time overhead, with stronger linear-in-machine-steps simulation in the reverse direction for fixed machine. Relates both simulation and boolean-string relation computability, proves halting many-one equivalence, and introduces a Hoare-logic layer combining functional correctness with termination/time bounds for Turing-machine programs. Records the exact closed-term and encoding restrictions, heap compression and output-size dependence needed for size explosion, costed heap-machine transition/refinement, concrete 11-tape/30-symbol simulation, total-function extraction versus manually defined divergence, Hoare tape invariants and constructive machine-definition choices. Reads included worked run and all formal rules, preserving several printed variable/type/zero-size problems rather than treating a prose theorem as an audited source build.
    - limits: §§1/3, pp.2–8: L has de Bruijn-indexed terms, weak reduction outside lambda bodies and beta reduction only on abstractions; variables are not values. Closed terms are the main simulation input. Term size counts unary indices. Reduction may choose either side of an application, but uniform confluence yields unique terminating value and beta-step count. Small-step and big-step characterization agree on closed terms. Theorem 1/§1, pp.3–4: L-to-TM simulation returns a shared heap encoding the result, not necessarily its fully expanded syntax. Expansion can be exponential in source size and beta-step count. Polynomial simulation bound depends on source size and steps; materializing the value additionally depends on output size. Pointer overhead can prevent constant-factor space equivalence; full time-and-space invariance is future work. Theorem 2/§3.1, pp.3/6: computability concerns k-ary relations over boolean lists and an output list. Complexity is actually a functional relation over input lengths, output length and time, written as a function on paper. This avoids requiring a globally total Coq time-bound function for undecidable domains. Polynomially bounded output gives equivalence of polynomial-time computability, in particular PTIME agreement. §3.2/Theorem 6, pp.7–8: compile variables to ref, application to concatenated operand code plus app, abstraction to lam/body/ret. Task and value stacks hold program/address closures; heap entries link arguments and prior environments. Lambda parsing matches nested lam/ret tokens; indexed heap lookup follows links. Optimized task push drops empty residual programs. Starting from a closed term prevents invalid free references. Theorem 6, p.8: beta evaluation in i steps is simulated by 3i+1 heap-machine steps, finishing with empty task stack and singleton closure value. Reachable machine-state encoding size is bounded by c(i+1)(i+||s||+1). Unfolding is a functional relation rather than an unrestricted recursive Coq function because malformed cyclic heaps may diverge. Reachability and acyclic construction matter. §4/Appendix A, pp.9–11/19–20: finite state and alphabet types, fixed finite tape count, total transition function, boolean halting flag and optional write/no-move actions. Tapes encode a contiguous finite symbol segment plus head position, with no built-in distinguished blank. User string-computability convention supplies a blank symbol distinct from true. These choices support constructive encodings and avoid an arbitrary noncomputable transition oracle. §4.2, pp.9–11: realization is partial correctness of terminating runs; a separate relation provides time-bounded termination. Labelled machines support Switch/While composition, alphabet retractions, selected-tape lifting and relabelling. Register encodings have START/STOP delimiters with head at START; unspecified auxiliary tapes are implicitly void in §5. The framework builds actual machine descriptions, while user proofs connect inferred relations to intended specifications. §5/Theorem 11, p.12: Lookup/Parse use five tapes; Step and simulator use eleven tapes over a 30-symbol alphabet. Simulator is While Step. Printed bound p(i,m)=c(3i+2)^2(3i+1+m)m is polynomial in beta steps and input-term size. Conversely simulator termination implies source termination. Some displayed component specs contain variable/type slips; no independent artifact replay validates their corrected versions here. §6/Theorems 17/21, pp.13–14: certifying extraction translates total first-order Coq functions and generates time-recurrence obligations, discharged by solverec when a sufficient bound is supplied. A manually constructed recursion/loop term handles partial or divergent computation. For a fixed TM, transition cost is constant in tape contents but depends on machine parameters; generated obligations include 52|Q|²+130n+216. Fixed-machine simulation is linear in TM steps with machine-dependent constants. §7, p.14: input-list conversion, k-ary application/substitution, simulation and output decoding connect TM-computability to L-computability. Printed Theorem 21 bound is c*m*n1*...*nk*tau+c; zero-length arguments make this formula degenerate, so it should not be silently accepted without a size-plus-one convention or correction. No such restriction is stated in the supplied definition. §8, p.15: weak Hoare triples express conditional realization; total triples combine it with a termination budget under the same precondition. Per-tape assertions describe encoded value, voidness or exact tape equality, plus an optional cross-tape/label invariant. Combinator rules enable symbolic execution; a user first proves correctness, adds a cost, replays the script and discharges accumulated arithmetic. Automatic synthesis of a useful cost function is future work. Theorem 23/§9, p.16: L-to-TM relation compiler prepares a task stack, runs heap simulation, unfolds the resulting boolean-list value and decodes it. For N=sum input lengths, bound c(i+1)(i+N+1)((N+1)(i+1)+m) is cubic in i, quadratic in N, linear in output length m. Constants may depend on the fixed source program/arity. Explicit +1 factors avoid zero-input collapse in this direction. §10, pp.16–18: development including dependencies is reported as 30,000 lines and about 18 minutes compilation on an Intel i7-6600U 2.60GHz; new code 7,800 lines, about 40% specifications/60% proofs. These are author measurements, not an independent benchmark. Framework scaling is conjectured; proof automation sometimes fails or is slow and needs annotations for every recursive helper. MetaCoq and automatic cost generation are proposed extensions. §8/References, pp.15/18: full Hoare rule details are in a separate externally linked Appendix B, not the supplied 20-page PDF. This reading covers all supplied pages and explicitly leaves that supplement and source build unchecked. No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+ model or LLM specification/proof-generation evaluation is reported.

- A Mechanized Proof of the Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem for Countable Networks (2021)
    - what: Isabelle/HOL formalization of the existence of an orthogonal flow-cut pair in countable networks with finite individual capacities. Corrects a failed reduction invariant and quotient/trimming definitions in Aharoni et al. An alternative proof under finite total outgoing capacity at every non-source vertex uses finite-network MFMC and majorised convergence. Tracks the full network→web→maximal wave→trimming/quotient→bipartite linkage→network chain; distinguishes loose from unhindered webs, finite vertex weights from locally finite graphs, orthogonality from numeric optimization, arbitrary chains from countable convergence sequences, and bounded from unbounded proof effort. Includes the infinite-ray counterexample showing that even an orthogonal cut need not have minimum numeric value.
    - limits: Theorem 1/Definitions 2–5 and §5, pp.1/3/12–13: countability is stated for edges. Each edge capacity is finite and nonnegative, but total incoming/outgoing capacity may be infinite. The formal locale requires distinct source and sink, zero capacity off edges, and finite capacities. The informal Theorem 1 omits the distinctness condition, although its cut requires the source inside and sink outside. Formal graph vertices are edge endpoints, eliminating isolated vertices; the carrier type need not itself be countable. Definitions 4–5, pp.3–4: a network flow respects edge capacities and equates incoming/outgoing sums at internal vertices, potentially infinity on both sides. Orthogonality saturates each outgoing cut edge and sets every incoming cut edge to zero. This is a local edge property; it does not establish a minimum numerical cut or maximum numerical source outflow in all infinite networks. Definitions 6–11, pp.4–5: webs place finite weights on vertices rather than edges. A current bounds both degrees by each weight, reflects outgoing flow in incoming flow outside A, has no inflow to A or outflow from B, and may leak current internally. A web-flow additionally conserves internal current. Saturation and exhaustion differ; a terminal vertex is a saturated sink. Definitions 8–11, pp.4–5: an essential vertex has a path to B avoiding other vertices of the separating set. Roofing collects vertices separated from B; strict roofing removes essential vertices. A wave has separating terminal vertices and zero outgoing current outside their roofing. These path-based properties describe bottlenecks, not an algorithmically computed finite cut. §3.1/Lemma 13, pp.5–7: each network edge becomes a web vertex weighted by its capacity; incident original edges yield web edges. This records how an incoming contribution splits among outgoing edges, avoiding subtraction of two infinite aggregate flows. The recovered network edge flow is max(in-degree,out-degree). The local reduction assumes distinct endpoints, no sink outgoing edges, no direct source-sink edge and positive capacities; additional reductions remove the extra restrictions before the final result. §3.2/Definitions 14–15, p.7: pointwise ordered currents/waves form chain-complete partial orders. Zorn yields a maximal wave. A trimming decreases current, conserves current in strict roofing outside A, and preserves essential terminal vertices outside A. Decreasing one-step scaling at a leaking vertex reaches a fixpoint by Bourbaki–Witt; this is an existence construction, not a terminating executable flow algorithm. Definition 16/Lemma 19, pp.8–9: the quotient retains edges with source outside strict roofing and target outside all roofing. Its A side consists of essential terminal vertices minus B−A; terminal vertices in B receive zero weight. Adding a quotient linkage to a trimming gives an orthogonal web-flow. The maximal-wave quotient is loose: no nonzero waves and zero is not a hindrance. Definition 18/Figure 7, p.8: absence of nonzero waves alone is insufficient for linkability. A hindrance is a wave leaving a positive deficit at a nonessential A vertex. Looseness requires the zero wave not be a hindrance too. Unhindered means there is no hindrance, allowing nonzero waves. §3.4/Lemmas 20–21, p.9: bipartite reduction assumes no incoming edges to A, no outgoing edges from B, no loops, and disjoint sides. Internal vertices are duplicated into left/right copies with a diagonal edge and original-edge cross links. Loose input implies unhindered bipartite output, not necessarily loose output. Bipartite linkage can require a further trimming to restore flow conservation in the original web. §4.1/Theorem 25, pp.10–11: the simpler linkage proof assumes the sum of weights of the neighbours of each A vertex is finite. The corresponding network result bounds outgoing capacity individually at every vertex other than the source; no uniform global bound or finite-neighbour requirement is imposed. A finite-set Hall-type weight inequality plus countable matrices, diagonalization and majorised convergence yield a linkage. Proposition 24, p.10: prescribed countable nonnegative row/column marginals have equal finite total, and all subsets satisfy the neighbour-sum inequality. The constructed matrix vanishes off the allowed relation. The formalization adapts the special case of Kellerer directly using finite MFMC; it does not import an unverified infinite-network theorem. §4.2/Definition 26/Lemma 27, p.11: general linkability maintains that the residual web after subtracting allocated degree weights is unhindered. Saturate one enumerated A vertex while preserving that invariant, add the current to the previous current, and take the increasing edgewise supremum. Bipartite structure makes every current a web-flow. This removes the bounded-neighbour assumption. Theorem 28/Lemmas 29–31, pp.11–12: the saturation proof uses flow attainability under no loops/no incoming source edges and finite total incoming OR outgoing capacity at each non-sink vertex. Perturbation lemmas control finite total weight reductions and positive slack. These are helper hypotheses established in the proof, not added assumptions on every final network. §5, pp.12–14: graph/network/web records group data; locales enforce countability, finite weights/capacity, and side restrictions as needed. Extended nonnegative reals and counting-measure integrals define total sums, avoiding summability proof obligations while retaining necessary finite-bound obligations. Zero off edges allows degree sums over the entire type and avoids changes of graph parameter. §5, p.13: Bourbaki–Witt replaces explicit ordinal developments for trimming, linkage recovery and saturation. Arbitrary chains needed by Isabelle chain completeness are reconciled with sequential monotone convergence by selecting a countable subsequence, using countably many potentially nonzero edge coordinates. Supporting fixed-point and integral lemmas were added to the library. §6, pp.15–16: the original bipartite reduction fails to preserve looseness, and also fails to preserve unhinderedness for arbitrary unhindered input. The corrected route specifically uses loose→unhindered and proves linkability for the larger class of unhindered bipartite webs. The induction invariant and saturation lemma must both be strengthened. §6, pp.15–16: allowing quotient edges back into essential terminal vertices can invalidate the sum of wave and quotient current. Corrected quotient excludes them and adjusts sides/weights. Original trimming equality used all terminal vertices on one side; replacing that with essential terminal vertices handles zero-weight sinks. §§5/7–8, pp.14/16–17: evaluation consists of a formal development, proof reductions, counterexamples, line-count comparison and prior theorem reuse. No runtime, proof-check time, hardware, algorithm benchmark or independent artifact execution is reported here. Further restrictions that avoid infinite-ray anomalies remain unformalized. AFP version and separate report are available but were not checked in this reading.

- A Verified Decision Procedure for Univariate Real Arithmetic with the BKR Algorithm (2021)
    - what: Isabelle/HOL correctness proof of a BKR-style univariate real-arithmetic decision procedure with rational-coefficient polynomial atoms. Computes exact realizable sign assignments by recursive matrix combination and reduction using Tarski queries, then decides existential/universal closure of Boolean polynomial formulas. Supplies executable SML and supporting matrix/rank theorems, with ten illustrative microbenchmarks. Connects formula semantics to complete sign determination, reduces unrestricted sign regions to roots of coprime polynomials using squarefree factorization/Rolle/root bounds, and proves the matrix equation separately from invertibility. Kronecker combination preserves invertibility but temporarily includes impossible sign patterns; zero-count column removal and rank-preserving pivot-row selection restore an invertible reduced system. Proves cached matrix consistency and coverage invariants, and exposes coefficient growth as the practical bottleneck despite fewer queries.
    - limits: Formal input grammar has atoms p>0,p≥0,p=0 with rational-coefficient univariate p, combined by conjunction/disjunction. The proved top-level operations decide ∀x phi or ∃x phi over one real variable. Negation/disequality can be normalized using signed polynomials, but arbitrary multivariate quantifier alternation and full real QE are not delivered here. Restricted sign theorem requires p!=0 and each q coprime to p, ruling out zero signs for q at p roots. Preliminary squarefree/pairwise-coprime factorization and separate zero-root cases are needed to cover unrestricted input atoms, including signs0. A Renegar variant avoiding coprimality was formalized after acceptance but its full details are omitted. M*w=v needs distinct candidate sign vectors covering every realizable assignment and valid subset indices. The theorem alone does not imply square/invertible M; separate inductive invariants establish it. Roots and actual count-vector definitions are semantic/nonconstructive specifications, not procedures for explicitly isolating real algebraic roots. The algorithm maintains distinct sign vectors of correct length, all realizable signs included, a cached matrix equal to the matrix computed from subset/sign lists, and matrix invertibility. Only reduction guarantees exact signs; base/combination may overapproximate. Column deletion retains full column rank, then selected rows form a square full-rank matrix. The empty polynomial-list restricted case is handled separately: no roots of p gives no consistent assignment; otherwise the result is the singleton empty vector. The sampling construction using derivative of the product is presented for nontrivial factors; constant/degenerate preprocessing cases should not be inferred from that displayed formula alone. Optimized univariate BKR has potential for parallel polylogarithmic time, but this development is unoptimized/sequential and does not formalize that complexity theorem. Both parallelization and a compatible formal complexity framework remain future work. The cited Tarski-query arithmetic-operation estimate excludes coefficient bit growth. Export to SML compiled by MLton supplies experimental executables, not automatically a kernel-checked Isabelle proof result for each native run. Making BKR practical as an Isabelle tactic is future work. By contrast the measured univ_rcf comparator explicitly checks untrusted Mathematica certificates by reflection inside Isabelle. Bivariate/multivariate AppendixA is informal motivation, not a verified multivariate algorithm. The original multivariate BKR complexity analysis has a known error; the paper proposes future variants and does not claim to repair/formalize all multivariate complexity bounds. Performance evidence is ten microbenchmarks on one laptop, one-hour cutoff, three-decimal reported seconds. No repetitions/variance or broader representative suite is given. Naive matrix-equation implementation is unverified, and the external-solver tactic includes startup overhead. No LLM-agent, distributed-protocol, Rust/Verus or TLA+ result is measured.

- Active Learning of Abstract System Models from Traces using Model Checking (2021)
    - what: Combines trace-based symbolic automata learning with software model checking to actively refine a finite-state abstraction until it admits all implementation behaviors over chosen observable variables. Defines a symbolic NFA over valuations, extracts local completeness conditions from incoming/outgoing predicates, checks them with CBMC, converts valid counterexamples into new traces, and proves that satisfying all conditions implies trace inclusion. It separates spurious-counterexample checking via k-induction, quantifies completeness alpha and transition match d, and evaluates T2M+CBMC on reverse-engineered Simulink Stateflow C implementations against random passive sampling.

    - number: random sampling failed to produce alpha=1 for 50% of remaining benchmarks; some active runs timed out (e.g., FrameSyncController)

The k bound should meet system diameter for a completeness guarantee, but is often estimated and poor values add spurious behavior. Experiments use auto-generated Simulink C and an a-priori finite alphabet; generalization to other software/code generators is unestablished. CBMC may time out or segmentation-fault on models.

- Avis (2021)
    - title: Avis: In-Situ Model Checking for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
    - what: Introduces Avis, an in-situ model checker for UAV control firmware. It builds portable flight workloads, injects clean sensor failures at operating-mode transitions using the SABRE stratified breadth-first schedule, and checks physical-state invariants in simulation.

- Bridging arrays and ADTs in recursive proofs (2021)
    - what: Presents a fully automatic method for synthesizing recursively defined relational invariants that prove equivalence of paired object implementations when one uses arrays and the other algebraic data types (ADTs). The method encodes initialization, paired transitions, applicability and output equality as CHCs; Algorithm 1 builds a recursive invariant schema, Algorithm 2/3 bridge producer/consumer operations for linear scans, and Algorithm 4/5 use noop observations for sets/maps. Candidate relations are validated by structural induction with AdtInd/Z3. The paper formalizes equivalence as an inductive invariant over a composition of two deterministic objects, with initialization, consecution for every paired operation, precondition applicability in both directions, and output equality. It defines producer/consumer/noop classifications via a partial ordering on ADT states and synthesizes a Skolem-like updated array state plus matching constraints. Recipe 1 handles stacks/queues with an index and can infer loop invariants; Recipe 2 handles sets, multisets and maps by updating only the observed array cell while preserving all other inputs. Validation is structural induction rather than recursion-free SMT checking, and user lemmas are optional (one multiset lemma was needed in evaluation).
    - number: 10 benchmark variants in Table 1
    - number: stack 2.81 s and queue 40.61–42.18 s
    - number: set 2.12/19.24 s; multiset 32.62/3.59 s; map 1.95/5.83 s
    - number: MacBook Pro 2 GHz Intel Core i5, 8 GB RAM
    - limits: Objects are modeled syntactically as predicates obtained from symbolic execution; loop effects must already be expressed as quantified formulas. Programs are deterministic and each enabled precondition has a successor/output. The approach targets finite sets of operations and list-shaped ADTs; it assumes suitable classifications/recipes and SMT quantifier-elimination/array reasoning. CHC solving is undecidable in general, proof search can dominate runtime, and the evaluation is textbook data structures rather than large real software. The method requires monotonic/structural-induction support in AdtInd and may need user lemmas for harder cases.

- Brief Announcement: On Strong Observational Refinement and Forward Simulation (2021)
    - what: Shows by example that ordinary forward simulation need not preserve hyperliveness or strong observational refinement when finite and infinite traces are allowed. Defines progressive forward simulation with a well-founded decrease on concrete steps mapped to an empty abstract sequence; states that it implies strong observational refinement. Full theorem proof is external. The counterexample composes a forward-simulated LL/SC implementation with fetch-and-add. A particular LL/SC implementation permits SC failure merely because another thread executed LL, without any intervening write. Alternating threads can therefore prevent both operations from returning. The formal scheduler requirement is nonempty enabled actions after every consistent finite trace, plus object determinism; it does not impose per-thread fairness. Definition 1 forbids infinite internal stuttering through a well-founded concrete-state order. Necessity of the progress condition is future work.

Full proof of Theorem 2 deferred to external reference [3]; no machine-checked artifact or empirical measurements in supplied brief. The motivating text says LL at F2 although pseudocode labels LL at F1; record interprets the operation rather than reproducing that line typo.

Those nonzero hypotheses justify cancellation, rather than assuming all determinants are invertible (p.70). Section2 works in a projective space described by collinearity. Proposition6 transports the initial and crossing incidences into eight convenient orderings. Proposition7 gives four noncollinear triples from two distinct lines and explicit distinctness; Proposition8 changes the reference frame while re-establishing18incidence/inequality/nonincidence clauses. These are formal hypothesis-management steps, not new Pappus conclusions (pp.71–73). Propositions9/10 give disjunctions of failures to rule out degenerate configurations. Proposition11 separates an intersection from c2; Propositions12/13 recover collinearity within each original line; Propositions14/15 derive further distinctness; Proposition16 proves a crossing point noncollinear with a specified pair. Exact hypotheses differ, so these statements do not authorize arbitrary point coincidences (p.73). Proposition17 uses a reference point o and two lines through it, with(o,p1,q1) noncollinear. It requires o distinct from p2,p3,q2,q3, the three p points pairwise distinct and the three q points pairwise distinct. Crossings are r3 on p1q2 and q1p2, r2 on p1q3 and p3q1, r1 on p2q3 and p3q2.     - what: Diffy verifies selected parameterized array programs by induction on positive array-size parameter N. It splits PN into QN-1 plus a peeled suffix, relates QN-1 to PN-1 through product-program difference invariants, transfers the smaller-program postcondition, and verifies the peel with iterative strengthening or recursively reduced loop nesting. At60seconds it proves151/157 safe cases and detects142/146 unsafe cases on an enhanced303-program suite. Distinguishes QN-1 (only loop bounds truncated, with data-dependency repairs) from PN-1 (all N replaced), explains required precondition splitting and cross-program coverage, records conditional peel simplification and failed loop propagation, and retains the strengthen-transfer obligation rather than treating arbitrary quantifier elimination as sufficient. Complete category results, timeout sensitivity, baseline wins and source formula/indexing gaps qualify headline superiority.

Upper bounds use N, constants and enclosing counters, not arbitrary mutable data. N is a positive integer size parameter. It does not cover arbitrary C pointers, concurrency, recursion or distributed failures. §3: properties are universal arithmetic-index guards implying quantifier-free array/integer arithmetic predicates, or quantifier-free formulas. Scalars and arrays undergo SSA renaming, including separate array versions per loop and distinct writes. The mathematical domain is integers/arrays; the paper does not establish C overflow, pointer aliasing, division edge cases or machine memory-safety semantics end to end. §§2,4.1: PN-1 replaces all occurrences of N by N-1; QN-1 truncates loop-bound N while preserving data-expression N, then repairs uses affected by moving peels. Correct construction must establish PN semantically equivalent to QN-1;peel(PN). It is not enough to append last iterations without propagating all data/control dependencies. §4.1: nested-loop exposition assumes inner-body writes are not used later in outer fragments, and outer writes used by the inner body are not overwritten again. Relaxations are delegated to extended[13]. Algorithm1 aborts a needed substitution from a peel that is still a loop; implementation sometimes uses closed-form summaries, unused-write reasoning or conservative overapproximation. Thus it does not automatically transform every grammar-accepted nested array program. §4.1/Lemma1: strictly smaller maximum nesting depth is proved for linear upper bounds in N/enclosing counters, whose difference on replacing N by N-1 is constant. Corollary that a nonnested program has loop-free peel inherits conditions; general nonlinear bounds need not yield constant many peeled iterations. Missed-iteration construction also needs sensible nonnegative ordered bounds; grammar alone does not state all monotonicity/boundary conditions. The theorem should not be generalized to arbitrary decreasing/negative bounds without additional validation. §4.2: phi(N) must imply phi-prime(N-1) and delta-phi-prime(N), with split remainder facts not modified by PN-1/QN-1 as needed. For conjunction over indices0..N-1, restrict only index range for phi-prime and retain N inside each conjunct; remainder is last-index conjunct if untouched. If no iterated conjunction, proposed default is phi-prime=phi(N),delta=True. Correct input coupling between the two program runs is essential. §4.3: product graph has synchronized loop iteration structure; corresponding branches synchronize only after establishing equivalent guards, otherwise all four branch pairs are considered.     - title: A Variant of Wagner’s Theorem Based on Combinatorial Hypermaps
    - what: Doczkal reports a constructive Coq proof that a finite simple graph with neither K5 nor K3,3 minor and no isolated vertices admits a genus-zero combinatorial hypermap embedding. Converse and a bridge to actual real-plane drawings remain outside the completed result. H-free excludes H as a minor, not merely as a subgraph. k-connected requires k<|G| and all separators size≥k. Their cycles encode edges, nodes and faces; retaining redundant third permutation helps symmetry reasoning. Plain means every edge cycle has two darts; loopless means paired darts lie in different node cycles; simple means at most one edge cycle links any two node cycles. Genus=((2C+|D|)-(E+N+F))/2, where C counts components and E,N,F permutation cycles. Inherited Euler inequality and evenness ensure natural subtraction does not truncate and division has no remainder; planar means genus 0 (§5). - DSS (2021)
    - title: Detectable Sequential Specifications for Recoverable Shared Objects
    - what: Defines detectability by transforming an ordinary sequential object specification into a detectable sequential specification (DSS). Per-process abstract state remembers a prepared operation and its response. prep-op announces the operation, exec-op performs it, and resolve reports whether it took effect and its response; ordinary operations remain available without detection. Section 2 gives the state transformation and four operation axioms. prep-op and resolve are total and idempotent, while exec-op requires the matching prepared operation with no recorded response. An auxiliary parity bit can distinguish repeated identical operations. DSS is combined with a separate concurrency correctness condition and leaves nesting recovery to the application. Section 3 derives a queue from the Michael–Scott/durable queue: tagged per-thread pointers record operation preparation and completion, CAS and helping maintain the linked list, and Appendix A supplies a centralized recovery scan. A variation replaces centralized recovery with individual recovery. Theorem 1 states lock-freedom and strict linearizability, but the article omits the analysis and detailed model. Section 4 measures failure-free queue throughput on real Optane memory.
    - number: up to 20 threads on 20 cores
    - number: 30-second runs, ten runs per point, standard deviation <2% of mean
    - number: non-detectable DSS nearly 3× detectable DSS throughput at low parallelism
    - number: MS up to 1.5× non-detectable DSS at two threads
    - limits: A recovering process must retain its identifier across crashes to query its previous operation; this conflicts with the fresh-identifier model underlying durable linearizability. DSS specifies sequential behavior and requires a separate concurrent correctness condition. The queue uses asynchronous shared memory, persistent memory, volatile caches, explicit flushes and system-wide crashes. Correct nesting is an application responsibility. The correctness theorem is stated rather than proved in this article. Experiments cover failure-free runs, use debug compilation at O0 and sequentially consistent atomics, and do not measure crash recovery latency. The log queue comparator is the authors’ implementation and could be optimized further.

    - title: Recursive Variable-Length State Compression for Multi-Core Software Model Checking
    - what: Introduces dtree, a concurrent chain-of-balanced-trees storage structure for variable-length model-checker states, supporting partial reconstruction and incremental delta updates; integrates it into the DMC multi-core checker. The paper contrasts dtree with TreeDBS and Compact Tree, explains why fixed alignment fails under dynamic allocation, and defines a StateID combining root index and length. Its API supports insert, delta, full/partial get and nested sub-states, enabling models to update heap regions without reconstructing complete states. Dtree experiments model Michael-Scott queues, sorted linked lists and concurrent hash maps, then compare 118 BEEM fixed-length models against LTSmin/TreeDBS, Compact Tree and SPIN Collapse. Results expose the trade-off: dtree wins on variable-length variance but loses compression on fixed-length vectors because its chain can be less balanced.

DMC's search core is simple parallel BFS; experiments use 64 threads on one 96-core machine, so results are implementation- and workload-dependent. Future work includes better root tables and work stealing.

- Ghost Signals: Verifying Termination of Busy Waiting (2021)
    - what: Develops a modular Hoare/separation-logic approach to termination of busy-waiting programs under fair scheduling. Ghost signals represent conditions other threads must establish; linear obligations require setting them. A well-founded partial order forbids waiting on a signal at or above any obligation held by the waiter. Data-structure invariants tie signals to real conditions, allowing resource-local proof of waiting over arbitrary shared structures. §2 derives the logic through thread-safe physical signals, non-thread-safe signals guarded by mutexes, arbitrary heap cells, then erasure into ghost state. An augmented operational semantics makes a thread get stuck if it exits with outstanding obligations; fork transfers obligations rather than discarding them. A program-order graph tracks the path carrying each obligation. A minimal infinitely-waited signal would have an infinite obligation path that can wait only on finitely-waited lower signals, yielding contradiction under fairness. Points-to/signal ownership prevents races. Mutex acquisition creates a release obligation and also obeys the level order. §3 splits signal-ID allocation from initialization so a fixed finite collection of signal IDs can be named early without creating premature obligations. Loop iterations may select from a finite signal set, and outer productive loops use ordinary decreasing counters. §5 explains call/wait permissions and thread phases; permission consumption only in descendant phases prevents a self-fueling busy loop. §6 describes a possible reduction of termination to instrumentation safety for higher-order step-indexed logics.

    - title: Justness: A Completeness Criterion for Capturing Liveness Properties
    - what: Defines justness as a completeness criterion for transition-system paths: once a non-blocking transition enabled by parallel components is not interfered with, some component must eventually act.     - what: Defines sure infinite-time-horizon safety for Bayesian neural-network policies in closed-loop discrete-time systems and computes a safe subset of the weight posterior.     - what: Coq/SSReflect formalization of Hanoi variants, including uniqueness and optimality for three-peg regular perfect-state transfers, optimal arbitrary-state strategies for three pegs, and Frame–Stewart optimality between perfect states for four-peg regular and outer-to-outer star puzzles. Four-peg proofs reconstruct technical mathematical lower bounds rather than merely verify a recursive solution. Records finite-function state encoding, peg-relation-parametric legal moves, projection with adjacent-repeat deletion, equality-sensitive minimality induction, greedy counterexample and linear variant, triangular-number valuation for four regular pegs, 2^i3^j sequence and alternating multi-state penalty invariant for four-star pegs. Distinguishes puzzle variant and endpoint scopes, stated optimality from generated legal paths, proof effort and printed formula/side-condition errors.
