A configuration is a finite function from each disk to its peg, uniquely inducing sorted stacks. Thus every encoded state is stack-legal; on_top checks no smaller disk on that peg. Finite-function equality/extensionality comes from the finite representation, not an assumed axiom for arbitrary Coq functions. §2, pp.3–7: auxiliary-peg selector is symmetric but guaranteed different from both pegs only for at least three pegs. General move requires one chosen disk on top before and after, an allowed peg relation and all other disks unchanged. If the relation is reflexive, unchanged states may qualify; regular/linear/star relations are irreflexive. This is a discrete sequential graph, with no simultaneous moves. §2, pp.6–7: regular relation allows every distinct pair; linear relation allows consecutive ordinal pegs; star relation requires distinct pegs and at least one equal zero, so zero is center. Three-peg linear/star graphs are isomorphic after relabelling, not equal under the displayed labels (linear center 1 versus star center 0). Endpoint role matters for distances. §2–2.1, pp.5–8: transforms remove/add largest disks, split/merge size ranges, or restrict arbitrary disks/pegs. Projecting a legal path can produce identical adjacent states when a removed disk moves, so rm_rep deletes adjacent repetitions before applying the smaller-puzzle path theorem. It need not delete all repeated states or establish shortestness. §2.1, pp.7–8: distance is least length of a connecting path in a finite state graph; gpath combines path legality, endpoint and size equal to distance. Paper does not spell out its convention for disconnected arbitrary relations. Uses in the Hanoi results have connected move graphs; an unconditional metric theorem for every arbitrary peg relation should not be inferred. §3.1, pp.8–9: recursive perfect-state transfer has 2^n−1 configurations after the starting state, and is a legal path when source differs from destination. Equality-sensitive comparison proves every such transfer path is at least this length and equals it iff it is the generated path. Double induction on disks and path length handles the largest disk moving once, twice or returning. Uniqueness applies to these regular perfect endpoints, not all shortest paths in all variants. §3.1, p.10: in regular three-peg arbitrary-state transfer, a greedy largest-disk destination move may be suboptimal. Greedy is optimal if one endpoint is perfect; for two arbitrary endpoints compare one- and two-jump strategies for the largest disk whose location differs, leaving larger disks fixed. The paper describes these formalized results but does not print all algorithm/optimality proofs. §3.2, pp.10–11: for linear three pegs, greedy is optimal. Distinct adjacent perfect pegs have distance (3^n−1)/2; the two outer pegs have 3^n−1; identical endpoints have zero. With 3^n states, a shortest outer transfer visits every configuration exactly once. This is a state-graph result, not a measured search benchmark. §4.1, pp.11–12: Frame–Stewart parks top m<n disks using four pegs, transfers remaining n−m using three while avoiding the occupied peg, then retrieves m. Choose m minimizing 2T4(m)+T3(n−m). The generic k-peg recurrence yields an algorithm; its optimality for arbitrary k is stated open at publication. This paper proves four-peg regular and four-peg star scopes only. §4.2, pp.12–13: regular four-peg optimal perfect-transfer cost Phi(n) is the prefix sum of 2^(triangular_root i), and satisfies the Frame–Stewart recurrence with 2^(n−m)−1. The proof uses a valuation Psi of an arbitrary disk set E, defined through a max over L with capped triangular-root exponents. If v uses only two pegs avoiding p0, then Psi of disks on p0 in u bounds d(u,v) below. Distinct p0,p2,p3 and the codomain restriction are essential. §4.2, p.13: strong induction follows first/last visits of the largest disk and a selected disk T through a geodesic, splits at critical configurations and modifies/project paths to fit the induction hypothesis. Combined with the generated upper bound, this yields exact Phi(n) for distinct perfect endpoints. The 1000-line proof formalizes a six-page main argument, with most details referred to Bousch rather than reproduced. §5, pp.13–15: star theorem concerns two different outer pegs. Transfer parks small disks on the third outer peg, uses a three-peg outer-to-outer linear transfer for the rest, then retrieves. Cost is 2S1(n), where S1 sums increasing distinct numbers 2^i3^j starting at 1. Its recurrence contains (3^(n−m)−1)/2; doubled cost satisfies the star Frame–Stewart recurrence. §5, p.14: lower bound generalizes from two endpoints to l+1 configurations, with intermediate codomains alternating between pairs of outer pegs. Sl(n) and its differences alpha_l plus endpoint penalty beta support induction on n and splitting into alternating subpaths. Convexity in n and concavity in l combine lower bounds. At l=1 and perfect outer endpoints penalties vanish, matching the algorithm upper bound. §5–6, pp.15–16: star main argument spans about 3500 Coq script lines versus 15 informal pages, organized into three sublemmas and a without-loss-of-generality step. Proofs use little automation and natural numbers. Replacing subtraction inequalities with addition needs the source proof’s bounds; truncated natural subtraction is not ordinary integer subtraction. §6, pp.15–16: evaluation is formal theorem reconstruction, counterexamples and proof-size descriptions.     - what: The paper develops GoL, a process-calculus model for shared memory, locks, read-write locks, and later channels, with behavioural types that encode happens-before synchronization. Type soundness and progress connect processes to µ-calculus types; model checking these types detects data races, lock safety/liveness, and mixed channel/shared-memory errors. In-logic compilation removes the compiler from the final statement; it does not eliminate trust in the logic, prover implementation or fidelity of source/machine/hardware models.     - title: Ascoli-Arzelà Theorem
    - what: Yamazaki, Miyajima and Shidama formalize Ascoli–Arzelà for continuous maps from a compact metric domain into a complete normed target. Compactness of the family’s closure in the supremum norm is equivalent to equicontinuity and compact closure of each pointwise value set. Definitions and finite-net/closure lemmas connect normed, metric and topological representations. The paper also handles a common compact target range. Closure bars disappear in the raw extraction, so interpreting this as compactness of the unclosed family would change the theorem. Records uniform versus pointwise family moduli, compact-domain uniformization, closure rather than raw-subset completeness/compactness, finite-net consequences, evaluation-set conditions, topology transport and the common-compact-range corollary.

Main setting has nonempty metric M, nonempty compact topological S equal to M_top, complete normed linear topological T, and a nonempty family F of continuous maps S→T with its supremum norm. G is the same underlying function set in the metric-domain representation (pp.87,90–93). Definition 1 explicitly introduces closure of a metric subset through the induced topology. Rendered closure bars on Y,Z,H,F and pointwise sets are lost in raw extraction. Theorems 7–12,16–19,23 must therefore be read from the renderings. This record uses cl(F) for closure and distinguishes it from F; exact quotations preserve extraction and their pointers warn about missing bars (entire paper). Definition 2 equiboundedness gives one finite K for all functions and all domain points: ||f(x)||≤K. Definition 3 equicontinuity at x0 gives one delta for each epsilon and x0, uniform over f but allowed to depend on x0. Definition 4 uses one delta for each epsilon uniformly over all functions and all pairs x1,x2. These quantifier orders are distinct (pp.88–89). Theorem 3 expresses continuity by open neighborhoods and norm differences; Theorem 4 converts continuity on compact metric M into uniform continuity. Theorem 5 makes pointwise family equicontinuity equivalent to its uniform Definition 4 on compact M. Its proof takes half-radius neighborhoods, a finite subcover and a positive minimum radius, then uses an epsilon/2 triangle argument (pp.88–89). Theorem 2 proves a finite union of compact subsets compact by induction on finite-sequence length. It is supporting topology infrastructure, not a general assertion that arbitrary unions of compact sets are compact (p.88). Theorem 6 equates norm completeness and metric completeness. Theorem 7 says a closed subset cl(H) of complete Z is complete, not that arbitrary H is complete. Theorem 8 says H is totally bounded iff cl(H) is; Theorems 9/10 combine this with completeness to relate total boundedness of H and compactness/sequential compactness of cl(H), across metric/norm/topological representations (pp.89–90). The continuous-function space C(S,T) is complete when S is compact and T complete, imported through the existing normed continuous-function library. Theorems 11/12 give sequential compactness/compactness of the closure of a family iff its metric subspace is totally bounded. No closedness assumption on the original family is needed because the conclusions concern its closure (pp.90–91). Theorem 13 starts with a totally bounded nonempty family in the sup norm. A finite cover by radius-one balls, representatives and K=maximum representative norm+1 give a uniform bound. Smaller sup-norm nets and uniform continuity of finitely many representatives give a shared continuity modulus. The PDF prints the bound construction and asserts the final modulus, rather than a complete expanded derivation (p.91). Theorem 14 says each evaluation set H_x={f(x):f∈H} is totally bounded and the family equicontinuous. Evaluation is norm nonexpansive: ||f(x)-g(x)||≤||f-g||_sup, explaining transfer of finite nets. This inequality is this reading’s explanation, not a reproduced checker trace (pp.91–92). Theorem 15 aligns the distance-by-norm, MetricSpaceNorm and TopSpaceNorm constructions when a normed structure and norm topology agree. This avoids treating equality of underlying elements as automatic equality of every topology/metric representation. Theorems 20/21 similarly transport compactness, and22 gives completeness of a compact normed linear topological space (pp.92–93). Theorem 16 characterizes total boundedness of H by uniform family equicontinuity and compactness of cl(H_x) for every point x. Target completeness turns totally bounded pointwise sets into compact closures. For the converse, the standard finite-net reasoning combines finitely many domain sample neighborhoods with finite approximations to their evaluation sets. The displayed proof merely states existence of finite epsilon-ball covers and omits that detailed construction; it was not audited from Mizar source (p.92). Theorems 17/18 express the same criterion as sequential compactness of cl(H) or compactness of cl(F), respectively. Theorem19 replaces uniform equicontinuity by equicontinuity at every point using Theorem5. These are relative compactness criteria for the family, not assertions that an arbitrary unclosed family F is itself compact (pp.92–93). Theorems 16–19 require pointwise relative compactness, stronger than equiboundedness in a general infinite-dimensional Banach target. A bounded family of constant maps taking orthonormal unit-vector values would be equicontinuous and equibounded but have no compact evaluation-set closure. This is an illustrative mathematical check of the necessary distinction, not an example supplied or benchmarked in the paper. Theorem23 assumes every member range lies in one compact subset U of T. Then the pointwise closures lie in that compact set, so equicontinuity suffices for compactness of cl(F); conversely compact cl(F) gives equiboundedness and equicontinuity. The compact-range premise is a substantive additional restriction, not merely boundedness of U (p.93). Presented evaluation is a library-based formal theorem development with definitions, short proof sketches and dependency references. No executable finite-net construction, computational complexity, checking times/proof sizes, empirical comparison, checker log or artifact run is supplied. Imported ASCOLI source and continuous-function Banach-space proof [11] not independently inspected. No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM proof/specification-agent evaluation (all pages).

- ACL2 multiplier rewriter (2020)
    - title: Automated and Scalable Verification of Integer Multipliers.
    - what: Gives an ACL2-verified rewrite procedure for functional correctness of concrete signed/unsigned multiplier circuits. It proves symbolic SVL execution equals ACL2 integer multiplication with specified extensions and bit truncation. First proves hierarchical adder modules and replaces them with sum/carry specifications s(x)=x mod 2 and c(x)=floor(x/2). Separate multiplier rules flatten summation trees, combine carries through a temporary d(x)=x/2 representation, and simplify Booth/sign-extension partial products. Syntactic restrictions contain polynomial expansion and keep conflicting adder/multiplier rules in separate phases. The specification is rewritten via a proved multbycol function to the same per-output-bit form; syntactic equality concludes the theorem. Lexicographic measures justify termination of the core rule sets.
    - number: Eight 1024×1024 signed/unsigned cases: 322–397 s; DK takes 13,247–15,198 s and AM times out
    - number: Proof time grows 4.5–6× for 4× circuit-size growth; largest runs consume up to 30 GB
    - number: Simple Wallace-like designs spend about 40% in rewrite simplification; Booth designs spend over 70% in partial-product simplification
    - limits: Requires preserved circuit hierarchy, adder module names/I/O sizes, multiplier I/O widths and signedness. ACL2 proves the rewriting and resulting circuit theorem relative to SVL semantics and the supplied specification; completeness is unproved. Failed proofs lack friendly diagnostics or counterexamples. Array multipliers scale poorly. Comparison excludes Verilog translation time; DK includes certificate generation/checking, while AM produces no certificate. Benchmarks are arbitrarily selected, emphasizing Wallace-like circuits. The termination section omits detailed discussion of elementary algebraic rules.

    - what: # ODE liveness needs enough solution duration and a valid path through its domain (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Tan and Platzer develop deductive proofs that an ordinary differential equation (ODE) solution lasts long enough to reach a target without leaving its allowed domain. This record reads the complete 61-page arXiv:2004.14561v2 report, dated 9 August 2020, including all appendices. The contribution is a library of small refinement steps in differential dynamic logic (dL), a logic for discrete and continuous programs, plus derived existence/liveness rules and a KeYmaera X implementation. The authors derive corrected forms of several earlier liveness arguments; the earlier publications themselves were not independently checked for this record. The approach yields proofs that the solution of a given > ODE exists long enough to reach a given target region without leaving a given evolution domain. Numerous subtleties > complicate the generalization of discrete liveness verification techniques, such as loop variants, to the continuous set- > ting. For example, ODE solutions may blow up in finite time or their progress towards the goal may converge to zero. > These subtleties are handled in dL by successively refining ODE liveness properties using ODE invariance properties > which have a complete axiomatization. This approach is widely applicable: several liveness arguments from the > literature are surveyed and derived as special instances of axiomatic refinement in dL. These derivations also correct > several soundness errors in the surveyed literature, which further highlights the subtlety of ODE liveness reasoning > and the utility of an axiomatic approach. An important special case of this approach deduces (global) existence prop- > erties of ODEs, which are a fundamental part of every ODE liveness argument. Thus, all generalizations of existence > properties and their proofs immediately lead to corresponding generalizations of ODE liveness arguments. Overall, > the resulting library of common refinement steps enables both the sound development and justification of new ODE > existence and of liveness proof rules from dL axioms. Global existence is expressed by adding a clock and proving that every arbitrary finite clock threshold can be exceeded. The dependency-order rule builds the ODE in groups whose right-hand sides use only earlier groups and themselves. Each group needs either a squared-norm bound depending on earlier groups/time or a suitable linear bound on its squared-norm derivative. Derived cases include globally Lipschitz fields and affine dependency groups. Example 2, u′=u and v′=uv, has provably global solutions despite lacking a global Lipschitz constant for the whole vector field. The bounded-existence rule says a solution either reaches any requested time horizon or leaves a bounded region; invariance of that region then proves global existence. The combined rule allows affine groups alongside bounded nonlinear groups. For an unconstrained target, an atomic differential variant is a quantity whose derivative is bounded below by one fixed positive constant until the goal. Strict positivity alone can decay toward zero and fail to reach the goal. A constant positive rate also fails if another coordinate blows up before enough time passes. Corollary 12 therefore makes sufficient duration explicit or uses provably global solutions. Equational goals use continuity; higher-order variants use a positive higher Lie derivative to obtain polynomial-in-time progress. Staging-set rules keep the trajectory in a region until the goal and force exit: a bounded set bounds continuous terms, while a compact set lets a strictly positive derivative attain a positive minimum. The set-Lyapunov rule requires compact K and open target P, correcting a merely closed-K version reported in the survey. The running linear spiral reaches a smaller circle and then an enclosing annular target by continuity. The nonlinear spiral u′=−v−u(1/4−u²−v²), v′=u−v(1/4−u²−v²) can blow up outside its small stable region, yet still reaches squared norm 2 from the unit circle using compact staging in 1≤u²+v²≤2. Thus global existence is one useful sufficient condition, not a necessary property of every successful finite reachability proof. For constrained variants, the initial target-false condition and open/closed domain requirements remain explicit. A closed annulus can permit reaching its outer boundary; excluding that boundary from the domain makes the same target impossible. The combined and compact-eventuality rules join higher derivatives, compact staging and domain refinement. The implementation offers an existential variant rule that lets arithmetic search find the positive derivative lower bound, with a manual-instantiation option to avoid that search. A semialgebraic variant rule handles disjunctions/conjunctions of polynomial inequalities through a progress formula and invariant reasoning, rather than adding a nonsmooth min/max function to the logic. Example 8 proves u′=−u eventually enters [−1,1]. Closed-domain refinement uses an interior-set obligation. Its practical strictification of nonstrict inequalities underapproximates that interior; Appendix B explicitly explains why it need not equal the interior, for example x≤x versus x<x. Proof support obtains dependency groups by topologically sorting strongly connected components of the ODE variable-dependency graph. Affine groups can be handled automatically; nonlinear groups can need user-provided bounds, with an additional arithmetic method for an isolated univariate nonlinear group. Compatible invariant assumptions can strengthen box premises only when the antecedent ODE/domain permits at least the relevant trajectories. This is a controlled use of context: arbitrary initial-state assertions cannot be retained as if they were invariants. - APKeep: Realtime Network Verification for Real Networks (2020)
    - what: APKeep incrementally checks a symbolic model of network forwarding, filtering and header rewriting. Its Port-Predicate Map separates logical functions and their applications, and maintains Boolean packet equivalence classes by splitting only for changed behavior and merging equal port sets. An informal inductive proof establishes a minimum partition for the basic immediate-merge algorithm; experiments measure update-plus-loop-check cost, partition sizes, memory, link-failure queries and synthetic NAT updates. Records the precise EC equivalence relation, rule priority/hit analysis, split/transfer/merge algorithm, rewrite closure, delayed merging and separate partition optimizations, invariant and policy traversal, vendor PBR case, all dataset and comparison tables, partial-run counting and synthesized workloads. Distinguishes the basic minimum-partition theorem from optimized execution and exposes printed formula/pseudocode/data inconsistencies without inferring implementation faults.
    - limits: §2.1: Every element sends each header to exactly one logical action port. Headers in an EC must select the same port at every element, even elements the header never reaches. This partition can be finer than physical device behavior or reachable paths.     - title: AVR: Abstractly Verifying Reachability.
    - what: Presents AVR, a push-button word-level model checker for source-level transition systems. It combines syntax-guided abstraction/refinement with word-level IC3, SMT backends, BMC and interpolation, and emits independently checkable inductive-invariant certificates or BTOR2 counterexample witnesses. - Cloud spatial model checking (2020)
    - title: Cloud Deployment Tradeoffs for the Analysis of Spatially-Distributed Systems of Internet-of-Things
    - what: Builds a runtime spatial-verification architecture for resource-constrained IoT systems. Trajectory-derived accessibility graphs become closure spaces evaluated with Spatial Logic for Closure Spaces (SLCS); model checking is packaged as microservices and deployed on VMs, containers, AWS Lambda FaaS, or a hybrid. The paper explains how points of interest and trajectories induce a quasi-discrete closure model, how SLCS closure/surround operators express bike-sharing requirements, and how services maintain model/state updates. It compares monolithic VM, containerized ECS, FaaS and hybrid load balancing, using a Beijing taxi trace and a 30-second SLA. A mobile-device baseline averages 99 seconds per invocation. Lambda stays near 12 seconds across load rates; monolith is 9–12 seconds through 20× load but violates SLA at higher peaks; containers time out at 20× or more due to scale-up; hybrid splits 65–35% monolith/FaaS at 60× and has about 20 seconds median calls, with load-balancer overhead under 300 ms.

The architecture centralizes verification and can suffer network latency, privacy and single-point-of-failure issues; edge decentralization and quantitative/metric properties are future work.

- Context-bounded multithreaded liveness (2020)
    - title: Context-Bounded Verification of Liveness Properties for Multithreaded Shared-Memory Programs
    - what: Proves decidability and complexity results for termination, fair non-termination and fair starvation of dynamically spawning recursive threads under a fixed context-switch bound, introducing VASS with balloons as the key intermediate model. The paper formalizes Dynamic Networks of Concurrent Pushdown Systems (DCPS), thread identities, scheduler swaps/resumptions and fairness. Ordinary termination reduces through downward closures to VASS non-termination, yielding the 2EXPSPACE result. Fairness is not downward-closure preserving, so VASS with balloons stores semi-linear multisets of future spawns; progressive runs and a shallow-run theorem reduce DCPS fair behavior to VASSB reachability, then to ordinary VASS reachability. A separate Ramsey/pumping and consistency construction reduces starvation to fair termination. The paper gives proof machinery rather than an implementation or empirical benchmark.
    - number: For K ≥ 1, K-bounded non-termination is 2EXPSPACE-complete
    - number: For every K, fair non-termination and fair starvation are decidable
    - number: Fair decision procedures are non-elementary, already for K=0 via VASS reachability
    - number: VASSB has decidable progressive runs and every progressive run has a shallow counterpart
    - limits: The bound K is fixed per decision instance and fairness means every thread ready infinitely often is eventually scheduled (with identity-equivalence subtleties handled by an angelic scheduler argument). Results concern the DCPS model: finite global state, pushdown stacks, shared global control and restricted scheduler rules. Fair problems are decidable but non-elementary; unbounded context switching remains outside the decidability claim.

- EEV BNN verification (2020)
    - title: Efficient Exact Verification of Binarized Neural Networks
    - what: Presents EEV, an exact (sound and complete) verifier for binarized neural networks. BNN layers compile to reified cardinality constraints; MiniSatCS adds native propagation for these constraints. BinMask induces balanced layer-wise sparsity, Cardinality Bound Decay (CBD) shrinks threshold bounds, and adaptive gradient cancelling trains networks whose exact robustness is tractable. The SAT encoding uses {0,1} activations, sparse {-1,0,1} weights, quantized inputs, thermometer-encoded perturbation intervals, and cached network clauses. The paper explains why balanced sparsity matters more than total sparsity and why lower cardinality bounds reduce sequential-counter encoding size, improve propagation, and make outputs predictable. Standard hard-tanh straight-through adversarial training can produce high PGD but low exact robustness; tanh/adaptive gradients and verifier-generated adversaries narrow this gap. EEV also encodes ensemble reject queries requiring all models to agree on the same wrong class.
    - number: MiniSatCS >100x over unmodified SAT

    - number: BinMask solve 756.288→0.002s MNIST and 0.267→0.003s CIFAR10
    - number: CBD mean bound 148.3→2.7 MNIST; 123.8→2.1 CIFAR10
    - limits: Exactness applies to the quantized BNN and encoded infinity-norm perturbation domain, not arbitrary floating-point inference. Inputs are quantized (s=1/255 or 2epsilon), final batch normalization is restricted to scalar statistics, and verification remains NP-hard with timeouts for harder settings. Robustness/accuracy tradeoffs are severe on CIFAR10 at large epsilon; CBD can reduce natural accuracy. Results use MNIST/CIFAR10 architectures and do not prove properties of real-valued or distributed systems.

    - what: Gauntlet finds P4 compiler crashes with well-formed random programs, semantic mistakes in accessible compiler passes through SMT equivalence checking, and backend miscompilations through model-derived input/output packet tests. Its symbolic P4 interpreter supplies both oracles. The authors report96confirmed distinct bugs across P4C,BMv2 and Tofino over eight months,54fixed, and six specification changes. This is compiler bug finding with conditional translation validation of tested transformations, not verification of every compiler execution or correctness of the user network program. Captures generator probability/size controls, independent block semantics, symbolic table encoding and parameter directions, undefined-behavior taint and unstable-code distinction, parser/ToP4 dependencies, per-pass reparse/check workflow, constrained backend test generation and dropped-test limits. - GSPACER (2020)
    - title: Global Guidance for Local Generalization in Model Checking
    - what: Adds explicit global guidance to local IC3-style lemma generation. Three general rules—implemented as GS PACER on top of Z3 SPACER—use the current lemma set to introduce blocking states/lemmas and mitigate locality failures.     - title: Parameterised Complexity of Model Checking and Satisfiability in Propositional Dependence Logic
    - what: Classifies parameterized complexity of model checking (MC), satisfiability (SAT), and exact-team-size satisfiability (m-SAT) for propositional dependence logic (PDL). It proves a dichotomy: most listed parameters yield fixed-parameter tractability, while team-size, dependence-atom arity, or split count can make problems paraNP-complete. The paper defines team semantics and syntax-circuit treewidth, then gives explicit reductions and algorithms. MC parameterized by team-size is solved by bottom-up enumeration of subteams in time polynomial in formula size and O*(2^(2k)); MC by split count is paraNP-complete via a 3-coloring reduction with three team splits. SAT reduces to singleton assignments because PDL is downward closed, making dependence atoms true and split disjunction classical; SAT by split count is solved by partial assignments with conflict markers and at most 2^k candidates. m-SAT adds a unary requested team size and is FPT for number of variables, formula size, or depth but paraNP-complete for team-size or dep-arity. The table leaves m-SAT under formula-treewidth and split count unresolved.

    - title: Checking Qualitative Liveness Properties of Replicated Systems with Stochastic Scheduling.
    - what: Develops Presburger stage graphs for sound and complete verification of stable-termination/liveness properties of replicated systems with an unknown number of indistinguishable agents and stochastic scheduling. A stage graph is a finite DAG of inductive Presburger configuration sets with ranking certificates. The authors give a decidability/completeness result, an incomplete practical constructor using Z3, well-quasi-order and Petri-net techniques, and evaluate it on population protocols, leader election and mutual exclusion. The paper formalizes replicated systems as 1-conservative Petri/VAS-style multiset rewriting and assumes a scheduler whose transition probabilities depend only on the current configuration and are nonzero for every enabled transition. Proposition 2 characterizes fair-run progress by ranking certificates; Proposition 3 and Theorem 2 establish stage-graph soundness/completeness, while Theorem 3 reduces candidate checking to Presburger satisfiability. Algorithm 1 starts from a potential-reachability overapproximation, computes eventually dead transitions (linear ranking or layer functions), and splits stages when needed. Exact dead-state sets are computable via backward reachability but can be doubly exponential; the practical procedure is incomplete. Z3 experiments build mostly chains of at most three stages (five for approximate majority), verify infinite families of protocols, and produce independently checkable invariant/ranking certificates.

    - what: Tiramisu verifies distributed routing configurations by building multilayer graphs of routing processes, VLANs, physical links and route attributes. It chooses a policy-specific algorithm: path-vector simulation for actual path selection, integer linear programs for quantitative path metrics, and graph traversal for potential path existence. A Yen-based accelerator avoids enumerating some failures. The paper gives conditional handwritten correctness arguments and performance comparisons on real and synthetic configurations. Records RAG tainting and TPG construction, L2 contraction, routing-algebra operations and convergence boundary, physical-failure correlation, complete ILPs and TDFS/TYEN listings, ACL repair example, all tables, detailed baseline conditions/core counts, unsupported feature combinations, and qualified printed-formula/listing/proof concerns rather than treating broad speed or correctness claims as universal.
    - limits: §§4.1–4.2: A routing adjacency graph (RAG) is built per destination subnet. Vertices are routing processes and static-route holders; paired edges encode BGP/OSPF adjacency and directed edges encode redistribution. Route-origin vertices are tainted, propagating except across consecutive iBGP edges. This preliminary phase assumes active adjacencies and no filtering; traffic propagation graphs (TPGs) subsequently model those dependencies and filters. §4.2: A TPG is built per source/destination subnet pair. Vertices include process RIBs, per-device VLAN ingress/egress, source and destination. Edges encode physical VLAN-compatible links, L2 flooding, process dependence on L2 or OSPF routes to BGP next hops, and attachments to processes tainted for destination. VRFs replicate process vertices. Parsing/device configuration, topology, protocol settings and concrete advertised prefixes form the trusted input. §4.2: Prefix/neighbor route filters and source/destination IP ACLs prune edges. Other edge labels add/remove/block route tags or carry metric vectors (administrative distance, local preference, AS-path length, OSPF cost). Import/export actions are placed on importing-process outgoing edges. Traffic traverses opposite to route advertisements: blocked-tag information propagates toward tag-adding edges. Shared physical-link variables correlate multiple logical protocol edges under failures. §5.1: Layer-3 TPG contracts L2 paths whenever connectivity exists, combining non-overlapping labels. Routing algebra has signatures, a preference relation, labels, a composition operator and origination signature. Composition and comparison are per protocol: BGP sets local preference, adds AS-path length and uses OSPF tie-breaking; administrative distance mediates protocol choice. Full protocol implementation semantics and parser refinement are not mechanized. §5.1/Algorithm 1/Appendix C.1: TPVP starts destination with origination and other nodes empty, repeatedly composes neighbor paths/signatures and picks locally preferred paths in shared-memory order until paths stop changing. Theorem 1 is conditional on network convergence and supported routing algebras. Lemmas 2–6 argue permitted-path, contraction and ranking correspondence by node/protocol cases, then compare round-robin TPVP to path-vector protocol scheduling. Footnote 4 assumes the algebra has all properties needed for convergence; no general termination theorem for arbitrary configurations. - Two-Layer HLC/SMT Monitor (2020)
    - title: Efficient Two-Layered Monitor for Partially Synchronous Distributed Systems
    - what: Combines an efficient HLC γ-extension filter with an accurate SMT predicate detector. The filter controls false-positive/false-negative trade-offs; the SMT second layer checks only marked windows, yielding constant-size clocks and large monitoring-time reductions for partially synchronous distributed systems. The model assumes bounded clock skew ε but no message-delay bound, and expresses violations as predicates over process variables. ε-extension considers all states within skew to remove false negatives for supported predicates, while γ<ε reduces candidate windows at the cost of recall. The second layer encodes event intervals, causality, skew, and predicate truth as SMT constraints; batching 100 windows amortizes solver calls. Experiments simulate 10 round-robin processes (one million iterations each) and evaluate precision/recall across message probability α, state-true probability β, delay δ, skew ε, and duration ℓ, then test mutual exclusion in time-division multiplexing.
    - number: γ=0.045 setting: precision falls 0.929→0.295 as γ goes 0.1ε→ε while recall rises 0.009→1
    - number: for n=10, δ=10, ε=100, α=0.1: two-layer 3.1 s versus single-layer 81 s
    - number: average cost reduction 90%, minimum 85%; second-layer maximum 2.5 s
    - number: γ=0.25ε example costs 228 ms with false-negative rate 0.627
    - limits: Partial synchrony and known (or estimated) ε are required for the accuracy guarantees; predicate detection remains NP-complete in general. HLC γ-extension cannot handle all predicates and may produce false negatives when γ<ε. The two-layer monitor has perfect precision because SMT filters false positives, but recall is only perfect at γ=ε and runtime may become a bottleneck if the filter marks too many windows. Experiments are simulations and one mutual-exclusion application.

- Unbounded SDE safety (2020)
    - title: Unbounded-Time Safety Verification of Stochastic Differential Dynamics.
    - what: Reduces infinite-horizon probabilistic safety for nonlinear polynomial Ito SDEs to finite-horizon verification. Exponential stochastic barrier certificates give an exponentially decreasing tail bound; time-dependent polynomial barriers and SDP then bound the selected finite interval. Defines the stopped diffusion and infinitesimal generator, uses vector supermartingales and Doob maximal inequality to prove tail bounds, and gives sufficient conditions for time-dependent finite-time certificates. The reduction picks a horizon after which the tail is below any requested epsilon. SDP templates synthesize both certificate types, while matrix exponentials handle vector certificates. The full paper evaluates three examples: scalar population dynamics, a noisy harmonic oscillator and a two-dimensional nonlinear drift system.

    - what: Presents an integrated VerifAI design workflow for an industrial Boeing TaxiNet aircraft-taxiing controller: Scenic models semantic runway environments, active search drives X-Plane closed-loop simulation, counterexamples are analyzed and targeted tests confirm causes, and retraining uses discovered failures. The paper extends Scenic with externally assigned parameters so active samplers can replace fixed probabilistic draws, and implements a VerifAI client/server interface to X-Plane datarefs. In the six-dimensional case study, 4,000 nominal runs found only 55.2% satisfying the eventually-centerline property and 9.1% leaving the runway. Visualization localized failures to dim lighting, cloud/time interactions, runway intersections around 1,450 m, and aircraft shadows; disabling shadows confirmed the hypothesized root cause. Replacing the neural net with ground-truth errors made every counterexample satisfy the property, localizing faults to perception. Generic, Halton, and specialized retraining raised satisfaction to 82%, 83%, and 86%, respectively, and reduced runway departures to 3.9%, 0.6%, and 0.5%; cross-entropy sampling learned a failure-focused distribution, but augmentation experiments sometimes regressed performance.

- A Process Calculus for Formally Verifying Blockchain Consensus Protocols (2019)
    - what: # Whole-paper read: A Process Calculus for Formally Verifying Blockchain Consensus Protocols (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Wolfgang Jeltsch; arXiv1911.08033v1,19November2019,16pages. The result is the ♮-calculus, pronounced “natural calculus,” and an Isabelle/HOL theory for reasoning about process behavior. It is infrastructure for a proposed verified Ouroboros implementation. The paper says, “We plan to very soon start using our process calculus for developing a formally verified implementation of the Ouroboros family of consensus protocols.” It does not report that implementation or a consensus safety/liveness proof. [Q0,Q1,Q12]  ## Language and execution model  A process calculus describes communicating programs and the steps they may take. This one embeds its terms in a functional host language. Higher-order abstract syntax means a binder is represented by a host-language function: Receive takes a function from received data to the remainder process, and NewChannel takes a function from the fresh channel to the remainder process. The host handles variable binding, renaming and ordinary computation. The paper focuses on Isabelle/HOL; it describes Haskell execution and automatic conversion to Isabelle terms as the intended workflow, deferring discussion of that embedding. No verified Haskell translation or runtime correspondence result is supplied here. [Q2,Q3]  The five constructors are Stop, Send, Receive, Parallel and NewChannel. Processes are coinductively defined, allowing infinite terms. Examples include forwarding a received value to two channels, forwarding only when the value differs from a given value, and replication represented by p∞=p∥p∞. Send has no continuation. Although the communication rule synchronizes sender and receiver, this restriction makes synchrony unobservable in the stated calculus. There is no explicit nondeterministic-choice constructor; this does not make concurrent scheduling deterministic. Computation, branching and recursion are placed in the host language. [Q3]  The calculus permits arbitrary transmitted data, including pairs or lists containing several local channels. Publishing such data can open several channel scopes at once. A single conventional transition rule would then combine sending, scope opening and closing. The paper separates these concerns into two layers. Basic transitions expose opening as its own step. Proper transitions combine opening steps with sending, while receiving and internal communication refer back to basic transitions. The printed one-channel and two-channel publication rules show how this composition works. Some symmetric/general rules and the complete proper-residual datatype are omitted from the exposition, with formalization sources linked separately. [Q4,Q5]  A residual bundles a transition's label with its target process, because a label's bound channel can also bind occurrences in that target. Thus transitions relate a source process to a residual rather than treating source, label and target as independent entities. Basic residuals have acting and opening constructors; nesting residuals supports later composition. To compare residuals, a lifting operation extends a relation on processes to matching labels and related targets. In the opening case the targets must be related for every channel argument. Bisimilarity then means each process can match the other's transitions while preserving that relation. [Q5,Q6]  ## Generic results and assumptions  The main reuse mechanism is to prove transition theory once for an abstract residual lifting operation, then establish its axioms for each concrete residual type. Section3.1 prints preservation of equality, relational composition and converse. These are presented as the laws of a relator, a mapping on types and relations that preserves that structure. This differs from an ordinary Haskell functor on types and functions. Isabelle-generated datatype relators supply the intended concrete instances. The source locale additionally makes monotonicity explicit; the printed three-law presentation and actual locale assumptions should therefore be kept distinct. I do not establish whether that additional law is derivable from the printed ones. [Q7,Q8,S3]  Strong bisimilarity matches individual steps. Weak bisimilarity permits internal communication to be ignored. Since the generic residual interface hides labels, the paper introduces silent, which adds a silent label, and fuse, which removes silence from nested residuals. Weak transitions are inductively generated by strong steps, empty silent steps and composition through lifted weak transitions followed by fuse. Five printed laws—two naturality laws, two neutrality laws and associativity—give a monad structure on types and relations. They are assumptions of the reusable construction, not proved facts about every possible transition system. The paper reports formal proofs that weak bisimilarity equals mixed bisimilarity, where strong steps are matched by weak ones, and that strong bisimilarity is contained in weak bisimilarity. [Q9]  For the usual single silent label, Section3.3 requires a natural silent relation that is left-total and unique on both sides. It derives fuse as the union of the converse of silent and its lifted converse, and states that these satisfy the general weak-residual laws. This reduces the per-instance proof burden. These are generic behavioral-equivalence results; no fairness, adversarial stake model, probabilistic security, real-time bound or consensus termination theorem is established in this paper. [Q10]  ## Known limits and concrete counterexample  The proper transition system can open a scope even when the channel is not transmitted. The author explicitly gives νb.a◁x → a◁νb.x with target0, where x does not depend on b, and says a fix is under investigation. This is a disclosed semantic issue in the presented concrete calculus. It does not by itself invalidate the generic theorems conditional on residual laws, which are largely independent of this calculus. [Q5]  Higher-order abstract syntax also permits process structure to depend on channels, including local channels. Such channel-dependent branching is unwanted here, while branching on ordinary data is intended. Related work excludes or separately characterizes these terms; the author explains that making channels abstract does not eliminate them in classical Isabelle/HOL. Preventing channel-dependent behavior while retaining host-language binding remains future work. These unresolved expressiveness/semantics restrictions matter before treating the calculus as an adequate model of a particular network implementation. [Q11,Q12]  ## Evaluation and pinned source inspection  The evidence is mathematical construction, worked syntax/transition examples and reported Isabelle formalization. The paper says “large parts” of the calculus and the “complete theory of transition systems” were formalized, and that the document was produced from Isabelle source checked against that formalization. It gives no runtime experiment, benchmark table, proof-development time, proof-size accounting, end-to-end protocol case or comparison of verification effort. Its acknowledgements mention network-equivalence proofs, without presenting a measured evaluation of them. There are18references and no numbered figures or tables. [Q1,Q12]  Reference10 pins input-output-hk/fm-ouroboros at bbeec3136ae68e7bb6800680e216b12db6c1113a. I statically read seven saved files: README, Channels.thy, Processes.thy, Residuals.thy, Weak_Residuals.thy, Std_Weak_Residuals.thy and Weak_Transition_Systems.thy. They total28,155bytes; each SHA256 and Git-blob identity matches the nontruncated188-entry pinned tree. The source directories use Chi_Calculus naming. Channels declares abstract chan/val types, Processes has the five constructors, and the weak-transition theory includes explicit proof scripts for weak/mixed equivalence and strong-bisimilarity inclusion. This is a targeted sample, not an audit of the complete calculus or dependency closure. Imported theories, the referenced binder-preservation ML and Haskell implementation were not read or run. [S0–S6]  The pinned weak-residual interface uses silent plus an absorb operation, deriving lift from them; the paper instead presents lift/silent/fuse. Its weak-transition composition rule is correspondingly expressed through absorb. The standard-weak-residual theory proves a sublocale interpretation into that interface. These are source/presentation differences, not a checked equivalence between the two formulations. Residuals.thy explicitly assumes lift monotonicity; Weak_Residuals.thy assumes absorb monotonicity and notes that this is needed for the inductive weak-transition definition. [S3–S6]  The README specifies Isabelle2018 and offers a default properly build rejecting sorry, plus a qnd build accepting fake proofs. I did not run either mode, so the build instructions do not establish a fresh successful check. No assertion about the admission status of the entire uninspected dependency closure follows from this source sample. The paper's machine-checking statements remain author-reported; the saved source supplies statically inspectable declarations and proof scripts. [S0,S2–S6]  ## Contribution to the requested topic  This adds an approach to reusable mechanized semantics for distributed programs: represent binding in residuals, separate channel-scope handling from communication, and prove behavioral-equivalence infrastructure against explicit algebraic interfaces. For specification/proof agents, my inference is to evaluate semantic adequacy, locale assumptions, concrete instantiations, source-version correspondence and intended protocol properties separately from the presence of proof scripts. The paper contains no Verus/verified-Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment. [Q2,Q5,Q7–Q12,S3–S6]  Read all16pages,18references,every printed constructor/rule/formula/example and all16page renders. Official and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. Read the seven static source files above. No author code or embedded ML was executed/imported; no compiler, checker, prover or solver was run; no serialized scientific results were loaded.

- A Verified Compositional Algorithm for AI Planning (2019)
    - what: HOL4 soundness proof for synthesizing a concrete plan by composing instantiated solutions to an augmented descriptive quotient. Builds a polymorphic factored transition-system library, sufficient subplan precedence/coverage conditions and an action-filtering repair. Formalization exposes two missing assumptions in an earlier mathematical algorithm and generalizes soundness beyond Boolean finite-state symmetry-derived quotients. Needed initial assignments, a pairwise precedence relation, coverage by actual subproblems, bijective variable renaming, cross-instantiation variable consistency and restoration of shared needed resources jointly justify concatenation. A total no-op semantics for inapplicable actions makes individually harmless plan steps dangerous after composition; rem-cless deletes them before instantiation/concatenation. The final theorem is conditional on supplied quotient, valid instantiations and a quotient solution, not a verified general-purpose planner search procedure.
    - limits: States are finite maps from variable type α to arbitrary value type β. Actions are pairs of finite maps for preconditions/effects; applying one with unsatisfied preconditions leaves the state unchanged. Effects override existing assignments. This differs from classical planning semantics that prohibit inapplicable steps. Valid problems require the initial-state domain equal the union of action domains and the goal domain contained there. Although β and the action set can be infinite/uncountable, each valid state is a finite map and a returned plan is a finite action list. Generic assignment semantics does not already formalize arbitrary continuous dynamics or functional numeric preconditions/effects. A solution consists of actions from the problem’s action set and reaches a state extending the goal. Theorems establish soundness when the premises hold; they do not promise finding a quotient, a plan, complete reachability search, optimality, termination of a subplanner, or successful planning for every solvable concrete input. Needed assignments include initial assignments occurring in any action precondition or the goal. They are conservative sufficient support, not a claimed smallest plan-dependent set. Transfer of a plan to another compatible state also requires every step’s precondition hold when run from the needed partial state. Precedence requires the first goal contain the second problem’s shared needed assignments and both goals have identical assignments on the intersection of the two problem domains. Concatenation requires this relation for every earlier/later pair, not merely adjacent problems. Subproblem coverage requires consistent initial submaps, action-set inclusion and covering every concrete goal assignment. Variable instantiations must be bijective on relevant variable sets, and pwise-valid prevents distinct quotient variables from colliding across different instantiations. Shared quotient variables may map to the same concrete variable. Final HOL statement additionally requires distinct instantiation functions and injectivity of the induced instantiated-problem mapping. The quotient goal is augmented to restore initial values of common needed variables; the final theorem requires the augmented instantiated problems cover the concrete problem. Any ordering of a finite valid instantiation list then works after rem-cless filtering. No assumption that the quotient came from symmetry is needed once these explicit conditions hold. The assurance is HOL4 theorem derivation over the specified action semantics/library. The paper does not give an extracted implementation refinement, end-to-end parser/executable proof, verified symmetry detector or verified subplanner. Reader did not rerun the available scripts. No distributed-system implementation, Verus/Rust proof, TLA+ integration, LLM agent experiment or user study is evaluated. Murphi compositional model checking is a suggested adaptation, not a verified result of this development.

Formal verification of hybrid systems is of significant practical interest because the CPSs > they model frequently operate in safety-critical settings. Bounded staging removes the global Lipschitz requirement: the trajectory stays in a bounded staging region until the target, and one fixed positive derivative forces it to exit. Compact staging needs only a strictly positive derivative because a continuous derivative attains a positive minimum there. - Approximate synthesis (2019)
    - title: Synthesizing Approximate Implementations for Unrealizable Specifications
    - what: Synthesizes reactive implementations against environments whose infinite input words have bounded ultimately periodic representations. A k-lasso-precise implementation satisfies the specification for every input word represented by a lasso of length at most k. An ε-k approximation instead satisfies it on at least a 1−ε fraction of those distinct input words. Sections 3–4 formalize transition systems, lassos and the difference between bounding input words and bounding environment state. Proposition 1 connects the two using an implementation-size factor. A deterministic automaton recognizes bounded-lasso prefixes; an exponential lower bound shows why this recognition is costly. Composing it with a deterministic parity specification yields an exact synthesis algorithm. Section 5 gives a bounded-state QBF encoding with O(|φ|+n²+k²) formula size as stated by the paper, with input-alphabet size present in the variable count. Section 6 reduces approximation to maximum model counting over transition/output choices and input words. Auxiliary unrollings of length 2k prevent double counting different lassos that denote the same infinite word. Section 7 implements the encodings with CAQE and MaxCount and evaluates greedy and round-robin arbiters.
    - number: 11 experimental rows
    - number: round-robin: 2 states, k=4, rate 0.5 in 26 s
    - number: round-robin: 4 states, k=2, exact 12.15 s, approximate rate 0.88 in 283 s
    - number: greedy: 1 process, 2 states, k=2, exact 0.41 s, rate 1 in 0.79 s
    - limits: All correctness and approximation claims are relative to bounded input lassos, not unrestricted environments or an empirical probability distribution. A bounded environment state space and bounded lasso length are related but distinct restrictions. The automata algorithms are exponential in k; symbolic instances also grow quickly with state bound and process count. Table 1 contains timeouts and an approximate solver result of 0.88 even for a case where exact QBF synthesis succeeds, so the reported MaxCount solutions need not reach the optimal rate. Hardware and timeout duration are not specified in the experimental section.

- ATL star vCGS undecidability (2019)
    - title: Model Checking ATL* on vCGS
    - what: Shows that model checking ATL* and ATL on visible concurrent game structures (vCGS) is undecidable by a polynomial-time reduction from imperfect-information concurrent game structures (iCGS). The construction adds an environment agent, atoms encoding actions, states and indistinguishability classes, visibility predicates, turn variables and guarded commands. It simulates each iCGS step with two vCGS transitions, so formulas duplicate each next operator. Theorem 1 states PTIME reducibility and Corollary 1 transfers undecidability; under positional strategies, the known PSPACE/ΔP2 completeness results also transfer.
    - number: PTIME reduction
    - number: ATL* and ATL undecidable under imperfect information/perfect recall
    - number: positional-strategy cases PSPACE-complete and ΔP²-complete
    - limits: The reduction is for the specified vCGS semantics and imperfect-information/perfect-recall iCGS source; it establishes decidability limits rather than an executable implementation. Formula translation duplicates next operators, and the complexity claims distinguish unrestricted perfect recall from positional strategies. No experiments are reported.

- Bayer et al. DPRM 2019 (2019)
    - title: The DPRM Theorem in Isabelle
    - what: Reports ongoing Isabelle work toward the Davis-Putnam-Robinson-Matiyasevich theorem, that recursively enumerable natural-number sets are Diophantine. Completed components include an exponentiation representation and register-machine execution implying satisfaction of 15 encoded equations. The converse direction and two Diophantine relation proofs remain unfinished in this paper; the later halting-undecidability connection is also future work. Reads both arithmetization directions and unfinished dependency chain, variable-binding/representation difficulties, finite-base trace packing, initial validity conditions, exponentiation proof resources and two boundary errors in the printed arithmetic statements. Distinguishes a whole-paper reading from a completed formalization.
    - limits: Polynomials use integer constants with natural parameters and existential natural witnesses. A predicate is Diophantine when equivalent to an existential polynomial-zero equation. Closure under conjunction/disjunction requires correct relabeling and separation of witnesses; it does not imply closure under arbitrary negation or universal quantification (§2). Tuple choices include finite lists versus index-to-natural maps, with separate or combined parameter/witness namespaces. The currently most successful implementation uses one nat⇒nat map for both. Exchange/relabeling is a major proof burden; alternative implementations are still being explored. These representation choices are consequential proof-engineering evidence rather than an automatic general compiler (§2). Binary orthogonality forbids shared 1 bits; masking requires each bit of a to be at most the corresponding bit of b. AND is characterized by c masking both a,b and residuals (a−c),(b−c) orthogonal. Number-theoretic digit operations and Lucas’s theorem support these reductions, but §6 explicitly leaves binary AND/masking Diophantine integration unproved. A displayed mathematical relation is not evidence every is_diophantine obligation was discharged (§2). Exponentiation uses α_b(0)=0, α_b(1)=1 and α_b(n+2)=b*α_b(n+1)−α_b(n), b≥2. α_2 is linear; larger b gives exponential bounds. A 2×2-matrix route supplies divisibility/congruence facts and, for b>3, 15 equations in eight witnesses plus a,b,c parameters for a=α_b(c). This 15-equation system is distinct from the later 15 register-machine equations (§3). Theorem 4’s exponentiation representation is reported fully formalized in 2800 lines and 86 intermediate lemmas, plus 270 lines for is_diophantine Pexp. This component does not complete the register-machine or overall DPRM proof. No formal source audit/checker rerun was performed (§3). Reader-identified printed errors, confirmed on rendered p.33:4: the q=0 branch uses r<0 despite all variables natural, so cannot express 0^r=0 for positive r. Example p=0,q=0,r=1 has true exponentiation but no displayed branch: the first/second fail, and the third has m=bq−q²−1≤0, making p<m impossible. Intended branch is r>0. Also the preceding congruence q^r≡q*α_b(r)−α_b(r−1) needs r≥1 under the declared natural indexing: at r=0 the truncated r−1 gives right side 0, not 1 modulo m>1. The later expanded formula avoids the negative index. These presentation defects do not establish a false underlying formal theorem. Minsky machines have finitely many natural-valued registers and states; program states contain increment-and-jump, conditional decrement-and-jump or halt. Configuration is (program counter, register list), and execution follows a fetch/update/step cycle. Initial validity includes in-bounds register/state references and exactly one halt state. The paper does not enumerate all implementation invariants or provide machine instruction code (§4 and footnote 2). Arithmetization introduces register values, one-hot state indicators and nonzero indicators at each time. To replace an input-dependent number of time-indexed equations, packs each finite history into digits of one natural number using a sufficiently large power-of-two base; masking expresses zero-indicator bit bounds. Existentially encoded finite traces establish halting, not a fixed universal time bound for every input (§4). The reported completed direction is halting of an initially valid machine implies satisfaction of the 15 time-independent equations (2400 lines). The reverse, equation satisfaction implies an actual halting execution, is unfinished (1100 lines so far), needing equation properties and digit utilities. This missing direction matters: without it, spurious arithmetic witnesses have not been formally excluded (§4). §5 defines recursively enumerable sets through machines starting at counter 0 and tape [a,0,…,0], halting exactly for members. Theorem 6 prints the intended implication is_recursively_enumerable A⇒is_diophantine A, but §6 states the overall formalization remains incomplete. Treat Theorem 6 as the target mathematical theorem and dependency assembly, not a finished end-to-end Isabelle proof. Even completing DPRM does not by itself constitute this project’s formalized undecidability proof of Hilbert’s tenth problem. §6 still requires a bridge to halting undecidability for this specific machine implementation, either proving equivalence to existing Abacus/Turing formalizations or proving its undecidability directly. Mathematical equivalence known externally does not discharge that formal proof obligation. Project reports 20 months elapsed and implementation by undergraduates with no prior formalization experience; supervisor was not directly implementing. The first-major-nonexpert claim is qualified by the authors’ knowledge. This is a descriptive experience report, not a controlled study of novice performance or proof-agent productivity. No runtime, resource benchmark or proof-checking metrics are reported (§6). Paper links the evolving GitLab formalization and plans an AFP submission. Present-day repository completion was not investigated; record reflects this 2019 paper only. No artifact run, distributed-system protocol, Verus/verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM evaluation. Relevance to proof/specification evaluation is a reader inference about accounting for missing directions and dependencies.

- Brown et al. HOTG 2019 (2019)
    - title: Higher-Order Tarski Grothendieck as a Foundation for Formal Proof
    - what: Constructs a standard model of higher-order Tarski Grothendieck set theory assuming a 2-inaccessible cardinal, then combines Isabelle/HOL and Isabelle/Mizar results by proving representation bijections and preservation of operations. Demonstrates number-theory theorem transfer and alignment of lists, functions, groups and rings. Separates mathematical model construction from the explicitly Isabelle-formalized integration section; records the least-universe/choice construction, restricted domains, type and index conversions, concrete theorem scope, two repairable printed errors, manual integration and the limited evaluation evidence.
    - limits: §2 uses Church simple types, nonempty Henkin domains, logical equality/quantifiers and Hilbert choice. Standard frames contain all functions between domains; general Henkin frames may contain subsets. Models require a total logical interpretation of terms. Soundness/completeness is cited from existing literature; this paper focuses on axiom sets rather than a new proof calculus. §3 adds set type ι and membership, empty set, union, powerset, replacement and an explicit least-universe constructor. Ten axioms include extensionality, membership induction and four universe clauses. Choice is required for the claimed equivalence between explicit universes and existence-only presentations. §2 leaves equivalence of alternative HOTG axiomatizations to future work; do not treat that equivalence as already formally proved here. §4 assumes ordinary well-founded set theory and large cardinals. A 2-inaccessible cardinal is a regular limit of inaccessible cardinals, whose existence is assumed, not proved. Theorem 9 supplies a sufficient relative satisfiability result, not unconditional consistency, a converse or an equiconsistency theorem. The model interprets set objects as Vκ, truth values as {0,1}, and arrow types as full function spaces. Universes are transitive and closed under pairs, powersets and indexed unions, giving union/image closure. For each A, an inaccessible κ′ above its rank and below κ supplies a containing universe; intersecting all such universes yields the least one. Choice on Vκ+ω supplies variables and typed choice operators. Higher-order function objects need not themselves be members of the set domain Vκ (§4, Theorems 7–9). Theorem 7 checks each HOTG axiom for a standard set-theoretic interpretation with a universe function. Theorem 8 constructs that interpretation under the 2-inaccessible assumption. These are written mathematical proofs. The paper explicitly says all §5 definitions/theorems were formalized in Isabelle; it does not explicitly make the same machine-formalization claim for the §4 model construction. Reader-identified printed error, visually confirmed on p.9:7: the UnivMin proof defines f on ℘(℘A), then writes f(A)=x. An arbitrary A need not belong to that domain. The witness f(℘A)=x repairs the pair argument because A∈℘A and ℘A∈℘(℘A), with f(∅)=y. This local presentation error does not establish a false main result or an unsound formal artifact. Reader-identified printed error, visually confirmed on p.9:8: Definition 10 types s2h:ι→σ and h2s:σ→ι but its last condition is ∀x:σ.s2h(x)∈d, generally ill-typed. The displayed Isabelle definition on the same page correctly uses h2s(y) in d. The intended range condition is h2s(x)∈d; no formal-source defect inferred. §5 uses two object logics inside the Isabelle logical framework, with separate HOL/set equalities and meta/object implication. This is not a verified import of arbitrary native Mizar kernel derivations. §6 limits this work to the Isabelle specification of Mizar and re-formalized MML parts. Introductory library sizes describe context, not complete successful integration of those libraries. beIsoS combines inverse equations, restricting the set-to-HOL inverse to elements of d, and the HOL-to-set range condition. Since HOL types are nonempty, the corresponding set must be inhabited. Type/domain restrictions remain necessary even when syntactic contexts hide them. A matching name or unproved correspondence is insufficient: transfer uses proved bijections and operator-preservation equations (§5). Natural-number alignment relates Mizar’s least limit ordinal and HOL’s subtype of individuals. Recursive zero/successor maps are inverse on Nat; the inverse is defined on all sets with undefined outside Nat. Termination uses proper subset ordering on Peano naturals. Proved preservation includes addition, multiplication, comparison, divisibility and primality (§5.1). Transfers Lagrange’s four-square theorem and Bertrand’s postulate by higher-order rewriting. Integer alignment is analogous; missing exponentiation is lifted by converting set inputs to HOL, applying the HOL operation and converting its output back. Fermat-divides-3-4 covers integer x,y,z and natural n divisible by 3 or 4, concluding xyz=0 if x^n+y^n=z^n. This is not the full Fermat theorem for every exponent above 2 (§5.1). Polymorphic HOL lists (Nil/Cons) correspond to one-based finite-sequence functions, parameterized by the element bijection. Cons maps to singleton concatenation; the inverse takes index 1 and shifts the tail. Its termination follows length. Length/concatenation/index preservation includes the zero-based HOL versus one-based Mizar successor offset. Set-of-pairs functions correspond to HOL functions under domain/range bijections and preserve application (§5.2). Group and ring alignment must reconcile HOL type classes/records with explicit set carriers, named fields and intersection types. Mizar additive and multiplicative groups have distinct library theories. Omitting an explicit unit field in one forward representation does not remove the neutral-element proof obligation; the inverse selects 1.g. Ring mapping preserves zero, one, addition, multiplication and ring validity; the integer ring is aligned explicitly (§5.3). Introduction claims transfers involving Euclidean spaces, Brouwer fixed points and topological invariance results, while detailed §5 examples cover numbers, lists, functions, groups and rings. The printed paper supplies no displayed topological transfer derivation; the linked artifact remains unread, so those introduction claims are not independently confirmed by artifact inspection. Evaluation is a model argument plus formal examples and reported proof-development size: 18 definitions, 135 theorems, 2667 proof lines. No transfer runtime, proof-checking runtime, automatic alignment accuracy, benchmark comparison or repeated-run measurements are reported. Integration is described as mostly manual. Dependent-type foundation integration is future work (§§1,7). The Isabelle/TLA mention is related-work context about higher-order features in object logics, not an evaluated TLA+ distributed-protocol verification. No distributed algorithm, verified Rust/Verus implementation or LLM proof/specification agent experiment appears. Relevant methodological lessons about preserving meaning across representations are reader inferences. Artifact not fetched or executed.

- Characteristic Formulae for Liveness Properties of Non-Terminating CakeML Programs (2019)
    - what: Extends CakeML characteristic formulae and Hoare triples to prove total-correctness liveness properties of diverging programs. Divergent results carry lazy I/O traces; a clocked big-step semantics defines divergence as timeout at every clock and the supremum of finite-clock I/O prefixes. A transfinite-induction rule for repeat loops reduces proofs to terminating loop-body triples plus a limit-stream equation. A verified source transformation rewrites tail-recursive functions to repeat form. The framework is mechanized in HOL4 and integrated with CakeML. The semantics adds Div and FFIDiv results and POSTd predicates while preserving local separation reasoning. The repeat rule has base, successor and limit cases and a limited_parts side condition controlling all FFI resources. The transformation injects a runtime error in non-tail return branches so a transformed terminating function cannot be incorrectly treated as diverging; it is proved sound only for POSTd. Examples include silent pureLoop, conditional condLoop, infinite/finite catLoop over lazy input, cyclic pointerLoop, uncurried myRepeat, and a seL4 UAV filter. The filter proof shrinks from 1,971 lines of direct operational-semantics HOL to 1,479 lines with CF and yields an operational theorem; compiler liveness transfer remains conditional on no out-of-memory.
