- Deconstructing Stellar Consensus (Extended Version) (2019)
    - what: # Reading: Deconstructing Stellar Consensus (Extended Version) (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  García-Pérez and Schett's arXiv 1911.05145 v3 (13 December 2019) gives a mathematical account of Stellar's ballot protocol. Its main construction separates federated voting, an idealized abstract consensus protocol and a concrete protocol that compresses voting statements. Read all 43 pages, eight main sections, Appendices A–E, four algorithms, four figures, all numbered arguments and 16 references. The paper has five theorem statements, four corollaries and 44 lemmas. All 43 page renders inspected through 11 contacts; pages 5, 12, 23, 29, 30, 33, 36 and 37 individually. The paper supplies mathematical proofs and illustrative executions, not a mechanically checked development or an evaluation of deployed Stellar code.  The model fixes a finite universe V. A correct node follows the protocol; an honest node may additionally stop; a malicious node may deviate otherwise. Every pair has an authenticated perfect link. Partial synchrony provides a finite unknown GST after which message delays are bounded; correct timers have bounded disagreement over a given delay after GST. Trust configuration is an input to the proofs. Open membership motivates federated quorums, but this model does not prove dynamic membership changes, trust-list discovery or correctness of a complete blockchain (§§1–2).  A federated Byzantine quorum system (FBQS) assigns each node a nonempty family of slices, each containing that node. A nonempty set is a quorum if every member has a slice wholly within it. Two correct nodes are intertwined when any quorum containing the first intersects any quorum containing the second in a correct node. An intact set I is itself a quorum and its projection has the required intersection between its members. Lemma 3 gives intersection inside I for any two quorums that touch I; Lemma 4 makes intersecting intact sets merge, hence distinct maximal intact sets are disjoint. Agreement is local to an intact set. The four-node Example 2 with faulty v3 has maximal intact sets {v1,v2} and {v4}; the two sets can disagree. In contrast, the classical 3f+1 construction with 2f+1 slices and at most f faults has all correct nodes in one maximal intact set (§2; Appendix A).  The specification requires output once, agreement within each maximal intact set, and weak validity conditional on every node being honest. Under that condition, unanimous proposals force their value and any decided value must have some proposer. It does not require a correct proposer when malicious nodes exist. Its liveness condition is non-blocking: from any prefix, an undecided intact node eventually decides in every admissible continuation where all malicious nodes stop. The authors explicitly say that continuing malicious traffic with good timing can delay termination permanently for their chosen timeout strategy. Thus this is not unconditional Byzantine termination. Section 3's subsequent broad sentence about entailing usual weak consensus in 3f+1 systems, and its phrase “if every correct node is honest,” need that earlier condition retained: correctness already entails honesty, and cardinality quorum intersection alone does not remove the continuing-malicious-traffic case (§3, pp4–5).  Federated voting (FV) is a tagged Bracha-style primitive. A node first sends VOTE(a); a quorum containing the recipient enables READY(a); a set intersecting every one of that recipient's slices also enables READY(a); a quorum containing the recipient enables delivery. Those slice-intersecting sets are called v-blocking. Each intact node's blocking set touches I. Therefore its first READY for a value is justified by a quorum, preventing conflicting READY values inside I. Theorem 6 proves no duplicate deliveries, totality inside I, consistency for intertwined nodes and delivery when all nodes in I vote alike. A finite propagation argument yields an unknown bounded post-GST delivery delay δ_I once one node in I has delivered. FV alone does not guarantee a decision from arbitrary split votes (§4; Appendix B).  The condition that the recipient belong to the supporting quorum is essential. In Example 2, {v3} is a quorum. If v3 is malicious and the recipient-membership condition is removed, it can send different READY values to v1 and v2 and make these intact peers deliver differently. Figure 1 gives a separate benign voting pattern over four classical nodes: two correct nodes vote false, one votes true and the malicious node helps false. The last correct node changes from its VOTE(true) to READY(false) after a blocking set persuades it. Changing a readiness value relative to one's vote is intended behavior, rather than equivocation (§4, Figure 1, Example 8).  The abstract SCP (ASCP) uses ballots (n,x), ordered first by positive round n and then totally ordered value x, plus a null ballot. It runs a Boolean FV instance for each ballot. Voting false aborts that ballot; voting true tries to commit it. To prepare b, a node delivers false for every lower ballot carrying a different value. It may then raise its candidate to the prepared ballot and vote true. Committing b decides x and stops the node. Safety combines Lemma 9, that a committed ballot had an intact preparer, with Lemma 10, that preparing a higher incompatible ballot excludes an intact READY-to-commit for a lower one. Lemma 11 tracks a largest prepared value back to some proposal when all nodes are honest. Ready-trees, whose leaves are voting quorums, support this validity argument (Algorithm 2; §§5 and Appendix C).  ASCP is an idealization: it allocates infinitely many FV states and can process infinitely many ballot messages in one step. Batched network semantics sends possibly infinite sequences atomically and processes an entire received batch atomically in ballot order. These semantics do substantive proof work; they are not a measured implementation optimization. A formalization must specify admissible ordered sequences and existence of the maxima used by later definitions; a bare totally ordered value domain does not by itself provide every enumeration or maximum. The paper abstracts from Stellar's nomination protocol and assumes arbitrary consensus proposals, so its result covers the ballot protocol, not nomination, transaction validation or a ledger implementation (§5, including footnote 1).  A quorum of messages endorsing higher rounds starts or restarts a timer with delay F(round). A timeout advances to the next round, retaining the largest prepared value if any, otherwise the candidate's value. F doubles with the round. The liveness proof defines a round's prepare-footprint as contributing voting-quorum leaves, its abort interval as their sending interval, and its window as δ_I after the first intact preparation. Lemma 12 claims that sufficiently late windows stop overlapping when faulty nodes stop. Corollary 29 then synchronizes the largest prepared ballot across I; Theorem 13 concludes the peers either commit it or advance together with its value. Figure 2 depicts the required inequality F(n) > δ_A(n)+δ_P+δ_I. A machine proof must bound the round-dependent abort interval and justify eventual domination and persistence of this inequality; doubling F alone does not establish those steps. No numerical termination bound is supplied (§5; Appendix C, pp22–24).  Concrete SCP (CSCP) replaces the infinite FV array with one bunched-voting (BV) process. A prepare statement for b summarizes aborting all lower incompatible ballots; a commit statement names b. BV stores the highest ballots voted, readied and delivered for a prepare statement, plus sets of ballots voted, readied and delivered for commit. A node votes prepare only as its maximum rises; commit voting additionally requires b to equal its maximum voted prepare. Quorum and blocking conditions combine prepare statements by inclusion of the lower-incompatible sets. Algorithm 4 keeps the abstract candidate/prepared/round logic and replaces Boolean FV calls with prepare/commit indications. State is finite at each finite execution prefix; the growing ballot numbers and commit sets are not a fixed finite-state bound (§6, Algorithms 3–4).  The printed Algorithm 3 has a material guard mismatch. Line 8 checks max-voted-prep < b, whereas the surrounding explanation and the corresponding Appendix D proof use max-readied-prep < b. The statement in the prose describing lower-incompatible inclusion also reverses its direction relative to the displayed formula. A hand case exposes the guard consequence: use four correct nodes with classical three-node quorums, values {0,1}, and unanimous proposals 0. After all invoke prepare((1,0)), their maximum voted prepare is (1,0); the greatest ballot justified by those matching VOTE messages is also (1,0), so the printed strict guard rejects it. With no READY messages, the blocking rule cannot start. In a lockstep execution, timeouts make every node prepare((r,0)) before that round's votes arrive, repeating the same rejected equality each round despite timely delivery. This identifies behavior of the literal displayed guard; it does not refute the intended max-readied-prep version. The paper's own Figure 4 readiness steps also require the intended version (Algorithm 3, p12; §6, p13; Appendix D, p33).  Theorem 14 claims observational refinement: every CSCP execution has an ASCP execution with the same proposal/decision history projected to I. Appendix D defines a simulation σ that expands prepare statements into abort batches, commit messages into true-voting batches, and preserves external events. It proves candidate/prepared/round agreement and several voting-state invariants, then checks all concrete event cases. Lemma 37 handles finite prefixes; the theorem extends to complete traces. These are paper proofs, not a simulation run or proof-tool output (§6; Appendix D).  Several simulation details need explicit repair or justification before mechanization. Definition 31's φ is a maximum over ballots whose lower incompatible ballots have delivered false, and its commit expansion uses φ(σ(τ)) < b′ ≤ b. One must fix the implicit node parameter, establish that the maximum exists, and explain which pre- or post-preparation cutoff includes the true votes generated during preparation. Lemma 33 states a readied commit ballot is at most max-delivered-prep, but Lemma 35 invokes it as a bound by max-readied-prep; the statement and use need reconciliation. The READY(cmt) cases in Lemma 37 assume b > max-readied-prep, a guard not present in Algorithm 3's commit-readiness rules. Receiving a message at a correct recipient also does not by itself rule out contradictory earlier messages from a malicious sender. These are identified proof/encoding obligations, not completed disagreement executions (Appendix D, pp29–35).  The step from finite prefixes to complete traces and the transfer of conditional properties require more than proposal/decision equality. A fair infinite concrete run must map to an admissible fair abstract run with the relevant timing and stopped-malicious-node conditions. Otherwise every finite prefix could be legal while the infinite execution starves an enabled action. Likewise, weak validity's all-honest premise must survive the construction of abstract behavior outside I, whose external proposals are absent from I's history. Corollary 15 cites history equality to transfer all four properties without separately spelling out these premise-preservation arguments. This reading records the claimed refinement and non-blocking result while leaving those obligations open; it supplies no general refutation of SCP (§6; Appendix D, p36).  The authors illustrate matching abstract/concrete histories in Figures 3 and 4 with correct proposals 3, 3 and 1. Nodes first prepare (1,1), then prepare (1,2) with malicious support, fail to gather a commit quorum, timeout, then commit (2,2) and decide 2. The displayed concrete trace is inconsistent with Algorithm 3: besides the already identified READY-prep guard mismatch, v4 votes commit((1,2)) without ever voting prepare((1,2)). Its max-voted-prep remains (1,1), so the line-18 commit guard rejects that vote even after fixing line 8. This is an author illustration, not a certified literal execution of the printed pseudocode; the local mismatch does not by itself establish disagreement or refute the repaired protocol. No correct node proposed 2, which is permitted by the stated validity under malicious behavior. The abstract execution expands an infinite abort batch when entering round two; the concrete one represents it with one prepare statement. These are worked executions, not empirical benchmark results (Appendices C–D, Examples 30 and 38).  Subjective FBQS permits each correct node to have its own view of malicious nodes' slices, while all correct-node slices agree across views. The intact sets coincide across these views (Lemma 16); any two known quorums touching I intersect inside I (Lemma 17). These facts lift FV, ASCP and the refinement to that setting, yielding Theorems 18–19 and Corollary 20. Appendix E gives the lifted lemmas and analogous proofs. It does not allow correct nodes to disagree arbitrarily about each other's slices, nor does it prove that a real trust configuration contains an intact set. The self-reference in Lemma 50's proof is a visible citation error; its intended non-subjective precursor is Lemma 11 (§7; Appendix E).  There are no measured performance results, production-code equivalence claim backed by an artifact, test statistics, TLA+ model, verified Rust/Verus development or LLM-agent experiment in this edition. Its contribution to distributed verification is the explicit guarantee boundary around intact sets, reusable voting lemmas and a concrete-to-abstract proof structure. The guard mismatch, assumption-preserving refinement and finite-prefix/fairness distinctions are concrete cases for evaluating specification/proof agents; that use is a reader inference. No author code, compiler, checker, solver, prover, model checker or scientific-result artifact was executed or loaded. Hand cases above are source reasoning only.
    - limits: fixed finite universe, authenticated perfect links, eventual bounded message delay/timer disagreement; intact-set local agreement; weak validity all-honest; malicious stopping for non-blocking; infinite atomic batches in abstract model; intended concrete guard differs from print; assumption/fairness-preserving refinement obligations

    - what: Coq/CFML verification of an OCaml incremental directed-cycle detector, proving functional correctness and worst-case amortized asymptotic complexity together. Replaces Bender et al. fixed backward-search threshold with the source vertex current level, giving an online algorithm with total sequence bound O(m min(sqrt(m),n^(2/3))+n). Extends separation logic to integer time credits and reports a machine-checked metatheory update. A modular six-statement interface hides representation and potential while exposing telescoping credit charges. Cycle results consume the valid graph capability, so clients cannot keep using the structure after a rejected edge. Local replete-level invariants and partially relaxed forward-search invariants connect correctness to complexity. Negative credits remove repeated subtraction side conditions, but debt may not be discarded; this is backed by an updated soundness argument.

IsGraph owns the graph exclusively and entails acyclicity. No concurrent-client or distributed execution theorem is provided. On Ok, add_edge_or_detect_cycle restores IsGraph for G plus the new edge. On Cycle, it proves reachability w→*v in the original G but returns no IsGraph ownership. Subsequent calls are unsupported, even if a particular failure branch happened not to mutate anything. Time model counts one unit per function call and zero for other primitives. Source-level asymptotic claims do not bound physical CPU time, memory allocation/GC, machine stack or wall-clock latency on a specified platform. OCaml signed integers are modeled as mathematical Z, and the paper explicitly ignores finite-precision overflow. Level increments, marks and fuel reasoning therefore retain this ideal-integer assumption. No verified OCaml compiler/runtime theorem is supplied. Auxiliary graph/mark/level/adjacency operations have specifications and constant-time requirements; a concrete implementation is supplied and verified according to the authors. Generated allocation calls use C calloc/free with architecture-dependent size_t; generator refuses potentially lossy size downcasts. Allocation-failure code exits1 after an error.     - what: Develops model checking for Halpern–Shoham interval temporal logic (HS) over finite Kripke structures and timeline-based system models. It compares HS variants with LTL, CTL, and CTL* under homogeneous semantics, then relaxes homogeneity using regular expressions while preserving or increasing fragment complexity. For dense-time timelines, unrestricted planning is undecidable; simple future trigger rules are decidable via timed automata, with EXPSPACE completeness for non-singular intervals and PSPACE completeness for intervals in Intv(0,∞). MITL model checking reduces inclusion to timed-automata emptiness.

    - what: # Reading: porting Paxos optimizations to Raft* (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Wang, Zhao, Mu, Chen and Li study a modified Raft called Raft*, not a proof that original Raft and Paxos are interchangeable. The whole 61-page extended paper, Appendices A–C, six printed TLA+ modules, 15 figures and 67 references were read. Exact supporting passages are staged in quotes.json with section and PDF-page anchors.  The central construction starts with already-correct specifications A, its optimization AΔ, and B refining A. A non-mutating optimization introduces state/actions or conjuncts without changing A's existing state updates. Given state and action-parameter mappings, translating the added clauses produces BΔ. Section 4.3 sketches BΔ refining both AΔ and B, preserving their invariants. This is a conditional specification transformation, not a general liveness or performance theorem. Added guards can prevent progress; added actions must explicitly preserve old state, and initialization and new-variable frames must be compatible. The paper leaves implementation to developers and states in §1 that correctness is guaranteed only at specification level.  Raft* prevents deletion of accepted entries by returning extra log entries during elections, selecting safe suffix values, and rejecting shorter appends. A separate accepted-ballot field distinguishes an entry's original Raft term from its latest Paxos acceptance ballot. Figure 3 maps leader self-acceptance as well as explicit messages. One Raft* action can cover multiple Paxos operations, so porting must account for every relevant action, including implicit self-acceptance.  The two implemented cases are quorum leases (PQL) and Mencius. PQL allows a leaseholder to read locally only after relevant pending writes are applied; writes notify the leaseholders of an intersecting quorum. Translating f+1 Paxos acknowledgments to f remote Raft acknowledgments must include the leader's implicit acknowledgment and its own leaseholders. The authors describe a handwritten version that omitted those leaseholders. Mencius assigns default log-slot proposers round-robin. Nondefault recovery proposes no-ops; skipTags allow default no-ops to become executable early. The optimization must be applied to every action corresponding to Paxos acceptance, including BecomeLeader and AppendEntries, not only ReceiveAppend. Appendix B abstracts leases with one global timer; distributed-clock and real lease-expiry correctness require additional implementation assumptions.  Evaluation uses five AWS regions (Oregon, Ohio, Ireland, Canada, Seoul), two m4.xlarge instances per region for client/server, 4 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM, SSD and stated 750 Mbps network. WAN latency spans 25–292 ms. Closed-loop YCSB-like workloads use 100,000 keys, a configurable shared hot-key probability and otherwise region-partitioned uniform keys. Each trial lasts 50 seconds with a stated 10 seconds for warm-up and cool-down; whether 10 seconds applies jointly or separately is unclear. Results are medians of five trials. Implementation builds on etcd c4fc8c09, retaining custom networking/batched forwarding that the authors say improves throughput 2.4×. Oregon is the favorable Raft leader placement.  PQL uses 2-second leases, renewal every 0.5 seconds, default 90% reads and 5% conflict, and 50 clients per region for latency. About 90% of reads take 1 ms; leader-lease leader reads take 1.6 ms, while a 1% follower tail reaches approximately 137 ms from conflicting writes. PQL reports 1.6× throughput at 90% reads and 1.9× at 99%; write latency rises because leaseholders must acknowledge. Figure 9(d)'s x-axis runs from 50% conflict on the left to 0% on the right. Its rising speedup therefore agrees with the prose that lower conflict helps. An earlier apparent contradiction came from overlooking that reversed axis and is withdrawn. Figure 9 captions/legends use Raft where parts of the prose discuss Raft*; keep that baseline wording distinction.  Mencius uses 100% puts, 0% or 100% conflict, and 8-byte or 4-KB payloads. The CPU case reaches about 55,000 versus 41,000 operations/s (about 1.34×); the network case reports 70% higher throughput than Raft-Oregon. Oregon itself beats Seoul by 30% in the stated comparison. Execution can still wait for remote earlier slots: the paper reports roughly 360 ms versus 110 ms for Mencius conflict/no-conflict cases, and about 79 ms at the Raft-Oregon leader. These are workload/deployment measurements, not a verification result, fault campaign, or universal optimization guarantee.  The paper claims a machine-checkable TLAPS refinement proof in §6. Appendix C is a manual prose proof outline, and Appendix B supplies specifications and invariant statements, not executable TLAPS proof bodies. The referenced GitHub master-tree request and, after waiting over five minutes, repository metadata endpoint returned HTTP 404 on 19 October 2026 UTC. No external proof source was recovered; artifact-acquisition.json records the later response. A missing retrieval does not disprove that a historical proof existed. Appendix C calls a batch-to-sequence correspondence 'stuttering', although true stuttering leaves the mapped abstract state unchanged. Its one-step simulation statement needs an abstract batch action or a justified intermediate-state argument. Its BecomeLeader safe-prefix/suffix claims are asserted without derivation in this outline. Its mapping table also uses lastLogEntry.Term where the main text distinguishes the accepted ballot.  Several printed specifications require repair before treating them as checker inputs. These omissions can affect semantics, so they are not classified as merely cosmetic syntax errors. Figure 4 leaves unrelated state unconstrained, uses logs'[i]=v in B versus singleton {v} in A/BΔ, and BΔ initialization quantifies k while referring to i. Appendix B's quorum assumption prints Q⊆Quorum rather than Q⊆Acceptor (Raft variants print both). UpdateLog prints logBallot'[i] without the acceptor index. ProposeEntries prints IF i1=0 THEN raftlogs[a][i1−1][1] ELSE −1, reversing the expected initial-index test. Some modules omit introduced variables from vars/init and omit frames for new variables; PQL Apply, GrantLease and UpdateTimer preserve MP!vars but leave other PQL variables unconstrained. These are findings about the printed artifact, not executed counterexamples against the authors' implementation or an independently obtained historical proof.  For distributed-system verification, this contributes a concrete specification-transformation method and useful cases of implicit acknowledgments, state mappings and safe optimization transfer. It also separates invariant preservation from progress and measured speed, and highlights the need to check exact proof artifacts, initialization, frame conditions and batch simulation. It contains no Verus, verified-Rust or LLM proof-agent experiment. No author code, prover or model checker was run.

- SecCSL (2019)
    - title: SecCSL: Security Concurrent Separation Logic.
    - what: SecCSL extends concurrent separation logic with relational assertions for data-dependent value sensitivity and location sensitivity. Assertions can express pointers, arrays, shared invariants, and security labels; lock invariants combine functional heap facts with policies for attacker-observable sinks. The logic's compositional noninterference property is timing-sensitive, so branches on secret values are forbidden. The authors mechanize soundness in Isabelle/HOL and implement SecC, a symbolic-execution verifier for a C subset. The central case study is a lock-protected record whose classified flag controls data sensitivity and whose public OUTPUT_REG sink must never receive secret data; a variant of Covern's CDDC case study and known benchmark problems are reported as verified within milliseconds in the abstract/overview.

- tree ensemble robustness verification (2019)
    - title: Robustness Verification of Tree-based Models
    - what: Develops exact and anytime lower-bound verification for decision-tree ensembles under l∞ perturbations. A single tree is verified in linear time; an ensemble is reduced to maximum K-clique search in a K-partite box-intersection graph, and a multilevel clique algorithm gives progressively tighter robustness lower bounds. Each leaf corresponds to a d-dimensional axis-aligned box. Ensemble leaf tuples are feasible exactly when their boxes intersect, yielding a K-clique; Theorem 1 bounds exact verification by min{O(n^K), O((2Kn)^d)} for at most n leaves/tree and d features. The multilevel algorithm merges T tree parts into pseudo-nodes, preserving boxes and refining a bound level by level until exact. It also handles multiclass attacks, arbitrary query boxes, unimportant features and anchor-like analyses. Across nine datasets and standard/robust GBDTs (500 examples where feasible, 10-step binary search), bounds are close to MILP while up to roughly 3000x faster; for robust MNIST the reported bound ratio is 0.96 and 12.6s versus MILP hundreds of seconds.

Each generated time-to-failure eventually signals fail[id], and the template can be instantiated for several independent faults. The system-level STA is then driven by those fault events. The SPX example has one component and enters failure on its fault. The TMR example has three independently failing replicas; after the first fault it remains operational in faulty1, stores which replica failed, and enters failure when a different second replica faults. Reliability properties are estimated with UPPAAL SMC; an example asks for reaching M.failure within 100000 time units. Probability uncertainty ε controls the accuracy/cost trade-off.     - title: Formal Specification and Verification of Dynamic Parametrized Architectures
    - what: Defines Dynamic Parametrized Architectures (DPAs), where indexed component sets, connections, initial configurations, invariants and reconfiguration transitions are first-order formulas over unbounded index sets.     - what: Introduces HOT-PDL, a dynamic logic over higher-order traces (HOTs) with call/return (CR), caller-to-callee (CC) and returned-function-to-caller (RC) pointers. The lock example refines CAS/RESET spinlock to an ownership-aware abstract lock and then skip; Civl uses Boogie and has verified a garbage collector and race detector, with about fifty smaller examples including ticket lock and lock-free stack.

    - number: around fifty smaller Civl programs
    - number: Section 6: around fifty smaller programs; large cases are a concurrent garbage collector and a data-race detector

The result is safety/refinement only, not liveness. The paper reports no new quantitative benchmark table; executable code generation, scalability, and IDE integration remain open, and concrete atomic-action gates remain trusted specification points.

- Lazy Self-composition for Security Verification. (2018)
    - what: Combines symbolic path-sensitive taint analysis of one program copy with precise two-copy safety verification to avoid eager full self-composition. Ifc-CEGAR validates candidate taint leaks, transfers relational invariant information and refines taint updates. Ifc-BMC duplicates only possibly tainted computations while unrolling, and can prove safety early when all live initial taint disappears. SeaHorn prototypes are compared to eager composition on small security benchmarks. Details observability/declassification predicates, the one-sided meaning of taint, proof-trace rewriting versus strengthening and the model refinement needed to restore induction. Keeps conditional completeness separate from prototype support; preserves no-fresh-secret condition for BMC termination, unknown handling, bitvector/struct limitations, all benchmark values and the narrow evidence behind scalability/constant-time claims.
    - limits: §§3–4: transition-system variables and quantifier-free first-order theory formulas describe Init, Tr and Bad. Tr is assumed reflexive so either program copy may stutter. H identifies initially secret variables and L is its complement. Security is defined relative to the chosen operational model and observation predicates, not every possible timing/cache/network observation. §4: Obs_x specifies when a low variable is adversary-observable. The terminal-output policy, concurrently executing observers and selected declassification contexts are modeled by these predicates. Setting Obs false or explicitly marking a value untainted changes the permitted policy and must be justified externally; it is not a derived no-leak theorem. §4.1: taint marks high variables true and low variables false initially. Theta(expression) disjoins taint of its variables; conditional update taint includes condition taint and the chosen branch expression. It tracks explicit and implicit flows but overapproximates value dependence, e.g. different expressions with the same result. The final prose reverses x1/x2 dependency direction; the displayed update gives the intended meaning. §4.2: self-composition starts low variables equal and leaves high values independent. Bad requires one low value unequal while both copies satisfy its observation predicate. Results concern this paired-execution definition under the chosen stuttering model; termination behavior or microarchitectural leakage is not automatically covered. §5 Corollaries1–2: real self-composition leaks imply possible taint leaks; no taint leak proves no modeled leak. A tainted output alone does not prove insecurity. Untainted implies equality across the related copies, whereas equality need not imply untainted in the original abstraction. §5.1 Algorithm1: taint solver SAFE ends the check; a taint counterexample triggers a constrained self-composed problem. One described Constraint choice bounds all self-composed executions by the counterexample length k rather than merely replaying one control path. An actual paired witness gives UNSAFE; a spurious one supplies relational facts for refinement. §5.1: ReWrite adds single-copy facts and entailed equalities/disequalities while preserving claimed inductive traces, without itself improving the taint abstraction. Strengthening additionally uses proved equalities to require no taint, which can destroy induction. Refine changes selected next-taint functions under the strengthened frame condition to restore induction; it is not merely adding an unproved invariant to the original model. §5.1 Theorem1 assumes a sound and complete first-order-theory model checker maintaining inductive traces. It states Ifc-CEGAR soundness/completeness under that assumption and gives a proof sketch, not unconditional decidability or termination for arbitrary C/CHCs or a proof that Spacer always terminates. Lemma claims/trace transformations are not mechanically verified here. §5.1 printed formula issues, visually confirmed: equations10/12 initialize a trace over Y=X∪Xt using Init_d, which is defined over X∪Xd; displayed component-preservation implications on p.145 use frame i on both sides instead of i+1; equation13 switches superscript d to s. The record follows the stated algorithmic intent without silently treating the typeset formulas as a complete executable correctness proof. §5.2 Algorithms2–3: an UNSAT taint query permits the duplicate value to reuse the original computation. SAT or UNKNOWN conservatively duplicates it. At BND without a conclusive result return UNKNOWN; failure to find a bounded counterexample alone is not safety. The simplified bad formula omits Obs only for exposition. §§1,5.2: early safety requires no live variable tainted and no leak found in the checked prefix. Initial secret taint must be exhausted and no new secret input introduced later; the introduction explicitly states this assumption and says later tainted inputs need a modified check. Does not provide a general finite completeness bound for ongoing distributed services. Algorithm notation issues: Algorithm2 calls LazySC(M,Mt), whereas Algorithm3 header orders(Mt,M); Algorithm1 advertises UNKNOWN but main loop has no solver-UNKNOWN branch, and its UNKNOWN return follows until-infinity. These are high-level sketches; practical resource/solver-unknown handling is not completely specified. Algorithm2 also does not explicitly distinguish an unknown composed-property query before its early-safety check. §§6–6.2: prototype initially described as not bit-precise and not supporting complex lists. More specifically CEGAR uses LLVM instrumentation plus Spacer and cannot handle benchmark structs or bitvector operations; BMC works over CHCs with Z3 and handles all evaluated programs. Do not generalize CEGAR restrictions to the list/BV BMC rows or infer full C bit-precise semantics from them. §§6.2–6.4: Intel Core i7-4578U,8GB RAM;300s timeout. Eager comparisons use the same backend on two copies. All seven CEGAR rows are safe, only pwdcheck2 needs one refinement; the other six are discharged by taint analysis with no self-composition refinement. Eight BMC rows include two unsafe variants. These selected small/microbenchmarks are not a large deployed-code security audit. §6.4: Table3 runtime at array size64 is85.44s, supporting under2min on that instance. Author statement of exponential runtime growth is a qualitative characterization of eight observations, not a proved asymptotic bound or scaling to unbounded arrays. Exact BND values, program sizes, solver versions, repetition variance and memory consumption are not supplied. §§7–8: security-type, dynamic-taint and product-program comparisons are discussion claims without separate head-to-head benchmark data here. General k-safety and quantified relational invariants for unbounded data structures are future work. No verified implementation, certificate validation, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM evaluation is reported. Frontend, instrumentation, policy and solvers remain trusted.

- LLUMC (2018)
    - title: Unbounded Software Model Checking with Incremental SAT-Solving
    - what: Presents LLUMC, translating optimized LLVM IR from sequential C into four DimSpec CNF formulas for unbounded reachability, solved by incremental SAT (IncPlan) or IC3 (MinireachIC3). It targets assertion failures and undefined signed arithmetic overflows. The encoding uses curr/pred basic-block identifiers and selected live variables as bit-vectors; I, G, U, and T represent initial, goal, universal-state, and transition constraints. Explicit assert/assume/error calls and nsw arithmetic generate error transitions. The paper states a soundness claim but omits a structural proof, relying on assumptions about C-to-LLVM preservation and closed state transitions. IC3 can prove safety, while incremental SAT finds counterexamples and may not terminate on unreachable goals.
    - number: 24 benchmarks: 14 incorrect and 10 correct, 14–646 LOC, 151–116,777 clauses
    - number: MinireachIC3 solved 20/24 within 600 s; IncPlan frequently timed out on safe cases
    - number: larger erroneous s3 client: 198.93 s and 940.5 MB (abcdSat)
    - number: overflow smaller: IC3 0.83 s; gcd-4 safe: IC3 6.853 s
    - limits: Only sequential C supported; memory accesses, floating point, recursion, concurrency, and unsupported LLVM operations are excluded in evaluation. Global memory is ignored by the bit-vector encoding. Error means failed assert or specified signed overflow, not all undefined behavior. The authors explicitly say the central claim lacks a formal structural induction proof. SAT reachability alone cannot prove unreachability and large instances time out.

- Local/global distributed proof complexity (2018)
    - title: Local Verification of Global Proofs
    - what: Compares local labels, one shared global proof, and mixed proofs for constant-radius distributed verification, quantifying the cost of distributing global evidence. Defines local, global and mixed certificate sizes s_l, s_g and s_m and proves s_l≤s_m≤s_g, s_m≤n s_l and s_g≤n s_l+O(n log n). The price of locality is n s_l/s_m. Uniform local proofs yield Θ(n) price; At-most-one-selected (Amos) has O(log n) uniform labels and Θ(n) price. Minimum Spanning Tree has O(log²n) local proofs and O(n log n) global proof, giving Θ(log n). At-least-one-selected requires Ω(n log n) mixed proof, and reversing decision therefore needs Ω(log n) local or Ω(n log n) global evidence. A block-neighborhood counting argument supplies the lower bound and is lifted to leader election, spanning tree and odd-cycle. Bipartite global proofs are conjectured Θ(n log n), with bounds depending on identifier range. The paper connects local/global nondeterministic hierarchies to communication-complexity hierarchies.
    - number: s_l≤s_m≤s_g
    - number: s_g≤n s_l+O(n log n)
    - number: Amos price Θ(n)
    - number: MST price Θ(log n)
    - limits: Verification radius is constant and verifiers are uniform unless explicitly discussing identifier range; IDs are polynomial-range O(log n) bits for the main model. Local labels are assumed equal size, so concatenation is exactly n times one label. Lower bounds use oriented cycles/blocks and can depend on connectedness, IDs and proof model. The Bipartite Θ(n log n) global lower bound remains a conjecture; communication-complexity hierarchy separations are open.

- Modular Paxos verification (2018)
    - title: Paxos Consensus, Deconstructed and Abstracted (Extended Version)
    - what: # Paxos Consensus, Deconstructed and Abstracted: whole paper reading (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Álvaro García-Pérez, Alexey Gotsman, Yuri Meshman and Ilya Sergey's extended Paxos Consensus, Deconstructed and Abstracted is arXiv:1802.05969v1,16 February 2018. All 44 pages were read: eight sections, Appendices A–E, all 17 figures, four theorems, five lemmata, four definitions, examples 1–6, all printed proof outlines and 32 references. All 11 contact sheets and individual15,18,21,22,28,32,33,44 were inspected. The original, local and official PDFs match. No author code, scientific-result artifact or formal checking tool was executed or loaded. [Evidence: Q0, frontmatter/v1 identity, PDF pp.1–1; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The paper separates two verification problems: proving single-decree Paxos through composable shared-memory object specifications, and deriving Multi-Paxos by transformations of message handling. It adapts Boichat et al.'s Paxos→Round-BasedConsensus→Round-BasedRegister decomposition. The lower specifications deliberately admit unsuccessful operations that nevertheless expose values to other operations. The aim is to preserve each unchanged module's proof when changing another module or the network implementation. Claims of being the first such modular verification belong to these authors; this reading does not establish historical priority. [Evidence: Q1, §1, two contributions, PDF pp.2–3; Q28, §7, complete comparisons/claimed novelty, PDF pp.24–25; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The setting is crash-stop, majority-quorum consensus, not Byzantine consensus or crash-recovery with durable storage. The basic network neither invents, changes, drops nor duplicates messages, delivers with unbounded delay, and has nonblocking send/blocking receive. Later transformations explicitly introduce selected read-request duplication. Leader election is omitted under an assumption that one correct process trusted by all other correct processes always exists. No failure-detector implementation, storage-recovery proof or general termination proof is supplied. Finite trace refinement and linearizability establish safety properties, not eventual completion: lower specifications may repeatedly choose failure. [Evidence: Q2, §3, decomposition/leader assumption, PDF pp.4–5; Q3, §3, network/imperative language, PDF pp.5–5; Q4, §1, safety scope, PDF pp.1–1; Q19, Definition1, full configuration traces, PDF pp.18–18; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Acceptors retain promised round r, accepted round w and value v. A read(k) gathers distinct-sender acknowledgments from ceil((n+1)/2) acceptors and chooses the value with highest accepted round, or undef. A write(k, v) gathers an equal majority; either operation can fail after a nack. Acceptors accept requests at k≥r and atomically update state with their acknowledgment send. A proposer uses rounds pid, pid+n, pid+2n,…; this guarantees disjoint rounds between processes under one continuing invocation per process. Reinvoking the printed entry operation resets k to pid, so repeated independent calls need fresh-instance state or persistent counters. Fixed process identities and trustworthy message origins under the assumed transport model, plus matching request rounds, are essential. [Evidence: Q6, Figure3/§3, complete read/write implementation, PDF pp.6–6; Q7, Figures4–5, acceptor and entry implementation, PDF pp.7–7; Q8, §3, entry and unique rounds, PDF pp.8–8; Q3, §3, network/imperative language, PDF pp.5–5; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The top sequential specification stores one value, choosing the first proposal and returning that value thereafter. Its concurrent implementation can decide another process's previously exposed proposal; ghost pending-thread entries let one invocation linearize that proposing operation first and then itself. This is helping: a thread's logical effect may occur during another thread's step. The proof assumes unique proposal values, one pending slot per process and single-assignment result cells. A concrete invocation identity or a justification that unique tagging preserves client-visible equality would be needed to generalize beyond that stated setting. Abstract results are declared Boolean in Figure 7 although proposal values have type val; this is a printed typing mismatch. [Evidence: Q5, Figure2, atomic entry specification, PDF pp.4–4; Q10, §4/Figure 7/Theorem 1, complete top refinement, PDF pp.9–10; Q30, Appendix A, complete top-level proof outline, PDF pp.27–29; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Figure 6 gives the reason for weakening the intermediate abstractions. A low-round write can fail overall yet reach one acceptor, after a higher-round quorum has already decided another value. An overlapping read may see that isolated value and complete successfully, although its subsequent write will fail. Real-time order and this information flow can require the failed write to linearize before the read. The abstract specifications therefore retain sets of exposed values rather than only the globally decided value, allow reads at stale rounds and allow a write at an otherwise eligible round to fail because a concurrent operation overtakes it. [Evidence: Q9, §3/Figure 6, complete histories and rationale, PDF pp.8–9; Q11, §4/Figure8, round consensus contract, PDF pp.10–12; Q12, Figure9/§4, complete register contract, PDF pp.12–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Round-BasedConsensus's atomic proposeRC(k, v0) nondeterministically selects vD and a success flag. If vD is already exposed or equals v0, it adds vD to valsRC even on failure; success additionally needs k≥roundRC and retains the first decided vRC. Round-BasedRegister is weaker: every write exposes its input, a successful eligible write updates roundRR and vRR, and a read may return any exposed value when its round is stale. Its vRR is not itself an immutable consensus decision. The enclosing read-before-write discipline and unique increasing rounds are needed to recover the deterministic top specification. Theorem 2 places logical effects at failed read or completed write. [Evidence: Q11, §4/Figure8, round consensus contract, PDF pp.10–12; Q12, Figure9/§4, complete register contract, PDF pp.12–12; Q13, Theorem 2, round consensus linearization, PDF pp.12–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The register proof uses prophecy variables: ghost values selected according to how an operation eventually returns. Successful reads are intended to linearize when the quorum-th read acknowledgment is sent, successful writes at the quorum-th write acknowledgment, failed reads at their nack return, and failed writes at the first accepting response or at the failure return if none accepted. These are proof annotations, not an implementable ability to predict network schedules. Ghost counters count acknowledgments sent, whereas concrete quorums count acknowledgments received. The basic no-duplication premise is used in relating those quantities. [Evidence: Q14, §4, register prophecy/linearization explanation, PDF pp.12–14; Q15, Figure10, complete instrumented read/write, PDF pp.14–14; Q16, Figure 11/Theorem3, complete annotated acceptor, PDF pp.14–15; Q32, Appendix C, complete register proof outline/invariants, PDF pp.31–41; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Reader source-level objection to the printed read annotation: Figure 11 requires both count_r[k]=quorum−1 and proph_r[k]=(true, v), where v is that particular acceptor's local value. The eventual read result is instead the maximum accepted-round value among received acknowledgments. With n=3, let A1 hold (vA, w=1) from a failed write and A2 hold undef. A read at k=3 returns vA after receiving A1's then A2's replies. When A1 sends, count=0 rather than 1; when A2 sends, count=1 but its undef differs from the prophecy vA. A third sender sees count=2. No successful-read annotation fires. This ordinary schedule substitution identifies a proof-instrumentation gap, not a conflicting-decision attack or an executed trace. The proof needs an annotation tied to the relevant quorum maximum, not equality with an arbitrary quorum-th sender's value. [Evidence: Q15, Figure10, complete instrumented read/write, PDF pp.14–14; Q16, Figure 11/Theorem3, complete annotated acceptor, PDF pp.14–15; Q32, Appendix C, complete register proof outline/invariants, PDF pp.31–41; Q9, §3/Figure 6, complete histories and rationale, PDF pp.8–9; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The incomplete-operation case also needs care. The paper leaves a never-returning write's prophecy undef and never linearizes it, although it may already change an acceptor and supply a value read by another operation. A standard linearizability proof can complete selected pending operations; this annotation needs to support those completions rather than erase every nonreturning writer. Separately, after correcting the acknowledgment predicate notation, Appendix C's intended Val(j, v) invariant equates the current value with existence of a historical write acknowledgment for v. After accepting v1 then v2, the retained message history still contains the acknowledgment for v1 but the current value is v2, contradicting the reverse implication. The intended invariant needs a latest-round qualification. These are reader proof obligations, not a rejection of Paxos's ordinary quorum argument. [Evidence: Q14, §4, register prophecy/linearization explanation, PDF pp.12–14; Q16, Figure 11/Theorem3, complete annotated acceptor, PDF pp.14–15; Q32, Appendix C, complete register proof outline/invariants, PDF pp.31–41; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The appendices contain additional transcription problems material to mechanization. Appendix A's loop annotations use pid=k mod n despite initializing k=pid and maintaining the owner formula ((k−1) mod n)+1; n=3, pid=3, k=3 gives3≠0. They also assert a false pending flag after an unsuccessful iteration, although that branch does not clear it. Appendix B's rely relation prints an index condition (k mod n)≠(k mod n), with no distinct index, which would exclude all interference literally. Appendix C's req/ack predicates reuse the same message identity for a request and its reverse-direction acknowledgment; for different endpoints those fields cannot both hold. These details must be corrected before treating the outlines as machine-checked proofs. [Evidence: Q30, Appendix A, complete top-level proof outline, PDF pp.27–29; Q31, Appendix B, complete round consensus proof outline, PDF pp.29–31; Q32, Appendix C, complete register proof outline/invariants, PDF pp.31–41; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The network layer models local states, protocol transition relations and a multiset of uniquely identified messages retained after reception with active=false. A simple execution chooses an internal step, send or receive at one node. Appendix D flattens proposer code, carries the residual program text in each local state and gives send/receive rules; it leaves ordinary WHILE-language semantics assumed. Thus program counters and auxiliary loop variables are part of this encoding, not invisible implementation details. Receive rules in Figures13–14 also print an unbound n where the destination-node update is intended. [Evidence: Q17, §5.1, local states/messages/transition relations, PDF pp.16–17; Q18, Figure13/§5.1, network steps, PDF pp.17–18; Q33, Appendix D, complete code-aware encoding, PDF pp.41–44; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Out-of-thin-air semantics adds selected read requests without changing local state, justified by predicate P when the proposer has reached at least that round. Lemma 1 claims its complete configuration traces are included in the simple semantics. Appendix E's entire argument says a read request does not change proposer state and has no nontrivial precondition. That does not directly match Appendix D's code-aware encoding, where executing send advances the residual program and loop, and a particular round/destination request is sent once. Extra duplicate requests with unchanged program state therefore need an explicit observation/projection or a different reusable-send protocol. The source's exact-trace inclusion is stronger than client-visible equivalence and its printed one-sentence proof does not bridge them. [Evidence: Q20, §5.2, complete OTA rule/predicate/Lemma 1, PDF pp.18–18; Q19, Definition1, full configuration traces, PDF pp.18–18; Q33, Appendix D, complete code-aware encoding, PDF pp.41–44; Q34, Appendix E, complete transformation/composition proofs, PDF pp.44–44; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Slot replication runs an independent single-decree instance per slot; projection to any slot recovers its base behavior up to stuttering. Widening then copies a triggering read request to all slots at the same recipient. Its refinement requires OTA compliance and P-monotonicity: a request justified at one sender slot must be justified at every other sender slot. Example 4 correctly excludes independently advancing rounds and supplies fixed-round instances as a positive case. Example 5 immediately invokes the unrestricted Section 3 implementation, whose rounds retry independently; the required synchronization/restriction is not established there. An independent-slot source-level case uses n=3, pid=1, with sender slots at rounds 4 and 1: request k=4 satisfies P in the first slot but not the second. The refinement must state a shared-round discipline rather than infer it from ordinary slot independence. [Evidence: Q21, §5.3/Figure14/Definition2/Lemma2, independent slots, PDF pp.18–20; Q22, §5.4/Definition 3, widening rule/OTA compliance, PDF pp.20–21; Q23, §5.4, Definition4/Examples4–5/Lemma3, PDF pp.21–21; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Two further printed conditions need explicit scope. Definition 3 introduces a triggering subset T but then quantifies all messages m∈M instead of m∈M∩T; its read-only P would reject ordinary write/ack messages. Optimized widening's receiveAndAct applies a received message to every slot without an explicit m∈T branch, despite T appearing in the rule's name. Applying a slot-specific write everywhere would not preserve independent slots. Restrict the optimized rule to triggering read requests and retain ordinary per-slot reception for other messages. These are literal-rule qualifications, not evidence about the linked Scala implementation. [Evidence: Q22, §5.4/Definition 3, widening rule/OTA compliance, PDF pp.20–21; Q24, §5.5, all-slot optimized rule/Lemma 4, PDF pp.21–22; Q23, §5.4, Definition4/Examples4–5/Lemma3, PDF pp.21–21; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Reader refinement qualification also applies to Lemmata 3–4. Widening consumes one active request and inserts replicas in the same transition; separate slot-replicating receive and OTA send transitions introduce intermediate configurations. Appendix E explicitly says, “This allows us to emulate this step by a per-slot execution of the OTASend.” That establishes a multistep simulation argument, while Lemma 3 states inclusion of complete configuration traces. Lemma 4 permits compression of intermediate configurations, but expanding receives also leaves inactive replica requests in message history; the optimized rule does not insert that same history. A specified observation/refinement mapping must account for grouped steps and internal request histories, not just remove intermediate configurations. These are source-level proof obligations, not executed counterexamples or consensus-safety violations. [Evidence: FR_FQ19, §5.1, observation definition, PDF pp.17–17; FR_FQ25, §5.4, WStepReceiveT adds replicas while consuming the original, PDF pp.20–20; FR_FQ26, §5.5, optimized widening has no triggering-set guard, PDF pp.21–21; FR_FQ27, §5.5, Lemma 4 configuration compression, PDF pp.22–22; FR_FQ40, Appendix E, Lemma 3 simulation uses multiple steps, PDF pp.44–44; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Optimized widening batches one recipient's per-slot receive, local and reply steps; Lemma 4 relates it to expanding those local sequences. Bunching packages the resulting replies in a message, caches/unpacks them on demand and maps them back to separate messages in Lemma 5. The intended benefit is amortized Phase 1 across slots while reusing single-decree proofs. Because the model permits infinitely many slots, its all-slot batch needs a finite or lazy representation before implementation. The register-provider interface exposes independent write-once slots; it does not itself prove client request deduplication, gap-free log execution, application linearizability or leader-lease correctness. [Evidence: Q24, §5.5, all-slot optimized rule/Lemma 4, PDF pp.21–22; Q25, §5.6/Figure15/Lemma 5, bunching/unpacking, PDF pp.22–23; Q26, §5.7–6, composition/interface/stability, PDF pp.23–24; Q27, §6, Scala/Akka prototype/Theorem 4, PDF pp.24–24; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Theorem 4 composes Theorem 1 with the transformation lemmata to claim refinement of an array of atomic write-once registers. Appendix E supplies short proofs of Lemmata 1–3 and Theorem 4; Lemmata 4–5 have statements/explanations in the body but no separate extended proofs. Stable rely/guarantee assertions are the stated condition for transporting program reasoning across network transformations. The paper's conclusion proposes Raft, PBFT, Mencius, master leases and epoch numbering as future applications, without establishing those results here. [Evidence: Q26, §5.7–6, composition/interface/stability, PDF pp.23–24; Q34, Appendix E, complete transformation/composition proofs, PDF pp.44–44; Q29, §8, contributions/proposed extensions, PDF pp.25–26; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Validation is a Scala/Akka proof-of-concept linked at github.com/certichain/protocol-combinators, plus handwritten specifications, annotations and proof outlines. The paper reports no benchmark configurations, performance measurements, experiment counts or machine-checked artifact for its own argument. “Executable” and “provably correct” are the authors' descriptions; source-code refinement and runtime-library correctness were not inspected in this reading. TLA+, PVS, Isabelle, EventML, PSync, Ivy, IronFleet, Verdi and Disel appear as related work, not tools used to check these particular proofs. [Evidence: Q27, §6, Scala/Akka prototype/Theorem 4, PDF pp.24–24; Q28, §7, complete comparisons/claimed novelty, PDF pp.24–25; Q34, Appendix E, complete transformation/composition proofs, PDF pp.44–44; literal spans in quotes.json.]  For this database the main contribution is proof reuse across both object abstraction and protocol-aware network optimization, with failed-write information flow as a concrete test of specification adequacy. Reader follow-ups are a TLA+ model of ghost-free concrete histories and slot/round synchronization; Verus/Rust ownership and typed sender/instance proofs for a finite lazy network adapter; and LLM proof-agent tasks checking prophecy coverage, pending-operation completions, stable interference assertions and exact refinement observations. No Verus, verified Rust or LLM evaluation is reported. These proposed checks should distinguish repairing printed proof outlines from discovering an actual consensus safety violation. [Evidence: Q1, §1, two contributions, PDF pp.2–3; Q14, §4, register prophecy/linearization explanation, PDF pp.12–14; Q23, §5.4, Definition4/Examples4–5/Lemma3, PDF pp.21–21; Q27, §6, Scala/Akka prototype/Theorem 4, PDF pp.24–24; Q29, §8, contributions/proposed extensions, PDF pp.25–26; literal spans in quotes.json.]
    - number: Module proofs can be reused across implementations

Handwritten proof annotations require repairs. Transformations need stable assertions, cross-slot P-monotonicity, triggering-message guards, and an observation/refinement mapping.

    - title: Peregrine: A Tool for the Analysis of Population Protocols.
    - what: Introduces Peregrine, a web tool for designing, simulating, statistically sampling and parameterized-verifying population protocols. The paper defines protocol/configuration/fairness semantics and illustrates majority voting. The UI supports graphical or script descriptions, manual/random simulation with rewind, convergence-speed statistics and JSON export. Verification first proves layered termination (a sufficient condition for silence), then searches an iteratively strengthened Presburger overapproximation for bad initial-to-terminal executions; candidate counterexamples are checked for concrete reachability by LoLA and replayed/exported. It distinguishes ordinary and increased-accuracy consensus classification, where LoLA checks whether a nonterminal consensus can later be broken.

Reachability is approximated, so satisfiable bad formulas require LoLA confirmation and unsatisfiable formulas prove correctness only under the approximation theorem. Fairness abstracts random interactions. Constraint-system size limits current verification to roughly 100 states and a few thousand transitions; arbitrary non-silent protocols and finite-state tools' scalability are outside scope.

- POS concurrency sampling (2018)
    - title: Partial Order Aware Concurrency Sampling
    - what: Presents POS, a randomized concurrency scheduler that samples partial orders rather than redundant total interleavings. It assigns random priorities to events, executes the highest-priority enabled event, and reassigns priorities of events racing with the executed event. The paper formalizes sequentially consistent concurrent machines, event independence, partial-order equivalence and minimum partial-order coverage probability. BasicPOS uses immutable priorities but suffers propagated constraints; POS versions priorities by per-object access counts, yielding bipartite constraints and a theorem with a race-count-dependent lower bound. Implementation supports read-only-event relaxation and a periodic priority reset workaround for busy loops. Micro benchmarks use 16 events across four threads/objects; macro tests use SCTBench and Maple, with explicit exclusions and conservative geometric-mean handling.
    - number: POS micro-benchmark geometric mean 2.87e−6 versus random walk 2.14e−8 and PCT 2.00e−8
    - number: POS about 7.0× better overall (134.1× excluding RAPOS and BasicPOS)
    - number: read-only POS* about 1.4× better than POS and 5.0× better than other methods
    - number: macro geometric mean POS about 2.6× PCT and 4.7× random walk
    - limits: The machine model assumes sequential consistency, each statement accesses at most one shared object, disabled events eventually enable, and executions terminate (finite traces). POS needs a race predicate and probabilistic priorities; fairness is probabilistic and implementation resets priorities every 10^3 voluntary context switches, with claimed minimal effect. Guarantees are lower bounds on partial-order coverage, not exhaustive testing; read-only relaxation depends on correctly classifying races.

- Program Analysis Is Harder Than Verification: A Computability Perspective (2018)
    - what: Defines a computability model of assertion domains, total recursive analyzers and total recursive verifiers, then studies when finding an assertion is reducible to checking one. An analyzer can always be converted constructively to an equally powerful verifier; the paper states a converse reduction for finite domains of assertions and an impossibility result for infinite domains under its stated conditions. An abstract domain is countable with a concretization into program sets and a decidable semantic implication relation; the base definition does not require a complete lattice. Verifiers return true or unknown, analyzers return an assertion, and soundness/completeness are defined independently. Extensional domains depend only on input-output semantics. Rice-style theorems 5.3/5.4 limit precise analyzers and nontrivial monotone precise verifiers to trivial extensional domains. Theorem 7.1 constructs a verifier by testing whether the analyzer result entails the requested assertion. Reasonable verifiers are nontrivial, monotone and finitely meet-closed. Theorem 7.6 constructs an equivalent analyzer on a nonempty finite domain by finite enumeration and a strongest verified assertion. Lemma 7.7 uses a countably infinite bounded-convergence domain whose equivalent analyzer would decide termination; Theorem 7.8 states the general impossibility of a total recursive verifier-to-equivalent-analyzer transformation for infinite domains. Examples distinguish semantic assertions from intensional resource assertions and connect the abstract framework to intervals and polyhedra.

    - number: Lemma 7.7/Theorem 7.8: infinite-domain impossibility via termination reduction

The finite converse requires the paper’s reasonable-verifier conditions, including finite meet closure. The infinite result concerns a general constructive reduction preserving assertion-proving power, not the claim that every concrete synthesis instance or infinite-domain analysis is uncomputable. These are computability statements, not practical running-time, NP-hardness or model-quality bounds. The theorem proofs are mathematical within the presented model; no mechanized proof artifact or empirical evaluation is reported.

    - title: Learning Task Specifications from Demonstrations
    - what: Formulates learning a temporal Boolean task specification from finite demonstrations as maximum-a-posteriori inference over a candidate concept class. For concept classes represented as chains/lattices, monotonicity enables binary-search or breadth-first algorithms that minimize expensive random-satisfaction queries. Computing random satisfaction is generally #P-complete, so Monte Carlo/BDD or SAT approximations are needed. - Symbolic liveness analysis (2018)
    - title: Symbolic Liveness Analysis of Real-World Software
    - what: Defines a generic liveness property for real-world programs—eventually consuming input or terminating—and implements symbolic lasso detection in KLEE to find violations. The paper formalizes transition systems with productive actions, deterministic computation except for input, and finite memory; it proves that any violating trace has a finite stem followed by a non-productive cycle. The implementation tracks per-path state fingerprints (register/memory fragments plus serialized path constraints), uses symbolic execution to cover input space, and reports concrete reproducing inputs. Evaluation covers GNU Coreutils, BusyBox and toybox, including interpreter behavior in sed, runaway counters, allocation-sensitive pointers and state explosion. Five previously unknown defects (three Coreutils, two BusyBox) were confirmed and fixed; all reported violations had concrete witnesses.

- Verifying concurrent software using movers in Cspec (2018)
    - what: Cspec is a Coq framework for implementing and proving concurrent systems through state-machine refinement, composable layers and reusable proof patterns. Right/left movers reduce interleavings to atomic execution of larger code blocks. Fully mechanized patterns verify a Maildir-like server, Cmail, and a locked counter over an x86-TSO model. Extracted Haskell Cmail scales on a twelve-core tmpfs benchmark. Records state/argument-dependent commutation and stable enablement, finite-prefix safety scope, protocol proof obligations, error-state elimination, zero-effect retries and partition lifting. Captures six concrete mail concurrency cases, conservative PID-filtered directory listing, two naming plans, all TSO layers and the previous-owner buffer invariant. Saves all framework/layer LOC and pattern counts, measured setup, development anecdotes and precise trusted boundaries.

Executables use Coq extraction to Haskell (OCaml is mentioned as an alternative). The result is not a proof of arbitrary compiled C, Rust or a native binary. §§5.2,7: Correctness is trace inclusion, with every finite prefix representing possibly infinite behavior. Only safety properties are targeted. No scheduler fairness, termination, starvation freedom, eventual successful delivery or lock acquisition follows. The proof may insert a never-executed stably enabled left-mover into an equivalent execution; it does not make the actual scheduler run it. §§1–2,8.6: Node failures are outside scope. File-system crash behavior and durability are not proved despite the Maildir motivation. Top-level intended behavior and bottom-level file-system model must be correct. Coq soundness and standard assumptions including functional extensionality, extraction/runtime, driver and concrete syscall mapping are trusted. §§1,5.3,8: SMTP/POP3 parsing and protocol implementation are unverified. The Haskell network/file-system driver lies outside the proof. Compatibility with Go SMTP, postal and rabid is testing, not protocol conformance proof. TLS, spam filtering and logging are absent. §6.1 Figures 10–12: Commutation must preserve both operations’ individual return values and final state across distinct PIDs. Atomic blocks have right-movers, at most one non-mover, then left-movers. State-dependent properties need only hold after the already-executed prefix but require proofs for all reachable modeled states, not sampled interleavings. §6.1: Disabled intermediate operations require stable enablement when moving an operation earlier: enablement survives undoing another process’s step. An existing locked-file read can be a left-mover although reading arbitrary newly created/temporary files is not. Lock ownership rules must ensure other processes cannot release this process’s lock. §6.2: Protocol semantics disables forbidden operations, such as unlocked accesses. Sound use requires proving every API user follows the protocol under unrestricted semantics. Merely restricting the environment would assume away the race; Cspec requires the refinement proof. §6.3 Figure 13: The abstraction pattern keeps operation types fixed, preserves the return value and relates successor states for every low-level step. Invariant introduction uses an identity relation. An absorbing abstract error state can relate to any low-level state, but a later protocol proof must show it unreachable before obtaining the final guarantee. §6.4: Retry-loop bodies must either perform the correct successful effect and exit, or have zero effect and retry. This supports a safety/atomicity proof without guaranteeing eventual success. Partition lifting requires proven single-shard refinement plus correct naming and disjoint decomposition at top and bottom. §§3–5 Figures 1,3,6: The displayed mail/file-system specifications permit a false delivery/link return with no effect, not solely a proved name-collision cause. They are permissive safety specifications and do not guarantee success. The paper uses atomic rename terminology later; earlier implementation/spec uses link followed by unlink, with no destination overwrite, so do not substitute unrestricted POSIX rename semantics. §8.1: With concurrent deletion, PID-filtered readdir deliberately permits a superset of existing names. It is a right-mover, not a both-mover, in that case. A name absent from the superset is free; a reported name need not still exist. Plan 2 describes random names but concretely uses the current timestamp and relies on retry rather than guaranteed collision freedom. §8.2 Figure 16: The x86-TSO case verifies a modeled counter built over shared memory and per-core store buffers. Any core may flush any portion of its buffer at each low-level operation. This is not validation of a physical processor, compiler memory model or executable counter benchmark. §8.3 Figure 17: Performance uses local simulated SMTP/POP3 requests on Linux tmpfs, avoiding network and persistent-storage bottlenecks. Authors implemented the unverified GoMail comparator. Request mix is 1:1 delivery versus read/delete over 100 random users. Message sizes, measurement durations, repetitions, error bars and raw runs are not supplied. §8.4 Figure 18: Effort is two people about six months part time, following another twelve months of failed alternative designs. Incremental deletion/naming/multi-user timings are author anecdotes, not controlled studies or independent replications. The text’s approximate 100–200 spec LOC per layer omits displayed extremes 63 and 323. §8.5 Figure 19: Proof-pattern counts are module uses and need not equal numbers of layers. The Cmail diagram describes naming plan 1; the count table also includes the retry pattern used in plan 2, which has one additional intermediate layer. §§2,8.6: The state-machine approach draws on TLA and I/O automata, but the work is not a TLA+ implementation/proof or a distributed node-failure theorem. No Verus, verified Rust or LLM-generated-specification/proof evaluation. Public artifact URL is recorded but not fetched or replayed.
