- Auxiliary Variables in TLA+ (2017)
    - what: # Auxiliary Variables in TLA+ (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Leslie Lamport and Stephan Merz, arXiv:1703.05121v2, paper dated 27 May 2017. This is a practical account of extending TLA+ specifications with history, prophecy and stuttering variables so that state expressions can connect different representations of a concurrent system. Its central requirement is equivalence after hiding the added variables, not just that an augmented specification has some behaviors of the original. The worked snapshot result concerns safety of a simplified algorithm whose reads may never terminate. General language-independent soundness and completeness proofs are explicitly deferred to future work (Q1,Q2,Q16,Q21).  ## Reading and evidence scope  Read the complete 71-page PDF: cover, abstract, contents, printed pages 1–69, all sections 1–6.6, two numbered theorems, displayed definitions/equations, all 27 figure listings and all nine bibliography entries. The introduction says 25 figures, but numbering continues through Figure 27. There are no numbered tables, appendix or checklist. References were read as bibliography entries, not recursively followed. All 71 page images were generated; only PDF pages 19,20,27,39,40,41,44,45,46,48,49,54,57,62,66,67,68,70 were individually inspected. Complete extracted text was read for every page; this does not claim visual inspection of every page.  Read the complete official project webpage, downloaded its 317-member ZIP, and read nine selected plaintext assets whole: Prophecy.tla, Stuttering.tla, AfekSimplified.tla, AfekSimplifiedH.tla, NewLinearSnapshotPS.tla, and both MC.cfg/MC.tla pairs under AfekSimplifiedH Model_1/Model_2. Other ZIP modules, prettyprints, model copies and result/log files were inventoried but not read. The retained files are exact archive bytes; each has a SHA256 and explicit scope. No author code, TLA+ module, TLC model, TLAPS proof or checker was executed/imported; no model/checkpoint or serialized experiment data was loaded. Static symbolic traces below are reader reasoning, not rerun results. The official webpage calls these “small TLC models”; their existence does not establish universal verification (W1,C1–C9).  ## What an auxiliary variable must preserve  A TLA+ specification describes behaviors, sequences of states allowing steps that leave the observed variables unchanged. Hiding a variable uses a temporal existential quantifier: it chooses an entire value sequence and includes the logic's treatment of stuttering. It is not ordinary quantification over one state value. The paper first gives an approximate behavior intuition, then explains why stuttering makes that intuition incomplete. Definitions must be expanded with bound-name renaming; its NotUnique substitution example demonstrates how naive textual replacement can turn a valid expression into a contradiction. Recursive definitions are treated as fixed-point abbreviations, not arbitrary source-text rewriting (Q3,Q4).  A refinement mapping substitutes state expressions for abstract variables; the implementation must imply that substituted specification. Forgetting auxiliary variable a must recover the original specification: ∃a:Spec_a is equivalent to Spec. Merely proving the projection implies Spec would permit the extension to remove original behaviors, even all of them. The examples teach how to avoid this loss, rather than offering an unbounded mechanized proof for every stated transformation (Q2,Q3,Q5).  ## History: remembering information the implementation discarded  MinMax1 stores all integer inputs in a set; MinMax2 stores only extrema. Both classify each input as Hi, Lo, Both or None. The set maps readily to its minimum and maximum, but an extrema-only state cannot reconstruct all forgotten intermediate inputs. MinMax2H adds h, initially empty, recording the inputs on response steps, which supplies the missing refinement state. Infinity and MinusInfinity are distinguished noninteger values; assumptions on these sentinels matter to empty-history handling (Q5,Q6).  Theorem 1 gives a syntactic history-variable rule: augment Init with h=exp_Init; choose a disjunctive representation of Next; replace each subaction A by A conjoined with h'=exp_A; include h in the variable tuple. Expressions must obey the stated variable/context restrictions after definition expansion. Earlier discussion permits using the old history value in updates. The point of a disjunctive representation is to expose each enabled choice and its bound identifiers without changing conjunction/disjunction scope (Q6,Q7).  Theorem 2 permits replacing a subaction A by B when they are equivalent under an invariant and for every identifier in the subaction's context. Equation 3.2 is an action formula, which the paper says TLAPS can prove but TLC cannot directly check; TLC can instead compare the full temporal specifications on chosen finite models. A reported successful small comparison is not a proof for arbitrary state domains. Adding history to a specification with liveness retains the original liveness conjunct. Fairness can be expressed through the augmented actions when the required correspondence and enablement hold (Q7,Q8).  ## Prophecy: exposing a later choice earlier in a proof  SendInt examples choose a sent integer at different stages. A history variable cannot manufacture a choice still in the future. A prophecy variable p predicts it, constrains the action consuming that prediction, and can then choose a fresh prediction. Validity requires that each reachable original action has an admissible good prediction, rather than demanding a prediction for every syntactically describable state pair. Predictions that are not consumed must keep their intended relationship across steps (Q9).  SendSetUndo lets an implementation remove pending elements; its prophecy array predicts send versus undo, and the mapping retains only predicted sends. SendSeqUndo adds ordering and shifting indices. A partial injection maps surviving old prediction identities to new identities. Injectivity prevents identifying distinct predictions and accidentally excluding behaviors. The prose in §4.5 calls DomInj a “partial function”, but both the formal condition and retained Prophecy module require membership in PartialInjections. The formal requirement is the one used here (Q10,Q11,C1).  The three conditions combined in ProphCondition are: an available good prediction, a partial injection with the correct old/new domains, and PredDom containing every index whose prediction can affect the action predicate. PredDom may overapproximate those dependencies; consuming extra predictions safely allows extra refreshes. NewPSet preserves predictions only along unconsumed mapped identities and leaves consumed/new ones free. These obligations are properties of reachable actions of the original specification. The paper explains why a TLC checking module may need to end before declaring p: the original Spec does not constrain that variable. It recommends checking these conditions before the final refinement, which gives useful intermediate debugging obligations (Q11,C1).  Liveness is retained from the original specification, not blindly replaced with fairness of the newly constrained NextP. In §4.6, allowing the prophecy value infinity would permit an endless stall in the safety formula; original weak fairness excludes that prophecy choice. Thus the combined formula can fail to be machine closed: its liveness condition rules out an otherwise allowed finite prefix, rather than only requiring later progress. The authors permit this as an intermediate proof instrument and caution against using it to describe an implementation. This is a scope condition on the method, not evidence that prophecy is unsound (Q12).  ## Stuttering: matching different internal step counts  The clock example connects a 24-hour counter to an hour/minute clock by inserting 59 steps that leave the original hour unchanged. A stuttering variable stores which action/context is being expanded and a value that advances toward a bottom value. Despite the name decr, the example's order can use j+1, initial 1 and bottom 59. A refinement expression recovers the minute from the auxiliary state. PreStutter requires a predicate equivalent to the chosen action's actual enablement; otherwise it could start an unfinished expansion of an action that cannot run (Q13).  PostStutter and PreStutter insert at least one step; MayPostStutter and MayPreStutter permit zero. Correctness needs a countdown closed in its domain and reaching bottom from every domain value, a valid initial countdown on reachable original actions, and correct enablement for the pre form. StutterConstantCondition expresses finite reachability of bottom through a recursive closure over Nat. The alternative version is justified for finite Sigma. Replacing Nat and Sigma with finite TLC domains checks those instances only (Q14,C2).  There is an actual paper/archive difference. Figure 16 sets MayPreStutter's first countdown to decr(initVal), whereas the retained root Stuttering.tla sets it to initVal. A static trace with bot=0, initVal=1, decr(j)=j−1 therefore adds one pre-action step in the printed version and two in the archived version. This concerns the exact extra-step count when initVal differs from bot; it does not by itself refute auxiliary preservation or the snapshot example, which uses MayPostStutter. The archive comment also says “one fewer” while giving 42 as both the original and May operator example count. Do not assume all embedded Stuttering copies are identical to this root file (Q13,C2,D1).  Section 5.4 treats a different problem: an implementation whose original variables halt may need to represent an abstract behavior with infinitely many internal steps. A history counter on an added unchanged-vars action, plus weak fairness for that auxiliary action, supplies infinitely many hidden steps. This is distinct from accidentally making an ordinary countdown infinite. Section 5.5 retains the original liveness conjunct and states preservation of machine closure for the described stuttering construction (Q15).  ## Snapshot case: assumptions and proof structure  The generic linearizable-object specification uses BeginOp, DoOp and EndOp with visible operation interfaces and hidden object/internal state. Type and closure assumptions establish the legal operations and results; weak fairness describes eventual internal execution and return. The snapshot specialization has disjoint logical Readers and Writers, a nonempty value set with an initial value, and a register per writer. One physical process may act in both logical roles. These are atomic shared-memory specifications, with no network failure, crash recovery, weak-memory or Rust implementation model (Q16).  The example simplifies the unbounded-storage Afek snapshot algorithm. Each atomic register contains a value paired with an unbounded write number, so repeated writes never look identical. A reader collects registers twice, in arbitrary order, and returns only when the tagged collections agree. The omitted helping mechanism in the full algorithm is what would ensure termination despite interference; this simplified reader can retry forever. The paper explicitly states that only safety is satisfied (Q17,C3).  A direct state mapping to the usual linearizable snapshot fails. A reader can collect an old register value, a writer can install a new value, and the reader can still finish with the old snapshot. Its abstract read must occur before the write, but the original state then lacks the future information needed to choose that point. The authors move the hard prophecy construction to a more permissive abstract specification, NewLinearSnapshot. It records for each active reader the sequence of memory values during that read and chooses the returned member at completion. This reformulation gives the implementation a simpler history-only connection to the intermediate specification (Q18).  NewLinearSnapshotPS predicts which positive sequence index each reader will return. It adds an auxiliary step after BeginRd if index 1 is predicted, and after a write for each reader whose newly appended memory value is the predicted one. A countdown set removes one chosen reader at a time; its refinement expression assigns the corresponding atomic abstract read to those added steps. The displayed module asserts separate safety and full-spec refinement theorems. Its assumptions include StutterConstantCondition over SUBSET Readers with one-element removal; that condition must hold, so it cannot silently be extended to an infinite reader set containing an infinite countdown subset (Q19,Q20,C5).  AfekSimplifiedH instead records the memory sequence h for each active reader. BeginRd starts it, writes append to active histories, successful read completion clears it, and failed retries retain it. The mapping uses the first component of each tagged register for abstract memory, h for rstate, and wrNum/interface/tag relationships for abstract writer state. Figure 27's final statement is exactly “theorem SpecH ⇒ NLS ! SafeSpec”. This is a safety target, even though some surrounding prose and a retained source comment loosely refer to the full Spec. No general liveness result for the simplified algorithm follows from that prose (Q21,C4).  ## Evaluation and released model boundaries  The paper reports the final theorem checked by TLC in about ten hours on a circa-2012 laptop, using two readers, two writers, two register values, reader/writer symmetry, a state constraint of at most three writes per writer and two workers. This is a finite, constrained example check. No state count, memory use, scaling sweep, repeated-runtime distribution or unbounded mechanized final proof is supplied. Some local algebraic obligations have displayed TLAPS proofs, such as Next/Nxt equivalence; the final refinement theorems in the selected source files have no accompanying TLAPS proof (Q22,C4,C5).  The two retained shipped AfekSimplifiedH models use the same 2/2/2 reader/writer/value cardinalities, SpecH, TypeOKH and NLS!SafeSpec. Model_1 replaces Nat with 0..2 and constrains wrNum[i]<2; Model_2 uses 0..3 and wrNum[i]<3. Each defines symmetry as permutations of writers only. These retained settings differ from the prose's reader-and-writer symmetry and at-most-three-writes description. Strict wrNum<3 permits completed initial-state transitions only while the counter is below 3; it is not an exact encoding of allowing the third increment while remaining inside the state constraint. Without the unread historical logs/configuration, neither file can be identified as the reported ten-hour run. The observations qualify source correspondence; no rerun discrepancy is claimed (C6–C9,D2).  ## Contribution to the requested topics  This is directly relevant to proving concurrent/distributed systems correct in TLA+: its concrete value is choosing additional proof state without restricting the system's original behaviors, checking intermediate prophecy/countdown conditions, and separating safety from progress. It supplies substantial worked specifications and a concurrent snapshot refinement, rather than an empirical comparison of tools. It contains no Verus, verified Rust or LLM experiment.  Possible applications to specification/proof agents are reader proposals: require the hiding-equivalence obligation, preserve fairness and parameter assumptions, distinguish finite model checks from general proofs, and record paper/source differences. An agent that merely obtains a passing refinement implication could have strengthened away required behaviors or proved only safety. This paper explains the mathematical obligations such an evaluation should expose; it does not measure agent performance.
    - limits: Temporal hiding equivalence;prophecy reachability/injection/dependency obligations;terminating countdown/correctenablement;originalfairness;atomicsharedmemory/unboundedtags;simplifiedreadmaynotterminate;finiteconstrainedTLCnotunboundedproof;paper/archiveandmodelcorrespondencedifferences.
    - how much was read: most of it read

- Developing Bug-Free Machine Learning Systems With Formal Mathematics (2017)
    - what: Presents Certigrad, an implementation of stochastic computation graphs in Lean, with a reported machine-checkable proof that stochastic backpropagation produces unbiased estimates of the mathematical gradient of expected cost. It demonstrates a workflow in which formal specifications and attempted proofs guide implementation and expose both code errors and missing assumptions. It also reports verified Gaussian integration/reparameterization optimizations and an MNIST variational-autoencoder experiment with performance comparable to TensorFlow. Separates an executable stochastic program from its mathematical expectation semantics using Dist n, built by primitive sampling, deterministic returns and composition. The paper gives expectation and RNG-threading equations for each constructor. The initial all-graphs unbiasedness specification is strengthened with WellFormed, GradsExist, IntegralsExist and CanDiffUnderInts preconditions. A simple single-parameter, nonmemoizing implementation is proved first; a multi-parameter memoizing implementation is then proved equivalent. A heuristic tactic proves model-specific preconditions for the transformed AEVB graph. The verified optimization sequence integrates Gaussian KL terms and replaces parameter-dependent Gaussian sampling with standard-normal sampling followed by scale/shift, preserving the objective while changing the gradient estimator.
    - limits: Correctness is relative to the stated mathematical specification and adopted axioms. The authors assume real numbers, integration and primitive mathematical laws rather than constructing their foundations. They report repairing initially unsound axioms by restoring integrability conditions, but this reading does not independently audit that axiom set. The final displayed scalar theorem requires unique node identifiers and scalar leaves (WellFormed), appropriate differentiability for all relevant stochastic choices (GradsExist), existence of integrals (IntegralsExist), and conditions allowing gradients through integrals (CanDiffUnderInts). The implementation is reported to handle arbitrary tensor shapes and multiple parameters; the displayed specification deliberately simplifies these. Proving the generic algorithm is insufficient for an arbitrary client graph: each graph must meet the preconditions. Some are undecidable in general, so the theorem-proving tactic is heuristic rather than a complete decision procedure. The proof concerns ideal infinite-precision real arithmetic. The authors explicitly say replacing reals with floating-point numbers technically invalidates the specification and may cause numerical instability; no floating-point error bound is established here. The running system trusts optimized Eigen tensor operations and a small C++ wrapper to match the formally reasoned operations, and relies on Lean VM/runtime and primitive pseudo-random sampling. The paper describes corresponding mathematical/procedural distribution interpretations but does not establish a checked correctness theorem for the concrete RNG, Eigen, C++ wrapper or execution platform. Unbiased stochastic gradients do not establish convergence of ADAM, bounded gradient variance, statistical validity, good generalization or model fit. The empirical AEVB training comparison addresses one example, not those general guarantees. The source repeatedly says proving exposes all implementation errors. The supported guarantee is absence of violations of the modeled specification under its assumptions; specification errors, inconsistent axioms and implementation layers outside the model remain material, as the paper itself discusses. Claims of reduced cognitive burden and finding all bugs early are the authors’ development experience, not a controlled developer study or complete empirical bug census. The paper reports increased overall workload but supplies no person-hour or proof-size measurements.

- DiVM: Model Checking with LLVM and Graph Memory (2017)
    - what: Presents DiVM, an LLVM-IR virtual machine with graph-organized memory and verification hypercalls, plus DiOS, a verification-oriented OS that supports POSIX-like C/C++ programs in explicit-state and abstraction-driven model checking. The VM represents heap objects as graph nodes linked by pointer edges, tracks pointer/definedness types in shadow memory, uses object-level allocation/free and stable object identifiers, and stores stacks as graph-linked activation frames. A small hypercall interface exposes nondeterministic choice, interrupt points, tracing, shared-object marking and machine control to a virtualized OS. This separation lets the verifier keep a simple initial/successor interface while the OS implements scheduling, threads, syscalls, monitors and faults. The paper explains τ and symmetry reductions, abstraction compatibility, and evaluates DIVINE 4 against DIVINE 3 and ESBMC.

- Epistemic Model Checking of Atomic Commitment Protocols with Byzantine Failures (2017)
    - what: # Epistemic Model Checking of Atomic Commitment Protocols with Byzantine faults (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Omar Ibrahim Al-Bataineh, arXiv1705.02515v3,10May2017. The official arXiv metadata calls the paper “Epistemic Model Checking of Atomic Commitment Protocols with Byzantine Failures”; the visible PDF title ends “with Byzantine faults” (M1,Q0). Official and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. The paper uses MCK to replace knowledge tests in a two-phase-commit program with concrete predicates, then studies cheating detection and termination in a synchronous reliable environment. The main qualification is its own Table2: global consistency, commit validity, abort validity and universal cheating detection fail. Eventual participant decisions and the stated coordinator/participant termination tests hold for the tested finite models. This is an analysis of a vulnerable protocol family, not a proof of Byzantine-correct atomic commitment (Q0,Q8,Q11).  ## Scope and semantics  Read all14PDFpages, sections1–8,17reference entries, all three protocol figures and three tables. Viewed individual renders7,8,9,12,13 to inspect complete pseudocode, formulas and tables. The PDF's visible version/date is2017; its creation metadata says2019, which is not substituted for the publication date. The bibliography is not a recursive reading of its cited sources. No MCK program, checker, author code or solver was executed/imported; no serialized model/experiment data was loaded.  Knowledge is defined through indistinguishability: Ki(phi) holds if phi holds at every point compatible with agent i's local information. Perfect recall retains past observations. A knowledge-based program chooses actions using such formulas, whereas its concrete implementation uses predicates of observable variables and explicit history variables. Correct implementation requires equivalence at the program points/times where each knowledge test is used. Merely obtaining the same outcome on one run, or making a safe conservative replacement, is a weaker condition (Q1,Q2,Q3).  The proposed workflow is partly automated. A human guesses a Boolean predicate/history update for each knowledge formula; MCK checks X^n(pc_i=l implies (predicate iff knowledge)). The human inspects counterexamples and revises the guess. The paper expressly says this requires “inspection and human reasoning” and possibly “some ingenuity.” It does not supply a fully automatic synthesis algorithm, a proof of search termination, or an agent evaluation. Its discussion of unique implementations depends on perfect recall and present-time knowledge tests, rather than arbitrary epistemic programs (Q3).  ## Model, cases and reported properties  One process coordinates a transaction and the others vote yes/no. An honest coordinator commits only when its own and all participant votes are yes; otherwise it aborts. It broadcasts its decision, receives acknowledgments and uses nested knowledge tests to decide when to stop. A Byzantine coordinator can choose an incorrect decision or send inconsistent decisions to different participants. The considered faults target outcomes rather than deliberately delaying or blocking termination (Q4,Q5,Q6,Q9).  The environment delivers messages, handles synchronization and exposes the trap/cheatingDetected variables to participants. Communication is synchronous and reliable in the evaluated context, with bounded delays and chosen wait parameters. The general pseudocode also mentions undefined votes and communication failures; those are not evidence that the reported Byzantine-context checks include message loss. There is no arbitrary asynchronous scheduler, unbounded delay, crash recovery or cryptographic refinement result (Q5,Q9).  A participant can detect cheating immediately when it voted no but receives commit. Participants may also open a run: they exchange their votes and received decisions, exposing contradictory decisions or a no vote paired with some commit instruction. A participant that detects cheating publishes that fact through the modeled variable. Such a publication mechanism assumes appropriate truth/correspondence in the environment; no executable authentication or dissemination implementation is supplied in the paper (Q5,Q7,Q10).  The coordinator's vote remains private to it. If every participant voted yes and the coordinator sends one consistent but incorrect decision, opening the participants' observations does not expose its private vote. The paper reports a counterexample to universal cheating detection in this case. Its speculative policy follows the received decision when the participant does not know cheating occurred. That differs from requiring knowledge that no cheating occurred; the latter conservative policy is discussed as preventing commits in this information setting (Q10,Q11).  Table1 gives three phase-specific predicate replacements. At point1, known cheating is a no vote paired with a received commit. At point2, detection also includes published cheating or an opened run with a no vote/commit pair or inconsistent decisions. Its point3 replacement for not knowing cheating is a yes vote with no publication/no trap, or a trap showing all participant votes yes and decisions equal. These are printed claimed equivalences, with the limitations below preserved (Q11).  Table2 reports:1a global consistency fails;1b eventual participant decision holds;2a commit validity fails;2b abort validity fails;3 complete cheating detection fails;4a coordinator termination holds;4b participant termination holds. Specifications2a/2b explicitly constrain the coordinator's decision variable, while1a/1b concern participant outcomes. These different variables should not be collapsed into a claim about every honest participant's valid outcome. Failure of one displayed formula does not by itself identify all possible implementation failures; no full counterexample traces for every table cell are supplied (Q8,Q11).  The models were checked for d=2,3,4,5 agents. The paper says “We conjecture that our present implementation can be shown to work for all number of agents” (§7,p13). Thus the all-size generalization is a conjecture, not a parameterized proof. It refers to “two contexts” there although this retained version presents only one Byzantine-context results row; a second unseen experiment is not inferred (Q12).  ## Formula and predicate qualifications  The explicit abbreviation Khat_i(decision) is Ki(decision=commit OR decision=abort). This says that agent i knows a decision has been made. It is weaker than knowing which decision: Ki(decision=commit) OR Ki(decision=abort). A two-point information set with commit at one point and abort at the other satisfies the first formula but neither disjunct of the second. Consequently the paper's prose “knows the final decision” should be interpreted with this written formula in view. The printed formula does not alone establish value knowledge, even if other model observations might establish it in particular phases (Q7,Q8; reader semantic example).  Table1 point3 also appears too narrow for its claimed equivalence to NOT Ki(cheating). Consider an honest coordinator sending abort after a participant voted no, with trap=false and cheatingDetected=false. Cheating is actually false. By the factivity of knowledge under the stated indistinguishability semantics, Ki(cheating) is false, so its negation is true. Yet both disjuncts of the printed replacement require the participant's vote yes, making the predicate false. The program can still retain its already assigned abort outcome; this example challenges exact epistemic equivalence rather than proving an additional disagreement execution. The paper's unreleased environment/control-point details would be needed to see whether it excludes this apparently ordinary reachable case (Q2,Q7,Q11; reader derivation).  The no-vote stopping explanation appeals to abort validity while Table2 reports abort validity fails for the coordinator's decision. Knowing the correct prescribed decision and knowing the actual Byzantine coordinator variable are different claims. The record preserves this ambiguity instead of deriving an unqualified early-stop theorem. Similarly, Specifications3/4a/4b and §7 use a free participant index i in the printed formulas; their prose talks about everyone. The coordinator pseudocode does contain an explicit conjunction over participants before breaking. Treat the displayed specifications as schematic per-participant tests unless the missing MCK model establishes their quantification (Q6,Q8,Q9).  ## Run-length method and evaluation  For a coordinator stopping condition T, the paper checks X^n(NOT T) universally over runs. Its first failed bound identifies an execution where T holds; the proposed doubling then binary search seeks the smallest such bound. To find a uniform upper bound it instead checks X^n(T), seeking the first bound where every run satisfies T; a counterexample at one step earlier illustrates a slow run. These are model time/communication bounds, not observed wall-clock latency or throughput (Q12).  Binary search requires a monotone bounded predicate. Perfect recall preserves knowledge of past facts but does not, by itself, preserve knowledge of an arbitrary proposition about a changing current state. The one-shot decision/stopping model may provide the required persistence; its complete environment/transition model is needed to establish that. An asserted universal eventual stop also need not yield a finite uniform bound for arbitrary infinite-state systems. The paper's finite tested cases and its explicit “if any” upper-bound search should remain visible (Q12; reader methodological qualification).  Table3 reports a shortest run of one round and d−1 messages, and a longest run of three rounds and3(d−1)messages. Figure3's optional participant all-to-all exchange can add2(d−1)(d−2) sends if each of d−1 participants sends both its vote and decision to each other participant. That is reader arithmetic from its loop. The paper does not explain how this optional traffic is charged in Table3, so its linear message totals should not become an unqualified bound including every opened-run exchange (Q8,Q12).  No MCK version, hardware, state-space counts, checker runtimes, iteration counts, full environment listing, complete counterexample archive or source URL appears in the retained paper. Therefore its model-checking outcomes and timing/message claims remain author-reported. This read does not reproduce them or certify its printed formulas against a saved executable model. Future work includes coordinator replication, cryptography and improved fault detection (Q12,Q13).  ## Contribution to the requested topic  This provides a concrete specification-to-predicate refinement workflow for distributed protocols: preserving local observations/history, checking epistemic equivalence at exact control points and learning from counterexamples. Its negative results demonstrate that termination and detection improvements do not establish atomic-commit safety. There is no Verus/Rust implementation, TLA+ experiment or LLM agent. A reader proposal for proof/specification agents is to check formula/prose agreement, exact versus merely outcome-preserving predicate replacements, finite versus all-size coverage, hidden environment assumptions and complete message accounting separately.

Legal inputs with corrupted certificates need not all accept. §1: at label distance at least epsilon*n, rejector density is at least alpha*epsilon. Lemma4 says existence of an error-sensitive scheme implies the universal scheme is error-sensitive. Their proofs and the regular-subgraph impossibility example are deferred to the full version. The saved text notes regular is locally checkable; local checkability alone does not imply robust rejection counts. §3 universal certificates: every node gets the same triple (T,M,L), containing all IDs, adjacency matrix and all input labels. Nonboundary nodes have identical one-hop views and accept, so alpha*d≤boundary size. Sufficiency uses universal certificates: remove edges with two rejecting endpoints, yielding components with consistent descriptions; isolate all-rejecting components, replace labels using their legal source descriptions, then invoke local stability. Intended distance bound is (beta+1)k, hence alpha=1/(beta+1). Printed label/boundary equalities need qualification below. §4/Definition9: strong local stability allows replacement of one shared subgraph’s labels between two legal graphs, with repair cost proportional to its two boundaries. Lemma10 says it implies local stability; proof deferred. Strict separation in general and equivalence on bounded-degree graphs are asserted with proof in full version. On an even path, opposing orientations toward endpoints pasted at the midpoint require at least n/2 pointer-label edits but any one-round verifier sees only two altered boundary neighborhoods. Conversely, symmetric adjacency-list tree representation admits compact robust certificates. A one-round conversion from pointers to incident lists does not preserve node-edit distance under reverse reconstruction. §5/Theorem14: certificate has root ID I(u), parent ID P(u), distance d(u). Intended checks enforce symmetric tree adjacency, agreement on root ID across every communication edge, parent existence and decreasing distances, and child consistency on selected edges. Root has P(u)=ID(u),d=0. Printed checks unconditionally demand a neighbor with P(u), contradicting self-parent at root on a loop-free graph, and do not explicitly require parent edge in the selected input tree. §5/Theorem14 repair: remove communication edges whose endpoints both reject and corresponding input incidences. - Gomes et al. SEC Isabelle (2017)
    - title: Verifying Strong Eventual Consistency in Distributed Systems
    - what: Builds a reusable Isabelle/HOL framework that formalizes strong eventual consistency (SEC), an asynchronous unreliable causal-broadcast network, and three operation-based CRDTs: Replicated Growable Array, Observed-Remove Set, and increment-decrement Counter. The abstract convergence theorem proves that distinct happens-before-consistent operation lists with the same set of operations yield the same state when concurrent operations commute, while a separate no-failure condition gives progress. The network locale has six axioms covering unique node histories, delivery cause, local delivery, globally unique message IDs, causal delivery, and valid broadcast operations; messages may be delayed, reordered, dropped, or nodes may crash permanently. RGA proof models immutable element IDs, tombstones, insertion ordering, causal validity, and proves concurrent operations commute and application never fails. ORSet uses add IDs and remove sets of observed IDs; Add/Remove commute only under a proved independence condition. Counter operations commute unconditionally. The framework is executable via Isabelle code generation; one counter implementation ran over TCP, but detailed performance/fault-tolerance evaluation was left for future work.
    - number: 3 CRDTs verified

The model uses crash-stop permanent node failure, not recovery, and does not model overlay implementation, timing, or resource limits. RGA retains tombstones; garbage collection is explicitly out of scope. The correctness claims are for operation-based CRDTs satisfying the five SEC locale obligations, not arbitrary distributed data types. Executable extraction demonstrates computability rather than performance.

    - title: Model Checking for Fragments of Halpern and Shoham’s Interval Temporal Logic Based on Track Representatives
    - what: Develops model checking for Halpern–Shoham interval-temporal-logic fragments over finite Kripke structures. For AABBE (and symmetrically AAEBE), it introduces finite track descriptors and bounded track representatives, yielding an EXPSPACE procedure and PSPACE-hardness; AABE/AB are PSPACE-complete and universal ∀AABE/Prop are coNP-complete. The paper maps every finite Kripke track to a homogeneous abstract interval model and defines B_k-descriptors encoding prefixes up to B-nesting depth k. Descriptor-element types, clusters, and k-indistinguishability identify repeated prefixes with identical descriptors; contraction replaces them while preserving the descriptor. The bound τ(|W|,k)=min(1+(1+|W|)^(2k+4)+|W|, 1+(k+3)|W|^(|W|²+1)+|W|) limits representative length. An unravelling algorithm explores forward/backward tracks with this bound, and recursive Check/ModCheck procedures are proved sound and complete. Examples encode scheduler mutual exclusion, reachability, and starvation; hardness reductions establish PSPACE-hard AABE/AB and coNP-hard propositional fragments.
    - number: AABBE model checking in EXPSPACE

    - number: ∀AABE and Prop coNP-complete
    - limits: Models are finite Kripke structures with left-total transitions; interval propositions use the homogeneity assumption (true on an interval iff true on all constituent states). The method bounds tracks for fixed B-nesting depth and can require exponential working space; descriptor counts are non-elementary in general. It addresses model checking, not satisfiability of full HS (known undecidable), and examples are illustrative rather than empirical system evaluations. Succinct formula encodings raise AABBE hardness to NEXP-hard.

    - what: Builds hybrid-system models of dynamic-window-style ground-robot controllers and proves safety and liveness in differential dynamic logic (dL). KeYmaera X proofs are converted into ModelPlex runtime monitors. The models make control-loop delay ε, robot acceleration/braking, obstacle speed, and circular motion symbolic. Theorems 1–4 prove collision properties using loop and differential invariants; Theorem 3 additionally proves an obstacle has an execution that can brake safely, and Theorem 4 limits responsibility to visible orientation sectors. Refinements prove safety with actual acceleration (Theorem 5), trajectory-distance sharp turns (Theorem 6), location uncertainty (7), actuator damping (8), velocity uncertainty (9), asynchronous obstacle decisions (10), and quantified arbitrary obstacles (11). Liveness proofs establish waypoint reachability (12), intersection crossing (13), and deadline variants (14–15). Concrete instantiations analyze indoor doors/corridors, and synthesized ModelPlex conditions check sensor/actuator samples against the verified model and trigger fail-safe stopping on deviations. Proof statistics show automation but nontrivial QE cost.

    - title: An Abstraction Technique for Parameterized Model Checking of Leader Election Protocols: Application to FTSP
    - what: Develops a simulation-preserving abstraction for parameterized timed leader-election protocols with unique identifiers and arbitrary topologies. It abstracts non-leader nodes and network edges around a shortest path to the future leader, approximates clock drift with finite schedulers, and incrementally checks FTSP root election for all graphs bounded by leader distance K. The method first maps identifiers/messages to future-root versus non-root values and relaxes irrelevant sequence/entry variables, then completes the graph outside a chosen shortest path and merges those nodes into an environment process. Simulation lemmas establish that checking the finite abstract model implies LTL properties on every topology in G_K. Approximate-synchrony scheduler S_a(Δ) over-approximates real clocks for a finite horizon derived from σ_l,σ_u,Δ. An incremental proof initializes already-converged path nodes and uses a non-interference guard to remove spurious environment messages. A NuSMV semi-algorithm finds optimal FG bounds without storing all reachable states.

    - title: Faster Statistical Model Checking for Unbounded Temporal Properties
    - what: Introduces SimAdaptive, a black-box statistical model-checking algorithm that monitors simulation prefixes to infer bottom strongly connected components (BSCCs), stopping runs early while retaining confidence guarantees for unbounded reachability, full LTL and mean-payoff properties. A path's candidate BSCC is defined by a suffix that is a graph BSCC; k-candidates and strong candidates bound false detection using the minimum positive transition probability pmin. Candidate lifetimes and a union bound yield Algorithm ReachedBSCC with error δ, which feeds sequential probability-ratio testing for reachability. The paper extends the construction to LTL and derives mean-payoff estimators with bounded expected error, then proves an expected runtime bound depending on transient depth R, BSCC size B and hitting time T. Prism experiments compare SimAdaptive against topology-agnostic simulation, topology-aware analysis and numerical model checking across huge benchmark chains.
    - number: pmin lower bound required
    - number: α=β=ε=0.01; δ=0.001 reachability
    - number: 1,000-step candidate-check optimization
    - number: runtime bound O(sim · k^(R+B) · B · T)
    - limits: The chain is finite, discrete-time, and sampled from a fixed initial state; a positive lower bound pmin on every nonzero transition is required. Statistical answers are only guaranteed outside an ε indifference region and have α/β/δ confidence parameters. Candidate detection can be slow for deep systems or large BSCCs, with runtime bound O(sim · k^(R+B) · B · T); the implementation checks candidates every 1,000 steps and modifies some Prism models (self-loops for deadlocks, one initial state). The approach is not a replacement for topology-aware methods and extension to MDPs is future work.

- Alloy meets TLA+: An exploratory study (2016)
    - what: # Alloy meets TLA+: An exploratory study (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Macedo and Cunha compare a manually embedded hotel locking model in Alloy and TLA+, then measure checking costs with Alloy Analyzer 4.2/MiniSat and TLC 2.08. This is a one-example exploratory study. Their scope is explicit: “using a concrete example” (§1, PDF p. 2, Q6). No general translator, equivalence theorem, implementation proof or named theorem is presented. The source is arXiv1603.03599v1, 11 March2016, 14pages; a further publication venue was not established.  ## What the model assumes and checks (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The front desk is disconnected from room locks. A lock accepts its current key or the next key in its room’s ordered, disjoint keypool; accepting a newer key invalidates the old one. Guests keep keys after checkout. Initially rooms are vacant, guests hold no keys and the front desk’s last-issued key equals the lock’s current key (§§2–2.1, PDF pp. 3–5, Q7–Q11). The authors describe the retained-key behavior directly: “allows the guest to keep the room key” (§2.1, PDF p. 5, Q11). The finite model has no fairness constraint (§3.1, PDF p. 9, Q22).  The prose says a guest should enter only its own room. The printed assertion is narrower: “(Entry[t, t’, g, r, k] and some FD.occupant.t[r]) implies g in FD.occupant.t[r]” (Figure 1, PDF p. 4, Q10). It tests entry into an occupied room and allows entry into an empty room. The TLA+ property has the same nonempty-occupant guard (Figure 3, PDF p. 7, Q17). The experiment checks safety; discussion of finite-trace liveness pitfalls is not a liveness evaluation.  The counterexample has five states: initialization; g0 checks into r1 with k1; g0 checks out; g1 checks into r1 with k2; g0 enters using k1 before g1 first uses k2 (Figure 2, PDF p. 6, Q15; §2.2, PDF p. 5, Q14). It demonstrates the delay between issuing a fresh key and updating a disconnected lock. The proposed restriction is to “assume that guests enter the room immediately” after check-in (§2.2, PDF p. 5, Q14). NoIntervening therefore changes allowed environment behavior. The authors report no counterexample after adding it in the checked models; this is not a verified implementation repair or an unbounded Alloy proof.  The printed models and prose contain a reproducibility mismatch. Figure 1 includes NoIntervening and prints “check NoBadEntry for 3 but 30 Time” (Q10), while §2.2 describes 3 elements/5 Time and a counterexample (Q13), and §4 calls Figure 1 an n = 4/t = 30 model (Q30). Figure 3 also includes NoIntervening in Spec, while Figure 4 shows a counterexample (Q17–Q18). The evaluation explicitly ran with and without the restriction (Q29); the printed restricted listings alone should not be described as producing those unrestricted traces.  ## What the embedding exposes (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The study distinguishes TLA+ expressiveness from TLC’s executable subset (§3, PDF p. 6, Q16). Alloy’s static structures range over possible assignments, while a TLC constant assignment fixes one structure. To preserve the intended search, Room, Guest and keypools are initialized nondeterministically as variables and then held unchanged. Fixing exactly 3 rooms and 3 keys misses this bug because a room needs two spare keys for the successive check-ins (§3.1, PDF p. 8, Q19). This is a concrete example of a checker returning no counterexample after the search universe has been narrowed incorrectly.  Alloy’s explicit Time ordering creates exact trace scopes. The authors warn that “there is no guarantee that counter-examples occurring” in smaller traces recur at larger exact scopes (§2.2, PDF p. 5, Q13). They therefore check every scope through t and accumulate the cost. A bound below 5 misses this bug. These are finite trace checks over finite key/room/guest universes, not a parameterized proof.  The TLA+ version encodes Alloy facts through TypeInv in Next. The authors separately report checking TypeInv as an invariant and observing preservation by the actions (footnote 2, PDF p. 9, Q23); this is a reported finite-model check. TLC’s enumeration/order/next-state requirements and relational encoding issues constrain the manual embedding (§3.1, PDF pp. 8–10, Q20–Q24). No general derivation algorithm is supplied.  Stuttering affects what counts as an observed event. When a registered key is used again, Entry changes no variable: “TLC will not recognize such” steps, “identifying instead a stuttering step” (§3.2, PDF p. 10, Q25). The box-action NoBadEntry accepts stuttering independently of its inner action condition. The paper leaves general action-semantic correspondence unresolved (§5, PDF p. 14, Q37). This record identifies that limit; it does not construct a reachable unauthorized stuttering entry or refute the restricted model. NoIntervening is rewritten from a constraint on three Time instants to a state predicate Post plus the next Entry; stuttering remains allowed and no fairness is added (Figures 1/3, Q10/Q17;Q22/Q27). Deadlock reporting was disabled for finite key exhaustion and state-preserving Entry (§3.2, Q26). No progress or deadlock-freedom result follows.  ## What was measured (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The study used a 1.8 GHz Intel Core i5, 4 GB, OS X 10.10, Alloy Analyzer 4.2 with MiniSat and TLC 2.08. Tests ran “multiple times”; no repetition count, variance or raw trials are supplied (§4, PDF p. 11, Q29). TLC breadth-first and depth-first searches were tested, with depth-first limited to 100. Thus the paper’s general description of unlimited TLC trace length must not be applied to every plotted curve.  Figure 5 contains six panels and five series: TLA BF, TLA DF, Alloy, TLA En, Alloy En (PDF p. 12, Q31 and figure-evidence.json). Panels a/b vary n with Alloy t = 30; c/d use the different exact universe; e/f vary t with n = 4. The vertical axis is logarithmic seconds. All panels were inspected; no exact point timings were inferred from raster curves. No error bars or raw trials are provided.  Here n denotes exact ordered-key count and maximum room/guest counts. Alloy’s time at t aggregates checks for all scopes 1 through t; BF finds a shortest witness directly (§4, Q30). The authors report that the Analyzer finds the n = 4 counterexample at t = 5 “in less than a second in contrast to TLC’s 415 seconds” (§4, PDF p. 11, Q30). The sentence does not identify which TLC search mode the 415 seconds denotes. This is verification runtime on this model and historical setup, not application latency or a general tool speedup.  Generating static configurations is expensive. The original model has 776 initial states at n = 3 and 18,960 at n = 4. A second model fixes exactly n rooms and n guests and uses n + 2 keys, giving 108 and 960 states. The paper explicitly says these universes “are not directly comparable” at the same n (§4, PDF pp. 12–13, Q32–Q33). Do not treat the change as a semantics-preserving reduction of the original universe.  A preliminary hybrid uses Alloy to enumerate initial structures and TLC to check each fixed structure. Alloy’s symmetry breaking reduces 18,960 to 520 representatives for n = 4, generated in “less than 2 seconds” (§4, PDF p. 13, Q34). Disabling symmetry recovers 18,960. The partition loses the global shortest-counterexample guarantee and state sharing. For counterexample timings the authors “considered a” portion of the initial states after measuring the fraction that produce a counterexample; neither fraction nor portion/order is supplied (§4, Q35). With NoIntervening they consider all initial states. The hybrid improves some TLC curves; its gains over pure Alloy “are not so evident” (Q35). No proven general translator or symmetry-preservation result accompanies this preliminary comparison.  ## What it adds to the requested topic (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The direct contribution is a detailed historical Alloy/TLA+ modeling comparison with a complete small example and measured checking costs. Distributed algorithms motivate systems with rich structures and dynamics (§1, Q3), but hotel locking is the sole evaluated case. No Verus, verified Rust or LLM experiment appears.  For evaluating LLM-written specifications, I infer concrete checks from this example: compare exact versus maximum cardinalities; read the property’s guard; separate an implementation repair from an environment restriction; check event/stutter correspondence; distinguish checked invariants from imposed constraints; compare trace coverage and cumulative timing; retain sampled-state caveats. These are reader-derived evaluation lessons, not measured LLM results. The authors’ own conclusion keeps the main performance limit explicit: “the obvious caveat of the bounded search space” (§5, PDF p. 14, Q37).  ## Evidence and limits of this read (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Read all 649 layout-text lines, all 14 pages, every printed Alloy/TLA+ definition/configuration, five figures including six Figure 5 panels, Table 1 and all 11 references. Inspected seven contact sheets and the fullsize plot page. The bundle retains 38 literal line/character/page-anchored excerpts, 17 reader diagnostics, numeric evidence, visual evidence and hashes. combined.quote-source.txt is the staging source; source_files contains path strings and raw hashes are separate. No separate model/benchmark archive URL was identified in the paper or obtained. No author code, checker, solver or prover was executed, and no serialized scientific/model/results data were loaded. Results are author-reported and statically inspected, not independently reproduced. Historical language/tool claims should not be projected onto current versions.

NoIntervening restricts environment behavior. Bounded exact Alloy trace scopes; finite TLC universes and depth-first limit 100. General translation and stutter/event correspondence unresolved. Printed scope/variant mismatch retained.

- Array Folds Logic (2016)
    - what: Array Folds Logic adds restricted deterministic folds and integer counting to finite unbounded-length integer arrays. Folds translate into reversal-bounded symbolic counter machines; products coordinate folds over the same array and Presburger encodings decide reachability. The paper claims PSPACE-complete satisfiability, NP-completeness for a fixed maximum number of folds per array, and undecidability with existential-universal quantification or concatenation. AFolder solves manually encoded parser, processor-mapping, loop-safety and histogram cases. Records the precise counter/control restrictions, implicit break semantics, model construction, why folds per array rather than total folds drives product cost, and the lack of automatic program-to-formula generation. Preserves all17 measured cases and source discrepancies in example code/formulas, a printed multiplication reduction, signed-value bounds, and a table count. These are reader observations about the chapter, not claims that the implementation or the underlying results have been disproved.
    - limits: §§2–2.2: arrays are finite integer sequences Z*, with natural array indices and integer elements/counters; length and values are unbounded across models. Free array/integer variables are implicitly existential. This models mathematical integers, not source-language bitvector overflow, pointer aliasing or C allocation. Read-over-write axioms are assumed, but out-of-bounds reads are not explicitly assigned a value in the supplied semantics. §2.1/Table1: fold input vector contains initial index and counters, with implicit state initially0. Each step consumes one current element; guards may also use integer terms with fixed array reads such as a[p]. It compares element/index/counter with an integer term and state with a constant, increments/decrements counters by constants, assigns constant control states, and increments index by1. No arbitrary multiplication, counter-to-counter update, arbitrary array mutation inside fold, or general higher-order lambda is allowed. §2.1: branch guards must be mutually exclusive; at most one update per implicit variable in a branch. If no guard matches, implicit break returns the current vector before consuming that element. Out-of-bounds index likewise terminates. Within each control-flow SCC, every counter has only nondecreasing or only nonincreasing updates; SCC changes bound reversals. Dropping this restriction invalidates the stated decision construction. §2.3: expressiveness examples include bounded values, a guessed pivot partition, alternating symbols, equal block counts, equal counts across arrays, histogram ratios, and length-prefixed fields. Sortedness requiring relationships between arbitrary pairs of indices is explicitly inexpressible; counting expressiveness does not subsume quantified array logics. Comparisons to other logics are the authors’ claims about cited contemporary fragments, not a survey of all later systems. §3: parser proof obligations use SSA names, fold summaries for inner loops, and bounded unfolding of the outer column loop. Satisfying formula gives a selected accepted-path test, not a proof of all parser behavior or safety. Last conditional’s failure branch is easy for Crest; accepted branch with required columns is hard. No fully automatic whole-program summarization front end is implemented in this paper. §4/Definitions1–3: SCM has finite control, a shared symbolic input integer per transition, constants/free parameters and counters; its product conjoins guards/input constraints and concatenates counter vectors. Products are needed when folds share an array, since independently satisfiable per-fold runs may require incompatible cell values. Arbitrary differing start/stop indices, negated fold equalities, reads/writes and signed counters need semantic handling beyond simply taking the displayed lockstep product. §4/Lemma1: claimed small model uses exponentially bounded array length and integer values, supporting polynomial-space guessing of parameter values and successive cells while simulating folds. Proof sketch chooses a satisfying Boolean valuation, uses counter regions/modes, compresses runs via integer linear programming and obtains short runs/cell values. Full proof is referred to separate arXiv version [14]. The statement prints an upper bound on signed integers but not an absolute-value/lower bound; the polynomial-bit representation conclusion needs both sides controlled. §4/Theorem1: PSPACE membership uses that small-model argument; hardness reduces DFA-intersection nonemptiness to simultaneous folds over one shared array. This is a formula satisfiability complexity theorem, not measured runtime or a proof of arbitrary array-program verification decidability. No formal proof-assistant mechanization is reported. §4.1: Theorem2 claims undecidability for ∃*∀* AFL via Hilbert’s Tenth Problem/multiplication. Corollary1 derives concatenation undecidability using a quoted existing word-equation result (Theorem3) plus definability of unary counts. The printed multiplication encoding has a concrete counterexample recorded below; distinguish the intended result from validation of this displayed proof. §5: deterministic encoding separates nonfold constraints, product-machine reachability and initial/final linking. Counter-bound parameters are assumed in a fixed order. Regions and at most O(|phi|³) modes lead to an NFA, Parikh counts and constraints enforcing counter feasibility; generated Presburger formula has stated size O(|phi|^(m+4)) with at most m folds per array. Handling arbitrary parameter order is not detailed; guessing an order is compatible with NP reasoning but literal deterministic enumeration need not have the same polynomial size. §5/Lemma2: fixed m-AFL is NP-complete; Presburger arithmetic already gives hardness for0-fold formulas. Fixing the total number of folds is stronger than needed. The relevant bound is folds per shared array, after identifying arrays that must be equal; many independent arrays can each have one fold and still avoid one large product. §5 model generation: solve Presburger constraints, instantiate Parikh multiplicities, form a transition multigraph, recover an Eulerian path and choose cell values satisfying associated input constraints. This is witness construction as described, not independent solver-certificate checking. Materializing an exponentially long array can cost more than deciding existence. §6: AFolder is C++ with Z3 Presburger backend. Ubuntu14.04 64bit/IntelCorei5-2540M2.60GHz. Formula size counts logical operators plus branches, not source LOC or bits. Table has17 selected instances,10sat/7unsat, no reported timeouts or run variance. Translation/solving times are separate; array length is longest array in a sat model. No current repository build, proof-kernel check or independent model replay was performed. §6/SV-COMP: six simple manually modeled safety conditions are UNSAT below1s translation and below1s solving each. Authors state most competing SV-COMP tools fail them, but provide no side-by-side tool list, configuration or comparative timing table in this chapter. These results do not establish an end-to-end safe verdict for every source program absent correctness of its encoding. §7: automated proof-obligation generation and loop summarization, combinations with other decidable array fragments and implementation optimizations are future work. IPv6/TLV is motivation, not a verified network protocol case study. NUMA example counts processor assignments per thread; no concurrent scheduling, distributed protocol, Rust/Verus/TLA+ or LLM proof-agent evaluation is given.

- Automaton learning for infinite safety games (2016)
    - title: An Automaton Learning Approach to Solving Safety Games over Infinite Graphs.
    - what: Learns finite-state winning controllers for safety games over infinite or very large graphs. Rational arenas encode vertex sets as regular languages and edges as rational relations; an ICE-like teacher returns positive, negative, existential-implication or universal-implication counterexamples, and a SAT-based learner constructs minimal consistent DFAs. The paper proves closure properties of rational relations, defines winning sets and a generic automata-theoretic teacher, and gives SAT encodings whose satisfiability is equivalent to existence of an n-state DFA consistent with the sample. The minimal-consistent-DFA algorithm increments n and terminates at the minimum; the full learner terminates with a winning set when one exists. An RPNI heuristic is sound but incomplete and restricted to finite out-degree. Examples include unary encodings of grid positions, implication counterexamples, diagonal/box/evasion/follow games and program repair.

    - number: 300 s timeout and 16 GiB memory
    - limits: Winner determination for rational safety games is undecidable, so the method is a semi-algorithm and assumes a winning set exists for the termination theorem. The SAT learner's passive DFA identification is NP-complete in general; RPNI cannot guarantee minimality or completeness and handles only finite implication languages. Experiments use regular-language/transducer encodings and finite-state safety objectives; results do not establish liveness synthesis or arbitrary infinite-state game classes.

    - title: Bounded Model Checking for Probabilistic Programs?
    - what: Develops an on-the-fly bounded model-checking method for conditional probabilistic programs. Each finite unrolling constructs a finite operational MDP, and monotonic growth of conditional reachability probabilities and expected rewards yields sound lower bounds; parametric iterations can permanently classify valuations that already violate a property.     - title: A Safety and Liveness Theory for Total Reversibility?
    - what: Defines CCSroll, a CCS extension with totally ordered keyed reductions and programmed rollback, and characterizes safety and liveness preorders using forward traces, rollback barbs and tree refusals. The syntax/semantics records memories and dependency histories so a rollback of key k deterministically returns all later reductions to the state before k. The authors prove rollback determinism and rollback/forward correspondence, then identify two semantic properties enabling forward-only reasoning. Observable trace inclusion is shown sound and complete for inverse may-testing safety; a rollback-aware tree-refusal model is sound and complete for should-testing liveness. Examples M1–M6 show safety conservatively extends CCS while rollback distinguishes systems that CCS cannot distinguish; the paper also gives compositional LTS, trace zipping/unzipping, and characteristic tests.

    - what: Gives a direct compositional translation from full LTL to limit-deterministic Büchi automata (LDBA). The construction supports the standard quantitative MDP model-checking algorithm by encoding jumps as product actions. The construction defines Reach(ϕ) via the after-function modulo propositional equivalence, then builds one deterministic G-monitor for each guessed G-subformula and a product of monitors, plus an auxiliary monitor for the G-free residual. Theorem 2 gives a double-exponential lower bound. Theorem 3 proves that the LDBA can be used directly in quantitative MDP checking by delaying the jump until a BSCC determines the eventual G-set. - Adam (2015)
    - title: Adam: Causality-Based Synthesis of Distributed Systems
    - what: Presents the Adam Java implementation of symbolic Petri-game synthesis: a separate controller for each process uses its causal past and exchanges knowledge at joint transitions. A winning strategy avoids bad places and avoids introducing deadlocks. The paper sketches a finite two-player reduction and reports controller-synthesis benchmarks. Cuts are maximal concurrent sets of places annotated by enabled decision sets and type-1/type-2 system tokens. Type-2 tokens will never synchronize, even indirectly, with the environment; type-1 tokens are blocked until its next move. Environment choices are delayed until an mcut so independent system choices cannot depend on unseen environment choices. The BDD encoding assigns places to tokens rather than arbitrary subsets of places. Phase 1 computes valid type-2 cuts by greatest fixed point; phase 2 combines greatest/least fixed points for winning mcuts and their predecessors; phase 3 extracts a strategy and per-player projections. Net invariants compact the place encoding.
    - number: CM 6/2: 15 tokens, 244 BDD variables, 46 places/48 transitions, 1042.2 s and 2.51 GB; strategy 105 places/36 transitions

    - number: DW 20: 22 tokens, 516 BDD variables, 1734.7 s and 15.85 GB; strategy 1264 places/861 transitions
    - limits: One environment player, an arbitrary but bounded number of system players, and safe nets (at most one token per place). Bounded nonsafe nets can be translated to safe nets. Players know their causal past and exchange it only when synchronizing; controllers need this modeled communication/memory. Safety plus deadlock avoidance is the objective, not general liveness: terminating net markings are permitted when the underlying unfolding itself has no enabled transition. Benchmark sizes and timings do not establish scalability for unbounded protocols. No TLA+, Rust, Verus, LLM, or machine-checked implementation evaluation.

    - what: Gives a direct alternating-Büchi-automaton construction for finite-state HyperLTL/HyperCTL* model checking, including quantifier alternation via nondeterminization and complementation. For a restricted alternation-free fragment, reduces checking to a small symbolic circuit with bad-state and strong-fairness constraints. Uses ABC to analyze hardware information flow, cross-execution symmetry of a finite Bakery implementation, and error-code Hamming distance. Preserves the temporal-placement restrictions in alternation-free syntax, current-path branching semantics, formula versus explicit-state complexity, latch-count encoding bound and assumptions behind circuit simplifications. Documents concrete invalid-ID, scheduling/tie-breaking and reset-polarity counterexamples, all benchmark rows, intended information flows versus vulnerabilities and missing quantitative-flow/experimental details.
    - limits: §2: Kripke structures have a successor from every state, hence infinite paths. Path assignments advance synchronously; a newly quantified path starts at the current state of the most recently quantified path epsilon. HyperLTL places all quantifiers in a prefix; HyperCTL* permits branching quantification inside temporal operators. These are finite-state model results, not parameterized proofs over arbitrary process counts. §3.1 Definition2: alternation-free means one quantifier type in negation normal form plus placement restrictions: no existential in the left of Until or right of Release; no universal in the right of Until or left of Release. Boolean combinations of separately checked blocks are handled. A formula with no textual ∀/∃ switch can still incur extra alternation through a forbidden temporal placement. §3.1: standard Boolean/Next/Until/Release automata are combined bottom up. Existential path elimination first applies Miyano–Hayashi nondeterminization, then products with the Kripke structure and projects a state component. This preserves a common witness path across alternating branches; projecting arbitrary alternating branches independently is not the construction. §3.1 Theorem2 states PSPACE-completeness in formula size and NLOGSPACE-completeness in explicit Kripke-structure size. This is not a logarithmic-space or polynomial-time claim in the number of circuit latches: a circuit represents an exponentially large state graph. Proposition1 gives correctness with structural-induction explanation; no mechanized metatheory or verified implementation is supplied. §3.2: full logic uses complementation of alternating automata and nondeterminization. With g(0,n)=n and g(k,n)=c^g(k-1,n), Theorem4 gives NSPACE(g(k,|formula|)) and NSPACE(g(k-1,|K|)), defining level-1 as NLOGSPACE. These are upper bounds parameterized by alternation depth; the practical circuit implementation/evaluation is for the restricted alternation-free fragment. §4: circuit transition is input-enabled and input-deterministic, with nonempty initial states. Associated Kripke structure adds a dummy initial state and shifts atoms by Next. Strong-fairness pair(a1,a2) requires a1 finitely often or a2 infinitely often. Validity is reduced to an initial formula output, no bad outputs and these fairness conditions; plain bounded safety search is not a complete substitute for fair reachability. §4 Proposition3 bounds latch count by |C|*k+|formula| for k path quantifiers; the paper defines circuit size as number of latches, abstracting the gate list. This does not bound every gate/transition-expression size by the same expression. Quantifier copies synchronize their starting latches; outputs track obligations and bad-state violations. Conjunction/Release circuit rules are explicitly omitted for space; correctness is sketched by structural induction. §5: implementation transforms AIGER circuits obtained by standard VHDL/Verilog synthesis; ABC supplies IC3/PDR, interpolation and BMC. Intel Core i5-4278U at2.6GHz. Defaults except starred Sym9; exact exceptional setting, timeout duration, RAM limit, repetitions and error bars are not specified. Dashes in BMC cells are not zero-second proofs, and TO is unresolved within an unspecified budget. §5.1: most I2C noninterference formulas intentionally fail because address/data transfer is the function of the bus. Failure alone is not a security vulnerability. NI3 holds with write enable off; NI5 fails because concurrent masters/arbitration affect later interpretation. Long-term NI7/8 fail, indicating information may persist. NI6 is listed/timed but has no separate prose explanation. §5.1: 3-bit address flow is determined for QNI1, while the log2(9)≈3.17-bit upper-bound query QNI2 times out. Neither quantitative-flow query is in Table1. The later assertion that all I2C properties were easily analyzed must be qualified by this reported timeout. §5.2: Bakery analysis is a synchronous finite Verilog model with select/pause inputs. Illegal select IDs advance process0. Excluding those paths, parameterizing tie resolution and contracting ID comparisons into one step change assumptions/model behavior before S3 is satisfied. Results do not show the unchanged original protocol is fully symmetric or prove starvation freedom/mutual exclusion under every scheduler. §5.2: printed S1–S3 use two universal path quantifiers, despite prose saying every execution has another swapped execution. Deterministic input-enabled circuit semantics support relating paired swapped inputs; do not silently rewrite the displayed formula to ∀∃. The weak-until rewrite removes a liveness-shaped part only under the stated input-determinism/input-enabledness conditions. §5.3: valid encoder properties depend on reset/control configuration and distinct data inputs. Huffman and8b10b are not error-correcting codes and only distance1 is expected. Hamming7–4 encodes4bits into7bits and is checked up to distance3. Active-high versus documented active-low reset is a specification/implementation discrepancy, not proof of failed correction on correctly configured messages. Printed source issues: §2 defines Release as ¬(¬phi1 U ¬phi1), repeating phi1 where standard duality uses phi2 on the right; visual PDF confirms. The §3.1 definition of K-equivalent languages is written only as an accepted-word implication, while later propositions use equivalence language. Record does not treat these presentation issues as an independent refutation of the algorithm. Hardware synthesis, circuit transformation, model semantics, specifications and ABC remain trusted. No proof certificates, independent checker or artifact execution are evaluated here. Claims of first/practical/industrial scale are author claims about selected cases. No Rust, Verus, TLA+ or LLM result is reported.
