- Automatic Completion of Distributed Protocols with Symmetry. (2015)
    - what: # Automatic Completion of Distributed Protocols with Symmetry (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Rajeev Alur, Mukund Raghothaman, Christos Stergiou, Stavros Tripakis and Abhishek Udupa, arXiv:1505.04409v1. The arXiv comments identify this as the “Full version of paper presented at CAV 2015.” The paper gives a solver-and-model-checker loop that fills missing guards and state updates in finite distributed protocol sketches, requiring determinism, symmetry, deadlock freedom, safety and liveness under supplied fairness assumptions. Its empirical results cover Peterson mutual exclusion, a four-process self-stabilizing line, and five missing cache-coherence corner cases. Guaranteed correctness is explicitly limited to the finite synthesized instance (Q1,Q2,Q6,Q13,W1,W2).  ## Reading and evidence scope  Read all 21 pages, sections 1–6, all displayed definitions/formulas, nine figures, the complete five-row Table 1, and all 31 bibliography entries. There is no appendix, checklist, numbered theorem/proof or numbered pseudocode algorithm. Figure 2 is the synthesis workflow; §4 gives textual algorithms. Individually inspected page renders 3,8,11,13,14,15,16,17,18,19, covering every figure, the table, protocol diagrams and the weakest-precondition formula. This does not claim visual inspection of all pages. References were read as bibliography entries, not recursively followed.  Retained the inventory PDF, raw/layout extractions and official arXiv metadata. The paper says the custom model checker is planned for future public release; it supplies no implementation URL. No implementation/model files or historical logs were acquired or read. A web-search tool request for code returned an error without results; this is not evidence that no code exists. No author contacted, author code executed/imported, checker/solver rerun, or model/checkpoint/serialized experiment data loaded. Source versions and reported runs were not independently reproduced (Q8,W1).  ## Problem and modeling assumptions  The designer provides extended state-machine sketches, not just an English request or temporal goal. Each process has finite control locations, finite typed variables/channels, an initial valuation, known and unknown typed functions, guarded transitions and fairness sets. All type cardinalities are required finite, including process-identity symmetric types and array domains. A completed function is initially a finite interpretation table. The environment is another specified machine with no unknown functions (Q3,Q4,Q6).  Composition synchronizes matching output/input channels and sequences their updates so the receiver sees the transmitted value; independent internal actions interleave. Buffered unordered communication in the cache example is modeled within these finite-state machines, not assumed to be an unbounded reliable network. The formal product assumes disjoint process state variables and output ownership. Safety means no reachable error location. Liveness means no infinite fair accepting run of the supplied monitors; deadlock freedom is separate. Thus a finite deadlock cannot pass just because no infinite violating run exists (Q3,Q4).  Weak fairness applies to a set of transitions: either the whole set is disabled infinitely often or some member occurs infinitely often. Strong fairness requires that a set enabled infinitely often has a member taken infinitely often. Fairness sets are attached to output/internal transitions; input behavior depends on the environment/composition. These assumptions matter to the guarantees. The paper argues that using only safety in synthesis permits trivial solutions that disable progress (Q2,Q3).  Symmetry means behavior is invariant under renaming values of the designated types. Permutations act on array entries and indices, channel/process parameters and states. Unknown functions are constrained to commute with renaming, f(π(d))=π(f(d)). This is stronger than merely using the same source text while permitting special treatment of one numeric identity. Quantifiers are expanded over finite domains for the solver. The discussion mentions other symmetry notions as possible extensions; the implementation/evaluation described uses the stated finite symmetry treatment (Q5,Q7).  The designer can restrict signatures to exclude irrelevant variables, fix known read-only updates, and add constraints across functions. The formal completion requires deterministic individual machines, a symmetric product, satisfaction of initial constraints, and a deadlock-free/safe/live composition. Determinism allows simultaneous input transitions only on distinct input channels. Guarantees concern that chosen environment, monitor and fairness model, not every implementation of the informal protocol name (Q6,Q7).  ## Algorithm and what its checks establish  The synthesis loop asks Z3 for interpretations satisfying current constraints, instantiates the protocol, then model-checks it. An erroneous candidate yields further necessary conditions excluding its counterexample or repairing the reason it violates the property. A successful interpretation may subsequently be converted to a symbolic expression using an enumerative syntax-guided synthesis solver. A symbolic grammar/output is therefore a later step; the initial solver does not directly synthesize arbitrary program syntax (Q6,Q10,Q13).  The custom checker combines a symmetry-reduced annotated quotient graph with permutation tracking in a threaded graph, then searches accepting strongly connected components under fairness. Tracking the renaming matters because a compressed path can stand for multiple original paths and fairness obligations must be adjusted accordingly. The described procedure removes states enabling unmet strong-fairness sets and recomputes components until it finds a fair accepting cycle or rules one out. The authors build on cited algorithms and describe the search as sound and complete; this paper supplies no separate numbered soundness/completeness proof or implementation certification. Their historical limitations of Spin, Murphi, SMC and NuSMV are reports about their tool attempts, not a current feature comparison (Q8).  For a deadlock, the next candidate must block the witnessed path or enable some outgoing action at its end. For a safety trace it must block the error path. The paper compiles product transitions to guarded commands, coalesces assignments and computes weakest preconditions; a guarded-command obligation uses guard implication, so a disabled step can break the trace. For liveness, a stem/cycle witness must become infeasible, fail to close, or become unfair. The Peterson example shows why simply banning the waiting loop is too strong: enabling a continuously neglected critical transition can make that loop unfair under the given fairness assumption (Q9,Q10).  There is a printed indexing problem worth preserving without treating it as an implementation defect. §4.3 indexes a trace cmd1,…,cmdn but defines pre_i using cmd_(n−i−1). With n=1 and i=1 this refers to cmd_−1 rather than the sole command. The intended reverse traversal would require a corrected index/convention; no source code was available to determine what the implementation uses. The rendered page 11 confirms the printed formula. The liveness recurrence also reuses notation inconsistently around the named union of fairness sets. These are presentation limits on mechanically following the text, not reproduced failures of the tool (Q10,D1).  Search heuristics prefer each error path to exercise few unknown functions while choosing diverse paths that collectively cover many. Shorter unknown-function dependencies can give stronger pruning constraints. Candidate costs favor minimally permissive guards, unchanged updates, then fewer input dependencies; bounds relax when the solver cannot satisfy them. Such constraints are search guidance, not protocol requirements. They strongly affect runtime, and Dijkstra required a different guard heuristic. No controlled ablation quantifies each optimization's benefit (Q11,Q12).  ## Concrete cases  Peterson has two processes with my/other identity parameters, shared flag/turn variables, a critical-section safety condition and a starvation monitor. Figure 1 removes the waiting/critical guards; the experiment additionally leaves flag-update expressions unspecified and requires that at least one guard hold. Weak fairness of selected non-input transitions suffices for the stated monitor. The authors report an interpretation in under one second and expressions matching the known protocol. Table 1 reports three unknown functions; this count is retained as printed rather than inferred by counting the distinct update sites mentioned in prose (Q3,Q12,T1).  The self-stabilizing case is four processes in a line, each with Boolean x/up state. The two middle processes have two unknown guarded commands, each with two unknown updates; corresponding middle-process completions must be identical. A legitimate state has exactly one globally enabled guarded command. The specification requires reaching legitimate states from arbitrary starts, staying legitimate thereafter, and reachability among legitimate states. The successful expressions match Dijkstra's displayed rules. This is synthesis/verification for N=4; the general-N illustration is not itself a parameterized correctness proof (Q12).  German/MSI has a directory, symmetric caches and one environment per cache; permissions are invalid/shared/exclusive. Its variant adds direct cache-to-cache data/acknowledgment, silent shared eviction and coordinated exclusive eviction. These optimizations create interactions absent from the simpler base protocol. One explicit race has a directory still listing a silently evicted cache as a sharer: that cache has already requested exclusive ownership when it receives an invalidation for another requester, and must acknowledge the invalidation despite its transient state. Two related races vary the pending read/write request (Q12,Q14).  Two remaining missing behaviors arise when exclusive eviction/writeback races with another cache's request: the cache receives an unexpected invalidation, while the directory receives unexpected writeback. The synthesized behavior treats the invalidation like a writeback acknowledgment for the evicting cache; the directory accepts the latest data and forwards it to the requester without requiring an extra acknowledgment. Figures 8/9 mark the missing behaviors and recovery messages. The designer still specifies which message kinds each unknown state must handle; §5.4 says this assistance was crucial to scaling. This is completion of supplied protocol structure, not autonomous discovery of all states, messages or correctness requirements (Q14,Q15).  ## Measured results and limits  Table 1 reports five configurations. Peterson: 3 unknown functions, search space 2^36, 60 states, 14 iterations, 97 ms SMT and 130 ms total. Dijkstra: 6 functions, 2^192 possibilities, about 2,000 states, 30 iterations, 27 s SMT and 64 s total. German/MSI-2: 16 functions, about 2^4700 possibilities, about 20,000 symmetry-reduced states, 217 iterations, 31 s SMT and 298 s total. German/MSI-4: 28 functions, about 2^7614, about 20,000 reduced states, 419 iterations, 898 s SMT and 1,545 s total. German/MSI-5: 34 functions, about 2^9000, about 20,000 reduced states, 525 iterations, 2,261 s SMT and 3,410 s total. The exponents were checked in the page render because the extraction flattens superscripts (T1).  The suffix -n counts the missing transitions among five corner cases, not the number of caches. The paper does not state the exact cache-count/channel-capacity/value-domain configuration used for these rows, preventing a precise independent reconstruction from the paper alone. All runs use a Linux desktop with a 3.4 GHz Intel Core i7 and 8 GB memory. Multiple SMT seeds were run and the worst runtimes reported, but the number of seeds, dispersion and exact tool versions are absent. There is no broad benchmark population or matched competing-system comparison. Long cases spend much time solving heuristic constraints; German/MSI-5's SMT fraction is 2261/3410≈66.3%, a reader calculation, not a new measurement (Q15,T1,D2).  The authors say synthesized symbolic expressions were parametric and worked on larger instances, but explicitly qualify that interpretations are “only guaranteed to be correct for the finite instance of the protocol”. No sizes/results for the larger checks or cutoff/induction proof is supplied. Symmetry reduces a fixed instance's state graph; it does not by itself prove correctness for every process count. Nor do these finite-state experiments establish crash/Byzantine tolerance or machine-code correctness (Q13).  ## Contribution to the requested topics  This is directly relevant distributed-protocol synthesis with safety and liveness checking, predating LLM-based agents. Its distinctive combination is finite extended state sketches, symmetry constraints, fine transition-set fairness, and automatically generated counterexample constraints. Its related-work claims distinguish earlier scenario completion, safety-only concurrent sketching, and template-based self-stabilization; these comparisons are attributed to the authors, without independently reading those cited works (Q2).  For Verus/TLA+/LLM-agent work, the transfer is a reader proposal: preserve explicit environment/fairness assumptions, use deadlocks and fair cycles as separate feedback, constrain identity symmetry and keep programmer-supplied structure visible in evaluation. An SMT table, a readable symbolic expression, a finite checked instance and a general verified protocol are different outputs. The paper measures the first stages and fixed-instance checks; it contains no Verus/Rust development, TLA+ model, LLM agent or general parameterized proof.
    - limits: Allfinite types;specifiedenvironment/monitors/fairness;humanprovidedstates/messagekinds;fixedinstancecorrectness;unknowncachecapacities/version/seeds;noimplementationread/rerun;printedrecurrenceindexproblemnotcodefailure.

    - title: Algebraic Approach to Algorithmic Logic
    - what: Bancerek formalizes an algebraic framework in Mizar: extensible sorted signatures, languages with substitution/free variables/equality, combined language/program algebras, and closed theories. It derives propositional and quantified logical laws and nine algorithmic consequences for assignment, composition and if/while constructs. Theorems concern membership in a theory satisfying explicit axiom/closure assumptions; no operational-semantics soundness/completeness or concrete program verification is supplied. Tracks fresh-symbol construction, algebra reduct preservation, sort-preserving substitution/capture avoidance, explicit theory closure and nonempty-versus-consistent distinction, stronger fresh-variable conditions for equality, exact loop premises and lack of termination theorem. Flags visually confirmed unusual Definition21 and its literal conflict with variable singleton support under later combined hypotheses, without claiming the unchecked Mizar artifact is inconsistent.

Stated foundations are Mendelson propositional/quantifier logic and Mirkowska–Salwicki Algorithmic Logic; program algebra and basic free-variable algebra are inherited. Includes 47 definitions and 162 propositions: foundation 1–34, propositional 35–105, quantifier/equality 106–153, algorithmic 154–162. Author reports formalized library results; reader did not rebuild Mizar or inspect full source proofs (p225, §§1–6). Base many-sorted signature Ω describes typed term operations. PC signature adds formula sort and six distinct properly typed Boolean connectives at positive offset n; QC adds two injectively indexed quantifiers per variable disjoint from Boolean connectives; AL adds a distinct program sort and three program×formula→formula operators. Correctness here denotes these signature/typing requirements, not semantic validity of every axiom (Definitions 4–6). Proposition 11 constructs an extension of any signature using ordinal suprema: formula sort sup(carrierΩ), program sort its successor, nine fresh connectives sup(operation-carrierΩ)+i, quantifiers tagged triples. Proof establishes disjointness using ordinals versus pairs, extends arities/result sort and pads connective sequence to chosen n. Essential signature additionally separates added operations/sorts from original Ω. Later disjoint renaming construction uses products and inverse first projections (Proposition 22). These are explicit symbol-allocation/type compatibility proofs, not parser correctness (§1–2). Tolerating means two functions agree on common domain. Extending variable families preserves old sort components, using empty sets for new sorts when required. Q is T-extension iff its Ω-reduct equals underlying algebra of T. Proposition 17 extends prescribed carriers on any subset I of new sorts; Proposition 18 preserves nonempty carriers given nonempty old algebra and new family. Proof uses override of sorted carriers and operations, not a claim that arbitrary chosen logical axioms are consistent (§1–2). Language combines sorted algebra, a free-variable map, sort-preserving substitution and equality operation on same-sort term pairs. Formula is an element of nonempty formula sort. Free variables for Boolean connectives are unions, for truth empty, and quantification removes bound singleton. Finite support is separate property. Capture-avoiding quantified substitution uses fresh z outside supports of replacement and body when binder occurs free in replacement; requires an available variable and records side conditions rather than eliding them (Definitions 8–37). Substitution-correct(1) gives identity x←x and homomorphism through nonquantifier operations; (2) replaces variable by same-sort term; (3) adds further support/renaming properties as literally printed. Equality substitution correctness distributes substitution over equality. Equality free-variable correctness gives support union and a variable its singleton support. Stronger equality theorems explicitly assume finite supports, infinite variable family in relevant sort and multiple substitution-correctness attributes (Definitions 16–17,21,44–45; §5). Reader source caveat: Definition 21 p. 236 literally requires y∉vf(τ1)(σ) for every variable y∈Y(σ) and arbitrary τ1, followed by additional conditional clauses. Visually confirmed, not extraction-only. Definition 45 p. 243 gives vf(y)=singleton y for a variable. Under later use Y=X extended by empty new sorts and nonempty/infinite X(σ), taking τ1=y makes these two printed requirements incompatible. Propositions 149–150 assume both substitution-correct(3) and vf-eq-correct plus infinite X(σ), so under a literal reading their premises cannot jointly hold. This is a reader deduction about printed definitions; no claim that actual Mizar code is inconsistent or that all other theorems are vacuous. Paper does not exhibit a model satisfying these combined stronger premises (§2–3, §5). Bialgebra combines language structure with program algebra carrier, characteristic operations and assignment map. AL-correct ties program carrier to program sort. If-while algebra packages nonempty/well-founded/nondegenerate strict syntax, base algebra extension, free-variable correctness, substitution and constructors for empty instruction, concatenation, conditional and while. Several attributes come from previous program-algebra paper and are not re-proved as operational semantics here. New M·α and union-like/intersection-like operators are algebraic formula constructors; flow extraction renders latter as d(M,α)/e(M,α), PDF shows large union/intersection symbols (Definitions 38–41, §3). PC theory is a subset of formulas containing classical Hilbert-style axiom schemas (including excluded middle) and closed under modus ponens. QC theory adds instantiation, side-conditioned quantifier movement, negation duality and universal generalization. Equality adds reflexivity and substitutivity. AL theory adds distribution, recurrence/monotonicity and assignment/composition/conditional/loop schemas relative to fixed formula φ. Theory membership α∈F is the result notion; paper does not identify it with truth under all state interpretations (Definitions 42–47). Existence of closed theories uses full formula carrier, which trivially contains every axiom and is closed under every rule. This proves nonemptiness/existence, not consistency, a proper nontrivial theorem set, or soundness/completeness. No claim of contradiction is inferred solely from this construction. No least theory construction, concrete state/transition model, solver runtime or empirical success rate supplied (§3). PC propositions 35–105 derive identity/transitivity/currying, conjunction/disjunction commutativity/associativity/distribution, contraposition, classical double negation, De Morgan laws and equivalence transport. Printed arguments mostly cite earlier proposition numbers; full derivation scripts are not reproduced. QC 106–145 derives monotonicity/duality/commutation, bound-variable support facts and moving fresh-independent formulas across quantifiers. For example x∉vf(α) needed for ∃x(α∧β)⇔α∧∃xβ; ∃x∀yα⇒∀y∃xα is one direction, not unrestricted exchange equivalence (§4–5). Equality 146–153 derives substitution stability, symmetry/transitivity, equality-mediated renaming/quantification and (α∧x=y)⇒α[x←y]. Proof assumptions vary: symmetry/transitivity add finite support, infinite variable sort and substitution(2)/(3); 149–150 additionally require vf-eq and vf-QC. Do not silently generalize all equality laws to arbitrary language structure; printed combined-premise caveat above applies (§5). AL closure explicitly assumes M distributes through binary conjunction/disjunction, union-like recurrence U(M,α)⇔α∨U(M,M·α), intersection-like recurrence I(M,α)⇔α∧I(M,M·α), and monotonicity for U/I. These fixed-point equations alone do not establish least/greatest fixed-point semantics over runs. Assignment substitutes term; sequential composition (M;M1)·α⇔M·(M1·α). Conditional evaluates algorithm M then tests fixed φ/¬φ before branch. These equations are theory axioms, not proved from a concrete execution model in this article (Definition 47). Nine final AL consequences: triple conjunction/disjunction distribution; U/I respect theory equivalence; two-step unrolling exposes α and M·α before recursive tail; variable-to-variable assignment is formula substitution; if-rule concludes from either test/branch pair; while-rule concludes if M·¬φ and α are known, or M·φ and M·(M1·(while M do M1·α)) are known. Recursive branch already mentions loop result. Thus Proposition 162 is not a loop-termination theorem, induction/invariant rule establishing arbitrary iterations, or a verified compiler/program implementation (Propositions 154–162). No concrete distributed protocol, fault/scheduling model, Rust/Verus, TLA+ translation, LLM agent or benchmark. No quantitative build-time/proof-size result. Contribution is reusable formal logic infrastructure; relevance to proof-agent evaluation is tracking definitional axioms versus derived facts, exact side conditions and possible vacuity of literal printed hypotheses. Archived release identifier is a source pointer, not reader validation.

    - title: Model Checking Existential Logic on Partially Ordered Sets
    - what: Classifies existential first-order model checking and embedding on finite posets by structural invariants, proving fixed-parameter tractability for bounded width and polynomial-time isomorphism there, while establishing hardness for neighboring bounded invariants. The bounded-width algorithm computes a chain partition, compiles tuples of chains into semilattice structures, uses perfect hash families/color coding to reduce embeddings to polynomial-time homomorphism instances, and runs in 2^{O(k log k)} n^{O(1)} for pattern size k. A proposition equates existential model checking and embedding in parameterized complexity. Reductions from Clique give W[1]-hardness at bounded cover-degree, and SAT encodings give NP-hard embedding at bounded width and bounded degree in classical complexity. A distributive-lattice construction solves isomorphism in polynomial time on bounded-width posets.

- Differential radical invariants (2014)
    - title: Characterizing Algebraic Invariants by Differential Radical Invariants
    - what: Characterizes invariant algebraic varieties of polynomial vector fields using a finite chain of successive Lie derivatives of one polynomial. The resulting differential-radical invariant rule is sound and complete for checking invariance over real-closed fields, and generation reduces to maximizing the kernel dimension (equivalently minimizing rank) of a symbolic matrix. Defines the Zariski closure of an ODE orbit as the smallest algebraic overapproximation, proves its soundness and differential-ideal property, and establishes the differential radical characterization theorem: h vanishes on an orbit iff finitely many Lie derivatives vanish initially. Theorem 2 gives a decidable invariant-variety check and a sound/complete proof rule; Theorem 3 says every invariant variety is a differential-radical ideal of one polynomial. Homogenization converts generation to biaffine symbolic linear algebra; Gaussian elimination searches parameter assignments and Proposition 3 gives a sound orbit overapproximation condition. Case studies recover trigonometric identities, airplane collision invariants, and three longitudinal-aircraft energy functions.

Generation is at least NP-hard and PSPACE under stated no-parameter assumptions; de-homogenization may fail for projective candidates. - Distributed Protocols and Heterogeneous Trust: Technical Report (2014)
    - what: # Distributed Protocols and Heterogeneous Trust: Technical Report (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Sheff, van Renesse and Myers use information-flow labels to reason about distributed protocols whose participants disagree about which machines may crash or lie. The central guarantee is participant-specific: a failure that violates one participant’s assumptions must not damage participants whose assumptions still hold (§1.1, Q2). They generalize Bosco Fast Consensus and the OARcast/Nysiad construction. Evidence consists of mathematical/prose proofs, an offline SMT threshold search, and small consensus simulations.  I read arXiv:1412.3136v1, stamped 9 December 2014 (Q1). The local PDF and the official v1 PDF retrieved on 19 October 2026 are byte-identical. Both have 2018/10/9 footers; those footers do not establish a new arXiv version or publication date. The report has 26 pages, six figures, Algorithm 1, Appendices A–B and 40 references, all read. There are no tables.  ## Model and assumptions (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  The network is asynchronous and permits all participants to communicate. Resending is assumed to make delivery reliable unless sender or receiver fails. A faulty participant cannot forge a correct participant’s source identity; signatures are suggested (§2.1, Q3). Almost-sure termination adds the assumption that repeatedly sent concurrent messages eventually arrive in every possible order. Section 5 phrases this as random ordering. Appendix B.5 additionally needs a selection function with nonzero probability for each input value (Q36). These assumptions matter: ordinary asynchronous message delivery alone does not establish the termination result.  A **guru** functions correctly and has true trust assumptions. A **chump** functions correctly but has false trust assumptions. The authors state that “chumps may receive ‘wrong’ results” (§2.2, Q4). Most guarantees concern gurus, rather than every participant that happens to execute correctly. The requirements also exclude some trust configurations: arbitrary mutual distrust is not automatically supportable (Q2).  The labels adapt the Decentralized Label Model. Each integrity or availability policy names an owner and a principal trusted to influence content or availability. Principals may be machines, people or compound authorities. Conjunctive principals combine authority; disjunctive principals describe alternative authority. Label ordering and join/meet track how message combinations trade integrity against availability (§§3–4, Appendix A, Q5–Q8, Q32, Q41). “More restrictive” labels correspond to weaker usable assurances. The paper describes static reasoning before execution; it does not report a compiler enforcing these policies or a complete implementation proof.  The simple synthesizers make the tradeoff concrete: accepting the first of three messages gives high availability but permits any sender to influence the value; requiring three identical messages increases integrity but makes each sender necessary. Contradiction can produce the detectable unavailable value `none` (§4.1, Q7, Q42). Survivor sets and failure-prone sets can be represented as labels separately for each principal’s crash and Byzantine expectations. For four participants tolerating any single failure, the system principal is the disjunction of the four triples, while the attacker principal is the disjunction of the six pairs (§4.2, Q8).  ## Consensus construction and proofs (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Algorithm 1 broadcasts a proposal, waits for a sufficiently available received set, and examines sets of identical messages. A high threshold D permits decision; a lower threshold C forces a value into the underlying consensus. Otherwise a selection function chooses from received values. The underlying protocol can recursively be another fast-consensus round. A deciding participant then broadcasts its decision once more so that the remaining participants can proceed consistently (§5, Q10–Q11). A deterministic selector may let an attacker prevent convergence, so randomness is advised (Q12).  The stated properties have different scopes (§5, Q9):  - Agreement: any two deciding gurus choose the same value, and repeated decisions by a guru agree - Unanimity: if **all correct participants** initially propose v, a deciding guru chooses v - Validity: if a participant decides and **all participants are correct**, some participant proposed the value - Progress: gurus eventually decide if the underlying consensus terminates - Termination: recursive fast consensus eventually decides for gurus with probability 1 under the extra random-network assumptions  Validity is deliberately weak: it does not guarantee a nonfaulty participant proposed the value in an execution containing Byzantine faults. Probabilistic termination is not a bounded worst-case or expected-round theorem.  For homogeneous assumptions, c is the total number permitted to be unavailable and b is the number permitted Byzantine, with c ≥ b. The received-set threshold is |R| ≥ n−c, decision requires |S| > (n+c)/2+b, and change requires |S| > (n−c)/2. The requirement is n > 3c+2b, reducing to n > 3c for crashes only and n > 5b when c=b. Tightness is attributed to earlier Bosco work, not newly proved here (§5.1, Q12).  For heterogeneous assumptions, each participant supplies its own availability threshold and change/decision labels. Constraints (1)–(6) ensure that sender failures bound message availability, tolerated failures cannot block a sufficient set, progressing parties can continue without blocked parties, decision thresholds imply change, liar/wrong sets cannot redirect other votes, and one guru’s decision forces other correct parties to enter the underlying consensus with that value (§§5.2–5.3, Q13–Q18). This is an explicit set of conditions to satisfy, rather than a theorem for every label assignment.  Appendix B proves agreement separately for decisions in the same round and different rounds. It uses constraints (4)–(6), unanimity/agreement of the underlying protocol, and continued participation by deciding parties. Unanimity propagates the common correct proposal through the underlying protocol. Fault-free validity follows from selecting received values and authentic message sources. Progress uses constraints (1)–(3) to ensure sufficient messages arrive (Q33–Q35).  The termination argument deserves a precise limit. Appendix B.5 concludes: “in any pair of consecutive rounds, there is a non-zero probability a guru will decide. Therefore, each guru, with probability 1, eventually decides” (Q36). Nonzero probabilities that can decrease across rounds do not alone justify almost-sure termination. The appendix does not explicitly supply a uniform conditional lower bound, independence, or a complete stochastic fairness argument. Its intended strong network/selection assumptions may provide that missing step. This read flags a proof-detail dependency; it does not supply a counterexample to the protocol.  Two notation concerns are visible in the PDF, not extraction artifacts. Equation (3) quantifies R ⊆ P but uses S in its body (p.12, Q16). Figure 3’s A_sys row for Bob/Carol/Dave/Eve prints an integrity-policy superscript I where the text describes an availability threshold (p.13, Q17). The record preserves both; it does not silently repair the formulas or claim a checked encoding.  ## Five-party case and measured results (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Alice tolerates arbitrary failure by Bob and no other failures. Bob, Carol, Dave and Eve tolerate Byzantine Alice plus at most one crash among themselves (§§1, 2.2, 5.4, Q19). The searched thresholds let these five reach consensus. A homogeneous envelope must allow one Byzantine failure and one additional crash, hence b=1, c=2 and n>8: nine participants (Q21). Five versus nine exploits different trust structure; it does not violate a lower bound for an identical failure model.  Alice sometimes must listen to Bob despite distrusting him. If Bob is Byzantine, the others’ trust assumptions fail and Alice alone may remain a guru. But when Bob is merely crash-prone, Carol and Dave might change their votes after hearing Bob and Eve. Alice therefore waits for Bob or Eve to preserve agreement in executions where those other participants are gurus (§5.4, Q20). This illustrates why individually “ignoring everyone distrusted” is not sufficient.  The authors simulated 1000 instances for homogeneous nine-party Bosco and the corresponding heterogeneous five-party protocol. Each round’s message ordering and the selector’s choice are uniform random. All parties begin with different values. They compute the mean probability of a participant deciding after each round and show standard-error bars (§5.4, Figs.4–5, Q21–Q23). Exact curve ordinates and error magnitudes are not tabulated. The captions say “in each round,” while the prose says “after each round” and the curves increase toward one; this record retains reported round quantiles without reconstructing the raw event distribution.  The explicit reported outcomes are (§5.4, Q21, Q24):  - no failures: heterogeneous median 3 rounds and 95th percentile 5; homogeneous median 5 and 95th percentile 8 - Alice Byzantine and Bob crashed: heterogeneous 95th percentile 4; homogeneous median 6 and 95th percentile 12  The heterogeneous median in the fault scenario is not explicitly stated in the prose, so none is invented. Byzantine Alice’s behavior is specific: she proposes a fresh never-before-seen value every round. This is a chosen attack, not comprehensive Byzantine exploration. The paper attributes the faster convergence partly to reduced contention among fewer active participants. It evaluates the whole customized configuration, without isolating label adaptation from the participant-count change. It reports no deployed throughput, wall-clock communication latency, hardware, random seed or raw per-run result file in the paper.  For threshold synthesis, the requirements are encoded in quantifier-free bitvector logic and Z3 is used offline. Four- to six-party protocols reportedly take “a few minutes for each protocol” (§5.4, Q25). There are no exact timings, hardware or Z3 version. Checking given labels is described as polynomial, placing the search problem in NP; precise hardness remains future work. This is not a claim of NP-completeness or polynomial-time synthesis.  Section 5.5 adds a distrusted client as a participant so the best case is client→servers→client, without waiting for inter-server communication. The construction is subject to threshold requirements and explicitly trades bandwidth for latency; there is no implementation timing experiment (Q26).  ## OARcast, Nysiad and artifact evidence (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  OARcast has a designated sender and echoers. Messages carry author and relay signatures plus sequence numbers. Echoers rebroadcast unseen sender messages, cease on conflicting sender-signed values for a sequence number, and deliver only after lower sequence numbers and a sufficient identical-echo threshold. Constraint (7) prevents two gurus from delivering different values for the same position (§6.1, Q27–Q28). If the sender is correct, no correct participant (even a chump) can simulate a different ordering. Liveness further requires a correct sender and enough uncompromised echoers. The report says its correctness proof “proceeds exactly as in [13, 14]”; it does not give a separate full OARcast appendix proof (Q28–Q29).  Nysiad simulates a crash-tolerant system of deterministic state machines. Each simulated machine gets an OARcast sender. A host accepts a simulated message only when its own simulation independently computes an identical message and the matching OARcast delivers it. Gurus thus simulate the same execution and ordering. A faulty designated sender can block availability without independently changing the derived message value/order; each host’s own integrity and availability still constrain its simulation (§6.2, Q30). Footnote 2 limits OARcast integrity to uniform guaranteed delivery and ordering; application content can have further constraints. A 3f+1 crash-Bosco conversion using a deterministic selection function is described as 3f+1 Byzantine consensus with best-case two sends, compared with Fast Byzantine Paxos “by this very simple metric” (Q30). Nysiad has no empirical evaluation here.  The linked Dropbox ZIP was recovered successfully. It contains only `pysmt/pylisp2.py` (9444 bytes) and `pysmt/pysmt.py` (40332 bytes). Both were read in full, 1151 LF-delimited lines including terminal empty lines. They are a Lisp parser and Python-2-style SMT converter/solver wrapper. The converter eliminates supported finite datatypes and Boolean interfaces, turns functions into bitvector lookup tables, unrolls quantifiers, emits QF_BV headers, and defaults to invoking `z3`. It includes local threshold optimization and HTML analysis modes (Q37–Q40). Its help explicitly notes that compactly declared bitvector lengths can entail exponential file expansion (Q37).  No README, protocol constraint input, simulator, dependency pin, historical commit identifier or experiment output is present in this particular archive. The source supports the existence of a QF_BV preparation and solver workflow, but cannot alone reproduce the five-party thresholds or plotted simulations. No author code was imported or executed; no solver, prover, verifier or compiler was run. Only reader extraction, rendering, hashing, arithmetic and validation scripts were used. Simulation and synthesis outcomes remain author-reported.  ## Relevance to the requested topic (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  This paper adds a useful formal-specification question for distributed systems: whose assumptions must hold for each guarantee? Its concrete contributions are a label-based description of integrity/availability, explicit threshold constraints, conditional consensus proofs, and a worked heterogeneous deployment comparison. It separates agreement from delivery availability and shows how Byzantine behavior can deny progress without corrupting the eventual ordering.  There is no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment. Transfer to agents writing specifications/proofs is reader inference: state trust and scheduling assumptions per participant, retain the weak validity quantifier, check threshold side conditions, and distinguish prose proof, SMT synthesis, simulation and implementation verification. A useful evaluation would test multiple trust graphs and adversarial schedules while pinning constraint encodings and the simulator. Confidentiality, self-interested behavior and general automatic protocol transformation remain future work (§7, Q31).  The quotation identifiers used above are defined in quotes.json and mirrored in the JSONL record; each definition includes its exact source span and section. Reading Figure 3’s vote combinations as distinct participants, its intended change threshold is two matching votes and its decision threshold three among Bob, Carol, Dave and Eve; Alice’s own vote does not contribute to those counts (Q17). This helps explain why she can need Bob’s message despite distrusting him.

    - what: Corrects prior complexity claims and gives a deterministic polynomial-space model-checking procedure for Dynamic Logic of Propositional Assignments and Coalition Logic of Propositional Control and Delegation. Its DL-PA algorithm represents valuations and iteration counters as k-bit strings, and uses mutually recursive deterministic Boolean procedures REL, MOD, and ITE. Divide-and-conquer evaluates α* by splitting iteration counts, while a well-founded order and induction establish soundness and completeness. Recursive depth is linear in formula/program size and k, yielding polynomial space. Polynomial reductions transfer the upper bound to DCL-PC; QSAT reductions make both logics PSPACE-complete.

- Graph- versus Vector-Based Analysis of a Consensus Protocol (2014)
    - what: # Whole-paper read: Graph- versus Vector-Based Analysis of a Consensus Protocol (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Giorgio Delzanno, Arend Rensink and Riccardo Traverso; GRAPHITE2014, EPTCS159, pp44–57, doi10.4204/EPTCS.159.5, arXiv1407.7931. This is a finite-state Paxos safety comparison between graph transformation in GROOVE and a PROMELA model in SPIN. It demonstrates how modeling and symmetry reduction affect reachable state counts and exploration cost. It does not establish a parameterized Paxos theorem or correspondence with a deployed implementation. [Q0,Q1,Q2,Q14]  ## Property and model assumptions  Definition1 requires every chosen value to have been proposed and all choices, including successive rounds, to agree. The general introduction permits arbitrarily delayed messages and crash/recovery retaining local information. The displayed models contain no explicit crash/recovery transitions. Each proposer sends at most one Prepare, and there is one learner. Authors argue that more proposers can mimic repeated rounds and that multiple learners have the same available information. These are modeling justifications; the paper supplies no formal cutoff theorem reducing arbitrary configurations to the finite instances measured. The one-Prepare restriction also prevents indefinite injection of new proposals; this is not a liveness proof for unrestricted Paxos. [Q1,Q2,Q3]  Prepare chooses a fresh round; Promise carries the acceptor's last accepted round/value; a quorum causes a proposer to reuse the highest previously accepted value, or its own initial value if none exists. Acceptors promise increasing rounds and accept rounds at least as high as their current promise. Learners choose a round/value after a quorum. Figure1 supplies the pseudocode, including fresh-round and maximum-prior-round selection requirements. [Q2,Q3]  ## What the two encodings do  GROOVE stores a configuration as a typed graph. Process/value nodes have no explicit identities; round numbers and counters remain integer attributes. Broadcasts are persistent message nodes connected to senders, rather than individually ordered channel contents. Isomorphic configurations can therefore merge. Nested quantification counts matching Promise/Learn nodes, negative conditions prevent duplicate Learn emission and select a maximal prior round, and control functions schedule large rule applications. onPromise removes isPrepared so a proposer accepts a quorum only once; changeMyval precedes sendAccept. A learner may choose again. Unsafe patterns test two distinct chosen values, including two choices by one learner, or a chosen value absent from all proposer values. Depth-first search stops at the first unsafe graph, or explores the complete reachable state space for that initial configuration. [Q4,Q5,Q6,Q7]  PROMELA represents each role as a process and communications as four bounded channels. Ordered send (!!) and matching receive (??) reduce irrelevant message-order variation. atomic/d_step blocks combine operations; the proposer scans Promise entries with a sentinel round9, restores them, and sends Accept after a quorum. Temporary variables are reset and learner counters saturate at the majority. Figures9–10 give proposer, acceptor, four-recipient broadcast and learner code. Printed MAX=10 bounds channels and the learner's round-indexed counter array; values use byte/short/int types. The paper does not provide separate complete experiment inputs or a formal GROOVE–PROMELA equivalence proof. The hardcoded four-recipient example is not itself every row's configuration. Atomicity, graph identity, message persistence, finite channels and representation differ together, so this is not a controlled isolation of one implementation feature. Potential blocking inside atomic blocks and fixed channel capacities are modeling limits, not independently demonstrated bugs. [Q8,Q9,Q10]  ## Evaluation and exact result scope  Table1 has22GROOVE configurations. Low majority searches all find a safety violation before exhausting the state space; their counts measure search to a counterexample. High majority searches report no violation and enumerate all reachable states of those finite models. Examples: two proposers/twelve acceptors/majority7 produce5,491,406states in14,794,452ms; three/six/majority4 produce12,247,549 in8,771,175ms; four/four/majority3 produce9,337,923 in4,523,411ms; seven/two/majority2 produce4,607,455 in1,154,561ms. Authors state that the next larger configurations exhaust memory. This is reported bounded exploration, not a proof for all process counts. [Q10,Q11]  Eight high-majority instances are also explored without graph isomorphism reduction. For two proposers/two acceptors,224states become78 (65.18% reduction); two/five:1,178,114→9,729 (99.17%); five/two:12,743,315→55,420 (99.57%). This within-GROOVE comparison more directly supports the symmetry-reduction claim. Reduction has a cost: the authors report over75% of time spent checking isomorphism for two proposers/eleven acceptors, and generation rates from under400 to over6,000states/s. Figures11–12 visualize growth/comparisons; changing quorum thresholds produces sawtooth growth. [Q11,Q12]  Table2 has11SPIN configurations, with ordinary and starred bit-hashing columns. Starred exploration is an underapproximation: finding an unsafe state supplies a witness, while finding none does not exhaustively establish safety. The caption says a hash factor above100 indicates high coverage; it is a heuristic, not a completeness guarantee. Nonempty reported factors are1.9,2.2,2.3,5.1,6.5,26, all below100. Retain distinct counts: for two proposers/five acceptors/low majority, ordinary226,306states versus starred387,982; for three/three/high,4,998,934 versus4,997,226. Larger starred counts must not be read as larger complete reachable state spaces. [Q12,Q13]  GROOVE used an i7-2600 3.4GHz, Windows7, Java6 and8GB memory; SPIN used an i7, Windows7,6GB, jSpin/SPIN6.2.5May2013 with default memory management. The paper states no repeated-run count or uncertainty estimate. Different resources and modeling choices limit causal claims about engine superiority. It reports search-state counts and verification time, not executable Paxos throughput/latency. [Q10,Q12,Q13]  ## Printed inconsistencies and presentation limits  The SPIN prose says ordinary search finds violations only through five acceptors with two proposers, and with three proposers finds violations only through three acceptors and proves safety only through two. Table2 nevertheless prints ordinary low-majority results for two/six (4,374,568states,118,000ms) and three/four (2,712,145,68,400ms), plus an ordinary high-majority result for three/three (4,998,934,71,700ms). I retain the table and flag its disagreement with the prose; I did not reproduce either. [Q12,Q13]  Two cells require literal preservation. Table2 two/two/high starred state count appears as “62 0” in layout extraction and as spaced “62 0” in the render; raw extraction yields620, matching the adjacent ordinary620. The normalized table records620 with this ambiguity. More materially, two/four/high ordinary Time is printed “3,5” while starred Time is “3,510”; caption units are milliseconds. The former is retained literally, with numeric normalization left unset, rather than silently interpreting it as3.5ms or3,500ms. [Q13]  Figure12's visible acceptor axis is labeled1–5, while its embedded spreadsheet text contains rows2–6. That text also differs from Tables1–2:234 versus224 for GROOVE/no-isomorphism/two-two;29,532 versus29,352 for SPIN/high/two-three;4,374,578 versus4,374,568 for SPIN/low/two-six. These are presentation/data discrepancies, not evidence of a model-checker defect. The record uses table values and preserves the figure's text separately. The graph compares early-stopped unsafe searches, complete safe GROOVE explorations and approximate SPIN explorations; its curves are not uniformly complete state-space sizes. [Q11,Q13,Q15]  ## Contribution and read scope  The paper contributes a concrete distributed-protocol modeling lesson: remove irrelevant process/value identity, message ordering and intermediate steps when that preserves the desired property, and measure the cost and benefit of reductions. For evaluating agents that generate specifications/proofs, my inference is to require an explicit property, finite bounds, preservation argument and completeness status for each reported result before comparing state counts or claiming verification. There is no Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment. [Q1,Q7,Q9,Q14]  Read all14PDFpages, all14references, all12figures, both result tables, all displayed pseudocode/PROMELA and graph rules; viewed all14page renders. Official arXiv and inventory PDFs are byte-identical. Publisher PDF bytes differ, but its full layout extraction is identical. No separate author artifact URL was identified in the paper's links; the printed models were inspected without execution. No compiler, model checker, solver or author-code run.

- Petri Games (2014)
    - title: Petri Games: Synthesis of Distributed Systems with Causal Memory
    - what: Models distributed synthesis as Petri-net games whose tokens are system or environment players and whose synchronizations exchange complete causal history. Strategies restrict branches in net unfoldings. Defines deterministic system choices, unrestricted local environment moves and deadlock avoidance. For concurrency-preserving games, global unfolded strategies can be distributed into one-token local controllers. mcut/ecut summaries support a reduction to finite complete-information games. Bounded one-environment-token safety synthesis is EXPTIME-complete; unbounded synthesis is undecidable.

- Proving Safety with Trace Automata and Bounded Model Checking. (2014)
    - what: Combines loop acceleration with trace automata to remove redundant accelerated executions before bounded model checking. Trace subsumption preserves reachable states while lowering the transformed program diameter, enabling safety proofs and faster bug finding. - Regression-Free Synthesis for Concurrency. (2014)
    - what: Defines concurrency repair that preserves sequential behavior and, when initially correct, complete preemption-free behavior, while eliminating assertion errors. Adds constraints learned from good traces to the constraints learned from counterexamples, aiming to prevent a repair from breaking previously good behavior. Names the generic positive-and-counterexample extension to CEGIS PACES. §2 precisely relates traces before and after adjacent within-basic-block instruction swaps or atomic-section insertion. A regression must preserve reads-from relationships into assume/await conditions and must originate from a good trace that could not already become bad by scheduler choices alone. §3 uses trace-analysis graphs with intra-thread, reads-from-conditional/assertion and non-free write-order edges. A cover proves the necessary happens-before edge; additional noninterference edges place other writes before the source write or after the read. Conjoining/disjoining cover constraints yields a polynomial-time sufficient regression-prevention algorithm; when no cover exists, the theoretical fallback fixes every current intra-thread order. Exact sound-and-complete constraints can be computed exponentially. Bad-trace elimination reuses partial-order generalization and cycle constraints from the 2013 predecessor. §4 maintains cumulative constraints and good-trace images as the program changes, formalizing correspondence more carefully than scheduler input reuse. Wait/notify repair is discussed for inputs outside the standard sequential-correctness precondition.

    - number: iwl3945.c: 66 LOC; mixed 1 iteration/3+2 s versus ce1 and ce2 2 iterations/2 s
    - number: lc-rc.c: 40 LOC; mixed 10 iterations/2+7 s; ce1 179/122 s; ce2 203/134 s
    - number: rtl8169.c: 405 LOC, five concurrency bugs; mixed 7 iterations/10+45 min; ce1 >100 iterations/>6 h; ce2 8/54 min
    - limits: Fixed number of threads in Cwhile; await is the only blocking operation and defines preemption points. All complete sequential traces must be good; preservation of preemption-free traces is conditional on their original correctness. Bugs are assumed data-independent: changing valuations without changing instruction-location sequence cannot change whether the trace is bad. Regressions are a restricted class requiring identical conditional reads-from, so newly enabled conditionals from different writes can evade the definition. Good-trace constraints cover seen traces, not all unobserved behavior; final correctness depends on Verify. The implementation uses CBMC and the evaluated finite/simplified driver models; no full Linux driver proof or weak-memory guarantee. Fair termination refers to choosing bad traces in the synthesis loop, not scheduler fairness for an executing repaired program. An unsound learner can still be followed by verification, but it lacks the stated intermediate-regression theorem.

- SACO (2014)
    - title: SACO: Static Analyzer for Concurrent Objects.
    - what: Presents SACO, a static analyzer for actor/concurrent-object programs that infers termination, resource bounds and deadlock freedom. Points-to and may-happen-in-parallel analyses feed circular termination reasoning, cost bounds and dependency-graph deadlock checks. The monitor/object model permits one active task per object, cooperative await, asynchronous sends and blocking future get. Allocation-site sequences parameterized by k give object-sensitive points-to information; polynomial MHP composition prunes impossible interleavings. Termination assumes shared data is updated finitely often and proves that assumption through termination of updating loops. Resource bounds combine local ranking functions with counts of interfering updates; deadlock graphs are pruned using MHP labels. The vending-machine example derives a coin+·n loop bound and an acyclic dependency graph.

- SATMC 3.0 (2014)
    - title: SATMC: A SAT-Based Model Checker for Security-Critical Systems
    - what: Describes SATMC 3.0, which combines planning-graph encodings with reactive-system bounded model checking to reduce bounded security-goal violations to SAT. ASLan models rewrite rules, Horn clauses, first-order LTL constraints and goals, with NuSMV generating LTL encodings and MiniSAT solving them. The formal framework defines states as facts closed under Horn clauses, rewrite-rule paths, closed-world semantics and first-order temporal satisfaction. Security systems compose a system model with a Dolev–Yao intruder and optional custom intruder; examples encode SAML messages, RBAC and PKCS#11 operations. SATMC specializes intruder rules, builds a monotone planning graph, grounds first-order LTL using only matching facts, and creates Φk whose satisfying assignments correspond exactly to length-k counterexamples. Iterative deepening is sound for each bound but can be semi-decision when kmax is infinite.

Planning graphs over-approximate reachable states and quantifier grounding can be expensive or infeasible for unbounded domains, although SAT encoding avoids false positives. Models rely on symbolic Dolev–Yao cryptography and user-specified constraints; the paper does not establish completeness for arbitrary unbounded security systems.

- Scilingo scenario SCR model checking (2014)
    - title: Analyzing Behavioural Scenarios over Tabular Specifications Using Model Checking
    - what: Introduces a free tool for specifying and checking families of behavioral scenarios over SCR tabular requirements. Scenario programs combine guarded state changes, tests, sequencing, and iteration; the tool translates SCR tables and scenario programs to Promela and checks an end-state safety assertion with SPIN. A pacemaker specification is the running case. The paper defines the scenario grammar (stateChange, guarded stateChange[f], tests [f], sequencing, and Kleene iteration) and compiles each sentence with a program counter; unrestricted changes rely on SCR table transitions, guards filter traces, and the final property becomes assert(pc==n+1 → PROP). In the pacemaker study, SPIN finds two counterexamples: POR can return to Normal while battery voltage remains low, and magnet release can fail when the bradycardia program is off. Refining transition-table guards fixes S1; narrowing S2 to cases with a configured program makes it hold. Compared with DynAlloy, Spin+ finds counterexamples in 90 ms/780 ms and verifies repaired scenarios in milliseconds, while DynAlloy exceeds 30 minutes for S1 at 20 loop unrolls. The notation supports safety only; liveness is identified as future work.

- The Formalization of Decision-Free Petri Net (2014)
    - what: Reports a Mizar-library formalization of decision-free Petri nets, alternating directed paths and simple circuits, natural-valued markings, enabled transitions and totalized firing. Proves that each circuit’s sum of place tokens is preserved by a transition and by every finite sequence under that firing operation. Separates genuinely firable sequences from total evaluation, where disabled transition attempts leave the marking unchanged. The decision-free condition requires exactly one incoming and one outgoing transition per place, not one input/output per transition. A key structural lemma shows that any transition incident to a circular path’s place must occur on that path. Alternating-position and almost-injective-sequence lemmas support the one-step circuit invariant, which extends to finite sequences through the firing composition law. Firing is explicitly a no-op when disabled, so the final theorem needs no enabled-sequence premise; this strengthens the total-function equality without establishing legal execution or liveness.
    - limits: Markings map places to natural numbers. Arcs are unweighted relations in the displayed definitions: a successful firing subtracts one at input-only places, adds one at output-only places, and leaves both/neither places unchanged. No timed transitions, capacities, inhibitor arcs, arc weights, failure model or scheduling fairness appear in this formalization, despite reference [19] being a timed-Petri-net textbook. Decision-free-like (Definition 7) says every place has exactly one predecessor transition and exactly one successor transition. A transition may have multiple input or output places. The final decision-free-net mode also assumes Petri-like and existence of a directed circuit. Underlying Petri-like/basic-net definitions are imported and not expanded in the article; this reading does not independently audit those MML definitions. Directed paths have odd length at least three, alternate place-to-transition and transition-to-place arcs, and end at a place. Circuits additionally are circular and almost one-to-one: they close at the first place without internal repetitions. The repeated endpoint is not counted twice, since token sums use the finite set of places in the sequence, not the sequence with multiplicities. Preliminaries define an enumeration of marking values on a finite place subset and sum it to obtain the token number. Empty subsets use the empty sequence. The paper also establishes finite-sequence uniqueness facts and a smallest example PN0 with place 0, transition 1 and both connecting arcs. It does not provide a new algorithm for finding every circuit in a large net. Propositions 5–10 locate initial/final arcs and show places occur at odd indices and transitions at even indices, with neighboring arcs around each internal occurrence. Proposition 15 uses unique per-place predecessors/successors to show that a transition incident to any place of a circular path is a transition of that path. Without that closure, a transition outside the circuit could inject or remove a circuit token. A transition is firable exactly when all its input places have positive token counts (Definition 11). Definition 12 makes firing total: if firable, update by incidence; otherwise return the original marking. Input-output self-loops still require a positive token even though their net update is zero. Disabled attempts are stuttering evaluations, not enabled transitions. Definition 13 separately defines a firable finite sequence using a chain of intermediate markings and an enabledness obligation at every position; the empty sequence qualifies. Definition 14 evaluates any finite transition list using the total one-step Firing function and returns the initial marking for an empty list. Its absence of enabledness conditions is deliberate in the displayed definition and determines the scope of Proposition 17. Propositions 11/12 connect a transition with its singleton list and their firability. Proposition 13 gives Firing(Q concatenated Q1,M)=Firing(Q1,Firing(Q,M)) without a firability premise. Proposition 14 derives prefix firability and suffix firability at the prefix result from firability of the concatenation; no converse is stated in the printed proposition. Proposition 16 quantifies over a decision-free net, one circuit, any natural marking and any transition. It preserves the sum over exactly that circuit’s place set. Proposition 17 extends this equality to any finite transition sequence, with no assumption that the sequence is firable. It does not establish global conservation of all places, boundedness of every place in an arbitrary net, liveness, deadlock freedom, fairness, reachability completeness or infinite-trace properties. Reader proof explanation: a disabled transition stutters. A transition disjoint from the circuit changes no circuit place. If it touches the circuit, Proposition 15 puts it on the circuit; almost injectivity and unique place incidence leave one circuit input and one circuit output (possibly the same place). Thus the one-step sum change is zero, and finite-sequence iteration preserves it. The article gives dependency lists rather than a complete displayed Mizar proof script for the final two propositions. The article identifies MML entry PETRI_DF, version 8.1.02 5.22.1199, and supplies formal theorem statements with short proofs/dependency references. This is evidence of a published formalized development, not an independent local check. No MML files, proof checker, executable simulator, benchmark, empirical protocol case study, proof-time measurements or artifact build was run or inspected here. The paper has no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent result. Its relevance is reusable transition-system invariants and precise enabledness semantics. Applying its invariant to a distributed protocol would require a proved model relation from protocol states/steps to this restricted net class. A claim that a resource count is preserved in deployed code would need that extra refinement argument.

    - title: Formalization of the Advanced Encryption Standard. Part I
    - what: Arai and Okazaki formalize a parametric AES-shaped cipher in Mizar and prove decryption after encryption for 128-bit blocks and keys of 128,192 or 256 bits. Byte substitution S and state mixing M are assumed permutations; concrete GF(2^8) definitions and invertibility are explicitly deferred. Work proves array representation and inverse-composition structure plus key expansion, rather than completing all concrete AES transformations or establishing cryptographic security. Records precise state serialization, inverse component proofs, all key-expansion cases and round counts, reverse-key schedule, missing final mixing step and reverse-index induction. Preserves arbitrary byte/state permutation assumptions, exact shift conventions and deferred finite-field semantics, avoiding substitution of generic round-trip validity for standard conformance.

Reuses previous DESCIP_1 sequence shifts/XOR and standard Mizar functions/finite sequences. FIPS197(2001) is specification reference. Paper says GF(2^8) treatment will be future work; does not instantiate standard AES S-box or prove concrete MixColumns matrix invertible. Reader did not build Mizar or inspect later installments (p171, §§1–7). State type is four rows of four 8-bit Boolean sequences, giving 128-bit block. Serialization maps row i,column j to eight bits starting 1+8(i−1)+32(j−1), one-based. Propositions 15–17 prove coverage/disjointness/unique byte interval  ; 18–19 prove array map injective and onto,20 its inverse equation. Not merely an assumed representation equivalence; paper supplies short proof arguments. No numerical endian/standard-layout test performed (§2). S is any permutation of Boolean^8, shared by encryption, decryption and key expansion. SubBytes applies S bytewise, inverse applies S^−1. Propositions 21–23 establish both cancellation directions and bijectivity from generic inverse-function lemma 14. State mixer M1/M2 is an arbitrary permutation of entire 128-bit state, not restricted to a columnwise GF matrix. Its inverse assumed through permutation type. This separates generic inverse proof from later instantiation obligations (§3, §7). ShiftRows sends row i through Op-Shift(x_i,5−i); InvShiftRows uses i−1. These shifts sum 4, row length, so cancellation follows from inherited cyclic-shift arithmetic. Under DESCIP_1 definition Op-Shift(s,n)[j]=s[((j−1+n) mod len s)+1], the forward shifts are left 0,3,2,1 modulo 4, inverse 0,1,2,3. Reader derivation preserves printed convention, without claiming FIPS conformance, an observed implementation failure or independently comparing external standard. Propositions 24–26 prove inverses for the written definitions (§4). AddRoundKey XORs corresponding bytes. Key helpers substitute bytes, rotate a four-byte word left and XOR words. Rcon has ten explicit words: first bytes 01,02,04,08,10,20,40,80,1b,36 in hexadecimal, other three bytes zero. These are enumerated bit patterns; finite-field derivation not supplied (§5–6). Key size parameter m∈{4,6,8} counts 32-bit words. Expanded word count 4(7+m) gives 44,52,60 words; group consecutive four words into 11,13,15 state keys (reader arithmetic). Initial m words copied; at index i≥m XOR prior i−m word with transform of previous word. If i mod m=0, transform RotWord then SubWord and XOR Rcon(i/m); for m=8 and i mod 8=4 additionally SubWord; otherwise unchanged. KeyExpansion is deterministic for supplied S, not separately a proved standard-conformance or security theorem (Definitions 7–13). Encryption begins AddRoundKey with first state key. Sequence length N=(7+m)−1=m+6; middle steps apply SubBytes, ShiftRows, M, then XOR next key. Final step omits M and uses last key. Thus 9/11/13 full middle rounds plus one final round:10/12/14 rounds for m=4/6/8. Count derived from index ranges, not empirical performance measurement. Decryption reverses same expanded key sequence, XORs key then applies M^−1 where appropriate, InvShiftRows, InvSubBytes; inverse final output cancels initial key (§7). Propositions 27–34 give mixer inverse, composed component cancellation and equal forward/reversed-key XOR cancellation. Main 35 holds m=4 or 6 or 8: AES-InvCipher(S,M,AES-Cipher(S,M,t,K),K)=t. Printed proof defines encrypt/decrypt state sequences, N=m+6 and invariant ds(i+1)=es(N−i) for i<N. Base cancels encryption final key plus no-mixing final layer; step cancels key/mixer/shifts/substitution; last XOR cancels first key. Full printed derivation includes induction dependency references; reader does not claim independent kernel replay (§7, pp180–181). Raw keys 128/192/256 are sliced into 4/6/8 four-byte words. Wrappers serialize 128-bit message to state, apply generic cipher/inverse with same S,M and parsed key, then deserialize. Propositions 37–39 prove respective DEC(ENC(message,key),key)=message using array inverse and 35. Block size remains 128 for every key length. Identity proves unique recovery of original message for fixed parameters and key; it does not prove resistance to wrong-key recovery or any cryptographic attack (§7). Article body permits natural m syntactically in cipher definitions, but key-expansion defining conditions and main inverse theorem require m=4,6,8; do not extend completed theorem to arbitrary key lengths. The permutation hypotheses are real semantic assumptions, not discharged by merely naming operations SubBytes/MixColumns. No concrete executable implementation, constant-time/side-channel model, security game, block mode/padding/authentication, benchmark or known-answer test reported (§§1–7). Paper is an example of modular inverse proofs over an abstract cipher skeleton. A concrete AES correctness claim additionally needs specified finite-field transformations instantiated as required permutations and agreement of arrays, shifts and key layout with standard. Those obligations are not established by generic round trip. No distributed fault model/protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+ development or LLM agent experiment.

    - title: Two Variable vs. Linear Temporal Logic in Model Checking and Games
    - what: Compares two-variable first-order logic (FO2) and linear temporal logic (LTL), including unary temporal logic UTL, stutter-free fragments, and the combined FO2[LTL]. It gives three formula-to-automata translations and derives tight or near-tight verification bounds for nondeterministic, recursive, probabilistic, and game models. Translation I relates UTL/FO2 to unambiguous limit-deterministic Büchi automata; Translation II exploits polynomially many FO2[<] subformula types under a unary-alphabet restriction; Translation III builds deterministic parity automata for FO2 using small-model representatives. These constructions yield NP for FO2[<] on Kripke/HSM/RSM, NEXP for FO2 on RSM, 2EXPTIME-complete two-player games, #P/PEXP probability bounds on Markov chains, PSPACE for FO2[<] on recursive Markov chains, and 2EXPTIME quantitative MDP bounds. FO2[LTL] inherits the maximum complexity of its components, while Let definitions make FO2[<] exponentially harder.

- Efficient Synthesis for Concurrency by Semantics-Preserving Transformations (2013)
    - what: Synthesizes assertion-safe concurrent libraries from sequentially correct libraries using sequential-semantics-preserving instruction reorderings and atomic sections. Generalizes a failing linear trace into a partial order representing many failing schedules, then eliminates all its linearizations with constraints obtained from a minimal cycle in a weighted elimination graph. §3 models deterministic instructions/CFG methods, arbitrary concurrent method invocations and sequential input/output behavior. §4 computes allowed within-block statement reorderings by commutativity checks, combines ordering and atomicity constraints, and motivates idempotent duplication without formally incorporating it. §5 defines error invariants that overapproximate states reachable along the trace and underapproximate states from which the error is forced. A complete generalization check is expensive; two sufficient rules exploit conditional commutativity or an error-preserving common postcondition, while checking intervening instructions preserve supporting invariants. Previously relaxed edges are rechecked. §6 encodes essential happens-before relations, available reorderings and atomicity additions as weighted graph edges; creating a cycle makes every represented trace infeasible. - On the complexity of model checking interval-valued discrete time Markov chains (2013)
    - what: The paper closes or sharpens complexity gaps for model checking finite interval-valued DTMCs under two semantics. UMC chooses one admissible DTMC once and uses it forever; IMDP can choose an admissible probability distribution whenever a state is visited. For reachability, minimum and maximum probabilities coincide across the two semantics and the problem is P-complete. Full PCTL differs: IMDP model checking is P-complete, whereas UMC model checking is shown Square-Root-Sum-hard. For reachability, Proposition 1 maps every fixed admissible DTMC to a simple IMDP scheduler and conversely uses the standard existence of an optimal simple scheduler, proving equality of extrema. For the upper bound, the authors formulate reachability as an LP whose constraints range over vertices of each state's interval-feasible probability polytope; there may be exponentially many such vertices. They invoke the ellipsoid method and construct a polynomial-time separation oracle: for a candidate vector, solve a compact LP at each state to find the minimizing feasible transition distribution; if a constraint is violated, a rational vertex of polynomial encoding size supplies a separating hyperplane. P-hardness is by reduction from ordinary MDP reachability, replacing an MDP action μ at s with an intermediate state (s,μ). For UMC PCTL, a reduction from Square-Root-Sum builds an IDTMC whose PCTL subformulas force three transition probabilities for each i to equal √x_i/q; a final next-state constraint tests whether Σ√x_i≤y. For IMDP PCTL, bottom-up PCTL labelling reduces until/until-like path formulas to optimal reachability; equality P=p is checked using whether p lies between the infimum and supremum. These are formal reductions/proofs rather than experimental algorithms.

The analytic extension represents schedulability as a disjunction of polyhedra over computation times, deadlines and jitters; the PTA approach uses IMITATOR’s Inverse Method and is necessary-and-sufficient for the modeled periodic system. The PTA model explicitly encodes pipeline activation, preemptive/non-preemptive processors, deadline-failure states and parameter valuations; tiles returned by the Inverse Method have uniform discrete behavior. Two test cases compare RTSCAN, MAST holistic analysis and IMITATOR: PTA regions contain the sufficient regions from analytic/holistic methods because they explore all synchronous periodic traces, while MAST can outperform RTSCAN when offset-based interference reductions apply.

    - limits: RTSCAN uses integer parameters and polyhedra; its guarantees are sufficient bounds and complexity increases with hyperperiod and unconstrained deadlines. IMITATOR’s current model supports only strictly periodic, zero-offset pipelines with end-to-end deadlines no larger than periods, and exhaustive region exploration is slow. MAST uses sampled parameter searches/slack computation and can miss exact regions or depend on step size. Scheduling support is preemptive fixed priority for CPUs and non-preemptive fixed priority for CAN networks; other protocols and multiprocessors are future work.
