- PSyHCoS: Parameter Synthesis for Hierarchical Concurrent Real-Time Systems (2013)
    - what: Presents a C#/.NET toolkit for timing-parameter synthesis and model checking of hierarchical concurrent systems specified in Parametric Stateful Timed CSP (PSTCSP). The inverse method starts from a reference parameter valuation and synthesizes a convex region with the same time-abstract action behavior. Evaluates full reachability, inverse synthesis and equivalent-state reductions on eight timing examples; Fischer mutual exclusion yields Delta<Epsilon from reference (3,4). The reference-valuation contract preserves time-abstract linear-time behavior, rather than finding all safe valuations or proving all timed properties. PSTCSP creates clocks implicitly as execution proceeds, supports nested processes and shared/programmatic data, and stores states as process/constraint identifiers. The paper exposes nontermination and memory limits, overhead of equivalent-state merging, and confounds in cross-tool comparisons caused by manual translation. Complete table includes negative performance cases as well as a Fischer instance enabled by reduction.
    - limits: PSTCSP is a process algebra with shared variables, data structures, user-defined programs, several choice/concurrency constructs and timing operators Wait[d], timeout[d], within[d], deadline[d]. Parameters are unknown constants representing timing delays, not the number of processes. The displayed Fischer model fixes N=3; benchmark Fischer4/5/6 separately fix those process counts. No theorem quantifies correctness over arbitrary N. Clocks are implicit and dynamically introduced, unlike an explicitly fixed timed-automaton clock set. Footnote 1 identifies PSTCSP with parametric closed timed epsilon-automata; expressiveness is stated incomparable with parametric timed automata. Formal semantics, inverse-method soundness, undecidability and equivalent-state reduction are imported from [3]/[4], not reproved in this six-page tool paper. IM takes a model and reference valuation pi and returns a convex constraint K guaranteeing the same time-abstract sequences of actions as pi. A known correct reference transfers the relevant linear-time properties to all valuations in K. Synthesis itself is not a test that the reference is correct, not necessarily a maximal safe region, and not a guarantee that all safe parameter choices are found. Clock-sensitive or bounded-time specifications require their own semantic encoding; equal untimed action traces alone do not establish identical event times. Parameter synthesis is undecidable; authors deliberately constructed examples where IM fails to terminate. They report termination on their practical cases, not on all models. Full parametric reachability can have an infinite reachable state set even where IM terminates. A finite evaluation timeout or memory-out does not establish mathematical nontermination, and the table itself marks M.O. rather than an infinite-time execution proof. Fischer model uses shared turn (initial Idle=-1) and counter (initial zero), with two parameters Delta and Epsilon. Processes read Idle, update turn within Delta, wait Epsilon, and enter iff turn still equals their ID. Entry increments counter, exit decrements it and resets turn. Reference Delta=3,Epsilon=4 gives Delta<Epsilon, which authors call the weakest known mutual-exclusion constraint. The record preserves that as their model-specific claim, not a proof of necessity for every Fischer variant. The toolkit reports LTL, deadlock and refinement checking, simulation/trace playback and full state graph generation. It also permits C# functions/data in models. The paper supplies no machine-checked implementation proof, proof-producing interface or verified semantics for arbitrary host functions. Correctness of tool implementation, parsing, polyhedral operations, host code and input model remains outside the article’s demonstrated formal guarantees. Implementation uses C#/.NET and Parma Polyhedra Library for constraints. Architecture has separate parser, internal representation, algorithms, simulator and GUI. Each semantic rule and algorithm is a separate class; authors propose reusing algorithms on labeled transition systems. Internal states pair string-coded process and constraint IDs. A string equality test is reported for constraint identity; exact normalization/interning correctness and cost are not specified here. Optimized reachAll+ and IM+ merge equivalent PSTCSP states. The technique can reduce state counts exponentially in the best case but requires costly operations. Both original and optimized variants are exposed to users. The article does not provide a new proof of equivalence preservation or a formal refinement relation to deployed concurrent-system code. Table 1 contains eight fixed examples: Bridge (four persons/17 time units), Fischer4/5/6, Jobshop scheduling, railway control RCS5/6, and TrAHV train. It reports parameters, state/transition counts, maximum clocks and seconds. IM groups omit transition counts. State counts with k are rounded; M.O. denotes memory-out in context, not an unsafe answer. Full numeric rows are stored separately in benchmark_table. Environment is Windows XP 32-bit, Intel Quad Core 2.4 GHz, 4 GB memory. No tool/compiler/PPL versions, run repetitions, variability, CPU utilization, exact memory peaks or common time limit are stated. Model sizes and chosen reference valuations depend on each benchmark; references for non-Fischer cases are standard valuations, and Fischer uses values satisfying known good-behavior constraints. IM+ can help sharply: Fischer5 states 133k→13k and seconds1176→84.5; Fischer6 IM is M.O. while IM+ reaches86k states in1144s. It also costs time: Bridge253→455s with identical2.8k states; RCS5 7.83→16.7s with identical5.6k states. These measured cases do not prove general speedup or guaranteed termination. Reader table check: the prose says state reduction makes IM+ faster whenever it reduces states, yet Jobshop has1112→877 states and17.1→22.8s. Also the stated up-to80% slowdown for Bridge is not the largest table slowdown: RCS5 has about113% overhead. These are discrepancies in the performance summary, not counterexamples to the inverse method’s correctness. The article reports deadlock checking when full reachability terminates and identifies Jobshop’s terminal deadlock as expected because every task runs once. A completed acyclic schedule is a counterexample to a naive deadlock-free requirement, not necessarily a scheduling failure. Exact checked LTL formulas and full per-model verification outputs are not tabulated. Authors say a synthesized True region for railway models allows timing constructs to be removed and claim this for all parameter valuations. The formal abstraction/refinement argument and full parameter-domain restrictions are not presented here. Record this as an author application claim; it does not by itself prove real-world railway safety or eliminate implementation timing requirements. IMITATOR comparison used the same hardware under Ubuntu11.10 64-bit, unlike the Windows32-bit main table. Authors explicitly call comparison inaccurate due to manual PSTCSP/PTA translation: each tool favors native models. IMITATOR Jobshop8.96s andTrAHV0.097s are reported; Fischer translations fail to terminate, Bridge/RCS are too large for manual translation. No fair overall cross-tool ranking follows; automated efficient translation remains future work. Sources, binaries, manual and models were linked at the historical PSyHCoS page http://lipn.univ-paris13.fr/~andre/software/PSyHCoS/. This reading used the saved paper only and did not fetch or run the artifact or import cited proofs. No verified Rust, Verus, TLA+, LLM-agent result or deployment-level distributed implementation is supplied.

- Complete symmetry reduction in safety verification (2012)
    - title: A Complete Method for Symmetry Reduction in Safety Verification
    - what: Introduces a complete symmetry-reduction method for safety verification of finite, parametrically defined multi-process systems without precomputed global symmetry. It defines weak symmetry relative to the safety property, learns state interpolants backward over the interleaving tree, transforms interpolants by process permutations, and prunes states whose symmetric future is covered. The DFS algorithm handles cycles with fixpoint interpolation. Weak symmetry compares program-counter tuples, safety truth under a permutation, and bijective matching of enabled/scheduled transitions while deliberately ignoring shared-variable values; strong symmetry additionally requires full state equality. The algorithm memoizes interpolants per program point, recursively conjoins weakest-precondition approximations for enabled and disabled transitions, detects cycles and computes path-invariant fixpoints, then prunes if a permuted memoized interpolant holds. Theorem 1 proves pruning sound; Theorem 2 proves completeness with respect to weak symmetry when precondition computation is monotonic and symmetry preserving. Examples show pruning despite differing sums and process IDs.

No completeness or success guarantee beyond this hypothesis space is shown. §3: CHECK_TYPE checks a function against its declared augmented type rather than inferring contract solely from uses. extern types are assumed for omitted bodies.     - title: Globally reasoning about localised security policies in distributed systems
    - what: Defines AspectKBL, a process-algebra language for distributed networks with security policies attached to locations, Belnap four-valued policy composition, labelled-transition semantics, and ACTL-like global safety obligations. It proposes checking each syntactic action directly instead of constructing the full LTS, yielding a safe over-approximation for finite systems. AspectKBL models parallel locations, tuple data, out/in/read actions, nondeterministic choice, and replicated processes; local aspects have pointcuts, applicability conditions, and four-valued recommendations. Policy-guarded transitions induce a pruned LTS. ACTLv obligations quantify over all paths and transitions matching a cut, checking predicates before/after interactions. The alternative checker unifies each action with an obligation cut, identifies source/target policies, collects recommendations as constraints, and certifies an action if policies deny it or their constraints imply the obligation predicate. It forbids replication to guarantee finite paths and avoid undecidable general model checking. Healthcare role/private-note examples and third-party-cookie models show both unsafe and policy-protected behavior. An Appendix gives a partial Haskell prototype; constraint solving, parser support, and a correctness proof remain incomplete.
    - number: 4 Belnap values: bottom, true, false, top
    - number: 2 extended case studies
    - number: 3 healthcare process variants
    - number: ACTLv safety obligations over all paths
    - limits: Soundness is claimed as a goal but not proved in the report. The finite-network restriction excludes replication; obligation cuts require constant target locations; direct action inspection may over-approximate impossible paths and return inconclusive false. Current tool handles only simple constraints by substitutions, lacks a parser and complete constraint solver, and uses a conservative liberal Belnap combination. The language is Turing-complete without restrictions, global logic covers safety rather than liveness, and examples are small abstractions.
    - how much was read: most of it read

- Interactive verification of Markov chains: Two distributed protocol case studies (2012)
    - what: # Interactive verification of Markov chains: Two distributed protocol case studies (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Johannes Hölzl and Tobias Nipkow, QFM 2012, EPTCS 103, pp.17–31, DOI 10.4204/EPTCS.103.2; arXiv:1212.3870v1, submitted 17 December 2012. This record covers all 15 PDF pages, §§1–6, acknowledgment, all 23 references and all 4 figures. The local PDF and freshly fetched official PDF are byte-identical. Exact excerpts, source lines, character offsets and PDF/printed pages are in quotes.json; Q-numbers below refer there. The AFP 2012 release and the current AFP source snapshot are distinct supporting artifacts, inspected statically in the ranges recorded in source-scope.json. No Isabelle, author code, model checker or solver was run.  ## What is established  The contribution is a parameterized mathematical verification of two finite-state discrete-time, time-homogeneous Markov-chain models in Isabelle/HOL. It proves formulas for ZeroConf address-collision probability, almost-sure termination and expected allocation cost, and for Crowds endpoint independence, exposure to collaborators, conditional predecessor identification and an information-leakage upper bound. “It can deal with infinite-state systems, although this paper considers only parameterized finite-state systems” (§1, p.17, Q1) is the scope to retain. Infinite path spaces still require measure theory. This is a proof about abstract global models, with formalization effort reported by the authors; it is not an implementation benchmark.  Several discrepancies constrain use of the printed results. The ZeroConf example’s named parameters do not satisfy its printed 10^-13 bound; its displayed cost formula has parentheses inconsistent with the model and retained source. The Crowds §4.2 independence display uses last-ncoll where its heading and definitions concern last-jondo. Finally, the retained information-flow theorem has an additional uniform-initiation hypothesis absent from the paper’s displayed theorem. These are separate issues, documented below rather than silently repaired.  ## Probability foundation and proof method (§2, pp.18–20)  The chain has a nonempty finite state set S and nonnegative transition weights whose row sums are 1 (Q4). Its path probability is constructed on all infinite state sequences from arbitrary product spaces, avoiding an encoding into infinite boolean choices (Q5). A specified start state precedes the measured sequence: the first measured index represents a transition from that start. Individual sequence elements need not satisfy the transition relation by the definition of path alone; the probability measure provides the operational meaning (Q4). Conditional probability is a quotient; AE means probability 1 (Q3).  The reusable tools are one-step equations for event probability, integrals and almost-everywhere predicates (Q6), qualitative reachability over nonzero transition edges and an until operator (Q7), and a theorem that almost every path is state fair (Q8). In the finite chain, if all states reachable before the target remain inside the allowed region or target, and every such non-target state can still reach the target, until holds almost surely (Q8). This is a theorem about the chain’s measure, not an extra fairness assumption on an adversarial scheduler. The model has no nondeterministic scheduler.  The hitting-time and accumulated nonnegative-reward definitions support expected termination cost (Q9). LEAST is total but underspecified if no witness exists: “If there is no such n, then the term has some arbitrary (defined!) value” (§2.1, p.18, Q2). Almost-sure termination and reachability lemmas make the meaningful cases explicit. Finiteness of expected hitting time uses the finite-state setting; it should not be generalized to arbitrary infinite chains. Likewise, the §3.4 prose that finiteness almost everywhere suffices for a finite integral is too broad in isolation. Here the finite chain, finite transition rewards and finite expected hitting time supply the needed integrability argument; the historical source explicitly invokes positive_integral_reward_until_finite before solving the cost equations (historical Zeroconf_Analysis.thy:187–196).  ## ZeroConf: model, result and concrete case (§3, pp.21–25)  The protocol allocates an unused IPv4 link-local address from 169.254.1.0 through 169.254.254.255, a pool of 65024 addresses. A new host chooses uniformly and probes using ARP. The probability q denotes choosing an occupied address; p denotes loss of the request/response exchange (Q10–Q11). This abstracts one allocation against a fixed occupancy/loss environment. Independent repeated choices and constant transition probabilities are encoded in the Markov model; changing occupancy, concurrent allocation races and correlated/history-dependent losses are not additional modeled transitions. Other cited PRISM/timed models contain more protocol features than this selected model (Q10).  The explicit assumptions are N∈Nat, 0<p<1, 0<q<1 and nonnegative real r,E (Q13). Thus zero loss, zero occupied addresses and endpoints 1 are outside the stated theorem context, even if limits can be considered separately. There are N+4 valid states: Start, Ok, Error and Probe 0…ProbeN. Ok and Error absorb. From Start, an unused choice reaches Ok with cost r(N+1); an occupied choice reaches Probe 0 with cost r. A successful probe response returns to Start with cost 0. A failed probe advances with probability p and cost r, or at ProbeN reaches Error with cost E (Fig.1, Q12,Q14). E is the repair penalty, not merely packet latency. The graph and formula use N+1 total probes; the prose step 5 says “N requests” (Q11), so N=2 means 3 probes as the numerical example and graph explicitly state.  The event is reaching Error, not proving collision impossible: P_err(s)=Pr_s(until S {Error}) (Q15). With p,q strictly positive, its derived Start probability is positive. The proof first establishes P_err(Error)=1 and P_err(Ok)=0, then the one-step recurrence. An unrestricted recurrence is unsuitable as an automatic rewrite because it loops: “using it would result in non-termination of the rewrite engine” (§3.3, p.24, Q16). State-specific rules and induction over the remaining probes yield  P_err(Start) = q p^(N+1) / [1−q(1−p^(N+1))].  The printed induction skeleton and theorem are retained in Q17; the historical source gives the same general formula (Q38). Most ZeroConf steps use rewriting, with induction and two rewrite steps for the probe recurrence (Q16–Q17). This is concrete evidence about proof organization rather than an assertion that theorem proving was automatic end to end.  The paper names 16 hosts, q=16/65024, p=.01 and N=2, then prints “Perr Start ≤ 1/1013” in extracted text, visually 10^-13 (Q18; PDF8/printed 24). Reader arithmetic with exact rational numbers gives 1/4063000001≈2.46123554×10^-10. It therefore satisfies neither 10^-13 nor 10^-12. This is an arithmetic inconsistency in the stated example, not a protocol execution or a failed prover replay.  Both inspected AFP versions instantiate locale arguments in order N,p,q,r,E/e as `2 "16 / 65024 :: real" "0.01" "0.002" "3600"` and state a 10^-12 bound (historical Q36,Q40; current Q46,Q48). That assigns p=16/65024 and q=.01, reversing the paper’s named meanings. Under that assignment the same formula gives 1/6645020000257≈1.50488637×10^-13, which does satisfy the retained 10^-12 claim, but exceeds 10^-13. Thus the retained proof text concerns a different concrete parameterization; it does not validate the numerical sentence as printed. The static source inspection establishes these statements and supplied proof scripts, without certifying that a historical checker run used precisely these downloaded bytes.  For expected cost, C_fin integrates transition rewards until Error or Ok. The chain reaches one of them almost surely (Q19,Q21). The model-consistent formula, also present in the historical and current source (Q39,Q47), is  C_fin(Start) = [q(r+p^(N+1)E+rp(1−p^N)/(1−p)) + (1−q)r(N+1)] / [1−q+qp^(N+1)].  The paper instead prints the successful-allocation term `(1−q)*(r*N+1)` (Q21, PDF9/printed 25); the model defines `r*(N+1)` (Q14). With the paper’s named parameters, r=.002 s and E=3600 s, the correct formula gives≈.006001383 s, consistent with the reported≤.007 s; the printed parentheses give≈1.004001383 s. With the retained swapped p,q values, the correct cost is≈.006020208 s and also≤.007 s. The 7 ms result is a symbolic expected rewarded-model bound under selected input parameters, not a measured latency, worst-case deadline or successful-allocation-only expectation. Both Error and Ok terminate the cost accumulation, and the error penalty is included.  ## Crowds: model and anonymity claims (§4, pp.25–29)  Crowds establishes routes by choosing a uniformly random next participant and deciding whether to forward again with probability p_f. Routes can revisit participants; Fig.2 uses J1−J4−J2−J7−J4−C1−S, while Fig.4 illustrates a different route J1−J4−J3−J5−J4−C1−S (Q20,Q25). Neither is a test trace generated by this reader. Fig.3 is a 3-participant transition-graph illustration, not the size limit for the theorem (Q23).  Let J be the number of jondos and H the number of honest/non-collaborating jondos. The set is finite and nonempty, collaborators form a nonempty strict subset, 0<p_f<1, and init is a nonnegative distribution with total 1 and zero mass on collaborators (Q24). The model states are Start, Init i for honest i, Mix j for all j and End: H+J+2 states. From Start the init distribution chooses the initiator. An Init state moves uniformly to a Mix participant; from Mix the next Mix identity has probability p_f/J, or the route ends with probability 1−p_f. End absorbs (Q26). Participants can select themselves, and collaborators follow these transitions: active route manipulation, arbitrary topology, timing observations and multiple correlated runs are outside this model.  The paper is explicit about the abstraction boundary: “We could model the individual behaviour of jondos in Isabelle/HOL and show that this induces our Markov chain model, but this is not in the scope of this paper” (§4, p.25, Q22). Hence these results do not constitute refinement from distributed node implementations, or whole-protocol anonymity against all observations. The starting state is excluded from the measured path; Init is at index 0. The displayed len value is the last zero-based Mix index, so a terminating path has len+1 Mix states. The paper’s wording calls len the number of Mix states, but its formula and i≤len lemmas count len+1 (Q27; historical Q42).  The intended §4.2 claim is that the final server-contacting participant is independent of the initiator, under the specified uniform routing. The displayed lemma instead contains last-ncoll, defined in the next subsection as the predecessor of the first collaborator, rather than last-jondo (Q28 versus Q27,Q29). Preserve this symbol discrepancy. The current AFP `server_view_indep` proves factorization of initiating and final-participant sets (Q49); the historical source has a `server_view` theorem equating the chance that final participant equals initiator to the reciprocal of the participant count; the historical source names that reciprocal J=1/card jondos (Q43; historical Crowds_Protocol.thy:97–98; Q45). The historical notation differs from the paper’s J=count notation. Independence gives no additional identity information from this modeled endpoint observation; it does not remove a nonuniform prior or give the server “no chance” of guessing in an absolute sense.  For collaborator exposure, hit-colls means at least one Mix participant is a collaborator, and last-ncoll denotes the participant immediately before the first such collaborator. Conditional identification is meaningful because the nonempty collaborator set makes the hit probability positive. The paper proves (Q29–Q31):  - Pr(hit-colls) = (1−H/J)/(1−(H/J)p_f) - Pr(first=i and last-ncoll=l | hit-colls) = init(i)[p_f/J + indicator(i=l)(1−(H/J)p_f)], for honest i,l - Pr(first=last-ncoll | hit-colls) = 1−((H−1)/J)p_f  The first expression approaches 0 when the number of collaborators and p_f remain fixed and J tends to infinity. This is not a limit with a fixed attacker fraction. The second and third account for revisiting the initiator; they concern predecessor equality, not a general optimal attacker-classification success rate. The probably-innocent bound≤1/2 requires H>1 and p_f≥J/[2(H−1)]. Since p_f<1, feasibility requires H>J/2+1, stronger than merely an honest majority. The paper gives the precise inequality 1/2<(H−1)/J and then loosely says “more than half” (Q31).  Reader-created arithmetic example, separate from the paper’s case: J=10,H=9,p_f=3/4 gives hit probability 4/13 and conditional predecessor-equals-initiator probability 2/5; its threshold is 5/8. For J=10,H=6 the threshold is 1, excluded by p_f<1. These examples clarify the parameter constraints; no simulation, model checking or author code produced them.  For information flow, the paper conditions its measure on hitting a collaborator and bounds mutual information between initiating identity and the predecessor of the first collaborator by [1−((H−1)/J)p_f]log2(H) bits (Q32). The formalization uses Radon–Nikodým-based information theory and reduces finite-range variables to the discrete probability/logarithm sum. Both retained historical and current `information_flow` theorems add `init_uniform`, requiring equal initiating probability 1/H for each honest participant (Q44,Q50). That hypothesis is absent from the displayed paper theorem and the general §4.1 context. The evidence-backed formal theorem should retain it. This inspection does not show that the numerical inequality is false for arbitrary init; it establishes that the inspected scripts prove the stated bound under an extra hypothesis. The bound covers this pair of identities under the conditional measure, not all data a real collaborator might observe.  ## Evaluation, related work and limits (§§5–6, pp.30–31)  The evaluation is two worked formal developments, exact parametric formulas and concrete rewrites for a selected ZeroConf instance. The authors report “a couple of days” and approximately 260 Isabelle/HOL lines for ZeroConf; Crowds needs approximately 1060 lines and “one person a couple of weeks,” including finding the information-gain estimate (Q34). These are author-reported effort/size figures with no controlled comparison, replication, distribution or detailed time log. The paper supplies no proof-checking runtimes, hardware measurements, packet experiments, implementation throughput, benchmark suite or user study. The two protocols are case studies, not statistical samples.  The related-work discussion matters to the opening comparison with model checking: it explicitly recognizes probabilistic CEGAR for infinite-state systems, parametric transition probabilities for a fixed state count, and quantitative invariants for linear probabilistic programs (Q33). Thus the broad opening PRISM/model-checker contrast should not become a claim that all model checking handles only one fixed numerical instance. This work builds on the authors’ previous pCTL model-checking formalization and measure theory, and compares other HOL/Coq probability frameworks and information-flow analyses. These are discussion-level comparisons, not reproduced comparative experiments. The probabilities here can be written in PCTL, while HOL permits more properties; Markov decision processes, continuous-time models and certification of model-checker runs are future work in this 2012 paper (Q34). Their presence on the modern AFP page is subsequent artifact evolution, not a result reported here.  ## What this adds to the requested topic  Directly, this is evidence that distributed-protocol questions can require quantitative guarantees over infinite executions: almost-sure termination, finite expected cost, conditional anonymity and information leakage differ from deterministic safety invariants. Isabelle’s reusable probability library supports proofs for arbitrary finite network/probe sizes and symbolic probabilities, with the global model and theorem hypotheses made explicit. The ZeroConf rewrite/induction presentation is useful concrete proof-engineering evidence. It also shows why a local literature database should compare printed statements, parameter meanings and source hypotheses, rather than treat a claimed proof as validation of every nearby prose sentence.  There is no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment in this paper. Reader inference for those areas: an agent producing a specification/proof should retain the global-model refinement boundary, distinguish probability 1 from every execution, check integrability assumptions, align locale argument order with physical parameter names, and preserve extra theorem hypotheses. Evaluating such an agent should inspect those semantic correspondences as well as checker acceptance. These are lessons drawn by this reader, not results measured by Hölzl and Nipkow.
    - limits: Finite nonempty time-homogeneous DTMCs, normalized nonnegative transitions. ZeroConf:N natural,0<p,q<1,r,E>=0; fixed global occupancy/loss abstraction,N+1 probes. Crowds:finite nonempty participants,nonempty strict collaborator subset,0<p_f<1,honest-only initiation,uniform routing; retained information-flow proof also requires uniform initiation. Global models without node-level refinement. Printed numerical,formula,symbol and source-hypothesis discrepancies retained. No proof replay.

- IOALERGIA DLMDP learning (2012)
    - title: Learning Markov Decision Processes for Model Checking
    - what: Introduces IOALERGIA, an adaptation of Alergia that learns deterministic labeled Markov decision processes from alternating input/output traces. It builds an IO frequency prefix tree, merges states using recursive Hoeffding compatibility including disabled-action errors, chooses epsilon by BIC, and produces a DLMDP suitable for PLTL and scheduler analysis. The paper gives formal LMDP/DLMDP and scheduler semantics, a fair-scheduler observation model with unbounded independent sequence lengths, explicit IOFPTA/merge algorithms, convergence to the true structure up to bisimulation and parameter convergence with probability one, and the limitation that analogous convergence does not carry to PCTL. It evaluates deterministic and nondeterministic slot machines, not just an abstract learner: model sizes, learning time, probability/reward approximation, optimal-action accuracy, and conditional-probability failures are reported.
    - number: deterministic models: 160k-5,000k symbols; learning 9.8-454.4 s; learned state counts 436-1727; IOFPTA up to 1,135,055 nodes
    - number: deterministic learned optimal actions improve with data and remain above 25% random baseline
    - number: nondeterministic hooked models: 160k-5,000k symbols; 9.7-460.3 s; 437-1725 states
    - number: for hooked model, real P(3 bars|C1)=0.30 while learned values range 0.0327-0.0714; C3 real=0.30 while learned 0.0835-0.0940
    - limits: Observed traces alternate outputs and inputs, begin/end in states, and are independent; nondeterministic actions are resolved by a fair scheduler that chooses each input infinitely often. Disabled actions produce an err output and a memoryless scheduler is used in data generation. Epsilon controls type-I compatibility error and BIC balances likelihood and model size. Learned models approximate observed/generating systems; exact conditional probabilities and PCTL guarantees need not transfer, especially for nondeterministic systems. PRISM computes the reported properties.

- Isabelle pCTL checker (2012)
    - title: Verifying pCTL Model Checking
    - what: Formalizes finite discrete-time Markov chains, their probability measure on infinite paths, pCTL syntax/semantics (next, bounded and unbounded until, cumulative/state/unbounded rewards), and the standard model-checking algorithm Sat in Isabelle/HOL. The authors prove Sat sound and complete. The formalization constructs a probability space from infinite products and Carathéodory extension, proves cylinder-measure and iterative integral equations, and formalizes state fairness and finite expected hitting time. Sat computes bounded operators recursively, probability-0/1 reachability by predecessor closure, and unbounded until/rewards through uniquely solvable linear systems and function-indexed Gauss–Jordan elimination. The final theorems connect an Isabelle result to the semantic state set and show termination under the unique-solution theorem; the authors discuss list-based extraction, certificate checking and parameterized protocol case studies.
    - number: Theorems 30, 32 and Corollary 33 establish soundness/completeness
    - number: about 4,480 AFP lines reported
    - number: finite nonempty state spaces
    - number: bounded and unbounded until plus three reward forms
    - limits: The chain has a finite nonempty state space, time-homogeneous transition matrix and nonnegative state/transition rewards; a starting state induces the path measure rather than an initial distribution. The set-based equations are almost executable but not directly handled by Isabelle code generation; arbitrary state indexing, the while-combinator and Gauss–Jordan adaptation require a future list-based SatL. This is foundational formalization without a runtime benchmark against PRISM.

- Lattice Tree Automata (2012)
    - title: Tree Regular Model Checking for Lattice-Based Automata
    - what: Introduces Lattice Tree Automata (LTA), extending tree automata with lattice-valued leaves to represent infinite sets of interpreted terms efficiently. A completion/evaluation algorithm computes finite over-approximations of reachable states for rewriting systems with arithmetic data. LTA Boolean operations, evaluation and completion support interpreted symbols without Peano encodings. Theorems establish sound over-approximation and completeness for left-linear term-rewriting systems under conditions; widening ensures termination of infinite numeric behavior. Examples model counters and Java-like data domains.

Theorem 4 assumes a left-linear TRS R, a tree automaton A and linear equations E, and requires completion to terminate; its conclusion is language inclusion over all R-reachable terms. Widening can lose precision; evaluation may not terminate without widening.

- Lock Removal for Concurrent Trace Programs (2012)
    - what: Removes redundant lock statements from concrete concurrent trace programs while preserving shared-memory-access partial orders. This reduces constraints for later SMT-based predictive bug analysis. The method goes beyond removing purely thread-local locks by checking which locks maintain impossible control-state transitions. §2 shows a lock around only local operations can still restrict the order of surrounding shared accesses; naive removal introduces an assertion failure. §3 defines visible successors of global control states and a conservative static successor relation ignoring data. Theorem 1 says equality of these static successor sets before and after removal preserves partial orders of global operations. §4 summarizes each local path between adjacent shared accesses/lock acquisitions (pairs of interest) by a lock access pattern: initial/final held sets, backward/forward acquisition histories, continuously held locks and acquired locks. Inconsistent pattern pairs expose reachability barriers. Retaining at least one blocking lockset per barrier preserves impossible transitions; remaining locks can become nops. Pattern equivalence classes avoid enumerating all program-counter tuples. §5 iterates removal in the running example: B is first removed, then A becomes removable. Other synchronization can be ignored conservatively or incorporated through a universal causality graph.
    - number: 20 table traces, 1–21 threads, 55–45653 total events, up to 41 named locks; acquisition history nesting depths 0 or 1
    - number: BarrierB2: 13 threads, 805 events, 49 initial critical sections and 21 in transformed trace; removal 1.6 s, symbolic check 54.5→7.4 s
    - number: account2: 21 threads, 1747 events, 140→60 critical sections; removal 2.6 s, check 8.7→2.4 s
    - number: Elevator1: 184→174 critical sections; removal 0.1 s, check 29.6→0.7 s
    - limits: Input is a finite trace program with a fixed finite thread/lock set: branch choices already made, calls inlined, loops and recursion unrolled, actual accessed addresses known. Preservation concerns alternative interleavings of those fixed local paths, not all paths or whole-program source optimization. Static reachability overapproximates by ignoring shared-data consistency; extra synchronization can only reduce executions. The decomposition assumes nested locks and is incomplete beyond two threads. Experiments assume sequential consistency and use Yices. No proof for relaxed memory, fences, dynamic whole-program lock sets, general liveness, or arbitrary executions. The claimed linear worst-case local analysis should be read with the fixed-pattern/thread/lock assumptions; the algorithm explicitly compares inconsistent pattern combinations. Most measured acquisition-history depths are zero, some one, so benchmarks do not establish behavior with deep nesting.

- McScM communicating-machines framework (2012)
    - title: McScM: A General Framework for the Verification of Communicating Machines
    - what: Introduces McScM, an OCaml platform for safety verification and controller synthesis of finite-state processes communicating over reliable unbounded FIFO channels. It unifies abstract interpretation, abstract regular model checking, CEGAR and lazy abstraction behind a common verify front end and symbolic queue-content representation. The paper specifies the CM input and bad-state representation, explains verify outputs (safe certificate, counterexample or resource-bounded abort), and details four algorithms sharing FCID/QDD infrastructure and path-invariant generators. It describes compile-time interface guarantees from OCaml modules/functors and on-the-fly validation of path invariants and inductive certificates. The control tool computes a safe restriction using distributed control. Benchmark analysis finds algorithm-dependent strengths: absint terminates but may be inconclusive, cegar is good when precision is local, and armc often handles global refinement better; no method dominates.

    - number: examples range from 5 global control states to about 10^4 for Peterson

    - number: absint solved safe examples quickly but was inconclusive on unsafe cases; cegar/armc/lart had complementary time/memory results

The algorithms are semi-algorithms or approximations and can abort under user resource/precision limits. absint always terminates without necessarily deciding safety; armc cannot handle a simple non-regular protocol in the benchmark. The release (1.2) is work in progress; future infinite local data (counters/timers) needs new abstractions and region algebras.

- Model Checking and the State Explosion Problem (2012)
    - what: Lecture notes develop finite-state temporal model checking and four approaches to state explosion: symbolic BDD representation, partial-order reduction, counterexample-guided abstraction refinement and SAT-based bounded model checking, emphasizing the last. Defines Kripke structures and CTL*/LTL/CTL syntax and semantics, including incomparability of LTL and CTL. Gives explicit-state EU labeling and fixed-point characterizations, reduced ordered BDD operations, and the importance of variable order. States abstraction conditions preserving universal CTL* and explains how spurious abstract traces drive refinement. Derives a bounded safety encoding from initial states, transition unrolling and a bad-state disjunction. Discusses diameter bounds and k-induction for completeness. For general LTL, gives loop-free bounded semantics, lasso encodings and improved linear-size until encodings with loop selectors and auxiliary variables. Ends with equisatisfiable Tseitin CNF, DPLL/unit propagation, conflict learning and watched literals.

Shared variables are a Boolean-valued flag function, a turn value initially 0, and the generated program-counter function pc. Initially both flags are false and both counters are at a0. Each process repeatedly sets its flag, gives the other process the turn, checks the other's flag and turn through two separate labeled tests, executes the critical-section skip, then clears its flag (Q5–Q8).  Atomicity is specified by PlusCal labels: an action runs from one label to the next. Figure 2 exposes seven action formulas per process, and Next existentially selects one process's action. Reads/writes and control changes have exactly the interleaving semantics of these formulas. The example supplies no weak-memory, compiler-reordering, machine-instruction, crash, recovery or network-message model. Correctness of a compiled Rust or C implementation would need a separate correspondence argument. The critical section itself is represented by an atomic skip; the paper's property is that the two program counters never simultaneously equal cs (Q6–Q9).  The full specification is Spec = Init ∧ □[Next]_vars, with vars collecting flag, turn and pc. Brackets admit either a Next transition or a step leaving all listed variables unchanged. A behavior is an infinite state sequence. Stuttering is included to simplify refinement, not to assert progress (Q7,Q8,Q10).  There is no fairness clause in the displayed Spec. A reader witness repeats the initial state forever: Init holds, every step satisfies UNCHANGED vars, and neither process ever reaches cs. Thus that exact Spec does not imply eventual entry into a critical section. This is compatible with its mutual-exclusion safety property. The paper says liveness can be expressed and proved in TLA+, but does not give the extra progress assumptions or a liveness proof here (Q4; math-witness.json). It would be wrong to infer starvation freedom merely from the safety theorem.  ## What is proved, and the checking boundary  The target is Spec ⇒ □MutualExclusion. Its three state-level obligations are Init ⇒ Inv, Inv ∧ [Next]_vars ⇒ Inv′, and Inv ⇒ MutualExclusion. Figure 3 and §3.1 explain how propositional reasoning plus temporal induction and monotonicity yield the temporal theorem from these premises. They then state: “TLAPS does not yet handle temporal reasoning, so we omit the proof of the qed step” (Q11). Figure 6 calls itself the “complete hierarchical proof” while visibly retaining that omission (Q19). This is a disclosed tool limitation, not evidence that the mutual-exclusion theorem is false.  Inv is TypeOK ∧ I. TypeOK constrains pc to seven labels per process, turn to {0,1}, and flag to Boolean-valued functions on {0,1}. I says a process from a2 through a4 has its flag set. A process at cs or a4 excludes the other from both cs and a4; if the other is still in either waiting-test location, turn favors the process already in that region (Q12). The stronger control-state conditions explain why the simple target predicate is preserved even across the entry/exit protocol.  Two small reader checks clarify the formula. Init satisfies TypeOK, while all control-state antecedents in I are false at a0. If pc[0]=cs, I for process 0 excludes pc[1]=cs; if pc[0]≠cs, MutualExclusion already holds. These checks cover initialization and implication to the target. They do not replace the preservation proof or independently certify the tool. TypeOK describes 7²×2×2²=392 possible valuations; that is a domain-size calculation, not the paper's reported 58 reachable states (math-witness.json).  The paper first reports TLC checking execution errors and MutualExclusion over all 58 reachable states of this particular finite model. It also checks inductiveness by replacing Init with Inv, model checking Inv ∧ □[Next]_vars. Starting from every state satisfying the candidate invariant tests preservation beyond the original reachable-state set. For more complicated or infinite-state specifications, the authors recommend small-instance model checking as a way to find errors, and explicitly limit its ability to establish general inductiveness (Q9,Q12). A successful finite instance is not a universal proof for arbitrary process counts or data domains.  The illustrated checks also reveal the human work. A leaf proof citing only Init and Inv fails because TypeOK and I remain uninterpreted. Supplying their definitions lets TLAPS prove initialization. Expanding definitions for the entire preservation obligation still fails with the default provers and produces a 65-line obligation. CVC3 through the SMT backend proves it “in a few seconds” (Q13–Q15). No hardware, precise solver versions, timeout, repeat count or full timing log accompanies that statement.  To demonstrate hierarchy rather than rely on this easy SMT success, the authors deliberately decompose the preservation proof using Zenon and Isabelle. The SUFFICES step replaces [Next]_vars with Next only after separately proving the unchanged-variable case. It then splits Inv′ into TypeOK′ and I′. Zenon proves the SUFFICES reduction; Zenon fails on the stated TypeOK′ proof but Isabelle succeeds. Both fail on I′ without further decomposition (Q16–Q17).  The next level introduces an arbitrary process j, names its invariant subexpression as I!(j), and picks the process i that performs the Next action. Instead of seven action-by-action cases, two cases, i=j and i≠j, suffice for the displayed example. Explicit facts and definition expansions then discharge the leaves. A case step's own name denotes its case assumption, so citing that name within its proof is not circular citation of its conclusion. NEW-bound assumptions and the PICK membership fact are automatically available within scope; ordinary facts still need the stated context discipline (Q18–Q19).  ## Proof management, reuse and trust  The Proof Manager translates proof steps into sequents with a goal and context of symbols, assumptions and previously established facts. It tracks context changes and sends leaf obligations to backends. It records success, failure, cancellation and omission. The interface can check one step, theorem or file, show the exact failing obligation, navigate back to the producing proof, and hide irrelevant portions of the hierarchy (Q21–Q22).  “Proof obligations are independent of one another” describes the ability to check conditional obligations in any order (Q21). It does not make a theorem valid while required assumptions or earlier steps remain unproved. The distinction matters in this very example: the state-level work can be developed independently while the final temporal QED is omitted. Global completion requires all needed obligations and the correct bridge to the stated property.  Fingerprinting stores an obligation's status under a canonical representation. Bound variables become de Bruijn indices, so renaming them does not change the representation; unused symbols and hypotheses are removed from the context. This supports reuse after proof reorganization, moving a step or removing and later reinserting it. Status can also be queried without launching proofs (Q23). The paper describes the mechanism but gives no hash-collision theorem, implementation-level soundness proof or controlled cache benchmark. Correct reuse depends on the representation preserving all relevant logical dependencies. This record did not inspect the fingerprint implementation.  The backends described are Isabelle/TLA+, Zenon and SMT solvers. Default attempts use Zenon, then Isabelle; the SMT route translates obligations into SMT-LIB for CVC3, with native Yices/Z3 alternatives. Isabelle is the most trusted backend. Zenon can emit Isar proofs that Isabelle checks. The paper says certification of SMT proof traces is future work, so a successful SMT result should not be silently counted as Isabelle-certified evidence in this article (Q3,Q15,Q27).  The trusted components also include translations and critical Proof Manager transformations such as distributing prime through addition. Users can disable fingerprints and reprove obligations, which addresses cache reuse concerns without removing the other trust dependencies. The authors further warn that an incorrect target formula can make a proof meaningless and that incorrect assumed mathematical facts can invalidate an apparent result. TLC can test those exact assumed formulas on instances; that supplies error-finding evidence, not a proof of every assumed mathematical statement (Q27–Q28).  ## Evaluation and concrete larger cases  The evaluation is a worked proof tutorial plus development experience, not a randomized user study or comparative prover benchmark. Its concrete local evidence comprises the 58-state TLC result, the failed/repaired leaf proofs, the 65-line preservation obligation, backend-specific outcomes and the qualitative CVC3 timing. There are no statistical estimates, repeated trials, task success rates, hardware budgets or uniform comparison across proof assistants (Q9,Q13–Q19).  Larger uses are named: Byzantine Paxos, the Memoir security architecture, and Pastry lookup/join protocols. These are cited case studies, not complete proofs reproduced in this article (Q20). A cited 1100-line invariance proof has 100 non-leaf steps, illustrating the scale at which the hierarchy acts like nested lemmas (Q22). The claim that 100 conventional linear lemmas would be unreadable is the authors' judgment, not a measured readability result.  The strongest maintenance anecdote concerns Lamport's Byzantine Paxos proof. He initially spent several weeks over several months on its safety proof while debugging TLAPS. Later he discovered the algorithm lacked the desired liveness property, changed it, repaired small bugs found by TLC, and re-established safety in a day and a half, about 12 hours of actual work. About three quarters of the new proof obligations had already been proved (Q24). This shows reported reuse during a real revision and separately shows why safety does not imply liveness. It does not report a newly checked liveness proof, an exact obligation count, or an isolated speedup attributable solely to fingerprinting.  The related-work discussion compares declarative proofs and interface features with Mizar/Isar, reuse with KIV, set-theoretic/refinement approaches with Rodin/Event-B, and high-level specifications with VCC/Why source-code verification. These are architectural comparisons and historical author assessments, not present-day benchmark rankings (Q25). The conclusion also lists proof constructs not exercised in the Peterson example, including existential witnesses, local definitions and facts supplied implicitly to backends. Temporal reasoning and improved sequence support are planned work in the article (Q26,Q29).  ## Static artifact findings  Both pinned Peterson modules contain the full PlusCal comment, generated actions, candidate invariant, ISpec for inductiveness testing, and two variants of the same safety proof. One variant uses SMT for preservation; the other expands the hierarchy. Both end their top-level theorem with PROOF OMITTED (Q31–Q35). This independently preserves the article's disclosed checking boundary in a usable example artifact. The source exists; no dynamic proof certificate or successful replay is supplied by this read.  The artifact retains ProcSet and uses USE DEF ProcSet, matching the paper's footnote about a definition inlined in Figure 2. MutualExclusion uses negated conjunction, logically equivalent to the paper's disjunction. Source leaf proofs often cite Inv, Next and proc(i) directly where Figure 6 cites numbered steps; the explanatory text explicitly permits such fact references (Q7,Q17,Q32–Q35). The FM directory copy differs only by an unused NeverCS predicate and DEF versus DEFS spelling in one leaf proof (Q36 and retained file comparison). Neither difference establishes an algorithm change or runtime failure. The two files remain exact downloaded bytes.  ## Contribution to the requested research topics  This is directly relevant to formal verification of distributed systems and TLA+: it gives a concrete path from a labeled algorithm to a temporal specification, tested invariant, structured proof obligations, backend checks and maintained proof status. It makes both the specification assumptions and proof-completion boundary visible. Its larger-system anecdotes link those mechanisms to distributed protocols while leaving those cited proofs outside this article's detailed evidence.  It contains no Verus or verified-Rust development, LLM agent, generated-specification benchmark or automatic invariant-synthesis evaluation. Its transferable design ideas are therefore reader proposals: give proof agents explicit sequents and scoped context; use checker feedback to distinguish missing definitions from difficult obligations; split proofs without dropping stuttering or other cases; cache normalized obligations only with valid dependencies; and report omitted steps and certification routes alongside success counts. The article does not measure those proposals with LLMs. Its most useful evaluation lesson is to keep a correct formalization, state-level proof success, temporal completion, liveness, certificate checking and proof-reuse evidence separate.

Larger case studies cited; maintenance/timing evidence is anecdotal.2026modulepin does not identify2012executables.

    - title: TRACER: A Symbolic Execution Tool for Verification
    - what: Presents TRACER, a symbolic-execution verifier for safety assertions in sequential C. It builds a finite overapproximating symbolic tree, learns weak interpolants from infeasible paths to subsume paths, and widens/refines loop invariants for unbounded loops. The implementation translates CIL programs (including pointers/arrays and alias partitions) to CLP(R), supports SP/WP/CLP interpolation and optional InterProc invariants, and reports proof trees or counterexamples.

- Effectively Nonblocking Consensus Procedures Can Execute Forever - a Constructive Version of FLP (2011)
    - what: # Effectively Nonblocking Consensus Procedures Can Execute Forever: whole paper reading (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Robert L. Constable's Effectively Nonblocking Consensus Procedures Can Execute Forever – a Constructive Version of FLP is arXiv:1109.3370v1,15 September 2011. Its frontmatter also gives July 17, 2008, a footnote describing changes through August 2011, and a May 20, 2021 print date. These identify the saved version rather than three independent research results. All 17 pages were read: Sections 1–2, their eight subsections, all lemma/theorem/corollary statements and proofs, Figures 1–7, the One Step Program, acknowledgments and ten references. All five contact sheets and individual4,10,14,16 were inspected. Original, local and official PDFs match. No author code, scientific-result artifact or formal checking tool was executed or loaded. [Evidence: Q0, frontmatter/abstract/dates, PDF pp.1–1; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The contribution is a constructive variant of the Fischer–Lynch–Paterson impossibility argument. Instead of only proving that some indecisive run exists, the paper assumes a computable nonblocking witness and explains how to calculate every finite prefix of an infinite indecisive execution. Its distinction is between an existence proof and an effective construction, not a new consensus protocol. Classical nonblocking alone is handled using excluded middle/choice; the stronger effective premise supplies the computational content. Historical claims that earlier proofs lack this construction are Constable's assessment of the cited work, not a literature-wide priority finding established here. [Evidence: Q1, §1.1, constructive versus classical problem, PDF pp.2–2; Q6, §1.4, full theorem/lemma/corollary summary, PDF pp.5–6; Q12, §2.2, full constructive/classical corollaries, PDF pp.10–11; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The model is deterministic binary consensus with crash failures, reliable FIFO message channels and unbounded asynchronous delay. Processes have private state and messages in queues; executions are serialized into individual actions. Fairness requires every message to a nonfailed process eventually be read and every enabled action at such a process eventually be taken. Uniform inputs require the corresponding decision, and all deciding processes agree. The main construction concerns tolerating one failure, although no process actually crashes in its resulting fair run. Randomized termination, known-delay synchrony and Byzantine fault behavior are outside the stated theorem. [Evidence: Q3, §1.2, complete computing/fairness model, PDF pp.3–4; Q4, §1.3, consensus/nonblocking/witness, PDF pp.4–4; Q11, §2.2, CFLP theorem/full proof, PDF pp.10–10; Q12, §2.2, full constructive/classical corollaries, PDF pp.10–11; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Constable defines the premise in §1.3: “P is called effectively nonblocking if from any reachable global state s of an execution of P and any subset Q of n − t nonfailed processes, we can find an execution α from s using Q and a process Pα in Q which decides a value v ǫ B.” Effective nonblocking is a total computable function wt(s, Q): for every reachable state s and every chosen set Q of n−t nonfailed processes, it returns a finite execution using Q, its deciding state and a process deciding a bit. This is an existential progress witness, not a promise that every continuation progresses. It is stronger information than an abstract claim that some extension exists. A constructive proof of nonblocking can supply such a witness; the paper cites Nuprl/Coq's constructive setting and Mark Bickford's nonblocking formalizations as motivation. It does not present a checked Nuprl or Coq development of this complete CFLP proof. [Evidence: Q4, §1.3, consensus/nonblocking/witness, PDF pp.4–4; Q2, §1.1, Nuprl/Coq and blocking motivation, PDF pp.3–3; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The paper's v-possible predicate asks whether one of finitely many wt(s, Q) results decides v. For one-failure tolerance this can be decided by n witness evaluations, one for each Q_i excluding P_i. That does not decide all possible future decisions. Effective bivalence instead includes explicit finite executions deciding 0 and 1; arbitrary bivalence remains undecidable according to the source. In particular, a witness may choose only 0-valued continuations even when another execution decides 1, so failure to find a 1 in those n selected witnesses does not establish univalence. The construction retains a known opposite-valued path rather than replacing that information by a finite sample of witness answers. [Evidence: Q5, §1.3, v-possible/effective bivalence, PDF pp.5–5; Q8, §2.1, finite witness-decision test, PDF pp.6–6; Q11, §2.2, CFLP theorem/full proof, PDF pp.10–10; Q13, §2.3, initialization/replay and witness independence, PDF pp.11–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]  Initialization starts at all-zero inputs and flips one process at a time until all-one inputs. It chooses the first initialization s_k for which some witness decides 1. At s_(k−1), the witness excluding P_k decides 0. Replay that finite execution from s_k: only P_k's initial state changed and it takes no step, so the other processes still decide0. This is ordinary explanatory substitution, not an executed trace. The witness itself need not return identical paths on the two inputs; the proof explicitly uses replay rather than assuming witness extensionality in unseen state. [Evidence: Q9, §2.1, full initialization proof, PDF pp.7–7; Q13, §2.3, initialization/replay and witness independence, PDF pp.11–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]  The One Step Lemma takes explicit bivalent paths and a process P_i, and constructs a reachable state b′ with two opposite-valued deciding paths using only Q_i. Its first proof walks backward along a finite 1-path, queries wt at predecessor states and uses agreement to transfer decisions across an isolated P_i action. The commutativity lemma permits executions of disjoint process sets to be replayed in either order while delaying cross-set messages. This depends on the asynchronous message model and on the selected actions remaining executable; it is not a general claim that arbitrary shared-memory operations commute. Figures 1–4 show the two decision branches and commuting diagrams. [Evidence: Q10, §2.1, full One Step proof/Figures 1–4, PDF pp.7–10; Q14, §2.3, both commutativity lemmata/proofs, PDF pp.12–12; literal spans in quotes.json.]  David Guaspari's alternative proof counts P_i actions on one branch of a fork. A fork is a pair of finite paths ending in different decisions; an i-fork has one branch avoiding P_i, and a full i-fork has both branches avoiding it. At the last P_i action, query the witness on Q_i. If its decision matches the branch already avoiding P_i, commutation produces a full i-fork after that action. If it matches the other branch, replace the suffix by the witness path and strictly decrease the number of P_i actions. Finite descent yields the One Step Lemma. The returned path length and witness-running time are unbounded by this paper; the finite descent measures distinguished-process actions, not total execution cost. [Evidence: Q15, §2.3, fork definitions/modification lemma, PDF pp.13–14; Q16, §2.3, alternative One Step proof, PDF pp.15–15; literal spans in quotes.json.]  CFLP then cycles through processes and selected enabled actions. Before executing P_i's action, it obtains a state b′ bivalent via Q_i; replaying the two Q_i decision paths after that action preserves bivalence by commutativity and agreement. If the action was already executed while reaching b′, it is not repeated. Repeating this procedure supplies longer indecisive prefixes while giving each process turns. The source asserts the resulting execution is fair and failure-free. A formal extraction should explicitly enumerate pending messages/enabled actions so process-level round robin also discharges its stronger message/action fairness definition. The printed proof does not give that queue-selection policy or an explicit total function for the n-th output action. This is an extraction/detail obligation, not a counterexample to classical FLP. Strong FLP instead assumes nonblocking without a computable witness and invokes choice/excluded middle to obtain an infinite run. The Blocking corollary states that a procedure terminating on all failure-free executions must have a reachable state where one process's failure prevents any decision. - Kartzow dissertation on pushdown model checking (2011)
    - title: First-Order Model Checking on Generalisations of Pushdown Graphs
    - what: Develops decidability and complexity results for first-order (FO) model checking on infinite structures arising from higher-order software models. It proves tree-automatic representations for level-2 collapsible pushdown graphs with regular reachability and L-mu predicates, FO decidability for nested pushdown trees, a new higher-order nested-pushdown-tree hierarchy with a level-2 algorithm, and decidability of FO extended with counting, infinity, and Ramsey quantifiers on automatic structures. The thesis supplies the constructions behind each theorem: encodings of level-2 stacks into trees; regular reachable configurations, stack operations and reachability predicates; product constructions combining automata and L-mu predicates; locality/Ehrenfeucht-Fraisse and pumping arguments for nested pushdown trees; relevant-ancestor equivalences and small-witness algorithms for higher-order nested trees; and tree-comb/Ramsey reductions. It proves a nonelementary lower bound for FO on level-2 collapsible pushdown graphs, gives 2-EXPSPACE bounds for nested trees, and includes an appendix reducing the Turing-machine halting problem to L-mu model checking on a bidirectional half-grid. The work is mathematical proof and automata construction, not an empirical tool evaluation.

- Quantitative concurrent synthesis (2011)
    - title: Quantitative Synthesis for Concurrent Programs.
    - what: The paper synthesizes a deterministic finite-state concurrent program by resolving nondeterministic synchronization choices in a partial program. A weighted-automaton performance model assigns architecture-sensitive costs to locking, context switches, memory/cache operations; a possibly probabilistic scheduler induces worst- or average-case limit-average objectives. Correctness is specification-free safety such as race or deadlock freedom. The synthesis problem reduces to imperfect-information stochastic graph games and is Nexp-complete; practical solving uses static strategy pruning, MDP strategy improvement, Gaussian elimination for Markov chains, and value-preserving data abstraction. A prototype handles producer-consumer, optimistic concurrency, and two other finite-state patterns. For two producers/two consumers and four cells, fine-grained locking is 19% better when copying costs 100x locking, while coarse locking is 25% better when costs are equal; measured optimistic-concurrency runtime peaks then declines as batch size n grows.

Correctness covers race/deadlock freedom rather than arbitrary functional specifications, and interleaving semantics assumes one scheduled thread at a time. Worst/average objectives are limit-average/mean-payoff. Results depend on chosen weighted automata and scheduler, so they do not claim universally optimal synchronization; desktop measurements are a sanity check against synthesis trends.

    - title: Policy Monitoring in First-Order Temporal Logic.
    - what: Defines an effectively monitorable safety fragment of metric first-order temporal logic (MFOTL): formulas Ψ = □Ψ′ with bounded future temporal operators, arbitrary nesting of metric past and bounded future operators, quantifier alternation, and finite or automatic structures. An incremental monitor rewrites violations into a finite-relation fragment, maintains auxiliary relations for temporal subformulas, queues future obligations, and emits violating assignments online. The algorithm handles events and duration-like states by encoding starts/finishes, supports point-based metric timestamps, and incrementally updates past-since and bounded-future relations rather than recomputing windows. The paper gives PPTL syntax and interval semantics, distinguishes finite and infinite normal-form paths, and removes finite paths to form NFG_inf. Its construction algorithm records self-loops and paired Rabin sets to exclude infinite repetition of strong chop; a Safra-style tree algorithm determinizes NFG_inf while merging equivalent PPTL formulas. The product construction labels accepting bottom strongly connected components and reduces formula probability to reachability of accepting BSCCs. A worked p;q chain yields an almost-sure result, illustrating the complete pipeline.
    - number: finite NFG for every PPTL formula
    - number: Rabin acceptance pairs
    - number: product state space S × V_inf(Q)
    - number: worked p;q probability 1
    - limits: Models are discrete-time Markov chains with a finite formula-generated graph and (for the stated theorem) a finite chain with a unique initial state. The paper relies on prior PPTL normal-form and equivalence decision procedures and sketches algorithms rather than reporting an implementation or complexity measurements. Determinization inherits Safra-style state blow-up; only infinite/omega-regular properties are handled in NFG_inf, while finite PPTL paths are discarded for this analysis. The conclusion says an actual probabilistic PPTL model checker is future work.

- Replication and Abstraction: Symmetry in Automated Formal Verification (2010)
    - what: Explains how process permutations identify equivalent states, and surveys explicit-state, BDD, SAT and probabilistic implementations, symmetry detection, counter abstraction and partially symmetric systems. Bisimilar symmetry quotients preserve CTL* over symmetric atomic propositions [Q1]. Defines group actions on shared and local variables, including process-identity references [Q3], and conditions on transitions, labels and initial states. Explains representative computation and its graph-isomorphism difficulty [Q2]; multiple representatives preserve information while reducing less [Q4]. Develops symbolic orbit-relation difficulties, on-the-fly selection and dynamic reduction [Q5–Q7]. Reviews Murphi, SymmSpin, TopSpin, SMC, ProB, RuleBase, PRISM, GRIP and BOOM. Separates conservative source-level symmetry detection from semantic checking, and compares ordinary quotients with annotated methods for partial symmetry [Q11–Q12].

    - number: Counter state-space bound (n+1)^l is polynomial in n only with l fixed; local variables can make l exponential (§6).

    - limits: Correctness requires a valid symmetry action and invariance of relevant transitions, initial states and atomic propositions. Identity-sensitive variables require moving process slots and renaming referenced identities [Q3]. General representative computation can be expensive [Q2]. Fixed underapproximation in one symbolic method may miss reachable states [Q5]; dynamic canonization guarantees require suitable groups [Q7]. PRISM symmetry declarations were user obligations in the surveyed version [Q8]. Counter abstraction needs a program translation and may suffer local-state explosion [Q9–Q10]. Tool status is historical (2010); no artifacts executed. Symmetry for a fixed instance does not alone prove all process counts [Q14].

- Robust GR(1) liveness robustness (2010)
    - title: Robustness in the Presence of Liveness
    - what: Defines robustness for liveness specifications by requiring a minimum number of system guarantees to remain true as environment assumptions fail. It reduces single and multiple counting requirements to Generalized Reactivity (GR) objectives and gives verification and synthesis algorithms for robust systems. The paper develops concrete robustness measures using dining philosophers, formalizes them as ordered sets of GR(1)-like implications, and shows that disjunctions of conjunctions of Büchi objectives can be exponentially simplified to generalized Büchi objectives. It proves DCB game solving co-NP-complete via a 3SAT reduction, then gives a counter-based construction reducing GR(1) games to one-pair Streett games. The construction preserves winning strategies, extends to GR(k), and yields verification and synthesis complexity bounds; synthesized strategies trade lower runtime for larger memory than Zielonka’s method.
    - number: GR(1) verification O(mn|Q|^2|δ|)
    - number: GR(1) synthesis O(|S||E|(mn)^2)
    - number: GR(k) synthesis O(|S|^k|E|(mn)^{k(k+1)}k!)
    - number: DCB game winning strategy problem co-NP-complete
    - limits: Specifications are finite products of deterministic Büchi automata over input/output signals and robustness is measured by counts of assumptions and guarantees, with a user-supplied total order. The model is reactive infinite-play games; liveness violations cannot be detected finitely, so safety guarantees cannot generally be sacrificed in response to a fairness-assumption violation. DCB-to-generalized-Büchi simplification is exponential and DCB game solving is co-NP-complete. The proposed GR(1) algorithm uses O(|S||E|(mn)^2) time but stores (m+1)(n+1) memory states (or n with an extra strategy computation); GR(k) incurs factorial/exponential factors. No implementation benchmark is reported beyond the worked examples and asymptotic analysis.

- Symbolic Model Checking Data Structures (2010)
    - title: On the size of data structures used in symbolic model checking
    - what: Analyzes whether preprocessing the model or temporal formula can make model checking tractable and proves conditional lower bounds on symbolic state representations. The paper models systems as synchronous or interleaved compositions of finite transition systems, reduces from planning, and uses compilability theory. The reductions establish k-arrow-PSPACE hardness/completeness even when one input part is preprocessed into polynomial space: interleaved model checking remains complete for full LTL and hard for the F fragment, while synchronous variants are hard. A separate state-membership problem shows that a polynomial-size BDD for legal initial states would collapse compilability classes; the argument extends to arbitrary decision diagrams whose evaluation lies in a polynomial-hierarchy level. Thus the worst-case blow-up is representation-independent under standard separation assumptions.

- Termination Analysis with Compositional Transition Invariants (2010)
    - what: Introduces Compositional Termination Analysis (CTA), replacing repeated expensive whole-program safety checks in Binary Reachability Analysis with ranking of loop-free unwindings and a transitivity check on a disjunctively well-founded candidate transition invariant. Increasing unwinding depth and removing already-ranked transitions permits short terminating fragments to yield a global termination argument. §2 defines transition invariants as supersets of transitive reachable transition closure, and disjunctive well-foundedness as finite unions of well-founded relations. §3 observes a transitive disjunctively well-founded relation is well-founded. Lemmas 1/2 accumulate rankings of increasingly deep, not-yet-covered unwindings and allow skipped intermediate depths; the implementation uses powers of two. Algorithm 1 tracks an overapproximation X of reachable states. A failed ranking produces a candidate nontermination precondition C: reachable C establishes nontermination; unreachable C is removed from X. Thus reachability checking remains where ranking fails rather than in every refinement. §4 slices each loop independently, havocs other loops and assignments depending on five or more variables, and uses CBMC symbolic execution to discover paths in loop-free fragments instead of enumerating all of them.
    - number: 87 drivers ×2 configurations =174 driver benchmarks
    - number: matched nontrivial successful BRA baseline: 99 terminating and 45 nonterminating cases
    - number: 3 GHz Xeon; 2 GB memory limit; 2 h per driver
    - number: precise CTA: average speedup 52; up to 3 orders of magnitude; more than 3× analyzed benchmarks at equal precision under the limit
    - limits: Soundness depends on the rank subprocedure returning a disjunctively well-founded superset or a genuine nontermination precondition, and on valid reachability checks. Finite-state nontermination completeness requires a complete rank procedure, unlike the implemented incomplete engine. Per-loop slicing/havoc overapproximates behavior and can lose termination proofs; practical heuristics replace assignments depending on at least five variables. Evaluations compare identical abstracted slices, not untouched drivers. Baseline is selected from BRA-successfully-analyzed, nontrivial loops, so speedup figures are conditional on that subset. Fast variants skip path-precondition checking or all reachability checking, potentially reporting false nontermination outside these benchmarks; the paper reports no precision loss on its measured examples. No scheduler fairness or busy-waiting progress argument is supplied for concurrent programs.
