- Verifying Safety Properties With the TLA+ Proof System (2010)
    - what: FirstpublicTLAPSrelease:hierarchical safety-proof management,backendtranslation/trust and Peterson/Bakery/incompletePaxoscases. # Verifying Safety Properties With the TLA+ Proof System (authored by agents unless marked 🧑)  Kaustuv Chaudhuri, Damien Doligez, Leslie Lamport, and Stephan Merz, IJCAR 2010, LNCS 6173, pp142–148; arXiv:1011.2560v1, 11 November 2010. The venue/pages are confirmed by Stephan Merz's author bibliography: “booktitle = {5th Intl. Joint Conf. Automated Reasoning (IJCAR 2010)}” and “{142-148}” (Q17; complete bibliography block in quotes.json). Read all seven PDF pages, §§1–5.1, acknowledgements and all 15 references; all seven page renders were inspected individually. The paper has no figures, tables, numbered theorems, benchmark suite, or appendix. This is the saved outside-index arxiv_all PDF, whose hash matches the reconstructed 352-path inventory. No author implementation or proof files were executed/imported, and no checkpoint or serialized data was loaded. Consultation and independent review are complete; the IJCAR bibliographic correction was applied. REVIEW.md records scope and root-only checks. The fetched author-hosted PDF has the same extracted body after removing the arXiv margin and declared glyph/spacing differences; author-copy-comparison.json records the comparison. No additional scientific content was inferred from that normalization.  The paper describes the first public TLAPS release, its proof-obligation processing, and three example developments. It directly concerns TLA+ verification of concurrent and distributed systems. Its reported support covers invariance and step simulation but excludes liveness proofs. TLA+ the language can specify liveness; this release's prover cannot establish those properties. These are historical 2010 capabilities, not a statement about today's TLAPS. The authors state: “It handles almost all the non-temporal part of TLA+ as well as the temporal reasoning needed to prove standard safety properties, in particular invariance and step simulation, but not liveness properties” (§1 p1, Q1).  ## Proof representation and what must be trusted  Specifications and proofs share the TLA+ language. A hierarchical proof decomposes a theorem into steps and ultimately leaf obligations, each citing facts and definitions. TLAPM flattens imported/instantiated modules and sends processed leaves to backends. A user can work with incomplete proofs and choose which steps to check; the release uses pragmas to exclude proofs from checking. Thus a successful check of selected leaves does not itself establish completion of every claimed theorem. This completion check is a practical evaluation requirement inferred from the workflow. Q2–Q4 preserve the architecture and selection semantics.  The backend called Isabelle/TLA+ implements the constant fragment as a dedicated Isabelle object logic. The paper explains that embedding into existing HOL/ZF logics was inconvenient because TLA+ is untyped, with no proposition/term distinction. Its single value type, classical first-order logic, equality, conditionals, Hilbert choice, Zermelo–Fränkel set axioms, and primitive function objects supply the mathematical basis. Natural numbers are introduced using a Peano structure whose existence follows from ZF; arithmetic is developed recursively. Tuples/sequences and records are functions, strings are character sequences. Ordinary “typing” facts become proof hypotheses: the paper's n+0=n example needs a numeric n. Boolean conjunction is described as Boolean-valued even on arbitrary arguments. These are semantics/proof-library facts reported by the authors, not a reader audit of the object logic. Q9/Q10 give the details.  Zenon searches for first-order proofs and emits Isabelle/Isar scripts checked against Isabelle/TLA+. The paper explicitly says “Zenon is therefore not part of the trusted code base of TLAPS” (§4.2 p5, Q11). That exclusion applies to this certificate-checking route; it does not make the entire TLAPS pipeline untrusted. TLAPM's priming rewrite engine is expressly trusted. The generic SMT-LIB backend and Cooper Presburger arithmetic backend are expressly non-certifying in this release. “Certifying veriT” is a planned integration even though veriT is already among solvers tried through the generic non-certifying interface. Distinguishing solver brand from integration mode prevents a false claim that all SMT results were certified. Q3/Q5/Q11/Q12 preserve these boundaries.  Backends reason over constant expressions. TLAPM moves primes through ordinary mathematical operators and leaves constants unchanged: (u=v+2c)' becomes u'=v'+2c when u,v are state variables and c is constant. Double priming is rejected by the syntactic analyzer. Defined operators are hidden by default and expand when made usable. Modal operators may fail substitution of equals: knowing u=42 now does not imply u'=42. Reader illustration: a transition from u=42 to u'=43 satisfies the former but violates the latter. Usable non-substitutive definitions are expanded; hidden applications become opaque hashes, conservatively losing some valid equivalences such as O(e∧f)=O(f∧e). This is a stated completeness tradeoff, not a collision/security guarantee or a proof of implementation soundness. Q5/Q6 give the transformation and example.  Positional and labelled references resolve subexpressions before later processing. In O(x,y)=x=20y+2, O(3,4)!2!1 selects 20·4. A label l on y·20 can keep referring to that term after unrelated surrounding syntax changes. The feature supports concise proof reuse, but the paper supplies no maintenance experiment. Default discharge tries Zenon, then Isabelle automation; pragmas can request tactics or other backends, often indirectly via a named standard theorem such as SimpleArithmetic. Q7/Q8 give these cases.  The generic arithmetic route rewrites obligations into SMT-LIB AUFLIRA, often dropping assumptions outside that theory, with conservative sort detection for bound variables. Reader inference: proving a conclusion from fewer assumptions is logically stronger, so omission alone is not a soundness defect; translation and sort handling must still preserve meanings. The paper reports successful use of Yices, CVC3, Z3, veriT, and Alt-Ergo, without solver-specific counts, timings or comparative accuracy. It does not prove the soundness/completeness of these translations in this note. Q12 records the exact scope.  ## Development practice and concrete evidence  The authors first check finite instances with TLC and then attempt proofs. On leaf failure, TLAPM prints usable hypotheses and the goal, expanding usable definitions. Their reported common failure is omission of a needed fact/definition. They split difficult obligations into lower-level assertions, verify the local qed, then prove those assertions in any order. The example case split proves (P1∨…∨Pn)⇒Q by each Pi⇒Q. This is a concrete incremental authoring/debugging workflow, not evidence that partial obligations are sufficient. The Toolbox then only hid proof portions; broader integration was future work, while an Emacs mode provided hierarchical viewing and proof selection. Q13/Q14 preserve this historical distinction.  The authors warn that unchecked “obviously true” assumptions can be wrong and recommend checking such data-structure facts with TLC. Finite model checking can expose counterexamples; it does not universally prove an unbounded assumption. That latter qualification is a reader inference, not a claim that the authors measured assumption-error rates. The claim that specification errors are likelier than TLAPS soundness bugs is also the authors' engineering judgment, with no quantified comparison in this paper. Q3/Q14 carry both source statements.  Section 5.1 gives these author-reported developments, without the actual full proof scripts:  - two-process Peterson mutual exclusion: about 12 PlusCal lines and a proof of about 130 lines - N-process Bakery with atomic reads/writes: an 800-line proof - high-level Paxos: 100 TLA+ specification lines covering a consensus abstraction and two refinements; first refinement completed with a 550-line proof, second mostly proved and estimated to exceed 1,000 lines  The Paxos case is explicitly incomplete, including the acknowledgement to Jean-Baptiste Tristan. The estimated second-proof length is not a measured completed artifact. Neither case length establishes checking time, human time, bug counts, proof coverage across implementations, liveness, or executable-code correctness. The N-process claim concerns the mathematical example as reported, not a finite-N experiment independently rerun here. Q15/Q16 preserve the complete cases.  The library is reported to contain more than 1,400 lemmas/theorems, about 200 pages of pretty-printed Isar. These size measures and the three case descriptions support feasibility of the release; no theorem about the verifier itself, controlled user study, performance comparison, memory result, automated success rate or systematic experiment is supplied. The full development files and checker outputs were not inspected/reproduced in this reading. “It has not turned out to be difficult once the proof idea has been understood” is an author experience report, rather than a measured proof-automation guarantee (§5.1 p7, Q16).  For the database, this is direct foundational evidence for high-level safety proofs and TLA+ proof tooling. It contributes explicit trust distinctions, partial-proof management, priming/substitution pitfalls, finite-model-checking practice, and a deliberately incomplete Paxos case. It has no Verus, verified Rust, or LLM experiment. A proposed use as an evaluation reference for proof agents is reader inference: record the precise theorem and unchecked assumptions, require every obligation, distinguish certificate-checked from trusted solver routes, and report whether the intended specification captures the requirement.

    - title: Formal Methods: Practice and Experience
    - what: Survey of industrial formal-methods practice combining a new questionnaire covering 62 projects, earlier surveys, eight highlighted industrial project families, and proposals for reusable verification experiments in the Verified Software Repository. The new survey collected structured questionnaires November 2007–December 2008; 56 project reports came from involved individuals and six from literature. Reports application areas, size bands, techniques, expertise/training, perceived time/cost/quality effects and intentions to reuse. Compares model-checking uptake across decades using Fisher exact tests. Discussion favors choosing rigor by component/property, robust supported tools, familiar design-language interfaces, and integration with existing development processes. Defines path probability measures, probabilistic temporal logics PCTL/CSL and expected rewards; explains graph preprocessing, linear-equation solving and CTMC uniformisation, then presents PRISM and three cited applications. - Probabilistic symbolic model checking with PRISM: a hybrid approach (2004)
    - what: The authors address the main weakness of pure MTBDD probabilistic model checking: transition matrices can remain compact while iterative solution vectors lose regularity, gain many distinct values, and become large and slow. Their hybrid PRISM engine keeps the probabilistic transition structure symbolic but stores the numerical iteration vector explicitly in an array, aiming for sparse-matrix-like numerical speed without sparse-matrix model-storage cost. The paper gives the implementation mechanism. Matrix-vector multiplication is performed by recursively traversing the MTBDD and extracting each nonzero matrix entry once. To avoid array slots for unreachable encoded states, it introduces offset-labelled MTBDDs: nodes carry row/column offsets counting reachable states; redundant-level removal is restricted so offsets remain available; node merging is optional where different reachability patterns require different offsets. The structure is constructed from an ordinary MTBDD before numerical solution by restoring skipped levels and computing offsets from a BDD for reachable states. An optimization replaces all nodes at a chosen MTBDD level by cached explicit sparse submatrices; the highest level fitting a 1024 KB storage cap is chosen. The same idea extends to MDPs through several matrix-vector products per iteration. The authors also identify a method restriction: ordinary Gauss-Seidel needs row/column access not provided by one recursive traversal; they point to a block Gauss-Seidel variant. No new general formal correctness theorem is proved in the supplied text; the main evidence is algorithmic explanation plus experiments.

- Scalable Distributed On-the-Fly Symbolic Model Checking (2000)
    - what: Combines BDD-based, breadth-first on-the-fly checking of RCTL safety properties with distributed reachability and memory balancing. Saves each breadth-first frontier in slices across processes, then cooperatively reconstructs a counterexample without gathering an entire frontier on one process. Starts sequentially until a memory threshold, partitions ownership, exchanges newly reached states with their owners and detects distributed termination or an error. Rebalancing can change each process's slice between iterations; correctness relies on the slices jointly covering the sequential frontier. During counterexample generation, processes extend a suffix backward locally, then broadcast a longest suffix and resume. Section 3.3 derives ways to reduce intermediate BDD memory: restrict transition partitions to the current frontier slice or once to the union of a process's saved slices, use simplify-assuming, and substitute a singleton target directly for next-state variables. Appendix A explains regular expressions describing finite bad computations and their reduction to reachability of a monitoring automaton.

- CoMuS hierarchical modular verification (2021)
    - title: Modular Verification of Concurrent Programs via Sequential Model Checking
    - what: CoMuS checks concurrent safety by iteratively generating sequential verification tasks for individual threads and their abstract environments. The main thread calls an initially havocing env_move function. A counterexample triggers an environment reachability query: infeasible interference refines env_move; feasible suffixes produce earlier promises of error as assertions. The environment uses try_start to represent reachable noninitial computations. Multiple threads are handled recursively in a chosen hierarchy. Termination is proved for finite variable domains, while progress alone is claimed for infinite domains.
    - number: Implementation uses Python 3.5, pycparser, SeaHorn and Z3. Dynamic-programming tests use a 3,600s timeout; chain/ring tests use 1,200s. Reordering the last two threads in long_th3_safe raises reported time from 10 to 25 seconds. Numeric figure cells not recoverable from extracted text were not inferred.
    - limits: Sequentially consistent shared memory, fixed thread count and a restricted C subset. The prototype lacks dynamic thread creation and alias analysis. Performance depends on an order matching the program's dependency hierarchy; the authors report other tools usually outperform it on their supported general SV-COMP subset. Full proofs are linked separately rather than supplied here.
    - how much was read: parts read

Causal analysis marks atomic propositions relevant to violation; highlighting/filtering and debugger-style stepping connect these components. The user study asks participants to diagnose system errors, edit a formula and find a violation in a larger trace pair.

The larger study case omits graph view because of system size. Causal explanation supports understanding of a returned counterexample, rather than proving the visual interface or every system correct. Tool execution and figures were not independently inspected.

- Equilibria-based probabilistic model checking (2019)
    - title: Equilibria-Based Probabilistic Model Checking for Concurrent Stochastic Games.
    - what: Extends rPATL and PRISM-games to synthesize subgame-perfect social-welfare-optimal Nash equilibria for two coalitions with distinct probabilistic or reward objectives. Finite-horizon objectives use recursive game solution; infinite-horizon objectives use approximate epsilon-equilibria and value iteration. Bimatrix equilibria are encoded through labelled polytopes and enumerated with Z3, with dominated-strategy filtering. The modeling language permits joint action-dependent updates and rewards.
    - number: Table 1 includes an Aloha model with 2,308,349 states and 10,362,711 transitions, and a robot model with 389,377 states and 27,267,419 transitions. Authors report under-two-hour solutions for their examples, while choice-dense models are limited to tens of thousands of states. Experiments use a 2.10GHz Xeon and 16GB RAM.
    - limits: Infinite-horizon probability queries exclude nonterminal end components; reward targets must be reached almost surely under every strategy profile. Without these conditions the presented value iteration need not converge. The coalition-based result is not an unrestricted multi-player Nash solver. Model size alone does not determine runtime: many per-state choices make local equilibrium solving expensive. Appendix convergence proofs and code were not reread.
    - how much was read: parts read
    - [source](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-30942-8_19)

    - limits: The argument is handwritten. The deployed Pacemaker is not machine-checked. The chained variant needs two consecutive correct leaders, and its liveness argument is omitted for brevity. Completing in a single view does not establish that this view is eventually selected (an inference).

    - what: Extends ESBMC-GPU with CUDA neural-library operational models and incremental bounded model checking for neuron-coverage conditions and adversarial inputs. Operational models approximate cuBLAS/cuDNN behavior for symbolic verification. Coverage assertions encode sign/value changes across neurons and input pairs; a nondeterministic image constrained by a distance bound searches for changed classifications. The experiments distinguish fast coverage checks from expensive bit-accurate adversarial search.

The displayed experiment command disables division-by-zero, pointer and bounds checks, so these runs cannot establish general CUDA memory safety. Direct tool comparison was limited by compatibility issues.

- A formal semantics for concurrent systems (1979)
    - what: Formalizes extended semaphore primitives using vector firing sequences and sketches a concurrency-preserving translation from bounded semaphore programs into COSY, a path/process notation for concurrent-system behavior. Available body pages introduce cyclic COSY paths/processes with sequencing, exclusive choice and iteration; distinguish identically named operations in separate processes; and represent histories using component sequences. Defines atomic pe operations requiring specified semaphores positive and other specified semaphores zero before simultaneous decrements, and ve operations incrementing selected semaphores. ESP programs are cyclic sequential processes without jumps or conditionals and use ESPs as their only synchronization. An inductive semantics tracks process histories, semaphore histories and integer valuations. Bounded semaphore behavior is encoded by finite COSY paths, with a replicator macro for repeated structure; semaphore tests/increments/decrements are replaced by corresponding program-operation choices. A second reader-writer example is translated, with maximum semaphore values w, r and 1 for w writers/r readers. A theorem states equality of vector-firing-sequence sets and valuation functions, with an induction proof sketch. An unbounded extension discusses infinite counters, directed limits and possible domain/fixed-point constructions rather than giving a completed construction.
    - number: Newcastle Technical Report132, April1979;16 physical scan pages.
    - number: Available body printed pages1–3 and6–14; printed4–5 absent.
    - number: Reader-writer example maximum A,R,M semaphore values: w,r,1.
    - limits: Recovered source is Newcastle University Technical Report 132, April 1979, with a cover saying to appear in Kyoto proceedings August 1978. DOI metadata identifies the same title/authors as a 1979 LNCS chapter pp.571–584; this scan is a report version, not demonstrated identical to the published chapter. All 16 supplied PDF images were viewed, but the scan skips printed pages 4–5: physical page7 is printed3 and physical8 is printed6. Missing pages include part of the COSY/VFS definitions. Thus this is a reading of the complete available scan, not a complete-paper reading. PDF text extraction supplies no usable body text; quotations are manual selected-passage transcriptions. Mathematical syntax/proof details were visually read where available, but not independently checked, mechanized or executed. The bounded translation is for a restricted semaphore-only coordination language, not arbitrary concurrent programs; its proof is explicitly a sketch. Unbounded completion is speculative in this report. No performance, industrial-scale validation or automatic verification tool is supplied.

- Watase STIRLIN1 Stirling formula 2025 (2025)
    - title: A Formal Proof of Stirling s Formula.
    - what: FORMALIZED MATHEMATICS Vol. 33, No. 1, pp.
    - limits: MML STIRLIN1 version8.1.15 5.95.1495 identifies the Mizar formalization. Target is the limit of n! divided by n^(n+1/2)e^-n, namely sqrt(2pi), not a numeric finite-n error bound or complexity result (pp.95,101). Definition2 calls f class C1 on a nonempty closed interval A only if f is differentiable throughout(-1,infinity), its derivative restricted there is continuous, and A is contained in that half-line which is contained in dom f. This is stronger than the ordinary statement f continuously differentiable just on[0,1]. Introduction’s prose references Def3 for C1, but actual predicate is Def2; Def3 is the restricted derivative (pp.96–97). D[01](n)=EqDiv([0,1],n+1) avoids a zero denominator at natural index0. Theorem1 identifies each cell[(k-1)/(n+1),k/(n+1)] for k in Seg(n+1); Theorems2/3 give mesh1/(n+1), nonzero and tending0. Truncated subtraction appears in formal natural-number indexing (pp.96–97). Definitions5/6 form upper/lower derivative values on each closed cell, and Definitions7/8 average them. Under C1, derivative continuity on compact cells supplies finite extrema and Riemann integrability. Theorem4 applies the fundamental theorem of calculus to f(b)-f(x0); Theorems5–8 sandwich that difference between cell derivative infimum/supremum times(b-x0) (pp.97–98). Definitions9/10 separately integrate a constant right-endpoint value and -f on each cell. Step(f,n) lists f(i/(n+1)); SumStep sums these; nIntegral(n)=(n+1) integral(-f); WSeq is their sum. Thus WSeq(n)=sum_i f(i/(n+1))-(n+1) integral f, with the integral subtraction occurring once (pp.98–99). Theorem10 states lim WSeq=one-half integral_0^1 f_prime. Intended squeeze: integrating each cell’s derivative bounds gives a factor one-half of cellwidth², summing and multiplying by n+1 bounds WSeq between one-half the lower/upper Riemann sums for f_prime; both approach the same integral. This derivation explains the displayed infrastructure, but the full Theorem10 proof is not printed (pp.97–99). For log(1+x),(-1,infinity) guarantees1+x>0; Theorems11–13 establish differentiability and derivative1/(1+x). Theorem14 differentiates(1+x)ln(1+x)-x; Theorem15 gives integral_0^1 ln(1+x)=ln(4/e)=2ln2-1. Theorems16/17 give integral of its derivative ln2 and WSeq limit(ln2)/2 (pp.99–100). Definition15 Step(f,m) is a zero-indexed sequence f(i/m) for m nonzero. Theorems18/19 convert its finite restriction to the leading f(0) followed by step(f,m-1); log(1+0)=0 removes that term in Theorem20. This connects library finite sums and sequences without silently changing the number of samples (pp.100–101). Theorems21/22 express WSeq for log(1+x) as ln A_m, A_m=(2m)!/m! times(e/(4m))^m for m=n+1. Factorials and e are positive, so continuity of exp converts limit ln A_m=(ln2)/2 into A_m→sqrt2, stated as convergent WStirl in Theorem23. No gamma-function construction is required (pp.100–101). Stirling ratio B_m=A_m/C_m with C_m=sqrt(m)(2m)!/(4^m(m!)²). Introduction identifies C_m as the square root of a Wallis product sequence and imports C_m→1/sqrt(pi) from Theorem51 of[12]. Nonzero limit justifies division to obtain sqrt(2pi). Theorem24 is labeled a consequence of23, but the Wallis dependency is essential and explained in the introduction, not re-proved here (pp.96,101). One erroneous summation and one potentially confusing notation occur on p.96: the displayed log application puts -n integral inside summation braces (subtracting it n times), while Lemma1/WSeq correctly subtract it once. The ratio denominator sqrt(n)(2n)!/(4^n(n!)²) is algebraically correct. Its identification as the square root of a Wallis-product sequence depends on that cited sequence’s definition; no second error is established. The intended factorial identity and Theorems21–24 are recorded, not the repeated-integral expression. Definition17 defines StirlSeq on natural indices including0; the classical ratio description is for positive n. A finite initial-index convention does not affect its limit, but the PDF does not discuss evaluation of0^(1/2) or division at0. No finite-n numerical approximation guarantee follows just from the limiting theorem (p.101). Introduction mentions HOL Light, Rocq, Isabelle, Metamath and Lean versions; these are related-work claims, not a measured comparison here. References include an explicit HOL Light source link and Isabelle AFP entry; those developments and Wallis source are not independently read in this record. PDF has no proof-size/check-time statistics, experiments, checker transcript or artifact run (pp.95,101–102). Exact quotations preserve raw PDF extraction including broken fraction/exponent ordering, the U+0016 restriction glyph and extracted inequality symbols. Renderings govern formula interpretations. Eight pages,17definitions,24numberedtheorems,14references and all supplied sketches read. No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM proof/specification-agent evaluation.

- Watase WALLIS01 integral and product 2025 (2025)
    - title: Formalization of Wallis Infinite Product Formula for π and the Wallis Integral
    - what: FORMALIZED MATHEMATICS Vol. 33, No. 1, pp.
    - limits: MML WALLIS01 version8.1.15 5.95.1495. The Introduction describes an elementary-calculus route toward Stirling, citing other proof assistants without proof-size, speed or automation comparisons. Stirling’s full formula is motivation rather than a theorem established in this paper (pp.85–86). Result1 gives 0<sin x<1 for 0<x<π/2; result2 gives x^m<x^n for natural n<m and 0<x<1, allowing n=0; result3 requires n≥1 and 0<x<π/2 for adjacent sine-power inequalities. Results42–43 later separate strict inequalities inside the interval from weak integral inequalities over the closed interval; endpoints are not silently covered by the strict premise (pp.87,92–93). Definition1 even-seq(m) permits m=0; Definition2 odd-seq(m) and subsequent product recurrences/formulas require positive m. Results4–13 track domains Seg n, lengths, positivity, monotonicity, restrictions and append operations. Results7 and12 duplicate the even-product recurrence as printed. Results8/11 explicitly give the first three even/odd lists (pp.87–88). Results14/15 prove product even-seq(k)=2^k k! and product odd-seq(k)=(2k)!/(2^k k!) for k≥1 by induction. No empty odd-sequence convention is used for these statements (p.88). Definitions3/4 use the same @ notation in both directions between a real-valued function on A and an element of RAlgebra A; @@ reduces back to the original object. Results16–22 reconcile pointwise multiplication, scalar action, addition, negation and subtraction. This is representation infrastructure, not approximation of functions (p.89). Result23 is the power successor law in a unital associative nonempty multiplicative magma. Result24 proves continuity of natural powers of a continuous total real function. Result25 identifies pointwise powers at positive values;26 covers a zero value for positive exponent. These printed pointwise statements do not claim the same arbitrary-real evaluation lemma for negative base values (pp.89–90). Result27 requires an open Z and a differentiable total real function, with positive exponent. Results28/29 obtain continuity of restrictions, integrability and boundedness on a nonempty closed interval, also after multiplication by an arbitrary real scalar. Result30 handles sin-power endpoints0 andπ/2 for positive exponent; zero exponent has its separate integral base case35 (pp.90–91). Result31 gives derivative of sin^(n+1) for n≥1. - Formalizing the Cholesky Factorization Theorem (2024)
    - what: Reports ACL2(r) proof that, for square symmetric A satisfying recursive positive-definite-p, the lower triangular part L of chol(A) obeys L L^T=A. Uses L as a witness for a Skolemized existence theorem. Develops partitioned-matrix support and a Schur-complement recognizer structurally aligned with chol to guide induction/rewrite automation. The bridge from this recognizer to ordinary quantified positive definiteness is justified informally in the paper, not established by a displayed machine theorem; floating-point backward-error/stability verification remains future work. Tracks exact theorem predicates, executable-versus-logical square-root distinction, totalization/guards, unchanged upper triangle, source-level witness and auxiliary hints. Records informal-equivalence boundary, a false printed determinant identity, proof-resource measurements and absence of a verified approximation/error theorem for chol-exec. These details prevent conflating an exact logical decomposition proof with floating-point numerical safety.
    - limits: Real square symmetric input is intended. Standard positive definiteness means v^T A v>0 for every nonzero compatible realv; the formal theorem instead assumes positive-definite-p(A), symmetry and equal row/column counts. Its recursive recognizer excludes nonmatrices/nonreal or nonpositive pivots, accepts the empty matrix and descends through rank-one Schur complements. The paper’s introductory phrase about positivity of diagonals of principal submatrices must be read as positivity of successive Schur pivots, not merely positive original diagonal entries. Partition A=[[α,a12^T],[a21,A22]]. Set λ=sqrtα>0, l=a21/λ, recursively factor S=A22−l l^T. chol stores updated diagonal/lower column and recursively processed trailing block while retaining original upper rowa12; therefore chol(A) itself is generally not lower triangular. Correct output factor is get-L(chol(A)). The equality proof uses symmetry a12=a21 to recover off-diagonal blocks and align recognizer and algorithm updates. ACL2 logical functions are total. Program1 returns an empty matrix for nonmatrix input, unchanged empty input, or same-dimension zero matrix for nonreal/nonpositive pivot. It handles nonsquare row/column cases for logic admission even though useful correctness is restricted. Program1 execution guards require matrixp, squareness and symmetry; they do not themselves assert positive definiteness. Guard checking is not a proof that arbitrary input is SPD. Logic/execution split uses mbe; equivalence must hold under verified guards. mbt is logically its argument but evaluates as true in runtime mode once guards justify skipping the check. The declaration’s dimension measure decreases through the trailing block. This is a functional list representation, not a demonstrated C/Rust memory-safety/in-place destructive-update proof. - Towards Solid Abelian Groups: A Formal Proof of Nöbeling’s Theorem (2024)
    - what: Formalizes in Lean4/Mathlib that the integer module of locally constant maps from any profinite space S to Z is free. Since Z is discrete this is the group C(S,Z) of continuous maps. Constructs a basis by well-ordering all clopen coordinates, selecting finite Boolean coordinate products not generated by earlier products, proving spanning through finite quotients and proving independence by ordinal induction. Supplies a detailed mathematical exposition and explains implementation choices and integration into Mathlib. Reconstructs the Boolean-product basis, spanning argument, exact sequence and three ordinal cases; tracks fixed ambient coordinates, closed-cover pasting contracts and well-founded recursion. Separates the proved profinite special case from the original bounded-function theorem and future structural results for solid condensed groups. Records actual final Lean statement and noncomputable basis, targeted pinned-source scope, qualitative code-size reports and lack of experimental comparison.
    - limits: Profinite means totally disconnected, compact and Hausdorff. No finite/countable or nonempty assumption on S. Integers carry the discrete topology. A free Z-module means a basis giving unique finite integer linear combinations; it is an algebraic assertion, not freeness as a topological group. Original Nöbeling theorem concerns bounded integer-valued functions on any set; this paper formalizes the profinite continuous-function special case, not that stronger statement. Any profinite S embeds as a closed subset of Bool^I by indicators of all clopen subsets. Total separation gives injectivity; continuity and compact-to-Hausdorff give closed embedding. A well-order on I uses classical choice. The basis is noncomputable; neither the theorem nor proof is an algorithm to enumerate a basis for an arbitrary profinite input. Products P are finite strictly decreasing lists in I, ordered lexicographically; empty product is1. eval multiplies 0/1 coordinate indicators. E(S) consists of products whose evaluations are outside the Z-span of all earlier evaluations. This greedy definition alone does not guarantee independence for arbitrary Z-generators; special Boolean geometry and ordinal argument establish it here. Projection πJ preserves coordinates in J and zeroes the rest, with source and target the same full product Bool^I. It does not change coordinate type to J. SJ is its image. Precomposition C(SJ,Z)→C(S,Z) is injective because the projection onto its image is surjective. Good products on SJ cannot contain a coordinate outside J, since their evaluation would be0. Spanning: P is well-ordered, so induction eliminates a non-good product through earlier products. S is the cofiltered limit of its images SJ for finite J; bijectivity uses separation by individual coordinates and directed closed compact nonempty fibers, with generalized Cantor intersection. Every continuous map into discrete Z factors through a finite quotient. Finite point-delta functions are products of ei or(1−ei), whose expansions are integer combinations of P. Ordinal induction fixes I throughout and proves independence, separately from already proved spanning. Predicate Q(μ) quantifies over all closed S⊆Bool^I with every true coordinate index<μ, for μ≤the order type of I. Merely saying E(S) is a basis while changing I does not specify the induction hypothesis used by this proof. The author identifies that ambiguity in earlier informal exposition. Zero case: S supported below0 is empty or the singleton false vector. Empty S yields the zero module and empty good-product basis; singleton yields the empty product1 as its basis. For a limit μ every finite product is supported below some μ′<μ, so E(Sμ) is a directed union of earlier good products; injective pullbacks preserve independence and directed unions of independent subsets are independent. Successor μ+1: split S by μ-coordinate into S0/S1 and put S′=S0∩πμ(S1), supported belowμ. Define g(f)(x)=f(x with coordinateμ set1)−f(x with coordinateμ set0). The sequence0→C(Sμ,Z)→C(S,Z)→C(S′,Z) is left exact: first map injective and its image is ker g. No terminal0 or surjectivity of g is claimed/needed. Kernel factorization pastes the restrictions on closed sets S0 and πμ(S1), agreeing on their intersection. Good products split into old E(Sμ) and new products startingμ. For newp, g(eval p)=eval(tail p) on S′. Contraposition plus exactness/spanning shows tail p is good on S′; the tail map on products startingμ is injective. Independence on both sides and the commutative left-exact diagram imply independence of the combined family. Printed Lemma38 defers its case proof to linked Lean, rather than giving all proof steps on paper. Lean Products I is a subtype of lists satisfying Chain′(>); adjacency plus transitivity yields strict decrease. GoodProducts.isGood tests nonmembership in Submodule.span of earlier evaluations. The final source combines GoodProducts.linearIndependent with GoodProducts.span through Basis.mk, then transports freeness across the clopen-coordinate closed embedding. LocallyConstant.piecewise pastes maps on two closed sets covering the whole ambient space, assuming agreement on the intersection and decidable membership. Variant piecewise′ allows C0⊆C1∪C2 with all sets in one ambient X and returns a map on C0. This avoids recasting the fixed Boolean ambient space as a nested subtype during induction. Printed isLocallyConstant:=omitted abbreviates exposition; it is not evidence of an admitted theorem in source. Paper links pin Mathlib commit ba9f2e5baab51310883778e1ea3b48772581521c. Saved the entire Nobeling.lean file at this immutable URL, but only introduction, relevant definitions and final proof sections were read. No dependency audit, admission/axiom audit, archive equivalence check, build or kernel execution performed. Nobeling_aux has an inhabited-coordinate context; final coordinates are clopen sets, inhabited by the empty clopen even when S is empty. Solid condensed group motivation is a future application. Define Z[S]^solid=lim Z[Si] over finite quotients; solid A means every map from free condensed Z[S] to A uniquely extends along Z[S]→Z[S]^solid. Combining discreteness characterization with Nöbeling gives a product-of-Z structural result in the mathematics, but paper says Lean3 supporting code must still be ported to Lean4 before formalizing that result in Mathlib. Do not credit this paper with a completed Lean4 solid-group construction. These are qualitative code-size comparisons with differing boundaries, not controlled measurements of effort/performance. Author calls comparison with full expanded §4 fairer. - Formalization of a Stochastic Approximation Theorem (2022)
    - what: Classical Coq formalization of regular and extended real-valued Dvoretzky stochastic-approximation convergence theorems, using the Derman–Sacks proof. A conditional-mean-zero noise process with summable second moments converges almost surely under a drift bound with vanishing error, summable multiplicative slack and divergent cumulative decrease. Supporting infrastructure includes general probability spaces, almost-everywhere reasoning, expectations, Lp spaces, conditional expectations and filtrations. Records every main theorem hypothesis, deterministic versus stochastic drift and nonmeasurable auxiliary controls, pointwise versus almost-sure assumptions, proof dependence on conditional-expectation factorization, du Bois-Reymond weighted-series lemma, Borel–Cantelli/Chebyshev and a deterministic backward-iteration argument. Preserves actual classical axioms, library representation choices and the distinction between mathematical applications and completed algorithm formalization.
    - limits: §2 Theorem4: Probability space(Ω,F,P), increasing filtration Fn⊆F, Fn-adapted real Xn, measurable deterministic history function Tn:R^n→R, noise Wn measurable at time n+1 and Xn+1=Tn(history)+Wn. Noise has E[Wn|Fn]=0 almost surely and sum E[Wn²]<∞. Noise need not be independent across times. Each second moment must be finite in the inspected formal source. §2 Theorem4: Fixed real target x*, nonnegative real sequences αn,βn,γn with αn→0,sumβn finite,sumγn=+∞. Drift condition for all histories:|Tn(history)−x*|≤max(αn,(1+βn)|xn−x*|−γn). Conclusion is Xn→x*almost surely, not just in probability, and not a finite-time bound, convergence rate or numeric implementation guarantee. §2 Theorem5/§4.2: Tn may be stochastic with its realized process Fn-adapted; α/β/γ become Ω→R functions and their limit/sum hypotheses hold almost surely. They are not required to be Fn-measurable; footnote6 says that original revisited-paper assumption was unused. Final source still assumes nonnegativity and the drift bound pointwise for all n,ω, while only asymptotic limit/sum conditions are almost sure. Do not weaken every source premise to almost everywhere merely because §4.2 uses that phrase broadly. Inspected source Results: Regular history map is vector R n→R with measurable-vector premise; extended map is(vector R n×Ts)→R and requires adaptedness of realized T. Both final corollaries construct X from X0,T,W and assume adapted X; H16 bounds only realized T′n(ω),X′n(ω), a weaker sufficient condition than the paper’s all-histories presentation. vector refers to the list of scalar history values, not a multidimensional/Hilbert-valued convergence theorem. §4.2: Alternative bound|max drift|≤max(αn,(1+βn−γn)|xn−x*|) is also formalized with remaining hypotheses intact, using an Abel-type rescaling of divergent positive series. This is a separate convenient corollary, not an unconditional relaxation of every standard drift condition. §3.1: pre_events are predicates Ts→Prop; sigma algebras close under countable union/complement/fullspace; events package membership proofs in a dependent pair. Probability spaces use nonnegative countably additive measures with mass1. Borel generation by half-open intervals/open sets is proved equivalent; generated sigma algebra intersection and inductive closure are equivalent so proofs can use induction. §3.2: almost P means P contains a measurable event of probability1, so P itself need not be measurable. almostR2 lifts an arbitrary binary relation and inherits suitable order properties. This definition is relevant to auxiliary control functions without measurability hypotheses; it does not silently assume a completed measure space. §3.3: Expectation is built from finite-range and nonnegative functions, then positive/negative parts. option Rbar distinguishes undefined infinity differences(None),finite expectations and signed infinity. The library extends Coquelicot limits to extended-real-valued sequences using coinciding inf/sup limits, avoiding direct use of a uniform-space filter construction. FiniteExpectation packages well-defined finite values to simplify side conditions. §3.4: Quotient random variables by almost-everywhere equality so the norm is definite. Paper reports Lp module/Banach results and Hilbert structure for L2. It prints IsLp with real exponent n and also mentions p=∞; no independent source inspection of the infinity endpoint was made. Extensionality and choice principles listed in footnote7 support the quotient; this is not an axiom-free constructive library. §3.5: Conditional expectation first has an indicator-integral universal property, uniqueness only almost everywhere, linearity/tower/factor-out/monotonicity/Jensen. Existence starts with L2 orthogonal projection using the Lax–Milgram Hilbert library, chooses an equivalence-class representative, approximates nonnegative L1 functions with min(f,n), and takes a limit. A wrapper adjusts null-set representatives to make simple properties exact where possible. §3.5: General conditional-expectation function can be defined broadly but the defining universal property is proved only for nonnegative or finite-expectation functions; an arbitrary signed nonintegrable function is not automatically covered. FiniteConditionalExpectation returns real values under finite-expectation premises. The paper reports contraction on Lp and L2-loss minimization, not executable sampling or an algorithm for evaluating conditional expectations. §§3.6–3.8: Filtrations/adaptedness encode available history. Library begins martingale theory but does not claim every martingale theorem. Finite-range value lists may contain duplicates/extraneous values. General random variables are supported, but product-space constructions and monotone convergence are limited to probability measures; general measure theory is only partial groundwork. §4.1: du Bois-Reymond lemma for nonnegative an:sum an converges iff some positive bn→∞ has sum an bn finite. Existing proofs assumed strictly positive terms or an unavailable integral test; formal proof handles zero terms/cases and uses a Rudin exercise. This supplies a vanishing threshold α with sum E[Wn²]/αn² finite, not an extra original noise assumption. §4.1: Center target at0 and set Zn=Wn sign(Tn). Measurability/adaptedness and conditional-mean-zero factor-out give the orthogonality needed for a Loève series theorem; summable second moments imply sum Zn converges almost surely. Chebyshev+Borel–Cantelli give eventual |Zn|≤αn. Then |Xn+1|≤max(2αn,(1+βn)|Xn|+Zn−γn) eventually almost surely. §4.1 Lemma8: Nonnegative a,b,c,ξ; a→0,sumb finite,sumc divergent,sumδ convergent(δ need not be nonnegative); eventual ξn+1≤max(an,(1+bn)ξn+δn−cn) implies ξ→0. Proof iterates backward, uses finite products/list maxima and Abel descending convergence. A separate random exceptional set must be removed before applying this deterministic pathwise statement. Classical assumptions: Coq standard real-number axioms, functional/propositional extensionality and constructive definite description(unique choice) for quotienting are explicitly reported; proof also invokes constructive indefinite description for a classical sequence case split. Similar names do not mean computationally constructive extraction. No complete transitive axiom audit or independent compilation was performed. §1 examples are motivation: sample mean, deterministic contraction/Bellman iteration and SGD/root estimation illustrate mathematical applicability. The formal main result is scalar and conditional. Q-learning convergence is explicitly future work in §6; no completed distributed RL implementation, verified optimizer executable, machine learning experiment or asymptotic rate is evaluated. §1 Example3 claims differentiation commutes with expectation because it is linear, even while the sampling distribution may depend on x. Linearity alone is insufficient: differentiating an x-dependent measure adds a term, and exchanging derivative/integral needs regularity. Thus this motivation does not establish arbitrary SGD convergence; the abstract theorem still requires its own drift/noise assumptions. - Mechanising Complexity Theory: The Cook-Levin Theorem in Coq (2021)
    - what: Coq formalization of polynomial-time computability, NP, reductions and Cook–Levin using weak call-by-value lambda calculus L as a concrete cost model. Proves SAT and3SAT NP-complete through a chain from a generic L bounded-halting problem, heap machine and Turing-machine problems, covering-card tableaux, binary tableaux, Boolean formulas and Tseitin CNF. All reduction functions and their runtime/output-size bounds are implemented and analyzed in L, even though TMs are intermediate objects. Records why output-size bounds are separate from beta-step bounds, admissible bounded-halting inputs and why they repair the one-sided compiler-time argument, the actual versus expositional reduction factorization, overlapping-card soundness/completeness and polarity invariants, flat encodings and two-stage correspondence proofs, exact reported proof effort, concrete SAT-verifier resource analysis, printed formula discrepancies and the formal certificate bound checked in official coqdoc.
    - limits: §§2–3: Constructive Coq type theory; finite alphabets mean decidable equality plus exhaustive enumeration. L is untyped weak call-by-value with de Bruijn indices and Scott encodings. Its uniformly confluent reduction makes every terminating path have the same beta-step count. Encodings determine the size model, so unary and binary arithmetic cannot be interchanged silently. §3 Definitions1–2: Polynomial boundedness uses a monotone polynomial majorant. Polynomial-time computability requires both a polynomial beta-step bound and polynomial encoded result size. The latter is explicit because L can construct exponentially large terms in few steps; it is required to make composition and comparison with TMs sound. §3 Definitions3–6: NP uses a polynomial-time decidable verifier relation with soundness and existence of a polynomially bounded certificate. The verifier need not reject oversized certificates; completeness promises a short one. Certificates are L terms; a generalized introduction permits other injectively encoded certificate types with polynomial-time decoding. Many-one reductions preserve yes/no equivalence, not merely a forward implication. Printed Definition4,p5 has a self-bound: size(enc y)≤f(size(enc y)), rather than an input-size bound. Official coqdoc polyCertRel.complete__pCR instead uses size(enc y)≤p__pCR(size(enc x)); this resolves the paper typo without inferring an artifact defect. The complete NP coqdoc file was read; it is source-text evidence, not an independent kernel check. §1/§8: Existing polynomial-time L/TM simulations justify equivalence of complexity classes mathematically, as the abstract says. However, §8 explicitly leaves mechanizing agreement of this NP definition with a TM-based NP definition to future work. Do not claim that equivalence theorem is mechanized in this paper. §§4–5: Generic inputs include program, unary certificate bound k and unary time bound t. The GenNP subtype restricts programs to closed abstractions and admissibility: whenever any certificate halts, some certificate within k halts; any halting certificate run finishes within t. Analogous restrictions apply to the multi-tape problem. The NP-hardness reduction constructs instances satisfying these conditions. §5: The actual mechanization factors GenNP→LMGenNP→mTMGenNP, with a structure-sharing heap machine and linear overhead. Footnote4 says the exposition instead separates a TM evaluator directly as a better factorization. CheckCert translates arbitrary guessed tapes into Boolean-list encodings and invalid encodings diverge; EvalL is a fixed interpreter, not a per-input compiled machine. §5: Multi-to-single compilation supplies an upper runtime bound and halting preservation. A short compiled run alone does not bound the original run. Admissibility supplies existence of a short certificate and the original time bound, allowing the reverse implication. The prose accidentally uses k/k′ for runtime in pp9–10; the definitions consistently assign k to certificate size and t to time. §§2,6.1: TM tapes have no distinguished blank symbol and use optional current symbols. Tableau encoding adds blank, delimiter and state/head symbols. The state symbol stays at the string center; moving the head shifts the whole tape representation. Uniform polarity tags enforce a common shift. §6.1 redefines k:=|in|+k_cert, the combined fixed-input and certificate-size bound. Thus z=k+t=|in|+k_cert+t, with two additional blanks per side; tableau width is O(|in|+k_cert+t). §6.1: Covering cards constrain every overlapping width3 window of each adjacent pair of rows. This differs from applying a single rewrite rule at one position. General CC permits card width ω, offset o, and final substrings. Binary conversion uses codes of length |Σ|, not logarithmic codes. Each binary cell becomes a Boolean variable, and initial/card/final gadgets are conjoined. §6.1 Theorems14–16: For a represented configuration with |tp|<z and a TM step, there is a unique CC successor representing that step. Initial tape length≤k, where §6.1 uses k=|in|+k_cert, and step bound t establish completeness and soundness of bounded runs. Halting-configuration replication pads runs that halt before t to exactly t covering steps. A separate nondeterministic prelude guesses the certificate using a disjoint alphabet. §§4,6.2–6.3: Tseitin conversion avoids exponential CNF distribution. SAT NP membership is proved by a polynomial-time assignment verifier; the paper omits its full correctness proof. Footnote8 strengthens the result to3SAT. - Learning dynamic polynomial proofs (2019)
    - what: DQN selects elementary polynomial inference steps, building a small set of nonnegative lemmas. A linear program combines those lemmas into an upper-bound certificate. A permutation-invariant polynomial embedding supports transfer across graph sizes. On dense random maximum-stable-set instances, reports tighter bounds with much smaller final LPs than tested static hierarchy levels. Learned search proposes steps; algebraic rules and final identities justify the certificates. Explains the distinction between a feasible stable set (existential lower bound) and a nonnegativity proof (universal upper bound). Gives strict-positivity completeness for hypercube certificates, a complete-graph dynamic degree-two derivation, and a supplementary n/l lower bound for the specified static LP. Constructs trilinear monomial-orbit features invariant to variable renaming plus max pooling over memories/equalities. Supplies dense LP-based rewards, cached action scoring, full DQN settings, a symmetry ablation and explicit rational graph certificates.
    - limits: Inference rules multiply an established nonnegative polynomial by x_i or 1−x_i and take nonnegative linear combinations. Their soundness requires x in [0,1]^n and correct initial axioms. Stable-set experiments also reduce modulo x_i^2=x_i and x_ix_j=0 for graph edges. Polynomial simplification and coefficient equality must preserve that quotient semantics. The main completeness theorem is quoted from Krivine: strictly positive polynomials on the compact hypercube have a finite nonnegative sum of x^alpha(1−x)^beta generators. The footnote restricts the completeness claim to strict positivity/refutation. It does not prove every merely nonnegative polynomial has such a certificate, nor that bounded-degree learned search is complete. Training uses random graphs with25 vertices and edge probability p in[0.5,1]. Generated memories start with2n inequality axioms and graph/Boolean equalities. Search is capped at100 additions and degree2 intermediate lemmas. Results do not establish performance on arbitrary polynomial optimization, sparse graphs, distributed programs or natural-language statements. No human proofs or optimal α(G) labels train the agent, but the dense reward depends on solving a mathematical LP after each addition. “Unsupervised” here means absence of supplied target proofs/optimum labels; it does not mean learning without an exact optimization environment. The orbit-based embedding and symmetric pooling establish architectural invariance under set enumeration and joint variable relabeling. Invariance is not injectivity or a proof of successful generalization. Fixed degree bounds the orbit feature dimension independently of sufficiently large n, while enumerating polynomials/actions still grows with n. Bounds are certified only if nonnegative coefficients and polynomial identities are checked accurately. Printed rational examples admit exact arithmetic; the paper does not provide a verified LP implementation or a systematic numerical-to-rational certificate-reconstruction/error protocol for every aggregate experiment. Supplementary theorem γ_l≥n/l concerns the precise product-generator hierarchy in Eq.10 with only Boolean and edge equalities. It is not a lower bound for every static method or for formulations strengthened by extra valid inequalities. Dynamic advantage is demonstrated against tested levels2–5 and random legal actions, not every proof search strategy. Only one training seed(0) and one NVIDIA V100 are specified. Test means cover100 random graph instances for each reported size. No intervals, multi-seed variability, end-to-end wall-clock comparison, total GPU training time or ground-truth optimality-gap table is supplied.

- Coalescing (2014)
    - title: Coalescing: Syntactic Abstraction for Reasoning in First-Order Modal Logics
    - what: The paper sends mathematical proof obligations to ordinary first-order provers. It sends temporal combinations (statements about how things change over time) to a propositional temporal prover. Each backend never sees the expressions it cannot interpret, since they are hidden.
    - limits: It does not claim to fully automate liveness. The implementation limits it describes are historical and do not describe current TLAPS.

- Pak TIETZE2 finite-dimensional extension 2014 (2014)
    - title: Tietze Extension Theorem for n-dimensional Spaces
    - what: Pąk extends the scalar Tietze extension principle to compact convex finite-dimensional targets with nonempty interior, then transports it to homeomorphic targets. The actual theorems preserve the target subset, stronger than merely extending into ambient Euclidean space. A converse for positive dimension derives normality from the universal extension property. Extensive hypercube/product-homeomorphism infrastructure tracks interiors and supports the finite-dimensional construction. Records coordinate assembly, hypercube range/face/interior facts, positive-radius and dimension contracts, boundary-preserving products, target-preserving transport and the positive-dimension converse with quantified closed domains.
    - limits: MML TIETZE_2 version8.1.02 5.22.1199 identifies a Mizar formalization. Normality is the domain-space separation property used by Tietze. In §3 A is a closed subset of T throughout; f has domain the subspace T restricted to A. This inherited closedness is essential though not restated in every theorem (pp.11,16–18). “Non boundary” for the convex compact targets means nonempty interior in the ambient Euclidean topology. Theorems23/24 require compactness, convexity and this property; they do not cover arbitrary nonconvex targets or infinite-dimensional normed spaces. Summary says extension g:T→E^n, while theorem23 actually gives g:T→E^n restricted to X, preserving the target X (pp.11,17). Proposition1 interchanges indexing of a family of coordinate functions with evaluation of their assembled product. Proposition21 states assembly into E^n is continuous when every coordinate function is continuous; n must be nonzero there. Coordinate continuity is a finite-product topology fact, not a claim that arbitrary separately continuous multivariable maps are jointly continuous (pp.12,16–17). Definition1 imports the open hypercube centered at p with common radius r; Proposition2 preserves membership on changing a coordinate inside its interval; Propositions3/4 give exact coordinate projections/membership. Definition2 uses potentially unequal half-widths R(i): all q(i) lie in[p(i)-R(i),p(i)+R(i)] (p.12). Propositions5/6 handle negative or nonnegative supplied half-widths, and nonnegative R makes the closed hypercube nonempty. Convexity/compactness are registered even for the general finite-sequence representation. Do not silently assume len R=n: Proposition9 explicitly requires n≤len R to compare an open cube with r≤inf rng R (pp.12–13). Proposition7 permits coordinate replacement within a closed interval; Proposition8 proves each coordinate projection is that interval when the whole closed cube is nonempty. Proposition10 characterizes boundary points by membership and some coordinate at an endpoint. For common radius r>0, Proposition12 identifies the interior with OpenHypercube; Propositions11/13/14 give center/inclusion/nested-radius facts. A positive-radius closed cube has nonempty interior (p.13). Proposition15 preserves homeomorphisms under products. Proposition16 maps a product of n- and m-dimensional closed cubes of positive radii onto the unit(n+m)-cube and sends the product of open interiors onto its open interior. Its proof normalizes each factor, uses a coordinate-concatenation homeomorphism E^n×E^m→E^(n+m), restricts to cubes and composes (pp.13–14). Proposition17 precomposes that cube map with arbitrary given homeomorphisms from nonempty T1,T2 and preserves the iff interior-membership condition. Proposition18 transports via boundary-preserving homeomorphisms for any compact convex bodies A,B,C with nonempty interior in dimensions n,m,n+m. It proves an existence homeomorphism, not an affine isomorphism or metric isometry (pp.14–16). Propositions19/20 specialize to products of positive-radius closed disks/balls and an(n+m)-dimensional unit closed disk, preserving the product of open balls as the open unit ball. The rendering has closure bars on balls in the proof and Proposition20, which raw extraction drops; ordinary open Ball and its closed version must not be conflated (p.16). Proposition22 extends f from closed A into the unit closed n-cube without leaving it. Intended construction extends each scalar coordinate to[-1,1] using the scalar Tietze result, assembles continuous coordinates (Proposition21), and uses coordinate-range characterization (Proposition8) to retain the cube. The PDF labels22 a consequence of8,1,21 but does not print the complete scalar-extension proof/source (p.17). Proposition23 transports a map into compact convex X with nonempty interior through a homeomorphism to a cube, applies22, then composes back. Proposition24 additionally transports to B subset S whenever B and such X are homeomorphic: if h:B→X, the extended map is h^-1 composed with an extension of h composed with f. Equality g restricted to A=f is exact, not approximation or equality only up to homotopy (p.17). Proposition25 requires T nonempty and n≥1. Its premise quantifies over every topological S, every nonempty closed A subset T, every B homeomorphic to an eligible n-dimensional X, and every continuous f:T|A→S|B. If all such maps extend into that same B, T is normal. This is a universal extension property, not a consequence of extending one selected map (pp.17–18). The converse sketch reduces to extension of scalar functions into[-1,1], which characterizes normality; a positive-dimensional cube permits embedding such a scalar coordinate and projecting an extension. This explains why the explicit n≥1 guard matters: a zero-dimensional singleton target cannot characterize normality. The PDF prints only the short scalar-extension reduction, not the full coordinate embedding instantiation (p.18). Forward results are existence theorems. No executable extension algorithm, numeric worked example, computational complexity, proof size/check time, empirical comparison or checker transcript is supplied. Library homeomorphism and scalar Tietze proofs are imported, not independently audited here. No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM proof/specification-agent evaluation (entire paper). Exact quotations preserve raw-extraction defects, especially lost ball closure bars, U+0016 restriction signs, product symbols and inequality glyphs. Renderings were inspected; interpretation distinguishes open/closed sets. Ninepages,twodefinitions,25propositions/allsuppliedsketches,onefootnote,44references and received date read; no artifact execution.

- Pak BROUWER2 convex-body fixed points 2011 (2011)
    - title: Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem in the General Case
    - what: Pąk formalizes Brouwer fixed-point existence for continuous selfmaps of compact convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space with nonempty ambient interior. The article first establishes ray/frontier facts,then gives a homeomorphism from each such convex body to the closed unit disk carrying its frontier to the unit sphere. It also obtains boundary-preserving homeomorphisms between two such bodies and proves that a nonempty boundary subspace cannot be a retract of its body. Records the full-dimensional interior guard,subspace topology,selfmap requirement and boundary-preserving homeomorphism contract. Separates the general ray supremum lemma from convex uniqueness,and distinguishes fixed-point existence from uniqueness,computation or an arbitrary compact-convex-set theorem without interior. Includes the non-retraction conclusion absent from the Summary.

- Pak RLAFFIN3 barycentric continuity 2011 (2011)
    - title: Continuity of Barycentric Coordinates in Euclidean Topological Spaces
    - what: Pąk formalizes ordered barycentric coordinates for finite affinely independent Euclidean vertex sets, their invariance under translation, nonzero scaling and injective linear maps, and continuity on the affine hull. Prefix coordinate maps reflect as well as preserve openness and closedness when fewer than all barycentric coordinates are retained. Full affine bases give global coefficient continuity; arbitrary affinely independent sets require the relative topology on their affine hull. Records cardinality/rank conditions, exact enumeration transport, zero-coordinate tests for affine hulls of vertex subsets, affine-to-linear basis conversion and the dimension limit on topology equivalences. Distinguishes affine-hull continuity from unsupported continuity on the entire ambient space.
    - limits: MML RLAFFIN3 version7.11.07 4.160.1126 identifies the formalization. V is a real linear space; the topological conclusions concern finite-dimensional Euclidean E^n. A2 is a finite affinely independent subset of V and A4 an affinely independent subset of E^n, automatically finite. Generic A1 need only be finite; barycentric uniqueness/topology conclusions use affine independence (pp.139–140). Propositions1/2 distribute interval boxes and Cartesian-product membership over finite-sequence concatenation. Propositions3–6 connect finite dimension with the whole carrier, establish dim(E^n)=n, bound |A|≤dim(V)+1 for affine independence, and characterize |A|=dim(V)+1 by Affin A=V. The overbar means cardinality, not closure (pp.139–140). Proposition7 makes a cylinder defined by the first k≤n ordinary coordinates open iff its base in E^k is open. Proposition8 gives the corresponding statement for the embedded subspace formed by appending n zeros. These distinguish ambient topology from subspace topology (p.140). Proposition9 states conv(A)∩Affin(B)=conv(B) for B⊆affinely independent A. Proposition10 distributes scalar multiplication over function images;11 identifies an affine hull containing zero with the carrier of its linear span. Proposition12 is |A|=|rA| iff r≠0 or A is trivial (at most one element), not the generally false set equality A=rA; bars are visible in the rendering but absent in extracted text (p.140). Definition1 makes an enumeration an injective finite sequence with range exactly X. Translation transports it elementwise (13); scaling transports an enumeration iff the scalar is nonzero or the set is trivial (14). Proposition15 requires an n×m matrix of rank n; in this row-vector convention its map E^n→E^m is injective, so vertex distinctness is preserved. Rank cannot be omitted (p.141). Definition2 orders the coefficient function x→A by composition with the enumeration E, yielding x→E with length |A| (16). Translation (17), nonzero scaling (18) and full-row-rank linear maps (19) leave this ordered coefficient vector unchanged when the vertex enumeration is transported with the point. Their point hypotheses restrict to the original affine hull; no arbitrary off-hull coefficient interpretation is inferred (p.141). Proposition20 characterizes membership in the affine hull of a vertex subset by zero coefficients at excluded vertices, assuming x∈Affin A2. Propositions21/22 specialize to first-k and remaining vertices: the excluded suffix or prefix of the ordered coordinate vector is zero. The first uses truncated natural subtraction |A2|−0k; the second explicitly assumes k≤|A2| (p.141). When zero is the last enumerated vertex, removing it leaves an ordered linear basis of the span (23); coefficients in that basis equal the first |A4|−1 barycentric coefficients (24). This supplies the affine-to-linear-coordinate bridge. The paper states propositions without their proofs, so this is a dependency/strategy reading, not a reconstruction of a Mizar proof trace (p.142). For a full affine basis |A4|=n+1,25/26 say A5⊆E^k is open/closed iff its first-k barycentric-coordinate inverse image is open/closed in E^n, provided k≤n. For an arbitrary A4,27/28 replace the ambient domain by E^n restricted to Affin A4 and require k<|A4|. Relative topology and the strict coordinate-count bound are material; these are stronger than one-way continuity (p.142). Reason for the coordinate-count limit (reading inference): all |A| barycentric coordinates satisfy sum=1, so the full coordinate image is an affine hyperplane rather than all E^|A|. For vertices0,1 in R, coordinates are (1−t,t). A nonempty closed singleton disjoint from that line has empty open inverse image but is not open in R², disproving the unrestricted reflected-openness claim. This is an illustrative derivation, not a printed example. Definition3 fixes a vertex/index x and defines the real coefficient function v↦(v→A)(x). Outside A it is identically0 (29); for affine independence the converse holds (30). Proposition31 proves continuity only after restriction to Affin A4;32 gives ambient continuity if |A4|=n+1. Nothing here establishes ambient continuity for a nonspanning vertex set (p.142). The paper also registers every Euclidean affine subset as closed, every halfline as closed, and conv(A4) as closed. Proposition33 states that Int A4 is open if |A4|=n+1. Its imported Int operator is not defined in this paper; the record preserves that notation rather than silently identifying it with ordinary topological interior of the vertex set (pp.142–143). No numerical example, executable barycentric algorithm, floating-point error bound, performance measurement, proof-size/check-time statistics or independent checker transcript appears. The 33 references include affine-independence, linear-coordinate and Euclidean-transformation libraries; those dependencies are not independently read for this record. No distributed protocol, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-agent evaluation. Exact quotations retain extraction defects: cardinality overbars disappear, restriction glyphs become U+0016/U+0017, finite-sequence concatenation renders as a and function-composition/application ordering is typographic. Renderings govern interpretation. All six pages/three definitions/33 propositions and reference/date material read; formal source/checker not executed.

- Pak SIMPLEX2 Brouwer simplex 2011 (2011)
    - title: Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem for Simplexes
    - what: Pąk formalizes Brouwer fixed-point existence for a continuous self-map of a full-dimensional Euclidean simplex. The article develops Lebesgue numbers,uniform bounds on simplex diameters,a geometric barycentric-subdivision mesh decay estimate,and a closed-face-cover intersection theorem. It also states that the small inductive dimension of the simplex and E^n is n. The quantitative decrease concerns individual-simplex mesh,not shrinkage of the whole realized domain. Records open-cover quantifiers,mesh supremum/fallback,subcomplex monotonicity,convex-hull diameter preservation,exact degree-dependent decay,closed-cover face conditions and fixed-map domain/range. Separates statements from an inferred KKM/barycentric proof route because no proof sketches are printed.
    - limits: MML SIMPLEX2 version7.11.07 4.160.1126 identifies the article. Main23/24 use A affinely independent in E^n with cardinality n+1,and f a continuous function from the subspace conv A into itself. They guarantee a fixed point in dom f,with no contraction,uniqueness,or rate-of-iteration hypothesis. Lower-dimensional simplices embedded in E^n are not directly covered by that full-dimensional displayed statement (pp.145,149). Definition1 uses a nonempty metric space whose topology is compact and an open covering family F. A Lebesgue number is positive and satisfies:for every p,there exists a member ofF containing the whole open ball at p of that fixed radius. The chosen cover member may depend on p. Theorems1–3 preserve the number under enlarging/coarsening the cover and under taking a smaller positive radius (pp.145–146). Theorem4 attains a finite nonempty metric subset’s diameter at two points. Definition2 M-bounded requires one uniform real bound on the diameter of every face in the complex’s family,not just boundedness of each face separately. Subcomplexes/skeletons inherit boundedness and finite-vertex complexes are bounded (5/6). The word topology here names the abstract complex’s face family;it is not an arbitrary family of ambient open sets (p.146). The complex diameter is mesh:the least upper bound on its simplex/face diameters. Definition3 includes a fallback value0 when the face family does not meet the metric carrier’s power set;Definition4 gives the simpler simplex-supremum characterization for M-bounded nonvoid subset-closed complexes. Theorems7–10 give nonnegativity,subcomplex/skeleton monotonicity,and equality to diam S for the complex generated by finite S (p.147). Definitions5/6 specialize metric boundedness/mesh to Euclidean complexes. Mesh does not bound distances between arbitrary vertices in different disconnected faces:as a reading illustration,singleton faces at all integer points in R have mesh0 but unbounded union. Subdivision therefore decreases local simplex size,not necessarily the diameter of the realized domain (pp.146–148). Theorem11 compares differences of barycenters from a nested finite face family. It gives a1−a2=r(b1−b2),with0≤r≤(|union F|−1)/|union F|. This is the vertex-count source of the subdivision contraction factor. K2 appears in the printed statement without an explicit local declaration;the imported complex-type conventions are not audited here (p.148). Theorem12 expresses a selected-vertex face as an intersection of facets missing excluded vertices,assuming dom E minus X is nonempty. The printed prefix notation conv A \{E(k)} must be grouped as conv(A\{E(k)}) for that facet reading;removing only the vertex from the already-convex set would not express the same identity. Parentheses are not printed and the source parse was not audited (p.148). Theorem13 places conv A in the closed ball centered at anyp∈conv A of radius diam A;the overbar is missing in raw extraction. Theorem14 preserves boundedness under convex hull and15 preserves diameter. A closed rather than open ball is essential when diameter is attained or zero (p.148). Theorems16–18 require a bounded finite-degree nonvoid simplicial complex and the explicit imported containment |K|⊆Omega_K. They give mesh(BCS K)≤d/(d+1)mesh(K),then mesh(BCS(k,K))≤(d/(d+1))^k mesh(K),and for every positive target r some k has mesh<r. For d≥0 the ratio is<1. The geometric containment is retained literally rather than assigned an unaudited interpretation (p.148). Theorems19/20 concatenate coordinates to a homeomorphism E^i×E^j→E^(i+j),mapping products of equal-radius open hypercubes to one open hypercube. Theorem21 characterizes Euclidean boundedness by containment in some open hypercube. Closed bounded Euclidean subsets and convex hulls of affine-independent sets are then registered compact (pp.148–149). Theorem22 is a closed-cover intersection condition:nonempty affinely independent A,enumeration E,a sequence F of |A| closed subsets of the subspace conv A,and for every index subset S,conv(E(S))⊆union(F(S)). Then the intersection of all F_i is nonempty. Closedness is relative to conv A and the face condition is required for every S,not only vertices or the whole simplex. This is the displayed KKM-type intermediary (p.149). Standard fixed-point route,reading inference rather than a supplied proof:write barycentric coordinates ofx andf(x),and define F_i={x:f_i(x)≤x_i}. Coordinate continuity makes the F_i closed. On a face indexedS,the x_i sum to1 overS while f_i are nonnegative and their sum overS is≤1,so at least onei∈S satisfies the inequality. The22intersection gives all coordinate inequalities;equal total sums force equality and hence f(x)=x. The article cites barycentric continuity and Sperner libraries but gives no full proof/dependency trace. Theorems23/24 state fixed-point existence;25 gives small inductive dimension ofconv A equaln when|A|=n+1,and26 gives ind(E^n)=n. Small inductive dimension is the topological dimension defined recursively through boundaries of neighborhoods;the imported formal definition and dimension proof are not reproduced or independently audited. At n=0 the full simplex has one vertex and the fixed-point conclusion is immediate (p.149). No executable fixed-point algorithm,worked numerical example,approximation error for a computed point,proof/check-time statistics,benchmark or checker transcript appears. The mesh decay is an analytic estimate rather than measured runtime. Thirty-five references include abstract complexes,Sperner,barycentric continuity and inductive dimension;those dependencies not independently read for this record. No distributed protocol,Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment. All six pages,five sections,six definitions,26numbered results/all clauses,unnumbered registrations,35references/date read. Exact quote text follows saved raw extraction,not a visual mathematical transcription;cardinality/closed-ball bars vanish,diameter becomes∅,composition and restrictions are distorted. Renderings checked,especially pp148/149. No formal-source/checker execution.
